Part 1 — Concept

What Is a Database?

A database is an organized, persistent collection of data that is stored electronically and managed by a Database Management System (DBMS).

Think of it this way:

text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        YOUR APPLICATION                          │
│              (Java / Spring Boot / Microservice)                 │
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │ SQL / API calls
                             ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    DATABASE MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (DBMS)             │
│  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  │
│  │ Security │  │ Query    │  │ Trans-   │  │ Concurrency  │  │
│  │ & Auth   │  │ Optimizer│  │ actions  │  │ Control      │  │
│  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────────┘  │
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │
                             ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      PHYSICAL STORAGE                            │
│         (Disk / SSD / Memory / Cloud Block Storage)              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Core Definitions

TermDefinition
DataRaw facts: numbers, text, dates, images, events
InformationData organized into meaningful context
DatabaseStructured collection of related data
DBMSSoftware that creates, manages, and controls access to databases
Database SystemDBMS + database + applications + users + policies
SchemaLogical structure: tables, columns, relationships, constraints
InstanceA running copy of a database at a point in time

The Three Layers of Abstraction

Every database system exposes data through layers so users and applications never touch raw disk bytes directly:

text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  EXTERNAL LEVEL (Views)                                       │
│  What each user/application sees                              │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  CONCEPTUAL LEVEL (Logical Schema)                            │
│  Tables, relationships, constraints — the "design"            │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  INTERNAL LEVEL (Physical Storage)                            │
│  Pages, blocks, B-Trees, indexes, WAL — how data lives on disk│
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why three layers? So you can change physical storage (e.g., move from HDD to SSD, add an index) without rewriting every application.

Types of Database Systems (Preview)

CategoryExamplesPrimary Use
Relational (RDBMS)Oracle, PostgreSQL, MySQL, DB2, SQL ServerStructured, transactional data
DocumentMongoDB, CouchDBFlexible JSON-like documents
Key-ValueRedis, DynamoDBCaching, session storage
Wide-ColumnCassandra, HBaseHigh-write, distributed workloads
GraphNeo4j, Amazon NeptuneRelationship-heavy data
Time-SeriesInfluxDB, TimescaleDBMetrics, IoT, monitoring
SearchElasticsearchFull-text search, log analytics
Note: We will explore each category deeply in later lessons. For now, understand that "database" is an umbrella term — not synonymous with "Oracle" or "PostgreSQL" alone.

Part 2 — History

The Evolution of Data Storage

Understanding history explains why today's databases look the way they do.

Timeline

text
1950s          1960s          1970s          1980s          1990s
   │              │              │              │              │
   ▼              ▼              ▼              ▼              ▼
Punch Cards   Hierarchical   Relational    Client-Server   Internet
File Systems  & Network DBs  Model (Codd)   RDBMS boom      OLAP/Data Warehousing
              (IMS, CODASYL) (Oracle, DB2)  (SQL standard)  (Teradata)

2000s                    2010s                    2020s
   │                        │                        │
   ▼                        ▼                        ▼
NoSQL movement           Cloud databases          Multi-model, Serverless,
(BigTable, Dynamo,       (RDS, Aurora,            AI/ML integration,
 MongoDB, Cassandra)      Cloud Spanner)           HTAP, Edge databases

Era 1: File-Based Storage (Pre-1960s)

Applications stored data in flat files:

text
orders.txt
-----------
1001|John|500.00|2024-01-15
1002|Jane|750.00|2024-01-16

Problems:

  • No standard structure
  • Duplicate data everywhere
  • No concurrent access control
  • Application code owned all data logic
  • Crashes caused corruption with no recovery

Era 2: Hierarchical & Network Models (1960s–1970s)

IBM's IMS (Information Management System) used a tree structure:

text
        Customer
       /    |    \
   Order  Order  Order
    /       |
  Item    Item

Problem: Rigid structure. A child could have only one parent. Real-world data has many-to-many relationships.

Era 3: The Relational Revolution (1970)

Edgar F. Codd, an IBM researcher, published "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks" (1970).

His insight: represent data as relations (tables) with rows and columns, connected by keys — not physical pointers.

text
CUSTOMER                    ORDER
┌────────┬──────────┐      ┌──────────┬─────────────┬────────┐
│ cust_id│ name     │      │ order_id │ customer_id │ amount │
├────────┼──────────┤      ├──────────┼─────────────┼────────┤
│ 1      │ John     │◄─────│ 101      │ 1           │ 500.00 │
│ 2      │ Jane     │◄─────│ 102      │ 2           │ 750.00 │
└────────┴──────────┘      └──────────┴─────────────┴────────┘

Why revolutionary: Logical independence. Change storage without changing application logic.

Era 4: SQL and Commercial RDBMS (1980s–1990s)

  • 1974: SEQUEL (Structured English Query Language) at IBM → became SQL
  • 1979: Oracle — first commercial SQL RDBMS
  • 1983: IBM DB2
  • 1989: Microsoft SQL Server
  • 1996: PostgreSQL (open source)
  • 1995: MySQL

The SQL standard (ANSI/ISO) unified how we talk to databases.

Era 5: The NoSQL Movement (2000s)

Web-scale companies (Google, Amazon, Facebook) hit RDBMS limits:

CompanyProblemSolution
GoogleIndexing the webBigTable (2006)
AmazonShopping cart at scaleDynamo (2007)
FacebookSocial graph, feedsCassandra, Memcached
LinkedInReal-time analyticsKafka + specialized stores

Not "No SQL" but "Not Only SQL" — different tools for different trade-offs.

Era 6: Cloud-Native & Multi-Model (2010s–Today)

  • AWS RDS/Aurora, Google Cloud Spanner, Azure Cosmos DB
  • HTAP (Hybrid Transactional/Analytical Processing): one system for OLTP + OLAP
  • Serverless databases: pay per query, auto-scaling
  • NewSQL: distributed systems with ACID (CockroachDB, TiDB)

Historical Lesson for Architects

Every database innovation was a response to a specific failure of the previous generation. When you choose a database, you are choosing which historical trade-offs to accept.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Do Databases Solve?

Before databases, enterprises faced these failures daily:

Problem 1: Data Duplication & Inconsistency

text
WITHOUT DATABASE:
  Sales System:     Customer "John Smith" → Address A
  Billing System:   Customer "John Smith" → Address B  ← WRONG
  Support System:   Customer "John Smith" → Address A

WITH DATABASE:
  Single source of truth → one row, one address, all systems read it

Problem 2: Concurrent Access

Two bank tellers withdraw from the same account simultaneously:

text
WITHOUT CONCURRENCY CONTROL:
  Teller A reads balance: $1000
  Teller B reads balance: $1000
  Teller A withdraws $800 → writes $200
  Teller B withdraws $600 → writes $400  ← Lost update! Should be -$400

Problem 3: Durability & Crash Recovery

Power failure mid-transaction. Without a database, half-written files corrupt data permanently.

Problem 4: Security & Access Control

Who can read salary data? Who can delete orders? File systems offer no fine-grained control.

Problem 5: Query Complexity

"Find all customers who ordered more than $10,000 in the last 90 days across 3 product categories" — impossible with flat files without writing custom code every time.

Problem 6: Scalability

Your e-commerce platform goes from 1,000 to 10 million users. File-based systems cannot scale reads, writes, or storage.

The Unified Problem Statement

Organizations need a reliable, secure, concurrent, queryable, durable system to store and retrieve structured data at scale — independent of any single application.

That is what a database exists to solve.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Do Databases Exist as a Separate Layer?

Separation of Concerns

text
BAD ARCHITECTURE (1960s style):
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│  Application                     │
│  ├── Business Logic              │
│  ├── File I/O                    │
│  ├── Index Management            │
│  ├── Concurrency Control         │
│  ├── Crash Recovery              │
│  └── Security                    │
└─────────────────────────────────┘

GOOD ARCHITECTURE (Modern):
┌──────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────────────┐
│  Application     │     │  Database (DBMS)              │
│  └── Business    │────▶│  ├── Storage Management       │
│      Logic ONLY  │     │  ├── Query Processing         │
└──────────────────┘     │  ├── Transaction Management   │
                           │  ├── Concurrency Control      │
                           │  ├── Recovery & Backup        │
                           │  └── Security                 │
                           └──────────────────────────────┘

Why separate?

  1. Reuse: 50 microservices share one customer database
  2. Expertise: DBAs optimize storage; developers write business logic
  3. Integrity: Central enforcement of rules (constraints, transactions)
  4. Performance: Decades of optimization in one layer
  5. Compliance: Audit trails, encryption, access logs in one place

Why Not Just Use Files / Object Storage (S3)?

RequirementFile System / S3Database
Structured queries❌ Manual code✅ SQL
ACID transactions❌ No✅ Yes
Concurrent writes❌ Risky✅ Controlled
Relationships❌ Manual joins in code✅ Native
Indexing❌ Manual✅ Automatic
Crash recovery❌ Application's problem✅ Built-in
Schema enforcement❌ No✅ Yes

S3 is excellent for blobs (images, logs, backups). It is not a database.

Part 5 — Internal Working

How a Database System Works (High-Level)

When your Spring Boot app executes:

java
customerRepository.findById(123L);

Here is what happens inside the database:

text
┌─────────────┐
│ Application │
└──────┬──────┘
       │ 1. JDBC/JPA sends SQL over network (TCP)
       ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    CONNECTION MANAGER                       │
│  - Authenticates user                                     │
│  - Assigns session                                        │
│  - Manages connection pool                                │
└──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                           │ 2. SQL: SELECT * FROM customer WHERE id = 123
                           ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    PARSER & VALIDATOR                       │
│  - Checks syntax                                          │
│  - Validates table/column names against catalog           │
│  - Checks permissions                                     │
└──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                           │ 3. Parsed query tree
                           ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    QUERY OPTIMIZER                          │
│  - Generates multiple execution plans                     │
│  - Estimates cost (I/O, CPU, memory)                      │
│  - Chooses cheapest plan (index scan vs full table scan)  │
└──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                           │ 4. Chosen execution plan
                           ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    EXECUTION ENGINE                         │
│  - Runs the plan (scan index, fetch rows, apply filters)  │
│  - Uses buffer pool (memory cache)                        │
└──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                           │ 5. Row data
                           ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    STORAGE ENGINE                           │
│  - Reads pages from disk (or cache)                       │
│  - B-Tree index lookup                                    │
│  - Returns data pages                                     │
└──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘
                           │ 6. Result set
                           ▼
                    Back to Application

Key Internal Components

ComponentRole
Catalog (Data Dictionary)Metadata: tables, columns, indexes, users, permissions
ParserConverts SQL text into an internal query tree
OptimizerChooses the fastest way to execute a query
Execution EngineRuns the plan step by step
Storage EngineManages how data is stored and retrieved from disk
Buffer Pool / Shared BuffersIn-memory cache of frequently accessed pages
WAL (Write-Ahead Log)Log changes before applying to data files (durability)
Lock ManagerControls concurrent access
Transaction ManagerEnsures ACID properties

Part 6 — Storage Internals

How Data Is Physically Stored (Introduction)

At the lowest level, databases do not store "tables" — they store bytes on disk organized into pages (blocks).

Page Structure

text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    DATA PAGE (8KB typical)       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Page Header  │ Row Directory │ Free Space       │
│ (metadata)   │ (offsets)     │                  │
├──────────────┴───────────────┴──────────────────┤
│ Row 1 │ Row 2 │ Row 3 │ ... │ Row N               │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
DatabaseDefault Page Size
PostgreSQL8 KB
Oracle8 KB (default, configurable)
MySQL (InnoDB)16 KB
SQL Server8 KB

Tablespaces and Data Files

text
DATABASE INSTANCE
├── SYSTEM Tablespace (metadata, catalog)
├── USER Tablespace
│   ├── customers.dbf  (data file 1)
│   ├── customers.dbf  (data file 2)  ← Oracle can span files
│   └── orders.dbf
├── INDEX Tablespace
│   └── idx_customers.dbf
└── TEMP Tablespace (sort operations)

Heap vs Index-Organized Tables

Heap Table (default): Rows inserted wherever space exists. Primary key lookup requires an index.

text
HEAP TABLE (unordered storage):
Page 1: [Row 5] [Row 2] [Row 9]
Page 2: [Row 1] [Row 7] [Row 3]
         ↑
    PK Index points here

Index-Organized Table (Oracle IOT, MySQL PK Clustered Index): Rows stored in PK index order.

text
CLUSTERED INDEX (PK order IS storage order):
Leaf Pages: [Row 1] [Row 2] [Row 3] [Row 5] [Row 7] [Row 9]
Architect note: This distinction affects every performance decision. We will go deep in Lesson 4 (Storage Engines).

Part 7 — Memory Usage

How Databases Use Memory

Databases are I/O-bound systems that use memory to avoid disk access (disk is ~1000x slower than RAM).

Memory Architecture

text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    DATABASE SERVER MEMORY                      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  BUFFER POOL / SHARED BUFFERS (largest consumer)     │    │
│  │  - Cached data pages and index pages                 │    │
│  │  - PostgreSQL: shared_buffers                         │    │
│  │  - Oracle: SGA Buffer Cache                           │    │
│  │  - MySQL InnoDB: innodb_buffer_pool_size              │    │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  WAL Buffers     │  │  Sort / Hash Memory             │  │
│  │  (redo log cache)│  │  (work_mem / sort_area_size)    │  │
│  └──────────────────┘  └────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Connection      │  │  Query Plan Cache               │  │
│  │  Memory          │  │  (prepared statements)          │  │
│  └──────────────────┘  └────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Buffer Pool — The Most Critical Memory Structure

text
READ REQUEST for Row ID = 123:

  1. Check Buffer Pool
     ├── HIT  → Return from memory (~0.1ms)     ✅ Fast
     └── MISS → Read from disk (~5-10ms)        ❌ Slow
                → Load page into Buffer Pool
                → Return row

Cache Hit Ratio = (Hits / (Hits + Misses)) × 100
Target in production: > 99%

Typical Memory Sizing (Production Guidelines)

ComponentRule of Thumb
Buffer Pool60–75% of dedicated DB server RAM
Work Memory (per query)4–64 MB depending on workload
WAL Buffers16–256 MB
Connections~10 MB per connection (avoid too many)

Memory vs Disk Trade-off

text
More Buffer Pool Memory
    ├── ✅ Faster reads (fewer disk I/O)
    ├── ✅ Better query performance
    ├── ❌ Less RAM for OS cache
    └── ❌ Diminishing returns after working set fits in memory

Part 8 — Execution Flow

End-to-End: A Single INSERT Statement

Let's trace what happens when a payment service inserts a transaction:

sql
INSERT INTO payments (id, account_id, amount, status, created_at)
VALUES (987654, 456, 250.00, 'PENDING', NOW());

Execution Flow Diagram

text
STEP 1: PARSE
  SQL text → Syntax tree
  Validate: table exists? columns match? user has INSERT privilege?

STEP 2: OPTIMIZE
  INSERT is simple → direct path, no complex plan needed

STEP 3: BEGIN TRANSACTION (implicit or explicit)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Transaction ID assigned: TXN-8847291    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

STEP 4: WRITE-AHEAD LOG (WAL) — BEFORE data file
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  WAL Record:                             │
  │  TXN-8847291 | INSERT | payments |       │
  │  row(987654, 456, 250.00, PENDING, ...)  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
  fsync WAL to disk ← DURABILITY GUARANTEE

STEP 5: MODIFY BUFFER POOL
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Data page in memory marked DIRTY        │
  │  Row inserted into page free space       │
  │  Index pages updated in memory           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

STEP 6: COMMIT
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  WAL record marked COMMITTED             │
  │  Client receives "OK"                    │
  │  (Dirty pages flushed to disk later)     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

STEP 7: BACKGROUND CHECKPOINT (async)
  Dirty pages flushed from buffer pool to data files

Why WAL Before Data File?

text
SCENARIO: Power failure after INSERT committed but before data file updated

WITHOUT WAL:
  Transaction lost forever. Customer charged but no record. 💀

WITH WAL:
  On restart, database replays WAL → reconstructs committed transaction ✅

This is the foundation of durability — covered deeply in Lesson 33 (ACID).

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Database Performance Fundamentals

Performance in databases is measured across four dimensions:

The Four Performance Dimensions

text
                    THROUGHPUT
                  (queries/second)
                        ▲
                        │
         LATENCY ◄──────┼──────► CONCURRENCY
         (response     │        (simultaneous
          time)        │         users)
                        │
                        ▼
                   RESOURCE
                  EFFICIENCY
                  (CPU, I/O, RAM)

Key Performance Metrics

MetricDefinitionTarget (OLTP)
Latency (p50)Median query response time< 10ms
Latency (p99)99th percentile response< 100ms
ThroughputTransactions per second (TPS)Workload-dependent
Cache Hit Ratio% reads from memory vs disk> 99%
I/O WaitTime waiting for disk< 5%
Connection UtilizationActive vs max connections< 70%
Lock Wait TimeTime waiting for locks< 1% of query time

The Performance Hierarchy (What to Fix First)

text
1. MISSING INDEXES          ← Fix first (biggest impact, easiest)
2. FULL TABLE SCANS         ← Add indexes or rewrite queries
3. N+1 QUERIES (ORM)        ← Fix fetch strategies
4. BUFFER POOL TOO SMALL    ← Memory tuning
5. LOCK CONTENTION          ← Transaction design
6. DISK I/O BOTTLENECK      ← Storage upgrade, partitioning
7. NETWORK LATENCY          ← Connection pooling, read replicas
8. HARDWARE LIMITS          ← Scale up/out (last resort)

OLTP vs OLAP Performance Profiles

CharacteristicOLTP (Banking, Payments)OLAP (Reporting, Analytics)
Query typeShort, simple, indexedComplex aggregations
Read/WriteRead + Write heavyRead-heavy
Latency target< 10msSeconds to minutes OK
ConcurrencyThousands of usersFew concurrent queries
Data size per queryFew rowsMillions of rows
ExampleUPDATE account SET balance = balance - 100SELECT region, SUM(revenue) GROUP BY region

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

Computational Complexity in Database Operations

Understanding Big-O complexity helps architects predict behavior at scale.

Common Operation Complexities

OperationWithout IndexWith B-Tree Index
Find by PKO(n) full scanO(log n)
InsertO(1) appendO(log n) index update
DeleteO(n) find + O(1) markO(log n)
Range ScanO(n)O(log n + k) k=results
SortO(n log n)O(n log n) or O(k) if indexed
Join (nested loop)O(n × m)O(n log m) with index
Hash JoinO(n + m)O(n + m)

Scale Impact Example

text
Table: 100 million rows

Full Table Scan:  O(100,000,000) → ~30 seconds on HDD
Index Lookup:     O(log₂ 100,000,000) ≈ 27 page reads → ~0.5ms

Difference: 60,000x slower without index

Complexity and Architecture Decisions

text
At 1,000 rows:       Any approach works
At 1,000,000 rows:   Indexes mandatory
At 1,000,000,000 rows: Partitioning + indexes + read replicas
At 10,000,000,000 rows: Sharding required

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Your First Database Interactions

We will use a banking domain throughout this course — familiar, regulated, and architecturally rich.

Step 1: Create a Database and Schema

sql
-- PostgreSQL syntax (similar across Oracle, MySQL, SQL Server with minor differences)

CREATE DATABASE banking_platform;

\c banking_platform;  -- Connect to database (PostgreSQL)

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id     BIGINT          PRIMARY KEY,
    first_name      VARCHAR(100)    NOT NULL,
    last_name       VARCHAR(100)    NOT NULL,
    email           VARCHAR(255)    UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    phone           VARCHAR(20),
    date_of_birth   DATE,
    status          VARCHAR(20)     DEFAULT 'ACTIVE',
    created_at      TIMESTAMP       DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_at      TIMESTAMP       DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id      BIGINT          PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id     BIGINT          NOT NULL,
    account_type    VARCHAR(20)     NOT NULL,  -- SAVINGS, CHECKING, LOAN
    currency        CHAR(3)         DEFAULT 'USD',
    balance         DECIMAL(18,2)   NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.00,
    status          VARCHAR(20)     DEFAULT 'ACTIVE',
    opened_at       TIMESTAMP       DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    CONSTRAINT fk_customer
        FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(customer_id)
);

Step 2: Insert Data

sql
INSERT INTO customers (customer_id, first_name, last_name, email, date_of_birth)
VALUES
    (1001, 'Ankur', 'Kumar', 'ankur@email.com', '1990-05-15'),
    (1002, 'Priya', 'Sharma', 'priya@email.com', '1988-11-22');

INSERT INTO accounts (account_id, customer_id, account_type, balance)
VALUES
    (5001, 1001, 'SAVINGS',  15000.00),
    (5002, 1001, 'CHECKING',  3500.00),
    (5003, 1002, 'SAVINGS',   8200.00);

Step 3: Query Data

sql
-- Basic SELECT
SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name, email
FROM customers
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';

-- Join: Customer with their accounts
SELECT
    c.first_name,
    c.last_name,
    a.account_type,
    a.balance
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN accounts a ON c.customer_id = a.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id = 1001;

-- Aggregation
SELECT
    c.first_name,
    COUNT(a.account_id) AS total_accounts,
    SUM(a.balance)      AS total_balance
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON c.customer_id = a.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name;

Step 4: Update and Delete

sql
-- Update balance (will be wrapped in transactions in later lessons)
UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 500.00
WHERE account_id = 5002;

-- Delete with safety (always use WHERE!)
DELETE FROM accounts
WHERE account_id = 5002 AND status = 'CLOSED';  -- Never delete active accounts

Step 5: Inspect Database Metadata

sql
-- PostgreSQL: List all tables
SELECT table_name, table_type
FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_schema = 'public';

-- Oracle equivalent
-- SELECT table_name FROM user_tables;

-- MySQL equivalent
-- SHOW TABLES;

Production Checklist for Any Database

text
✅ High Availability configured (replication, failover)
✅ Backups automated and tested (RPO/RTO defined)
✅ Monitoring: latency, connections, disk, replication lag
✅ Connection pooling (HikariCP in Spring Boot)
✅ Least privilege access (app user ≠ admin user)
✅ Encryption at rest and in transit (TLS)
✅ Index strategy documented
✅ Slow query log enabled
✅ Capacity planning (6-month growth projection)
✅ Disaster recovery runbook tested annually

FailureCausePrevention

Disk fullUnbounded log growthMonitoring + log rotation + partitioning
Replication lagHeavy writes on primaryRead replicas, async processing
Slow queriesMissing indexesQuery review, execution plan analysis
Data corruptionHardware failure, bugChecksums, backups, WAL

Part 13 — Spring Boot Integration

Connecting Spring Boot to a Database

Spring Boot abstracts database access through Spring Data JPA and HikariCP connection pooling.

Application Configuration

yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/banking_platform
    username: ${DB_USERNAME}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
    driver-class-name: org.postgresql.Driver
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 20        # Max connections to DB
      minimum-idle: 5              # Min idle connections
      connection-timeout: 30000    # 30 seconds
      idle-timeout: 600000         # 10 minutes
      max-lifetime: 1800000        # 30 minutes
      pool-name: BankingHikariPool

  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate           # NEVER use 'create' in production
    show-sql: false                # Use logging framework instead
    properties:
      hibernate:
        dialect: org.hibernate.dialect.PostgreSQLDialect
        format_sql: true
        jdbc:
          batch_size: 25
        order_inserts: true
        order_updates: true

logging:
  level:
    org.hibernate.SQL: DEBUG       # Dev only
    org.hibernate.type.descriptor.sql: TRACE

Why connection pooling? Opening a DB connection costs ~50–100ms (TCP + auth + memory). Pooling reuses connections.

Entity and Repository

java
@Entity
@Table(name = "customers")
public class Customer {

    @Id
    private Long customerId;

    @Column(name = "first_name", nullable = false)
    private String firstName;

    @Column(name = "last_name", nullable = false)
    private String lastName;

    @Column(unique = true, nullable = false)
    private String email;

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "customer", fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    private List<Account> accounts = new ArrayList<>();
}

@Repository
public interface CustomerRepository extends JpaRepository<Customer, Long> {

    Optional<Customer> findByEmail(String email);

    @Query("SELECT c FROM Customer c JOIN FETCH c.accounts WHERE c.customerId = :id")
    Optional<Customer> findByIdWithAccounts(@Param("id") Long id);
}

Service Layer

java
@Service
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public class CustomerService {

    private final CustomerRepository customerRepository;

    public CustomerService(CustomerRepository customerRepository) {
        this.customerRepository = customerRepository;
    }

    public CustomerDto getCustomer(Long id) {
        Customer customer = customerRepository.findById(id)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new CustomerNotFoundException(id));
        return CustomerDto.from(customer);
    }

    @Transactional  // readOnly = false for writes
    public Customer createCustomer(CreateCustomerRequest request) {
        Customer customer = new Customer();
        customer.setCustomerId(generateId());
        customer.setFirstName(request.getFirstName());
        customer.setLastName(request.getLastName());
        customer.setEmail(request.getEmail());
        return customerRepository.save(customer);
    }
}

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

How Hibernate Maps Objects to Relational Data

Hibernate is the JPA implementation that translates Java objects into SQL and back.

The Object-Relational Impedance Mismatch

text
JAVA WORLD                    RELATIONAL WORLD
─────────────                 ──────────────────
Object                        Row
Reference / Pointer           Foreign Key
Inheritance                   No native equivalent
List<Account>                 JOIN or separate query
null                          NULL (similar but semantics differ)

Hibernate bridges this gap.

When to Choose What (Architect Rules)

text
CHOOSE RDBMS (Oracle/PostgreSQL/MySQL) WHEN:
  ✅ Structured data with relationships
  ✅ ACID transactions required
  ✅ Complex queries (JOINs, aggregations)
  ✅ Strong consistency needed
  ✅ Moderate scale (< 10TB, < 100K TPS)

CHOOSE Cassandra WHEN:
  ✅ Write-heavy (> 100K writes/sec)
  ✅ Time-series or append-only data
  ✅ Multi-datacenter replication
  ✅ Can accept eventual consistency

CHOOSE Redis WHEN:
  ✅ Sub-millisecond reads
  ✅ Session storage, caching
  ✅ Leaderboards, rate limiting
  ✅ Pub/sub messaging

CHOOSE MongoDB WHEN:
  ✅ Flexible/evolving schema
  ✅ Document-oriented data
  ✅ Rapid prototyping
  ✅ Horizontal scaling with sharding

CHOOSE BOTH (Polyglot Persistence) WHEN:
  ✅ Different access patterns in same system
  ✅ Example: Oracle (transactions) + Redis (cache) + Cassandra (logs)

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistakes Developers and Architects Make

Mistake 1: Treating the Database as a Black Box

text
❌ "My query is slow, I'll add more CPU to the server"
✅ "Let me check the execution plan and see if an index is missing"

Mistake 2: No Connection Pooling

java
// ❌ WRONG: Creating connection per request
Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pass);

// ✅ CORRECT: Use HikariCP (Spring Boot default)
@Autowired
private DataSource dataSource; // Pooled connections

Mistake 3: Using ddl-auto: create in Production

yaml
# ❌ DESTROYS DATA ON RESTART
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto: create

# ✅ Production settings
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto: validate  # or 'none'
# Schema changes via Flyway/Liquibase migrations

Mistake 4: Selecting * in Production

sql
-- ❌ Reads all columns, wastes I/O and memory
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 1001;

-- ✅ Select only needed columns
SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name, email
FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 1001;

Mistake 5: No Index on Foreign Keys

sql
-- ❌ JOINs and CASCADE DELETE will full-scan
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    customer_id BIGINT REFERENCES customers(customer_id)
    -- Missing index on customer_id!
);

-- ✅ Always index foreign keys
CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_customer_id ON accounts(customer_id);

Mistake 6: Storing Files in Database

text
❌ BLOB columns for profile images (bloats buffer pool, kills performance)
✅ Store file path/URL in DB, actual file in S3/object storage

Mistake 7: One Database for Everything

text
❌ Oracle for transactions + analytics + logs + cache + search
✅ Oracle (OLTP) + Read Replica (reporting) + Redis (cache) + Cassandra (logs)

Mistake 8: Ignoring Transaction Boundaries in Spring

java
// ❌ Each repository call in its own transaction (default without @Transactional)
public void transferMoney(Long from, Long to, BigDecimal amount) {
    accountRepo.debit(from, amount);   // Commits immediately
    accountRepo.credit(to, amount);    // If this fails, debit is NOT rolled back!
}

// ✅ Single transaction boundary
@Transactional
public void transferMoney(Long from, Long to, BigDecimal amount) {
    accountRepo.debit(from, amount);
    accountRepo.credit(to, amount);    // Both succeed or both fail
}

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Lesson 1 Interview Question Bank

Junior Level (0–2 years)

Q1: What is a database?

An organized collection of structured data managed by a DBMS that provides persistent storage, query capabilities, concurrent access control, and data integrity.

Q2: What is the difference between a database and a DBMS?

A database is the data itself. A DBMS is the software that manages, stores, retrieves, and secures that data (e.g., PostgreSQL is a DBMS; banking_platform is a database).

Q3: What is SQL?

Structured Query Language — the standard language for interacting with relational databases. Used for querying (SELECT), modifying (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), and defining schema (CREATE/ALTER/DROP).

Q4: Name five relational databases.

Oracle, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server, IBM DB2.

Q5: What is a schema?

The logical structure of a database — tables, columns, data types, constraints, indexes, and relationships.

Mid-Level (2–5 years)

Q6: Explain the three levels of data abstraction.

External (user views), Conceptual (logical schema/design), Internal (physical storage). Each level provides independence — change physical storage without affecting applications.

Q7: What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP?

OLTP: Online Transaction Processing — short, frequent read/write operations (banking). OLAP: Online Analytical Processing — complex read-heavy aggregations (reporting). Different performance profiles require different design.

Q8: Why is a connection pool important?

Creating DB connections is expensive (~50–100ms). Pools reuse existing connections, reducing latency and preventing connection exhaustion under load.

Q9: What happens when you call repository.save() in Spring Data JPA?

Hibernate checks persistence context → generates INSERT or UPDATE SQL → sends to DB → on transaction commit, changes are flushed and committed.

Q10: What is polyglot persistence?

Using multiple database technologies in one system, each optimized for specific access patterns (e.g., Oracle for transactions, Redis for cache, Cassandra for logs).

Senior Level (5–8 years)

Q11: Explain the query processing pipeline in a database.

Parse → Validate → Optimize (cost-based plan selection) → Execute → Return results. The optimizer is the most complex component, using statistics to estimate I/O costs.

Q12: What is a buffer pool and why does cache hit ratio matter?

In-memory cache of data/index pages. Hit ratio > 99% means most reads avoid disk I/O. Low hit ratio indicates insufficient memory or full table scans polluting the cache.

Q13: Why does a database write to WAL before modifying data files?

Write-Ahead Logging ensures durability — if crash occurs after commit but before data file update, WAL replay reconstructs committed transactions on recovery.

Q14: How would you design data storage for a payment system?

Oracle/PostgreSQL for ACID ledger, Redis for idempotency keys, Kafka for event stream, Cassandra for audit logs. Separate OLTP from analytics. Define RPO/RTO for DR.

Q15: What is the Object-Relational Impedance Mismatch?

Objects (inheritance, references, graphs) don't map cleanly to relational tables (rows, FK, flat structure). ORMs like Hibernate bridge this but introduce performance trade-offs (N+1, lazy loading).

Technical Lead Level

Q16: How do you decide between Oracle and PostgreSQL for a new enterprise project?

Evaluate: licensing cost, team expertise, compliance requirements, HA features needed, cloud strategy, existing ecosystem. Oracle for strict enterprise/compliance; PostgreSQL for cost-sensitive cloud-native.

Q17: Design a database layer for 10 microservices. Database per service or shared?

Database per service (microservices principle) — each service owns its data. Use events (Kafka) for cross-service data needs. Shared database is an anti-pattern (coupling, scaling bottleneck).

Staff / Principal Engineer Level

Q18: Your system's p99 latency jumped from 20ms to 500ms. Walk through diagnosis.

Check: connection pool saturation → slow query log → buffer pool hit ratio → lock contention → replication lag → disk I/O → network. Layer by layer from application to storage.

Q19: How would you migrate a monolithic Oracle database to microservices with zero downtime?

Strangler fig pattern: identify bounded contexts → extract service by service → dual-write period → CDC (Change Data Capture) for sync → cutover with feature flags → decommission old schema gradually.

Solution Architect Level

Q20: Design the complete data platform for a digital bank launching in 3 countries.

Consider: regulatory data residency (country-specific DB instances), core banking on Oracle RAC, payment ledger with ACID, Redis for sessions/rate limiting, Kafka for events, Cassandra for transaction logs, read replicas for reporting, cross-region DR with defined RPO/RTO, encryption at rest/transit, PCI-DSS compliance, capacity planning for 10M users.

Q21: CAP theorem — how does it apply to your banking platform design?

CP for core ledger (Oracle — consistency + partition tolerance, sacrifice availability during partition). AP for audit logs (Cassandra — availability + partition tolerance, eventual consistency acceptable). CA for single-node Redis cache (consistency + availability within one node).

Scenario-Based Questions

Scenario 1: "Your e-commerce platform's product catalog query takes 30 seconds. 10 million products, 100 concurrent users. What do you do?"

Check execution plan → likely full table scan → add indexes → consider read replica for catalog → Redis cache for hot products → CDN for static content → partition table if needed.

Scenario 2: "Two microservices share one PostgreSQL database. The team says it's fine because they're in the same domain. Are they right?"

No. Shared database creates tight coupling — schema changes break both services, scaling is monolithic, no independent deployment. Refactor to database-per-service with event-driven sync.

Part 20 — Revision Sheet

Lesson 1 Quick Revision

Must-Know Definitions

  • Database = organized persistent data collection
  • DBMS = software managing databases
  • Schema = logical structure
  • Instance = running database at a point in time
  • SQL = language for relational databases
  • WAL = Write-Ahead Log for durability
  • Buffer Pool = in-memory page cache
  • OLTP = transactional workloads
  • OLAP = analytical workloads

Must-Know Architecture

text
App → Connection Pool → DBMS (Parser → Optimizer → Executor) → Storage Engine → Disk
                                                      ↑
                                               Buffer Pool (RAM)

Must-Know History Points

  • 1970: Codd's Relational Model
  • 1979: Oracle first commercial RDBMS
  • 2000s: NoSQL for web scale
  • 2010s: Cloud-managed databases

Must-Know Spring Boot

  • HikariCP for connection pooling
  • ddl-auto: validate in production
  • @Transactional for transaction boundaries
  • Flyway/Liquibase for schema migrations

Must-Know Architect Rules

  • Choose database based on access patterns, not popularity
  • Polyglot persistence is the enterprise norm
  • Separate OLTP from OLAP
  • Database per microservice
  • Always define RPO/RTO for DR

Part 1 — Concept

What Are RDBMS and NoSQL?

RDBMS — Relational Database Management System

An RDBMS stores data in tables (relations) consisting of rows (tuples) and columns (attributes). Relationships between tables are defined through foreign keys. Data access is primarily through SQL.

text
RDBMS DATA MODEL
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                              │
│  CUSTOMERS                    ORDERS                         │
│  ┌──────────┬──────────┐     ┌──────────┬──────────────┐  │
│  │ cust_id  │ name     │     │ order_id │ customer_id  │  │
│  │ (PK)     │          │     │ (PK)     │ (FK)         │  │
│  ├──────────┼──────────┤     ├──────────┼──────────────┤  │
│  │ 1        │ John     │◄────│ 101      │ 1            │  │
│  │ 2        │ Jane     │◄────│ 102      │ 2            │  │
│  └──────────┴──────────┘     └──────────┴──────────────┘  │
│                                                              │
│  Properties: Fixed schema, ACID, SQL, JOINs, Constraints   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Examples: Oracle, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server, IBM DB2

NoSQL — Not Only SQL

NoSQL is an umbrella term for database systems that do not follow the relational model. They trade some relational guarantees for scale, flexibility, or performance in specific dimensions.

text
NoSQL is NOT one thing — it is FOUR different data models:

┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐
│  DOCUMENT    │  │  KEY-VALUE   │  │ WIDE-COLUMN  │  │    GRAPH     │
│              │  │              │  │              │  │              │
│  MongoDB     │  │  Redis       │  │  Cassandra   │  │  Neo4j       │
│  CouchDB     │  │  DynamoDB    │  │  HBase       │  │  Neptune     │
│              │  │  Riak        │  │  ScyllaDB    │  │              │
└──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘
     JSON/BSON       Key → Value      Rows × Cols       Nodes + Edges

The Critical Misconception

text
❌ WRONG:  "NoSQL replaces SQL"
❌ WRONG:  "NoSQL means no SQL language"
❌ WRONG:  "NoSQL is always faster"
❌ WRONG:  "Choose one — RDBMS OR NoSQL"

✅ CORRECT: "NoSQL = Not Only SQL"
✅ CORRECT: Different models for different access patterns
✅ CORRECT: Enterprise systems use BOTH (Polyglot Persistence)
✅ CORRECT: The choice is a trade-off, not a winner-takes-all

Formal Definitions

TermDefinition
RDBMSDBMS based on the relational model (Codd, 1970); data in tables with defined relationships
NoSQLNon-relational DBMS optimized for specific scalability, availability, or flexibility requirements
SQLStructured Query Language — standard for querying relational databases
SchemaStructure definition (RDBMS: rigid upfront; NoSQL: flexible or schema-on-read)
Polyglot PersistenceUsing multiple database technologies in one system for different data needs
NewSQLModern distributed databases offering SQL + ACID + horizontal scale (CockroachDB, Google Spanner)

Part 2 — History

Why Two Worlds Exist

The Relational Era (1970–2005)

text
1970  Codd publishes relational model
1979  Oracle — first commercial SQL RDBMS
1980s IBM DB2, Sybase, Informix
1989  Microsoft SQL Server
1995  MySQL (open source, web adoption)
1996  PostgreSQL (open source, advanced features)

DOMINANT PARADIGM: One database does everything
  ├── OLTP transactions
  ├── Reporting / analytics
  ├── Session storage
  └── Full-text search (later)

For 30 years, RDBMS handled all enterprise data needs. This worked because:

  • Data volumes were manageable (GB, not TB)
  • Servers scaled vertically (bigger CPU, more RAM)
  • Web traffic was moderate
  • Schema was stable and well-understood

The Breaking Point (2005–2010)

Web giants hit walls that RDBMS could not scale past:

text
THE TRIGGER EVENTS:

2004  Google publishes MapReduce paper
      → Processing petabytes — RDBMS can't scale horizontally

2006  Amazon Dynamo paper
      → Shopping cart: always available, even during partition
      → RDBMS replication too slow for their needs

2007  Facebook hits MySQL limits
      → 500M users, social graph doesn't fit relational model cleanly
      → Builds Cassandra (2008) and Memcached

2009  Twitter fails over on MySQL
      → Timeline generation requires different access pattern
      → Builds FlockDB, later Manhattan

2010  Netflix moves to Cassandra
      → 100M+ streaming users, global distribution needed

The NoSQL Explosion (2009–2015)

text
2009  MongoDB launched (document)
2009  Redis open-sourced (key-value)
2008  Cassandra open-sourced by Facebook (wide-column)
2010  Riak, CouchDB mature
2012  Amazon DynamoDB (managed key-value)
2015  Elasticsearch dominates search

Coined "NoSQL" at a 2009 meetup in San Francisco
Original meaning: "No SQL" → quickly revised to "Not Only SQL"

The Correction Era (2015–Present)

The industry learned NoSQL was not a silver bullet:

text
2015+  "NoSQL backlash" — companies returning to SQL for critical data
       MongoDB adds multi-document ACID transactions (2018)
       Cassandra adds lightweight transactions
       Redis adds RedisJSON, RedisSearch

2015+  NewSQL emerges
       Google Cloud Spanner (globally distributed SQL + ACID)
       CockroachDB (PostgreSQL-compatible, distributed)
       Amazon Aurora (MySQL/PostgreSQL compatible, cloud-native)

2020+  Multi-model databases
       Azure Cosmos DB (document, key-value, graph, column)
       ArangoDB (multi-model native)

TODAY: Mature architects use RDBMS + NoSQL together
       Not as competitors — as complementary tools

Historical Timeline Diagram

text
RELATIONAL DOMINANCE          NoSQL MOVEMENT           CONVERGENCE
1970────────────────2005──────2010────────2015────────2025──────▶

[RDBMS Only]    [Scale Crisis]  [NoSQL Boom]   [NewSQL/Multi-model]
 Oracle            Google         MongoDB         Spanner
 DB2               Amazon         Cassandra       CockroachDB
 MySQL             Facebook       Redis           Aurora
 PostgreSQL                       DynamoDB        Polyglot Persistence
                                               (Industry Standard)

What History Teaches Architects

Every database generation solved the previous generation's bottleneck and introduced new trade-offs. RDBMS solved file-system chaos. NoSQL solved web-scale horizontal scaling. NewSQL attempts to combine both. Your job is to know which trade-offs apply to your workload.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problem Did NoSQL Emerge to Solve?

RDBMS is excellent at many things. But at web scale, specific problems emerged:

Problem 1: Vertical Scaling Ceiling

text
RDBMS SCALING MODEL (Vertical):
┌────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Single Powerful Server                 │
│  CPU: 128 cores                         │
│  RAM: 2 TB                              │
│  Disk: 100 TB SSD                       │
│  Cost: $500,000+                        │
│  LIMIT: Physics and budget              │
└────────────────────────────────────────┘

NoSQL SCALING MODEL (Horizontal):
┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐
│ Node 1   │  │ Node 2   │  │ Node 3   │  │ Node N   │
│ Commodity│  │ Commodity│  │ Commodity│  │ Commodity│
│ Server   │  │ Server   │  │ Server   │  │ Server   │
└──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘
     Cost: $5,000 each × N nodes = linear scale

Problem: A single Oracle RAC cluster costing millions couldn't handle Facebook's write load. They needed 1000 cheap nodes instead of 1 expensive one.

Problem 2: Schema Rigidity at Speed of Business

text
RDBMS SCHEMA CHANGE (Painful):
  ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN attributes JSON;
  → Locks table (millions of rows)
  → Downtime window required
  → All applications must handle new column
  → Migration scripts for existing data
  → DBA approval, change management, rollback plan
  → Timeline: days to weeks

NoSQL SCHEMA CHANGE (Flexible):
  db.products.insertOne({
    name: "Laptop",
    attributes: { ram: "16GB", storage: "512GB SSD", color: "Silver" }
  });
  db.products.insertOne({
    name: "T-Shirt",
    attributes: { size: "L", material: "Cotton" }  // Different shape — OK
  });
  → Timeline: immediate

Problem 3: Impedance Mismatch with Modern Applications

text
APPLICATION OBJECT (Java):
Customer {
  id: 1001,
  name: "John",
  addresses: [                    ← List/Array
    { type: "HOME", city: "NYC" },
    { type: "WORK", city: "LA" }
  ],
  preferences: {                  ← Nested object
    newsletter: true,
    language: "en"
  }
}

RDBMS NORMALIZED STORAGE (3+ tables):
  customers        (id, name)
  addresses        (id, customer_id, type, city)
  preferences      (customer_id, newsletter, language)

NoSQL DOCUMENT STORAGE (1 document):
  { id, name, addresses: [...], preferences: {...} }
  → Matches application object structure exactly

Problem 4: Specific Access Patterns RDBMS Handles Poorly

Access PatternRDBMS ChallengeNoSQL Solution
Session lookup by keyOverkill — full SQL parser for GET keyRedis: O(1) in-memory
Append-only time-series logsINSERT OK but DELETE/archival painfulCassandra: optimized for writes
Full-text searchLIKE '%term%' is O(n) scanElasticsearch: inverted index
Social graph traversalRecursive JOINs are expensiveNeo4j: native graph traversal
Global low-latency readsSingle primary, replicas lagDynamoDB Global Tables

Problem 5: CAP Theorem Constraints at Scale

When a network partition occurs between data centers:

text
RDBMS DEFAULT BEHAVIOR:
  Network partition → Primary can't reach replicas
  → Writes may block (consistency over availability)
  → Single point of failure without complex HA setup

NoSQL DESIGN CHOICE:
  Network partition → System keeps serving
  → Some nodes may have stale data (availability over strong consistency)
  → Tunable per operation (Cassandra: ONE, QUORUM, ALL)

The Unified Problem Statement for NoSQL

At web scale, with evolving schemas, diverse access patterns, and global distribution requirements, a single relational database cannot efficiently serve all workloads. Organizations need specialized storage engines optimized for specific access patterns — while retaining RDBMS for workloads requiring strong consistency and complex relationships.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Does NoSQL Exist Alongside RDBMS?

The Fundamental Trade-Off

No database can maximize all properties simultaneously. Every system makes trade-offs:

text
                    THE DATABASE TRADE-OFF TRIANGLE

                              CONSISTENCY
                             (All nodes see
                              same data)
                                   ▲
                                  / \
                                 /   \
                                /     \
                               /       \
                              /  PICK  \
                             /    TWO    \
                            /             \
                           /_______________\
                    AVAILABILITY          PARTITION
                   (System always        TOLERANCE
                    responds)           (Works when
                                        network splits)

RDBMS (Oracle):     Consistency + Partition Tolerance (CP)
                    → May reject writes during partition to stay consistent

Cassandra:          Availability + Partition Tolerance (AP)
                    → Keeps serving during partition, data may be stale

Redis (single):     Consistency + Availability (CA)
                    → Works perfectly until partition (then fails)

Why Not Just Scale RDBMS?

Engineers tried. It partially works, but hits hard limits:

Scaling TechniqueRDBMS Reality
Read Replicas✅ Works well — async replication, stale reads possible
Vertical Scaling✅ Works to a point — physics limits at ~2TB RAM
Sharding (manual)⚠️ Possible but painful — application-level routing, no cross-shard JOINs
Oracle RAC⚠️ Shared storage cluster — expensive, complex, not true horizontal scale
PostgreSQL Citus⚠️ Extension for sharding — improving but not native
Write Scaling❌ Single primary bottleneck — all writes go to one node
text
WRITE SCALING — THE HARD PROBLEM:

RDBMS:                          Cassandra:
┌──────────────┐               ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐
│   PRIMARY    │               │Node 1│ │Node 2│ │Node 3│
│  (ALL WRITES)│               │Writes│ │Writes│ │Writes│
│      │       │               │ 25%  │ │ 33%  │ │ 42%  │
│  Replicas    │               └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘
│  (read only) │               Writes distributed across ring
└──────────────┘
Single write bottleneck

Why RDBMS Still Dominates Critical Workloads

NoSQL did NOT replace RDBMS because:

  1. ACID transactions — Banking cannot use eventual consistency for account balances
  2. Complex queries — Business intelligence requires JOINs across 10+ tables
  3. Data integrity — Foreign keys, constraints enforced by DB, not application
  4. Maturity — 50 years of tooling, expertise, compliance certifications
  5. Ecosystem — Hibernate/JPA, reporting tools, migration utilities
  6. Regulatory — PCI-DSS, SOX, HIPAA audits expect relational audit trails

Why Both Exist: Polyglot Persistence

text
MODERN ENTERPRISE DATA PLATFORM (Your Target Architecture):

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    APPLICATION LAYER                             │
│         Spring Boot Microservices (Java/Kafka/AWS)              │
└──────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬─────────────┘
       │          │          │          │          │
       ▼          ▼          ▼          ▼          ▼
┌──────────┐┌──────────┐┌──────────┐┌──────────┐┌──────────┐
│  Oracle  ││  Redis   ││ Cassandra││ MongoDB  ││Elastic-  │
│  (RDBMS) ││(Key-Value││(Wide-Col)││(Document)││ search   │
│          ││          ││          ││          ││          │
│ Core     ││ Session  ││ Audit    ││ Product  ││ Log      │
│ banking  ││ Cache    ││ Logs     ││ Catalog  ││ Search   │
│ ledger   ││ Rate     ││ Events   ││ CMS      ││ Analytics│
│ ACID tx  ││ limit    ││ Time-    ││ Flexible ││ Full-text│
│          ││          ││ series   ││ schema   ││          │
└──────────┘└──────────┘└──────────┘└──────────┘└──────────┘

Each database chosen for ONE specific access pattern.
NOT because it's trendy — because the workload demands it.

Part 5 — Internal Working

How RDBMS and NoSQL Work Internally (Comparative)

RDBMS Internal Architecture

text
RDBMS INTERNAL ARCHITECTURE (e.g., PostgreSQL, Oracle)

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      SQL INTERFACE                           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Parser → Analyzer → Rewriter → OPTIMIZER → Executor      │
│                                      │                       │
│                              Cost-Based Plan                 │
│                              (statistics-driven)             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  TRANSACTION MANAGER                                         │
│  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐  │
│  │ Lock Manager │  │ MVCC Engine  │  │ WAL (Redo Log)   │  │
│  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────────┘  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  STORAGE ENGINE                                              │
│  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐  │
│  │ Buffer Pool  │  │ B-Tree Index │  │ Heap/Clustered   │  │
│  │ (page cache) │  │              │  │ Table Storage  │  │
│  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────────┘  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  DISK: Data Files + WAL Files + Index Files                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Key RDBMS internal behaviors:

  • Every query goes through a cost-based optimizer
  • MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) for read/write concurrency
  • WAL ensures durability before acknowledging commits
  • B-Tree indexes for O(log n) lookups
  • Lock manager prevents conflicting concurrent modifications

NoSQL Internal Architectures (By Type)

Document Store (MongoDB)

text
MONGODB INTERNAL ARCHITECTURE

Client Request
      │
      ▼
┌─────────────┐
│ Mongos      │  (Query Router — in sharded cluster)
│ (Router)    │
└──────┬──────┘
       │
       ▼
┌─────────────┐
│ Query Layer │  Parse BSON query → Select index or collection scan
└──────┬──────┘
       │
       ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WIRED TIGER STORAGE ENGINE              │
│  ┌──────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐│
│  │ B-Tree Index │  │ Document Store  ││
│  │ (_id, fields)│  │ (BSON on disk)  ││
│  └──────────────┘  └─────────────────┘│
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ Cache (50% RAM by default)       │  │
│  └──────────────────────────────────┘  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘

Key-Value Store (Redis)

text
REDIS INTERNAL ARCHITECTURE

Client: GET session:user:12345
      │
      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  REDIS SERVER (Single-threaded event loop)│
│                                          │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  Hash Table (dict)               │  │
│  │  Key: "session:user:12345"       │  │
│  │  Value: {userId, roles, expiry}  │  │
│  │  Lookup: O(1) average              │  │
│  └──────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                          │
│  ALL DATA IN RAM (primary)               │
│  Optional: RDB snapshots / AOF to disk   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘
Response time: ~0.1ms (vs ~5ms for disk-based DB)

Wide-Column Store (Cassandra)

text
CASSANDRA INTERNAL ARCHITECTURE (Distributed Ring)

         Node 1 (Token 0–33)
        /                        \
   Node 3                         Node 2
   (Token 67–99)                 (Token 34–66)

Write Path:
  Client → Any node (coordinator)
         → Hash(partition_key) → Determine token owner
         → Write to commit log (disk, sequential)
         → Write to MemTable (RAM)
         → Flush to SSTable (disk, immutable) when MemTable full
         → Replicate to N nodes based on replication factor

Read Path:
  Client → Coordinator node
         → Query MemTable + SSTables (Bloom filter skip)
         → Read repair if inconsistencies found
         → Return result (may be eventually consistent)

Internal Working Comparison Table

Internal ComponentRDBMSDocumentKey-ValueWide-Column
Query ProcessingFull SQL optimizerIndex scan / collection scanDirect key hash lookupPartition key routing
Storage StructureB-Tree pagesBSON documents + B-Tree indexHash table in RAMLSM Tree (MemTable + SSTable)
ConcurrencyMVCC + LocksDocument-level lockingSingle-threaded (Redis)Row-level, tunable consistency
DurabilityWAL (sync)Journal (WiredTiger)RDB/AOF optionalCommit log + SSTable
DistributionReplication (manual shard)Sharding (config servers)Redis Cluster slotsNative consistent hashing ring
JoinsNative optimizer$lookup (limited)Not supportedNot supported

Part 6 — Storage Internals

How RDBMS and NoSQL Store Data on Disk

RDBMS Storage: Page-Based Relational

text
RDBMS TABLE STORAGE (PostgreSQL Heap Table)

Table: accounts (100 million rows)
Data File: /var/lib/postgresql/data/base/16384/24576

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Page 1 (8KB)                                                │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │ Header │ ItemId │ Free │ account_id│customer_id│balance│   │
│  │        │ Array  │ Space│ 5001      │ 1001      │15000  │   │
│  │        │        │      │ 5047      │ 1023      │ 3200  │   │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Page 2 (8KB)  ... more rows ...                           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Page N (8KB)                                                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Separate Index File (B-Tree):
  account_id:5001 → Page 1, Offset 24
  account_id:5047 → Page 1, Offset 96

RDBMS storage characteristics:

  • Fixed column widths (or variable with length prefix)
  • NULL bitmap per row
  • Rows can move between pages (UPDATE that grows row)
  • Index is separate structure pointing to row location

MongoDB Storage: BSON Documents

text
MONGODB COLLECTION STORAGE

Collection: products
Document stored as BSON (Binary JSON):

Hex representation of one document:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 16 bytes: Document length                                 │
│ 1 byte:   Type (0x03 = embedded document)                │
│ String:   "_id"                                           │
│ 12 bytes: ObjectId (timestamp + machine + pid + counter)  │
│ String:   "name" → "MacBook Pro"                          │
│ String:   "category" → "Electronics"                      │
│ Embedded: "specs" → { ram: "16GB", storage: "512GB" }    │
│ End marker: 0x00                                          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Documents stored contiguously in data files.
_id index is ALWAYS created (clustered by _id).
Additional indexes are separate B-Trees pointing to document location.

Cassandra Storage: LSM Tree

text
CASSANDRA LSM (Log-Structured Merge) TREE

Write: payment_event
  partition_key: account_id=456, clustering: timestamp

Step 1: Commit Log (append-only, sequential disk write — FAST)
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ [write1][write2][write3][write4]...[writeN]                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Step 2: MemTable (in-memory sorted structure)
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ account:456|ts:100 → {amount:250, status:PENDING}          │
│ account:456|ts:101 → {amount:100, status:COMPLETED}        │
│ account:789|ts:99  → {amount:500, status:PENDING}          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Step 3: Flush to SSTable (immutable disk file, sorted)
┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐
│ SSTable-1.db     │  │ SSTable-2.db     │
│ (older data)     │  │ (newer data)     │
│ Bloom Filter     │  │ Bloom Filter     │
│ Index (sparse)   │  │ Index (sparse)   │
└──────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘

Read: Check MemTable → SSTable-2 → SSTable-1 (newest to oldest)
Compaction: Periodically merge SSTables, discard tombstones

Why LSM for Cassandra? Sequential writes are 100x faster than random writes on HDD/SSD. Perfect for write-heavy workloads.

Redis Storage: In-Memory with Optional Persistence

text
REDIS MEMORY STRUCTURE

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  redisDb (database 0)                                        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  dict (hash table)                                   │    │
│  │  ┌─────────────────────┬────────────────────────┐ │    │
│  │  │ Key                 │ Value (redisObject)    │ │    │
│  │  ├─────────────────────┼────────────────────────┤ │    │
│  │  │ "session:abc123"    │ {userId:1001, role:..} │ │    │
│  │  │ "ratelimit:ip:1.2"   │ counter: 47, TTL: 60s  │ │    │
│  │  │ "cache:product:99"  │ serialized JSON blob   │ │    │
│  │  └─────────────────────┴────────────────────────┘ │    │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Persistence Options:
  RDB:  Snapshot every N seconds → binary dump file
  AOF:  Append every write command → replay on restart
  None: Pure cache — data lost on restart (acceptable for sessions)

Storage Model Comparison

AspectRDBMSMongoDBCassandraRedis
Unit of storageRow in pageBSON documentRow in SSTableKey-value pair
SchemaFixed columnsFlexible documentFlexible columnsOpaque value
Primary storageDiskDisk (+ cache)Disk (LSM)RAM
Write patternRandom (update in place)Random (update document)Sequential (append)In-memory
Update costRead-modify-write pageRead-modify-write documentAppend new version (immutable)In-place (O(1))
DeleteMark row dead (vacuum later)Mark document deletedTombstone (removed on compaction)Immediate DEL command

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Memory Architecture: RDBMS vs NoSQL

RDBMS Memory Model

text
ORACLE SGA (System Global Area) / PostgreSQL Shared Buffers

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TOTAL DB SERVER RAM: 64 GB                                  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                              │
│  Buffer Cache / shared_buffers:     48 GB  (75%)            │
│  ├── Data pages cached                                       │
│  ├── Index pages cached                                      │
│  └── Undo/Rollback segments                                  │
│                                                              │
│  Shared Pool / work_mem:           8 GB   (12%)            │
│  ├── Parsed SQL plans                                        │
│  ├── Dictionary cache                                        │
│  └── Sort/hash operation memory                              │
│                                                              │
│  WAL / Redo Log buffers:           2 GB   (3%)             │
│  Connections (500 × 10MB):         5 GB   (8%)             │
│  OS Cache:                         1 GB   (2%)             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Key metric: Buffer Cache Hit Ratio > 99%
Miss = disk I/O = 5-10ms vs 0.1ms from RAM

NoSQL Memory Models

MongoDB Memory

text
MongoDB WiredTiger Cache (default: 50% of RAM - 1GB)

Server RAM: 32 GB
  WiredTiger Cache: 15 GB
    ├── Frequently accessed documents
    ├── Index B-Tree nodes
    └── Compression/decompression buffers

  Remaining: OS file system cache (also helps with reads)

If working set > cache → page faults → disk reads → latency spike
Monitor: db.serverStatus().wiredTiger.cache

Redis Memory

text
Redis: EVERYTHING in memory (by design)

Server RAM: 16 GB
  Redis data: up to ~13 GB (leaves room for overhead)
  maxmemory-policy: allkeys-lru (evict least recently used when full)

  1 million sessions × ~2KB each = ~2 GB
  10 million cache entries × ~1KB = ~10 GB

WARNING: Redis OOM → evictions or reject writes
Monitor: INFO memory, used_memory_peak

Cassandra Memory

text
Cassandra JVM Heap + Off-Heap

Server RAM: 32 GB
  JVM Heap: 8-16 GB (NEVER more than 16GB — GC pauses)
    ├── MemTable (active write buffer)
    ├── Bloom filters (in memory per SSTable)
    ├── Index summaries
    └── Key cache / Row cache (optional)

  Off-Heap / OS cache: 16-24 GB
    ├── SSTable data file cache (OS level)
    └── Compression buffers

MemTable flush threshold: memtable_heap_space (default ~256MB)
When MemTable fills → flush to SSTable → brief write pause

Memory Usage Comparison

SystemPrimary Memory UseTypical SizingOOM Risk
OracleBuffer cache (SGA)60-75% of RAMManaged — swaps to disk
PostgreSQLshared_buffers + OS cache25-40% shared_buffersManaged
MongoDBWiredTiger cache50% RAMPage faults to disk
RedisAll data in RAM80% RAM maxEviction or OOM error
CassandraMemTable + Bloom filtersHeap ≤ 16GBGC pauses if heap too large

Architect Memory Rule

text
FOR ANY DATABASE:

1. Identify WORKING SET (data accessed in normal operations)
2. IF working set fits in memory cache → excellent performance
3. IF working set > cache → expect disk I/O → tune or scale

Working Set Analysis:
  OLTP banking: Active accounts (last 90 days) ≈ 5% of total data
  Analytics: Full table scans — memory helps less
  Cache (Redis): Working set = ALL data (must fit in RAM)
  Time-series (Cassandra): Recent data hot, old data cold

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Query Execution: Same Request, Different Engines

Let's trace: "Get customer 1001 with all their accounts"

RDBMS Execution Flow (PostgreSQL)

sql
SELECT c.first_name, c.last_name, a.account_type, a.balance
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON c.customer_id = a.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id = 1001;
text
STEP 1: PARSE & ANALYZE
  Valid tables: customers, accounts ✓
  Join condition: customer_id ✓
  Filter: customer_id = 1001 ✓

STEP 2: OPTIMIZER (Cost-Based)
  Option A: Seq Scan customers + Nested Loop accounts    Cost: 150,000
  Option B: Index Scan customers(PK) + Index Scan accounts(FK)  Cost: 8  ← CHOSEN
  Option C: Hash Join + Seq Scan both                    Cost: 75,000

STEP 3: EXECUTE (Plan B)
  3a. Index Scan on customers PK → 1 row (0.05ms)
  3b. Index Scan on accounts(customer_id) → 2 rows (0.08ms)
  3c. Nested Loop Join → combine rows (0.01ms)
  Total: ~0.14ms

STEP 4: RETURN result set to client

MongoDB Execution Flow

javascript
db.customers.findOne(
  { _id: 1001 },
  { name: 1, accounts: 1 }  // Embedded — no join needed if denormalized
);

// OR if normalized (separate collections):
db.customers.aggregate([
  { $match: { _id: 1001 } },
  { $lookup: {
      from: "accounts",
      localField: "_id",
      foreignField: "customer_id",
      as: "accounts"
  }}
]);
text
NORMALIZED AGGREGATION EXECUTION:

STEP 1: Query Router receives aggregation pipeline

STEP 2: $match stage
  Index scan on _id → 1 customer document (0.1ms)

STEP 3: $lookup stage (equivalent to LEFT JOIN)
  For EACH customer doc (1 iteration):
    Index scan on accounts.customer_id → 2 account docs
  ⚠️ $lookup is essentially a nested loop join — slow at scale

STEP 4: Return combined document

DENORMALIZED (embedded accounts in customer doc):
  Single index lookup → 1 document with embedded accounts
  Total: ~0.1ms (no join)
  Trade-off: Update account → must update customer document too

Redis Execution Flow

text
Request: GET session:user:1001

STEP 1: Client sends RESP protocol command over TCP
STEP 2: Redis event loop receives command
STEP 3: Hash table lookup: key="session:user:1001"
  hashFunction(key) → bucket index → compare key → return value
  O(1) average case
STEP 4: Deserialize value → send to client
Total: ~0.1ms (all in memory, no parsing, no optimization needed)

Cassandra Execution Flow

sql
SELECT * FROM payments
WHERE account_id = 456
AND transaction_date >= '2024-01-01'
AND transaction_date <= '2024-01-31';
text
STEP 1: Coordinator node receives query
  partition_key = account_id (456) → determines which node owns data

STEP 2: Route to replica nodes (based on consistency level)
  Consistency QUORUM (RF=3): contact 2 of 3 replicas

STEP 3: On each replica:
  3a. Check MemTable for account_id=456
  3b. Check SSTables (newest first) — Bloom filter skip if not present
  3c. Merge results from MemTable + SSTables
  3d. Apply clustering column filter (date range)

STEP 4: Coordinator merges responses from replicas
  Read repair if versions differ (eventual consistency)

STEP 5: Return rows to client
Total: ~5-20ms (depends on consistency level, SSTable count)

Execution Flow Comparison

text
LATENCY HIERARCHY (same datacenter):

Redis GET:           ~0.1ms   █
RDBMS indexed query: ~0.5ms   ████
MongoDB _id lookup:  ~1ms     ████████
Cassandra read:      ~5ms     ████████████████████
RDBMS complex JOIN:  ~10ms    ████████████████████████████████████████
MongoDB $lookup:      ~50ms+   (depends on collection size)
RDBMS full scan:     ~30sec    (100M rows, no index)

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Performance Characteristics by Workload Type

Read Performance

WorkloadBest ChoiceWhy
Point lookup by keyRedisO(1) hash, in-memory
Point lookup by PKRDBMSB-Tree index, buffer pool
Range scan (indexed)RDBMSB-Tree range scan native
Full-text searchElasticsearchInverted index
Aggregations (OLAP)Column store / RDBMSVectorized execution
Graph traversalNeo4jNative pointer traversal

Write Performance

WorkloadBest ChoiceWhy
Single row update (ACID)RDBMSOptimized OLTP, row-level locking
Bulk append (logs, events)CassandraLSM sequential writes
High-frequency counterRedisINCR atomic, in-memory
Document upsertMongoDBSingle document write
Batch insert (1000s rows)RDBMS with COPY/bulkJDBC batch, pg_copy

Benchmark Reference (Orders of Magnitude)

text
Operation                    RDBMS      MongoDB    Cassandra   Redis
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Single PK read               0.5ms      1ms        5ms         0.1ms
Single PK write (sync)     2ms        3ms        5ms         0.1ms
Bulk insert (10K rows)     500ms      800ms      200ms       N/A
Complex JOIN (5 tables)    50ms       500ms*     N/A         N/A
Full table scan (1M rows)  5sec       8sec       3sec**      N/A
Aggregation GROUP BY       100ms      200ms      N/A         N/A

* MongoDB $lookup — not native join
** Cassandra requires partition key — no full scan allowed efficiently

Performance Anti-Patterns

text
❌ ANTI-PATTERN 1: Using MongoDB like RDBMS
   Multiple collections with $lookup joins
   → Redesign: embed documents or denormalize

❌ ANTI-PATTERN 2: Using Redis as primary database
   Redis crash = all data lost (without AOF/RDB)
   → Redis is a cache/accelerator, not source of truth

❌ ANTI-PATTERN 3: Using Cassandra for low-write, complex-query workloads
   No JOINs, no secondary index efficiency, no ad-hoc queries
   → Use RDBMS or MongoDB instead

❌ ANTI-PATTERN 4: Using RDBMS for time-series logs at billions of rows
   DELETE old data is expensive (vacuum, fragmentation)
   → Use Cassandra or TimescaleDB with TTL

❌ ANTI-PATTERN 5: Running analytics on primary OLTP database
   Full table scans evict buffer pool → OLTP queries slow down
   → Read replica or separate OLAP store

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Side-by-Side: Same Use Case, Different Databases

Use Case 1: Store and Retrieve a Customer

RDBMS (PostgreSQL):

sql
-- Create
INSERT INTO customers (customer_id, first_name, last_name, email)
VALUES (1001, 'Ankur', 'Kumar', 'ankur@email.com');

-- Read
SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name, email
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id = 1001;

-- Update
UPDATE customers SET email = 'ankur.new@email.com' WHERE customer_id = 1001;

-- Delete
DELETE FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 1001;

MongoDB:

javascript
// Create
db.customers.insertOne({
  _id: 1001,
  firstName: "Ankur",
  lastName: "Kumar",
  email: "ankur@email.com",
  createdAt: new Date()
});

// Read
db.customers.findOne({ _id: 1001 });

// Update
db.customers.updateOne(
  { _id: 1001 },
  { $set: { email: "ankur.new@email.com", updatedAt: new Date() } }
);

// Delete
db.customers.deleteOne({ _id: 1001 });

Redis:

bash
# Create / Update (same command)
SET customer:1001 '{"firstName":"Ankur","lastName":"Kumar","email":"ankur@email.com"}'

# Read
GET customer:1001

# Delete
DEL customer:1001

# With TTL (expire after 1 hour — useful for sessions)
SETEX session:1001 3600 '{"userId":1001,"role":"CUSTOMER"}'

Cassandra (CQL):

sql
-- Create (upsert semantics — INSERT = UPDATE in Cassandra)
INSERT INTO customers (customer_id, first_name, last_name, email, created_at)
VALUES (1001, 'Ankur', 'Kumar', 'ankur@email.com', toTimestamp(now()));

-- Read (must specify full primary key or partition key)
SELECT customer_id, first_name, last_name, email
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id = 1001;

-- Update (actually an INSERT with same primary key — LSM append)
INSERT INTO customers (customer_id, first_name, last_name, email)
VALUES (1001, 'Ankur', 'Kumar', 'ankur.new@email.com');

-- Delete (writes tombstone)
DELETE FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 1001;

Use Case 2: Payment Event Log (High-Volume Writes)

RDBMS — Works but not optimal at scale:

sql
CREATE TABLE payment_events (
    event_id        BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id      BIGINT NOT NULL,
    amount          DECIMAL(18,2),
    event_type      VARCHAR(50),
    created_at      TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_payment_events_account ON payment_events(account_id, created_at);

INSERT INTO payment_events (account_id, amount, event_type)
VALUES (456, 250.00, 'DEBIT');
-- At 100K inserts/sec: single primary bottleneck, index maintenance overhead

Cassandra — Designed for this:

sql
CREATE TABLE payment_events (
    account_id    BIGINT,
    event_time    TIMESTAMP,
    event_id      UUID,
    amount        DECIMAL,
    event_type    TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY (account_id, event_time, event_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (event_time DESC);

INSERT INTO payment_events (account_id, event_time, event_id, amount, event_type)
VALUES (456, toTimestamp(now()), uuid(), 250.00, 'DEBIT');

-- Query last 30 days for account (efficient — single partition scan)
SELECT * FROM payment_events
WHERE account_id = 456
AND event_time >= '2024-01-01'
AND event_time <= '2024-01-31';
-- Writes distributed across ring, no single primary bottleneck

Use Case 3: Session Cache

Redis — The right tool:

bash
# Store session on login
SETEX "session:token:abc123xyz" 1800 '{"userId":1001,"roles":["CUSTOMER"],"loginAt":"2024-01-15T10:00:00Z"}'

# Validate session on each request
GET "session:token:abc123xyz"
# Returns session data in 0.1ms — or nil if expired

# Extend session TTL on activity
EXPIRE "session:token:abc123xyz" 1800

# Rate limiting (100 requests per minute per IP)
INCR "ratelimit:192.168.1.1:2024011510"
EXPIRE "ratelimit:192.168.1.1:2024011510" 60
# If count > 100 → reject request

WHY each choice:
  Oracle RAC    → ACID transactions, row-level locking, regulatory compliance
  Redis         → Idempotency key check must be < 1ms (prevent double-charge)
  Cassandra     → Append-only audit log, 7-year retention, high write volume
  Kafka         → Event sourcing, downstream analytics, decoupling

Multi-Datasource Configuration

# application.yml — Polyglot Persistence Configuration
