Java Configuration Classes

java
// Primary Oracle DataSource
@Configuration
@EnableJpaRepositories(
    basePackages = "com.bank.repository.oracle",
    entityManagerFactoryRef = "primaryEntityManagerFactory",
    transactionManagerRef = "primaryTransactionManager"
)
public class OracleDataSourceConfig {

    @Primary
    @Bean
    @ConfigurationProperties("spring.datasource.primary")
    public DataSource primaryDataSource() {
        return DataSourceBuilder.create().build();
    }

    @Primary
    @Bean
    public LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean primaryEntityManagerFactory(
            EntityManagerFactoryBuilder builder) {
        return builder
            .dataSource(primaryDataSource())
            .packages("com.bank.entity")
            .persistenceUnit("primary")
            .build();
    }

    @Primary
    @Bean
    public PlatformTransactionManager primaryTransactionManager(
            @Qualifier("primaryEntityManagerFactory")
            EntityManagerFactory emf) {
        return new JpaTransactionManager(emf);
    }
}
java
// Redis Configuration
@Configuration
@EnableRedisRepositories(basePackages = "com.bank.repository.redis")
public class RedisConfig {

    @Bean
    public RedisTemplate<String, Object> redisTemplate(
            RedisConnectionFactory connectionFactory) {
        RedisTemplate<String, Object> template = new RedisTemplate<>();
        template.setConnectionFactory(connectionFactory);
        template.setKeySerializer(new StringRedisSerializer());
        template.setValueSerializer(new GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer());
        return template;
    }
}
java
// Cassandra Configuration
@Configuration
@EnableCassandraRepositories(basePackages = "com.bank.repository.cassandra")
public class CassandraConfig extends AbstractCassandraConfiguration {

    @Value("${cassandra.keyspace}")
    private String keyspace;

    @Override
    protected String getKeyspaceName() {
        return keyspace;
    }

    @Override
    protected String getLocalDataCenter() {
        return "datacenter1";
    }
}

Service Using Multiple Databases

java
@Service
@Slf4j
public class PaymentService {

    private final PaymentRepository paymentRepository;       // Oracle JPA
    private final RedisTemplate<String, Object> redis;       // Redis
    private final PaymentEventRepository eventRepository;  // Cassandra

    @Transactional  // Oracle transaction
    public PaymentResult processPayment(PaymentRequest request) {

        // Step 1: Idempotency check (Redis — outside DB transaction)
        String idempotencyKey = "payment:idempotency:" + request.getIdempotencyKey();
        Boolean isNew = redis.opsForValue()
            .setIfAbsent(idempotencyKey, "PROCESSING", Duration.ofHours(24));

        if (Boolean.FALSE.equals(isNew)) {
            return PaymentResult.duplicate(request.getIdempotencyKey());
        }

        try {
            // Step 2: ACID transaction in Oracle
            Payment payment = new Payment();
            payment.setAccountId(request.getAccountId());
            payment.setAmount(request.getAmount());
            paymentRepository.save(payment);

            accountRepository.debit(request.getAccountId(), request.getAmount());

            // Step 3: Audit log to Cassandra (async, eventual consistency OK)
            PaymentEvent event = PaymentEvent.from(payment);
            eventRepository.save(event);  // Cassandra — separate transaction

            // Step 4: Mark idempotency complete in Redis
            redis.opsForValue().set(idempotencyKey, "COMPLETED", Duration.ofHours(24));

            return PaymentResult.success(payment);

        } catch (Exception e) {
            redis.delete(idempotencyKey);  // Allow retry
            throw e;
        }
    }
}

Architecture Diagram: Spring Boot Multi-DB

text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  PaymentService (@Transactional)             │
│                                                              │
│  1. Redis SETNX (idempotency)     ← NOT in DB transaction   │
│  2. Oracle JPA save + debit       ← ACID transaction         │
│  3. Cassandra save event          ← Separate, async OK       │
│  4. Redis SET completed           ← NOT in DB transaction   │
└──────┬──────────────────┬──────────────────┬──────────────┘
       │                  │                  │
       ▼                  ▼                  ▼
┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐
│ Redis        │  │ Oracle       │  │ Cassandra        │
│ (Lettuce     │  │ (HikariCP +  │  │ (DataStax        │
│  Client)     │  │  Hibernate)  │  │  Driver)         │
│              │  │              │  │                  │
│ Idempotency  │  │ Ledger       │  │ Audit Events     │
│ TTL: 24h     │  │ ACID Tx      │  │ Append-only      │
└──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────────┘

⚠️ CRITICAL: Cannot use @Transactional across all three!
   Each database has its own transaction boundary.
   Pattern: Saga or Outbox for cross-DB consistency.

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

The Solution Architect's Framework for RDBMS vs NoSQL

The Five Questions Before Choosing Any Database

text
QUESTION 1: What is the ACCESS PATTERN?
  ├── Point lookup by key?        → Redis, RDBMS with PK index
  ├── Range scan?                 → RDBMS, Cassandra (within partition)
  ├── Full-text search?           → Elasticsearch
  ├── Graph traversal?            → Neo4j
  ├── Append-only log?            → Cassandra, Kafka
  └── Complex JOINs?              → RDBMS only

QUESTION 2: What CONSISTENCY does the business require?
  ├── Financial transaction?      → Strong ACID (RDBMS)
  ├── User profile update?        → Strong consistency preferred
  ├── Analytics dashboard?        → Eventual consistency OK
  ├── Session cache?              → Eventual consistency OK
  └── Audit log?                  → Eventual consistency OK (append-only)

QUESTION 3: What is the SCALE?
  ├── < 100GB, < 10K TPS          → Single RDBMS sufficient
  ├── 100GB - 1TB, < 100K TPS   → RDBMS + read replicas + Redis cache
  ├── 1TB - 100TB, > 100K TPS   → Sharding + Cassandra/NoSQL
  └── > 100TB, global             → Multi-region NoSQL + specialized stores

QUESTION 4: What is the LATENCY BUDGET?
  ├── < 1ms                       → Redis (in-memory)
  ├── < 10ms                      → RDBMS with proper indexes
  ├── < 100ms                     → Any database with tuning
  └── > 100ms OK                  → Batch, analytics workloads

QUESTION 5: What are OPERATIONAL CONSTRAINTS?
  ├── Team knows Oracle deeply?   → Leverage that expertise
  ├── Cloud-native startup?       → Managed services (RDS, DynamoDB)
  ├── Regulatory compliance?      → RDBMS with audit features
  └── Budget limited?             → PostgreSQL + Redis (open source)

CAP Theorem Applied to Real Systems

text
CAP THEOREM: In a distributed system during a network partition,
             you can guarantee at most TWO of:
             Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance

Network partitions WILL happen in distributed systems.
So the real choice is: CP or AP?

CP SYSTEMS (Consistency + Partition Tolerance):
  Oracle RAC, PostgreSQL synchronous replication
  → During partition: reject writes to maintain consistency
  → Use for: financial ledger, inventory counts

AP SYSTEMS (Availability + Partition Tolerance):
  Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB
  → During partition: accept writes, reconcile later
  → Use for: social feeds, analytics, audit logs

CA SYSTEMS (Consistency + Availability):
  Single-node Redis, single-node PostgreSQL
  → Works perfectly until network partition
  → Use for: cache, single-datacenter deployments

PRACTICAL REALITY:
  Modern systems tune consistency per operation:
  Cassandra: consistency ONE (fast, stale) vs QUORUM vs ALL
  DynamoDB: eventual vs strong consistency per read
  Spanner: TrueTime enables external consistency globally

NewSQL: The Third Path

text
NewSQL = SQL interface + ACID + Horizontal Scale

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Google Cloud Spanner                                        │
│  ├── SQL interface                                           │
│  ├── Globally distributed                                    │
│  ├── External consistency (TrueTime API)                     │
│  └── Used by: Google Ads, Google Play, Gmail                 │

└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

When to consider NewSQL:

  ✅ Global distribution with strong consistency
  ✅ Team knows SQL, doesn't want to learn Cassandra
  ❌ Cost (Spanner is expensive)
  ❌ Maturity vs Oracle for banking compliance

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

RDBMS vs NoSQL Anti-Patterns

Mistake 1: "NoSQL is Faster" — Blanket Statement

text
❌ "We switched from Oracle to MongoDB because NoSQL is faster"
✅ "We moved our product catalog to MongoDB because:
    - Schema changes weekly (new product attributes)
    - No complex JOINs needed (embedded documents)
    - Read-heavy, moderate write rate
    - Eventual consistency acceptable for catalog"

Mistake 2: Using Cassandra Without Understanding Partition Keys

sql
-- ❌ WRONG: Query without partition key → full cluster scan
SELECT * FROM payment_events WHERE event_type = 'DEBIT';
-- Scans EVERY node, EVERY SSTable — extremely slow, may timeout

-- ✅ CORRECT: Always include partition key
SELECT * FROM payment_events
WHERE account_id = 456          -- partition key FIRST
AND event_time >= '2024-01-01'; -- clustering column filter

Mistake 3: MongoDB as Primary Store for Financial Data

text
❌ Store account balances in MongoDB
   → Multi-document transactions added in v4.0 but not as mature as Oracle
   → No regulatory track record for core banking
   → Application must enforce referential integrity

✅ Oracle for balances, MongoDB for product catalog

Mistake 4: Redis Without Persistence for Critical Data

bash
# ❌ Idempotency keys in Redis with no persistence
# Redis crash → all keys lost → duplicate payments possible

# ✅ Configure AOF persistence + understand trade-offs
# redis.conf:
appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec  # Max 1 second data loss on crash

# ✅ Better: Use Redis for performance, Oracle for authoritative record

Mistake 5: Shared Database in Microservices

text
❌ ANTI-PATTERN: Database per Microservice violated

┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐
│ Order Service│     │Payment Service│
└──────┬───────┘     └──────┬───────┘
       │                    │
       └────────┬───────────┘
                ▼
         ┌──────────────┐
         │ Shared Oracle │  ← Coupling! Schema changes break both
         └──────────────┘

✅ CORRECT: Database per service + events for cross-service data

┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐
│ Order Service│     │Payment Service│
└──────┬───────┘     └──────┬───────┘
       │                    │
       ▼                    ▼
┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐
│ Order DB     │     │ Payment DB   │
│ (PostgreSQL) │     │ (Oracle)     │
└──────┬───────┘     └──────┬───────┘
       │                    │
       └────────┬───────────┘
                ▼
           Kafka Events
           (cross-service sync)

Mistake 6: Not Defining Data Ownership

text
❌ "The data team manages all databases"
✅ Each microservice team owns their database:
   - Order Service team owns Order PostgreSQL
   - Payment Service team owns Payment Oracle
   - Analytics team owns Cassandra (read-only replica via Kafka)

Mistake 7: Ignoring the Outbox Pattern for Cross-DB Consistency

java
// ❌ WRONG: Save to Oracle, then save to Cassandra
// If Cassandra write fails, Oracle is committed but audit log missing

@Transactional
public void processPayment(PaymentRequest req) {
    paymentRepo.save(payment);          // Oracle — committed
    cassandraRepo.save(event);          // Cassandra — may fail!
}

// ✅ CORRECT: Transactional Outbox Pattern
@Transactional
public void processPayment(PaymentRequest req) {
    paymentRepo.save(payment);          // Oracle
    outboxRepo.save(new OutboxEvent(event));  // Same Oracle transaction
    // Separate process reads outbox → publishes to Kafka → Cassandra consumer
}

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Lesson 2 Interview Question Bank

Junior Level

Q1: What is the difference between RDBMS and NoSQL?

RDBMS stores data in tables with fixed schema, supports SQL, ACID transactions, and JOINs. NoSQL encompasses non-relational databases (document, key-value, wide-column, graph) optimized for specific scale or flexibility requirements, often sacrificing full ACID or JOIN support.

Q2: Name the four types of NoSQL databases with examples.

Document (MongoDB), Key-Value (Redis), Wide-Column (Cassandra), Graph (Neo4j).

Q3: What does "Not Only SQL" mean?

NoSQL complements rather than replaces SQL databases. Modern systems use both — RDBMS for transactional data, NoSQL for caching, logs, search, etc.

Q4: Is Redis a database?

Yes — an in-memory key-value store. Used primarily as cache, session store, and message broker. Can persist to disk but designed for speed over durability.

Q5: Can MongoDB replace Oracle in a banking system?

Not for core banking (account balances, transactions). MongoDB lacks the ACID maturity, regulatory track record, and complex query capabilities Oracle provides for financial data. Could be used for non-critical data like product catalogs.

Mid-Level

Q6: Explain CAP theorem with examples.

During network partition: CP systems (Oracle) sacrifice availability to maintain consistency; AP systems (Cassandra) sacrifice consistency to maintain availability. CA systems (single-node Redis) work until partition occurs. Most systems tune consistency per operation.

Q7: What is polyglot persistence?

Using multiple database technologies in one system, each optimized for specific access patterns. Example: Oracle (transactions) + Redis (cache) + Cassandra (audit logs) + Elasticsearch (search).

Q8: When would you choose Cassandra over Oracle?

High write throughput (>100K/sec), time-series/append-only data, multi-datacenter replication, when eventual consistency is acceptable. NOT for complex queries, JOINs, or strong ACID requirements.

Q9: Explain the difference between schema-on-write and schema-on-read.

Schema-on-write (RDBMS): schema enforced at insert time — invalid data rejected immediately. Schema-on-read (MongoDB): schema validated at query time — flexible but inconsistent data possible.

Q10: What is the LSM Tree and which databases use it?

Log-Structured Merge Tree: writes go to in-memory MemTable, then flush to immutable SSTables on disk. Optimized for sequential writes. Used by Cassandra, RocksDB (MySQL InnoDB optional), LevelDB.

Senior Level

Q11: Design the data layer for a payment platform handling 50K TPS.

Oracle RAC for ACID ledger (strong consistency). Redis for idempotency keys (< 1ms). Kafka for event streaming. Cassandra for audit logs (append-only, 7-year retention). Read replicas for reporting. Define RPO/RTO. PCI-DSS encryption.

Q12: How do you handle transactions across Oracle and Cassandra?

Cannot use distributed 2PC across heterogeneous databases in practice. Use Saga pattern or Transactional Outbox: write to Oracle + outbox table in same transaction, async processor publishes to Kafka, Cassandra consumer writes audit log. Accept eventual consistency for non-critical path.

Q13: Explain MongoDB's WiredTiger storage engine.

Default storage engine since v3.2. B-Tree indexes, document-level locking, compression (snappy/zlib), checkpoint-based durability. Cache defaults to 50% RAM. MVCC for concurrent reads during writes.

Q14: What is consistent hashing and why does Cassandra use it?

Hash function maps keys to a ring (0 to 2^64-1). Each node owns a token range. Adding/removing nodes only remaps adjacent ranges — minimal data movement. Enables Cassandra's transparent horizontal scaling.

Q15: Compare Oracle RAC vs Cassandra for high availability.

Oracle RAC: shared storage cluster, strong consistency, complex/expensive, active-active reads, single-writer for data files. Cassandra: shared-nothing ring, tunable consistency, linear scale, any node accepts writes, eventual consistency default.

Technical Lead Level

Q16: Your team wants to migrate from Oracle to MongoDB to "modernize." How do you respond?

Ask: which workloads and why? Core banking data stays on Oracle (ACID, compliance). Identify candidates: product catalog, CMS, session data, logs. Propose polyglot approach, not rip-and-replace. Estimate migration cost, risk, team training.

Q17: How do you prevent the "distributed monolith" anti-pattern with multiple databases?

Strict database-per-service ownership. No cross-service SQL queries. Cross-service data via events (Kafka). API composition for reads needing multiple services. Saga for distributed transactions. No shared database.

Staff / Principal Engineer Level

Q18: Evaluate Google Spanner vs Oracle for a global banking platform.

Spanner: global SQL, external consistency via TrueTime, horizontal scale, cloud-native. Oracle: 40-year banking track record, regulatory certifications, team expertise, on-prem option. Consider: data residency laws, cost (Spanner per-node pricing), migration complexity, existing Oracle PL/SQL investment.

Q19: How would you design idempotency for a payment system at 100K TPS?

Redis SETNX with TTL (24h) for fast path. Key: payment:idempotency:{clientRequestId}. Value: PROCESSING → COMPLETED. Oracle stores authoritative payment record. If Redis miss but Oracle has record → return cached result. TTL expiry allows retry of genuinely failed requests.

Solution Architect Level

Q20: Design complete data platform for a neobank (0 to 10M customers, 3 regions).

Region 1 (Primary): Oracle for core banking (or CockroachDB if cloud-native). Redis cluster for sessions/cache. Kafka for events. Region 2/3: Read replicas + Cassandra for regional audit logs. Global: DynamoDB for idempotency (multi-region). Elasticsearch for transaction search. S3 for document storage. Define consistency per store. DR: RPO 0 for ledger, RPO 1hr for analytics.

Q21: CAP theorem — is it still relevant in 2024?

Yes, but nuanced. Modern systems offer tunable consistency (Cassandra, Cosmos DB). Spanner achieves consistency AND availability via TrueTime (GPS clocks). PACELC extends CAP: if Partition, choose A or C; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. Architects must understand the trade-off space, not just the theorem.

Scenario-Based Questions

Scenario 1: "E-commerce site uses MySQL. Product catalog has 500K products with varying attributes (electronics have RAM/CPU, clothing has size/color). Queries are slow. Team proposes MongoDB. Good idea?"

Yes, for the catalog specifically. Flexible schema handles varying attributes without NULL columns or EAV pattern. Embed variants in document. Keep MySQL for orders/payments (ACID). Add Redis cache for hot products. NOT a full MySQL replacement.

Scenario 2: "Cassandra cluster shows high read latency. Diagnostics?"

Check: consistency level (ALL vs ONE), number of SSTables (too many → compaction lag), partition key design (too wide partitions), Bloom filter false positives, GC pauses (heap too large), read repair overhead, network between datacenters.

Part 20 — Revision Sheet

Lesson 2 Quick Revision

Core Concepts

  • RDBMS = tables, SQL, ACID, schema-on-write, vertical scale + read replicas
  • NoSQL = Not Only SQL — four types: Document, Key-Value, Wide-Column, Graph
  • Polyglot Persistence = multiple databases in one system, each for specific pattern
  • CAP = Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance — pick 2 during partition
  • NewSQL = SQL + ACID + horizontal scale (Spanner, CockroachDB)

When to Choose What

text
ACID + JOINs + Complex queries     → RDBMS (Oracle/PostgreSQL)
Sub-ms key lookup + cache          → Redis
Flexible schema + document model   → MongoDB
High write rate + time-series      → Cassandra
Full-text search                   → Elasticsearch
Graph relationships                → Neo4j
Global SQL + strong consistency    → Spanner/CockroachDB

NoSQL Types Quick Map

text
Document:   MongoDB     → JSON documents, flexible schema
Key-Value:  Redis       → O(1) lookup, in-memory, TTL
Wide-Column: Cassandra → LSM tree, partition key, ring topology
Graph:      Neo4j       → Nodes + edges, traversal queries

Spring Boot Multi-DB

  • @EnableJpaRepositories for Oracle/PostgreSQL
  • Spring Data MongoDB with @Document
  • Spring Data Cassandra with @Table
  • Spring Data Redis with @RedisHash
  • Cannot @Transactional across different databases — use Saga/Outbox

Key Trade-offs

RDBMS WinsNoSQL Wins
ACID transactionsHorizontal write scale
Complex JOINsSchema flexibility
Strong consistencySub-ms latency (Redis)
Regulatory complianceAppend-only logs
50 years of toolingGeographic distribution

bash

M2: Given this Cassandra table design, explain why the query fails:

sql
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id UUID,
    customer_id BIGINT,
    order_date TIMESTAMP,
    amount DECIMAL,
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id)
);

-- This query fails or performs terribly. Why?
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1001;
Answer: customer_id is not the partition key. Cassandra can only efficiently query by partition key (order_id). This query triggers a full cluster scan. Fix: redesign with PRIMARY KEY (customer_id, order_date, order_id).

Part 1 — Concept

What Is Database Architecture?

Database architecture is the internal structure of a Database Management System (DBMS): how client applications connect, how queries are processed, how memory and processes are organized, how data is stored on disk, and how background services maintain durability, recovery, and availability.

A DBMS is not a single program. It is a multi-layered system of cooperating processes, memory regions, files, and protocols.

text
DATABASE SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE (Logical View)

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     CLIENT APPLICATIONS                          │
│        Java / Spring Boot / JDBC / Python / BI Tools             │
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │ Network Protocol
                             │ (TCP/IP, JDBC, ODBC, pg wire protocol)
                             ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     DATABASE SERVER (DBMS)                       │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  CONNECTION LAYER                                          │  │
│  │  Authentication, session management, protocol handling     │  │
│  └────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘  │
│  ┌────────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  QUERY PROCESSING LAYER                                    │  │
│  │  Parser → Rewriter → Optimizer → Executor                  │  │
│  └────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘  │
│  ┌────────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  TRANSACTION & CONCURRENCY LAYER                           │  │
│  │  Transaction manager, lock manager, MVCC, isolation       │  │
│  └────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘  │
│  ┌────────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  STORAGE ENGINE LAYER                                      │  │
│  │  Buffer pool, indexes, heap/clustered storage, WAL/redo    │  │
│  └────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘  │
│  ┌────────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  BACKGROUND SERVICES                                       │  │
│  │  Checkpoint, WAL writer, vacuum/autovacuum, archiver, etc. │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │
                             ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     PHYSICAL STORAGE                             │
│   Data files | Index files | WAL/Redo | Undo | Temp | Archive   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Core Architectural Components

ComponentPurpose
InstanceRunning DBMS processes + allocated memory
DatabasePhysical/logical collection of data files
Listener / PortAccepts client connections (Oracle Listener, PostgreSQL port 5432)
Connection / SessionOne authenticated client session
Process / Thread ModelHow work is executed (process-per-connection vs thread pool)
Shared MemoryBuffer pool, cache, lock tables shared by all sessions
Background ProcessesMaintenance, recovery, replication, checkpointing
Catalog / Data DictionaryMetadata about schemas, tables, privileges, statistics
Storage EngineHow rows/indexes/WAL are physically managed

Client-Server vs Embedded

ModelDescriptionExamples
Client-ServerSeparate DB server process; clients connect over networkOracle, PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server
EmbeddedLibrary inside application processSQLite, H2 (embedded mode), Derby
Cloud ManagedVendor runs client-server architecture for youAWS RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL

Enterprise systems almost always use client-server RDBMS architecture.

Part 2 — History

How Database Architecture Evolved

Era 1: Monolithic Programs (1960s)

Database logic lived inside application binaries. No separation between business logic and storage engine.

text
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│ Application + File Access  │
│ No shared access layer       │
└──────────────────────────────┘

Problem: Every application reimplemented indexing, locking, recovery.

Era 2: Hierarchical/Network DBMS (1960s–1970s)

IMS introduced a centralized DBMS, but architecture was still tightly coupled to physical data paths.

Era 3: Relational DBMS with Optimizer (1970s–1980s)

Codd's model + System R (IBM) introduced:

  • Logical/physical separation
  • Cost-based query optimizer
  • SQL as declarative interface

This created the modern layered architecture still used today.

Era 4: Multi-Process Enterprise Servers (1980s–1990s)

Oracle pioneered the instance + database split:

text
INSTANCE (Memory + Processes)     DATABASE (Files on Disk)
─────────────────────────────     ─────────────────────────
SGA                               Datafiles
Background processes              Redo logs
Shared buffer cache               Control files

DB2 and SQL Server followed similar enterprise models.

Era 5: Open Source Process Models (1990s–2000s)

PostgreSQL chose process-per-connection for stability. MySQL initially used thread-per-connection for lower overhead.

Both valid — different trade-offs.

Era 6: Cloud-Native Separation (2010s–Today)

Cloud databases separated compute from storage:

text
Traditional:                     Cloud-Native (Aurora example):
Compute + Local Disk               Compute nodes
                                   │
                                   └── Shared distributed storage layer

This enabled storage replication, faster failover, and independent scaling.

Architectural Lesson

Database architecture evolved to separate concerns: connection handling, query optimization, transaction control, and storage management — so each layer can evolve independently.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does DBMS Architecture Solve?

Problem 1: Many Clients, One Data Store

1000 Spring Boot instances must safely share one banking database without corrupting data.

text
Without centralized DBMS architecture:
  App 1 writes file
  App 2 writes file
  → Corruption, lost updates, no coordination

With DBMS architecture:
  All apps → one transaction manager → one storage engine

Problem 2: Query Complexity Hidden from Applications

Application should not decide:

  • Which index to use
  • Which join algorithm to apply
  • How to lock rows
  • How to recover after crash

The optimizer + storage engine handle this internally.

Problem 3: Durability Without Application Code

If the payment service crashes after commit, money must not disappear. Architecture must guarantee:

  • WAL/redo written before commit acknowledgment
  • Automatic crash recovery on restart

Problem 4: Concurrent Access at Scale

Thousands of sessions reading/writing simultaneously require:

  • Lock manager or MVCC
  • Buffer pool synchronization
  • Deadlock detection
  • Connection isolation

Problem 5: Operational Manageability

DBAs need to:

  • Backup while database is online
  • Monitor performance
  • Apply patches
  • Replicate to DR site

Architecture must support online operations.

Unified Problem Statement

Applications need a centralized, durable, concurrent, optimized data service with standardized access — independent of how data is physically stored or which hardware it runs on.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why DBMS Architecture Is Layered

Each layer exists because a specific class of problems was too complex to push to applications.

LayerWhy It Exists
Connection layerAuthentication, protocol, resource limits
ParserValidate SQL, reject invalid/dangerous queries early
OptimizerChoose best execution plan without developer micromanagement
ExecutorRun plans using buffer pool and storage engine APIs
Transaction managerGuarantee ACID across multiple rows/tables
Lock/MVCC layerSafe concurrent access
Buffer poolAvoid disk I/O — performance
WAL/RedoDurability and crash recovery
Background processesHousekeeping without blocking user sessions

Why Not One Big Process?

text
Monolithic design problems:
  - One bug crashes entire database
  - Hard to scale CPU cores efficiently
  - Difficult to isolate memory corruption
  - Background work competes with user queries

Layered/multi-process design benefits:
  - Fault isolation (PostgreSQL: one bad session kills one backend)
  - Specialized background workers
  - Shared memory for cache efficiency
  - Clear operational boundaries

Part 5 — Internal Working

DBMS Internal Architecture — Deep Dive

The Query Processing Pipeline

Every SQL statement passes through a pipeline:

text
SQL TEXT
   │
   ▼
┌──────────┐
│  PARSER  │  Syntax analysis → parse tree
└────┬─────┘
     ▼
┌──────────┐
│ ANALYZER │  Semantic validation against catalog
└────┬─────┘
     ▼
┌──────────┐
│ REWRITER │  View expansion, rule application
└────┬─────┘
     ▼
┌──────────┐
│ OPTIMIZER│  Generate plans, estimate cost, pick best
└────┬─────┘
     ▼
┌──────────┐
│ EXECUTOR │  Run plan operators (scan, join, sort, insert)
└────┬─────┘
     ▼
┌──────────┐
│ STORAGE  │  Buffer pool, indexes, WAL
│ ENGINE   │
└──────────┘

Process Models Across Major Databases

PostgreSQL — Process-per-Connection

text
                    ┌─────────────────┐
                    │  postmaster     │  (parent process)
                    │  (listener)     │
                    └────────┬────────┘
                             │
        ┌────────────────────┼────────────────────┐
        ▼                    ▼                    ▼
  ┌───────────┐       ┌───────────┐       ┌───────────┐
  │ backend   │       │ backend   │       │ background│
  │ process   │       │ process   │       │ processes │
  │ (session1)│       │ (session2)│       │ WAL writer│
  └───────────┘       └───────────┘       │ checkpointer│
                                          │ autovacuum │
                                          └───────────┘

Shared memory: shared_buffers, lock table, WAL buffers

Why processes? Memory isolation — one runaway query doesn't corrupt another session's memory space as easily.

Oracle — Instance Architecture (Processes + SGA)

text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     ORACLE INSTANCE                          │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ SGA (System Global Area) — Shared Memory               │  │
│  │  Database Buffer Cache | Shared Pool | Redo Log Buffer  │  │
│  │  Large Pool | Java Pool | Streams Pool                 │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│  Background Processes:                                       │
│  DBWn (Database Writer) | LGWR (Log Writer) | PMON | SMON   │
│  CKPT | ARCn | RECO | LREG | MMON | MMNL                     │
│  Server Processes:                                           │
│  Dedicated / Shared / PGA per session work areas             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
          │
          ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     ORACLE DATABASE (Files)                  │
│  Datafiles | Redo Logs | Control Files | Archive Logs        │
│  UNDO Tablespace | TEMP Tablespace                           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

MySQL InnoDB — Thread-per-Connection

text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     mysqld process                             │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ Connection Threads (one per client connection)         │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│  InnoDB Engine:                                              │
│   Buffer Pool | Change Buffer | Log Buffer | Adaptive Hash   │
│  Background Threads:                                         │
│   IO threads | Purge thread | Master thread | Page cleaner   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why threads? Lower memory overhead per connection than full OS process.

Connection Flow: Spring Boot → Database

text
Spring Boot App (HikariCP)
        │
        │ 1. Request connection from pool
        ▼
   HikariCP returns existing JDBC connection (or creates new)
        │
        │ 2. JDBC sends SQL over TCP
        ▼
   DB Listener / Port (1521 Oracle, 5432 PostgreSQL)
        │
        │ 3. Authenticate user/password, SSL, privileges
        ▼
   Assign Session (backend process / server process / thread)
        │
        │ 4. SQL processed through pipeline
        ▼
   Result set returned to JDBC → Hibernate → Service layer
        │
        │ 5. Connection returned to pool (NOT closed)
        ▼
   Ready for next request

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Physical Storage Architecture

Oracle Physical Architecture

text
ORACLE DATABASE FILE STRUCTURE

Database
├── Control Files          (database metadata, checkpoint info)
├── Redo Log Groups        (transaction log — circular)
├── Archive Logs           (optional copy of filled redo logs)
├── UNDO Tablespace        (rollback/MVCC old versions)
├── TEMP Tablespace        (sort/hash spill)
└── Data Tablespaces
     ├── USERS.dbf
     ├── INDEX.dbf
     └── SYSTEM.dbf

PostgreSQL Physical Architecture

text
PostgreSQL Cluster (Data Directory)
├── global/                (shared catalog)
├── base/                  (database OIDs → table files)
│   └── 16384/             (one database)
│       ├── 24576            (accounts table file)
│       └── 24577            (accounts index file)
├── pg_wal/                (WAL segments)
├── pg_xact/               (transaction commit status)
├── pg_multixact/          (row-level locking info)
└── postgresql.conf        (configuration)

MySQL InnoDB Architecture

text
InnoDB Tablespace
├── ibdata1 (system tablespace — data dictionary, undo)
├── table_name.ibd (per-table file if enabled)
├── redo log files (ib_logfile0, ib_logfile1)
└── undo tablespaces (separate undo logs in newer versions)

Tablespace Concept

A tablespace is a logical container mapping to one or more data files.

text
LOGICAL                    PHYSICAL
────────                   ────────
TABLESPACE users    →      /u01/oradata/users01.dbf
                           /u01/oradata/users02.dbf

Benefits:
  - Place indexes on fast SSD tablespace
  - Place archive data on cheap storage
  - Manage backup at tablespace level
  - Control quota and I/O patterns

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Memory Architecture Across DBMS Platforms

Oracle SGA vs PGA

text
ORACLE MEMORY MODEL

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ SGA (Shared by all sessions)                                 │
│  ├── Database Buffer Cache     (data/index blocks)           │
│  ├── Shared Pool               (SQL plans, dictionary cache) │
│  ├── Redo Log Buffer           (redo entries before disk)    │
│  ├── Large Pool                (RMAN, shared server)         │
│  └── Java Pool / Streams Pool                                │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ PGA (Private per server process)                             │
│  ├── Sort area                                               │
│  ├── Hash area                                               │
│  └── Session variables                                       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Memory AreaPurposeTuning Parameter
Buffer CacheCache data blocksDB_CACHE_SIZE / AMM
Shared PoolParsed SQL, metadataSHARED_POOL_SIZE
Redo Log BufferBatch redo writesLOG_BUFFER
PGASort/hash per sessionPGA_AGGREGATE_TARGET

PostgreSQL Memory

ComponentParameterPurpose
Shared Buffersshared_buffersPage cache for data/index
WAL Bufferswal_buffersWAL page cache
Work Memorywork_memSort/hash per operation
Maintenance Work Memmaintenance_work_memVACUUM, CREATE INDEX
Effective Cache Sizeeffective_cache_sizeHint to optimizer about OS cache
text
Per-query memory trap:
  work_mem = 256MB
  100 concurrent queries doing sorts
  Potential memory: 25GB+
  → Always size work_mem conservatively

MySQL InnoDB Memory

ComponentParameterPurpose
Buffer Poolinnodb_buffer_pool_sizeMain page cache
Log Bufferinnodb_log_buffer_sizeRedo log buffer
Change Buffer(inside buffer pool)Buffer secondary index changes
Adaptive Hash IndexautoHot page hash lookup

Memory Architecture Diagram

text
                    DATABASE SERVER RAM
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                              │
│  ████████████████████████████████████  Buffer Pool (60-75%) │
│  ████                                  WAL/Redo buffers      │
│  ██                                    Lock structures       │
│  ██████                                Connection overhead   │
│  ██                                    OS page cache (PG)    │
│                                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Goal: Working set in buffer pool → avoid disk reads

Part 8 — Execution Flow

End-to-End Execution Flow Examples

Example 1: SELECT with Index Scan (PostgreSQL)

sql
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 5001;
text
1. Client sends SQL
2. postmaster assigns backend process
3. Parser → Analyzer → Optimizer
   Plan: Index Scan on accounts_pkey → cost 8.0
4. Executor requests page from buffer pool
   ├── HIT: page in shared_buffers → read row
   └── MISS: read from disk → load into shared_buffers
5. Return balance to client
6. Backend waits for next command (connection stays open)

Example 2: COMMIT Flow (Oracle)

sql
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE account_id = 5001;
COMMIT;
text
UPDATE phase:
  ├── Generate redo entry in redo log buffer
  ├── Modify block in buffer cache (dirty)
  └── Generate undo in UNDO tablespace (for rollback/MVCC)

COMMIT phase:
  ├── LGWR writes redo from log buffer to redo log file
  ├── fsync redo log to disk
  ├── Return "COMMIT complete" to client
  └── DBWn writes dirty blocks to datafiles later (lazy write)

Crash recovery:
  SMON + redo apply replays committed changes not yet in datafiles

Transaction Flow Diagram

text
BEGIN ──▶ EXECUTE SQL ──▶ WAL/REDO WRITTEN ──▶ COMMIT
                              │                    │
                              ▼                    ▼
                         Dirty pages           Ack to client
                         in buffer pool        (durability guaranteed
                              │                 once WAL fsync'd)
                              ▼
                         Checkpoint/DB Writer
                         flush to data files
                         (async, later)

Background Process Interaction

text
USER SESSION                    BACKGROUND PROCESSES
────────────                    ────────────────────
INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE ────────▶ WAL Writer (flush WAL)
       │                   ──▶ Checkpointer (flush dirty pages)
       │                   ──▶ Autovacuum (reclaim dead rows - PG)
       │                   ──▶ Archiver (copy redo to archive - Oracle)
       │                   ──▶ Replication sender (stream WAL)
       ▼
   Response to client

How Architecture Affects Performance

text
Scenario: 200GB database, 64GB RAM

Buffer pool = 8GB (12%):
  Cache hit ratio ≈ 85-90%
  Most queries hit disk → slow

Buffer pool = 48GB (75%):
  Cache hit ratio ≈ 99%+
  Hot data stays in memory → fast

Working set analysis > generic percentage rules

BottleneckSymptomArchitectural Fix

Architectural Complexity by Operation

OperationPrimary Cost DriverComplexity

text
Single Instance Architecture Limits:
  Writes:  bound by one primary storage engine
  Reads:   scale with replicas + cache
  Memory:  bound by single server RAM

Beyond single instance → architectural change required:
  Read replicas
  Connection pooler (PgBouncer, RDS Proxy)
  Sharding
  Separation of OLTP and OLAP

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Inspecting Database Architecture

PostgreSQL — View Processes and Memory

sql
-- Active sessions and their queries
SELECT pid, usename, application_name, client_addr, state, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state != 'idle';

-- Buffer cache hit ratio
SELECT
    sum(heap_blks_hit) / nullif(sum(heap_blks_hit + heap_blks_read), 0)
        AS cache_hit_ratio
FROM pg_statio_user_tables;

-- Database size
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_database_size('banking_platform'));

-- Table and index sizes
SELECT
    relname AS relation,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(relid)) AS total_size
FROM pg_catalog.pg_statio_user_tables
ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(relid) DESC;
bash
# PostgreSQL process list
ps aux | grep postgres
# Shows: postmaster, background writer, checkpointer, walwriter, autovacuum

Oracle — Instance and Storage Views

sql
-- Instance info
SELECT instance_name, host_name, version, status, database_status
FROM v$instance;

-- SGA components
SELECT component, current_size/1024/1024 AS size_mb
FROM v$sga_dynamic_components;

-- Active sessions
SELECT sid, serial#, username, status, program, sql_id
FROM v$session
WHERE username IS NOT NULL;

-- Datafiles and tablespaces
SELECT tablespace_name, file_name, bytes/1024/1024 AS size_mb
FROM dba_data_files;

-- Buffer cache hit ratio (historical)
SELECT name, value
FROM v$sysstat
WHERE name IN ('consistent gets', 'db block gets', 'physical reads');

MySQL — InnoDB Status

sql
-- Show InnoDB engine status (buffer pool, locks, I/O)

-- Active connections
SHOW PROCESSLIST;

-- Buffer pool size
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_buffer_pool_size';

-- Table sizes
SELECT
    table_schema, table_name,
    ROUND(data_length/1024/1024, 2) AS data_mb,
    ROUND(index_length/1024/1024, 2) AS index_mb
FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_schema = 'banking'
ORDER BY data_length DESC;

sql

Production Spring Boot DB Configuration

yaml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://db-primary.internal:5432/banking
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 20
      minimum-idle: 5

Connection Pool Sizing Formula

text
Pool size per service instance ≈
  (Core count × 2) + effective_spindle_count   [PostgreSQL wiki rule]

Practical enterprise approach:
  Start with 10-20 per instance
  Monitor: hikaricp.connections.active, pending threads
  Total connections across all pods < DB max_connections × 0.7

Example:
  50 pods × 20 connections = 1000 connections
  PostgreSQL max_connections = 1500 → danger zone
  Fix: PgBouncer between app and DB

@Transactional and DB Session Relationship

java
@Transactional
public void transfer(Long from, Long to, BigDecimal amount) {
    // ONE connection borrowed from HikariCP for this thread
    // ONE DB session/process assigned
    // ONE transaction: BEGIN ... COMMIT/ROLLBACK
    accountRepo.debit(from, amount);
    accountRepo.credit(to, amount);
}   // Connection returned to pool — session may stay open on DB side

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

Hibernate in the Database Architecture Stack

Where Hibernate Sits

text
Application Layer
      │
 Hibernate/JPA Layer
  ├── EntityManager / Session
  ├── Persistence Context (L1 cache — per transaction/session)
  ├── L2 Cache (optional — shared across sessions)
  ├── JDBC Connection (from pool)
      │
 Database Architecture Layer
  ├── Parser / Optimizer / Executor
  └── Storage Engine

Session ↔ DB Session Mapping

text
IMPORTANT DISTINCTION:

Hibernate Session  ≠  Database Session

One HTTP request (with @Transactional):
  1 Thread
  1 Hibernate Session (Persistence Context)
  1 JDBC Connection
  1 Database backend process/thread
  1 Database transaction

Hibernate SQL Generation and Architecture Impact

java
// One findById — one SELECT
Customer c = customerRepo.findById(1001L).get();

// Hibernate generates:
// SELECT c.* FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = ?
// DB: parse → optimize → index scan → return

// Lazy collection access inside transaction
c.getAccounts().size();  // triggers second SELECT
// DB architecture: new query through full pipeline

open-in-view: false — Architectural Best Practice

text
open-in-view: true (DEFAULT — BAD for production):
  DB connection held open for ENTIRE HTTP request
  → Connection pool exhaustion
  → Long-running DB sessions
  → Lazy loading works "by accident" outside service layer

open-in-view: false (CORRECT):
  DB connection held only for @Transactional service method
  → Shorter session lifetime
  → Better pool utilization
  → Forces explicit fetch joins in service layer

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

Architect View of Database Architecture

Key Architectural Decisions

DecisionOptionsArchitect Consideration
DeploymentSelf-hosted vs RDS/Aurora vs RACOps burden, SLA, cost
Connection modelDirect vs pooler vs DRCPConnection count at scale
Read scalingReplicas vs caching vs bothStaleness tolerance
Storage layoutTablespace separationI/O isolation (index vs data)
HA modelActive-passive vs active-activeRPO/RTO, split-brain risk
Multi-tenancySchema-per-tenant vs DB-per-tenantIsolation vs cost

Instance Sizing Framework

text
Step 1: Estimate working set size (hot data accessed daily)
Step 2: Size buffer pool ≥ working set (target 99% hit ratio)
Step 3: Estimate peak connections (pods × pool size → use pooler if > 500)
Step 4: Estimate write TPS → WAL I/O requirements
Step 5: Estimate storage growth (12-24 month projection)
Step 6: Define HA: RPO/RTO → determines sync vs async replication

Cloud-Native Architecture Shift

text
Traditional Oracle Architecture:
  App → JDBC → Oracle RAC → SAN Storage

Cloud Architecture (Aurora PostgreSQL):
  App → RDS Proxy → Aurora Writer → Distributed Storage (6 copies, 3 AZ)
                  → Aurora Reader(s)

Architect benefit:
  Storage failure ≠ instance failure
  Failover ≈ 30 seconds (Aurora) vs minutes (traditional)
  Read scaling: add reader nodes independently

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Confusing Database with Instance

text
❌ "Delete the Oracle instance to remove data"
✅ Instance = running processes + memory
   Database = physical files
   You can stop instance (down) but data remains on disk

Mistake 2: One Connection Per Request Without Pooling

java
// ❌ Opens new DB session every call — 50-100ms overhead
Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pass);
// ✅ HikariCP — connection reused
@Autowired DataSource ds;

Mistake 3: Pool Size = Number of App Threads

text
❌ 200 Tomcat threads → maximum-pool-size: 200
✅ 200 threads → maximum-pool-size: 20
   Most threads don't need DB simultaneously
   200 DB sessions = memory exhaustion on PostgreSQL

Mistake 4: Ignoring max_connections

text
50 pods × 50 pool size = 2500 connections
PostgreSQL default max_connections = 100
→ "FATAL: too many connections"

Fix: Reduce pool size OR add PgBouncer OR increase max_connections (last resort)

Mistake 5: spring.jpa.open-in-view=true in Production

Holds DB connection for entire HTTP request — architectural anti-pattern. Set to false.

Mistake 6: Running Reports on Primary

text
❌ BI tool connected to primary OLTP database
   Full table scans → evict buffer pool → OLTP queries slow

✅ Dedicated read replica for reporting workloads

Mistake 7: Not Monitoring Background Process Health

text
PostgreSQL autovacuum stopped → table bloat → queries degrade over weeks
Oracle archiver failing → database hangs when redo log full
MySQL purge lag → undo tablespace grows → disk full

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is the difference between a database and an instance?

Database = files on disk containing data. Instance = running processes and memory that mount and access the database.

Q2: What is a buffer pool?

In-memory cache of data/index pages. Avoids disk I/O. Called shared_buffers (PG), buffer cache (Oracle), innodb_buffer_pool (MySQL).

Q3: What happens when you execute a SELECT query?

Parse → validate → optimize → execute → return results. Optimizer chooses index scan vs full scan based on statistics and cost.

Q4: Why use a connection pool?

Creating DB connections is expensive. Pool reuses open connections, reducing latency and preventing connection exhaustion.

Q5: What is WAL/redo log?

Transaction log written before data files. Ensures durability — committed transactions survive crashes via replay.

Mid-Level

Q6: Compare PostgreSQL process model vs MySQL thread model.

PG: one OS process per connection — better isolation, higher memory. MySQL: one thread per connection — lighter, shared address space risk.

Q7: Explain Oracle SGA vs PGA.

SGA: shared memory (buffer cache, shared pool). PGA: private per-session memory (sort areas, hash areas).

Q8: What is a checkpoint and why does it matter?

Checkpoint writes dirty buffer pool pages to datafiles, advances recovery starting point. Reduces crash recovery time but causes I/O spikes if poorly tuned.

Q9: How does HikariCP interact with PostgreSQL architecture?

Maintains N open TCP connections = N PostgreSQL backend processes. Each borrows a backend for query duration. Returns to pool without closing TCP connection.

Q10: What is the catalog/data dictionary?

System metadata: tables, columns, indexes, privileges, statistics. PostgreSQL: pg_catalog. Oracle: data dictionary views (DBA_ / V$).

Senior

Q11: Explain commit flow and why COMMIT is durable before data file update.

WAL/redo flushed and fsync'd on COMMIT. Client gets acknowledgment. Dirty data blocks written later by checkpoint/DB writer. Crash recovery replays WAL for durability.

Q12: How would you diagnose buffer pool thrashing?

Low cache hit ratio, high physical reads, increased I/O wait, queries previously fast now slow. Fix: increase buffer pool, eliminate full scans, partition large tables.

Q13: Design connection architecture for 100 microservice pods connecting to PostgreSQL.

Each pod: HikariCP max 10-15. Total ~1000-1500 → exceeds safe max_connections. Insert PgBouncer in transaction mode (200-300 DB connections). Monitor active/pending. Consider RDS Proxy on AWS.

Q14: Compare Oracle ARCHIVELOG vs NOARCHIVELOG mode architecturally.

NOARCHIVELOG: redo logs recycled, no point-in-time recovery. ARCHIVELOG: filled redo copied to archive — enables PITR and standby replication. Production banking: always ARCHIVELOG.

Technical Lead / Staff / Principal

Q15: Explain Aurora's compute-storage separation and why failover is faster.

Storage layer replicates data 6-way across AZs independently of compute. Writer failure → promote reader → storage already current → failover ~30 sec vs traditional replay/recovery.

Q16: How does autovacuum architecture prevent PostgreSQL transaction ID wraparound?

Autovacuum reclaims dead tuple space, freezes old transaction IDs. If autovacuum falls behind on large tables, XID wraparound risk → forced shutdown. Monitor pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup.

Q17: Design HA architecture for Oracle banking with RPO=0, RTO<60 seconds.

Oracle RAC (active-active) or Active Data Guard synchronous standby. ARCHIVELOG mode. Automatic failover (FSFO). Application TAF/FCF. Regular DR drill. Monitor redo apply lag (= 0 for sync).

Solution Architect

Q18: Single-region PostgreSQL vs Aurora vs Oracle RAC for a payment platform — evaluate.

PostgreSQL: cost-effective, strong features, manual HA. Aurora: managed, fast failover, storage auto-scale, PG compatible. Oracle RAC: highest enterprise maturity, highest cost, best for strict compliance. Decision: regulatory requirements + team skills + cloud strategy + TCO.

Scenario

Scenario: "After deployment, PostgreSQL CPU at 100%, pg_stat_activity shows 800 idle connections and 50 active."

800 idle = connection leak or pool misconfiguration (too many pods × large pools). 50 active queries likely slow. Fix: reduce pool sizes, add PgBouncer, investigate slow queries, enable leak detection. Root cause: missing pooler + open-in-view holding connections.
