Fundamentals
1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why This Exists5Internal Working6Storage Internals7Memory Usage8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Complexity Analysis11Code / SQL Examples12Production Usage13Spring Boot Integration14Hibernate/JPA Integration15Architect Perspective16Decision Matrix17Comparison Tables18Common Mistakes19Interview Questions20Revision Sheet21Summary Table*Practice

Part 1 — Concept

What Is a Key?

A key is one or more columns (or attributes) used to uniquely identify rows, establish relationships between tables, and enforce data integrity.

Keys are not optional design decoration. They define:

  • How rows are stored (clustered index — Lesson 4)
  • How tables are joined
  • How the ORM maps entities
  • How replication and sharding work at scale
text
KEY HIERARCHY (Relational Model)

SUPER KEY
  └── Any column set that uniquely identifies a row
       Example: {account_id}, {account_id, customer_id}, {account_number}

CANDIDATE KEY
  └── Minimal super key (no redundant columns)
       Example: {account_id}, {account_number}

PRIMARY KEY
  └── The chosen candidate key (one per table)
       Example: account_id

UNIQUE KEY / ALTERNATE KEY
  └── Other candidate keys enforced for uniqueness
       Example: UNIQUE(account_number)

FOREIGN KEY
  └── Column(s) referencing PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE key of another table
       Example: customer_id → customers.customer_id

Visual: Keys in a Banking Schema

text
CUSTOMERS                          ACCOUNTS
┌─────────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────────────────┐
│ PK  customer_id (BIGINT)│◄──────│ FK  customer_id (BIGINT)     │
│ UQ  email               │       │ PK  account_id (BIGINT)      │
│ UQ  ssn (encrypted)     │       │ UQ  account_number           │
│     first_name          │       │     account_type             │
│     last_name           │       │     balance                  │
└─────────────────────────┘       └──────────────────────────────┘
                                              │
                                              │ FK account_id
                                              ▼
                                  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
                                  │ PK  transaction_id (BIGINT)  │
                                  │ FK  account_id (BIGINT)      │
                                  │     amount                   │
                                  │     txn_type                 │
                                  │     created_at               │
                                  └──────────────────────────────┘

Types of Keys — Quick Reference

Key TypePurposeCount per TableNULL Allowed?
Primary Key (PK)Main row identifierExactly 1No (NOT NULL)
Foreign Key (FK)Reference to another table0 to manyDepends on design
Unique KeyAlternate identifier0 to manyYes (one NULL typically)*
Composite KeyPK/UK/FK spanning multiple columns—PK: no NULL in any part
Natural KeyBusiness-meaningful identifier——
Surrogate KeySystem-generated, no business meaning——

*PostgreSQL: multiple NULLs allowed in UNIQUE columns (NULL ≠ NULL). Oracle/MySQL: one NULL in UNIQUE.

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Key Design

text
1970    Codd defines relational model
        └── Primary key as fundamental requirement for a relation

1970s   Natural keys dominate
        └── SSN, ISBN, employee number, account number as PK

1980s   Surrogate keys emerge in practice
        └── Oracle sequences, auto-increment (Sybase → SQL Server → MySQL)
        └── Reason: natural keys change, composite keys complicate FKs

1990s   Composite keys common in legacy systems
        └── (branch_code, account_number) as PK
        └── ORM era makes composite PKs painful

2000s   Single-column surrogate BIGINT PK becomes standard
        └── Hibernate/JPA strongly prefer single @Id
        └── Natural keys demoted to UNIQUE constraints

2010s   UUID keys for distributed systems
        └── Microservices, multi-region, client-generated IDs
        └── UUID v4 (random) → UUID v7 / Snowflake (ordered)

2020s   Hybrid patterns
        └── BIGINT surrogate PK internally + UUID for external API
        └── Natural key as UNIQUE constraint for business integrity

Why Surrogate Keys Won

Natural Key ProblemExample
Can changeCustomer changes email used as PK
Composite(country_code, bank_code, branch, account) — 4-column PK everywhere
PrivacySSN as PK — regulatory nightmare
Distributed generationNo central sequence in microservices
PerformanceWide composite PK → wide FK columns → larger indexes
ORM frictionHibernate composite @EmbeddedId is verbose and error-prone

Historical Lesson

Codd required every relation to have a primary key. Modern practice: surrogate PK for internal identity, natural key as UNIQUE for business rules.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Do Keys Solve?

Problem 1: Row Identity — Which Row Is Which?

text
Without a key:
  "Update the account for John Smith" → Which John Smith? 47 matches.

With PK:
  "Update account_id = 5001" → Exactly one row.

Problem 2: Preventing Duplicates

text
Without UNIQUE constraint:
  INSERT customer email='ankur@email.com'  → OK
  INSERT customer email='ankur@email.com'  → OK again! Two accounts.

With UNIQUE(email):
  Second INSERT → ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint

Problem 3: Referential Integrity

text
Without FK:
  DELETE customer_id=1001 from CUSTOMERS
  ACCOUNTS still has rows with customer_id=1001 → orphan records

With FK:
  DELETE customer → RESTRICT (blocked if accounts exist)
                 → CASCADE (delete accounts too)
                 → SET NULL (orphan allowed if nullable)

Problem 4: Efficient Joins and Lookups

text
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id

Without index on FK (customer_id):
  Nested loop → full scan of accounts for each customer → O(n×m)

With index on FK:
  Index lookup per customer → O(n log m)

Problem 5: ORM and API Identity

java
customerRepository.findById(1001L);  // Requires stable, immutable PK

If PK changes (natural key update), every FK reference, cache key, and API URL breaks.

Unified Problem Statement

Keys provide unambiguous row identity, enforce uniqueness and relationships, enable efficient joins, and give applications a stable reference that survives business data changes.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Each Key Type Exists

Primary Key — Why Mandatory (Conceptually)

Codd's relational model treats a relation as a set of tuples — no duplicates. PK guarantees:

text
1. Uniqueness:   no two rows identical
2. Non-null:     every row identifiable
3. Immutability: (best practice) never UPDATE PK value
4. Stability:    ORM, FK, cache keys depend on it

Foreign Key — Why Not Application-Enforced Only?

text
Application-only integrity:
  Service A deletes customer
  Service B (different team, different deploy) still inserts orphan account
  Batch job bypasses application layer → orphans created
  Race condition: two services concurrently → inconsistent state

Database FK:
  Enforced at storage engine boundary
  Cannot be bypassed by any client (except superuser)
  Atomic with transaction — no window for orphans

Unique Key — Why Not Just Primary Key?

text
One PK per table, but business may require multiple uniqueness rules:

  PK:   customer_id (surrogate — internal)
  UQ:   email (business rule — one account per email)
  UQ:   ssn (regulatory — one person per SSN)

Cannot make all three PKs — only one PK allowed.
Unique constraints enforce alternate candidate keys.

Composite Key — When Still Valid

text
Valid composite PK use cases:
  Junction/associative tables: (order_id, product_id) for order_items
  Time-series partitioning key: (account_id, transaction_date, seq)
  Cassandra partition + clustering keys (Lesson 57)
  Legacy systems (migration cost too high)

Avoid composite PK on core entity tables in new OLTP design.

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Keys Work Internally

Primary Key → Index (Automatic)

When you declare a PRIMARY KEY, the database automatically creates a unique index:

text
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    ...
);

Internally created:
  UNIQUE INDEX accounts_pkey ON accounts (account_id)
  NOT NULL constraint on account_id

Storage (InnoDB): PK index IS the table (clustered — Lesson 4)
Storage (PostgreSQL): PK creates B+ tree index; heap stores rows separately

Foreign Key → Index (NOT Automatic in All DBs)

text
CRITICAL ARCHITECT FACT:

PostgreSQL: FK does NOT auto-create index on referencing column
Oracle:     FK does NOT auto-create index on referencing column
MySQL InnoDB: FK auto-indexes referencing columns ✅

CREATE TABLE accounts (
    customer_id BIGINT REFERENCES customers(customer_id)
);

Without index on accounts.customer_id:
  DELETE FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 1001
  → PostgreSQL must FULL SCAN accounts to check FK constraint
  → LOCK on accounts table during check
  → Slow + blocks concurrent access

ALWAYS: CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_customer_id ON accounts(customer_id);

FK Constraint Check Flow

text
DELETE FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 1001;

1. Lock customer row (or gap lock depending on isolation)
2. FK CHECK on accounts:
   SELECT 1 FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = 1001 LIMIT 1
   (Uses index if exists → fast; else seq scan → slow)
3. If rows found:
     RESTRICT → ERROR, rollback
     CASCADE  → DELETE matching accounts first
     SET NULL → UPDATE accounts SET customer_id = NULL
4. If no rows (or CASCADE complete): DELETE customer
5. COMMIT

Unique Constraint Internal Working

text
UNIQUE INDEX on email:

INSERT INTO customers (email, ...) VALUES ('ankur@email.com', ...);

1. B+ tree lookup: email = 'ankur@email.com'
2. Key found → ERROR duplicate
3. Key not found → insert into index + heap

NULL handling (PostgreSQL):
  UNIQUE allows multiple NULLs (NULL is distinct from NULL)
  Partial unique index for "one non-null value":
    CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_email ON customers(email) WHERE email IS NOT NULL;

Composite Key Internal Structure

sql
PRIMARY KEY (branch_code, account_number)

B+ Tree index key = concatenated (branch_code, account_number)
  'NYC' + '0012345678' → one composite key in index

Index prefix rule:
  Efficient: WHERE branch_code = 'NYC'
  Efficient: WHERE branch_code = 'NYC' AND account_number = '0012345678'
  NOT efficient: WHERE account_number = '0012345678' alone
                 (account_number is second column — no left-prefix)

Part 6 — Storage Internals

How Keys Affect Physical Storage

Surrogate BIGINT PK — Storage Profile

text
accounts table (1M rows):
  PK account_id BIGINT:     8 bytes × 1M = 8 MB in PK index
  FK customer_id BIGINT:    8 bytes × 1M = 8 MB in FK index
  Total key overhead:       ~16 MB + B+ tree overhead
  Rows per page:            ~120 (from Lesson 5 row size calc)

Composite 4-Column PK — Storage Profile

text
PK (country_code CHAR(2), bank_code CHAR(4), branch_code CHAR(6), account_num VARCHAR(20))

Composite key width: 2 + 4 + 6 + 20 + overhead ≈ 40 bytes per key
  vs BIGINT: 8 bytes

Every FK referencing this PK: 40 bytes per row in child tables
Every secondary index (InnoDB): includes PK as row pointer → 40 bytes extra

1M accounts:
  PK index: ~40 MB vs 8 MB (5× larger)
  Every child table FK index: 5× larger
  B+ tree: fewer keys per page → taller tree → more I/O

UUID PK Storage

text
UUID as VARCHAR(36):  37 bytes/row in index → worst
UUID as native (16B): 16 bytes/row → 2× BIGINT
UUID v4 random:       page split problems (Lesson 4)
UUID v7:              mostly sequential → acceptable

Key Column Order in Composite Index

text
INDEX (a, b, c):

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ B+ Tree sorted by: (a, b, c) lexicographic order             │
│                                                              │
│ ('NYC', '001', '001')                                        │
│ ('NYC', '001', '002')                                        │
│ ('NYC', '002', '001')                                        │
│ ('LA',  '001', '001')                                        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────�

Left-prefix usable:
  WHERE a = ?                    ✅ uses index
  WHERE a = ? AND b = ?          ✅ uses index
  WHERE a = ? AND b = ? AND c = ? ✅ uses index
  WHERE b = ?                    ❌ full index scan or no index use
  WHERE b = ? AND c = ?          ❌ same

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Key Width and Memory Impact

Buffer Pool — Cached Index Pages

text
Narrow PK (BIGINT):
  500 keys per 8KB page
  1M row index ≈ 2,000 pages ≈ 16 MB
  Entire index fits in buffer pool → all PK lookups from RAM

Wide composite PK (40 bytes):
  150 keys per 8KB page
  1M row index ≈ 6,667 pages ≈ 52 MB
  May not fit in buffer pool → disk I/O on lookups

Join Memory (Hash Join)

sql
SELECT c.name, a.balance
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON c.customer_id = a.customer_id;
text
Hash join builds hash table on join key:
  BIGINT customer_id: 8 bytes per hash entry
  Composite 4-col key: 40 bytes per hash entry

  1M customers in hash table:
    BIGINT: ~8 MB
    Composite: ~40 MB

  Larger keys → more work_mem consumed → more disk spills

Hibernate Persistence Context

java
// Entity identity in persistence context: primary key
Map<Object, Entity> identityMap;

// Composite PK: equals/hashCode must be correct across all key columns
@Embeddable
public class OrderItemId implements Serializable {
    private Long orderId;
    private Long productId;
    // Must implement equals() and hashCode() correctly
}
// More complex → more bugs → more memory for key objects

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Key Operations — Execution Flows

Flow 1: INSERT with PK + FK

sql
INSERT INTO accounts (account_id, customer_id, account_number, balance)
VALUES (5001, 1001, 'ACC-001', 0.00);
text
1. PK uniqueness check:
   B+ tree lookup account_id=5001 → not found ✅

2. FK referential check:
   B+ tree lookup customers.customer_id=1001 → found ✅
   (Requires index on customers.customer_id — PK already indexed)

3. UNIQUE check on account_number:
   B+ tree lookup 'ACC-001' → not found ✅

4. Insert row into heap/clustered index
5. Insert entries into all indexes (PK, FK index, unique index)
6. Write WAL
7. COMMIT

Flow 2: DELETE Parent with FK RESTRICT

sql
-- FK: accounts.customer_id → customers.customer_id ON DELETE RESTRICT
DELETE FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 1001;
text
1. Lock customer row 1001
2. FK check (accounts table):
   Index scan on accounts(customer_id=1001)
   ├── Index exists: O(log n) — finds 3 accounts → RESTRICT error
   └── No index: O(n) full table scan — same result, much slower, more locking
3. ROLLBACK or ERROR returned to client

Flow 3: CASCADE DELETE Chain

sql
-- transactions.account_id → accounts ON DELETE CASCADE
-- accounts.customer_id → customers ON DELETE CASCADE
DELETE FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 1001;
text
1. Find all accounts WHERE customer_id = 1001 (index scan)
2. For each account:
     Find all transactions WHERE account_id = ? (index scan)
     DELETE transactions
3. DELETE accounts
4. DELETE customer
5. COMMIT

Deep cascade chains are dangerous in production:
  One DELETE → thousands of child deletes → long transaction → lock contention
  Architect: prefer soft delete or async cascade via events

Flow 4: JOIN on Key

sql
SELECT c.first_name, a.balance
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON c.customer_id = a.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id = 1001;
text
Nested Loop Join (typical for selective filter):
  1. Index scan customers PK → customer_id=1001 → 1 row
  2. Index scan accounts(customer_id) → 3 rows
  3. Nested loop join → 3 result rows

Hash Join (typical for large joins):
  1. Build hash table on smaller table's join key
  2. Probe larger table
  Both join keys indexed → efficient build and probe

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Key Design Performance Impact

PK Type Performance Ranking (OLTP)

PK TypeInsertLookupFK overheadShardingORM
BIGINT SEQUENCE⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
UUID v7⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
UUID v4⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
Natural VARCHAR⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
Composite 3+ col⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Missing FK Index — Production Impact

text
Table: transactions — 500M rows
FK: account_id → accounts (no index on transactions.account_id)

DELETE one account:
  PostgreSQL scans 500M transactions → minutes of lock time
  All concurrent INSERTs to transactions blocked

Fix:
  CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_txn_account ON transactions(account_id);
  DELETE now: index seek → milliseconds

Unique Constraint vs Application Check — Race Condition

text
Application-only uniqueness check (TOCTOU bug):

  Thread A: SELECT email='x@.com' → not found
  Thread B: SELECT email='x@.com' → not found
  Thread A: INSERT email='x@.com' → OK
  Thread B: INSERT email='x@.com' → OK  ← DUPLICATE!

Database UNIQUE constraint:
  Thread B INSERT → immediate duplicate key error → safe
  Use ON CONFLICT (PG) or MERGE for idempotent upsert

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

Key Operation Complexity

OperationWith PK IndexWithout Index
PK lookupO(log n)O(n) table scan
INSERTO(log n) per indexO(log n) per index
FK check on DELETE parentO(log m) with FK indexO(m) child table scan
JOIN on indexed keysO(n log m) nested loopO(n × m)
UNIQUE checkO(log n)O(log n) via unique index
CASCADE DELETE depth d, k children eachO(d × k × log n)O(d × k × n) without indexes

Composite Key Complexity

text
Composite PK with k columns:
  Every FK in child tables: k columns propagated
  Every secondary index (InnoDB): includes full PK (k columns)
  Index size: O(k × row_count)
  Join complexity: same O(log n) but larger constant factor per comparison

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Key Definitions — Production SQL

Surrogate PK + Natural Unique Keys (Recommended Pattern)

sql
-- PostgreSQL
CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id     BIGSERIAL       PRIMARY KEY,          -- surrogate PK
    external_id     UUID            NOT NULL DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),  -- API identity
    email           VARCHAR(255)    NOT NULL,
    ssn_hash        VARCHAR(64)     NOT NULL,             -- hashed, not raw SSN
    first_name      VARCHAR(100)    NOT NULL,
    last_name       VARCHAR(100)    NOT NULL,
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ     NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),

    CONSTRAINT uq_customers_email    UNIQUE (email),
    CONSTRAINT uq_customers_ssn      UNIQUE (ssn_hash),
    CONSTRAINT uq_customers_external UNIQUE (external_id)
);

CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id      BIGSERIAL       PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id     BIGINT          NOT NULL,
    account_number  VARCHAR(20)     NOT NULL,
    balance         DECIMAL(18,2)   NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.00,
    status          VARCHAR(20)     NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE',

    CONSTRAINT fk_accounts_customer
        FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(customer_id)
        ON DELETE RESTRICT          -- cannot delete customer with accounts
        ON UPDATE NO ACTION,        -- PK never updated

    CONSTRAINT uq_accounts_number UNIQUE (account_number)
);

-- ALWAYS index FK columns (PostgreSQL/Oracle)
CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_customer_id ON accounts(customer_id);

Composite PK — Junction Table (Valid Use Case)

sql
CREATE TABLE order_items (
    order_id        BIGINT          NOT NULL,
    product_id      BIGINT          NOT NULL,
    quantity        INTEGER         NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    unit_price      DECIMAL(10,2)   NOT NULL,

    CONSTRAINT pk_order_items
        PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id),

    CONSTRAINT fk_order_items_order
        FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders(order_id)
        ON DELETE CASCADE,

    CONSTRAINT fk_order_items_product
        FOREIGN KEY (product_id) REFERENCES products(product_id)
        ON DELETE RESTRICT
);

CREATE INDEX idx_order_items_product ON order_items(product_id);
-- Index on order_id not needed — it's leading column of PK

Oracle Sequence-Based PK

sql
CREATE SEQUENCE customer_seq START WITH 1000000 INCREMENT BY 1 NOCACHE;

CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id   NUMBER(19)    DEFAULT customer_seq.NEXTVAL PRIMARY KEY,
    email         VARCHAR2(255) NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT uq_customers_email UNIQUE (email)
);

-- Hibernate allocationSize should match sequence cache setting
-- NOCACHE: allocationSize=1
-- CACHE 50: allocationSize=50

Partial Unique Index (Soft Delete Pattern)

sql
-- Allow only one ACTIVE account per email, but many deleted records
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_customers_email_active
    ON customers(email)
    WHERE status != 'DELETED';

-- Multiple rows with same email if status='DELETED' ✅
-- Only one row with email if status='ACTIVE' ✅

FK Actions Reference

sql
CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id      BIGSERIAL   PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id      BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    amount          DECIMAL(18,2) NOT NULL,

    CONSTRAINT fk_payments_account
        FOREIGN KEY (account_id) REFERENCES accounts(account_id)
        ON DELETE RESTRICT     -- block account delete if payments exist
        ON UPDATE NO ACTION      -- never update PK
);

CREATE TABLE account_audit (
    audit_id        BIGSERIAL   PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id      BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    change_type     VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    changed_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),

    CONSTRAINT fk_audit_account
        FOREIGN KEY (account_id) REFERENCES accounts(account_id)
        ON DELETE SET NULL       -- keep audit even if account deleted
        ON UPDATE NO ACTION
);

Part 12 — Production Usage

Key Design in Production Systems

Banking — Key Standards

text
INTERNAL IDENTITY:
  PK: BIGINT sequence (customer_id, account_id, transaction_id)
  Never expose internal BIGINT in public APIs

EXTERNAL IDENTITY:
  UUID (external_id) for API/integrations
  account_number: business unique key (UNIQUE constraint)
  IBAN: validated natural key (UNIQUE, checksum algorithm)

RELATIONSHIPS:
  All FKs indexed
  ON DELETE RESTRICT for core entities (customer, account)
  ON DELETE CASCADE never on financial core tables
  Audit tables: ON DELETE SET NULL or no FK (immutable log)

IMMUTABILITY:
  PK never updated
  Natural keys (account_number) changed via status='CLOSED' + new account, not UPDATE PK

Microservices — Key Boundaries

text
ANTI-PATTERN: Shared PK across services

  Order Service DB:  order_id (PK)
  Payment Service DB: order_id (FK?) → cannot enforce cross-DB FK

CORRECT:
  Each service: own surrogate PK
  Cross-service reference: store external ID (UUID) as plain column, NOT as FK
  Integrity: eventual consistency via Saga/events

  payments table (Payment Service):
    payment_id   BIGINT PK
    order_id     UUID NOT NULL   -- reference to Order Service, NO FK constraint
    CONSTRAINT uq_payments_order UNIQUE (order_id)  -- idempotency

Sharding Implications (Preview — Lesson 43)

text
Shard key must be chosen carefully:

  BAD shard key:  status ('ACTIVE'/'CLOSED') → 2 hot shards
  BAD shard key:  country_code → uneven distribution

  GOOD shard key: customer_id (hash) → even distribution
  GOOD shard key: account_id with consistent hashing

  PK choice affects sharding:
    BIGINT sequence: central generation → shard-local sequences or Snowflake
    UUID v7: client-generated → no coordination needed

Part 13 — Spring Boot Integration

Keys in Spring Data JPA

Surrogate PK Entity (Standard)

java
@Entity
@Table(name = "accounts",
       uniqueConstraints = @UniqueConstraint(name = "uq_accounts_number",
                                               columnNames = "account_number"))
public class Account {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "account_seq")
    @SequenceGenerator(name = "account_seq", sequenceName = "account_seq",
                       allocationSize = 50)
    @Column(name = "account_id")
    private Long accountId;

    @Column(name = "account_number", nullable = false, length = 20, unique = true)
    private String accountNumber;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    @JoinColumn(name = "customer_id", nullable = false,
                foreignKey = @ForeignKey(name = "fk_accounts_customer"))
    private Customer customer;
}

External UUID + Internal BIGINT (API Pattern)

java
@Entity
@Table(name = "customers")
public class Customer {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "customer_seq")
    private Long customerId;          // Internal — never in public API

    @Column(name = "external_id", nullable = false, updatable = false,
            columnDefinition = "UUID")
    private UUID externalId = UUID.randomUUID();  // Public API identity

    @Column(name = "email", nullable = false, unique = true)
    private String email;
}

// REST controller exposes externalId, never customerId
@GetMapping("/customers/{externalId}")
public CustomerDto getCustomer(@PathVariable UUID externalId) {
    return customerService.findByExternalId(externalId);
}

Composite PK — Junction Entity

java
@Entity
@Table(name = "order_items")
public class OrderItem {

    @EmbeddedId
    private OrderItemId id;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    @MapsId("orderId")
    @JoinColumn(name = "order_id")
    private Order order;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    @MapsId("productId")
    @JoinColumn(name = "product_id")
    private Product product;

    @Column(name = "quantity", nullable = false)
    private Integer quantity;
}

@Embeddable
@Data
@NoArgsConstructor
@AllArgsConstructor
public class OrderItemId implements Serializable {
    private Long orderId;
    private Long productId;

    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;
        if (!(o instanceof OrderItemId that)) return false;
        return Objects.equals(orderId, that.orderId)
            && Objects.equals(productId, that.productId);
    }

    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(orderId, productId);
    }
}

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

Hibernate Key Management

Entity Identity in Persistence Context

text
Hibernate uses PK as entity identity within a Session:

  session.get(Account.class, 5001L)  → cache key = (Account.class, 5001L)

  Two entities with same PK class in same session → same instance (guaranteed)

  Composite PK: cache key = (OrderItem.class, OrderItemId(1, 99))
  → equals/hashCode on @Embeddable MUST be correct

@GeneratedValue Strategies and Key Generation

StrategyKey TypeDB ImpactRecommendation
SEQUENCEBIGINTOracle/PG sequence✅ Best for Oracle/PG
IDENTITYBIGINTAuto-increment per row✅ MySQL; bad for batch inserts
AUTOVariesHibernate decides⚠️ Unpredictable across DBs
UUIDUUIDRandom UUID⚠️ Only with UUID v7 generator
TABLEAnyLocking table❌ Never in production

Natural Key Lookup with @NaturalId

java
@Entity
public class Customer {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "customer_seq")
    private Long customerId;

    @NaturalId
    @Column(name = "email", nullable = false, updatable = false)
    private String email;

    // Hibernate caches @NaturalId lookups in separate cache region
}

// Repository
public interface CustomerRepository extends JpaRepository<Customer, Long> {
    Optional<Customer> findByEmail(String email);  // uses uq index
}

// Session-level natural id cache (L1):
session.byNaturalId(Customer.class).using("email", "ankur@email.com").load();

FK and Cascade in Hibernate

java
@Entity
public class Customer {

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "customer", cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST)
    // NEVER CascadeType.REMOVE on financial entities in production
    private List<Account> accounts = new ArrayList<>();
}

// Hibernate cascade ≠ DB ON DELETE CASCADE
// Hibernate cascade: application-level object graph operations
// DB FK cascade: SQL DELETE statement level
// Use both deliberately — understand which layer handles what

Optimistic Locking with Version Key

java
@Entity
public class Account {

    @Id
    private Long accountId;

    @Version
    @Column(name = "version")
    private Long version;  // Not a "key" but critical for concurrent update safety

    @Column(name = "balance", precision = 18, scale = 2)
    private BigDecimal balance;
}

// UPDATE accounts SET balance=?, version=version+1
// WHERE account_id=? AND version=?
// Zero rows updated → OptimisticLockException → concurrent modification detected

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

Key Design Decision Framework

The Key Design Decision Tree

text
START: Design keys for a new table

Is this a junction/associative table (many-to-many)?
  YES → Composite PK (entity1_id, entity2_id) ✅
  NO  ↓

Is this a core business entity?
  YES → Surrogate BIGINT/BIGSERIAL PK ✅
        + UNIQUE on natural business identifiers
        + UUID for external API if microservice
  NO  ↓

Is this an audit/log/event table?
  YES → BIGSERIAL PK or (partition_key, sequence) composite
        No FK CASCADE from core tables
  NO  ↓

Is this a reference/lookup table (< 1000 rows)?
  YES → Natural key as PK acceptable (currency_code CHAR(3)) ✅
  NO  → Surrogate PK

Natural vs Surrogate — Decision Matrix

FactorNatural Key as PKSurrogate PK + Natural UNIQUE
Key stability❌ Business keys change✅ Surrogate never changes
FK simplicity❌ Wide composite FKs✅ Single BIGINT FK
Index size❌ Large✅ Compact
Business meaning in PK✅ Self-documenting❌ Requires JOIN
ORM support⚠️ Composite @EmbeddedId✅ Simple @Id Long
Distributed generation❌ Hard✅ UUID/Snowflake
Lookup tables✅ currency_code CHAR(3)⚠️ Overkill
RecommendationLookup tables onlyAll core OLTP entities

Key Design Standards Document (Template)

text
ORGANIZATION KEY STANDARDS:

1. All core entity tables: BIGSERIAL/BIGINT surrogate PK
2. All PK columns: NOT NULL, never updated after insert
3. All FK columns: indexed, BIGINT, NOT NULL (unless SET NULL design)
4. ON DELETE RESTRICT: default for all core FK relationships
5. ON DELETE CASCADE: only on pure junction/detail tables, never on money
6. Natural business identifiers: UNIQUE constraint, never PK
7. External API identity: UUID external_id column, UNIQUE, not PK
8. Composite PK: only on junction tables and sharded time-series
9. Sequence allocationSize: match DB sequence CACHE setting
10. Never expose internal BIGINT PK in public REST APIs

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: No Index on Foreign Key Columns

sql
-- ❌ FK without index (PostgreSQL/Oracle)
ALTER TABLE accounts ADD CONSTRAINT fk_customer
    FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(customer_id);
-- Missing: CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_customer_id ON accounts(customer_id);

-- ✅ Always add immediately after FK creation

Mistake 2: Natural Key as PK on Core Entity

sql
-- ❌ Email as PK — changes when user updates email
CREATE TABLE customers (email VARCHAR(255) PRIMARY KEY, ...);

-- ✅ Surrogate PK + unique email
CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    ...
);

Mistake 3: ON DELETE CASCADE on Financial Tables

sql
-- ❌ Delete customer → silently deletes all accounts and payments
FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(customer_id)
    ON DELETE CASCADE

-- ✅ RESTRICT — force explicit business process for deletion
ON DELETE RESTRICT

Mistake 4: Exposing Internal PK in API

java
// ❌ Public API uses internal database ID
@GetMapping("/accounts/{accountId}")
public AccountDto get(@PathVariable Long accountId) { ... }
// Enumeration attack: iterate accountId 1, 2, 3...
// Coupling: internal ID exposed forever

// ✅ Use external UUID
@GetMapping("/accounts/{externalId}")
public AccountDto get(@PathVariable UUID externalId) { ... }

Mistake 5: Updating Primary Key Values

sql
-- ❌ Never update PK — breaks FK references, ORM identity, cache keys
UPDATE customers SET customer_id = 9999 WHERE customer_id = 1001;

-- ✅ PK is immutable. Business key changes update non-PK columns only.

Mistake 6: @GeneratedValue(strategy = AUTO) in Production

java
// ❌ Hibernate picks different strategy per DB — untestable, unpredictable
@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.AUTO)

// ✅ Explicit strategy matched to your database
@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "account_seq")

Mistake 7: Composite PK Without equals/hashCode

java
// ❌ Missing equals/hashCode on @Embeddable composite key
// → Hibernate identity map breaks → duplicate entities in session → data corruption
@Embeddable
public class OrderItemId {
    private Long orderId;
    private Long productId;
    // MUST override equals() and hashCode()
}

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is a primary key?

Column(s) that uniquely identify each row. NOT NULL, unique, one per table. Automatically creates a unique index.

Q2: What is a foreign key?

Column referencing PK or UNIQUE key of another table. Enforces referential integrity — prevents orphan records.

Q3: Difference between PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE?

PK: one per table, NOT NULL, identifies main row identity. UNIQUE: multiple allowed, permits NULL (usually one), enforces alternate uniqueness.

Q4: What is a surrogate key?

System-generated identifier (BIGINT sequence, UUID) with no business meaning. Used as PK for stability and performance.

Q5: Why index foreign key columns?

Without index, DELETE/UPDATE on parent table requires full scan of child table for FK check — extremely slow and locking on large tables.

Mid-Level

Q6: Surrogate vs natural key — when to use each?

Surrogate (BIGINT) for all core OLTP entities — stable, narrow, ORM-friendly. Natural key as UNIQUE constraint for business rules. Natural key as PK only for small lookup tables (currency_code, country_code).

Q7: Explain ON DELETE RESTRICT vs CASCADE.

RESTRICT: blocks parent delete if children exist — safe for financial data. CASCADE: automatically deletes children — acceptable for junction tables, dangerous for core entities.

Q8: Why is UUID v4 a bad PK for InnoDB?

Random insertion order → B+ tree page splits → insert latency spikes → fragmented pages. Use BIGINT sequence or UUID v7 (time-ordered).

Q9: What is a composite key? Give a valid use case.

PK spanning multiple columns. Valid: order_items(order_id, product_id) junction table. Invalid: core customer table with (first_name, last_name, dob) — use surrogate instead.

Q10: How does Hibernate use the primary key?

PK is entity identity in persistence context (L1 cache). session.get(Entity.class, pk) uses PK as cache key. Composite PK requires @EmbeddedId with correct equals/hashCode.

Senior

Q11: Design keys for a payment system with idempotency.

payment_id BIGSERIAL PK. client_request_id UUID UNIQUE (idempotency key). account_id BIGINT FK indexed. Never CASCADE on money tables. external_id UUID for API. ON CONFLICT (client_request_id) DO NOTHING for idempotent insert.

Q12: Why can't you have FK between microservice databases?

FK requires both tables in same database. Cross-service: store external UUID as plain column with UNIQUE constraint. Enforce integrity via Saga pattern and event-driven eventual consistency.

Q13: Explain deferred FK constraints (PostgreSQL).

DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED: FK checked at COMMIT, not per statement. Allows inserting parent and child in same transaction in any order. Useful for complex bulk loads.

Q14: How does PK choice affect sharding?

Shard key often equals or includes PK. BIGINT sequence requires coordinated generation across shards (Snowflake, per-shard sequences). UUID v7 allows client-side generation without coordination. Poor shard key choice → hot shards.

Staff / Principal / Architect

Q15: Organization has 200 tables with no FK constraints ("for performance"). Evaluate.

FK checks are O(log n) with indexes — negligible overhead. Without FKs: orphan data guaranteed at scale, application bugs cause silent corruption, every service must reimplement integrity. Recommendation: add FKs with proper indexes, use RESTRICT not CASCADE, deferrable for bulk loads.

Q16: Design key strategy for global neobank with data residency requirements.

Internal BIGINT PK per region. UUID external_id for global API routing. Natural keys (IBAN) as UNIQUE per region. No cross-region FK — each region is independent DB. Global identity resolution service maps external_id → region + internal_id.

Scenario

Scenario: "DELETE customer takes 45 seconds, locks accounts table."

Missing index on accounts.customer_id FK column. DELETE triggers FK check → full table scan of accounts. Fix: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_accounts_customer_id ON accounts(customer_id). Verify with EXPLAIN on the FK check query.

Part 20 — Revision Sheet

Must-Know Rules

  1. Every table → surrogate BIGINT PK (core entities)
  2. Natural business keys → UNIQUE, not PK
  3. Every FK column → indexed (PG/Oracle manual, InnoDB auto)
  4. ON DELETE RESTRICT for financial core tables
  5. PK never updated after insert
  6. Never expose internal PK in public APIs — use UUID
  7. Composite PK → junction tables only
  8. UUID v4 → avoid as InnoDB PK; use UUID v7 or BIGINT
  9. FK in DB, not just application — enforced at storage boundary
  10. @EmbeddedId → equals/hashCode mandatory

Key Hierarchy

text
Super Key → Candidate Key → Primary Key (chosen)
                          → Alternate Key (UNIQUE constraint)
Foreign Key → references PK or UNIQUE of parent

ASCII: PK + FK + Index

text
CUSTOMERS                    ACCOUNTS
PK: customer_id (indexed) ◄── FK: customer_id (MUST index!)
UQ: email (indexed)          PK: account_id (indexed)
                             UQ: account_number (indexed)

Part 21 — Summary Table

TopicKey Takeaway
Primary KeyOne per table, NOT NULL, unique, auto-indexed, immutable
Foreign KeyEnforces referential integrity — always index referencing columns
Unique KeyEnforces alternate candidate keys — email, account_number
Surrogate KeyBIGINT/UUID system ID — standard for core OLTP entities
Natural KeyBusiness identifier — use as UNIQUE, not PK (except lookups)
Composite KeyValid for junction tables — avoid on core entities
StorageNarrow PK → smaller indexes → more rows/page → faster I/O
PerformanceMissing FK index = production outage on parent DELETE
Spring/JPA@Id Long + @SequenceGenerator + @NaturalId for business keys
MicroservicesNo cross-DB FK — UUID references + eventual consistency
ArchitectSurrogate PK internal + UUID external + UNIQUE natural keys

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why This Exists5Internal Working6Storage Internals7Memory Usage8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Complexity Analysis11Code / SQL Examples12Production Usage13Spring Boot Integration14Hibernate/JPA Integration15Architect Perspective16Decision Matrix17Comparison Tables18Common Mistakes19Interview Questions20Revision Sheet21Summary Table*Practice

Part 1 — Concept

What Are Constraints?

A constraint is a rule enforced by the database on column or table data. It rejects invalid rows before they are committed, regardless of which application, script, or batch job inserted them.

text
WITHOUT CONSTRAINTS                         WITH CONSTRAINTS
─────────────────────                       ────────────────
App A validates balance >= 0                Database rejects balance < 0
App B forgets validation        vs          for ALL clients consistently
Batch job bypasses app logic                One rule, one enforcement point
Microservice C inserts NULL email           NOT NULL blocks at INSERT time

Constraints are the database boundary for data integrity. Keys (Lesson 6) are a special category of constraints; this lesson covers the full integrity model.

Constraint Taxonomy

text
DATABASE CONSTRAINTS

├── ENTITY INTEGRITY
│   └── PRIMARY KEY          — row identity, NOT NULL + UNIQUE
│
├── REFERENTIAL INTEGRITY
│   └── FOREIGN KEY          — parent/child relationship rules
│
├── DOMAIN INTEGRITY
│   ├── NOT NULL             — column must have a value
│   ├── CHECK                — boolean expression must be true
│   ├── DEFAULT              — value when none supplied
│   └── Data type            — implicit domain (Lesson 5)
│
├── UNIQUENESS INTEGRITY
│   └── UNIQUE               — no duplicate values (except NULL rules)
│
└── BUSINESS / CUSTOM
    ├── Triggers             — arbitrary logic (Lesson 23)
    └── Exclusion (PG)       — prevent overlapping ranges

Constraint vs Application Validation

LayerRoleBypassed by
Application validationUX, early feedback, complex workflowsOther services, SQL clients, migrations
Database constraintFinal gate — invalid data never persistsSuperuser (sometimes), SET session_replication_role
Both togetherBest practice—
Architect rule: Validate in the app for user experience; enforce in the database for correctness.

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Integrity Enforcement

text
1970    Codd: entity, referential, domain integrity as relational foundations
1970s   PRIMARY KEY and FOREIGN KEY in early RDBMS (limited FK support)
1981    SQL-81: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY standardised
1989    SQL-89: CHECK constraint standardised (weak adoption initially)
1990s   Oracle, DB2 add CHECK; MySQL InnoDB adds FK (2001)
1992    SQL-92: full integrity constraint model
2000s   Application-layer validation dominates (Hibernate Validator, Bean Validation)
        └── Many teams skip DB constraints "for flexibility" — anti-pattern emerges
2010s   Microservices expose cost of no DB constraints (orphan data, duplicate payments)
2020s   Return to "database as last line of defense"
        PostgreSQL: EXCLUDE, DEFERRABLE constraints, rich CHECK
        Flyway/Liquibase: constraints as versioned schema code

Why Constraints Were Sometimes Removed

Reason ( flawed )Reality
"FKs are slow"FK check is O(log n) with index — negligible
"We use microservices"Each service DB still needs its own integrity
"ORM handles it"Batch jobs, migrations, ad-hoc SQL bypass ORM
"Hard to change schema"Flyway/Liquibase makes constraint changes manageable

Historical Lesson

Constraints were in the relational model from the start. Teams that removed them traded short-term deployment convenience for long-term data corruption certainty.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Do Constraints Solve?

Problem 1: Invalid Domain Values

text
Without CHECK:
  INSERT INTO accounts (balance) VALUES (-50000);   → Accepted
  Bank owes customer money on a savings account — logic error in production

With CHECK:
  CONSTRAINT chk_balance_nonneg CHECK (balance >= 0)
  → ERROR: check constraint violated

Problem 2: Missing Required Data

text
Without NOT NULL:
  INSERT INTO customers (first_name) VALUES (NULL);
  Account opened with no customer name — regulatory failure

With NOT NULL:
  → Rejected at insert

Problem 3: Duplicate Business Identifiers

text
Without UNIQUE:
  Two accounts with same account_number — reconciliation nightmare

With UNIQUE(account_number):
  Second insert fails atomically

Problem 4: Orphan Records

text
Without FK:
  Account references customer_id = 9999 — customer never existed

With FK:
  INSERT rejected if parent row missing

Problem 5: Concurrent Race Conditions

text
Two threads check-then-insert same email:
  Both pass application check → two rows with same email

UNIQUE constraint:
  Second INSERT fails — database serialises conflict

Problem 6: Inconsistent Defaults Across Clients

text
Service A: status defaults to 'ACTIVE'
Service B: status defaults to NULL
Batch job: status defaults to 'PENDING'

DEFAULT 'ACTIVE' on column:
  One authoritative default for all clients

Unified Problem Statement

Constraints guarantee that invalid, incomplete, duplicate, or orphaned data cannot enter the database — regardless of which client or process writes the data, and even under concurrent access.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Enforce Rules in the Database?

The Enforcement Boundary Argument

text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Clients: Spring Boot, Batch ETL, DBA scripts, BI tools,     │
│           migration tools, future services not yet built      │
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                             │ All paths hit same gate
                             ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CONSTRAINT LAYER (database)                                 │
│  NOT NULL | CHECK | UNIQUE | FK | DEFAULT                   │
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                             │ Only valid rows pass
                             ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STORAGE ENGINE                                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why Each Constraint Type Exists

ConstraintProblem it solves
NOT NULLOptional when required — incomplete records
DEFAULTInconsistent implicit defaults across code paths
CHECKValues outside business domain
UNIQUEDuplicate alternate keys
PRIMARY KEYDuplicate rows, NULL identity
FOREIGN KEYOrphan references, broken joins
EXCLUDE (PG)Overlapping bookings, double-booked resources

CHECK vs Trigger vs Application

text
Use CHECK when:
  Rule is row-local boolean expression
  balance >= 0, end_date > start_date, status IN (...)

Use TRIGGER when:
  Cross-row or cross-table logic
  Audit logging, complex cascades (Lesson 23)

Use APPLICATION when:
  Multi-step workflow, external API validation
  But still add DB constraint as safety net for invariants

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Constraints Are Enforced Internally

Constraint Storage in Catalog

Every constraint is metadata in the data dictionary:

text
PostgreSQL: pg_constraint, pg_class, information_schema
Oracle:     USER_CONSTRAINTS, USER_CONS_COLUMNS
MySQL:      information_schema.TABLE_CONSTRAINTS

Catalog entry stores:
  constraint name, type, table, columns, expression (CHECK)
  referenced table (FK), ON DELETE/UPDATE action
  DEFERRABLE / NOT DEFERRABLE (PG, Oracle)

Enforcement Timing

text
IMMEDIATE (default):
  Constraint checked at end of each SQL statement

DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED (PostgreSQL, Oracle):
  Constraint checked at COMMIT
  Allows temporary violation within transaction

NOT NULL — Internal Working

text
Row insert/update:
  1. Parse column null bitmap
  2. For each NOT NULL column: if null bit set → ERROR immediately
  3. No index involved — O(1) per column check
  Cost: negligible

CHECK — Internal Working

text
INSERT/UPDATE row:
  1. Evaluate CHECK expression with new row values
  2. Expression false → ERROR
  3. Expression true or unknown (NULL) → pass*
  
  * CHECK (balance >= 0): NULL balance → passes CHECK in SQL三值逻辑
    Combine with NOT NULL for mandatory validated columns

Storage: expression stored in catalog, evaluated per row change
Cost: CPU per row — cheap for simple checks; expensive for subqueries

UNIQUE — Internal Working

text
INSERT/UPDATE:
  1. B+ tree probe on unique index
  2. Key exists → ERROR duplicate key
  3. Key not found → insert into index + heap

UPDATE changing unique column:
  Delete old index entry + insert new (same as delete+insert)

FOREIGN KEY — Internal Working

text
INSERT into child (accounts):
  1. For each FK column: lookup parent PK/UNIQUE index
  2. Parent row not found → ERROR
  3. Parent found → proceed

DELETE from parent (customers):
  1. Scan/index child table for matching FK values
  2. Children found + RESTRICT → ERROR
  3. Children found + CASCADE → delete children first
  4. No children → delete parent

Cost: O(log n) with index on FK column; O(n) without — always index FKs

DEFAULT — Internal Working

text
INSERT without specifying column:
  1. Parser sees missing column
  2. Substitutes DEFAULT expression before constraint checks
  3. DEFAULT NOW() evaluated at insert time
  4. DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() evaluated per row

DEFAULT does NOT apply on UPDATE when column omitted
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = 100  — status unchanged, not reset to default

Constraint Check Order (Conceptual)

text
INSERT flow:
  1. Apply DEFAULTs for missing columns
  2. NOT NULL checks
  3. Data type coercion/validation
  4. CHECK constraints
  5. UNIQUE / PRIMARY KEY
  6. FOREIGN KEY (may require parent row to exist first)
  7. Write row + indexes + WAL

Part 6 — Storage Internals

How Constraints Affect Physical Storage

Index-Backed Constraints

text
These constraints CREATE indexes automatically:

  PRIMARY KEY  → unique B+ tree index (clustered in InnoDB)
  UNIQUE       → unique B+ tree index

Storage cost:
  One index entry per row per unique/PK constraint
  Wider columns in unique key → larger index (Lesson 5, 6)

CHECK and NOT NULL — No Extra Storage

text
NOT NULL: 1 bit in row null bitmap — already part of row header
CHECK:    expression in catalog only — zero per-row storage overhead
DEFAULT:  expression in catalog — zero per-row storage unless value stored

FK — Storage Impact

text
FK column storage:
  Same as regular column (e.g., BIGINT = 8 bytes)

Required FK index (manual in PG/Oracle):
  Additional B+ tree: 8 bytes × row_count + tree overhead

Without FK index:
  No extra index storage — but catastrophic DELETE/UPDATE performance

Partial Unique Index (Constraint Pattern)

sql
-- Constraint enforced only on subset of rows
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_active_email
    ON customers (email)
    WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';

Storage:
  Index contains ONLY active rows → smaller index
  Deleted/inactive rows excluded → multiple inactive same email allowed

Constraint Metadata Diagram

text
TABLE: accounts (heap/clustered file)
├── Row data pages
├── INDEX accounts_pkey (PK constraint backing)
├── INDEX uq_accounts_number (UNIQUE constraint backing)
├── INDEX idx_accounts_customer_id (FK performance — not auto in PG)
└── Catalog metadata:
      chk_balance_nonneg: CHECK (balance >= 0)
      fk_accounts_customer: FK → customers(customer_id) RESTRICT
      def_status: DEFAULT 'ACTIVE'
      nn_balance: NOT NULL on balance

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Constraint Memory Impact

ConstraintRuntime MemoryNotes
NOT NULLNone (bitmap in row)Zero overhead
CHECKExpression evaluation stackTrivial for simple expressions
DEFAULTNoneEvaluated at insert
UNIQUE/PKIndex pages in buffer poolSame as any index — cached pages
FKIndex pages + lock structuresParent delete may acquire child index locks

Buffer Pool — Unique Indexes

text
UNIQUE index on email (1M customers):
  ~30 MB index (VARCHAR average)
  Cached in buffer pool like any index
  INSERT: index probe + possible page split → brief latch contention on hot unique indexes

FK Locking Memory

text
DELETE parent with RESTRICT:
  Row-level locks on parent
  Shared or exclusive locks on child index pages during FK scan
  High concurrency on same parent row → lock queue buildup

Not a "memory" issue but operational: FK enforcement consumes lock manager resources

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Constraint Violation Execution Flows

Flow 1: Successful INSERT

sql
INSERT INTO accounts (account_id, customer_id, account_number, balance, status)
VALUES (5001, 1001, 'ACC-5001', 0.00, NULL);
-- status omitted → DEFAULT 'ACTIVE' applied
text
1. DEFAULT: status = 'ACTIVE'
2. NOT NULL: account_id ✓ customer_id ✓ account_number ✓ balance ✓ status ✓
3. Type check: DECIMAL ✓ BIGINT ✓
4. CHECK (balance >= 0): 0.00 >= 0 ✓
5. PK unique index: 5001 not found ✓
6. UNIQUE account_number: 'ACC-5001' not found ✓
7. FK customer_id=1001: found in customers ✓
8. Insert row + all indexes
9. WAL write
10. COMMIT → success

Flow 2: CHECK Violation

sql
INSERT INTO accounts (..., balance) VALUES (..., -100.00);
text
1-3. Pass NOT NULL and types
4. CHECK (balance >= 0): -100 >= 0 → FALSE
   → ERROR: new row violates check constraint "chk_balance_nonneg"
   → Transaction aborted (if no savepoint)
   → No row written, no WAL data change
   → Client receives SQLException

Flow 3: FK RESTRICT on DELETE

sql
DELETE FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 1001;
-- 3 accounts exist for this customer
text
1. Lock customer row 1001
2. FK check: index scan accounts(customer_id=1001) → 3 rows
3. ON DELETE RESTRICT → ERROR: update or delete on "customers"
   violates foreign key constraint "fk_accounts_customer"
4. Transaction rolled back
5. Customer row unchanged, accounts unchanged

Flow 4: DEFERRABLE FK — Load Pattern

sql
BEGIN;
SET CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED;

INSERT INTO orders (order_id, customer_id) VALUES (9001, 9999);
-- customer 9999 does not exist yet — OK (deferred)

INSERT INTO customers (customer_id, ...) VALUES (9999, ...);

COMMIT;
-- At COMMIT: FK checked → customer 9999 now exists → success
text
DEFERRABLE CONSTRAINT FLOW:

Statement time: FK violation allowed temporarily
COMMIT time:    All deferred constraints evaluated
                Any violation → entire transaction ROLLBACK

Flow 5: UNIQUE Race (Two Sessions)

text
Session A                          Session B
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
BEGIN                              BEGIN
INSERT email='x@.com'              INSERT email='x@.com'
  unique index: OK                   waits on A's lock OR
COMMIT                               tries insert → DUPLICATE KEY
                                   ERROR → ROLLBACK

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Constraint Performance Impact

Cost Summary

ConstraintInsertUpdateDelete ParentStorage
NOT NULL~0~0—0
DEFAULT~0——0
CHECK (simple)Low CPULow CPU—0
CHECK (subquery)HighHigh—0
UNIQUE/PKO(log n) indexO(log n)—Index size
FK (indexed)O(log n)O(log n)O(log n) child checkFK index
FK (no index)O(log n) parent—O(n) child scan—

Expensive CHECK Anti-Pattern

sql
-- ❌ CHECK with subquery — evaluated per row, may scan other tables
CONSTRAINT chk_max_accounts CHECK (
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM accounts a
     WHERE a.customer_id = customer_id) <= 5
);

-- ✅ Enforce in application or trigger; or use materialised count column + trigger
-- Keep CHECK row-local: CHECK (balance >= 0)

FK and Throughput

text
Myth: "Remove FKs for performance"

Reality at 10K INSERT/sec on child table:
  FK check = index lookup on parent PK ≈ 0.01ms
  Total FK overhead ≈ 10% vs unvalidated insert — acceptable for integrity gained

Remove FK → orphan rate 0.1% → manual reconciliation cost >> 10% insert overhead

UNIQUE Index Hot Spot

text
INSERT high-rate idempotency key (same second, many keys):
  Unique index on random UUID keys → spread across tree → no hot spot

INSERT sequential unique key on single table:
  Generally fine — B+ tree handles sequential inserts (Lesson 4)

Contention: multiple sessions inserting same duplicate value simultaneously
  → one wins, others fail fast — correct behaviour

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

OperationNOT NULLCHECKUNIQUEFK (indexed)
INSERTO(1)O(1) simpleO(log n)O(log n)
UPDATE columnO(1)O(1)O(log n)O(log n) if FK col changes
DELETE parent———O(k log n) k=children
SpaceO(1)O(1) catalogO(n) indexO(n) FK index

Rule: Keep CHECK O(1). Keep FK indexed O(log n). Avoid O(n) child scans.

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Production Constraint Patterns

Banking Account Table — Full Constraint Set

sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id      BIGSERIAL
                        CONSTRAINT pk_accounts PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id     BIGINT         NOT NULL,
    account_number  VARCHAR(20)    NOT NULL,
    account_type    VARCHAR(20)    NOT NULL,
    currency        CHAR(3)        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'USD',
    balance         DECIMAL(18,2)  NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.00,
    credit_limit    DECIMAL(18,2),
    status          VARCHAR(20)    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE',
    opened_at       TIMESTAMPTZ    NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    closed_at       TIMESTAMPTZ,

    CONSTRAINT uq_accounts_number
        UNIQUE (account_number),

    CONSTRAINT chk_accounts_balance
        CHECK (balance >= 0),

    CONSTRAINT chk_accounts_credit
        CHECK (credit_limit IS NULL OR credit_limit >= 0),

    CONSTRAINT chk_accounts_type
        CHECK (account_type IN ('SAVINGS', 'CHECKING', 'LOAN')),

    CONSTRAINT chk_accounts_status
        CHECK (status IN ('ACTIVE', 'SUSPENDED', 'CLOSED')),

    CONSTRAINT chk_accounts_closed
        CHECK (
            (status = 'CLOSED' AND closed_at IS NOT NULL)
            OR (status != 'CLOSED' AND closed_at IS NULL)
        ),

    CONSTRAINT fk_accounts_customer
        FOREIGN KEY (customer_id)
        REFERENCES customers (customer_id)
        ON DELETE RESTRICT
        ON UPDATE NO ACTION
);

CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_customer_id ON accounts (customer_id);

Oracle Equivalent

sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id      NUMBER(19)       NOT NULL,
    customer_id     NUMBER(19)       NOT NULL,
    account_number  VARCHAR2(20)     NOT NULL,
    balance         NUMBER(18,2)     DEFAULT 0 NOT NULL,
    status          VARCHAR2(20)     DEFAULT 'ACTIVE' NOT NULL,
    opened_at       TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT SYSTIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    closed_at       TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE,

    CONSTRAINT pk_accounts PRIMARY KEY (account_id),
    CONSTRAINT uq_accounts_number UNIQUE (account_number),
    CONSTRAINT chk_balance CHECK (balance >= 0),
    CONSTRAINT chk_status CHECK (status IN ('ACTIVE','SUSPENDED','CLOSED')),
    CONSTRAINT fk_customer FOREIGN KEY (customer_id)
        REFERENCES customers (customer_id)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_customer ON accounts (customer_id);

PostgreSQL EXCLUDE — Prevent Double Booking

sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;

CREATE TABLE appointment_slots (
    doctor_id   BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    slot        tstzrange   NOT NULL,
    patient_id  BIGINT      NOT NULL,

    EXCLUDE USING gist (
        doctor_id WITH =,
        slot WITH &&
    )
);

-- INSERT overlapping slot for same doctor → ERROR

Adding Constraints to Existing Table

sql
-- Safe migration: validate without blocking writes (PostgreSQL 9.1+)
ALTER TABLE accounts
    ADD CONSTRAINT chk_balance CHECK (balance >= 0) NOT VALID;

-- Scan existing rows in background
ALTER TABLE accounts VALIDATE CONSTRAINT chk_balance;

-- NOT VALID: new rows checked; existing unvalidated until VALIDATE completes

Naming Convention

text
Pattern: {type}_{table}_{column(s)}

pk_accounts              PRIMARY KEY
fk_accounts_customer     FOREIGN KEY
uq_accounts_number       UNIQUE
chk_accounts_balance     CHECK
nn_accounts_balance      NOT NULL (documentation; PG implicit)

Constraints in Production Domains

Banking

RuleConstraint
Balance never negative (savings)CHECK (balance >= 0)

Closed account has close dateCHECK (status='CLOSED' ↔ closed_at IS NOT NULL)
One active account per product per customerPartial UNIQUE index

Payments

sql
CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    client_request_id   UUID         NOT NULL,
    account_id          BIGINT       NOT NULL,
    amount              DECIMAL(18,2) NOT NULL,
    status              VARCHAR(20)  NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING',

    CONSTRAINT uq_payments_idempotency UNIQUE (client_request_id),
    CONSTRAINT chk_amount_positive CHECK (amount > 0),
    CONSTRAINT chk_status CHECK (status IN ('PENDING','COMPLETED','FAILED')),
    CONSTRAINT fk_payments_account FOREIGN KEY (account_id)
        REFERENCES accounts (account_id) ON DELETE RESTRICT
);

Healthcare (HIPAA)

text
NOT NULL on required PHI fields
CHECK on date ranges (discharge >= admission)
FK RESTRICT — never CASCADE delete patient records
Audit tables: no FK to patient (immutable log survives patient merge)

Microservices — Within Service Boundary

text
Order Service DB:
  FK order_items.order_id → orders.order_id  ✅ same database
  CHECK quantity > 0  ✅

Cross-service:
  payments.order_id UUID — NO FK to Order Service DB
  UNIQUE (order_id) for idempotency  ✅
  Integrity via Saga + events  ✅

FailureCauseFix
ORA-02291 / FK violationOrphan insertFix data + add FK if missing
Duplicate paymentMissing UNIQUE on idempotency keyAdd UNIQUE constraint
Negative balanceMissing CHECKAdd CHECK + reconcile existing
Slow DELETE customerFK without indexIndex FK column
Migration failsADD CONSTRAINT on dirty dataClean data, NOT VALID + VALIDATE

Part 13 — Spring Boot Integration

Constraints with JPA / Hibernate / Flyway

Entity Mapping to Constraints

java
@Entity
@Table(name = "accounts",
    uniqueConstraints = {
        @UniqueConstraint(name = "uq_accounts_number", columnNames = "account_number")
    }
)
public class Account {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "account_seq")
    @SequenceGenerator(name = "account_seq", sequenceName = "account_seq", allocationSize = 50)
    private Long accountId;

    @Column(name = "account_number", nullable = false, length = 20, unique = true)
    private String accountNumber;

    @Column(name = "balance", nullable = false, precision = 18, scale = 2)
    private BigDecimal balance;

    @Column(name = "account_type", nullable = false, length = 20)
    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    private AccountType accountType;

    @Column(name = "status", nullable = false, length = 20)
    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    private AccountStatus status = AccountStatus.ACTIVE;

    @Column(name = "opened_at", nullable = false)
    private OffsetDateTime openedAt = OffsetDateTime.now();
}

CHECK Constraints — Prefer Flyway/Liquibase

sql
-- V003__account_constraints.sql (Flyway)
ALTER TABLE accounts ADD CONSTRAINT chk_accounts_balance
    CHECK (balance >= 0);

ALTER TABLE accounts ADD CONSTRAINT chk_accounts_type
    CHECK (account_type IN ('SAVINGS', 'CHECKING', 'LOAN'));
yaml
spring:
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate   # Hibernate checks NOT NULL, UNIQUE, FK — not CHECK expressions
Hibernate validate verifies column nullability and unique constraints mapped via annotations. CHECK constraints must be in SQL migrations — Hibernate does not generate them from annotations (Bean Validation @Min is app-layer only).

Handling Constraint Violations

java
@RestControllerAdvice
public class DatabaseExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(DataIntegrityViolationException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse> handleDataIntegrity(DataIntegrityViolationException ex) {
        Throwable root = NestedExceptionUtils.getMostSpecificCause(ex);
        String message = "Data integrity violation";

        if (root instanceof ConstraintViolationException cve) {
            String name = cve.getConstraintName();
            message = mapConstraintName(name);  // uq_accounts_number → "Account number already exists"
        }

        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT).body(new ErrorResponse(message));
    }
}

Bean Validation vs DB Constraint

java
public class CreateAccountRequest {

    @NotNull
    @DecimalMin(value = "0.00", inclusive = true)  // App layer — fast feedback
    private BigDecimal initialDeposit;

    @NotBlank
    @Email
    private String email;
}

// DB still needs:
// CHECK (balance >= 0), NOT NULL, UNIQUE(email)
// @DecimalMin does NOT protect against batch SQL or other services

java
@ManyToOne(optional = false)
@JoinColumn(name = "customer_id", nullable = false,
    foreignKey = @ForeignKey(name = "fk_accounts_customer"))
private Customer customer;

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

Constraint Strategy for Solution Architects

Defense in Depth Model

text
Layer 1: API validation (Bean Validation)     — user experience
Layer 2: Domain model invariants (Java)       — business logic
Layer 3: Database constraints                 — correctness guarantee
Layer 4: Audit + reconciliation jobs          — detect drift

Never rely on Layer 1 or 2 alone.

What Must Be a Database Constraint

InvariantDB Constraint?
Balance >= 0✅ CHECK
Email unique✅ UNIQUE
Customer exists before account✅ FK
Idempotency key unique✅ UNIQUE
Valid enum status✅ CHECK or FK to lookup
Complex multi-table ruleTrigger or app + periodic audit
"User must be 18+"App (CHECK possible but rarely in DB)
Rate limitingRedis / app — not DB constraint

Constraint Migration Strategy

text
Adding constraint to production with existing data:

1. Identify violations: SELECT rows that fail proposed CHECK
2. Fix data (batch update, manual review)
3. ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID  (PG — no full table lock for validation)
4. VALIDATE CONSTRAINT during low traffic
5. Monitor application error rates for constraint violations

Removing constraint:
  Usually safe — but understand why it was added before dropping

Microservices Constraint Boundaries

text
┌─────────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────────┐
│   Order Service     │     │  Payment Service    │
│   DB: orders        │     │  DB: payments       │
│   FK: order_items   │     │  UNIQUE(order_ref)  │
│       → orders ✅   │     │  NO FK to orders ❌ │
│   CHECK qty > 0 ✅  │     │  CHECK amount > 0 ✅│
└─────────────────────┘     └─────────────────────┘

Each bounded context owns its constraints.
Cross-context: eventual consistency, not FK.

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Validation Only in Application

java
// ❌ Only @Min in DTO — batch job bypasses
@Min(0) private BigDecimal balance;

// ✅ DB constraint
// CHECK (balance >= 0)

Mistake 2: FK Without Index (PostgreSQL/Oracle)

sql
-- ❌ FK added, no index on customer_id
-- ✅ CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_customer_id ON accounts(customer_id);

Mistake 3: CASCADE on Financial Tables

sql
-- ❌ ON DELETE CASCADE on payments → account
-- ✅ ON DELETE RESTRICT

Mistake 4: CHECK with NULL Loophole

sql
-- balance NULL passes CHECK (balance >= 0) in SQL!
CONSTRAINT chk_balance CHECK (balance >= 0)
-- column allows NULL → negative check bypassed via NULL

-- ✅
balance DECIMAL(18,2) NOT NULL,
CONSTRAINT chk_balance CHECK (balance >= 0)

Mistake 5: ddl-auto=update Instead of Migrations

yaml
# ❌ Production
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto: update

# ✅ Flyway owns constraints
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto: validate
spring.flyway.enabled: true

Mistake 6: Generic Error on Constraint Violation

java
// ❌ Return 500 Internal Server Error for duplicate email
// ✅ Map uq_customers_email → 409 Conflict "Email already registered"

Mistake 7: Overloaded CHECK with Subquery

sql
-- ❌ Per-row subquery COUNT — kills insert throughput
-- ✅ Row-local CHECK only; cross-row rules in trigger or app

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is a constraint?

Rule enforced by the database on data — NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE, PK, FK. Invalid data rejected at insert/update.

Q2: Difference between NOT NULL and CHECK?

NOT NULL: column cannot be missing. CHECK: expression on value must be true (e.g., balance >= 0).

Q3: Why use FOREIGN KEY?

Ensures child references exist in parent — prevents orphan rows. Enforced for all clients, not just application.

Q4: What happens on UNIQUE violation?

INSERT/UPDATE fails with duplicate key error. Transaction aborts unless handled.

Q5: Does DEFAULT apply on UPDATE?

No. DEFAULT only when column omitted from INSERT. UPDATE omitting column leaves value unchanged.

Mid-Level

Q6: Application validation vs database constraint?

App: UX, complex rules. DB: final guarantee against all writers including batch/SQL. Use both; never DB-only for user messages, never app-only for invariants.

Q7: Explain ON DELETE RESTRICT vs CASCADE.

RESTRICT: block parent delete if children exist. CASCADE: delete children first. RESTRICT for financial data; CASCADE for owned detail rows only.

Q8: Why index foreign key columns?

DELETE/UPDATE parent scans child for FK violations. Without index: O(n) table scan, locks, slow. With index: O(log n).

Q9: What is DEFERRABLE constraint?

Checked at COMMIT instead of each statement. Allows temporary violation within transaction — useful for bulk loads with ordered inserts.

Q10: How add CHECK to table with existing bad data?

PostgreSQL: ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID, fix data, VALIDATE CONSTRAINT. Avoids long lock on full validation during ADD.

Senior

Q11: Design constraints for payment idempotency.

UNIQUE(client_request_id). CHECK(amount > 0). FK account RESTRICT. NOT NULL on status. No CASCADE. Handle duplicate via ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING or catch unique violation.

Q12: Can you have FK between microservice databases?

No — different databases. Use UNIQUE on external reference ID, enforce via Saga. DB constraints within each service boundary only.

Q13: CHECK (status IN ('A','B')) vs lookup table FK?

CHECK: simple, no join, harder to extend (DDL change). Lookup FK: extensible, referential, extra join. Lookup table for values that change; CHECK for stable enums.

Q14: Partial unique index for soft delete?

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... ON customers(email) WHERE status != 'DELETED' — allows multiple deleted same email, one active.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Team removed all FKs "for microservices." Response?

Microservices ≠ no FK within service DB. Each service owns its schema — FKs within that DB remain best practice. Cross-service: events not FK. Removing internal FKs guarantees orphan data and erodes trust in analytics.

Q16: Constraint strategy for zero-downtime migration adding NOT NULL to 500M row table.

Add column nullable → backfill default → ADD CONSTRAINT NOT NULL using NOT VALID (PG) or check enabled novalidate (Oracle) → validate in batches → set DEFAULT for new rows. Avoid single ALTER that locks table for full scan.

Scenario

Scenario: Duplicate payments with same client_request_id after 6 months in production.

Root cause: idempotency enforced only in Redis (TTL expired) or app check (race). Fix: UNIQUE(client_request_id) in DB. Reconcile duplicates manually. Application: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING or catch DataIntegrityViolationException.

  • PK — UNIQUE + NOT NULL
  • FK — referential integrity; always index (PG/Oracle)

text

CASCADE  — junction/detail only

Migration Pattern (PG)

ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID;
-- fix data --
VALIDATE CONSTRAINT ...;
