Lesson 08

Normalization

Phase 1: DATABASE FUNDAMENTALS | Previous: Constraints | Next: Denormalization

Fundamentals
1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why This Exists5Internal Working6Storage Internals7Memory Usage8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Complexity Analysis11Code / SQL Examples12Production Usage13Spring Boot Integration14Hibernate/JPA Integration15Architect Perspective16Decision Matrix17Comparison Tables18Common Mistakes19Interview Questions20Revision Sheet21Summary Table*Practice

Part 1 — Concept

What Is Normalization?

Normalization is a systematic process of organizing data in a relational database to:

  1. Eliminate redundancy (same fact stored in multiple places)
  2. Prevent update, insert, and delete anomalies
  3. Enforce logical data dependencies through table structure

Normalization splits large, wide tables into smaller related tables connected by keys (Lesson 6) and protected by constraints (Lesson 7).

text
DENORMALIZED (BAD)                         NORMALIZED (GOOD)

ONE BIG TABLE                              MULTIPLE RELATED TABLES
┌─────────────────────────────────┐       CUSTOMERS          ORDERS
│ order_id | cust_name | email   │       ┌──────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐
│ product  | price | qty | total │  →    │ customer_id  │◄───│ order_id    │
│ cust_name repeated every order  │       │ name, email  │    │ customer_id │
└─────────────────────────────────┘       └──────────────┘    └─────────────┘
                                                              ORDER_ITEMS
                                                              ┌─────────────┐
                                                              │ order_id    │
                                                              │ product_id  │
                                                              │ qty, price  │
                                                              └─────────────┘

Normal Forms Hierarchy

text
UNNORMALIZED DATA
       │
       ▼
    1NF  — Atomic values, no repeating groups
       │
       ▼
    2NF  — No partial dependency on composite PK
       │
       ▼
    3NF  — No transitive dependency on non-key attributes
       │
       ▼
   BCNF  — Every determinant is a candidate key
       │
       ▼
    4NF  — No multi-valued dependencies
       │
       ▼
    5NF  — No join dependencies (decomposed correctly)

Core Terminology

TermDefinition
Functional Dependency (FD)If A determines B, knowing A tells you B: A → B
DeterminantLeft side of FD (A in A → B)
Candidate KeyMinimal set of attributes that uniquely identify a row
Partial DependencyNon-key attribute depends on part of composite PK
Transitive DependencyNon-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute
AnomalyProblem caused by redundancy: update, insert, delete
DecompositionSplitting one table into multiple without losing information

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Normalization Theory

text
1970    Edgar F. Codd — relational model
1971    Codd introduces normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF concepts)
1972    Codd: "Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model"
1974    Ronald Fagin defines 4NF (multi-valued dependencies)
1977    Fagin defines 5NF (join dependencies)
1970s   Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) — stricter than 3NF

1980s–90s  Normalization taught as mandatory design discipline
           ER modeling + normalization = standard DBA curriculum

2000s   ORM era: developers skip normalization theory
        "I'll just add columns" → wide denormalized tables

2010s   Web scale: intentional denormalization (Lesson 9)
        Read replicas, caching, document embedding
        Normalization remains OLTP standard; denormalization for read scale

2020s   Hybrid: normalized OLTP core + denormalized read models (CQRS)
        Data warehouses star schema (denormalized by design)

Why Normalization Theory Was Created

Before normalization, databases looked like flat files:

text
ORDER_FLAT_FILE:
order_id|customer_name|customer_email|product1|qty1|product2|qty2|...

Every schema change, every customer rename, every duplicate product name was a production incident. Codd and others formalized rules to prevent this structurally.

Historical Lesson

Normalization is not academic pedantry — it was the engineering response to real data corruption in 1970s enterprise systems. It remains the default for OLTP; denormalization is a deliberate later choice (Lesson 9).

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does Normalization Solve?

The Three Anomalies

Update Anomaly

text
DENORMALIZED TABLE: orders_with_customer

order_id | customer_name | customer_email     | product | amount
---------|---------------|--------------------|---------|-------
101      | John Smith    | john@old.com       | Laptop  | 999
102      | John Smith    | john@old.com       | Mouse   | 25
103      | John Smith    | john@new.com       | Keyboard| 75  ← email updated here only

Problem: John has two emails in the same database.
Fix with normalization: customer_email stored ONCE in customers table.

Insert Anomaly

text
Cannot add a new customer until they place an order:

order_id | customer_name | customer_email
---------|---------------|---------------
(empty — no orders yet)

INSERT customer "Jane" with no order_id → impossible or NULL order_id hack

Normalized: INSERT into customers without any order.

Delete Anomaly

text
Delete last order for a customer → lose customer contact info entirely.

DELETE order 103 → last record with John's email gone

Normalized: DELETE order does not delete customer row.

Problem 4: Storage Waste

text
1 million orders, 50,000 unique customers
Denormalized: customer_name + email × 1M rows = massive duplication
Normalized: 50,000 customer rows + 1M order rows with customer_id FK (8 bytes each)

Problem 5: Integrity Drift

text
Same fact in two places → eventually inconsistent without strict application logic
Normalization + FK + UNIQUE = database enforces single source of truth

Unified Problem Statement

Without normalization, redundant data causes update/insert/delete anomalies, wastes storage, and makes integrity impossible to guarantee at scale. Normalization decomposes data so each fact is stored exactly once in exactly one place.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Normal Forms Exist

Each normal form eliminates a specific class of redundancy:

Normal FormEliminatesMechanism
1NFRepeating groups, non-atomic valuesOne value per cell; separate rows/tables
2NFPartial dependenciesMove partially dependent columns to new table
3NFTransitive dependenciesMove transitively dependent columns out
BCNFAll non-key determinantsStricter decomposition
4NFMulti-valued dependenciesSeparate independent multi-valued facts
5NFJoin dependenciesEnsure decomposition is lossless and correct

Why Not Stop at 1NF?

text
1NF alone still allows:

order_id, product_id (PK) | product_name | category_name

product_name → category_name (transitive via product_id)
Change category for a product → update every order line — update anomaly

3NF: products table holds product_name, category_name once

When Normalization Is the Wrong Tool

Normalization optimizes for write correctness and storage — not read performance. That is why Lesson 9 (Denormalization) exists. Architects normalize OLTP cores; denormalize read paths deliberately.

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Normalization Works — Functional Dependencies

Functional Dependency Notation

text
A → B  means: for any two rows, if A values are equal, B values must be equal

Examples (banking):
  account_id → balance           (one balance per account)
  customer_id → email            (in customers table)
  account_id → customer_id       (each account belongs to one customer)
  (order_id, product_id) → qty   (composite determinant)

Dependency Analysis Diagram

text
ACCOUNTS (violates 3NF if we add customer email here)

account_id → customer_id, balance, customer_email
customer_id → customer_email   ← TRANSITIVE (through non-key customer_id)

Decomposition:
  CUSTOMERS: customer_id → customer_email, name
  ACCOUNTS:  account_id → customer_id, balance
  FK: accounts.customer_id → customers.customer_id

Normalization Algorithm (Conceptual)

text
1. Identify all functional dependencies
2. Find candidate keys
3. Check current normal form
4. If violation found:
     a. Create new table with determinant as key
     b. Move dependent attributes to new table
     c. Add FK from old table to new table
5. Repeat until target normal form achieved
6. Verify lossless join decomposition

Lossless Join Decomposition

text
Decomposition is LOSSLESS if natural join recreates original data exactly:

R(A, B, C) split into R1(A, B) and R2(B, C) where B → C

If join adds spurious rows → lossy decomposition (BAD)
Always verify: R = R1 ⋈ R2 (no extra tuples)

Part 6 — Storage Internals

How Normalization Affects Physical Storage

Before and After Storage Profile

text
DENORMALIZED: order_flat (1M orders, 50K customers)

Columns per row: order_id, cust_name(50B), cust_email(50B), product(50B), ...
Approx row: 200 bytes × 1M = 200 MB data
Customer data repeated ~20× average → ~95 MB wasted on duplicate customer fields

NORMALIZED:
  customers: 50K × 120 bytes = 6 MB
  orders: 1M × 40 bytes = 40 MB
  order_items: 2M × 30 bytes = 60 MB
  Total: ~106 MB + index overhead

Storage saving: ~50% in this example
Buffer pool: more unique rows fit per page → better cache efficiency

Index Impact

text
Denormalized:
  Index on customer_email in order table → huge index (email repeated per order)

Normalized:
  Unique index on customers.email → 50K entries only
  FK index orders.customer_id → 1M entries (8-byte keys)

Normalized indexes are smaller and more selective

JOIN Cost Trade-off

text
Normalized read:
  SELECT o.*, c.email FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON ...
  = 2 index lookups + nested loop or hash join

Denormalized read:
  SELECT * FROM order_flat — no join, but wider rows, more I/O

Normalization trades JOIN CPU for storage integrity and smaller indexes
Lesson 9 addresses when to denormalize for read performance

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Normalization and Memory

Buffer Pool — Normalized Schema

text
Query: get order with customer email (normalized)

Step 1: Load order page from buffer pool (narrow row — more rows/page)
Step 2: Load customer page via FK index (likely already cached — hot customers)

Hot customer row cached once — shared across all their order queries
Denormalized: customer email duplicated in every order page — cache pollution

Hash Join Memory

sql
-- Normalized join
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id

Hash table key: customer_id BIGINT (8 bytes)
vs denormalized duplicate email VARCHAR(255) in every order row for comparison

Hibernate Persistence Context

java
// Normalized: one Customer entity, many Order entities reference it
Customer c = order.getCustomer();  // lazy or eager — one instance in session

// Denormalized embedded customer fields in Order:
// customer name change on one order object ≠ other orders — identity confusion

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Query Execution: Normalized vs Denormalized

Normalized Read Path

sql
SELECT o.order_id, o.order_date, c.first_name, c.email, oi.product_id, oi.quantity
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
WHERE o.order_id = 9001;
text
EXECUTION FLOW:

1. Index scan orders PK → order_id = 9001 → 1 row
2. Index scan customers PK → customer_id from order → 1 row
3. Index scan order_items(order_id) → N rows
4. Nested loop or hash join assembles result
5. Return joined result set to client

I/O: 3 index lookups + heap fetches (all likely buffer pool hits)

Update Path — Normalized Advantage

sql
-- Customer changes email — ONE row updated
UPDATE customers SET email = 'new@email.com' WHERE customer_id = 1001;

1. Index scan customers PK
2. Update ONE row in heap
3. Update ONE entry in email unique index (if changed)
4. WAL: one row change
5. COMMIT

Denormalized equivalent:
  UPDATE millions of order rows where customer_name = 'John' — catastrophic

Delete Path

sql
-- Delete order — customer preserved
DELETE FROM order_items WHERE order_id = 9001;
DELETE FROM orders WHERE order_id = 9001;
-- customers row untouched ✅

Denormalized: last order deleted → customer info lost ❌

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Normalization Performance Trade-offs

OLTP (Write-Heavy) — Normalize

AspectNormalizedDenormalized
INSERTSingle fact per tableDuplicate copies
UPDATEOne row per factMany rows per fact
DELETESurgicalRisk of orphan/lost data
StorageEfficientBloated
IntegrityFK + constraintsApplication-only

OLAP / Reporting — Often Denormalize

AspectNormalized (3NF)Star Schema (denormalized)
Complex aggregationsMany JOINsFew JOINs
Query simplicityHardEasy
StorageLessMore
Load ETLTransform requiredFlat facts

When 3NF Hurts Read Performance

text
Reporting query joining 8 normalized tables:
  8-way join on 100M rows → seconds to minutes

Solutions (not "denormalize everything"):
  1. Read replica with denormalized materialized view
  2. CQRS read model
  3. Data warehouse star schema (Lesson 59)
  4. Targeted denormalization (Lesson 9)

Over-Normalization Anti-Pattern

text
❌ EXCESSIVE:

account_balance_history:
  account_id, balance_date, balance_amount, currency_code

currencies:
  currency_code, currency_name, symbol

For 3 ISO codes — separate table adds JOIN for every balance query
✅ Acceptable: CHECK (currency IN ('USD','EUR','GBP')) or CHAR(3) without FK
   for tiny stable lookup sets (architect judgment)

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

Normalization and Computational Complexity

Join Complexity by Schema Shape

text
Tables: T1, T2, ... Tn
Join on indexed FK keys:

2-table join:  O(n1 log n2) nested loop with index
k-table join:  O(product of selectivities) — grows with depth

Normalized star around customer:
  customer → accounts → transactions → transaction_details
  4-way join for full history

Denormalized flat:
  O(n) scan — simpler but larger n (more bytes per row)

Dependency Testing Complexity

text
Analyzing FDs for schema with m attributes:
  Possible FDs: O(2^m) — exponential
  Practical design: focus on business keys and obvious transitivity
  Automated tools: normalization algorithms for teaching, not daily DBA work

Design Complexity vs Runtime

text
Normalized:
  Higher design complexity (more tables, ER diagrams)
  Lower runtime update complexity (single row)
  Moderate read complexity (JOINs)

Denormalized:
  Lower design complexity initially
  Higher runtime update complexity (fan-out updates)
  Lower read complexity (single table)

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Normalization Walkthrough — Banking Example

Unnormalized Starting Point

sql
-- ❌ 0NF / bad design: repeating groups
CREATE TABLE account_statements_bad (
    account_id      BIGINT,
    customer_name   VARCHAR(100),
    customer_email  VARCHAR(255),
    statement_date  DATE,
    txn1_desc       VARCHAR(100),
    txn1_amount     DECIMAL(18,2),
    txn2_desc       VARCHAR(100),
    txn2_amount     DECIMAL(18,2),
    txn3_desc       VARCHAR(100),
    txn3_amount     DECIMAL(18,2)
);
-- Repeating groups (txn1, txn2, txn3) violate 1NF

Step 1: First Normal Form (1NF)

sql
-- ✅ Atomic values, one txn per row (still redundant customer data)
CREATE TABLE account_statements_1nf (
    statement_id    BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id      BIGINT,
    customer_name   VARCHAR(100),
    customer_email  VARCHAR(255),
    statement_date  DATE,
    txn_description VARCHAR(100),
    txn_amount      DECIMAL(18,2)
);
-- 1NF achieved: no repeating groups
-- Still: customer_name, customer_email repeated per txn row

Step 2: Second Normal Form (2NF)

sql
-- Assume composite PK (statement_id, line_no) — skip if using surrogate PK
-- Partial dependency: customer_name depends only on account_id, not full PK

-- ✅ Split partial dependencies
CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id     BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    first_name      VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    last_name       VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    email           VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id      BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id     BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
    account_number  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    balance         DECIMAL(18,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (balance >= 0)
);

CREATE TABLE statement_lines (
    line_id         BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id      BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(account_id),
    statement_date  DATE NOT NULL,
    txn_description VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    txn_amount      DECIMAL(18,2) NOT NULL
);
-- 2NF: no non-key attribute depends on part of composite key

Step 3: Third Normal Form (3NF)

sql
-- Transitive dependency example to fix:
-- account_id → branch_id → branch_name, branch_address
-- branch_name depends on branch_id, not directly on account_id

CREATE TABLE branches (
    branch_id       BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    branch_code     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    branch_name     VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    city            VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE accounts_3nf (
    account_id      BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id     BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
    branch_id       BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES branches(branch_id),
    account_number  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    balance         DECIMAL(18,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (balance >= 0)
);
-- 3NF: no transitive dependency on non-key attributes

BCNF Example

sql
-- Violation: teacher teaches one subject; multiple teachers per subject possible
-- (student, subject) → teacher
-- teacher → subject  (teacher determines subject — teacher is not candidate key)

CREATE TABLE enrollments_bad (
    student_id      BIGINT,
    subject         VARCHAR(50),
    teacher         VARCHAR(100),
    PRIMARY KEY (student_id, subject)
);

-- BCNF decomposition:
CREATE TABLE teacher_subject (
    teacher         VARCHAR(100) PRIMARY KEY,
    subject         VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE enrollments (
    student_id      BIGINT,
    teacher         VARCHAR(100) REFERENCES teacher_subject(teacher),
    PRIMARY KEY (student_id, teacher)
);

4NF — Multi-Valued Dependency

sql
-- Customer has independent multi-valued facts: products purchased AND hobbies
-- (customer_id →→ product) and (customer_id →→ hobby) — independent

-- ❌ One table creates spurious combinations:
-- customer_id | product | hobby
-- 1           | Laptop  | Skiing
-- 1           | Laptop  | Chess   ← MVD spurious row

-- ✅ 4NF:
CREATE TABLE customer_products (
    customer_id BIGINT REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
    product_id  BIGINT REFERENCES products(product_id),
    PRIMARY KEY (customer_id, product_id)
);

CREATE TABLE customer_hobbies (
    customer_id BIGINT REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
    hobby       VARCHAR(50),
    PRIMARY KEY (customer_id, hobby)
);

Verify Lossless Join

sql
-- After decomposition, join should equal original row count (no spurious rows)
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM accounts a
JOIN customers c ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id;
-- Should match COUNT of accounts (if 1:N, each account once)

Part 12 — Production Usage

Normalization in Production Systems

Banking Core — Typically 3NF / BCNF

text
ENTITIES (normalized OLTP):
  customers, accounts, transactions, branches, products, loan_schedules

WHY:
  Regulatory accuracy — balance stored once
  Customer update — one row
  Audit trail — transaction immutability with FK to account

DENORMALIZED elsewhere:
  Monthly statement PDF cache (document store)
  Regulatory reporting mart (star schema)
  Customer 360 read model (CQRS projection)

E-Commerce

text
NORMALIZED OLTP:
  products, categories, orders, order_items, inventory, payments

READ DENORMALIZED:
  product_search_index (Elasticsearch — denormalized product + category + reviews)
  cart cache (Redis — embedded JSON document)

Pattern: normalize writes, denormalize reads (Lesson 9)

Healthcare EHR

text
NORMALIZED:
  patients, encounters, diagnoses (ICD codes FK), providers, medications

LOOKUP TABLES (normalized reference data):
  icd_codes, drug_codes, procedure_codes

Avoid duplicating drug name on every prescription row — FK to drug_catalog

When Teams Under-Normalize

text
Symptoms in production:
  "Customer address wrong on some orders but not others"
  "Report totals don't match ledger"
  "Migration to update product category took 6 hours"
  "Can't add customer without order"

Root cause: flat denormalized tables from "move fast" phase
Fix: incremental normalization with migration windows (expensive)
Prevention: start 3NF for OLTP core

Part 13 — Spring Boot Integration

JPA Entity Design Reflecting Normalization

Normalized Entity Relationships

java
@Entity
@Table(name = "customers")
public class Customer {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "customer_seq")
    private Long customerId;

    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true)
    private String email;

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "customer", cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST)
    private List<Account> accounts = new ArrayList<>();
}

@Entity
@Table(name = "accounts")
public class Account {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "account_seq")
    private Long accountId;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "customer_id", nullable = false)
    private Customer customer;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "branch_id", nullable = false)
    private Branch branch;

    @Column(precision = 18, scale = 2, nullable = false)
    private BigDecimal balance;
}

Anti-Pattern: Denormalized Embedded Fields

java
// ❌ Violates 3NF — customer email duplicated on every account entity
@Entity
public class Account {
    @Id private Long accountId;
    private String customerName;   // redundant
    private String customerEmail;  // redundant — update anomaly
    private BigDecimal balance;
}

// ✅ Reference normalized Customer entity
@ManyToOne private Customer customer;

DTO Projection for Read Performance (Without Denormalizing Schema)

java
// Normalized schema + read optimization without schema denormalization
public interface AccountSummaryDto {
    Long getAccountId();
    String getAccountNumber();
    BigDecimal getBalance();
    String getCustomerEmail();  // from JOIN in query
}

@Query("""
    SELECT a.accountId AS accountId, a.accountNumber AS accountNumber,
           a.balance AS balance, c.email AS customerEmail
    FROM Account a JOIN a.customer c WHERE a.customer.customerId = :customerId
    """)
List<AccountSummaryDto> findSummariesByCustomer(@Param("customerId") Long customerId);

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

ORM and Normalization Alignment

@Embedded vs Separate Entity

java
// Value object — no independent identity — OK to embed (part of 1NF atomicity)
@Embeddable
public class Address {
    private String street;
    private String city;
    private String postalCode;
}

@Entity
public class Customer {
    @Embedded
    private Address homeAddress;  // 1:1 component — not a separate table need
}

// If Address shared by multiple customers → normalize to address table
@ManyToOne
@JoinColumn(name = "address_id")
private Address address;

@ElementCollection — Normalization Warning

java
// ❌ @ElementCollection creates separate collection table but
//    tempts storing multi-valued attributes without proper entity
@ElementCollection
private List<String> phoneNumbers;  // OK for simple cases

// For complex repeated data with own lifecycle → @OneToMany separate entity
@OneToMany(mappedBy = "customer")
private List<PhoneNumber> phoneNumbers;

Fetch Strategy and Normalized Schema

text
Normalized schema + LAZY loading:
  order.getCustomer().getEmail()  → 2 queries (N+1 risk)

Solutions (without denormalizing schema):
  JOIN FETCH in repository query
  @EntityGraph
  DTO projection (above)

Normalization is schema design — not an excuse for N+1 (Lesson 53)

Cascade and Normalized Boundaries

java
// Normalized aggregate root pattern (DDD):
// Customer owns Accounts for creation — not for deletion in banking
@OneToMany(mappedBy = "customer", cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST)
private List<Account> accounts;

// NEVER CascadeType.REMOVE on financial child entities

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

Normalization Decision Framework

Target Normal Form by System Type

System TypeTarget Normal FormNotes
OLTP banking/payments3NF / BCNFNon-negotiable for core ledger
E-commerce orders3NFProduct catalog may use JSONB hybrid
Data warehouseStar/snowflake (denormalized dimensions)Lesson 59
Read models / CQRSDenormalizedBuilt from normalized source
Reference/lookup data3NF or flat lookup tableSmall stable sets
Event logsOften flat / time-seriesAppend-only, not normalized ER

Normalization Checklist for New Schema

text
□ Each table has single clear purpose (one entity type)
□ Every non-key column depends on the whole key
□ No non-key column depends on another non-key column
□ Repeating groups extracted to child tables
□ Lookup/reference data in separate tables with FK
□ Each fact stored in exactly one place
□ FK constraints on all relationships
□ Surrogate PK + natural business keys as UNIQUE (Lesson 6)
□ Read performance addressed separately (views, replicas, cache)

When to Stop Normalizing

text
Stop at 3NF/BCNF when:
  ✅ All anomalies eliminated
  ✅ Schema understandable to team
  ✅ JOIN count per common query ≤ 4-5 (or mitigated by indexes/views)

Go to 4NF/5NF when:
  Multi-valued dependencies cause spurious query results
  Rare in typical enterprise OLTP — know the theory for interviews

Do NOT normalize further if:
  Tiny lookup (< 20 rows) → separate table adds JOIN noise (judgment call)
  Read path requires 10-way joins → denormalize read side, not break OLTP

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Storing Everything in One "God Table"

sql
-- ❌ 80 columns, repeating data, mixed entities
CREATE TABLE banking_everything (...);

-- ✅ Entity-per-table: customers, accounts, transactions, branches

Mistake 2: Duplicating Customer Data on Every Order

java
// ❌ customerEmail on Order entity
// ✅ @ManyToOne Customer customer

Mistake 3: Confusing 1NF with "One Table Per Application Screen"

text
1NF ≠ one table total
1NF = atomic values within each table
Screens can JOIN multiple normalized tables

Mistake 4: Over-Normalizing Tiny Lookups

sql
-- ❌ Separate currency_names table for 3 currencies with JOIN on every row
-- ✅ CHAR(3) currency + CHECK or enum; or small currencies table (50 rows — fine)

Mistake 5: Denormalizing OLTP Core for Report Speed

text
❌ Add report columns to transactions table
✅ Materialized view or read replica star schema

Mistake 6: Ignoring Functional Dependencies During Design

text
Jumping to CREATE TABLE without asking:
  "Does this column depend on the full primary key?"
  "Does this column depend on another non-key column?"
→ Schema accumulates redundancy over sprints

Mistake 7: @ElementCollection Instead of Proper Entity

java
// Phone numbers with type, verified flag, country code → separate PhoneNumber entity
// Not List<String> in element collection if attributes grow

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is normalization?

Process of organizing tables to reduce redundancy and prevent update, insert, delete anomalies by decomposing tables based on functional dependencies.

Q2: What is 1NF?

Each cell contains a single atomic value; no repeating groups or arrays in columns.

Q3: Name the three anomalies normalization prevents.

Update anomaly (inconsistent duplicates), insert anomaly (can't add fact without unrelated fact), delete anomaly (deleting one fact loses another).

Q4: What is a foreign key's role in normalized schema?

Connects related tables; enforces that reference exists in parent — maintains referential integrity across decomposed tables.

Q5: What is 3NF?

Every non-key attribute depends only on the primary key — no transitive dependencies through other non-key attributes.

Mid-Level

Q6: Explain partial vs transitive dependency with example.

Partial: (order_id, product_id) → product_name but product_name depends only on product_id. Transitive: account_id → branch_id → branch_name where branch_name depends on branch_id not account_id directly.

Q7: Difference between 3NF and BCNF?

3NF allows non-key determinants if B is a prime attribute (part of candidate key). BCNF: every determinant must be a candidate key — stricter.

Q8: When would you NOT normalize further?

Tiny stable lookup sets, read models, data warehouses (star schema), or when JOIN cost exceeds redundancy cost — targeted denormalization on read path only.

Q9: How does normalization affect storage and joins?

Less redundant storage, smaller indexes, single-row updates. More JOINs on reads — mitigated by indexing FKs, views, caching, read replicas.

Q10: Is MongoDB "non-normalized"?

Document model often embeds related data (denormalized by design). References between documents analogous to FK — application-enforced. Different trade-off for flexible schema and read speed.

Senior

Q11: Design normalized schema for e-commerce: customers, orders, products, payments.

customers, products, orders (FK customer), order_items (FK order, product, qty, price at time), payments (FK order, amount, status). Price on order_items not products — historical fact. 3NF with FK indexes.

Q12: OLTP normalized vs warehouse star schema — explain coexistence.

OLTP 3NF for correctness. ETL to star schema (fact_sales, dim_customer, dim_product) for analytics. Same enterprise, different models for different access patterns — polyglot persistence at schema level.

Q13: Customer address on order table — normalize or denormalize?

Normalize: FK to customer/address for current mailings. Denormalize snapshot: ship_to_address on order as historical fact (address at order time) — not redundancy, it's a valid immutable fact. Distinguish redundancy from intentional snapshot.

Q14: Lossless join decomposition — why it matters?

Bad decomposition creates spurious rows when tables rejoined — wrong query results. Always verify join equals original data cardinality for the business rule.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Team has 200-table 3NF schema; reports take 10 minutes. Strategy?

Do NOT denormalize OLTP. Add: read replica, materialized views, columnar warehouse, CQRS read models, index tuning. Denormalize only read path. Preserve 3NF core for writes.

Q16: Microservices and normalization — one database per service?

Each service owns normalized schema for its bounded context. No shared normalized schema across services. Cross-service data via IDs and events — not shared 3NF database (anti-pattern).

Scenario

Scenario: "Product category changed but old orders show new category in reports."

Bug: order_items uses live FK join to products.category without storing category at sale time. Fix: add category_id or category_name to order_items at order time (snapshot — valid denormalization of historical fact, not a 3NF violation for transactional record).

Part 20 — Revision Sheet

Normal Forms (Memorize)

  • 1NF — atomic values, no repeating groups
  • 2NF — no partial dependency on composite PK
  • 3NF — no transitive dependency on non-key attrs
  • BCNF — every determinant is candidate key
  • 4NF — no multi-valued dependencies
  • 5NF — lossless join decomposition

Dependencies

text
Partial:     (PK part) → non-key attr        → 2NF fix
Transitive:  non-key → non-key → non-key    → 3NF fix
MVD:         A →→ B and A →→ C independent  → 4NF fix

Anomalies

text
UPDATE  — change fact in one place, miss duplicates
INSERT  — can't add fact without unrelated fact
DELETE  — remove one fact, lose another

Architect Rules

  1. OLTP core → 3NF minimum
  2. Historical facts (order price) → snapshot on line item — OK
  3. Read performance → views/replicas — not break OLTP normalization
  4. Every FK indexed; every fact stored once
  5. Lesson 9 denormalization is deliberate, not lazy design

Part 1 — Concept

What Is Denormalization?

Denormalization is the intentional introduction of redundancy into a database schema (or read model) to improve read performance, query simplicity, or scalability — after accepting the trade-offs that normalization (Lesson 8) was designed to prevent.

text
NORMALIZATION (Lesson 8)              DENORMALIZATION (Lesson 9)
────────────────────────              ────────────────────────────
Each fact stored once                 Same fact stored in multiple places
Fewer anomalies                       Risk of update/insert/delete anomalies
More JOINs on read                    Fewer or zero JOINs on read
Optimized for OLTP writes             Optimized for read-heavy workloads
Default for core transactional data   Deliberate choice for specific paths

Critical Distinction

text
❌ BAD "Denormalization":
   Lazy design — one giant table because JOINs are "hard"
   No plan for consistency
   Duplicated data with no ownership rules

✅ GOOD Denormalization:
   Measured trade-off documented in architecture
   Clear source of truth (normalized OLTP)
   Controlled refresh or sync strategy
   Acceptable staleness defined (RPO for reads)

Forms of Denormalization

text
DENORMALIZATION TECHNIQUES

├── SCHEMA-LEVEL
│   ├── Redundant columns (copy customer_name onto order)
│   ├── Pre-joined tables (flat reporting table)
│   ├── Aggregates stored (order_count on customer)
│   └── Summary tables (daily_balance_snapshot)
│
├── VIEW-LEVEL
│   ├── Materialized views (precomputed JOIN results)
│   └── Indexed views (SQL Server)
│
├── ARCHITECTURE-LEVEL
│   ├── Read replicas serving denormalized queries
│   ├── CQRS read models (event projections)
│   ├── Data warehouse star schema
│   └── Cache layers (Redis embedded documents)
│
└── DOCUMENT / NOSQL
    ├── Embedded documents (MongoDB product with reviews)
    └── Wide-column denormalization (Cassandra query-driven tables)

Denormalization vs Normalization — Not Opposites in Production

text
PRODUCTION ENTERPRISE PATTERN:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WRITE PATH (Source of Truth)          NORMALIZED 3NF        │
│  Oracle / PostgreSQL — customers, accounts, transactions   │
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                             │ CDC / Kafka / ETL
         ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
         ▼                   ▼                   ▼
┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐
│ Materialized    │ │ Elasticsearch   │ │ Star Schema     │
│ View (PG)       │ │ Product Index   │ │ (Warehouse)     │
│ DENORMALIZED    │ │ DENORMALIZED    │ │ DENORMALIZED    │
└─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Denormalization

text
1970s   Normalization dominates — denormalization seen as "bad practice"
1980s   Data warehouses born (Inmon, Kimball)
        └── Star schema = intentional denormalization for analytics

1990s   OLAP cubes (MOLAP/ROLAP) — pre-aggregated denormalized data
        Materialized views in Oracle 8i (1999)

2000s   Web scale: read >> write on many workloads
        Memcached, Redis — denormalized cache as standard layer
        MySpace/Facebook denormalize feeds, social graphs

2010s   CQRS + Event Sourcing (Fowler, Young)
        Separate write model (normalized) and read model (denormalized)
        MongoDB: "embed vs reference" = denormalization decision

2015+   Read replicas, Aurora, streaming ETL (Kafka + Flink)
        Real-time denormalized projections (customer 360, search indexes)

2020s   HTAP systems (TiDB, AlloyDB) blur line — columnar scan on normalized data
        Denormalization still required for Elasticsearch, Redis, Cassandra access patterns

Historical Lesson

Denormalization became respectable when the industry separated transactional correctness (OLTP, normalized) from analytical and read scale (OLAP, denormalized). The mistake is applying warehouse patterns to OLTP cores.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does Denormalization Solve?

Problem 1: Expensive Multi-Table JOINs at Scale

sql
-- Normalized 6-way join on 100M rows — 30 seconds on primary OLTP
SELECT c.name, a.account_number, t.amount, p.product_name, ...
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON ...
JOIN transactions t ON ...
JOIN products p ON ...
JOIN categories cat ON ...
JOIN branches b ON ...
WHERE t.created_at >= '2024-01-01';

Denormalized fact table or materialized view: single table scan — 2 seconds.

Problem 2: Read-Heavy Workloads Overwhelming OLTP

text
E-commerce product page:
  10,000 reads/sec per hot product
  1 write/sec (price update)

Normalized: 5 JOINs × 10K RPS = 50K query operations/sec on primary
Denormalized Redis/Elasticsearch document: 10K simple GETs/sec

Problem 3: Analytics on Operational Database

text
BI tool connected to OLTP:
  Full table scans evict buffer pool
  Aggregations lock rows
  Reports slow down payments

Denormalized warehouse/star schema on read replica:
  Analytics isolated from OLTP

Problem 4: API Response Latency Budget

text
Mobile banking app: p99 < 200ms for account summary
Normalized: 4 round trips or 4 JOINs
Denormalized read model: 1 query, pre-joined, pre-aggregated

Problem 5: Distributed / NoSQL Access Patterns

text
Cassandra: no JOINs — must denormalize at write time
MongoDB: embed reviews in product document — denormalized by design
Query pattern drives table design — not ER normalization

Unified Problem Statement

When read performance, query simplicity, or distributed access patterns cannot be met by normalized OLTP schema and indexing alone, controlled denormalization — with explicit consistency rules — solves the read-scale problem normalization intentionally does not address.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Denormalize After Normalizing?

Normalization optimizes write correctness. Many systems optimize for read patterns that normalization penalizes:

Read PatternNormalized CostDenormalized Benefit
Dashboard aggregationsMany JOINs + GROUP BYPre-computed summary
Search / faceted browseMulti-table JOINFlat search index
Product catalog pageJOIN product + inventory + reviewsSingle document
Account summary APIJOIN customer + accounts + balancesPre-joined read model
Time-series reportsScan + aggregate billionsPre-aggregated rollups

The CAP / Consistency Trade-off in Denormalization

text
Denormalized copy is ALWAYS stale relative to source of truth (unless synchronous):

  Source (Oracle):     balance = 1000  (committed)
  Redis cache:         balance = 1000  (synced)
  — payment of 100 —
  Source:              balance = 900   (committed)
  Redis (before sync): balance = 1000  (stale by milliseconds to seconds)

Architect must define: acceptable staleness for each denormalized copy

Denormalization Is Not a Replacement for Indexes

text
Before denormalizing, verify:
  □ Missing indexes on FK and filter columns? (Lesson 26)
  □ Buffer pool sized correctly? (Lesson 3)
  □ Query plan suboptimal? (Lesson 25)
  □ N+1 from ORM? (Lesson 53)

Denormalize when structural JOIN cost remains too high AFTER tuning

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Denormalization Works Internally

Type 1: Redundant Column (Same Database)

sql
-- Normalized source: customers.email
-- Denormalized copy on orders for historical snapshot OR read speed

ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN customer_email VARCHAR(255);

-- Populated at INSERT time from customers.email
-- NOT updated when customer changes email (snapshot semantics)
-- OR updated via trigger/application (active copy — anomaly risk)
text
WRITE PATH (INSERT order):
  1. Read customer.email (JOIN or separate SELECT)
  2. Insert order row with customer_email copied
  3. Single table read later — no JOIN

INTERNAL STORAGE:
  Extra column bytes per order row
  Wider rows → fewer rows per page → more I/O on full scan
  Trade-off: avoid JOIN CPU vs extra storage I/O

Type 2: Materialized View (Precomputed JOIN)

sql
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_account_summary AS
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.first_name,
    c.last_name,
    c.email,
    a.account_id,
    a.account_number,
    a.balance,
    a.status
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON c.customer_id = a.customer_id;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_mv_account_summary ON mv_account_summary(account_id);

-- Refresh strategies:
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_account_summary;                    -- locks (PG old)
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY mv_account_summary;       -- no read block (needs unique index)
text
INTERNAL WORKING:

  Base tables (normalized) ──REFRESH──▶ Materialized storage (physical copy)
  
  Query hits mv_account_summary:
    Optimizer chooses sequential/index scan on flat table
    No JOIN at query time — JOIN done at refresh time

  Storage cost: duplicate of joined result on disk
  Freshness: refresh interval (cron, trigger, or CDC stream)

Type 3: CQRS Read Model (Event Projection)

text
WRITE MODEL (normalized)              READ MODEL (denormalized)
────────────────────────              ──────────────────────────
PaymentService                        AccountSummaryReadModel
  Oracle: payments, accounts            PostgreSQL read DB or Redis:
  ACID transaction                      { customerId, accounts: [...], totalBalance }

         PaymentCompletedEvent ──Kafka──▶ ProjectionConsumer
                                              UPDATE read model
text
INTERNAL FLOW:

1. Payment committed in Oracle (normalized)
2. Event published to Kafka (after outbox)
3. Projection consumer receives event
4. Consumer updates denormalized read model:
     read_db.account_summary SET total_balance = total_balance - 100
5. API reads from read model — fast, flat structure

Lag: event processing latency (typically 100ms–2s)
Consistency: eventual

Type 4: Star Schema (Warehouse)

text
FACT TABLE (measures, foreign keys to dimensions):
  fact_sales(sale_id, date_key, customer_key, product_key, amount, qty)

DIMENSION TABLES (denormalized descriptive attributes):
  dim_customer(customer_key, name, email, city, segment, ...)  -- wide
  dim_product(product_key, name, category, subcategory, brand, ...)
  dim_date(date_key, day, month, quarter, year, is_holiday, ...)

Dimension denormalization: category + subcategory in dim_product (avoid snowflake JOINs in reports)

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Physical Storage Impact of Denormalization

Redundant Columns — Row Width Growth

text
NORMALIZED order row: ~40 bytes
  order_id, customer_id, order_date, status

DENORMALIZED order row: ~200 bytes
  + customer_name (50B), customer_email (50B), ship_address (100B)

Page capacity (8KB):
  Normalized: ~200 orders/page
  Denormalized: ~40 orders/page

Full order table scan: 5× more pages to read
Point lookup by PK: similar (one page either way)
Reporting query avoiding JOIN: faster despite wider rows

Materialized View Storage

text
Base tables total: 50 GB
Materialized view (join + filter): 15 GB additional disk

Oracle: segment in tablespace, indexes on MV
PostgreSQL: physical heap file like a table
Refresh: rewrite or incremental (depends on DB/log-based CDC)

Monitor: pg_total_relation_size('mv_account_summary')

Aggregate / Summary Tables

sql
CREATE TABLE daily_account_balance (
    account_id      BIGINT,
    balance_date    DATE,
    closing_balance DECIMAL(18,2),
    txn_count       INTEGER,
    PRIMARY KEY (account_id, balance_date)
);

-- Populated by nightly batch or stream aggregation
-- Storage: one row per account per day vs millions of transactions
-- Query "balance trend 90 days": 90 rows vs scan 1M transaction rows

Cassandra Denormalization — Query-Driven Tables

sql
-- Same payment data, two tables for two query patterns (full duplication)

CREATE TABLE payments_by_account (
    account_id BIGINT,
    event_time TIMESTAMP,
    payment_id UUID,
    amount DECIMAL,
    PRIMARY KEY (account_id, event_time, payment_id)
);

CREATE TABLE payments_by_merchant (
    merchant_id BIGINT,
    event_time TIMESTAMP,
    payment_id UUID,
    account_id BIGINT,
    amount DECIMAL,
    PRIMARY KEY (merchant_id, event_time, payment_id)
);

-- Write once → write to BOTH tables (application or dual-write pattern)
-- Storage: 2× — traded for read performance without JOINs

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Denormalization and Memory

Buffer Pool — Wider Denormalized Rows

text
Denormalized flat table in buffer pool:
  Fewer rows per page → more page faults for sequential scans
  BUT: one table vs three tables for JOIN → fewer total pages for equivalent report query

Example:
  JOIN path: touch customers page + accounts page + index pages
  Flat path: touch mv_account_summary pages only
  
  Hot reporting query: flat table wins if MV fits in buffer pool

Redis / Cache — Denormalized Documents

json
// Key: account:summary:1001
{
  "customerId": 1001,
  "name": "Ankur Kumar",
  "email": "ankur@email.com",
  "accounts": [
    { "accountId": 5001, "type": "SAVINGS", "balance": 15000.00 },
    { "accountId": 5002, "type": "CHECKING", "balance": 3500.00 }
  ],
  "totalBalance": 18500.00
}
text
Memory: entire summary in one Redis key — ~1-2 KB
Read: O(1) GET — no JOIN, no SQL parser
Invalidation: on PaymentCompleted event → recompute or patch totalBalance
Stale window: event consumer lag

Pre-Aggregated Rollups — Minimal Memory Footprint

text
Transaction table: 500M rows — won't fit in buffer pool
daily_account_balance: 365 × 1M accounts = 365M rows max — still large
monthly rollup: 12 × 1M = 12M rows — fits in buffer pool easily

Architect: tier aggregation (hourly → daily → monthly) for dashboard queries

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Denormalization Execution Flows

Flow 1: Read from Materialized View

sql
SELECT account_id, balance, email
FROM mv_account_summary
WHERE customer_id = 1001;
text
1. Parser → accounts MV as heap table (not a view join at runtime)
2. Optimizer: index scan on customer_id (if indexed) or filter
3. Sequential read of matching rows from MV storage
4. No access to customers or accounts base tables
5. Return results

Latency: ~5ms (indexed) vs ~50ms (3-table JOIN on normalized)
Staleness: last REFRESH time

Flow 2: INSERT with Denormalized Snapshot

sql
-- Application service (Spring Boot)
INSERT INTO orders (order_id, customer_id, customer_email, ship_address, ...)
SELECT nextval('order_seq'), 1001, c.email, c.address, ...
FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = 1001;
text
1. Read customer row (indexed PK lookup)
2. Copy email, address into order INSERT
3. Commit order — snapshot frozen at order time
4. Future customer email change does NOT update order (intentional)
5. Read order history: no JOIN to customers needed

Execution: 1 SELECT + 1 INSERT vs 1 INSERT + JOIN on every read
Write cost increases slightly; read cost decreases significantly

Flow 3: CQRS Projection Update

text
PaymentService.processPayment():
  1. BEGIN (Oracle)
  2. UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100
  3. INSERT payments (...)
  4. INSERT outbox_events (PaymentCompleted)
  5. COMMIT

OutboxPoller → Kafka: PaymentCompleted { accountId, newBalance, customerId }

AccountSummaryProjector:
  6. Consume event
  7. UPDATE read_model.account_summary
     SET total_balance = :newBalance WHERE customer_id = :customerId
  8. UPDATE Redis cache key account:summary:{customerId} (TTL refresh)

Mobile app read:
  9. GET read_model or Redis — denormalized, <10ms
  (May be 200ms stale if consumer lag)

Flow 4: Nightly ETL to Star Schema

text
02:00 — Extract from OLTP (normalized) via CDC or batch export
02:30 — Transform: join dimensions, compute measures
03:00 — Load fact_sales, update dim_customer (SCD Type 2 if history needed)
06:00 — BI dashboards query warehouse — zero load on OLTP primary

OLTP: normalized, untouched
Warehouse: denormalized star — optimized for GROUP BY, slice/dice

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Denormalization Performance Trade-offs

Read Performance Gains

PatternNormalized LatencyDenormalized LatencyTypical Gain
Account summary API50–200ms (JOINs)5–20ms (flat/MV)5–10×
Product search500ms+ (SQL LIKE)20ms (Elasticsearch)25×+
Dashboard KPIMinutes (OLTP scan)Seconds (rollup table)100×+
Hot cache read5ms (SQL)0.1ms (Redis doc)50×

Write Performance Cost

TechniqueWrite Overhead
Snapshot column on INSERT+1 SELECT (customer lookup)
Maintain aggregate column+1 UPDATE on parent per child INSERT
Dual Cassandra tables2× writes
MV REFRESH FULLPeriodic batch — spikes I/O
CQRS projectionAsync — doesn't block write path
Star schema ETLBatch — no OLTP write impact

Consistency Cost

text
ACTIVE DENORMALIZATION (update copy on every source change):
  Customer email change → UPDATE all orders? (millions of rows — disaster)
  → NEVER for mutable attributes across many rows

SNAPSHOT DENORMALIZATION (copy at point in time):
  Order stores email at purchase — never updated — ✅ correct semantics

COMPUTED DENORMALIZATION (MV, CQRS, cache):
  Refresh on schedule or event — staleness bounded by lag — ✅ acceptable for reads

When Denormalization Hurts

text
❌ Mutable data copied to many rows (customer name on every transaction line)
❌ Full MV refresh every minute on 500GB join — I/O storm
❌ Denormalized OLTP core with no sync strategy — anomalies guaranteed
❌ 80-column "reporting table" on primary DB — buffer pool pollution

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

Complexity of Normalized vs Denormalized Operations

OperationNormalized 3NFDenormalized FlatCQRS Read Model
Point read (PK)O(log n) + k JOINsO(log n)O(1) cache / O(log n)
Range reportO(k joins × n)O(n) scan flatO(n) on rollup
Insert factO(log n) one tableO(log n) + copy fieldsO(log n) write + event O(1)
Update mutable attrO(1) one rowO(n) all copiesO(1) source + async projection
StorageO(facts) minimalO(facts × redundancy factor)O(facts) + O(projection)
ConsistencyStrong (ACID)Application-managedEventual

Redundancy Factor

text
Redundancy R = (denormalized_size / normalized_size)

R = 1.0  → fully normalized
R = 1.5  → moderate (snapshot columns, MV for hot queries)
R = 3.0  → heavy (Cassandra dual tables, wide star dimensions)
R = 10+  → search indexes, document stores with embedded arrays

Higher R → faster reads, harder writes, more sync complexity

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Denormalization Patterns in SQL

Pattern 1: Historical Snapshot (Valid Denormalization)

sql
CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id         BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
    -- Snapshot at order time — NOT updated when customer changes
    customer_name       VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    customer_email      VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    ship_to_address     TEXT NOT NULL,
    order_total         DECIMAL(18,2) NOT NULL,
    ordered_at          TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
    order_item_id       BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id            BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(order_id),
    product_id          BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES products(product_id),
    product_name        VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,  -- snapshot — price/name at sale time
    unit_price          DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
    quantity            INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0)
);

Pattern 2: Materialized View (PostgreSQL)

sql
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_customer_account_totals AS
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.first_name,
    c.last_name,
    c.email,
    COUNT(a.account_id)     AS account_count,
    COALESCE(SUM(a.balance), 0) AS total_balance
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name, c.last_name, c.email;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_mv_cust_totals ON mv_customer_account_totals(customer_id);

-- Refresh every 5 minutes via pg_cron or application scheduler
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY mv_customer_account_totals;

Pattern 3: Summary / Rollup Table

sql
CREATE TABLE account_daily_summary (
    account_id          BIGINT NOT NULL,
    summary_date        DATE NOT NULL,
    opening_balance     DECIMAL(18,2) NOT NULL,
    closing_balance     DECIMAL(18,2) NOT NULL,
    total_credits       DECIMAL(18,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    total_debits        DECIMAL(18,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    txn_count           INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    PRIMARY KEY (account_id, summary_date)
);

-- Populated by batch job reading normalized transactions table
INSERT INTO account_daily_summary (...)
SELECT account_id, txn_date::date, ...
FROM transactions
WHERE txn_date >= CURRENT_DATE - 1
GROUP BY account_id, txn_date::date;

Pattern 4: Oracle Materialized View with FAST Refresh

sql
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW LOG ON accounts WITH ROWID, SEQUENCE
    (account_id, customer_id, balance, status) INCLUDING NEW VALUES;

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_active_accounts
BUILD IMMEDIATE
REFRESH FAST ON COMMIT  -- or ON DEMAND
AS
SELECT a.account_id, a.customer_id, a.balance, c.email
FROM accounts a
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = a.customer_id
WHERE a.status = 'ACTIVE';

-- FAST refresh: applies only changed rows from MV log — not full rebuild

Pattern 5: Trigger-Maintained Aggregate (Use Carefully)

sql
-- Denormalized order_count on customers — maintained by trigger
ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN active_order_count INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION trg_update_order_count()
RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
BEGIN
    IF TG_OP = 'INSERT' THEN
        UPDATE customers SET active_order_count = active_order_count + 1
        WHERE customer_id = NEW.customer_id;
    ELSIF TG_OP = 'DELETE' THEN
        UPDATE customers SET active_order_count = active_order_count - 1
        WHERE customer_id = OLD.customer_id;
    END IF;
    RETURN NULL;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER orders_count_trigger
AFTER INSERT OR DELETE ON orders
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION trg_update_order_count();

-- ⚠️ Adds write overhead; race conditions if not careful; prefer event projection for scale

Part 13 — Spring Boot Integration

Denormalized Read Models in Spring Boot

CQRS-Style Separate Read Repository

java
// WRITE side — normalized JPA entity (Oracle)
@Entity
@Table(name = "accounts")
public class Account { /* normalized — Lesson 8 */ }

// READ side — denormalized projection (PostgreSQL read DB or same DB MV)
@Entity
@Table(name = "account_summary_read_model")
@Immutable  // Hibernate: no writes through this entity
public class AccountSummaryReadModel {

    @Id
    private Long customerId;

    private String customerName;
    private String email;
    private BigDecimal totalBalance;
    private Integer accountCount;
    private Instant lastUpdated;
}

@Repository
public interface AccountSummaryReadRepository
        extends JpaRepository<AccountSummaryReadModel, Long> {
    // Single-table query — no JOIN
}

Event-Driven Projection

java
@Component
@Slf4j
public class AccountSummaryProjector {

    private final AccountSummaryReadRepository readRepo;

    @KafkaListener(topics = "payment-completed")
    @Transactional("readTransactionManager")
    public void onPaymentCompleted(PaymentCompletedEvent event) {
        readRepo.findById(event.getCustomerId())
            .ifPresent(summary -> {
                summary.setTotalBalance(event.getNewTotalBalance());
                summary.setLastUpdated(Instant.now());
                readRepo.save(summary);
            });
    }
}

Cache-Aside Denormalized DTO

java
@Service
public class AccountSummaryService {

    private final AccountSummaryReadRepository readRepo;
    private final RedisTemplate<String, AccountSummaryDto> redis;

    public AccountSummaryDto getSummary(Long customerId) {
        String key = "account:summary:" + customerId;

        AccountSummaryDto cached = redis.opsForValue().get(key);
        if (cached != null) return cached;

        AccountSummaryDto dto = readRepo.findById(customerId)
            .map(AccountSummaryDto::from)
            .orElseThrow();

        redis.opsForValue().set(key, dto, Duration.ofMinutes(5));
        return dto;
    }

    @KafkaListener(topics = "payment-completed")
    public void invalidate(PaymentCompletedEvent event) {
        redis.delete("account:summary:" + event.getCustomerId());
    }
}

Snapshot on Write — Order Service

java
@Transactional
public Order createOrder(CreateOrderRequest request) {
    Customer customer = customerRepo.findById(request.getCustomerId())
        .orElseThrow();

    Order order = new Order();
    order.setCustomerId(customer.getCustomerId());
    // Denormalized snapshot — intentional, immutable
    order.setCustomerName(customer.getFirstName() + " " + customer.getLastName());
    order.setCustomerEmail(customer.getEmail());
    order.setShipToAddress(request.getShipAddress());

    return orderRepo.save(order);
}

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

ORM and Denormalization

When to Map Denormalized Tables

java
// Materialized view or read model — read-only entity
@Entity
@Table(name = "mv_customer_account_totals")
@Immutable
public class CustomerAccountTotalsView {
    @Id
    private Long customerId;
    private String email;
    private BigDecimal totalBalance;
    private Integer accountCount;
}

// Repository — no save(), no cascade
// ddl-auto: validate — MV created by Flyway, not Hibernate

@Formula — Virtual Denormalization (Read-Time)

java
@Entity
public class Account {

    @Id
    private Long accountId;

    @Formula("(SELECT c.email FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = customer_id)")
    private String customerEmail;  // computed on every SELECT — NOT true denormalization

    // ⚠️ @Formula causes subquery per row — N+1 risk — avoid for lists
    // Use JOIN FETCH or MV instead for production read paths
}

@Embedded Snapshot Value Object

java
@Embeddable
@Data
public class CustomerSnapshot {
    private String name;
    private String email;
    // Immutable after order creation — set only in factory method
}

@Entity
public class Order {
    @Embedded
    private CustomerSnapshot customerSnapshot;  // denormalized snapshot columns in orders table
}

Avoid Hibernate @SecondaryTable for Denormalization

text
@SecondaryTable — splits entity across two physical tables (normalization tool)
Not denormalization — use redundant columns or separate read entity instead

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

When to Denormalize — Architect Decision Tree

text
START: Read path too slow after index tuning (Lesson 26-32)

Is data immutable historical fact (order price at sale)?
  YES → Snapshot column on INSERT ✅ (not a consistency risk)

Is query for analytics/reporting?
  YES → Star schema / MV on read replica ✅
  NO ↓

Is read:write ratio > 100:1 on this path?
  YES → Redis cache or CQRS read model ✅
  NO ↓

Is JOIN count > 4 and query latency > SLA?
  YES → Targeted MV or flat read model ✅
  NO ↓

Is access pattern in Cassandra/NoSQL (no JOIN)?
  YES → Query-driven denormalized tables ✅
  NO ↓

Stay normalized — optimize indexes and queries first

Consistency Model per Denormalized Copy

CopyConsistencyOwnerInvalidation
Order snapshot columnsImmutableOrder ServiceNever
MV account summaryEventual (5 min)DBA / batchREFRESH CONCURRENTLY
Redis account cacheEventual (TTL 5 min)Account ServiceEvent or TTL
Elasticsearch productEventual (seconds)Catalog ServiceCDC / event
Warehouse factsEventual (daily)Data teamETL schedule

Anti-Patterns for Architects

text
❌ Denormalize core ledger tables
❌ Update denormalized copies synchronously in same transaction across DBs (2PC)
❌ No staleness SLA documented for read models
❌ BI on primary OLTP — "just add indexes" without read replica
❌ Copy mutable customer attributes to all transaction rows
❌ Full MV refresh every minute on huge dataset

Snapshot vs Active Copy

TypeUpdated when source changes?Anomaly riskExample
SnapshotNeverNoneOrder line unit_price
Active copyShould be — rarely done correctlyHighcustomer_name on all orders
ProjectedAsync via event/MVBounded stalenessAccount total_balance read model
CachedTTL or invalidationBounded stalenessRedis product page

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Denormalizing the OLTP Core

text
❌ Merge customers + accounts + transactions into reporting_mega_table on primary DB
✅ Normalized OLTP + MV or warehouse on replica

Mistake 2: Active Copy of Mutable Data

sql
-- ❌ Copy customer_name to every transaction — 10M rows to update on name change
-- ✅ Snapshot only for immutable historical context (order ship name at order time)

Mistake 3: Materialized View on Primary Without CONCURRENTLY

sql
-- ❌ REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW during business hours — locks reads
-- ✅ REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY + unique index, off-peak schedule

Mistake 4: Cache as Source of Truth

text
❌ Balance stored only in Redis
✅ Balance authoritative in Oracle; Redis is cache with TTL + invalidation

Mistake 5: No Invalidation Strategy

text
Redis cache populated but never invalidated on payment
→ User sees stale balance until TTL expires
✅ Kafka event → cache delete or update

Mistake 6: @Formula Instead of Real Denormalization

java
// ❌ Subquery per row in list of 1000 accounts
@Formula("(SELECT ...)")
// ✅ MV or JOIN FETCH in repository query

Mistake 7: Denormalizing Before Index Tuning

text
Reports slow → team adds 15 redundant columns
Root cause: missing index on transactions(account_id, created_at)
Fix indexes first — denormalize only if JOIN cost still exceeds SLA

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is denormalization?

Intentional redundancy to improve read performance or simplify queries, trading off normalization benefits.

Q2: Difference between normalization and denormalization?

Normalization eliminates redundancy for write integrity. Denormalization reintroduces redundancy for read speed — deliberately.

Q3: Give one valid reason to denormalize.

Expensive JOINs on read-heavy reporting path; pre-compute via materialized view or summary table.

Q4: What is a materialized view?

Physical storage of a query result — refreshed periodically. Queries hit flat pre-joined data instead of runtime JOINs.

Q5: Is denormalization bad?

Not inherently — bad when applied to OLTP core without consistency strategy. Good for read models, caches, warehouses.

Mid-Level

Q6: Snapshot denormalization vs active copy?

Snapshot: copy at INSERT, never updated — correct for order price/address. Active copy: tries to mirror source — update anomaly risk across many rows.

Q7: Explain CQRS in context of denormalization.

Command side: normalized write model, ACID. Query side: denormalized read model updated via events. Eventual consistency between them.

Q8: When would you use a summary/rollup table?

Dashboard KPIs, trend charts — pre-aggregate daily/monthly from billions of transactions. Avoid scanning fact table repeatedly.

Q9: How keep Redis cache consistent with database?

Cache-aside: read through cache, populate on miss. Invalidate or update on write event (Kafka). TTL as safety net. Never write-only cache without invalidation.

Q10: Star schema — normalized or denormalized?

Denormalized dimensions (wide dim_product with category embedded). Fact table normalized to dimension keys. Designed for analytics, not OLTP.

Senior

Q11: Design read path for mobile banking account summary (p99 < 100ms).

Normalized Oracle for writes. CQRS projection or MV on read replica: customer_id, accounts[], totalBalance. Redis cache with Kafka invalidation on PaymentCompleted. Staleness SLA: 2 seconds acceptable.

Q12: Order line stores product_name — normalization violation?

No — intentional snapshot of historical fact (name at sale time). Not redundancy — immutable business record. Distinct from copying mutable current product name without snapshot semantics.

Q13: FULL vs CONCURRENTLY MV refresh?

FULL: rebuilds entire MV, may lock reads. CONCURRENTLY: incremental rebuild using unique index, no read block — requires UNIQUE index on MV. Use CONCURRENTLY in production.

Q14: Denormalize in Cassandra for payment queries by account and merchant?

Two tables: payments_by_account PK(account_id, time), payments_by_merchant PK(merchant_id, time). Dual write on payment insert. 2× storage, 0 JOINs — standard Cassandra pattern.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Team wants to denormalize Oracle core tables for reporting. Alternative?

Read replica + materialized views + nightly ETL to warehouse. Preserve 3NF primary for ACID. Define staleness SLA for reports (e.g., 15 min). Never flat mega-table on primary.

Q16: Evaluate trigger-maintained aggregate vs event projection for order_count on customer.

Trigger: synchronous, simple, adds write latency, doesn't scale across services. Event projection: async, scalable, eventual consistency — preferred for microservices. Trigger OK for low-volume monolith.

Scenario

Scenario: "Customer changed name; legal documents and old orders show different names. Compliance issue?"

If orders store snapshot (correct — legal record at transaction time): not a bug — document policy. If orders copy mutable name and weren't updated: design bug — should be snapshot semantics, not active copy. Future orders use new name; old orders retain old name.

Part 20 — Revision Sheet

Core Concepts

  • Denormalization = intentional redundancy for read scale
  • Not a substitute for normalization on OLTP core
  • Snapshot = immutable copy at point in time ✅
  • Active copy = mutable duplicate across rows ❌
  • MV = precomputed JOIN, refreshed async
  • CQRS = normalized write + denormalized read via events
  • Star schema = denormalized dimensions for BI

Decision Flow

text
Tune indexes first → still slow?
  Historical fact → snapshot column
  Analytics → MV / warehouse
  Hot read API → CQRS / Redis
  Cassandra → query-driven dual tables

Consistency

text
OLTP source:     strong ACID
MV/cache/read:   eventual — define staleness SLA
Never:           denormalized copy as sole source of truth for money
