Part 1 — Concept

What Is ER Modeling?

Entity-Relationship (ER) modeling is a visual and logical technique for describing the structure of data in a business domain: what things exist (entities), how they relate (relationships), and what rules govern those connections (cardinality, optionality, constraints).

An ER model is the blueprint between business requirements and physical database schema.

text
BUSINESS REQUIREMENTS          ER MODEL              RELATIONAL SCHEMA
─────────────────────         ────────              ──────────────────
"Customer opens                ┌──────────┐          customers
 accounts and                  │ Customer │          accounts
 makes payments"        →      └────┬─────┘    →     payments
                                  │ 1:N              (+ FKs, constraints)
                             ┌────▼─────┐
                             │ Account  │
                             └────┬─────┘
                                  │ 1:N
                             ┌────▼─────┐
                             │ Payment  │
                             └──────────┘

Core ER Components

ComponentSymbol (Chen)Definition
EntityRectangleObject type with independent existence (Customer, Account)
Weak EntityDouble rectangleDepends on another entity for identity (OrderItem depends on Order)
RelationshipDiamondAssociation between entities (Customer opens Account)
AttributeOvalProperty of entity or relationship (email, balance)
Key AttributeUnderlined ovalUniquely identifies entity instance
Cardinality1, N on linesHow many instances participate (one-to-many, etc.)

Crow's Foot Notation (Industry Standard)

text
Crow's Foot (used in Lucidchart, draw.io, ERwin, pgModeler):

││  exactly one (mandatory one)
o|  zero or one (optional one)
│<  one or many (mandatory many)
o<  zero or many (optional many)

Examples:
Customer ││─────<││ Account     One customer has one-or-many accounts
         ││─────o│ Order       One customer has zero-or-one active cart
Branch   ││─────<││ Employee  One branch employs one-or-many employees

ER Model Types

ModelLevelAudience
Conceptual ERHigh-level entities and relationshipsBusiness stakeholders, architects
Logical ERFull attributes, keys, cardinalityDB designers, developers
Physical modelTable names, types, indexes, partitionsDBAs, implementation

Part 2 — History

Evolution of ER Modeling

text
1976    Peter Chen publishes "The Entity-Relationship Model — Toward a Unified View of Data"
        └── ER model born at MIT — bridges business concepts and relational algebra

1980s   Chen notation (rectangles, diamonds, ovals) taught universally
        CASE tools: ERwin, PowerDesigner, Oracle Designer

1990s   Crow's Foot notation dominates industry tools (more compact than Chen)
        UML Class Diagrams partially replace ER for OO teams
        IDEF1X standard in government/enterprise

2000s   ORM tools (Hibernate) drive "entity-first" design from Java classes
        Risk: developers skip ER modeling → schema grows organically (bad)

2010s   Domain-Driven Design (DDD) aligns bounded contexts with ER sub-models
        Microservices: one ER diagram per service, not one giant enterprise diagram

2020s   Data mesh, event storming complement ER for distributed systems
        ER remains essential for relational OLTP design within each service

Historical Lesson

Chen created ER modeling because business stakeholders and programmers spoke different languages. ER diagrams remain the contract between product owners, architects, and DBAs before a single CREATE TABLE is written.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does ER Modeling Solve?

Problem 1: Ambiguous Requirements

text
Business says: "Track customer orders"

Without ER model — ambiguous:
  Can one order have multiple customers?
  Can a product appear in multiple orders?
  Is shipping address stored on customer or order?
  Are payments tied to order or account?

With ER model — explicit:
  Customer 1:N Order
  Order M:N Product (via OrderItem associative entity)
  Order has ship_to_address attribute (snapshot)
  Payment N:1 Order

Problem 2: Schema Design Errors Discovered Late

text
Skip ER → developers create tables ad hoc:
  Week 1: customers, orders
  Week 4: discover need order_items junction table — painful migration
  Week 8: payment doesn't link to order — reconciliation broken

ER model upfront → associative entities and FKs defined before coding

Problem 3: Normalization Violations Built In

text
ER modeling forces you to ask:
  "Is product_name an attribute of Order or of Product?"
  → Product entity → normalized
  → OrderItem stores unit_price snapshot → valid denormalization (Lesson 9)

Without ER: product_name on order table → update anomalies (Lesson 8)

Problem 4: Communication Across Teams

text
Architect, DBA, backend dev, QA, business analyst:
  All reference same ER diagram
  "The Payment entity" = unambiguous shared vocabulary

Problem 5: Microservice Boundary Drawing

text
ER modeling per bounded context:
  Payment Service ER: payments, refunds, payment_methods
  Order Service ER: orders, order_items, carts
  Shared concept "customer_id" as external reference — not shared table

Unified Problem Statement

ER modeling translates ambiguous business requirements into a precise, reviewable structural blueprint — preventing schema errors, normalization violations, and cross-team miscommunication before implementation.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why ER Modeling Precedes SQL

Separation of Logical and Physical Design

text
ER MODEL (WHAT)                    PHYSICAL SCHEMA (HOW)
───────────────                    ─────────────────────
Customer entity                    CREATE TABLE customers (...)
  - customer_id (PK)                 BIGINT PK, SEQUENCE
  - email (unique)                   VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL
  - date_of_birth                    DATE

Relationship: Customer opens Account   FK accounts.customer_id → customers
Cardinality: 1:N                       INDEX idx_accounts_customer_id

ER captures business rules independent of Oracle vs PostgreSQL vs MySQL.

Why Not Jump Straight to CREATE TABLE?

Skip ERWith ER
Miss M:N relationshipsJunction entities identified
Wrong cardinalityOptionality explicit (optional order?)
Attributes on wrong entityNormalization guided structurally
Missing entities discovered in prodCompleteness reviewed upfront
No shared documentationDiagram = living architecture artifact

ER and Normalization Are Linked

text
ER modeling naturally produces normalized schema:

Entity → Table
Attribute of entity → Column
M:N relationship → Junction table (2NF/3NF)
1:N relationship → FK on "many" side
Multi-valued attribute → separate entity (1NF)

Part 5 — Internal Working

ER Concepts — Deep Dive

Entities vs Attributes vs Relationships

text
ENTITY: exists independently, has own identity
  Customer, Account, Product, Branch

ATTRIBUTE: describes entity — cannot exist alone
  email, balance, order_date

RELATIONSHIP: association — may have its own attributes
  Customer PLACES Order
  Employee WORKS_AT Branch (with start_date attribute on relationship)

ATTRIBUTE ON RELATIONSHIP vs ENTITY:
  OrderItem.quantity → attribute of associative entity (M:N resolved)
  Employee.start_date on WORKS_AT → relationship attribute → column in junction/assignment table

Cardinality and Optionality

text
CARDINALITY: how many on each side
  1:1   One customer has at most one loyalty account
  1:N   One customer has many accounts
  M:N   Many students enroll in many courses

OPTIONALITY: minimum participation
  Customer ││──<││ Account     Customer MUST have account? No — optional on customer side: o<││
  Order ││──││ Payment         Order MUST have payment? Mandatory: ││──││

Full notation examples:
  Customer o│─────<││ Account
    A customer MAY have zero or many accounts
    An account MUST belong to exactly one customer

  Order ││─────<││ OrderItem
    An order MUST have at least one line item
    A line item MUST belong to exactly one order

Weak Entities

text
WEAK ENTITY: cannot be uniquely identified by own attributes alone
  Depends on identifying entity (owner)

Example: OrderItem
  Partial key: line_number (unique only within an order)
  Identifying relationship: Order ──< OrderItem
  Full key: (order_id, line_number) or surrogate order_item_id

Chen notation: double rectangle for weak entity, double diamond for identifying relationship

Modern practice: use surrogate PK (order_item_id) + FK to order — simpler ORM mapping
  Weak entity concept still guides design: OrderItem meaningless without Order

Subtype / Inheritance (ISA)

text
        ┌──────────┐
        │  Account │  (supertype)
        └────┬─────┘
             │ ISA
       ┌─────┴─────┐
       ▼           ▼
┌────────────┐ ┌────────────┐
│  Savings   │ │  Checking  │  (subtypes)
│  int_rate  │ │  overdraft │
└────────────┘ └────────────┘

Mapping options:
  1. Single table (all subtype columns, account_type discriminator)
  2. Table per subtype (accounts base + savings_accounts + checking_accounts)
  3. Table per concrete class

Banking often: single accounts table + account_type CHECK + nullable subtype columns
  OR separate tables for complex subtype behavior

Associative (Junction) Entities

text
M:N: Student enrolls in Course

  Student M:N Course  →  resolve to:

  Student 1:N Enrollment N:1 Course

  Enrollment (associative entity):
    student_id (FK)
    course_id (FK)
    enroll_date
    grade
    PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id) or enrollment_id surrogate
text
ASCII ER (Crow's Foot):

┌──────────┐       ┌────────────┐       ┌──────────┐
│ Student  ││─────<│ Enrollment │>─────││ Course   │
└──────────┘       └────────────┘       └──────────┘
                   enroll_date
                   grade

Part 6 — Storage Internals

ER-to-Relational Mapping — Physical Result

Every ER construct maps to storage structures (Lessons 4–6):

Mapping Rules

ER ConstructRelational MappingStorage
Strong entityTable with PKHeap/clustered file + PK index
Weak entityTable with FK to owner + partial key or surrogate PKSame
1:1 relationshipFK on either side (or both for mandatory)FK index
1:N relationshipFK on "many" sideFK index
M:N relationshipJunction table with two FKsTwo FK indexes
Simple attributeColumnRow bytes
Multi-valued attributeSeparate tableExtra table + FK
Composite attributeFlatten to columns (street, city, zip)Row bytes
Derived attributeUsually omit — compute in query/viewNo storage (or MV)
Relationship attributeColumn in junction/FK tableRow bytes

Banking ER — Physical Schema Result

text
ER ENTITIES                          PHYSICAL TABLES
───────────                          ───────────────
Customer                             customers (PK: customer_id, 8B)
Account                              accounts (PK: account_id, FK: customer_id)
Transaction                          transactions (PK: transaction_id, FK: account_id)
Branch                               branches (PK: branch_id)
Employee                             employees (PK: employee_id, FK: branch_id)
Customer-Account (1:N)               accounts.customer_id → customers
Account-Transaction (1:N)            transactions.account_id → accounts
Employee-Branch (N:1)                employees.branch_id → branches

Estimated row widths from Lesson 5 type choices → pages per table

Part 7 — Memory Usage

ER Design Decisions and Memory Impact

Entity Granularity Affects Buffer Pool

text
COARSE ER (few entities, wide attributes):
  Customer entity includes all accounts as JSON column
  → Wide rows, fewer customers per page, TOAST for JSON (Lesson 5)

FINE ER (many normalized entities):
  customers + accounts + transactions separate
  → Narrow hot rows, more customers per page in cache
  → Point lookup on customer: 1 page; account list: index scan on FK

M:N Resolution — Junction Table Memory

text
Order M:N Product → order_items junction

Memory for query "order with items":
  Normalized: order page + N order_item pages (index on order_id)
  vs embedded JSON items in order document (MongoDB style):
    One page if small order — but wide document

ER junction table → predictable B-tree index on order_id — buffer pool friendly

Derived Attributes in ER

text
ER diagram shows: total_balance as derived attribute on Customer
  dotted oval (derived)

Storage decision:
  ❌ Store on customer row — must update on every transaction (active denormalization)
  ✅ Compute: SELECT SUM(balance) FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = ?
  ✅ Or MV / read model (Lesson 9) for dashboard

ER marks it derived → architect knows not to store on OLTP row without sync plan

Part 8 — Execution Flow

From ER Diagram to Query Execution

Design-Time Flow

text
1. Gather business requirements (interviews, user stories)
2. Identify nouns → candidate entities
3. Identify verbs → candidate relationships
4. Assign attributes to entities (not relationships, unless M:N)
5. Define cardinality and optionality
6. Identify keys (PK, candidate keys)
7. Resolve M:N → associative entities
8. Check normalization (Lesson 8) — fix transitive/partial deps
9. Map to relational schema
10. Add constraints (Lesson 7), indexes (Lesson 26)
11. Review with stakeholders
12. Implement via Flyway/Liquibase + JPA entities

Runtime Flow — ER Guides Join Path

sql
-- ER defined: Customer 1:N Account 1:N Transaction
-- Query: "All transactions for customer 1001 in January"

SELECT t.*
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN transactions t ON t.account_id = a.account_id
WHERE c.customer_id = 1001
AND t.created_at >= '2024-01-01'
AND t.created_at < '2024-02-01';
text
EXECUTION (guided by ER FK structure):

1. Index scan customers PK → customer_id = 1001 (1 row)
2. Index scan accounts(customer_id) → N account rows
3. For each account: index scan transactions(account_id, created_at) → M rows
4. Nested loop or hash join assembles result

ER model ensured:
  FK indexes exist on accounts.customer_id and transactions.account_id
  Join path is valid — no orphan possible if FK enforced

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

ER Design Performance Implications

Good ER → Good Performance Foundation

ER DecisionPerformance Impact
Surrogate PK on all entitiesSequential inserts, narrow FK indexes
M:N resolved to junction tableIndexed lookups both directions
Derived attrs marked derivedAvoid accidental write amplification
Subtype as single table + discriminatorOne query vs JOIN across subtype tables
Separate Product entityProduct updates don't touch order_items snapshot

Bad ER → Performance Debt

ER MistakePerformance Cost
M:N not resolved (array in column)Full scan, no index on elements
Too many entities (over-normalization)8-way JOINs on every read
Missing associative entity attributes on wrong sideRedundant storage, update anomalies
Giant "Entity" for entire domainWide rows, buffer pool pollution
No weak entity distinctionComposite PK everywhere — wide indexes

ER and Read Path Planning (Lesson 9)

text
During ER modeling, annotate:

  [OLTP path]  Customer → Account → Transaction (normalized)
  [Read path]  Customer360ReadModel (denormalized projection — Lesson 9)
  [Search]     ProductSearchDocument (Elasticsearch — outside ER OLTP)

ER captures OLTP structure; supplementary read models documented alongside

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

ER Schema Complexity

DesignTablesJoin depth (typical query)Design complexityIntegrity
Single entity (god table)10LowPoor
3NF ER (10 entities)10-152-4MediumExcellent
3NF ER (50 entities)50-803-6HighExcellent
ER + read models+3-5 per hot path0-1 on read pathHigherGood (eventual on reads)

M:N Resolution Complexity

text
M:N with attributes:
  n entities, m relationships
  Each M:N → +1 junction table, +2 FKs, +2 indexes

100 M:N relationships → 100 junction tables
  Design complexity O(m)
  Query join complexity O(path length) not O(m) if indexed properly

Complete ER-to-Schema Example — Digital Banking

Step 1: Conceptual ER (Described)

text
ENTITIES:
  Customer, Account, Transaction, Branch, Employee, Loan, Payment

RELATIONSHIPS:
  Customer 1:N Account
  Account  1:N Transaction
  Account  1:N Payment
  Branch   1:N Employee
  Branch   1:N Account (account opened at branch)
  Customer 1:N Loan
  Loan     1:N LoanPayment (associative / weak-like)
  Employee N:1 Branch (works at)

Step 2: ASCII ER Diagram (Crow's Foot)

text
                    ┌──────────┐
                    │  Branch  │
                    └────┬─────┘
                         ││
              ┌──────────┼──────────┐
              ││         ││         ││
         ┌────▼────┐ ┌───▼───┐ ┌───▼────┐
         │Employee │ │Account│ │ (other)│
         └─────────┘ └───┬───┘ └────────┘
                           ││
              ┌────────────┼────────────┐
              ││           ││           ││
         ┌────▼────┐ ┌─────▼─────┐ ┌───▼────┐
         │Transaction│ │ Payment │ │  Loan  │
         └─────────┘ └───────────┘ └───┬────┘
                                         ││
                                    ┌────▼──────┐
                                    │LoanPayment│
                                    └───────────┘

         ┌──────────┐
         │ Customer ││────────────────────────────<││ Account
         └────┬─────┘│────<││ Loan
              ││
         (external ref in Payment Service: customer_id UUID — no FK cross-DB)

Step 3: Logical ER → SQL Schema

sql
-- BRANCH
CREATE TABLE branches (
    branch_id       BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    branch_code     VARCHAR(10)  NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    branch_name     VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    city            VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    region          VARCHAR(50)  NOT NULL
);

-- EMPLOYEE
CREATE TABLE employees (
    employee_id     BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    branch_id       BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES branches(branch_id),
    employee_number VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    first_name      VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    last_name       VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    role            VARCHAR(50)  NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX idx_employees_branch ON employees(branch_id);

-- CUSTOMER
CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id     BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    external_id     UUID NOT NULL DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() UNIQUE,
    email           VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    first_name      VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    last_name       VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    date_of_birth   DATE NOT NULL,
    status          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE'
        CHECK (status IN ('ACTIVE','SUSPENDED','CLOSED')),
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- ACCOUNT (Customer 1:N Account, Branch 1:N Account)
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id      BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id     BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(customer_id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
    branch_id       BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES branches(branch_id),
    account_number  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    account_type    VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL
        CHECK (account_type IN ('SAVINGS','CHECKING','LOAN')),
    currency        CHAR(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'USD',
    balance         DECIMAL(18,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (balance >= 0),
    status          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE',
    opened_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_customer ON accounts(customer_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_branch ON accounts(branch_id);

-- TRANSACTION (Account 1:N Transaction)
CREATE TABLE transactions (
    transaction_id  BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id      BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(account_id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
    txn_type        VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL
        CHECK (txn_type IN ('DEBIT','CREDIT','TRANSFER')),
    amount          DECIMAL(18,2) NOT NULL CHECK (amount > 0),
    reference       VARCHAR(100),
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);
CREATE INDEX idx_transactions_account ON transactions(account_id, created_at DESC);

-- LOAN (Customer 1:N Loan)
CREATE TABLE loans (
    loan_id         BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id     BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
    account_id      BIGINT REFERENCES accounts(account_id),
    principal       DECIMAL(18,2) NOT NULL CHECK (principal > 0),
    interest_rate   DECIMAL(5,4) NOT NULL CHECK (interest_rate >= 0),
    term_months     INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (term_months > 0),
    status          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE'
);

-- LOAN PAYMENT (Loan 1:N LoanPayment — weak entity pattern)
CREATE TABLE loan_payments (
    loan_payment_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,  -- surrogate (ORM-friendly)
    loan_id         BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES loans(loan_id),
    payment_number  INTEGER NOT NULL,
    due_date        DATE NOT NULL,
    amount_due      DECIMAL(18,2) NOT NULL,
    amount_paid     DECIMAL(18,2),
    paid_at         TIMESTAMPTZ,
    UNIQUE (loan_id, payment_number)  -- partial key uniqueness
);
CREATE INDEX idx_loan_payments_loan ON loan_payments(loan_id);

Step 4: M:N Example — Customer and Product (Investment Portfolio)

sql
-- ER: Customer M:N Product via Holding (associative entity)
CREATE TABLE holdings (
    holding_id      BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id     BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(customer_id),
    product_id      BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES investment_products(product_id),
    units           DECIMAL(18,6) NOT NULL CHECK (units > 0),
    acquired_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    UNIQUE (customer_id, product_id)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_holdings_product ON holdings(product_id);

Part 12 — Production Usage

ER Modeling in Production Domains

Banking — Core ER Boundaries

text
CORE BANKING ER (single Oracle schema — 3NF):
  Party (Customer, CorporateCustomer subtype)
  Account, Transaction, Product, Branch
  PartyAccountRole (M:N with role attribute — joint accounts)

KEY ER DECISIONS:
  Joint account: M:N Customer-Account via account_holders junction
    account_holders(customer_id, account_id, role: PRIMARY/JOINT)
  Transaction always belongs to ONE account (1:N)
  Product catalog separate from Account (Account IS-A product instance)

E-Commerce ER

text
Customer 1:N Order
Order 1:N OrderItem N:1 Product
Customer 1:1 Cart (optional — 0:1)
Cart 1:N CartItem N:1 Product
Order 1:N Payment
Product N:1 Category
Product M:N Tag via product_tags

READ MODELS (outside OLTP ER):
  ProductSearchDoc, OrderSummaryReadModel

Healthcare ER

text
Patient 1:N Encounter
Encounter 1:N Diagnosis N:1 ICDCode
Encounter 1:N Prescription N:1 Drug
Provider N:1 Department
Patient N:1 PrimaryCareProvider (Provider)

PRIVACY: Patient entity isolated — strict access controls
AuditLog entity — append-only, no FK DELETE CASCADE from Patient

Microservices — ER Per Service

text
┌─────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────┐
│   ORDER SERVICE ER  │  │  PAYMENT SERVICE ER │
│   Order             │  │  Payment            │
│   OrderItem         │  │  Refund             │
│   Cart              │  │  PaymentMethod      │
│   (customer_id ref) │  │  (order_id UUID ref)│
└─────────────────────┘  └─────────────────────┘
         No shared ER diagram — integration via IDs and events

Part 13 — Spring Boot Integration

From ER Diagram to JPA Entity Model

ER Entity → JPA Class Mapping

ER ConstructJPA Mapping
Entity@Entity class
PK attribute@Id + @GeneratedValue
Simple attribute@Column field
1:N relationship@OneToMany / @ManyToOne
M:N via junction@ManyToMany or two @OneToMany (preferred: explicit junction entity)
Weak entity@ManyToOne required + @Id or @EmbeddedId
Unique attribute@Column(unique=true)
Subtype (ISA)@Inheritance SINGLE_TABLE / JOINED / TABLE_PER_CLASS

Banking ER as JPA

java
@Entity
@Table(name = "customers")
public class Customer {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "customer_seq")
    private Long customerId;

    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true)
    private UUID externalId = UUID.randomUUID();

    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true)
    private String email;

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "customer", cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST)
    private List<Account> accounts = new ArrayList<>();

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "customer")
    private List<Loan> loans = new ArrayList<>();
}

@Entity
@Table(name = "accounts")
public class Account {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "account_seq")
    private Long accountId;

    @ManyToOne(optional = false, fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    @JoinColumn(name = "customer_id", nullable = false)
    private Customer customer;

    @ManyToOne(optional = false, fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    @JoinColumn(name = "branch_id", nullable = false)
    private Branch branch;

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "account", cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST)
    private List<Transaction> transactions = new ArrayList<>();

    @Column(precision = 18, scale = 2, nullable = false)
    private BigDecimal balance;
}

M:N — Explicit Junction Entity (Preferred over @ManyToMany)

java
// ER: Customer M:N Account via AccountHolder (with role attribute)
@Entity
@Table(name = "account_holders")
public class AccountHolder {

    @EmbeddedId
    private AccountHolderId id;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    @MapsId("customerId")
    @JoinColumn(name = "customer_id")
    private Customer customer;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    @MapsId("accountId")
    @JoinColumn(name = "account_id")
    private Account account;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    @Column(name = "holder_role", nullable = false)
    private HolderRole role;  // attribute on relationship → junction entity column
}

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

ER Modeling Pitfalls in ORM

@ManyToMany Hidden Junction Table

java
// ❌ Hibernate creates hidden join table — no place for relationship attributes
@ManyToMany
@JoinTable(name = "student_course")
private List<Course> courses;

// ✅ Explicit associative entity from ER model
@OneToMany(mappedBy = "student")
private List<Enrollment> enrollments;

Bidirectional Relationship Ownership

text
ER relationship Customer 1:N Account
JPA: "many" side (Account) owns FK (@JoinColumn on Account)
     "one" side (Customer) uses mappedBy

Rule: FK column lives on "many" side — matches ER-to-relational mapping

Aggregate Roots (DDD + ER)

text
ER entities that are aggregate roots (independent lifecycle):
  Customer, Order, Account

Entities that cannot exist alone (dependent/weak):
  OrderItem, Transaction, LoanPayment

JPA:
  CascadeType.PERSIST on composition relationships only
  Never CascadeType.REMOVE on Account → Transaction in banking

ER Derived Attribute → @Formula or Read Model

java
// ER: total_balance derived on Customer
// ❌ @Formula SUM subquery on entity
// ✅ Service method or read model entity (Lesson 9)
public BigDecimal getTotalBalance(Long customerId) {
    return accountRepo.sumBalanceByCustomerId(customerId);
}

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

ER Modeling Process for Solution Architects

Step-by-Step Methodology

text
PHASE 1: DISCOVERY
  □ Identify bounded contexts (microservices boundaries)
  □ List nouns (candidate entities) from requirements
  □ List verbs (candidate relationships)
  □ Identify reports and read paths (plan read models — Lesson 9)

PHASE 2: CONCEPTUAL ER
  □ Draw entities and relationships (no attributes yet)
  □ Validate cardinality with business stakeholders
  □ Resolve ambiguities ("can an order exist without customer?")

PHASE 3: LOGICAL ER
  □ Add attributes with types (Lesson 5)
  □ Assign PKs (surrogate — Lesson 6)
  □ Resolve M:N → junction entities
  □ Mark derived attributes (dotted)
  □ Mark snapshot attributes (order line price)
  □ Apply normalization check (Lesson 8)

PHASE 4: PHYSICAL MODEL
  □ Map to DDL with constraints (Lesson 7)
  □ Index FK columns and query paths
  □ Partition strategy for large entities (Lesson 42)
  □ Document read models separately

PHASE 5: REVIEW
  □ Walk through user stories against ER diagram
  □ Security: which entities contain PII?
  □ Compliance: audit requirements?
  □ Sign-off from business + DBA + lead developer

ER Review Checklist

text
□ Every entity has clear definition and single responsibility
□ Every relationship has documented cardinality AND optionality
□ No M:N without junction entity
□ No multi-valued attributes in columns (1NF)
□ Snapshot vs live copy decisions documented
□ PK strategy consistent (BIGINT surrogate)
□ FK ON DELETE actions defined per relationship
□ PII entities identified
□ Read models identified for hot paths
□ One ER diagram per microservice bounded context

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Skipping ER — Coding Tables Directly

text
❌ CREATE TABLE as requirements arrive
✅ ER diagram reviewed → then Flyway migrations

Mistake 2: M:N Not Resolved

text
❌ orders.product_ids VARCHAR (comma-separated)
✅ order_items junction table

Mistake 3: Attribute on Wrong Entity

text
❌ product_name on Order (update anomaly)
✅ product_name on Product; unit_price snapshot on OrderItem

Mistake 4: Wrong Cardinality

text
❌ "One order belongs to many customers" (usually wrong)
✅ Order N:1 Customer (one customer per order; joint account is different pattern)

Mistake 5: @ManyToMany for Relationship with Attributes

text
❌ Hidden join table — can't add enroll_date, grade
✅ Enrollment associative entity

Mistake 6: One Enterprise ER for All Microservices

text
❌ 200-entity diagram spanning all services — shared database anti-pattern
✅ One ER per bounded context; integration via events and external IDs

Mistake 7: Storing Derived Attributes Without Plan

text
❌ total_balance column on Customer with no sync strategy
✅ Derived in query, MV, or CQRS read model (Lessons 8-9)

Mistake 8: Confusing Optional Relationship with Nullable FK

text
ER: Customer o│──<││ Account (customer may have zero accounts)
Implementation: accounts.customer_id NOT NULL (account must have customer)
  Optionality on "many" side: account MUST have customer
  Optionality on "one" side: customer MAY have zero accounts
  → FK NOT NULL on accounts.customer_id is correct

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is an entity in ER modeling?

Object type with independent existence and identity — Customer, Order, Product. Maps to a table.

Q2: What is cardinality?

Number of instances participating in a relationship — 1:1, 1:N, M:N.

Q3: How do you represent M:N in a relational database?

Decompose into two 1:N relationships via junction (associative) table with FKs to both entities.

Q4: What is a primary key in ER terms?

Attribute(s) uniquely identifying each entity instance. Maps to PRIMARY KEY constraint.

Q5: Difference between conceptual and logical ER model?

Conceptual: high-level entities and relationships for business. Logical: full attributes, keys, cardinality for implementation.

Mid-Level

Q6: Explain weak entity with example.

Entity that cannot be uniquely identified without owner — OrderItem identified by (order_id, line_number). Depends on Order. Modern: surrogate order_item_id + FK + UNIQUE(order_id, line_number).

Q7: Where does FK go in 1:N relationship?

On "many" side — accounts.customer_id references customers.customer_id.

Q8: Attribute on relationship vs entity — how to decide?

If attribute describes relationship between two entities (enrollment grade, account_holder role) → junction table column. If it describes one entity (customer email) → entity table column.

Q9: ER model for joint bank account (two customers, one account)?

M:N Customer-Account via account_holders(customer_id, account_id, role). Junction entity with role attribute.

Q10: How does ER modeling relate to normalization?

Proper ER decomposition naturally achieves 1NF-3NF. Each entity → table, M:N → junction, no transitive attrs on wrong entity.

Senior

Q11: Design ER for e-commerce: cart, order, payment, inventory.

Customer 1:0..1 Cart 1:N CartItem N:1 Product. Customer 1:N Order 1:N OrderItem N:1 Product (unit_price snapshot). Order 1:N Payment. Product 1:1 Inventory or quantity on Product. Resolve M:N with junction entities.

Q12: ISA subtype in ER — map Savings and Checking accounts.

Option 1: Single accounts table, account_type discriminator, nullable subtype columns. Option 2: accounts base + savings_accounts + checking_accounts (joined). Choose based on subtype complexity and query patterns.

Q13: ER modeling for microservices — one diagram or many?

One ER per bounded context/service. Cross-service references as external IDs (UUID), not FK. No shared ER spanning services.

Q14: Snapshot attribute in ER — how to document?

Mark on logical ER as snapshot (e.g., order_items.unit_price with note "frozen at sale"). Not derived — immutable denormalization (Lesson 9). Distinct from derived total_balance.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Walk through ER modeling process for new payment platform module.

Discovery → bounded context → conceptual ER (stakeholder review) → logical ER (attributes, keys, normalization) → physical DDL → identify read models → security (PII entities) → Flyway + JPA implementation.

Q16: Legacy 80-table schema with no ER documentation — approach?

Reverse engineer ER from information_schema (pg_dump, Oracle SQL Developer datamodeler). Interview stakeholders to validate relationships. Identify anomalies vs business rules. Incremental documentation — prioritize core entities. Fix critical FK gaps.

Scenario

Scenario: "Business says one employee can work at multiple branches simultaneously."

Change Employee-Branch from N:1 to M:N via employee_assignments(employee_id, branch_id, start_date, end_date, is_primary). Junction entity with temporal attributes. Index both FKs. ER update before any CREATE TABLE.

ER Components

  • M:N → always junction entity

Mapping Rules (Memorize)

text
1:1  → FK on either (optional side preferred)
1:N  → FK on many side
M:N  → junction table with 2 FKs
Relationship attribute → junction table column
Multi-valued attribute → new entity/table

text

Part 1 — Concept

What Is SELECT?

SELECT is the SQL statement that retrieves data from one or more tables, views, or other query sources. It is the most frequently executed statement in production databases and the foundation of every report, API read, ORM query, and analytics pipeline.

sql
SELECT column_list
FROM   table_source
[WHERE  condition]
[GROUP BY columns]
[HAVING condition]
[ORDER BY columns]
[LIMIT / FETCH rows];

SELECT Does Not Mean "Read Only"

text
SELECT can:
  ✅ Read rows from tables and views
  ✅ Compute expressions (SELECT 1+1, SELECT NOW())
  ✅ Call functions and subqueries
  ✅ Lock rows (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE)
  ✅ Read from CTEs, joins, derived tables

SELECT does NOT:
  ❌ Modify data (unless combined with INTO or used in CREATE TABLE AS)
  ❌ Guarantee row order without ORDER BY
  ❌ Guarantee unique rows without DISTINCT

SQL Query Logical Processing Order

Critical: SQL is not executed top-to-bottom as written. The engine processes clauses in this logical order:

text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  LOGICAL EXECUTION ORDER (not written order)                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  1. FROM          — identify source tables                     │
│  2. JOIN          — combine tables                             │
│  3. WHERE         — filter rows (before grouping)              │
│  4. GROUP BY      — aggregate groups                           │
│  5. HAVING        — filter groups                              │
│  6. SELECT        — project columns/expressions  ◄── here     │
│  7. DISTINCT      — remove duplicate rows                      │
│  8. ORDER BY      — sort result                                │
│  9. LIMIT/OFFSET  — restrict row count                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Written:   SELECT → FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY
Executed:  FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT

Why this matters: You cannot use a SELECT alias in WHERE (WHERE runs before SELECT). You can use it in ORDER BY (runs after SELECT).

SELECT Clause Components

ComponentPurposeExample
Column listProject specific columnsSELECT account_id, balance
*****All columns (avoid in production)SELECT *
alias.colDisambiguate joined columnsSELECT c.email, a.balance
ExpressionComputed valueSELECT balance * 1.05 AS projected
LiteralConstant in resultSELECT 'USD' AS currency
FunctionTransform valueSELECT UPPER(name), NOW()
SubqueryNested SELECTSELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM accounts) AS cnt
DISTINCTUnique rowsSELECT DISTINCT status FROM accounts
AS aliasRename output columnSELECT balance AS current_balance

Part 2 — History

Evolution of SELECT

text
1974    SEQUEL (Structured English Query Language) at IBM
        "SELECT name FROM employees WHERE dept = 'SALES'"
        └── Declarative: WHAT you want, not HOW to get it

1979    Oracle V2 — first commercial SQL with SELECT
1986    SQL-86 standard — SELECT, FROM, WHERE standardized
1992    SQL-92 — major expansion: JOIN syntax, subqueries, set operations
        ANSI JOIN: FROM a INNER JOIN b ON a.id = b.id

1999    SQL:1999 — COMMON TABLE EXPRESSIONS (WITH clause) — Lesson 18
2003    SQL:2003 — WINDOW functions — Lesson 19
2008    SQL:2008 — FETCH FIRST, OFFSET
2011+   Database-specific extensions:
        PostgreSQL: RETURNING, DISTINCT ON, LATERAL
        Oracle: ROWNUM → FETCH FIRST, CONNECT BY (hierarchical)
        MySQL: LIMIT (non-standard origin, now widely supported)

2020s   ORMs generate SELECT for every JPA findById, JPQL query
        Query optimizers evolved to rewrite SELECT internally
        Columnar engines push SELECT into storage layer (projection pushdown)

Historical Lesson

SELECT introduced declarative querying — the programmer describes the result set; the optimizer (Lesson 30) decides index scans, join algorithms, and memory usage. This separation is why SQL scales better than row-by-row application code.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does SELECT Solve?

Problem 1: Data Access Without Knowing Physical Storage

text
Application should not know:
  Which disk page holds account_id = 5001
  Whether to use index or full scan

Application writes:
  SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 5001;

DBMS optimizer chooses:
  Index scan on PK → 0.5ms

Problem 2: Projection — Avoid Reading Unneeded Data

text
Banking app needs only account_id and balance for list screen.

SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts;   -- 16 bytes/row

SELECT * FROM accounts;                      -- 200 bytes/row (includes TOAST, LOB pointers)

Projection reduces I/O, buffer pool usage, network transfer (Lesson 5)

Problem 3: Computed Results Without Application Round-Trips

sql
-- Compute in database (single round-trip, uses DB CPU)
SELECT
    account_id,
    balance,
    balance * 0.0525 / 12 AS monthly_interest,
    CASE WHEN balance < 1000 THEN 'LOW' ELSE 'OK' END AS balance_tier
FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001;

Problem 4: Consistent Read View

text
SELECT sees committed data per isolation level (Lesson 37):
  READ COMMITTED: sees latest committed rows
  REPEATABLE READ: snapshot at transaction start (MVCC — Lesson 36)

One SELECT semantics — all clients agree on what "read" means

Problem 5: Security — Column-Level Access

sql
-- Role sees only permitted columns
GRANT SELECT (account_id, balance) ON accounts TO teller_role;
-- Teller cannot SELECT ssn, internal_notes

Unified Problem Statement

SELECT provides a declarative, optimized, secure way to project exactly the data needed from structured storage — without exposing physical layout or requiring application-side row iteration.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why SELECT Is Separate from WHERE, JOIN, etc.

SQL separates clauses because each maps to a relational algebra operation:

SQL ClauseRelational AlgebraPurpose
FROMRelation sourceInput set
WHERESelection (σ)Filter rows
SELECTProjection (π)Choose columns
JOINJoin (⋈)Combine relations
GROUP BYGroupingAggregation
ORDER BYSortPresentation order
text
Relational algebra composition:
  π_{account_id, balance}(σ_{customer_id=1001}(accounts))

SQL equivalent:
  SELECT account_id, balance
  FROM accounts
  WHERE customer_id = 1001;

Why declarative? Optimizer can rewrite (σ then π) as (index scan projecting columns) — equivalent result, different performance path.

Part 5 — Internal Working

How SELECT Works Internally

Query Processing Pipeline (SELECT-focused)

text
SQL: SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = 1001;

┌──────────┐
│  PARSER  │  Build parse tree: QuerySpec(SelectList, FromClause, WhereClause)
└────┬─────┘
     ▼
┌──────────┐
│ ANALYZER │  Resolve: accounts exists, columns exist, types compatible
│          │  Check GRANT SELECT privileges
└────┬─────┘
     ▼
┌──────────┐
│ REWRITER │  Expand views, apply rules (view → base table SELECT)
└────┬─────┘
     ▼
┌──────────┐
│ OPTIMIZER│  Generate plans:
│          │  Plan A: Seq Scan accounts + Filter customer_id=1001
│          │  Plan B: Index Scan idx_accounts_customer + Filter  ◄── chosen
│          │  Cost: A=150000, B=8
└────┬─────┘
     ▼
┌──────────┐
│ EXECUTOR │  Run plan: Index Scan → for each row project (account_id, balance)
└────┬─────┘
     ▼
┌──────────┐
│  CLIENT  │  Result set sent via JDBC/protocol
└──────────┘

Projection Internals

text
Executor reads full row from storage engine (page in buffer pool)
Projection: extract only requested columns from row bytes

Row on disk: [account_id|customer_id|balance|status|opened_at|...]
SELECT account_id, balance → extract 2 fields → send 16 bytes to client
SELECT * → extract all fields → send 200 bytes to client

Column store engines (analytics): read only requested column files — no full row read

DISTINCT Internals

sql
SELECT DISTINCT status FROM accounts;
text
Execution options:
  1. Hash aggregate: build hash table of status values → unique keys
  2. Sort + unique: sort rows by status → scan removing duplicates
  3. Index-only scan: if index on status exists — read unique index entries

Memory: hash/sort uses work_mem — may spill to disk if many distinct values

Expression Evaluation

sql
SELECT balance * 1.05 AS adjusted_balance FROM accounts;
text
For each row passing WHERE:
  1. Read balance column (DECIMAL)
  2. Multiply by 1.05 (exact decimal arithmetic)
  3. Build result tuple with alias adjusted_balance
  4. Send to client

CPU cost per row — negligible unless millions of rows without filter

Part 6 — Storage Internals

SELECT and Physical Storage Interaction

Heap Table Read (PostgreSQL)

text
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 5001;

1. B-tree index scan on accounts_pkey → ctid (page 847, slot 3)
2. Fetch heap page 847 into shared_buffers (if not cached)
3. Read slot 3 row bytes → extract balance column from row structure
4. Return DECIMAL value

Index-only scan (if covering — Lesson 28):
  If index includes balance → skip heap fetch entirely

Clustered Index Read (InnoDB)

text
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 5001;

1. Clustered PK index scan → leaf page contains full row
2. Extract balance from leaf — ONE I/O (no separate heap fetch)
InnoDB advantage for PK lookups + projection from PK leaf

SELECT * and TOAST (PostgreSQL)

text
Table with large JSONB metadata column:

SELECT * FROM customers;
  → Reads main page + TOAST fetch for large columns — expensive

SELECT customer_id, email FROM customers;
  → Main page only — TOAST not accessed if columns inline

Architect rule: never SELECT * in production services (Lesson 5, 18)

Sequential Scan Storage Pattern

sql
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts WHERE status = 'INACTIVE';
-- No index on status → Seq Scan

Reads ALL pages of accounts table sequentially:
  Page 1 → Page 2 → ... → Page N
  Filter status = 'INACTIVE' in executor
  Project account_id, balance from matching rows

I/O: entire table size on disk — why missing index hurts (Lesson 26)

Part 7 — Memory Usage

SELECT Memory Consumption

Buffer Pool (Shared)

text
Every SELECT that reads data pages uses buffer pool:
  Cache hit → read from RAM (~0.1ms)
  Cache miss → read from disk (~5ms), page loaded into buffer pool

Large SELECT * full table scan:
  Reads every page → may evict hot pages from buffer pool (cache pollution)
  OLTP impact: reporting SELECT on primary without LIMIT hurts other queries

work_mem — Sort and Hash for SELECT

sql
SELECT DISTINCT status FROM accounts;           -- hash table in work_mem
SELECT account_id FROM accounts ORDER BY balance; -- sort buffer in work_mem
text
work_mem per operation (PostgreSQL default ~4MB):
  If DISTINCT/sort exceeds work_mem → external sort/hash on disk (slow)

100 million row DISTINCT → work_mem exhausted → temp files on disk
Fix: add WHERE filter, index, or increase work_mem for session only

Client / JDBC Memory

java
// Fetch all rows into List — heap memory = rows × row width
List<Account> all = accountRepo.findAll();  // 1M rows × 500 bytes = 500MB JVM

// Streaming cursor — constant memory
@QueryHints(@QueryHint(name = "org.hibernate.fetchSize", value = "1000"))
Stream<Account> streamAll();

Result Set Size

QueryRowsWidthNetwork + JVM
SELECT account_id, balance1M~16 B~16 MB
SELECT * wide table1M~200 B~200 MB
SELECT * + LOB1K~5 MB~5 GB 💀

Part 8 — Execution Flow

SELECT Execution Flows — Detailed

Flow 1: Simple PK Lookup with Projection

sql
SELECT account_id, balance, currency
FROM accounts
WHERE account_id = 5001;
text
Step 1: Parse → validate columns
Step 2: Optimizer → Index Scan using accounts_pkey, cost=8.0
Step 3: Executor:
         a. Descend B+ tree to account_id=5001 leaf
         b. Read row from leaf (InnoDB) or follow ctid (PostgreSQL)
         c. Project 3 columns → result tuple (5001, 15000.00, 'USD')
Step 4: Send 1 row to client
Latency: ~0.5ms (buffer pool hit)

Flow 2: Filter + Projection (Secondary Index)

sql
SELECT account_id, balance
FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001 AND status = 'ACTIVE';
text
Step 1: Optimizer choices:
         A: Index Scan idx_customer_id + Filter status     cost=50
         B: Index Scan idx_status + Filter customer_id   cost=5000
         C: Bitmap Index Scan both + AND                   cost=100
         Choose A if idx_accounts_customer exists

Step 2: Index Scan idx_accounts_customer_id → 3 rows
Step 3: Filter status='ACTIVE' → 2 rows
Step 4: Project account_id, balance
Step 5: Return 2 rows

Flow 3: SELECT with Expression and CASE

sql
SELECT
    account_id,
    balance,
    CASE
        WHEN balance >= 10000 THEN 'PREMIUM'
        WHEN balance >= 1000  THEN 'STANDARD'
        ELSE 'BASIC'
    END AS tier
FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001;
text
For each row from index scan:
  1. Evaluate CASE expression (CPU)
  2. Build output row (account_id, balance, tier)
  3. No storage write — read-only MVCC snapshot
  4. Return result set

Flow 4: SELECT DISTINCT

sql
SELECT DISTINCT currency FROM accounts;
text
Step 1: Seq Scan or Index Scan on accounts
Step 2: Hash Aggregate: hash(currency) → unique values
         'USD' → bucket
         'EUR' → bucket
Step 3: Return hash table keys as result rows
Memory: O(distinct values) — small for currency (~200 ISO codes max)

PostgreSQL Execution Plan Example

sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = 1001;

-- Output:
-- Index Scan using idx_accounts_customer on accounts
--   (cost=0.42..8.44 rows=3 width=16)
--   (actual time=0.025..0.028 rows=3 loops=1)
--   Index Cond: (customer_id = 1001)
--   Buffers: shared hit=4
-- Planning Time: 0.15 ms
-- Execution Time: 0.05 ms

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

SELECT Performance Factors

Performance Hierarchy

text
FASTEST → SLOWEST (typical OLTP):

1. SELECT pk_col FROM t WHERE pk = ?           -- PK index, 1 row
2. SELECT cols FROM t WHERE indexed_col = ?    -- Index scan, few rows
3. SELECT cols FROM t WHERE partial_match      -- Index scan + filter
4. SELECT DISTINCT indexed_col FROM t        -- Index-only scan
5. SELECT cols FROM t WHERE unindexed_col = ? -- Sequential scan
6. SELECT * FROM huge_table                   -- Full table read
7. SELECT * with LOB/TOAST columns            -- Multi-page per row
8. SELECT with complex expression per row × millions -- CPU bound

SELECT Anti-Patterns

sql
-- ❌ SELECT * in production service
SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = 1001;

-- ❌ Function on indexed column — prevents index use (Lesson 25)
SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE UPPER(status) = 'ACTIVE';

-- ✅ Sargable (Search ARGument ABLE):
SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';

-- ❌ SELECT without WHERE on large table
SELECT account_id FROM accounts;  -- 100M rows to application

-- ✅ Pagination (Lesson 13 preview)
SELECT account_id FROM accounts ORDER BY account_id LIMIT 100;

Projection Pushdown

text
Smart ORM / API:
  Request: GET /accounts?fields=accountId,balance
  SQL: SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts  -- not SELECT *

Reduces:
  Buffer pool pages read
  Network bytes (JDBC → app)
  JVM object size
  Serialization time (JSON API)

Read Replica for Heavy SELECT

text
Heavy reporting SELECT:
  Route to read replica — not primary OLTP
  Same SQL, different instance — protects buffer pool on primary
  Staleness: replication lag (typically ms to seconds)

SELECT Computational Complexity

OperationComplexityNotes

DISTINCT (hash)O(n) time, O(d) spaced = distinct count
ORDER BY (no index)O(n log n)External sort if large

text
n = 1,000        Any plan works
n = 1,000,000    Index mandatory for point lookups
n = 100,000,000  Index + partition pruning (Lesson 42) for scans

FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001;

    CASE account_type
        WHEN 'SAVINGS'  THEN balance * 0.025
        WHEN 'CHECKING' THEN 0
        WHEN 'LOAN'     THEN balance * -0.065
    END                                             AS annual_interest,

SELECT Without FROM (Valid in PostgreSQL, Oracle)

sql

Scalar Subquery in SELECT List

sql

    c.customer_id,

    c.last_name,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id)
        AS account_count,

FROM customers c

Part 12 — Production Usage

SELECT in Production Systems

Banking — Teller Account Lookup

sql
-- Production: explicit columns, indexed WHERE, no SELECT *
SELECT
    a.account_id,
    a.account_number,
    a.account_type,
    a.balance,
    a.currency,
    a.status,
    c.first_name,
    c.last_name
FROM accounts a
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = a.customer_id
WHERE a.account_number = :accountNumber   -- bind variable — never string concat
AND a.status = 'ACTIVE';

API Pagination Pattern

sql
-- Keyset pagination (better than OFFSET at scale — Lesson 13)
SELECT account_id, balance, opened_at
FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = :customerId
AND account_id > :lastAccountId    -- cursor from previous page
ORDER BY account_id
LIMIT 20;

Reporting on Read Replica

sql
-- Heavy aggregate — run on replica, not primary
SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC('month', t.created_at) AS month,
    a.account_type,
    COUNT(*)                          AS txn_count,
    SUM(t.amount)                     AS total_amount
FROM transactions t
JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = t.account_id
WHERE t.created_at >= '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;
-- Route to: jdbc:postgresql://read-replica.internal:5432/banking

Monitoring Queries

sql
-- PostgreSQL: currently running SELECT statements
SELECT pid, usename, state, query_start,
       LEFT(query, 100) AS query_preview
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'active'
AND query ILIKE 'SELECT%'
ORDER BY query_start;

-- Oracle
SELECT sid, serial#, username, sql_id, status
FROM v$session
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' AND type = 'USER';

How Hibernate Builds SELECT

Entity Load → SELECT

JPQL SELECT Syntax

@Query("SELECT a FROM Account a WHERE a.balance > :minBalance")

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: SELECT * in Production

sql
-- ❌ Reads all columns including TOAST/LOB
SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = 1001;
-- ✅
SELECT account_id, account_number, balance, currency, status FROM accounts ...

Mistake 2: Assuming Row Order Without ORDER BY

sql
-- ❌ "Last inserted account" without ORDER BY — undefined order
SELECT account_id FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = 1001 LIMIT 1;
-- ✅
SELECT account_id FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = 1001
ORDER BY opened_at DESC LIMIT 1;

Mistake 3: Using OFFSET for Deep Pagination

sql
-- ❌ OFFSET 100000 — scans and discards 100K rows
SELECT account_id FROM accounts ORDER BY account_id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000;
-- ✅ Keyset pagination (Lesson 13)
SELECT account_id FROM accounts WHERE account_id > :lastId ORDER BY account_id LIMIT 20;

Mistake 4: Scalar Subquery Instead of JOIN

sql
-- ❌ N correlated subqueries
SELECT c.name, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id) ...
-- ✅ JOIN + GROUP BY (Lesson 14)

Mistake 5: String Concatenation in SQL (SQL Injection)

java
// ❌ CRITICAL SECURITY FLAW
jdbcTemplate.query("SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE account_number = '" + userInput + "'");

// ✅ Bind parameter
jdbcTemplate.query("SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts WHERE account_number = ?",
    accountNumber);

Mistake 6: findAll() on Large Table

java
// ❌ SELECT * FROM accounts — 10M rows into JVM heap
List<Account> all = accountRepo.findAll();
// ✅ Paginated or streaming
Page<Account> page = accountRepo.findAll(PageRequest.of(0, 100));

Mistake 7: Alias in WHERE

sql
-- ❌ ERROR: alias not visible in WHERE (logical order)
SELECT balance AS bal FROM accounts WHERE bal > 1000;
-- ✅ Repeat expression or use subquery/CTE
SELECT balance AS bal FROM accounts WHERE balance > 1000;

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What does SELECT do?

Retrieves data from tables. Projects columns, evaluates expressions, returns result set to client.

Q2: What is the difference between SELECT and WHERE?

SELECT chooses which columns appear in result. WHERE filters which rows are included. Different logical execution order: WHERE before SELECT.

Q3: Does SELECT guarantee row order?

No. Must use ORDER BY for deterministic ordering.

Q4: What is DISTINCT?

Removes duplicate rows from result set. All selected columns must match for rows to be considered duplicates.

**Q5: Why avoid SELECT * in production?**

Reads unnecessary columns, increases I/O, network, memory; breaks when schema changes; triggers TOAST/LOB fetches.

Mid-Level

Q6: Explain SQL logical processing order.

FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. Explains why alias unavailable in WHERE but available in ORDER BY.

Q7: What is projection pushdown?

Reading only requested columns from storage — reduces I/O. Explicit column list enables this. Column stores take it further.

Q8: DTO projection vs full entity load in JPA?

Full entity: SELECT all mapped columns, builds managed entity in persistence context. DTO: SELECT only needed columns, no entity management — faster for lists.

Q9: Sargable predicate — example?

WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01' — index usable. Non-sargable: WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2024-01-01' — function prevents index.

Q10: How does SELECT interact with MVCC?

SELECT reads snapshot of committed rows per isolation level. Non-locking read (default). No blocking of writers in MVCC databases (PostgreSQL, InnoDB).

Senior

Q11: Keyset vs OFFSET pagination — when and why?

OFFSET: simple but O(offset) cost — slow at page 10000. Keyset: WHERE id > last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT n — O(limit) always. Use keyset for infinite scroll, large tables.

Q12: Explain index-only scan in context of SELECT.

Index contains all columns in SELECT and WHERE — heap not accessed. Requires covering index (Lesson 28). PostgreSQL needs visibility map check.

Q13: Heavy reporting SELECT impacting OLTP — architect solution?

Read replica, materialized view (Lesson 9), columnar warehouse, restrict to off-peak, add WHERE date partition filter, never run on primary.

Q14: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE — when?

Pessimistic locking: lock rows for update in same transaction. Banking transfer: SELECT balance FOR UPDATE → check → UPDATE. Prevents lost update (Lesson 40).

Staff / Architect

Q15: Design read API for account list returning 50 fields, 10M accounts queried paginated.

DTO with 50 fields explicit in JPQL constructor SELECT. Keyset pagination on indexed column. Read replica. Cache hot customers in Redis. No entity load. Monitor p99. EXPLAIN on first page and page at depth.

**Q16: Team uses SELECT * everywhere via ORM. Migration strategy?**

Enable query logging, identify top 20 queries by frequency×width. Introduce interface projections and DTO constructors. Lint rule: ban findAll() without Pageable. Code review standard: no SELECT * in native queries. Measure buffer pool hit ratio improvement.

Scenario

Scenario: "API returns account list in 3 seconds. EXPLAIN shows Seq Scan on accounts, 2M rows."

Root cause: WHERE customer_id unindexed or missing WHERE entirely. Fix: CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_customer_id, add WHERE customer_id = ?, SELECT explicit columns not *, add LIMIT. Verify Index Scan in EXPLAIN. Latency target: <50ms.

Part 20 — Revision Sheet

Must-Know

  • SELECT = projection (columns), not filtering (WHERE) or sorting (ORDER BY)
  • Logical order: FROM before SELECT; alias in ORDER BY not WHERE
  • Never SELECT * in production
  • ORDER BY required for deterministic order
  • DISTINCT removes duplicate full rows
  • Bind parameters — never concatenate input
  • DTO projection for list APIs
  • Keyset pagination over OFFSET at scale
  • Sargable predicates for index use

ASCII: Query Pipeline

text
SQL → Parse → Analyze → Optimize → Execute → Result Set
                      ↑
              chooses Index Scan vs Seq Scan

Hibernate

text
findById()     → SELECT all entity columns
DTO projection → SELECT only needed columns ✅
Lazy load      → additional SELECT (N+1 risk)
