Part 1 — Concept

What Is WHERE?

The WHERE clause filters rows before they are grouped, projected, or sorted. It implements the relational algebra selection operation (σ).

sql
SELECT column_list
FROM   table_source
WHERE  condition          -- ← filters ROWS (not columns)

WHERE vs Other Clauses

ClauseFiltersOperates On
WHERERowsIndividual row columns
SELECTColumnsProjection — which columns appear
HAVINGGroupsAfter GROUP BY (Lesson 15)
ONJoin rowsDuring JOIN (Lesson 16)
text
Logical execution order:

FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT
                  ▲
            rows filtered here
            before aggregation and projection

What WHERE Can Contain

text
WHERE condition types:

├── Comparison:       =, <>, !=, <, >, <=, >=
├── Logical:          AND, OR, NOT
├── Range:            BETWEEN ... AND ...
├── Set membership:   IN (...), NOT IN (...)
├── Pattern match:    LIKE, ILIKE (PG), NOT LIKE
├── NULL check:       IS NULL, IS NOT NULL
├── Subquery:         EXISTS, IN (SELECT ...), comparison to subquery
├── Boolean expr:     (condition1) AND (condition2)
└── Extensions:       ANY, ALL, SOME (subquery quantifiers)

Core Principle

WHERE reduces the number of rows the database must process for all subsequent operations. A selective WHERE on an indexed column is the single most impactful performance lever after schema design.

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Row Filtering in SQL

text
1974    SEQUEL: WHERE clause in original IBM language
        "SELECT * FROM employees WHERE dept = 'SALES'"

1970s   Query optimizers add cost-based selection pushdown
        Filter applied as early as possible in plan (predicate pushdown)

1980s   Index-based WHERE optimization becomes standard
        B+ tree range scans for WHERE col > value

1990s   SQL-92: BETWEEN, IN, EXISTS standardized
        Optimizer learns to rewrite OR conditions to UNION for index use

2000s   Function-based indexes (Oracle) — partial workaround for non-sargable WHERE
        PostgreSQL: partial indexes matching common WHERE predicates

2010s   Query store / pg_stat_statements — identify bad WHERE patterns in production
        Parameter sniffing problems with prepared statement WHERE values

2020s   Auto-index advisors (AWS RDS, Google Cloud SQL)
        ML-based cardinality estimation for complex WHERE predicates

Historical Lesson

Early systems did full table scans for every WHERE. Modern optimizers push predicates to index scans and combine filters with bitmap/intersection — but only when the WHERE clause is written in an index-friendly (sargable) form.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does WHERE Solve?

Problem 1: Reading Entire Table When Few Rows Needed

sql
-- Without WHERE: 100 million rows read
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts;

-- With WHERE: 3 rows read
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = 1001;
-- 33 million times less data processed (with index)

Problem 2: Business Rules as Data Filters

text
"Teller sees only ACTIVE accounts for customer X"
"Report only transactions in January 2024"
"Find payments over $10,000 for fraud review"

WHERE encodes business scope into every query

Problem 3: Security — Row-Level Filtering

sql
-- Application always adds tenant filter
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE tenant_id = :currentTenantId    -- multi-tenancy isolation
AND customer_id = :customerId;

-- PostgreSQL Row Level Security (RLS) enforces WHERE at DB level:
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON orders
    USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::bigint);

Problem 4: Consistent Filtering Across Clients

text
Without WHERE in shared view:
  App A filters status='ACTIVE'
  Batch job forgets → processes CLOSED accounts

CREATE VIEW active_accounts AS
SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';
-- All clients querying view get consistent filter

Problem 5: Join Reduction Before Cartesian Product

sql
-- Filter before join reduces join input size
SELECT c.name, a.balance
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id = 1001;   -- 1 customer, 3 accounts — not 1M × 1M

Unified Problem Statement

WHERE eliminates irrelevant rows as early as possible in query execution — reducing I/O, CPU, memory, and network transfer while enforcing business scope and security boundaries.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Filter Before SELECT and GROUP BY?

Predicate Pushdown — Optimizer Philosophy

text
GOAL: Filter rows as early as possible

Query:
  SELECT account_type, SUM(balance)
  FROM accounts
  WHERE customer_id = 1001
  GROUP BY account_type;

Optimizer pushes WHERE before GROUP BY:
  1. Filter to customer_id = 1001  (3 rows from 1M)
  2. GROUP BY account_type on 3 rows
  NOT: group 1M rows then filter

Early filtering = less work for every downstream operation

WHERE vs HAVING — Why Two Filters?

sql
-- WHERE: filter rows BEFORE grouping
SELECT account_type, COUNT(*)
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'        -- filters individual rows
GROUP BY account_type;

-- HAVING: filter groups AFTER grouping
SELECT account_type, COUNT(*)
FROM accounts
GROUP BY account_type
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;           -- filters aggregated groups (Lesson 15)
UseClause
Filter individual rowsWHERE
Filter aggregated groupsHAVING
Filter on non-aggregated columnWHERE (preferred — earlier)
Filter on aggregate resultHAVING

Part 5 — Internal Working

How WHERE Works Internally

Predicate Evaluation

text
For each row candidate (from scan or index):

  Evaluate WHERE expression as TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN (NULL)

  TRUE    → include row in result
  FALSE   → discard row
  UNKNOWN → discard row (NULL is treated as false in WHERE)

Example: WHERE balance > 1000
  balance=1500 → TRUE  → include
  balance=500  → FALSE → exclude
  balance=NULL → UNKNOWN → exclude

Access Path Selection Based on WHERE

text
WHERE account_id = 5001
  → Optimizer: equality on PK → Index Unique Scan → O(log n)

WHERE customer_id = 1001
  → Index Scan on idx_accounts_customer_id → O(log n + k)

WHERE balance > 10000
  → Index Range Scan on idx_balance (if exists) → O(log n + k)

WHERE UPPER(status) = 'ACTIVE'
  → Function on column → Seq Scan + Filter → O(n)  ❌

WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' AND customer_id = 1001
  → Bitmap Index Scan (both indexes) + AND → O(log n)  ✅

Index Scan with Filter Diagram

text
WHERE customer_id = 1001 AND status = 'ACTIVE'

Plan: Index Scan idx_customer_id + Filter status

Index on customer_id:
  customer_id=1001 → rows: (5001, ACTIVE), (5002, CLOSED), (5003, ACTIVE)

Filter step (in executor):
  (5001, ACTIVE)   → status='ACTIVE' → ✅ include
  (5002, CLOSED)   → status='CLOSED' → ❌ exclude
  (5003, ACTIVE)   → status='ACTIVE' → ✅ include

Index gets close rows; filter removes rest without full table scan
Better: composite index (customer_id, status) — index-only filter (Lesson 27)

Parameterized WHERE (Bind Variables)

sql
-- Prepared statement:
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = $1;

First execution: optimizer chooses plan for customer_id = 1001 (3 rows)
Second execution: customer_id = 9999 (500 rows) — same plan reused

Parameter sniffing: plan optimized for first value may be wrong for second
PostgreSQL: adaptive plans (PG 14+), Oracle: bind peeking, SQL Server: recompile hints

Boolean Logic Short-Circuit

text
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' AND balance > 1000

Evaluation order not guaranteed in SQL (unlike Java &&)
Optimizer may reorder for index use:
  If index on status (high selectivity): filter status first
  If index on balance: may choose balance index instead

AND: all conditions must be TRUE
OR:  any condition TRUE → include row
     OR often prevents index use → UNION rewrite (advanced)

Part 6 — Storage Internals

WHERE and Physical Storage

Index-Assisted WHERE

text
Table: accounts (100M rows)
Index: idx_accounts_customer_id (customer_id)

WHERE customer_id = 1001:

B+ Tree lookup:
  Root → Branch → Leaf pages with customer_id=1001
  Returns 3 row pointers (ctid or PK leaf)

Pages read: ~3-4 index pages + 3 data pages = ~6 pages
vs Seq Scan: 100M rows / 120 rows per page = ~833,000 pages

Index reduces I/O by ~100,000× for selective predicates

Sequential Scan with Filter

text
WHERE status = 'INACTIVE'   (no index, 2% of rows)

Seq Scan:
  Read page 1 → evaluate status for each row → keep matches
  Read page 2 → ...
  Read all pages (must touch every page)

PostgreSQL: visibility check per row (MVCC)
Even "empty" pages after vacuum may be skipped via visibility map

Partial index opportunity:
  CREATE INDEX idx_inactive ON accounts(account_id) WHERE status = 'INACTIVE';
  → index only 2% of rows — tiny, fast (Lesson 26)

Clustered Index and Range WHERE

sql
-- InnoDB clustered PK: rows physically sorted by account_id
WHERE account_id BETWEEN 5000 AND 6000;

Range scan on clustered index:
  Sequential leaf pages from 5000 to 6000
  Sequential I/O — OS read-ahead helps — very fast

Same range on non-indexed column:
  Full table scan — random I/O — slow

Partition Pruning and WHERE

sql
-- Table partitioned by month (Lesson 42)
WHERE created_at >= '2024-06-01' AND created_at < '2024-07-01';

Optimizer: partition pruning
  Only scan transactions_2024_06 partition
  Skip other 11 monthly partitions
  WHERE on partition key → massive I/O reduction

Part 7 — Memory Usage

WHERE and Memory

Filter Reduces Downstream Memory

text
Query without selective WHERE:
  Hash Aggregate on 100M rows → work_mem exhausted → disk spill

Same query with WHERE customer_id = 1001 (3 rows):
  Hash Aggregate on 3 rows → trivial memory

WHERE selectivity directly affects work_mem for GROUP BY, DISTINCT, SORT

Bitmap Index Scan Memory

text
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' AND account_type = 'SAVINGS'
  (two separate indexes, PostgreSQL bitmap scan)

1. Scan idx_status → bitmap of matching row locations
2. Scan idx_account_type → bitmap
3. Bitmap AND operation in memory
4. Fetch matching heap rows

Bitmap fits in work_mem — for very large result sets → bitmap heap scan spills

JDBC/Hibernate — WHERE Limits Result Set Memory

java
// Without WHERE — loads all rows
List<Account> all = accountRepo.findAll();  // O(all rows) heap

// With WHERE — bounded result
List<Account> active = accountRepo.findByCustomerCustomerIdAndStatus(1001L, ACTIVE);
// O(matching rows) heap — typically small

Part 8 — Execution Flow

WHERE Execution Flows

Flow 1: PK Equality (Most Selective)

sql
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 5001;
text
1. Parse WHERE: account_id = 5001
2. Optimizer: unique index scan, cost=8, rows=1
3. Executor: B+ tree descent → 1 leaf page → 1 row
4. Evaluate WHERE: TRUE (exact match guaranteed)
5. Project columns → return 1 row
Time: ~0.5ms

Flow 2: Composite Condition

sql
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001 AND status = 'ACTIVE' AND balance >= 1000;
text
1. Optimizer statistics:
     customer_id=1001: 3 rows (highly selective)
     status='ACTIVE': 80% of rows
     balance>=1000: 60% of rows

2. Choose: Index Scan idx_accounts_customer_id (most selective first)
   Filter: status='ACTIVE' AND balance>=1000 (residual predicate)

3. For each of 3 index entries:
     Evaluate remaining conditions
     Include if all TRUE

4. Return matching rows (likely 1-3)
Time: ~1ms

Flow 3: OR Condition

sql
SELECT account_id FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001 OR customer_id = 1002;
text
Option A: BitmapOr of two index scans on customer_id
  Scan idx for 1001 → bitmap
  Scan idx for 1002 → bitmap
  OR bitmaps → fetch rows

Option B: Seq Scan + Filter (if optimizer thinks cheaper)

Option C: UNION ALL rewrite (optimizer may transform):
  SELECT account_id FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = 1001
  UNION ALL
  SELECT account_id FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = 1002;

Flow 4: NULL Handling

sql
SELECT account_id FROM accounts WHERE closed_at IS NULL;
text
For each row:
  closed_at = NULL → IS NULL → TRUE → include
  closed_at = '2024-01-15' → IS NULL → FALSE → exclude

⚠️ WHERE closed_at = NULL  → always UNKNOWN → zero rows returned
   Always use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL

Flow 5: Subquery in WHERE

sql
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE status = 'SUSPENDED');
text
Execution (semi-join):
  1. Execute subquery → set of suspended customer_ids (hash table)
  2. Scan accounts (index or seq)
  3. For each account: customer_id IN hash set?
  4. Include matching rows

Alternative: Hash Join accounts.customer_id = subquery.customer_id (semi-join)

EXPLAIN Example

sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001 AND status = 'ACTIVE';

-- Index Scan using idx_accounts_customer on accounts
--   Index Cond: (customer_id = 1001)
--   Filter: ((status)::text = 'ACTIVE'::text)
--   Rows Removed by Filter: 1
--   Buffers: shared hit=4

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

WHERE Performance Rules

Selectivity Formula

text
Selectivity = matching_rows / total_rows

customer_id = 1001:     3 / 1,000,000 = 0.000003  (0.0003%)  ← excellent
status = 'ACTIVE':      800,000 / 1,000,000 = 80%             ← poor alone
balance > 10000:        200,000 / 1,000,000 = 20%

Rule: most selective predicate should drive index choice
Composite index: (most_selective_col, next_selective_col) — Lesson 27

Sargable vs Non-Sargable Predicates

Sargable (index-friendly)Non-Sargable (blocks index)
col = valueUPPER(col) = value
col > valuecol + 1 > value
col BETWEEN a AND bYEAR(col) = 2024
col LIKE 'prefix%'col LIKE '%suffix'
col IS NULLCOALESCE(col, 0) = 0
col IN (1,2,3)CAST(col AS TEXT) = '123'
sql
-- ❌ Non-sargable — forces seq scan
SELECT account_id FROM accounts WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM opened_at) = 2024;

-- ✅ Sargable range — index on opened_at usable
SELECT account_id FROM accounts
WHERE opened_at >= '2024-01-01' AND opened_at < '2025-01-01';

WHERE Performance Checklist

text
□ Indexed column in equality or range predicate?
□ Most selective condition uses index?
□ Avoid functions on indexed columns?
□ IS NULL vs = NULL correct?
□ OR conditions — consider UNION or bitmap?
□ LIKE uses leading literal (not leading wildcard)?
□ Statistics up to date (ANALYZE)? (Lesson 31)
□ EXPLAIN shows Index Scan not Seq Scan for large tables?

Common WHERE Anti-Patterns

sql
-- ❌ Implicit type conversion — index blocked
WHERE account_id = '5001'   -- string vs BIGINT (may cast column)

-- ✅ Match types
WHERE account_id = 5001

-- ❌ Negative condition on indexed column — often seq scan
WHERE status <> 'CLOSED'    -- 95% of rows match anyway

-- ❌ OR on different columns — index merge overhead
WHERE customer_id = 1001 OR branch_id = 50
-- ✅ Consider UNION if both selective

-- ❌ NOT IN with NULLs in subquery — unknown result semantics
WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM blacklist)
-- blacklist has NULL customer_id → zero rows returned!
-- ✅ NOT EXISTS instead

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

WHERE PatternWith IndexWithout Index
PK equalityO(log n)O(n)
Equality on indexed colO(log n + k)O(n)
Range on indexed colO(log n + k)O(n)
LIKE 'prefix%'O(log n + k)O(n)
LIKE '%suffix'O(n)O(n)
Function on colO(n)O(n)
AND of indexed colsO(log n + k) composite/bitmapO(n)
OR of indexed colsO(k1 + k2) bitmap/unionO(n)
IN (small list)O(m × log n) m=list sizeO(n)
EXISTS subqueryO(n × subq) or hash semi-join O(n+m)O(n × subq)

k = matching rows, n = total rows, m = IN list size

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

WHERE Masterclass Examples

Comparison Operators

sql
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts WHERE balance > 10000;
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts WHERE balance BETWEEN 1000 AND 5000;
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts WHERE account_type <> 'LOAN';
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts WHERE account_type != 'LOAN';  -- same

Logical Operators

sql
-- AND: all conditions must be true
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001
AND status = 'ACTIVE'
AND balance >= 0;

-- OR: any condition true
SELECT account_id FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'SUSPENDED' OR status = 'CLOSED';

-- NOT
SELECT account_id FROM accounts
WHERE NOT status = 'CLOSED';           -- prefer <>
WHERE NOT (balance < 0 OR status = 'CLOSED');

-- Parentheses for precedence: AND binds tighter than OR
SELECT account_id FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001 AND (status = 'ACTIVE' OR status = 'SUSPENDED');

IN and NOT IN

sql
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE account_type IN ('SAVINGS', 'CHECKING');

SELECT account_id FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id IN (1001, 1002, 1003);

-- IN with subquery
SELECT account_id FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id IN (
    SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE region = 'APAC'
);

-- ⚠️ NOT IN — NULL trap
SELECT account_id FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM blocked_customers);
-- If blocked_customers has NULL customer_id → returns ZERO rows
-- ✅ Safe alternative:
SELECT account_id FROM accounts
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM blocked_customers b
    WHERE b.customer_id = accounts.customer_id
);

BETWEEN

sql
-- Date range (sargable)
SELECT transaction_id, amount, created_at FROM transactions
WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01'
AND created_at < '2024-02-01';   -- preferred over BETWEEN for timestamps

-- BETWEEN is inclusive both ends
WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-01-31 23:59:59';

-- Balance range
WHERE balance BETWEEN 1000.00 AND 10000.00;

LIKE Pattern Matching

sql
-- Prefix search (sargable with btree index in some DBs)
SELECT account_id FROM accounts WHERE account_number LIKE 'ACC-2024%';

-- Contains search (NOT sargable with standard btree)
SELECT account_id FROM accounts WHERE account_number LIKE '%12345%';
-- Use: full-text search (Elasticsearch) or pg_trgm index (PostgreSQL)

-- Single char wildcard
WHERE account_number LIKE 'ACC-____-___';  -- _ = one character

-- PostgreSQL case-insensitive
WHERE email ILIKE 'ankur@%';

-- ESCAPE character
WHERE description LIKE '%50%%' ESCAPE '%';  -- literal % in pattern

NULL Semantics

sql
-- ✅ Correct NULL checks
SELECT account_id FROM accounts WHERE closed_at IS NULL;
SELECT account_id FROM accounts WHERE closed_at IS NOT NULL;

-- ❌ WRONG — returns no rows (NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN)
SELECT account_id FROM accounts WHERE closed_at = NULL;

-- NULL in comparisons
WHERE balance > 1000;     -- NULL balance → UNKNOWN → excluded
WHERE balance IS DISTINCT FROM NULL;  -- PostgreSQL: explicit NULL equality test

-- COALESCE in WHERE — often non-sargable
WHERE COALESCE(status, 'ACTIVE') = 'ACTIVE';
-- ✅ Better: (status = 'ACTIVE' OR status IS NULL) if needed

EXISTS (Semi-Join)

sql
-- Accounts that have at least one transaction over $10,000
SELECT a.account_id, a.balance
FROM accounts a
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM transactions t
    WHERE t.account_id = a.account_id
    AND t.amount > 10000
);

-- Customers with no accounts
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id
);

ANY / ALL

sql
-- Balance greater than ANY (some) savings account average — unusual
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts a
WHERE balance > ANY (
    SELECT AVG(balance) FROM accounts GROUP BY account_type
);

-- Balance greater than ALL other accounts of same type — rare
WHERE balance > ALL (
    SELECT balance FROM accounts a2
    WHERE a2.account_type = a.account_type AND a2.account_id <> a.account_id
);

Part 12 — Production Usage

WHERE in Production Systems

Banking — Mandatory Filters

sql
-- Always filter by indexed columns; bind parameters
SELECT account_id, account_number, balance, currency, status
FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = :customerId          -- indexed FK
AND status IN ('ACTIVE', 'SUSPENDED')    -- business scope
AND tenant_id = :tenantId;               -- multi-tenancy (indexed)

Payment Fraud — Time-Window WHERE

sql
SELECT payment_id, account_id, amount, created_at
FROM payments
WHERE created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour'   -- partition + index friendly
AND amount > 10000
AND status = 'COMPLETED'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 100;

Soft Delete Pattern

sql
-- Application convention: always exclude deleted
SELECT customer_id, email FROM customers
WHERE status <> 'DELETED';   -- or status = 'ACTIVE'

-- Partial index matches this WHERE exactly:
CREATE INDEX idx_customers_active ON customers(email) WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';

Multi-Tenancy with RLS (PostgreSQL)

sql
-- Application sets tenant on connection
SET app.tenant_id = '1001';

-- RLS policy applies WHERE automatically
CREATE POLICY tenant_policy ON accounts
    USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::bigint);

-- Application query — no explicit tenant WHERE needed (but defense in depth: add both)
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = 5001;

Audit — Immutable Log Queries

sql
-- Append-only audit: WHERE on time range + indexed entity
SELECT event_id, event_type, payload, created_at
FROM audit_events
WHERE entity_type = 'ACCOUNT'
AND entity_id = :accountId
AND created_at >= :fromDate
AND created_at < :toDate
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 500;

Part 13 — Spring Boot Integration

WHERE via Spring Data JPA

Method Name Queries → WHERE Generation

java
public interface AccountRepository extends JpaRepository<Account, Long> {

    // WHERE customer.customerId = ?1 AND status = ?2
    List<Account> findByCustomerCustomerIdAndStatus(Long customerId, AccountStatus status);

    // WHERE balance > ?1 AND status = 'ACTIVE'
    List<Account> findByBalanceGreaterThanAndStatus(BigDecimal min, AccountStatus status);

    // WHERE openedAt BETWEEN ?1 AND ?2
    List<Account> findByOpenedAtBetween(Instant from, Instant to);

    // WHERE accountType IN (?1)
    List<Account> findByAccountTypeIn(Collection<AccountType> types);

    // WHERE customer.customerId = ?1 AND closedAt IS NULL
    List<Account> findByCustomerCustomerIdAndClosedAtIsNull(Long customerId);
}

JPQL with WHERE

java
@Query("""
    SELECT a FROM Account a
    WHERE a.customer.customerId = :customerId
    AND a.status = :status
    AND a.balance >= :minBalance
    """)
List<Account> findActiveAccountsAboveBalance(
    @Param("customerId") Long customerId,
    @Param("status") AccountStatus status,
    @Param("minBalance") BigDecimal minBalance);

Specification API — Dynamic WHERE

java
public static Specification<Account> hasCustomer(Long customerId) {
    return (root, query, cb) -> cb.equal(root.get("customer").get("customerId"), customerId);
}

public static Specification<Account> hasStatus(AccountStatus status) {
    return (root, query, cb) -> cb.equal(root.get("status"), status);
}

accountRepo.findAll(
    Specification.where(hasCustomer(1001L)).and(hasStatus(ACTIVE))
);
// Generates: WHERE customer_id = ? AND status = ?

Native Query — Always Use Bind Parameters

java
@Query(value = """
    SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
    WHERE customer_id = :customerId
    AND status = 'ACTIVE'
    AND opened_at >= :fromDate
    """, nativeQuery = true)
List<Object[]> findActiveSince(
    @Param("customerId") Long customerId,
    @Param("fromDate") LocalDate fromDate);

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

Hibernate WHERE Behavior

Automatic WHERE on Load

java
accountRepo.findById(5001L);
// SQL: SELECT ... FROM accounts a1_0 WHERE a1_0.account_id = ?

accountRepo.findByCustomerCustomerIdAndStatus(1001L, ACTIVE);
// SQL: SELECT ... FROM accounts a1_0
//      WHERE a1_0.customer_id = ? AND a1_0.status = ?

@Where — Hibernate Filter (Soft Delete)

java
@Entity
@Table(name = "accounts")
@SQLRestriction("status <> 'DELETED'")   // Hibernate 6 (was @Where)
public class Account {
    // All queries automatically add: WHERE status <> 'DELETED'
    // Including findById, findAll, JPQL
}
// ⚠️ Document this — native queries bypass @SQLRestriction

@Filter — Session-Scoped WHERE

java
@Entity
@FilterDef(name = "tenantFilter", parameters = @ParamDef(name = "tenantId", type = Long.class))
@Filter(name = "tenantFilter", condition = "tenant_id = :tenantId")
public class Account { ... }

// In service:
session.enableFilter("tenantFilter").setParameter("tenantId", 1001L);
// All Account queries now include WHERE tenant_id = 1001

Criteria API

java
CriteriaBuilder cb = entityManager.getCriteriaBuilder();
CriteriaQuery<Account> cq = cb.createQuery(Account.class);
Root<Account> root = cq.from(Account.class);

cq.select(root).where(
    cb.and(
        cb.equal(root.get("customer").get("customerId"), 1001L),
        cb.equal(root.get("status"), AccountStatus.ACTIVE),
        cb.greaterThanOrEqualTo(root.get("balance"), new BigDecimal("1000"))
    )
);

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

WHERE Design for Solution Architects

Index-WHERE Alignment

text
For every frequent WHERE predicate, ask:
  1. Is there an index on this column (or composite leading column)?
  2. Is the predicate sargable?
  3. What is selectivity (ANALYZE statistics)?
  4. Should this be a partial index matching exact WHERE?

Example:
  Query: WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' (80% of rows) — index alone not helpful
  Query: WHERE customer_id = ? AND status = 'ACTIVE' — composite index (customer_id, status)

Multi-Tenancy WHERE Strategy

text
Layer 1: Application WHERE tenant_id = ? on every query
Layer 2: Hibernate @Filter or @SQLRestriction
Layer 3: PostgreSQL RLS policy
Layer 4: Composite index (tenant_id, business_key) — tenant_id leading column

Defense in depth — never rely on application WHERE alone for security

WHERE in API Design

text
REST: GET /customers/{id}/accounts?status=ACTIVE&minBalance=1000

Maps to:
  WHERE customer_id = :id
  AND status = :status
  AND balance >= :minBalance

Architect rules:
  □ Every filter param maps to indexed column
  □ Reject unindexed filter on large table (400 Bad Request or async export)
  □ Max date range enforced (prevent full table scan via wide date range)
  □ Pagination mandatory (Lesson 13)

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: = NULL Instead of IS NULL

sql
-- ❌ Returns zero rows always
WHERE closed_at = NULL;
-- ✅
WHERE closed_at IS NULL;

Mistake 2: Function on Indexed Column

sql
-- ❌ Index on opened_at unused
WHERE DATE(opened_at) = '2024-01-15';
-- ✅
WHERE opened_at >= '2024-01-15' AND opened_at < '2024-01-16';

Mistake 3: NOT IN with NULL Subquery

sql
-- ❌ Zero rows if subquery contains NULL
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM blocked WHERE reason IS NOT NULL OR id IS NULL);
-- ✅
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM blocked b WHERE b.id = accounts.id);

Mistake 4: Implicit Type Mismatch

sql
-- ❌ May cast column — index blocked
WHERE account_id = '5001';   -- string literal
-- ✅
WHERE account_id = 5001;

Mistake 5: Unbounded Query — Missing WHERE

java
// ❌ No WHERE — full table scan
accountRepo.findAll();
// ✅ Always filter + paginate
accountRepo.findByCustomerCustomerId(customerId, PageRequest.of(0, 20));

Mistake 6: OR Preventing Index Use

sql
-- ❌ Optimizer may seq scan
WHERE customer_id = 1001 OR balance > 100000;
-- ✅ If both selective — UNION ALL
SELECT account_id FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = 1001
UNION ALL
SELECT account_id FROM accounts WHERE balance > 100000 AND customer_id <> 1001;

Mistake 7: Filtering in Application After Full Load

java
// ❌ SELECT all → filter in Java
List<Account> all = accountRepo.findAll();
return all.stream().filter(a -> a.getStatus() == ACTIVE).toList();
// ✅ WHERE in SQL
return accountRepo.findByStatus(ACTIVE);

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What does WHERE do?

Filters rows before grouping and projection. Only rows where condition is TRUE are included.

Q2: Difference between WHERE and HAVING?

WHERE filters individual rows before GROUP BY. HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

Q3: Why WHERE col = NULL returns no rows?

NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, not TRUE. Use IS NULL.

Q4: What is sargable?

Search ARGument ABLE — predicate written so optimizer can use index (no function on column).

Q5: AND vs OR precedence?

AND binds tighter. Use parentheses: a AND (b OR c).

Mid-Level

Q6: Explain selectivity and index choice.

Selectivity = fraction of rows matching predicate. Most selective column should lead composite index. Optimizer uses statistics to estimate rows and choose plan.

Q7: NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS — when to use which?

NOT EXISTS always safe with NULLs. NOT IN fails if subquery returns NULL. Prefer NOT EXISTS in production.

Q8: Why is LIKE '%abc%' slow?

Leading wildcard prevents B-tree index use — requires full scan. Use full-text search or pg_trgm for contains queries.

Q9: How does WHERE interact with MVCC?

WHERE evaluated on visible row versions per snapshot. Dead tuples excluded by visibility check before predicate evaluation.

Q10: Parameter sniffing problem?

Prepared statement plan optimized for first bind value may be wrong for subsequent values. Fix: adaptive plans, recompile hints, generic plans, or pg_stat_statements analysis.

Senior

Q11: Query slow with WHERE customer_id = ? — diagnosis steps?

EXPLAIN ANALYZE: Seq Scan? Missing index? Stale statistics? Implicit cast? Function on column? Low selectivity making index scan slower than seq scan? Run ANALYZE, CREATE INDEX, verify bind type matches column type.

Q12: Design WHERE strategy for multi-tenant SaaS on shared schema.

tenant_id on every table, composite indexes (tenant_id, business_key), RLS policy, Hibernate @Filter, application WHERE defense-in-depth, never query without tenant filter.

Q13: OR conditions and index usage — optimization strategies?

BitmapOr (PostgreSQL), index merge (MySQL), UNION ALL rewrite, or restructure to IN list if same column: status IN ('A','B') instead of status='A' OR status='B'.

Q14: Partial index matching WHERE — example?

CREATE INDEX idx_active ON accounts(customer_id) WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' — index only active rows, smaller, matches common WHERE status='ACTIVE'.

Staff / Architect

Q15: API allows arbitrary filter combinations on 100M row table. Risk and mitigation?

Risk: unindexed filter → full scan → outage. Mitigate: whitelist filterable fields, require indexed columns, max date range, mandatory pagination, async export for heavy queries, query timeout, read replica routing.

Q16: Compare RLS, @SQLRestriction, and application WHERE for tenant isolation.

Application WHERE: bypassed by native SQL, bugs. @SQLRestriction: Hibernate only. RLS: DB-enforced, all clients. Use all three for defense in depth; RLS is strongest guarantee.

Scenario

Scenario: "Query WHERE status <> 'CLOSED' takes 30 seconds on 50M row table."

90% of rows match — optimizer correctly chooses Seq Scan. Fix: invert predicate if minority desired (status = 'CLOSED' for closed only), partial index on closed rows, or restructure query. If need active: status = 'ACTIVE' may be selective enough with index, or accept seq scan and move to read replica/MV.

Part 20 — Revision Sheet

Must-Know

  • WHERE filters rows — runs before GROUP BY, SELECT, ORDER BY
  • IS NULL not = NULL
  • NOT EXISTS not NOT IN (with NULL subquery)
  • Sargable: no function on indexed column; use ranges not YEAR()
  • Selectivity drives index choice
  • AND tighter precedence than OR — use parentheses
  • LIKE 'prefix%' maybe indexed; %suffix never
  • Bind parameters — never string concat
  • WHERE in SQL not Java stream filter on full table

Logical Order

text
FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT

NULL Rules

text
= NULL     → always fails
IS NULL    → correct
NOT IN + NULL subquery → zero rows trap

ORDER BY

Phase 2: SQL MASTERCLASS | Previous: WHERE | Next: GROUP BY

Foundation
1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why This Exists5Internal Working6Storage Internals7Memory Usage8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Complexity Analysis11Code / SQL Examples12Production Usage13Spring Boot Integration14Hibernate/JPA Integration15Architect Perspective16Decision Matrix17Comparison Tables18Common Mistakes19Interview Questions20Revision Sheet21Summary Table*Practice

Part 1 — Concept

What Is ORDER BY?

ORDER BY sorts the result set by one or more columns or expressions after filtering (WHERE) and grouping (GROUP BY) but before row limiting (LIMIT/FETCH).

sql
SELECT column_list
FROM   table_source
[WHERE  condition]
[GROUP BY columns]
[HAVING condition]
ORDER BY sort_expression [ASC | DESC] [, sort_expression ...]
[LIMIT n OFFSET m];

Critical Rule: Order Is Not Guaranteed Without ORDER BY

text
❌ MYTH: "Rows come back in primary key order" or "insertion order"
✅ TRUTH: Without ORDER BY, row order is UNDEFINED and may change anytime

Same query, two executions:
  Run 1: rows 5, 2, 8, 1
  Run 2: rows 2, 5, 1, 8   ← both correct without ORDER BY

Reasons order may shift:
  Parallel query workers
  Index scan direction change
  Vacuum reordering heap pages
  Plan change after ANALYZE
  Buffer pool state

ORDER BY Logical Position

text
Execution order:
  FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT

Implications:
  ✅ Can use SELECT alias in ORDER BY (SELECT runs before ORDER BY logically... 
     actually in SQL standard SELECT alias IS available in ORDER BY)
  ✅ Can ORDER BY column not in SELECT list
  ❌ Cannot use ORDER BY alias in WHERE (WHERE runs before SELECT)
  ✅ LIMIT applied AFTER sort — sorts entire result then truncates (unless optimized)

ORDER BY Components

ComponentPurposeExample
ColumnSort by table columnORDER BY balance
AliasSort by SELECT aliasORDER BY total DESC
ExpressionSort by computed valueORDER BY balance * 1.05
Column positionSort by SELECT positionORDER BY 3 DESC (fragile — avoid)
ASCAscending (default)ORDER BY name ASC
DESCDescendingORDER BY balance DESC
NULLS FIRST/LASTNULL placement (PG, Oracle)ORDER BY closed_at DESC NULLS LAST
Multiple columnsTie-breaking sortORDER BY status, balance DESC

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Sorting in SQL

text
1974    SEQUEL includes ORDER BY — one of original clauses
1970s   Sort implemented as external merge sort on disk (tape → disk)

1980s   In-memory quicksort for small result sets
        Index-based ORDER BY: if index order matches, skip explicit sort

1990s   SQL-92: ASC/DESC explicit; NULL ordering implementation-defined

2000s   Top-N optimization: ORDER BY + LIMIT → heap scan stops early
        Oracle: ROWNUM workaround for pagination (pre-12c)
        MySQL: LIMIT/OFFSET widely adopted

2012    Oracle 12c / SQL Standard: FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY
        OFFSET ... FETCH NEXT — standard pagination syntax

2010s   Keyset pagination (seek method) emerges as OFFSET alternative at scale
        GitHub, Stripe, Facebook engineering blogs document OFFSET problems

2020s   Incremental sort (PostgreSQL 13+) — sort partially sorted input faster
        Optimizer: index-only scan + ordered index → no sort step
        Hybrid sorting: in-memory + external sort with work_mem tuning

Historical Lesson

ORDER BY was expensive on tape systems. Modern databases can avoid sorting entirely when an index provides the desired order — one of the highest-value optimizations for list APIs and pagination.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does ORDER BY Solve?

Problem 1: Undefined Row Order

text
"Teller needs accounts listed by balance, highest first"
Without ORDER BY: random order — unusable UI
With ORDER BY balance DESC: deterministic, business-correct

Problem 2: Pagination Requires Sort

text
Page 1: accounts 1-20
Page 2: accounts 21-40

Without stable ORDER BY:
  Page 2 may repeat rows from page 1 or skip rows
  Concurrent inserts between page requests → inconsistent pages

Fix: ORDER BY unique column (account_id) as tie-breaker
  ORDER BY balance DESC, account_id ASC

Problem 3: Top-N Queries

text
"10 largest transactions today"
ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 10

Without ORDER BY + LIMIT: must fetch all rows to application, sort in Java — catastrophic

Problem 4: Report Presentation

text
Regulatory report: transactions by date, then by account
ORDER BY created_at ASC, account_id ASC
Human-readable output requirement

Problem 5: Merge Join Prerequisite

text
Optimizer uses Merge Join when both inputs sorted on join key:
  accounts sorted on customer_id + customers sorted on customer_id
  ORDER BY / index order enables merge join — query planner benefit

Unified Problem Statement

ORDER BY provides deterministic, business-meaningful sequence for display, pagination, Top-N selection, and query optimization — transforming an unordered set into an ordered result.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Sort After WHERE, Not Before?

text
Correct pipeline:
  1. Filter 100M rows → 1000 rows (WHERE)
  2. Sort 1000 rows (ORDER BY)
  3. Return top 20 (LIMIT)

Wrong mental model:
  Sort 100M rows then filter → 100× more sort work

Optimizer enforces: WHERE pushed before SORT in execution plan
Exception: subquery/CTE inlining may reorder but semantically equivalent

Why Separate ORDER BY from WHERE?

ConcernClause
Which rows belong in resultWHERE
In what sequence rows appearORDER BY
Which groups pass thresholdHAVING
How many rows to returnLIMIT

Mixing sort logic into WHERE (e.g., window functions aside) breaks relational algebra composition and optimizer rewrite rules.

NULL Sort Order

text
SQL standard: NULL sort order implementation-defined

PostgreSQL default:
  ASC  → NULLS LAST
  DESC → NULLS LAST (PG 15+ default changed for consistency)

Oracle:
  ASC  → NULLS LAST
  DESC → NULLS FIRST (default)

Explicit control (portable in PG/Oracle):
  ORDER BY closed_at DESC NULLS LAST
  ORDER BY closed_at ASC  NULLS FIRST

Part 5 — Internal Working

How ORDER BY Works Internally

Sort Algorithms Used by Databases

text
SMALL result set (fits in work_mem):
  Quicksort in memory — O(n log n)

LARGE result set (exceeds work_mem):
  External merge sort:
    1. Sort chunks in memory → write to temp disk files
    2. Merge sorted chunks — multi-pass
    O(n log n) but with disk I/O — 10-100× slower

INDEX ORDER scan (no explicit sort):
  If index column order = ORDER BY columns:
    Index Scan (Backward) or Forward — rows already sorted
    O(k) where k = rows returned — no sort step in plan
    "Incremental Sort" avoided entirely

Execution Plan Sort Types

text
PostgreSQL EXPLAIN nodes:

Sort                  — explicit quicksort / external merge sort
Incremental Sort      — optimize partially ordered input (PG 13+)
Index Scan            — index provides order (no Sort node)
Index Only Scan       — covering + ordered
Backward Index Scan   — DESC order from ascending index

Example — sort required:
  Sort Key: balance DESC
  Sort Method: quicksort  Memory: 256kB

Example — index avoids sort:
  Index Scan using idx_accounts_balance on accounts
  (no Sort node above)

Top-N Heap Optimization

sql
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
ORDER BY balance DESC
LIMIT 10;

Optimizer may use:
  TOP-N HEAP: maintain heap of 10 largest — O(n log 10) ≈ O(n)
  vs full sort O(n log n)

  Or: Index Scan backward on balance index — stop after 10 rows
  Best case: O(log n + 10) — index seek to max + scan 10 entries

Multi-Column Sort Internals

sql
ORDER BY status ASC, balance DESC, account_id ASC
text
Sort comparison function (tuple comparator):
  Compare status first
  If tie → compare balance (reversed for DESC)
  If tie → compare account_id

Index match requirement for skip-sort:
  Composite index (status ASC, balance DESC, account_id ASC)
  Must match ORDER BY direction exactly (PG, MySQL 8+)
  Or index scan + sort remaining (partial index help)

ORDER BY + LIMIT Interaction

text
Plan without optimization:
  Sort ALL matching rows → take first N

Plan with Top-N / LIMIT pushdown:
  Partial sort or index scan stopping at N rows
  Critical for: ORDER BY indexed_col LIMIT 20 on 100M row table

Part 6 — Storage Internals

ORDER BY and Index/Storage Interaction

Index That Matches ORDER BY

sql
-- Index:
CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_customer_balance
    ON accounts (customer_id, balance DESC);

-- Query:
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001
ORDER BY balance DESC
LIMIT 10;

Plan: Index Scan on idx_accounts_customer_balance
  Rows already sorted by balance within customer_id partition
  No Sort node — reads index leaf in order — stops after 10 rows
text
B+ Tree leaf order (matching index):

customer_id=1001: [balance=50000] [balance=15000] [balance=3500] [balance=0]
                  ▲ scan backward for DESC — first 10 rows immediately

Clustered PK Order (InnoDB)

sql
SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY account_id;
-- InnoDB clustered index: rows physically in account_id order
-- Index Scan on PK — no sort — sequential I/O — very fast

SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY balance;
-- Not clustered order → explicit Sort or secondary index on balance

Sort Spill to Disk

text
work_mem exceeded during sort:

PostgreSQL temp files:
  base/pgsql_tmp/pgsql_tmpPID.seq

Oracle TEMP tablespace:
  Sort segments in TEMP tablespace

Symptom: query slow, temp file I/O high
Fix: reduce rows sorted (better WHERE), increase work_mem session-only,
     add matching index to eliminate sort

Heap Table vs Index Order (PostgreSQL)

text
SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY created_at;
No index on created_at:
  Seq Scan all pages → Sort all rows → return
  Pages read in physical storage order (not created_at order)

With index on created_at:
  Index Scan in order → no sort

Part 7 — Memory Usage

ORDER BY Memory Consumption

work_mem — Sort Memory Budget

text
PostgreSQL work_mem (default ~4MB per sort operation):

Sort 1000 rows × 100 bytes = 100KB → in-memory quicksort ✅
Sort 1M rows × 100 bytes = 100MB → external merge sort to disk ❌

Multiple sorts in one query (JOIN + ORDER BY + GROUP BY):
  Each sort operation gets its own work_mem allocation
  4 sorts × 4MB = 16MB per query possible

Rule: work_mem × concurrent_queries must fit in RAM
  Don't set work_mem = 1GB globally — OOM risk
  SET work_mem = '64MB' for specific reporting session only

Sort Memory Formula (Approximate)

text
Memory ≈ num_rows × (sort_key_width + row_pointer)

ORDER BY balance (8B) on 500K rows:
  ~500K × 16 bytes = 8MB → may fit in default work_mem

ORDER BY customer_name (200B) on 500K rows:
  ~500K × 216 bytes = 108MB → spills to disk

OFFSET Memory Trap

sql
ORDER BY account_id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000;

Database must:
  Sort (or index scan) 100,020 rows
  Discard first 100,000
  Return 20

Memory/CPU: O(offset + limit) — grows linearly with page depth
Page 5000 with OFFSET 100000 → scans 100K rows every request

Client Memory — Sorted Result Set

java
// Fetching sorted page into List
Page<Account> page = accountRepo.findByCustomerId(1001L, PageRequest.of(5000, 20));
// DB sorted 100,020 rows; returned 20 to JVM — OK

// Fetching ALL sorted rows
List<Account> all = accountRepo.findByCustomerIdOrderByBalanceDesc(1001L);
// Entire sorted result in JVM heap — dangerous if unbounded

Part 8 — Execution Flow

ORDER BY Execution Flows

Flow 1: Index Scan — No Sort (Ideal)

sql
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001
ORDER BY account_id
LIMIT 20;
text
1. WHERE customer_id = 1001 → index idx_customer_id
2. Index already sorted by (customer_id, account_id) if composite
   OR sorted by account_id within filter
3. Return first 20 rows in index order — no Sort node
4. Execution time: ~1ms

Flow 2: Explicit Sort

sql
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
ORDER BY balance DESC
LIMIT 10;
text
1. Index Scan idx_status → filter ACTIVE rows (800K rows)
2. Sort node: quicksort 800K (balance, account_id) tuples
   OR Top-N heap if optimizer chooses
3. Limit → return 10 rows
4. If 800K × 16B = 12.8MB > work_mem → external sort → slow
Better: CREATE INDEX idx_active_balance ON accounts(balance DESC) WHERE status='ACTIVE';

Flow 3: Pagination with OFFSET

sql
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001
ORDER BY account_id
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000;
text
1. Index Scan idx_customer (customer_id=1001) in account_id order
2. Scan and discard rows 1..100000
3. Return rows 100001..100020
4. Time increases linearly with OFFSET depth
   OFFSET 0:    ~1ms
   OFFSET 100K: ~500ms

Flow 4: Keyset Pagination (Seek Method)

sql
-- Page 1:
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001
ORDER BY account_id
LIMIT 20;
-- Last row: account_id = 5042

-- Page 2:
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001
AND account_id > 5042          -- cursor from previous page
ORDER BY account_id
LIMIT 20;
text
1. Index Seek to account_id > 5042 within customer_id=1001
2. Return next 20 rows — no OFFSET discard
3. Time: O(limit) regardless of page depth — ~1ms for page 5000
Requirement: unique, immutable sort key (or composite tie-breaker)

Flow 5: Multi-Column ORDER BY

sql
SELECT account_id, status, balance FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001
ORDER BY status ASC, balance DESC, account_id ASC;
text
Sort comparator:
  Row A vs Row B:
    Compare status → if equal
    Compare balance (desc) → if equal
    Compare account_id

Stable sort preserves relative order of equal keys (implementation detail)
Tie-breaker account_id ensures deterministic pagination

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

ORDER BY Performance Rules

Performance Hierarchy

text
FASTEST → SLOWEST:

1. ORDER BY PK + LIMIT (clustered/index order, stop early)
2. ORDER BY indexed column + WHERE indexed + LIMIT (index scan, no sort)
3. ORDER BY indexed column — full result
4. Top-N heap on filtered set (LIMIT small, no matching index)
5. In-memory Sort (fits work_mem)
6. External sort spill to disk (large result)
7. ORDER BY expression on column (sort after compute — no index)
8. ORDER BY unindexed column on full table scan

Index + ORDER BY Alignment Checklist

text
For query:
  WHERE customer_id = ?
  ORDER BY balance DESC
  LIMIT 20

Ideal index: (customer_id, balance DESC)
  Includes WHERE equality + ORDER BY direction

Partial index if WHERE status='ACTIVE' always present:
  CREATE INDEX ... ON accounts(balance DESC) WHERE status='ACTIVE';

Pagination Strategy Comparison

MethodPage 1Page 5000ConsistencyRequirement
OFFSETFastSlow O(offset)Duplicates/skips on concurrent writesSimple
Keyset (seek)FastFast O(limit)Stable if cursor usedUnique sort key
Cursor (server)FastFastBestStateful connection

ORDER BY Anti-Patterns

sql
-- ❌ No ORDER BY on paginated API
SELECT account_id FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = 1001 LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40;

-- ❌ OFFSET at scale
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 500000;

-- ❌ Sort by non-indexed expression
ORDER BY UPPER(last_name);   -- compute + sort, no index

-- ❌ Sort column not in indexed path with WHERE
WHERE customer_id = 1001 ORDER BY opened_at;  -- no composite index

-- ✅ Stable keyset pagination
WHERE customer_id = 1001 AND account_id > :cursor
ORDER BY account_id LIMIT 20;

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

OperationComplexityNotes
Sort (explicit)O(n log n)n = rows after WHERE
Top-N heapO(n log k)k = LIMIT
Index ordered scanO(log n + k)k = rows returned
OFFSET paginationO(offset + limit)Linear in page depth
Keyset paginationO(log n + limit)Constant page depth cost
Multi-column sortO(n log n)Same as single column
External merge sortO(n log n) I/O boundDisk spills dominate
text
n = 100M rows after WHERE:
  Full sort:     ~100M × log(100M) ≈ 2.4B comparisons + possible disk I/O
  Index + LIMIT 20: ~log(100M) + 20 ≈ 27 index steps — 6 orders of magnitude faster

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

ORDER BY Masterclass Examples

Basic Sorting

sql
-- Ascending (default)
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001
ORDER BY balance;

-- Descending
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001
ORDER BY balance DESC;

-- Multiple columns
SELECT account_id, status, balance FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001
ORDER BY status ASC, balance DESC;

NULL Handling

sql
-- PostgreSQL / Oracle
SELECT account_id, closed_at FROM accounts
ORDER BY closed_at DESC NULLS LAST;   -- active accounts first (NULL closed_at)

SELECT account_id, closed_at FROM accounts
ORDER BY closed_at ASC NULLS FIRST;

-- MySQL: NULLs first in ASC, NULLs last in DESC (default)
-- ISNULL(closed_at) trick for explicit control in MySQL:
ORDER BY ISNULL(closed_at), closed_at DESC;

ORDER BY Expression and Alias

sql
SELECT
    account_id,
    balance,
    balance * 0.0525 AS annual_interest
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
ORDER BY annual_interest DESC;   -- alias valid in ORDER BY

-- Expression sort
ORDER BY ABS(balance) DESC;

-- ⚠️ Column position (avoid in production — fragile)
SELECT account_id, balance, status FROM accounts
ORDER BY 2 DESC;   -- sorts by 2nd column (balance)

Pagination — OFFSET (Simple, Limited Scale)

sql
-- PostgreSQL / MySQL
SELECT account_id, balance, opened_at
FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001
ORDER BY opened_at DESC, account_id ASC   -- stable tie-breaker
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40;   -- page 3 (0-indexed page 2)

-- Oracle 12c+ / SQL Standard
SELECT account_id, balance
FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001
ORDER BY opened_at DESC, account_id ASC
OFFSET 40 ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY;

-- SQL Server
ORDER BY opened_at DESC, account_id ASC
OFFSET 40 ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY;

Keyset Pagination (Production Scale)

sql
-- First page
SELECT account_id, balance, opened_at
FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001
ORDER BY opened_at DESC, account_id DESC
LIMIT 20;
-- Response includes last row: (account_id=4988, opened_at='2024-06-15')

-- Next page (cursor from last row)
SELECT account_id, balance, opened_at
FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001
AND (
    opened_at < '2024-06-15'
    OR (opened_at = '2024-06-15' AND account_id < 4988)
)
ORDER BY opened_at DESC, account_id DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- Simpler keyset when sorting by unique PK only:
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001 AND account_id > :lastAccountId
ORDER BY account_id ASC
LIMIT 20;

Top-N Queries

sql
-- Top 10 balances bank-wide
SELECT account_id, customer_id, balance
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
ORDER BY balance DESC
LIMIT 10;

-- PostgreSQL: DISTINCT ON alternative for top-N per group (Lesson 11)
SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id)
    customer_id, account_id, balance
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
ORDER BY customer_id, balance DESC;
-- Highest balance account per customer

ORDER BY in Subquery / Window (Preview Lesson 19)

sql
-- Window function avoids self-join for ranking
SELECT account_id, balance,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY balance DESC) AS rn
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';
-- Filter rn = 1 for top account per customer

Part 12 — Production Usage

ORDER BY in Production Systems

Banking — Transaction History

sql
-- Mobile app: latest transactions, keyset pagination
SELECT transaction_id, amount, txn_type, created_at
FROM transactions
WHERE account_id = :accountId
AND created_at < :cursorTimestamp
ORDER BY created_at DESC, transaction_id DESC
LIMIT 50;

-- Index: (account_id, created_at DESC, transaction_id DESC)

E-Commerce — Product Listing

sql
-- Sort options: price, rating, newest
-- Each sort option should have supporting index or accept sort cost

-- Price low to high:
ORDER BY price ASC, product_id ASC

-- Newest:
ORDER BY created_at DESC, product_id DESC

-- Architect: whitelist sort columns — never dynamic ORDER BY on user input without validation

Reporting — Deterministic Export

sql
-- Regulatory export: fixed order for reproducible diffs
SELECT transaction_id, account_id, amount, created_at
FROM transactions
WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2024-02-01'
ORDER BY created_at ASC, transaction_id ASC;
-- Run on read replica

Dynamic ORDER BY — Safe Pattern

java
// ❌ SQL injection risk
"ORDER BY " + userSortColumn;

// ✅ Whitelist
private static final Set<String> ALLOWED_SORT = Set.of("balance", "opened_at", "account_id");

String sortCol = ALLOWED_SORT.contains(request.getSort()) ? request.getSort() : "account_id";
String direction = "desc".equalsIgnoreCase(request.getDir()) ? "DESC" : "ASC";

// Use in @Query with SpEL or Criteria API — never raw concatenation from user input

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

ORDER BY Architecture Decisions

List API Design Template

text
GET /accounts?customerId=1001&sort=balance&dir=desc&limit=20&cursor=5042

Rules:
  1. sort field whitelist: balance | openedAt | accountId
  2. dir: asc | desc
  3. limit: max 100 (cap)
  4. cursor: opaque token encoding last (sortValue, tieBreakerId)
  5. default sort: accountId ASC (unique, indexed)
  6. never expose OFFSET to client at scale — keyset only
  7. index per whitelisted sort path + WHERE filters

When to Pre-Sort (Denormalize Order)

text
Leaderboard (gaming, loyalty points):
  Real-time ORDER BY score on 10M users — expensive
  Alternative: Redis Sorted Set (ZADD score member) — O(log n) rank
  OR: periodic batch recompute of top-100 table (Lesson 9)

Not every ORDER BY belongs in SQL — match tool to access pattern

Sort + Filter Index Design Matrix

Query PatternIndex
WHERE customer_id=? ORDER BY account_id(customer_id, account_id)
WHERE customer_id=? ORDER BY balance DESC(customer_id, balance DESC)
WHERE status='ACTIVE' ORDER BY opened_at DESCPartial: (opened_at DESC) WHERE status='ACTIVE'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50 (no WHERE)(created_at DESC) — time-series feed

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: No ORDER BY on Paginated Query

sql
-- ❌ Undefined order — page 2 may differ from page 1 logic
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20;
-- ✅
ORDER BY account_id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20;

Mistake 2: Deep OFFSET at Scale

sql
-- ❌ Page 10000
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 200000;
-- ✅ Keyset
WHERE account_id > :cursor ORDER BY account_id LIMIT 20;

Mistake 3: Unstable Sort (Non-Unique ORDER BY)

sql
-- ❌ Many rows with same balance — pages overlap on concurrent insert
ORDER BY balance DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20;
-- ✅ Add unique tie-breaker
ORDER BY balance DESC, account_id ASC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20;

Mistake 4: Dynamic ORDER BY from User Input (SQL Injection)

java
// ❌ CRITICAL
"ORDER BY " + request.getParameter("sort");
// ✅ Whitelist only

Mistake 5: Assuming Heap Insertion Order

java
// ❌ "Last inserted account"
accountRepo.findTopByCustomerCustomerIdOrderByAccountIdDesc(customerId);
// Must explicitly ORDER BY — verify column reflects insert order (serial PK OK)

Mistake 6: Sort in Application After Unbounded SELECT

java
// ❌
List<Account> all = accountRepo.findByCustomerCustomerId(1001L);
all.sort(Comparator.comparing(Account::getBalance).reversed());
// ✅ ORDER BY in SQL with LIMIT

Mistake 7: Missing Index for Production Sort Path

text
API sorted by opened_at DESC — 10M rows — no index on opened_at
→ every request sorts millions of rows
→ add index or restrict date range in WHERE

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What does ORDER BY do?

Sorts result rows by specified column(s) or expressions. ASC ascending (default), DESC descending.

Q2: Is row order guaranteed without ORDER BY?

No. Order is undefined and may change between executions.

Q3: Can you use SELECT alias in ORDER BY?

Yes. ORDER BY runs after SELECT logically — alias is available. Not available in WHERE.

Q4: Difference between ORDER BY and WHERE?

WHERE filters rows. ORDER BY sorts remaining rows.

Q5: What is LIMIT?

Restricts number of rows returned after sort. Applied last in logical order.

Mid-Level

Q6: OFFSET vs keyset pagination?

OFFSET skips N rows — O(offset) cost, unstable under concurrent writes. Keyset uses last seen key (WHERE id > :cursor) — O(limit), stable, preferred at scale.

Q7: How can an index eliminate explicit sort?

If index column order matches ORDER BY columns and directions, optimizer uses Index Scan in order — no Sort node in plan.

Q8: Why add tie-breaker column to ORDER BY?

Non-unique sort keys cause non-deterministic order — pagination returns duplicate/missing rows. Add unique PK as final sort column.

Q9: What happens when sort exceeds work_mem?

External merge sort to temp disk — query slows dramatically. Fix: better WHERE, matching index, or session work_mem increase.

Q10: NULL sort order in PostgreSQL?

Default: NULLS LAST for ASC and DESC (PG 15+). Explicit: NULLS FIRST / NULLS LAST.

Senior

Q11: Design pagination for transaction API, 500M rows, infinite scroll.

Keyset on (created_at DESC, transaction_id DESC). Index (account_id, created_at DESC, transaction_id DESC). Cursor token encodes both values. No OFFSET. Max 100 per page. Read replica.

Q12: EXPLAIN shows Sort on 2M rows — optimization steps?

Add composite index matching WHERE + ORDER BY. Reduce rows with WHERE. Increase work_mem session-only if index impossible. Consider MV for dashboard. Verify Top-N optimization with LIMIT.

Q13: ORDER BY expression — index options?

Function-based index: CREATE INDEX ON accounts ((balance * 1.05)) (PG) or virtual column (MySQL). Or materialized computed column maintained by trigger.

Q14: Top-N vs full sort — when does optimizer use Top-N heap?

When LIMIT is small relative to filtered rows and no suitable index. O(n log k) vs O(n log n). Check EXPLAIN for Limit node above Sort or special Top-N plan.

Staff / Architect

Q15: REST API allows sort by any of 8 columns on 50M row table. Strategy?

Whitelist 8 columns. Composite index per (mandatory_filter_col, sort_col DESC). Cap limit at 100. Keyset pagination only. Reject unindexed sort+filter combo. Async export for full sorted dump. Monitor pg_stat_statements for sort spills.

Q16: Redis sorted set vs SQL ORDER BY for leaderboard?

Redis ZSET: O(log n) insert/rank, in-memory, eventual sync from DB. SQL ORDER BY: durable, ACID source, expensive at scale. Pattern: Oracle/PostgreSQL source of truth + Redis projection for read path (Lesson 9).

Scenario

Scenario: "Users report duplicate transactions across pages in mobile app."

Root cause: ORDER BY created_at DESC without tie-breaker — many txs same timestamp. Concurrent inserts between page loads. Fix: ORDER BY created_at DESC, transaction_id DESC + keyset pagination replacing OFFSET.

Part 20 — Revision Sheet

Must-Know

  • No ORDER BY = undefined order — never assume PK order
  • ORDER BY after WHERE — filter then sort
  • Alias OK in ORDER BY, not in WHERE
  • Stable pagination: unique tie-breaker column (PK)
  • OFFSET: simple, bad at depth — O(offset)
  • Keyset: WHERE id > :cursor ORDER BY id LIMIT n — production standard
  • Index matching ORDER BY eliminates Sort node
  • work_mem — sort spills to disk when exceeded
  • Whitelist dynamic sort columns — SQL injection prevention

EXPLAIN Check

text
Look for:
  Sort node → explicit sort (expensive)
  Index Scan without Sort → optimal
  Sort Method: external merge → disk spill
  Limit + Top-N → heap optimization
