GROUP BY

Phase 2: SQL MASTERCLASS | Previous: ORDER BY | Next: HAVING

Foundation
1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why This Exists5Internal Working6Storage Internals7Memory Usage8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Complexity Analysis11Code / SQL Examples12Production Usage13Spring Boot Integration14Hibernate/JPA Integration15Architect Perspective16Decision Matrix17Comparison Tables18Common Mistakes19Interview Questions20Revision Sheet21Summary Table*Practice

Part 1 — Concept

What Is GROUP BY?

GROUP BY divides rows into groups based on one or more column values, then applies aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) to each group — collapsing many rows into fewer summary rows.

sql
SELECT
    account_type,
    COUNT(*)           AS account_count,
    SUM(balance)       AS total_balance,
    AVG(balance)       AS avg_balance
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY account_type;
text
BEFORE GROUP BY (many rows):          AFTER GROUP BY (one row per group):

account_type | balance              account_type | count | total  | avg
─────────────┼─────────             ──────────────┼───────┼────────┼──────
SAVINGS      | 15000                 SAVINGS      | 2     | 23000  | 11500
CHECKING     | 3500                  CHECKING     | 1     | 3500   | 3500
SAVINGS      | 8000                  LOAN         | 1     | 50000  | 50000
LOAN         | 50000

Logical Execution Position

text
FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT
                       ▲           ▲
                  form groups   filter groups

WHERE  filters ROWS before grouping
HAVING filters GROUPS after aggregation
SELECT projects group results (including aggregates)

Aggregate Functions

FunctionPurposeNULL Handling
**COUNT(*)**Count all rows in groupIncludes NULL rows
COUNT(col)Count non-NULL valuesIgnores NULL
COUNT(DISTINCT col)Count unique non-NULLIgnores NULL
SUM(col)Sum numeric valuesIgnores NULL
AVG(col)AverageIgnores NULL
MIN(col)Minimum valueIgnores NULL
MAX(col)Maximum valueIgnores NULL
STRING_AGG (PG)Concatenate stringsConfigurable

GROUP BY Rules (SQL Standard)

text
Every column in SELECT must be either:
  1. Listed in GROUP BY, OR
  2. Inside an aggregate function (SUM, COUNT, ...)

❌ INVALID:
SELECT customer_id, account_type, SUM(balance)
FROM accounts
GROUP BY account_type;
-- customer_id not in GROUP BY and not aggregated — ERROR

✅ VALID:
SELECT account_type, SUM(balance)
FROM accounts
GROUP BY account_type;

✅ VALID:
SELECT customer_id, account_type, SUM(balance)
FROM accounts
GROUP BY customer_id, account_type;

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Grouping in SQL

text
1974    SEQUEL includes GROUP BY and aggregate functions
1970s   Implementation: sort-based aggregation (sort on group key, scan groups)

1980s   Hash-based aggregation introduced
        Build hash table keyed by group columns — O(n) average

1990s   SQL-92: GROUP BY rules standardized; HAVING clarified
        ROLLUP, CUBE extensions proposed

1999    SQL:1999 — GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP, CUBE in standard
        Oracle 8i ROLLUP/CUBE; PostgreSQL adds gradually

2000s   Columnar databases optimize GROUP BY via vectorized aggregation
        Parallel aggregation in Oracle, SQL Server, PostgreSQL

2010s   Approximate aggregation: HyperLogLog, approximate COUNT DISTINCT
        Real-time OLAP: pre-aggregated rollups (Materialized Views — Lesson 9)

2020s   Hybrid HTAP engines push GROUP BY to column store
        Streaming: Kafka + Flink continuous GROUP BY windows

Historical Lesson

GROUP BY moved from sort-based (1970s) to hash-based (1980s+) aggregation. Hash aggregation is O(n) average — critical for billion-row fact tables when sort order is not pre-established.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does GROUP BY Solve?

Problem 1: Summary Without Application Code

text
Without GROUP BY:
  Fetch 1M transaction rows to Java
  Loop: Map<accountType, BigDecimal> totals = new HashMap<>();
  Network: 1M rows × 100 bytes = 100MB transfer

With GROUP BY:
  SELECT account_type, SUM(amount) FROM transactions GROUP BY account_type;
  Returns 3 rows — database does aggregation near storage

Problem 2: Multi-Dimensional Analysis

sql
-- Total balance by account type AND currency
SELECT account_type, currency, SUM(balance), COUNT(*)
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY account_type, currency;
-- 3 types × 2 currencies = up to 6 summary rows from millions of accounts

Problem 3: Per-Entity Aggregates

sql
-- Total balance per customer (for customer list screen)
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS account_count, SUM(balance) AS total_balance
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY customer_id;
-- Replaces N scalar subqueries in SELECT list (Lesson 11 anti-pattern)

Problem 4: Existence and Frequency Analysis

sql
-- Customers with more than 5 accounts (HAVING — Lesson 15 preview)
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM accounts
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

Problem 5: Dashboard KPIs

text
Daily transaction volume, monthly revenue by region, average order value by category
All require GROUP BY at scale — core of OLAP and BI

Unified Problem Statement

GROUP BY collapses large row sets into meaningful summaries at the database layer — minimizing data transfer, leveraging storage-proximal computation, and enabling multi-dimensional business analysis.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Aggregate in the Database?

Relational Algebra Foundation

text
GROUP BY implements the **partition** + **aggregate** operation:

γ_{account_type, SUM(balance), COUNT(*)}(accounts)

Composition with selection:
  GROUP BY after WHERE = aggregate only filtered rows
  (optimizer pushes WHERE before GROUP BY always)

Why Not Aggregate in Application?

FactorDB GROUP BYApp aggregation
Data transferk group rowsn detail rows
CPU locationNear data, parallelJVM, single node
Memorywork_mem hash tableFull dataset in heap
CorrectnessSingle query semanticsPagination breaks totals
ParallelismMulti-core DB workersManual

GROUP BY vs DISTINCT

sql
-- DISTINCT: unique combinations — no aggregates
SELECT DISTINCT account_type, currency FROM accounts;

-- GROUP BY: unique combinations + summary stats
SELECT account_type, currency, COUNT(*), SUM(balance)
FROM accounts
GROUP BY account type, currency;

Use DISTINCT when you only need unique keys
Use GROUP BY when you need counts, sums, averages

GROUP BY vs Window Functions (Preview Lesson 19)

sql
-- GROUP BY: collapses rows — one row per group
SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) FROM accounts GROUP BY customer_id;
-- Returns 1 row per customer

-- Window function: keeps all rows — adds aggregate column
SELECT account_id, balance,
       SUM(balance) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_total
FROM accounts;
-- Returns 1 row per account with running customer total

Part 5 — Internal Working

How GROUP BY Works Internally

Two Aggregation Algorithms

Hash Aggregate

text
HASH AGGREGATE (most common for unsorted input):

1. Initialize empty hash table
2. For each input row (after WHERE):
     a. Compute hash of GROUP BY key (account_type value)
     b. Find or create hash bucket for that key
     c. Update aggregate state: count++, sum+=balance
3. Output one row per hash bucket

Memory: O(distinct groups) — fits in work_mem if small enough
Spill: hash table exceeds work_mem → HashAggregateDisk (temp files)

Best when: input NOT sorted on group key, many groups
text
Hash table internal state:

Key: 'SAVINGS'  → { count: 2, sum: 23000.00, min: 8000, max: 15000 }
Key: 'CHECKING' → { count: 1, sum: 3500.00,  min: 3500, max: 3500 }
Key: 'LOAN'     → { count: 1, sum: 50000.00, min: 50000, max: 50000 }

Sort + Group Aggregate

text
GROUP AGGREGATE (sort-based):

1. Sort all rows by GROUP BY columns (external sort if needed)
2. Scan sorted rows — consecutive equal keys = one group
3. Accumulate aggregates within each group boundary
4. Emit one row per group

Best when: input already sorted on group key (index order)
           or sort is needed anyway for ORDER BY same columns

Optimizer Choice

text
PostgreSQL EXPLAIN nodes:

HashAggregate
  Group Key: account_type
  -> Seq Scan on accounts

GroupAggregate (sort-based)
  Group Key: customer_id
  -> Index Scan on idx_accounts_customer  (pre-sorted)

Parallel HashAggregate (PostgreSQL, Oracle):
  Each worker builds partial hash → merge partial results
  Scales CPU for large aggregations

Partial Aggregation (Multi-Stage)

text
Parallel workers on 100M rows:

Worker 1: partial hash → { SAVINGS: sum=50M, count=500K }
Worker 2: partial hash → { SAVINGS: sum=48M, count=480K }
Worker 3: partial hash → { SAVINGS: sum=52M, count=520K }
Finalize: merge → { SAVINGS: sum=150M, count=1.5M }

Reduces single-thread bottleneck

FILTER Clause (PostgreSQL, SQL Server)

sql
SELECT
    COUNT(*)                                    AS total_accounts,
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'ACTIVE')   AS active_accounts,
    SUM(balance) FILTER (WHERE account_type = 'SAVINGS') AS savings_total
FROM accounts;

-- Single scan, multiple conditional aggregates — more efficient than 3 subqueries

Part 6 — Storage Internals

GROUP BY and Storage Interaction

Scan Volume Determines Aggregation Cost

sql
SELECT account_type, SUM(balance)
FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001
GROUP BY account_type;

-- Index Scan customer_id → 3 rows → hash 3 groups trivial
-- I/O: 3-4 pages

SELECT account_type, SUM(balance)
FROM accounts
GROUP BY account_type;

-- Seq Scan 100M rows → hash aggregate 100M updates
-- I/O: entire table — why WHERE before GROUP BY matters

Index-Only Group Aggregate

sql
-- Covering index: (customer_id, account_type, balance)
SELECT customer_id, account_type, SUM(balance)
FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id BETWEEN 1000 AND 2000
GROUP BY customer_id, account_type;

Index Only Scan on covering index:
  Read index pages only — no heap fetch
  Pre-sorted on (customer_id, account_type) → GroupAggregate, no hash

Partition-Wise Aggregation (Lesson 42 Preview)

text
Table partitioned by txn_date (monthly):

SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', txn_date), SUM(amount)
FROM transactions
WHERE txn_date >= '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY 1;

Partition pruning → scan only 2024 partitions
Parallel: one worker per partition → partial aggregates → merge
Massive speedup on time-series GROUP BY

Pre-Aggregated Storage (Lesson 9)

text
Instead of GROUP BY on 1B raw transactions every dashboard load:

account_daily_summary table (pre-aggregated):
  account_id, summary_date, txn_count, total_debits, total_credits

Dashboard GROUP BY:
  SELECT summary_date, SUM(total_debits) FROM account_daily_summary
  GROUP BY summary_date;
-- Scans thousands of rows not billions — intentional denormalization

Part 7 — Memory Usage

GROUP BY Memory Consumption

Hash Aggregate Memory

text
work_mem budget for hash table:

Each group entry:
  Group key bytes + aggregate state (count, sum, min, max)
  ≈ key_width + 32-64 bytes per aggregate function

Query:
  GROUP BY customer_id (8B key) on 1M customers:
    1M × (8 + 32) ≈ 40 MB → exceeds default work_mem (4MB) → disk spill

Query:
  GROUP BY account_type (20B key) on 3 groups:
    3 × 52 ≈ 156 bytes → trivial in memory

Spill to Disk — HashAggregateDisk

text
EXPLAIN ANALYZE output:
  HashAggregate
    Batches: 4  Memory Usage: 4096kB  Disk Usage: 512MB

Symptom: query was fast on small data, slow after growth
Fix:
  Add WHERE to reduce rows before GROUP BY
  Increase work_mem for session (not global)
  Pre-aggregate to summary table
  Use approximate aggregates if exact not required

Sort-Based Group Memory

text
GroupAggregate requires sorted input:
  Sort node uses work_mem separately from HashAggregate
  Two memory consumers in same query possible:
    Hash Join (work_mem) + HashAggregate (work_mem) + Sort (work_mem)

JDBC Result Set

java
// GROUP BY returns small result — low JVM memory
List<Object[]> summary = em.createQuery(
    "SELECT a.accountType, SUM(a.balance) FROM Account a GROUP BY a.accountType"
).getResultList();
// Returns 3 rows — not 1M rows — efficient

Part 8 — Execution Flow

GROUP BY Execution Flows

Flow 1: Hash Aggregate with WHERE

sql
SELECT account_type, COUNT(*), SUM(balance)
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY account_type;
text
1. Seq Scan accounts (or Index Scan on status)
2. Filter: status = 'ACTIVE' (WHERE — per row)
3. HashAggregate:
     For each active row:
       hash(account_type) → update {count, sum}
4. Output 3 rows (SAVINGS, CHECKING, LOAN)
5. No sort needed

EXPLAIN:
  HashAggregate  Group Key: account_type
    -> Seq Scan on accounts  Filter: status = 'ACTIVE'

Flow 2: Group Aggregate (Index Sorted)

sql
SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance)
FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id BETWEEN 1000 AND 1010
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY customer_id;
text
1. Index Scan idx_accounts_customer_id (customer_id 1000-1010)
   Rows returned in customer_id order
2. GroupAggregate: detect group boundaries as customer_id changes
3. Emit SUM per customer
4. Already sorted — ORDER BY satisfied without extra Sort node

Flow 3: Multi-Column GROUP BY

sql
SELECT customer_id, account_type, COUNT(*), SUM(balance)
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY customer_id, account_type;
text
Hash key = composite (customer_id, account_type)
  (1001, 'SAVINGS')  → { count: 1, sum: 15000 }
  (1001, 'CHECKING') → { count: 1, sum: 3500 }
  (1002, 'SAVINGS')  → { count: 1, sum: 8000 }

Output: one row per unique (customer_id, account_type) pair
Index opportunity: (customer_id, account_type, balance) covering

Flow 4: GROUP BY with JOIN

sql
SELECT c.region, COUNT(a.account_id), SUM(a.balance)
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE a.status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY c.region;
text
1. Hash Join customers ⋈ accounts (or nested loop)
2. Filter status = 'ACTIVE'
3. HashAggregate on region
4. Output regional summary

Join cardinality affects hash table input size:
  1M accounts × 1 customer each → 1M rows into aggregator
  Push WHERE before join when possible (predicate pushdown)

Flow 5: COUNT(DISTINCT) — Expensive

sql
SELECT account_type, COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)
FROM accounts
GROUP BY account_type;
text
Requires tracking unique customer_ids per group:
  HashAggregate with nested hash set per group — memory heavy
  OR Sort + Unique + GroupAggregate — two-pass

Much more expensive than COUNT(*)
HyperLogLog approximation for scale: COUNT(DISTINCT ...) APPROX in some DBs

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

GROUP BY Performance Rules

Performance Hierarchy

text
FASTEST → SLOWEST:

1. GROUP BY low-cardinality column (3 groups) + selective WHERE
2. HashAggregate on filtered set fitting in work_mem
3. GroupAggregate on index-sorted input
4. HashAggregate with disk spill (HashAggregateDisk)
5. COUNT(DISTINCT col) on large groups
6. GROUP BY on full table scan (no WHERE) — billions of rows
7. GROUP BY expression (non-indexed): GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', created_at)

Optimization Checklist

text
□ WHERE before GROUP BY — minimize input rows?
□ Group key low cardinality where possible?
□ Covering index on (group_cols, aggregate_col)?
□ work_mem sufficient for hash table (EXPLAIN ANALYZE)?
□ COUNT(DISTINCT) necessary — or HyperLogLog acceptable?
□ Pre-aggregated summary table for repeated dashboard queries?
□ Parallel aggregation enabled (max_parallel_workers_per_gather)?
□ Run heavy GROUP BY on read replica?

GROUP BY Anti-Patterns

sql
-- ❌ Full table GROUP BY on OLTP primary repeatedly
SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) FROM accounts GROUP BY customer_id;
-- Called every 5 seconds by dashboard — cache or MV instead

-- ❌ GROUP BY non-indexed expression on huge table
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('day', created_at), COUNT(*)
FROM transactions   -- 500M rows, no index on expression
GROUP BY 1;
-- ✅ Filter date range + index on created_at
WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2024-02-01'

-- ❌ Scalar subquery instead of GROUP BY (Lesson 11)
SELECT c.name, (SELECT SUM(balance) FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id)
FROM customers c;
-- ✅
SELECT c.name, SUM(a.balance) FROM customers c JOIN accounts a ON ... GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name;

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

OperationTimeSpace
HashAggregateO(n) avgO(g) groups in work_mem
GroupAggregate + SortO(n log n)O(n) sort buffer
HashAggregate disk spillO(n) I/O boundDisk temp files
COUNT(DISTINCT) per groupO(n) to O(n log n)O(g × distinct_per_group)
Parallel partial aggO(n/p) per workerO(g) merge
GROUP BY + JOINO(join cost) + O(n) aggCombined

n = input rows after WHERE, g = number of distinct groups

text
Cardinality impact:
  GROUP BY account_type (3 values):     g=3    — always fast
  GROUP BY customer_id (1M values):     g=1M   — large hash table
  GROUP BY (customer_id, account_type): g≤3M   — even larger

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

GROUP BY Masterclass Examples

Basic Aggregation

sql
-- Count and sum by account type
SELECT
    account_type,
    COUNT(*)              AS account_count,
    SUM(balance)          AS total_balance,
    AVG(balance)          AS avg_balance,
    MIN(balance)          AS min_balance,
    MAX(balance)          AS max_balance
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY account_type;

Multi-Column GROUP BY

sql
SELECT
    customer_id,
    account_type,
    currency,
    COUNT(*)         AS cnt,
    SUM(balance)     AS total
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY customer_id, account_type, currency
ORDER BY customer_id, account_type;

GROUP BY with JOIN

sql
SELECT
    c.region,
    c.status           AS customer_status,
    COUNT(a.account_id) AS account_count,
    COALESCE(SUM(a.balance), 0) AS total_balance
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY c.region, c.status
ORDER BY total_balance DESC;

Replacing Scalar Subqueries

sql
-- ❌ Slow: correlated subquery per customer
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS cnt
FROM customers c;

-- ✅ Fast: single pass
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email, COUNT(a.account_id) AS cnt
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.email;

GROUP BY Expression

sql
-- Monthly transaction volume
SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC('month', created_at)   AS month,
    COUNT(*)                          AS txn_count,
    SUM(amount)                       AS total_amount
FROM transactions
WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01'
AND created_at < '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', created_at)
ORDER BY month;

-- Oracle
SELECT TRUNC(created_at, 'MM') AS month, COUNT(*), SUM(amount)
FROM transactions
GROUP BY TRUNC(created_at, 'MM');

COUNT Variations

sql
SELECT
    account_type,
    COUNT(*)                    AS all_rows,          -- includes NULLs in rows
    COUNT(balance)              AS non_null_balance,  -- excludes NULL balance
    COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS unique_customers
FROM accounts
GROUP BY account_type;

FILTER Clause (PostgreSQL)

sql
SELECT
    customer_id,
    COUNT(*)                                           AS total,
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'ACTIVE')          AS active,
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'SUSPENDED')       AS suspended,
    SUM(balance) FILTER (WHERE account_type = 'SAVINGS') AS savings_balance
FROM accounts
GROUP BY customer_id;

ROLLUP — Subtotals (Preview)

sql
-- PostgreSQL / Oracle / SQL Server
SELECT
    account_type,
    currency,
    COUNT(*)     AS cnt,
    SUM(balance) AS total
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY ROLLUP(account_type, currency);
-- Produces: detail rows + subtotals per account_type + grand total

GROUPING SETS

sql
SELECT
    account_type,
    currency,
    SUM(balance)
FROM accounts
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS (
    (account_type, currency),
    (account_type),
    ()   -- grand total
);

Part 12 — Production Usage

GROUP BY in Production Domains

Banking — End-of-Day Summary

sql
-- Run on read replica after market close
SELECT
    branch_id,
    account_type,
    COUNT(*)         AS account_count,
    SUM(balance)     AS total_balance
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY branch_id, account_type
ORDER BY branch_id, account_type;
-- Index: (status, branch_id, account_type) or partial WHERE status='ACTIVE'

Payments — Hourly Volume Dashboard

sql
SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC('hour', created_at) AS hour,
    status,
    COUNT(*)                       AS payment_count,
    SUM(amount)                    AS total_amount,
    AVG(amount)                    AS avg_amount
FROM payments
WHERE created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '24 hours'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;
-- Pre-aggregate to hourly_summary table if queried every minute (Lesson 9)

E-Commerce — Sales by Category

sql
SELECT
    p.category_id,
    DATE_TRUNC('day', o.ordered_at) AS order_date,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)      AS order_count,
    SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.ordered_at >= :fromDate AND o.ordered_at < :toDate
GROUP BY p.category_id, DATE_TRUNC('day', o.ordered_at);

Logistics — Shipments by Status and Region

sql
SELECT
    origin_region,
    status,
    COUNT(*)              AS shipment_count,
    AVG(delivery_days)    AS avg_delivery_days
FROM shipments
WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'
GROUP BY origin_region, status;

When to Pre-Aggregate Instead

text
If same GROUP BY runs every 30 seconds on 500M rows:
  ❌ Repeated full aggregation on primary
  ✅ Materialized view refreshed every 5 minutes
  ✅ Or streaming rollup (Kafka Flink) → summary table

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

ORM and GROUP BY

Non-Entity Results

text
GROUP BY queries return aggregate results — NOT managed entities:
  List<Object[]> — untyped
  Interface projection — typed, recommended
  DTO constructor — typed, recommended

Never map GROUP BY result to @Entity — no single PK, not a row in one table

JPQL GROUP BY Rules

java
// ✅ Valid JPQL
@Query("""
    SELECT a.customer.customerId, COUNT(a), SUM(a.balance)
    FROM Account a
    GROUP BY a.customer.customerId
    """)

// ❌ Invalid — name not in GROUP BY
@Query("""
    SELECT a.customer.customerId, a.customer.email, SUM(a.balance)
    FROM Account a
    GROUP BY a.customer.customerId
    """)
// Fix: add a.customer.email to GROUP BY (functionally dependent in SQL — PG allows, JPQL strict)

Criteria API GROUP BY

java
CriteriaBuilder cb = entityManager.getCriteriaBuilder();
CriteriaQuery<Object[]> cq = cb.createQuery(Object[].class);
Root<Account> root = cq.from(Account.class);

cq.multiselect(
    root.get("accountType"),
    cb.count(root),
    cb.sum(root.get("balance"))
)
.where(cb.equal(root.get("status"), AccountStatus.ACTIVE))
.groupBy(root.get("accountType"));

List<Object[]> results = entityManager.createQuery(cq).getResultList();

text

  if email is functionally dependent on customer_id (PK)

JPQL/Hibernate may still require all non-aggregated columns in GROUP BY
Use native query or add all columns to GROUP BY for portability

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

GROUP BY Architecture Decisions

OLTP vs OLAP GROUP BY

text
OLTP (few groups, selective WHERE):
  Real-time: SELECT account_type, SUM(balance) WHERE customer_id = ?
  Index + hash 3 rows — milliseconds OK on primary

OLAP (many groups, full scans):
  SELECT region, month, SUM(revenue) FROM fact_sales GROUP BY 1,2
  Run on warehouse / read replica — never primary OLTP
  Or pre-aggregated cube / MV

Caching Aggregate Results

text
Dashboard KPI "total active balance":
  Expensive: GROUP BY on 10M accounts every page load
  Pattern:
    1. CQRS read model updated on AccountBalanceChanged event
    2. Redis key: bank:total_active_balance → single value
    3. Fallback: MV refreshed every 5 min

GROUP BY at query time vs pre-computed — staleness SLA decides

API Design for Aggregates

text
GET /reports/accounts/summary?groupBy=accountType,region

Architect rules:
  □ Whitelist groupBy dimensions
  □ Require date range filter for transaction GROUP BY
  □ Max groups returned (LIMIT on aggregate result)
  □ Route to read replica or warehouse
  □ Timeout 30s for ad-hoc GROUP BY
  □ Async export for unlimited GROUP BY results

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Non-Aggregated Column Not in GROUP BY

sql
-- ❌ SQL error (except MySQL ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY off — silent wrong results!)
SELECT customer_id, account_type, SUM(balance)
FROM accounts GROUP BY account_type;

-- ✅
SELECT account_type, SUM(balance) FROM accounts GROUP BY account_type;
-- OR
SELECT customer_id, account_type, SUM(balance)
FROM accounts GROUP BY customer_id, account_type;

Mistake 2: Filtering Aggregates in WHERE Instead of HAVING

sql
-- ❌ ERROR: aggregate in WHERE
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) FROM accounts
WHERE COUNT(*) > 5
GROUP BY customer_id;

-- ✅ HAVING (Lesson 15)
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) FROM accounts
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

Mistake 3: GROUP BY on Primary for Heavy Dashboard

text
Same expensive GROUP BY every 30 seconds → primary buffer pool pollution
Fix: MV, read replica, or cached aggregate

Mistake 4: COUNT(DISTINCT) When Not Needed

sql
-- ❌ Expensive
COUNT(DISTINCT session_id)  -- when rows are already unique per session

-- ✅ If one row per session guaranteed
COUNT(*)

Mistake 5: Missing WHERE Before GROUP BY

sql
-- ❌ Aggregates entire 500M transaction table
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('day', created_at), SUM(amount)
FROM transactions
GROUP BY 1;

-- ✅ Always bound time range
WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2024-02-01'

Mistake 6: Mapping Aggregate Query to Entity

java
// ❌ Invalid — result is not an Account entity
@Query("SELECT a.accountType, SUM(a.balance) FROM Account a GROUP BY a.accountType")
List<Account> getSummary();  // Wrong return type

// ✅

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What does GROUP BY do?

Divides rows into groups by column values and applies aggregate functions to each group, returning one row per unique group key combination.

Q2: Difference between WHERE and HAVING?

WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Cannot use aggregate functions in WHERE.

Q3: What columns can appear in SELECT with GROUP BY?

Columns in GROUP BY list or columns inside aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, etc.).

**Q4: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col)?**

COUNT(*) counts all rows including NULLs. COUNT(col) counts rows where col IS NOT NULL.

Q5: Does GROUP BY guarantee sort order?

No. Use ORDER BY for sorted output.

Mid-Level

Q6: Hash aggregate vs sort aggregate?

Hash: build hash table keyed by group columns — O(n). Sort: sort by group key then scan groups — O(n log n) but free if already sorted via index.

Q7: Why is COUNT(DISTINCT) expensive?

Must track all unique values per group — nested hash or sort — high memory. Approximate alternatives for scale.

Q8: Replace correlated subquery with GROUP BY — example?

Per-customer account count: JOIN + GROUP BY customer_id + COUNT() instead of (SELECT COUNT() FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = c.customer_id) per row.

Q9: GROUP BY vs window function SUM() OVER?

GROUP BY collapses rows to one per group. Window function keeps all rows adding aggregate column.

Q10: work_mem and hash aggregate spill?

Hash table must fit in work_mem. Exceeds → HashAggregateDisk spills to temp files — slow. Fix: filter rows, increase session work_mem, or pre-aggregate.

Senior

Q11: Optimize GROUP BY on 500M transactions by month.

WHERE date range + partition pruning on txn_date. Parallel HashAggregate. Index on created_at if filtering. Better: pre-aggregated monthly_summary table or MV. Run on read replica.

Q12: Explain ROLLUP vs GROUP BY.

ROLLUP(account_type, currency) produces detail rows + subtotal per account_type + grand total in one query — avoids UNION of multiple GROUP BY queries.

Q13: GROUP BY with LEFT JOIN — COUNT pitfall?

COUNT(a.account_id) counts non-null joined accounts. COUNT() counts customers including those with zero accounts. Use COUNT(a.account_id) vs COUNT() deliberately.

Q14: Functional dependency and GROUP BY (PostgreSQL).

PK functionally determines other columns — PG allows GROUP BY customer_id while selecting email. MySQL ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY rejects. JPQL typically requires all columns in GROUP BY.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Real-time dashboard needs 10 KPIs each aggregating 100M rows. Design.

Don't run 10 GROUP BY on primary. Pre-aggregate: streaming (Flink) → summary tables, MV refresh 1 min, Redis for hot KPIs, warehouse for historical. Define staleness SLA per KPI.

Q16: GROUP BY in microservice vs data warehouse?

OLTP service: GROUP BY with selective WHERE on service's own small bounded data OK. Cross-service analytics: ETL to warehouse, star schema, GROUP BY on facts — not cross-service JOIN + GROUP BY.

Scenario

Scenario: "Report shows total balance per region doesn't match sum of account balances."

Check: LEFT JOIN vs INNER JOIN (missing customers?), WHERE filtering wrong rows, duplicate rows from JOIN (M:N join explosion), SUM including closed accounts in one query not another, MV stale. Debug: compare GROUP BY on accounts alone vs JOIN query row counts.

Must-Know

  • GROUP BY = partition rows + aggregate per group

  • SELECT rule: only GROUP BY columns or aggregates
  • WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups (Lesson 15)
  • HashAggregate O(n) — watch work_mem spill
  • **COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) vs COUNT(DISTINCT col)**
  • GROUP BY ≠ sorted — need ORDER BY
  • Filter before group — always bound WHERE on large tables
  • Heavy GROUP BY → read replica / MV / pre-aggregate

Part 1 — Concept

What Is HAVING?

HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY has formed them and aggregate functions have been computed. It is the group-level equivalent of WHERE, which filters individual rows before grouping.

sql
SELECT
    customer_id,
    COUNT(*)       AS account_count,
    SUM(balance)   AS total_balance
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'          -- filter ROWS first
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1              -- filter GROUPS second
AND SUM(balance) > 10000;
text
EXECUTION PIPELINE:

  All accounts
       │
       ▼ WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'     ← row filter (Lesson 12)
  Active accounts only
       │
       ▼ GROUP BY customer_id        ← form groups (Lesson 14)
  One group per customer
       │
       ▼ HAVING COUNT(*) > 1         ← group filter (this lesson)
  Customers with 2+ active accounts
       │
       ▼ SELECT / ORDER BY / LIMIT
  Final result

HAVING vs WHERE — One-Line Summary

ClauseFiltersCan Use Aggregates?Runs When
WHEREIndividual rows❌ NoBefore GROUP BY
HAVINGGroups✅ YesAfter GROUP BY

What HAVING Can Contain

text
Valid HAVING predicates:
  HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
  HAVING SUM(balance) > 10000
  HAVING AVG(amount) BETWEEN 100 AND 1000
  HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT account_type) >= 2
  HAVING MAX(created_at) >= '2024-01-01'

Valid with GROUP BY column (already aggregated context):
  HAVING customer_id = 1001        -- equivalent to WHERE if customer_id in GROUP BY
  (prefer WHERE for group key equality — filters rows earlier)

Invalid in WHERE:
  WHERE COUNT(*) > 5               -- ❌ ERROR: aggregate in WHERE
  WHERE SUM(balance) > 10000       -- ❌ ERROR

Part 2 — History

Evolution of HAVING

text
1974    SEQUEL includes HAVING alongside GROUP BY
        Needed because WHERE cannot reference aggregate results

1970s   Early implementations: filter groups after sort-based aggregation

1980s   Hash aggregation: HAVING evaluated as hash buckets finalized
        Optimizer begins pushing HAVING conditions when possible

1990s   SQL-92 clarifies:
        - WHERE: pre-aggregation filter
        - HAVING: post-aggregation filter
        - SELECT aliases NOT available in HAVING (unlike ORDER BY)

2000s   Optimizer rewrite rules:
        "HAVING group_key = constant" → pushed to WHERE when equivalent
        Reduces rows entering hash aggregate

2010s   Columnar engines: vectorized HAVING on aggregate vectors
        BI tools generate HAVING for report filters ("show regions with sales > $1M")

2020s   Window functions reduce some HAVING use cases:
        Filter on ROW_NUMBER() in outer query instead of HAVING MAX(...)
        HAVING remains essential for true group-level aggregate thresholds

Historical Lesson

HAVING exists because aggregates do not exist until groups are formed — WHERE runs too early in the pipeline to see COUNT(*) or SUM(balance). The two-clause design preserves correct relational algebra ordering.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does HAVING Solve?

Problem 1: Filter on Aggregate Values

text
Business question: "Which customers have total balance over $50,000?"

Cannot use WHERE:
  WHERE SUM(balance) > 50000  ← ERROR — SUM not computed yet

HAVING:
  GROUP BY customer_id
  HAVING SUM(balance) > 50000  ✅

Problem 2: Filter on Group Size

text
"Customers with more than 3 accounts"
"Product categories with fewer than 10 orders — discontinue"

HAVING COUNT(*) > 3
HAVING COUNT(*) < 10

Problem 3: Filter on Group Quality

text
"Regions where average transaction amount exceeds $500"
"Branches where maximum account balance is below regulatory threshold"

HAVING AVG(amount) > 500
HAVING MAX(balance) < 1000000

Problem 4: Multiple Aggregate Conditions

text
"Customers with 2+ accounts AND total balance > $10,000 AND at least one savings account"
Often combined with conditional aggregates (FILTER clause) or subqueries
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 AND SUM(balance) > 10000

Problem 5: Excluding Empty or Degenerate Groups

text
LEFT JOIN producing groups with COUNT = 0 for missing accounts:
HAVING COUNT(a.account_id) > 0
-- Excludes customers with no matching accounts from grouped result

Unified Problem Statement

HAVING filters groups based on aggregate results or group-level conditions that only exist after GROUP BY — enabling business questions about totals, counts, averages, and extremes per group.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Not Use WHERE for Everything?

Aggregates Don't Exist at WHERE Time

text
Logical order enforced by relational algebra:

  σ_{status='ACTIVE'}(accounts)           -- WHERE (selection)
  γ_{customer_id, COUNT(*), SUM(balance)} -- GROUP BY (aggregation)
  σ_{COUNT(*) > 1}(...)                   -- HAVING (selection on groups)

Cannot reorder HAVING before GROUP BY without changing semantics

When HAVING = WHERE Semantically (Prefer WHERE)

sql
-- GROUP BY customer_id — customer_id is unique per group

-- ❌ Less efficient — filters after aggregating all customers
SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance)
FROM accounts
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING customer_id = 1001;

-- ✅ Better — filters rows before grouping
SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance)
FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001
GROUP BY customer_id;
-- Same result, fewer rows aggregated

Rule: If condition references only non-aggregated columns that appear in GROUP BY, put it in WHERE not HAVING.

When HAVING Is Mandatory

sql
-- Aggregate condition — only HAVING works
HAVING SUM(balance) > 10000
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
HAVING AVG(amount) <> MAX(amount)  -- unusual but valid

HAVING vs Subquery Alternative

sql
-- HAVING approach
SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) AS total
FROM accounts
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(balance) > 10000;

-- Equivalent subquery (sometimes optimizer rewrites to same plan)
SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) AS total
    FROM accounts
    GROUP BY customer_id
) sub
WHERE total > 10000;

-- Modern optimizers: typically identical plans
-- HAVING is cleaner and standard for group filters

Part 5 — Internal Working

How HAVING Works Internally

Execution Within Hash Aggregate

text
HASH AGGREGATE with HAVING:

1. Scan input rows (after WHERE)
2. For each row:
     hash(group_key) → update aggregate state in bucket
3. After ALL input rows processed:
     For each hash bucket:
       Evaluate HAVING predicate on aggregate state
       If TRUE  → emit output row
       If FALSE → discard bucket (group excluded from result)

HAVING is evaluated ONCE per group — not per input row
Cost: O(g) where g = number of groups — negligible vs O(n) aggregation
text
Hash bucket state when HAVING evaluated:

Bucket (customer_id=1001):
  { count: 3, sum: 25000 }
  HAVING SUM(balance) > 10000 → 25000 > 10000 → TRUE → emit row

Bucket (customer_id=1002):
  { count: 1, sum: 500 }
  HAVING SUM(balance) > 10000 → 500 > 10000 → FALSE → discard

HAVING Pushdown Optimization

text
Optimizer may rewrite:

  GROUP BY customer_id
  HAVING customer_id IN (1001, 1002, 1003)

To:

  WHERE customer_id IN (1001, 1002, 1003)
  GROUP BY customer_id

Because filtering group key before aggregation is equivalent and cheaper.

Does NOT push down:
  HAVING SUM(balance) > 10000  -- depends on aggregates

HAVING with DISTINCT Aggregates

sql
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT account_type) >= 2;

Internal:
  Each hash bucket maintains secondary hash set of distinct account_types
  After all rows: count distinct values in set
  Evaluate HAVING on that count
  Memory per group proportional to distinct values per customer

Parallel Aggregation + HAVING

text
Parallel workers:
  Each builds partial hash aggregate
  Merge partial buckets
  Evaluate HAVING on merged final aggregate state
  Emit passing groups only

HAVING evaluation is cheap — aggregation dominates cost

Part 6 — Storage Internals

HAVING and Storage Interaction

HAVING Does Not Reduce Input I/O

text
Critical insight:

  WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'  → reduces pages read from disk ✅
  HAVING SUM(balance) > X  → all matching rows still read and aggregated ❌

HAVING filters OUTPUT groups — not INPUT rows
To reduce I/O: maximize WHERE selectivity before GROUP BY

Exception: Predicate Pushdown to WHERE

sql
-- Optimizer pushes group key equality to WHERE
HAVING customer_id = 1001
→ WHERE customer_id = 1001  -- reads only that customer's rows

Index Cannot Directly Support HAVING on Aggregates

text
Index on balance does NOT help:
  HAVING SUM(balance) > 10000

Because SUM is computed after reading all group rows.

Possible architectures to avoid HAVING on huge data:
  Pre-aggregated summary table with index on total_balance
  SELECT customer_id FROM customer_balance_summary WHERE total_balance > 10000
  Materialized view refreshed periodically (Lesson 9)

Covering Index Helps Input to Aggregation

sql
SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance)
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(balance) > 10000;

Index: (status, customer_id, balance) WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
  Index Only Scan → all data from index → hash aggregate → HAVING filter
  HAVING still evaluates post-aggregate but input I/O minimized

Part 7 — Memory Usage

HAVING and Memory

HAVING Adds Negligible Memory

text
Hash aggregate memory determined by:
  Number of distinct groups (g) × (key size + aggregate state)

HAVING evaluation:
  One boolean check per group after aggregation
  O(g) CPU — no additional memory structure

Bottleneck remains hash table size — not HAVING clause

When HAVING Indirectly Affects Memory

sql
-- Without HAVING: return 1M groups to client
SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) FROM accounts GROUP BY customer_id;

-- With HAVING: return 50K groups to client
HAVING SUM(balance) > 10000;

Client/JDBC memory: 50K rows vs 1M rows — significant reduction
Database memory during query: same — all groups built before HAVING filters

Mitigation: Filter Input with WHERE

sql
-- Reduce groups formed (lower g → smaller hash table):
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' AND opened_at >= '2020-01-01'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(balance) > 10000;

Fewer input rows → fewer groups in hash table → less work_mem
HAVING cannot replace this WHERE optimization

Part 8 — Execution Flow

HAVING Execution Flows

Flow 1: Standard HAVING on Aggregate

sql
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt, SUM(balance) AS total
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 AND SUM(total) > 5000;
-- Note: typo fix - SUM(balance)
text
Step 1: Seq/Index Scan accounts WHERE status='ACTIVE'
Step 2: HashAggregate — build buckets per customer_id
Step 3: For each bucket evaluate:
          COUNT(*) > 1  AND  SUM(balance) > 5000
Step 4: Emit passing groups (e.g., 500 of 50,000 groups)
Step 5: SELECT projects customer_id, cnt, total
Step 6: ORDER BY if present

EXPLAIN (PostgreSQL):
  GroupAggregate / HashAggregate
    Filter: (count(*) > 1 AND sum(balance) > 5000::numeric)
    -> Seq Scan on accounts  Filter: status = 'ACTIVE'

Flow 2: HAVING COUNT on LEFT JOIN

sql
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email, COUNT(a.account_id) AS account_count
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.email
HAVING COUNT(a.account_id) > 0;
text
Step 1: Hash Join customers LEFT JOIN accounts
Step 2: Groups include customers with 0 accounts (COUNT = 0)
Step 3: HAVING COUNT(a.account_id) > 0 → excludes zero-account customers
Equivalent to INNER JOIN in this case — optimizer may rewrite

Flow 3: HAVING vs WHERE — Same Result, Different Cost

sql
-- Query A ( inefficient HAVING on group key )
SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance)
FROM accounts
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING customer_id = 1001;

-- Query B ( efficient WHERE )
SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance)
FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001
GROUP BY customer_id;

Query A: aggregate ALL customers → discard all except 1001
Query B: read 3 rows for customer 1001 → aggregate 1 group
Plan B: always preferred

Flow 4: HAVING with ROLLUP (Subtotal Rows)

sql
SELECT account_type, SUM(balance)
FROM accounts
GROUP BY ROLLUP(account_type)
HAVING GROUPING(account_type) = 0;  -- exclude grand total row
-- PostgreSQL GROUPING() function identifies subtotal/supertotal rows

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

HAVING Performance Rules

Golden Rules

text
1. Use WHERE for row filters — always maximize before GROUP BY
2. Use HAVING only for aggregate conditions that require it
3. Never put GROUP BY key equality in HAVING — use WHERE
4. HAVING does not reduce aggregation work — only output size
5. Pre-aggregate for repeated HAVING queries on huge data
6. Run heavy GROUP BY + HAVING on read replica

Performance Comparison

PatternAggregation InputHAVING EvalTotal Cost
WHERE selective + HAVINGSmall nO(g)Low
No WHERE + HAVINGFull table nO(g)High
WHERE on group key vs HAVING on group keyAll vs filteredSameWHERE wins
HAVING on pre-aggregated MVSmall nO(g)Lowest

Common HAVING Anti-Patterns

sql
-- ❌ Aggregate in WHERE
SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) FROM accounts
WHERE SUM(balance) > 10000   -- ERROR
GROUP BY customer_id;

-- ❌ Group key in HAVING
GROUP BY customer_id HAVING customer_id = 1001;
-- ✅ WHERE customer_id = 1001

-- ❌ HAVING without GROUP BY (valid but unusual — treats whole table as one group)
SELECT SUM(balance) FROM accounts HAVING SUM(balance) > 0;
-- Valid SQL: one group (entire table), HAVING filters that single group
-- Equivalent to: SELECT SUM(balance) FROM accounts WHERE ... if no GROUP BY needed

-- ❌ Duplicate filter in WHERE and HAVING unnecessarily
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
HAVING status = 'ACTIVE'  -- redundant if status in GROUP BY — pick WHERE

When HAVING on Pre-Computed Column Helps

sql
-- Materialized view with pre-computed totals:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_customer_totals AS
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt, SUM(balance) AS total
FROM accounts GROUP BY customer_id;

SELECT customer_id, total
FROM mv_customer_totals
WHERE total > 10000;   -- now WHERE works — aggregate already computed
-- Refresh MV periodically — no runtime GROUP BY + HAVING on 100M rows

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

OperationComplexityNotes
GROUP BY (hash)O(n) avgn = rows after WHERE
HAVING evaluationO(g)g = groups formed
WHERE before GROUP BYReduces nMost impactful
HAVING on group key onlyO(n) agg wastedPush to WHERE → O(n')
Full pipelineO(n) + O(g)HAVING term negligible vs aggregation
text
Example:
  n = 100M rows, g = 1M customers
  Hash aggregate: O(100M) — dominates
  HAVING SUM > 10000: O(1M) boolean checks — trivial

  Optimizing HAVING: focus on reducing n via WHERE, not HAVING itself

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

HAVING Masterclass Examples

Basic HAVING

sql
-- Customers with more than one active account
SELECT
    customer_id,
    COUNT(*)         AS account_count,
    SUM(balance)     AS total_balance
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- Customers with total balance exceeding $50,000
SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) AS total
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(balance) > 50000
ORDER BY total DESC;

Multiple HAVING Conditions

sql
SELECT
    customer_id,
    COUNT(*)              AS cnt,
    SUM(balance)          AS total,
    AVG(balance)          AS avg_bal
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
AND SUM(balance) > 10000
AND AVG(balance) > 3000;

HAVING with Conditional Aggregates (PostgreSQL)

sql
SELECT customer_id
FROM accounts
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE account_type = 'SAVINGS') >= 1
AND COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE account_type = 'CHECKING') >= 1;
-- Customers with both savings AND checking accounts

HAVING vs WHERE — Side by Side

sql
-- ✅ CORRECT split
SELECT account_type, COUNT(*), SUM(balance)
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'              -- row filter: active only
AND currency = 'USD'                 -- row filter: USD only
GROUP BY account_type
HAVING SUM(balance) > 100000;         -- group filter: high total only

-- Result: USD active account types with combined balance > $100K

HAVING on JOIN Result

sql
-- Regions with average account balance > $5,000
SELECT
    c.region,
    COUNT(a.account_id)  AS account_count,
    AVG(a.balance)       AS avg_balance
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE a.status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY c.region
HAVING AVG(a.balance) > 5000
AND COUNT(a.account_id) >= 10;

HAVING Without GROUP BY (Single Group)

sql
-- Entire table as one group — HAVING filters the single aggregate result
SELECT SUM(balance) AS bank_total
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
HAVING SUM(balance) > 1000000000;
-- Returns one row if total > 1B, zero rows if not
-- Unusual pattern — often rewritten as subquery with WHERE on alias

HAVING with Subquery Equivalent

sql
-- HAVING form
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM payments
WHERE status = 'COMPLETED'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(amount) > (
    SELECT AVG(total) FROM (
        SELECT SUM(amount) AS total
        FROM payments WHERE status = 'COMPLETED'
        GROUP BY customer_id
    ) sub
);
-- Customers paying above average total

Excluding Groups from LEFT JOIN

sql
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.email,
    COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
    AND o.ordered_at >= '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.email
HAVING COUNT(o.order_id) > 0;
-- Customers with at least one order in 2024
-- (INNER JOIN would be simpler here)

Part 12 — Production Usage

HAVING in Production Domains

Banking — High-Value Customer Identification

sql
-- Run on read replica — monthly batch
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.email,
    COUNT(a.account_id)  AS account_count,
    SUM(a.balance)       AS total_balance
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE a.status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.email
HAVING SUM(a.balance) > 100000
OR COUNT(a.account_id) >= 5
ORDER BY total_balance DESC;

Payments — Fraud: High-Frequency Accounts

sql
SELECT
    account_id,
    COUNT(*)         AS txn_count_1h,
    SUM(amount)      AS total_amount_1h
FROM payments
WHERE created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour'
AND status = 'COMPLETED'
GROUP BY account_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 20
OR SUM(amount) > 50000;
-- Alert on accounts exceeding velocity thresholds

E-Commerce — Underperforming Categories

sql
SELECT
    p.category_id,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS order_count,
    SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM order_items oi
JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.ordered_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '90 days'
AND o.status = 'COMPLETED'
GROUP BY p.category_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) < 10
OR SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) < 1000;

Logistics — Delayed Routes

sql
SELECT
    route_id,
    COUNT(*)                          AS shipment_count,
    AVG(delivery_days)                AS avg_days,
    COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE delivery_days > 5) AS late_count
FROM shipments
WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'
GROUP BY route_id
HAVING AVG(delivery_days) > 3
OR COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE delivery_days > 5) > 10;

Replace Repeated HAVING with Summary Table

sql
-- Instead of hourly HAVING COUNT > 20 on raw payments:
CREATE TABLE payment_velocity_summary (
    account_id      BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    txn_count_1h    INTEGER NOT NULL,
    total_amount_1h DECIMAL(18,2) NOT NULL,
    updated_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);
-- Updated by stream job; alert query becomes simple WHERE
SELECT account_id FROM payment_velocity_summary
WHERE txn_count_1h > 20;

    Long getCustomerId();
    long getAccountCount();

}

           COUNT(a) AS accountCount,

Native SQL with HAVING

java
@Query(value = """
    SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*), SUM(balance)
    FROM accounts
    WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
    GROUP BY customer_id
    HAVING COUNT(*) > :minCount AND SUM(balance) > :minBalance

List<Object[]> findCustomersNative(

Criteria API HAVING

java
CriteriaBuilder cb = entityManager.getCriteriaBuilder();
CriteriaQuery<Object[]> cq = cb.createQuery(Object[].class);
Root<Account> root = cq.from(Account.class);

Expression<Long> count = cb.count(root);
Expression<BigDecimal> sum = cb.sum(root.get("balance"));

cq.multiselect(root.get("customer").get("customerId"), count, sum)
  .where(cb.equal(root.get("status"), AccountStatus.ACTIVE))
  .groupBy(root.get("customer").get("customerId"))
  .having(
      cb.and(
          cb.gt(count, 1L),
          cb.gt(sum, new BigDecimal("10000"))
      )
  );

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

ORM and HAVING

JPQL HAVING Rules

text
JPQL supports HAVING with aggregate functions:
  HAVING COUNT(a) > 1
  HAVING SUM(a.balance) > 10000

JPQL HAVING cannot reference SELECT aliases:
  SELECT SUM(a.balance) AS total ... HAVING total > 10000  -- ❌ invalid JPQL
  HAVING SUM(a.balance) > 10000                            -- ✅

Native SQL may allow alias in HAVING (database-dependent) — avoid for portability

HAVING vs Application Filter

java
// ❌ Fetch all groups, filter in Java
List<Object[]> all = repo.findAccountCountByCustomer();  // all customers
return all.stream()
    .filter(row -> (Long) row[1] > 1 && ((BigDecimal) row[2]).compareTo(min) > 0)
    .toList();

// ✅ HAVING in query — filter at database
return repo.findHighValueCustomers(1L, minTotal);

Spring Data Limitation

text
Spring Data derived query methods do NOT support HAVING:
  findBy...Having... — not available

Use @Query with explicit HAVING clause or Criteria API

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

HAVING Architecture Decisions

When HAVING Belongs in OLTP vs Batch vs Stream

ContextHAVING Appropriate?Alternative
Real-time API filter on aggregates⚠️ If small dataPre-computed summary
Batch report (nightly)✅ Read replica—
Fraud detection (1-hour window)✅ With time WHEREStream aggregation
Dashboard KPI threshold❌ Repeated HAVINGMV / Redis
Alert rule engine✅ Bounded window+ indexed created_at

HAVING Threshold Configuration

yaml
# Externalize thresholds — don't hardcode in SQL strings
banking:
  high-value-customer:
    min-total-balance: 100000
    min-account-count: 5

# JPQL parameter binding:
HAVING COUNT(a) > :minAccounts AND SUM(a.balance) > :minTotal

Architect Decision Tree

text
Need filter on aggregate (SUM, COUNT, AVG)?
  NO  → use WHERE only
  YES ↓
Can aggregate be pre-computed (MV, summary table)?
  YES → query summary table with WHERE on total ✅
  NO  ↓
Is input bounded by WHERE (date range, tenant, status)?
  NO  → add mandatory WHERE bounds first
  YES ↓
Run on read replica with timeout
Use HAVING for aggregate threshold

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Aggregate in WHERE

sql
-- ❌ ERROR
WHERE SUM(balance) > 10000
-- ✅
HAVING SUM(balance) > 10000

Mistake 2: Group Key in HAVING

sql
-- ❌ Aggregates all customers first
GROUP BY customer_id HAVING customer_id = 1001;
-- ✅
WHERE customer_id = 1001 GROUP BY customer_id;

Mistake 3: Expecting HAVING to Reduce Scan

sql
-- ❌ Thinking HAVING reduces rows read — it doesn't
FROM accounts GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(balance) > 10000;
-- Still scans all accounts — add WHERE to limit input

Mistake 4: HAVING on SELECT Alias

sql
-- ❌ Invalid in standard SQL / JPQL
SELECT SUM(balance) AS total ... HAVING total > 10000;
-- ✅
HAVING SUM(balance) > 10000

Mistake 5: Wrong COUNT on LEFT JOIN

sql
-- ❌ COUNT(*) includes customers with zero orders
HAVING COUNT(*) > 0  -- always true for every customer in LEFT JOIN

-- ✅ Count the joined column
HAVING COUNT(o.order_id) > 0

Mistake 6: Filtering Aggregates in Application

java
// ❌ Load all groups — filter in Java
// ✅ HAVING in SQL or query pre-aggregated summary with WHERE

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is HAVING?

Filters groups after GROUP BY based on aggregate conditions like COUNT(*) > 5 or SUM(balance) > 10000.

Q2: Difference between WHERE and HAVING?

WHERE filters rows before grouping; cannot use aggregates. HAVING filters groups after aggregation; can use aggregates.

**Q3: Can you write WHERE COUNT(*) > 5?**

No — aggregate functions are invalid in WHERE. Use HAVING.

Q4: Does HAVING reduce rows scanned from disk?

No — HAVING filters output groups after aggregation. Use WHERE to reduce input rows.

Q5: Execution order of WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING?

WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.

Mid-Level

Q6: GROUP BY customer_id HAVING customer_id = 1001 vs WHERE customer_id = 1001?

Same result; WHERE is more efficient — filters rows before aggregating all customers.

**Q7: HAVING COUNT(*) > 0 on LEFT JOIN — pitfall?**

COUNT(*) counts group rows including NULL joins — always > 0. Use COUNT(joined_column) > 0.

Q8: How is HAVING evaluated internally?

After hash aggregate completes, one predicate evaluation per group bucket — O(g), cheap compared to O(n) aggregation.

Q9: HAVING vs subquery with WHERE on alias?

Semantically equivalent; optimizers often produce identical plans. HAVING is idiomatic for group filters.

Q10: Can HAVING exist without GROUP BY?

Yes — treats entire result as one group. SELECT SUM(x) FROM t HAVING SUM(x) > 0 filters the single aggregate row.

Senior

Q11: Optimize query with HAVING SUM(amount) > 10000 on 500M payments.

Mandatory WHERE on created_at range. Index on (created_at, customer_id, amount). Read replica. Consider pre-aggregated customer_payment_totals MV — filter with WHERE total > 10000 instead of runtime HAVING.

Q12: HAVING AVG vs WHERE on average — can you pre-filter rows?

HAVING AVG(amount) > 500 means group average — cannot replace with WHERE amount > 500 (that filters individual rows, not group average). Different semantics.

Q13: Push HAVING to WHERE — when does optimizer do this?

When HAVING condition references only GROUP BY columns without aggregates — e.g., HAVING region = 'APAC' → WHERE region = 'APAC'.

Q14: Design fraud alert: > 20 transactions per account per hour.

WHERE created_at >= NOW() - interval '1 hour' (mandatory). GROUP BY account_id. HAVING COUNT(*) > 20. Index (created_at, account_id). Stream alternative for real-time. Parameterize threshold.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Team puts all filters in HAVING for convenience. Problem?

Row-level filters in HAVING force full aggregation before discard. Performance disaster on large tables. Enforce coding standard: row filters in WHERE, aggregate thresholds in HAVING. Code review + pg_stat_statements audit.

Q16: Replace nightly HAVING query with MV architecture — design.

MV: customer_totals refreshed nightly. Alert query: SELECT * FROM customer_totals WHERE total_balance > threshold (WHERE not HAVING). Incremental refresh for intraday if needed. Document staleness SLA.

Scenario

Scenario: "Query returns customers with 0 accounts despite HAVING COUNT() > 0."*

Likely COUNT(*) vs COUNT(a.account_id) confusion with LEFT JOIN, or HAVING on wrong column. Fix: HAVING COUNT(a.account_id) > 0 or use INNER JOIN. Verify with EXPLAIN and sample groups.

Part 20 — Revision Sheet

Must-Know

  • HAVING = filter groups after GROUP BY
  • WHERE = filter rows before GROUP BY
  • Aggregates only in HAVING — never WHERE
  • Group key equality → WHERE not HAVING
  • HAVING does not reduce I/O — WHERE does
  • Execution order: WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT
  • **COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col)** in HAVING with LEFT JOIN
  • JPQL: no alias in HAVING — repeat aggregate expression
  • Heavy HAVING → read replica / pre-aggregated MV

Quick Decision

text
Row attribute filter?           → WHERE
Aggregate threshold?            → HAVING
GROUP BY column = constant?     → WHERE (not HAVING)
Repeated same aggregate filter? → MV + WHERE
