Part 1 — Concept

What Is a JOIN?

A JOIN combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column (typically a foreign key relationship), producing a wider result set that connects related data from the normalized schema (Lesson 8).

sql
SELECT
    c.first_name,
    c.last_name,
    a.account_number,
    a.balance
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.status = 'ACTIVE';
text
CUSTOMERS (1 side)              ACCOUNTS (N side)
┌─────────────┬──────────┐     ┌─────────────┬─────────────┐
│ customer_id │ name     │     │ account_id  │ customer_id │
├─────────────┼──────────┤     ├─────────────┼─────────────┤
│ 1001        │ Ankur    │────▶│ 5001        │ 1001        │
│ 1001        │          │────▶│ 5002        │ 1001        │
│ 1002        │ Priya    │────▶│ 5003        │ 1002        │
└─────────────┴──────────┘     └─────────────┴─────────────┘

JOIN RESULT (INNER):
┌──────────┬───────┬───────────────┬─────────┐
│ name     │       │ account_number│ balance │
├──────────┼───────┼───────────────┼─────────┤
│ Ankur    │       │ ACC-5001      │ 15000   │
│ Ankur    │       │ ACC-5002      │ 3500    │
│ Priya    │       │ ACC-5003      │ 8200    │
└──────────┴───────┴───────────────┴─────────┘

JOIN Types Overview

Join TypeReturnsUse When
INNER JOINRows with match in both tablesOnly related data needed
LEFT OUTER JOINAll left rows + matched right (NULL if no match)Keep left even without match
RIGHT OUTER JOINAll right rows + matched leftRare — rewrite as LEFT JOIN
FULL OUTER JOINAll rows from both; NULL where no matchReconciliation, data quality
CROSS JOINCartesian product (every combination)Generating combinations (rare)
SELF JOINTable joined to itselfHierarchies, comparisons
SEMI JOINRows from left where match exists in right (EXISTS)Existence check — no right columns
ANTI JOINRows from left where NO match in right (NOT EXISTS)Missing relationship detection

ANSI JOIN Syntax (SQL-92 — Standard)

sql
-- ✅ Modern standard syntax
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id

-- ❌ Legacy Oracle/Sybase syntax (avoid in new code)
FROM customers c, accounts a
WHERE c.customer_id = a.customer_id(+)   -- Oracle outer join operator

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Joins in SQL

text
1970s   Relational algebra defines join operations (⋈)
        Codd: natural join, theta join, outer join concepts

1980s   SQL-86: comma-separated FROM + WHERE for equi-joins only
        Oracle (+) outer join operator — confusing, non-standard

1992    SQL-92: explicit JOIN ... ON syntax — industry standard
        INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER standardized
        Separation of join conditions (ON) from row filters (WHERE)

1990s   Query optimizers develop join algorithms:
        Nested Loop, Sort-Merge, Hash Join

2000s   Cost-based optimizers choose join order for N tables
        Star schema join optimization in data warehouses

2010s   Parallel hash join, bloom filter semi-join (Oracle, PostgreSQL)
        Adaptive join (SQL Server): runtime switch nested loop ↔ hash

2020s   Join pushdown to storage / foreign data wrappers
        HTAP engines optimize star joins across row/column stores

Historical Lesson

SQL-92 JOIN ... ON syntax exists because mixing join conditions in WHERE with (+) outer join operators caused ambiguous, error-prone queries. Always use explicit JOIN syntax in production code.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Do Joins Solve?

Problem 1: Normalized Data Lives in Multiple Tables

text
Lesson 8 normalization stores:
  customers in customers table
  accounts in accounts table
  FK: accounts.customer_id → customers.customer_id

Application needs: customer name + account balance together
JOIN reassembles related facts at query time

Problem 2: Avoiding Data Duplication

text
Without JOIN (denormalized):
  Store customer_name on every account row — update anomaly

With JOIN:
  customer_name stored once in customers
  SELECT joins at read time — normalized integrity

Problem 3: Multi-Entity Queries

sql
-- Customer + account + latest transaction
SELECT c.name, a.account_number, t.amount, t.created_at
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN transactions t ON t.account_id = a.account_id
WHERE t.created_at = (SELECT MAX(created_at) FROM transactions ...);
-- Three-table join — common in reporting

Problem 4: Finding Missing Relationships

sql
-- Customers without any account (anti-join)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE a.account_id IS NULL;
-- Or: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id)

Problem 5: Existence Checks Without Duplication

sql
-- Customers who HAVE at least one active account (semi-join)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM accounts a
    WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
);
-- Avoids JOIN duplication when only existence matters

Unified Problem Statement

JOINs reconstruct logical relationships between normalized tables at query time — enabling multi-entity reads, existence checks, and reconciliation without storing redundant copies of related data.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Join Instead of Multiple Queries?

N+1 Problem (Application Anti-Pattern)

java
// ❌ 1 + N queries
List<Customer> customers = customerRepo.findAll();           // 1 query
for (Customer c : customers) {
    List<Account> accounts = accountRepo.findByCustomerId(c.getId());  // N queries
}
// 1001 queries for 1000 customers

// ✅ Single JOIN query
SELECT c.*, a.* FROM customers c JOIN accounts a ON ...
// 1 query — database optimizes join internally

Relational Algebra Composition

text
Join is composable:
  (customers ⋈ accounts) ⋈ transactions

Optimizer can reorder:
  (accounts ⋈ transactions) ⋈ customers
  if cheaper based on statistics — application cannot do this across round trips

Join vs Denormalized Document

ApproachReadWriteIntegrity
JOIN normalized tablesJoin costSingle-row updateFK enforced
Embedded document (MongoDB)Single readUpdate many copiesApp enforced
Denormalized flat tableSingle readUpdate anomalyPoor

Enterprise OLTP: JOIN normalized schema; denormalize read paths separately (Lesson 9).

Part 5 — Internal Working

Join Algorithms — Internal Working

The optimizer chooses among three primary join algorithms (Lesson 29 deep dive):

1. Nested Loop Join (NLJ)

text
FOR each row in outer table:
    FOR each matching row in inner table (index lookup):
        emit joined row

Best when: outer table is SMALL, inner has INDEX on join column
Cost: O(n × log m) with index on inner
Cost: O(n × m) without index — catastrophic

Example:
  customers (1 row, customer_id=1001) ⋈ accounts (index on customer_id)
  → 1 index lookup → 3 account rows — ~0.5ms
text
NESTED LOOP DIAGRAM:

Outer (customers)          Inner (accounts via index)
┌──────────────┐          ┌─────────────────────────┐
│ id=1001      │─────────▶│ idx: 1001→[5001,5002]  │
└──────────────┘          └─────────────────────────┘
                          Emit 2 joined rows

2. Hash Join

text
Build phase:  Read smaller table → build hash table on join key
Probe phase:  Read larger table → hash lookup join key → emit matches

Best when: both tables moderate/large, no useful index, equi-join (=)
Cost: O(n + m) average
Memory: hash table must fit in work_mem — else spills to disk

Cannot use for: non-equi joins (>, <, BETWEEN range joins)
text
HASH JOIN DIAGRAM:

Build (smaller: customers filtered)     Probe (accounts)
┌─────────────────────┐                ┌──────────────────┐
│ Hash Table:         │                │ account row      │
│ 1001 → cust row     │◀──hash(1001)───│ customer_id=1001 │
│ 1002 → cust row     │                └──────────────────┘
└─────────────────────┘                Emit joined row

3. Sort-Merge Join

text
Sort both inputs on join key (or use existing index order)
Merge like merge step in merge sort — emit matches when keys equal

Best when: both inputs already sorted on join key (index order)
Cost: O(n log n + m log m) if sort needed; O(n + m) if pre-sorted
Used for: large tables, equi-join, parallel execution
text
SORT-MERGE DIAGRAM:

Table A (sorted)     Table B (sorted)
customer_id          customer_id
1001 ─────────────── 1001  → match, emit
1002 ─────────────── 1002  → match, emit
1003                 1005  → 1003 no match, advance A
                     1005  → advance B

Join Order Optimization

text
3-table join: customers ⋈ accounts ⋈ transactions

Possible orders:
  (customers ⋈ accounts) ⋈ transactions
  (accounts ⋈ transactions) ⋈ customers
  (customers ⋈ transactions) ⋈ accounts  -- may be invalid if no FK

Optimizer tries all valid permutations (N! for N tables)
Uses statistics: row counts, selectivity, index availability
Picks minimum cost plan — join order matters enormously

Semi-Join and Anti-Join Internals

text
SEMI-JOIN (EXISTS):
  Hash join variant: probe side emits row only once per match
  Does not duplicate left rows when multiple right matches

ANTI-JOIN (NOT EXISTS):
  Hash anti-join: left rows with no hash match in right table
  More efficient than LEFT JOIN + IS NULL for existence checks

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Joins and Physical Storage

Index Requirements for Efficient Joins

text
FK column MUST be indexed (Lesson 6, 7):

accounts.customer_id → customers.customer_id
CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_customer_id ON accounts(customer_id);

Without index:
  Nested Loop → full scan accounts for EACH customer row
  Hash Join → full scan both tables anyway (better than NLJ without index)

With index:
  Nested Loop → O(log n) per outer row — excellent for selective joins

Clustered PK Join (InnoDB)

text
JOIN accounts ON customers.customer_id = accounts.customer_id

InnoDB:
  accounts.customer_id in secondary index → points to clustered PK leaf
  Two B+ tree lookups per account row in nested loop

Covering index on accounts(customer_id, account_id, balance):
  Index-only scan — skip clustered lookup — faster join

Join and Buffer Pool

text
Hash Join build table + probe scans:
  Both tables' pages loaded into buffer pool
  Large join of two big tables → evicts other hot pages (cache pollution)

Mitigation:
  Selective WHERE before join (reduce build/probe size)
  Join on read replica for reporting
  Pre-filter smaller table first

Cartesian Product (CROSS JOIN) Storage Disaster

sql
-- ❌ Accidental CROSS JOIN — missing ON clause
SELECT * FROM customers, accounts;  -- no WHERE join condition
-- 50,000 customers × 1,000,000 accounts = 50 BILLION rows

Always use explicit INNER JOIN ... ON

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Join Memory Consumption

Hash Join Memory

text
work_mem allocated for hash table (build side):

Build table: customers filtered to 10,000 rows × 200 bytes = 2MB → fits in work_mem ✅
Build table: 5M rows × 200 bytes = 1GB → Hash Join spill to disk ❌

PostgreSQL: HashJoin with batches — splits to disk when work_mem exceeded
Monitor: EXPLAIN ANALYZE → Hash Batches: 8, Disk Usage: 2GB

Sort-Merge Join Memory

text
Sort both inputs:
  Each sort uses work_mem independently
  2 sorts in merge join → 2× work_mem potential

Parallel sort: workers sort chunks → merge — distributes memory

Nested Loop Memory

text
Minimal memory:
  One outer row + inner index lookup at a time
  O(1) memory per iteration — best for memory-constrained systems
  But high I/O if outer large and inner not indexed

JDBC Result Set Width

java
// JOIN multiplies column count in each row — not row count (INNER JOIN 1:N increases rows)
Customer-Account 1:N join: 1 customer + 3 accounts = 3 result rows (not 1)
Each row: customer columns + account columns → wide result
Use DTO projection selecting only needed columns

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Join Execution Flows

Flow 1: INNER JOIN — Nested Loop with Index

sql
SELECT c.first_name, a.account_number, a.balance
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id = 1001;
text
1. Index Scan customers PK → customer_id = 1001 (1 row) — outer
2. Nested Loop:
     Index Scan accounts(customer_id) → 3 matching rows — inner
3. Combine: emit 3 joined rows
4. Project first_name, account_number, balance

Plan:
  Nested Loop
    -> Index Scan customers PK
    -> Index Scan idx_accounts_customer
Time: ~1ms

Flow 2: INNER JOIN — Hash Join

sql
SELECT c.region, a.account_type, COUNT(*)
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE a.status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY c.region, a.account_type;
text
1. Seq Scan accounts WHERE status='ACTIVE' (800K rows) — probe side
2. Seq Scan customers (50K rows) — build hash on customer_id
3. Hash Join: probe each account → hash lookup customer
4. HashAggregate on (region, account_type)

Plan:
  HashAggregate
    -> Hash Join (accounts.customer_id = customers.customer_id)
         -> Seq Scan accounts (Filter: status='ACTIVE')
         -> Hash
              -> Seq Scan customers

Flow 3: LEFT JOIN — Preserve Unmatched Left Rows

sql
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email, a.account_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
WHERE c.status = 'ACTIVE';
text
1. Hash Left Join (or Nested Loop Outer)
2. All active customers in result
3. Customers with no active account: account_id = NULL
4. WHERE c.status = 'ACTIVE' — filters customers before/during join

⚠️ Filter on right table belongs in ON (not WHERE) to preserve outer rows:
  WHERE a.status = 'ACTIVE'  -- converts LEFT JOIN to INNER JOIN behavior!
  ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'  -- ✅ correct

Flow 4: Anti-Join — Customers Without Accounts

sql
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id
);
text
1. Hash Anti Join (or Nested Loop Anti Join)
2. For each customer: check if any account exists
3. Emit customer only if no match
4. More efficient than LEFT JOIN + WHERE a.account_id IS NULL
   (doesn't materialize NULL account columns)

Flow 5: Many-to-Many Join Explosion

sql
-- ❌ Accidental M:N explosion
SELECT c.customer_id, a.account_id, t.transaction_id
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN transactions t ON t.account_id = a.account_id;
-- 1 customer × 3 accounts × 1000 transactions = 3000 rows — expected

-- If join condition wrong (missing account_id in second join):
JOIN transactions t ON t.customer_id = c.customer_id  -- wrong FK!
-- Cartesian explosion within customer — WRONG RESULTS

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Join Performance Rules

Algorithm Selection by Optimizer

ScenarioLikely Algorithm
Small outer + indexed innerNested Loop
Large tables, equi-join, no indexHash Join
Large sorted/indexed inputsSort-Merge Join
EXISTS / IN subqueryHash Semi Join
NOT EXISTSHash Anti Join
Very small inner (PG)Nested Loop with materialize

Join Performance Checklist

text
□ Index on FK (join) column on BOTH sides where applicable
□ Filter (WHERE) tables BEFORE join — reduce build/probe size
□ JOIN condition in ON — not WHERE (correctness + optimizer)
□ Avoid SELECT * on wide joined tables
□ Use EXISTS instead of JOIN when only checking existence
□ Use INNER JOIN when outer rows without match not needed
□ 3+ table joins: verify FK paths — no accidental Cartesian
□ Heavy joins on read replica
□ EXPLAIN ANALYZE for new multi-table queries
□ Consider denormalized read model for hot join paths (Lesson 9)

Join Anti-Patterns

sql
-- ❌ Filter right table in WHERE with LEFT JOIN
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE a.status = 'ACTIVE';  -- eliminates NULLs → INNER JOIN effect

-- ✅ Move right filter to ON
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'

-- ❌ Join without index on FK
-- 50K customers × seq scan 1M accounts each = disaster

-- ❌ OR in join condition
ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id OR a.joint_holder_id = c.customer_id
-- Often prevents hash/merge join — slow nested loop

-- ❌ Implicit cross join
FROM t1, t2 WHERE t1.id = t2.id  -- use explicit INNER JOIN

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

Join AlgorithmTimeSpaceRequires Index
Nested Loop (indexed inner)O(n × log m)O(1)Inner index
Nested Loop (no index)O(n × m)O(1)No
Hash JoinO(n + m) avgO(min(n,m)) hashNo
Sort-Merge JoinO(n log n + m log m)O(n + m) sortOptional
Cross JoinO(n × m)O(1)No

n = outer rows, m = inner rows after WHERE filters

text
Join result size:
  1:1 join:  max(n, m) rows
  1:N join:  up to n × avg_matches rows
  N:M join:  up to n × m rows (junction table avoids direct N:M)

3-table join cost:
  Depends on join order — optimizer picks minimum
  Worst case: O(n × m × p) for naive nested loops

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Join Masterclass Examples

INNER JOIN

sql
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.first_name,
    c.last_name,
    a.account_id,
    a.account_number,
    a.balance
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.status = 'ACTIVE'
AND a.status = 'ACTIVE';

LEFT JOIN

sql
-- All customers with their accounts (NULL if no account)
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.email,
    a.account_id,
    a.balance
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN accounts a
    ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
    AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'    -- filter in ON — preserves customers without accounts
WHERE c.status = 'ACTIVE';

-- Customers with NO accounts (anti-join via LEFT JOIN)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE a.account_id IS NULL;

RIGHT JOIN (Rewrite as LEFT)

sql
-- RIGHT JOIN — rarely used; rewrite for readability
SELECT c.customer_id, a.account_number
FROM customers c
RIGHT JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id;

-- Equivalent:
SELECT c.customer_id, a.account_number
FROM accounts a
LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = a.customer_id;

FULL OUTER JOIN

sql
-- Reconciliation: find mismatches both directions
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    a.account_id,
    CASE
        WHEN c.customer_id IS NULL THEN 'ORPHAN_ACCOUNT'
        WHEN a.account_id IS NULL THEN 'CUSTOMER_NO_ACCOUNT'
        ELSE 'MATCHED'
    END AS match_status
FROM customers c
FULL OUTER JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL OR a.account_id IS NULL;
-- PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server support FULL OUTER JOIN
-- MySQL: no native FULL OUTER — emulate with UNION of LEFT + RIGHT

SELF JOIN

sql
-- Employees and their managers
SELECT
    e.employee_id,
    e.first_name  AS employee_name,
    m.first_name  AS manager_name
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.employee_id = e.manager_id;

-- Accounts with balance higher than customer's average
SELECT a1.account_id, a1.balance, a1.customer_id
FROM accounts a1
JOIN (
    SELECT customer_id, AVG(balance) AS avg_bal
    FROM accounts GROUP BY customer_id
) avg_table ON avg_table.customer_id = a1.customer_id
WHERE a1.balance > avg_table.avg_bal;

M:N via Junction Table

sql
-- Customer M:N Account via account_holders (joint accounts)
SELECT
    c.first_name,
    a.account_number,
    ah.holder_role
FROM customers c
JOIN account_holders ah ON ah.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = ah.account_id
WHERE a.status = 'ACTIVE';

SEMI JOIN (EXISTS)

sql
-- Customers who have at least one active account
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM accounts a
    WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id
    AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
);

-- Equivalent IN (semi-join):
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email
FROM customers c
WHERE c.customer_id IN (
    SELECT a.customer_id FROM accounts a WHERE a.status = 'ACTIVE'
);

ANTI JOIN (NOT EXISTS)

sql
-- Customers with no accounts at all
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id
);

-- ⚠️ NOT IN with NULL trap — avoid
WHERE c.customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM accounts);  -- safe if customer_id NOT NULL

CROSS JOIN (Intentional)

sql
-- Generate all currency × account_type combinations for fee schedule
SELECT c.currency_code, t.account_type
FROM currencies c
CROSS JOIN account_types t;

-- Equivalent: FROM currencies c, account_types t (no WHERE)
-- Result rows = |currencies| × |account_types| — must be intentional

LATERAL JOIN (PostgreSQL)

sql
-- Top 3 transactions per account (correlated subquery as join)
SELECT a.account_id, t.transaction_id, t.amount
FROM accounts a
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT transaction_id, amount
    FROM transactions t
    WHERE t.account_id = a.account_id
    ORDER BY t.created_at DESC
    LIMIT 3
) t;

Part 12 — Production Usage

Joins in Production Domains

Banking — Customer Account Statement

sql
SELECT
    c.first_name || ' ' || c.last_name  AS customer_name,
    a.account_number,
    a.account_type,
    a.balance,
    t.transaction_id,
    t.amount,
    t.created_at
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT transaction_id, amount, created_at
    FROM transactions t
    WHERE t.account_id = a.account_id
    ORDER BY created_at DESC
    LIMIT 5
) t ON true
WHERE c.customer_id = :customerId
AND a.status = 'ACTIVE';
-- Index: accounts(customer_id), transactions(account_id, created_at DESC)

Payments — Order with Payment Status

sql
-- Microservices: NO cross-DB join — application composes or uses read model
-- Within Payment Service DB:
SELECT p.payment_id, p.order_ref, p.amount, p.status, r.refund_amount
FROM payments p
LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.payment_id = p.payment_id
WHERE p.order_ref = :orderRef;

E-Commerce — Order Details

sql
SELECT
    o.order_id,
    o.ordered_at,
    c.email,
    oi.product_id,
    p.product_name,
    oi.quantity,
    oi.unit_price
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.order_id = :orderId;
-- 4-table join — each FK indexed

Data Quality — Orphan Detection

sql
-- Accounts referencing non-existent customers (FK should prevent — audit check)
SELECT a.account_id, a.customer_id
FROM accounts a
LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = a.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL;
-- Should return zero rows if FK enforced

Part 13 — Spring Boot Integration

Joins via JPA

JPQL JOIN

java
@Query("""
    SELECT c, a FROM Customer c
    JOIN c.accounts a
    WHERE c.customerId = :customerId
    AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
    """)
List<Object[]> findCustomerWithActiveAccounts(@Param("customerId") Long customerId);

// Better: return DTO
@Query("""
    SELECT new com.bank.dto.CustomerAccountDto(
        c.customerId, c.firstName, a.accountId, a.accountNumber, a.balance)
    FROM Customer c
    JOIN c.accounts a
    WHERE c.customerId = :customerId AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
    """)

JOIN FETCH — Avoid N+1

java
@Query("""
    SELECT c FROM Customer c
    JOIN FETCH c.accounts a
    WHERE c.customerId = :customerId
    AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
    """)
Optional<Customer> findByIdWithAccounts(@Param("customerId") Long customerId);
// Single SQL with JOIN — accounts loaded in same query
// Without FETCH: lazy load triggers N+1 (Lesson 53)

LEFT JOIN FETCH

java
@Query("""
    SELECT c FROM Customer c
    LEFT JOIN FETCH c.accounts a
    WHERE c.status = 'ACTIVE'
    """)
List<Customer> findAllActiveWithAccounts();
// Customers without accounts included — accounts collection empty

Entity Graph

java
@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"accounts"})
Optional<Customer> findWithAccountsByCustomerId(Long customerId);
// Spring Data generates LEFT OUTER JOIN FETCH equivalent

Native Join

java
@Query(value = """
    SELECT c.customer_id, c.email, a.account_id, a.balance
    FROM customers c
    INNER JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
    WHERE c.customer_id = :customerId
    """, nativeQuery = true)
List<Object[]> findNativeJoin(@Param("customerId") Long customerId);

ORM Join Mapping

Relationship Annotations = Join Structure

java
@Entity
public class Customer {
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "customer", fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    private List<Account> accounts;
    // Hibernate: accounts loaded via
    // SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = ? (separate query if lazy)
}

@Entity
public class Account {
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    @JoinColumn(name = "customer_id", nullable = false)
    private Customer customer;
    // FK side owns the join
}

Join Types in Hibernate

Hibernate/JPQLSQL Equivalent
JOININNER JOIN
LEFT JOINLEFT OUTER JOIN
JOIN FETCHINNER JOIN (eager in same query)

Cartesian Product Warning

java
// ❌ Multiple JOIN FETCH collections — Cartesian product
SELECT c FROM Customer c
JOIN FETCH c.accounts
JOIN FETCH c.loans  // 3 accounts × 2 loans = 6 rows per customer in result

// ✅ Fetch one collection; batch fetch second
@BatchSize(size = 25)  // on loans collection

@JoinColumn and FK

java
@ManyToOne
@JoinColumn(name = "customer_id", nullable = false,
    foreignKey = @ForeignKey(name = "fk_accounts_customer"))
private Customer customer;
// Maps to: INNER JOIN ON accounts.customer_id = customers.customer_id
// Database FK ensures referential integrity

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

Join Architecture Decisions

When to JOIN vs Denormalize vs Compose

text
JOIN in OLTP (same DB, indexed FK):
  ✅ Customer + accounts for teller screen
  ✅ Order + order_items in Order Service DB

NO JOIN across microservices:
  ❌ Payment Service JOIN Order Service DB
  ✅ API composition or read model with denormalized data

Denormalized read model (Lesson 9):
  Customer360View table — pre-joined for dashboard
  Refreshed by events — avoids 5-table join on every page load

Join Depth Guidelines

Join CountGuidance
1-2 joinsNormal OLTP — index FKs
3-4 joinsOK with selective WHERE — verify EXPLAIN

API Composition Pattern (Microservices)

GET /customers/1001/account-summary

Account Service:
  SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE customer_id=1001

Customer Service:
  SELECT name, email FROM customers WHERE customer_id=1001

BFF/API Gateway composes response — no cross-DB JOIN
OR: CQRS read model pre-joins for this screen

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: RIGHT Table Filter in WHERE with LEFT JOIN

sql
-- ❌ Converts LEFT JOIN to INNER JOIN behavior
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE a.status = 'ACTIVE';

-- ✅
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id AND a.status = 'ACTIVE';

Mistake 2: Missing FK Index

sql
-- Join on unindexed customer_id — nested loop disaster
-- ✅ CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_customer_id ON accounts(customer_id);

Mistake 3: Accidental Cartesian Product

sql
-- ❌ Missing join condition
FROM orders o, order_items oi WHERE o.status = 'ACTIVE';  -- no o.order_id = oi.order_id

-- ✅
FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id WHERE o.status = 'ACTIVE';

Mistake 4: JOIN When EXISTS Suffices

sql
-- ❌ Duplicates customers with 3 accounts into 3 rows
SELECT DISTINCT c.customer_id FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE a.status = 'ACTIVE';

-- ✅
SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id AND a.status = 'ACTIVE');

Mistake 5: N+1 Instead of JOIN FETCH

java
// ❌ 1 + N queries
Customer c = customerRepo.findById(1001L);
c.getAccounts().size();

// ✅ JOIN FETCH in one query
customerRepo.findByIdWithAccounts(1001L);

Mistake 6: Cross-Service SQL JOIN

sql
-- ❌ Impossible in microservices — different databases
SELECT o.*, p.* FROM order_db.orders o JOIN payment_db.payments p ON ...
-- ✅ Event-driven read model or API composition

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is an INNER JOIN?

Returns rows where join condition matches in both tables. Unmatched rows excluded.

Q2: Difference between INNER and LEFT JOIN?

INNER: only matches. LEFT: all left rows kept; right columns NULL when no match.

Q3: Why put filter on right table in ON vs WHERE for LEFT JOIN?

WHERE on right column eliminates NULL rows (unmatched left) — acts like INNER JOIN. ON preserves outer rows.

Q4: What is a CROSS JOIN?

Cartesian product — every row of A paired with every row of B. n × m rows.

Q5: What is FK index importance for joins?

Nested loop inner side uses index for O(log n) lookup. Without index: O(n×m) scans.

Mid-Level

Q6: Explain nested loop, hash, and merge join.

NLJ: for each outer row, probe inner (needs index). Hash: build hash on smaller table, probe larger. Merge: sort both on key, merge scan.

Q7: EXISTS vs INNER JOIN?

EXISTS (semi-join): returns left rows once if match exists — no duplication. JOIN: includes right columns, duplicates for 1:N.

Q8: How to find customers without accounts?

LEFT JOIN + WHERE account_id IS NULL, or NOT EXISTS (preferred — clearer intent).

Q9: What causes join result explosion?

Missing/incorrect join condition, M:N without junction table, multiple 1:N joins multiplying rows.

Q10: JOIN FETCH in Hibernate?

Eagerly loads associated collection in same SQL JOIN — prevents N+1 lazy load queries.

Senior

Q11: Optimize 4-table join on OLTP primary taking 30 seconds.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE: identify seq scans, join order, row estimates. Add missing FK indexes. Push selective WHERE early. Consider covering indexes. Route to read replica if reporting. Denormalize read model if hot path.

Q12: Hash join spilling to disk — fix?

Increase work_mem session-only, reduce rows via WHERE before join, update statistics ANALYZE, ensure build side is smaller table after filtering.

Q13: Semi-join vs anti-join internal execution?

Semi-join: emit left row once on first match. Anti-join: emit left row when no hash match in right. Both avoid row duplication of regular join.

Q14: Microservices — can Order Service JOIN Customer Service tables?

No — separate databases. Use customer_id reference, API call, event replication, or CQRS read model with pre-joined data.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Design read path for customer dashboard needing data from 5 bounded contexts.

No cross-service JOIN. Options: BFF composes 5 API calls (parallel); CQRS read model fed by Kafka events with denormalized CustomerDashboardDoc; GraphQL federation. Cache in Redis. Define staleness SLA.

Q16: Join order for A⋈B⋈C — how does optimizer decide?

Statistics: row counts, selectivity of WHERE filters, index availability. Tries permutations; picks minimum cost. DBA influence: extended statistics, index design — not manual join order hints except emergency.

Scenario

Scenario: "Report count of orders per customer is 3× expected."

Likely join explosion: missing join key, M:N join without junction, or duplicate rows in dimension table. Debug: compare COUNT(*) vs COUNT(DISTINCT order_id). Fix join conditions. Use EXISTS or subquery with DISTINCT if needed.

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why This Exists5Internal Working6Storage Internals7Memory Usage8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Complexity Analysis11Code / SQL Examples12Production Usage13Spring Boot Integration14Hibernate/JPA Integration15Architect Perspective16Decision Matrix17Comparison Tables18Common Mistakes19Interview Questions20Revision Sheet21Summary Table*Practice

Part 1 — Concept

What Is a Subquery?

A subquery (inner query, nested query) is a SELECT statement embedded inside another SQL statement — in WHERE, FROM, SELECT, HAVING, or INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. The outer query uses the inner query’s result as a value, table, or filter.

sql
-- Scalar subquery in WHERE
SELECT account_id, balance
FROM accounts
WHERE balance > (
    SELECT AVG(balance) FROM accounts WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
);

-- Subquery in FROM (derived table / inline view)
SELECT customer_id, total
FROM (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) AS total
    FROM accounts
    GROUP BY customer_id
) sub
WHERE total > 10000;

Subquery Classification

text
SUBQUERIES

├── By result shape
│   ├── Scalar subquery      → returns 1 row, 1 column (single value)
│   ├── Row subquery         → returns 1 row, multiple columns
│   ├── Table subquery       → returns multiple rows and columns
│   └── Column subquery      → returns 1 column, multiple rows (IN, ANY)
│
├── By correlation
│   ├── Non-correlated       → inner query runs once, independent
│   └── Correlated           → inner query references outer row, runs per outer row
│
├── By placement
│   ├── WHERE / HAVING       → filter (most common)
│   ├── FROM                 → derived table / inline view
│   ├── SELECT list          → scalar per row (usually correlated)
│   └── INSERT / UPDATE      → source for DML
│
└── By logical role
    ├── Semi-join              → EXISTS, IN (match exists)
    ├── Anti-join              → NOT EXISTS, NOT IN
    └── Comparison             → >, <, = scalar subquery

Subquery vs Join — When Each Wins

NeedOften Better
Filter by aggregate thresholdJOIN + GROUP BY or derived table
Existence check (any match?)EXISTS (semi-join)
Absence check (no match?)NOT EXISTS (anti-join)
Single scalar value (avg, max)Scalar subquery (non-correlated)
Per-row computed columnCorrelated subquery or window function (Lesson 19)
Multi-column result setJOIN or derived table in FROM

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Subqueries in SQL

text
1970s   SEQUEL includes subqueries in WHERE — early systems executed naively
        Correlated subquery: re-run inner query for EVERY outer row

1980s   Query optimizers begin subquery unnesting (flattening to joins)
        Oracle: "subquery coalescing" — rewrite IN to semi-join

1990s   SQL-92 formalizes:
        - Scalar, row, table subqueries
        - EXISTS, IN, ANY, ALL quantifiers
        - Derived tables in FROM

2000s   Cost-based unnesting: optimizer chooses subquery vs join plan
        MySQL historically weak at subquery optimization (pre-5.6)
        PostgreSQL: pull-up sublinks, semi-join deduplication

2010s   Window functions reduce some correlated subquery patterns
        EXISTS often preferred over IN for NULL safety and plan stability

2020s   Adaptive plans; decorrelation in PostgreSQL 12+ (initplans, hash semi-join)
        ORMs generate subqueries from lazy loading (N+1) — architectural concern

Historical Lesson

Early databases executed correlated subqueries once per outer row — O(n×m) disaster. Modern optimizers decorrelate (unnest) many subqueries into joins or semi-joins automatically. You still must write subqueries that can be unnested.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Do Subqueries Solve?

Problem 1: Compare to Aggregate Without Extra Join

sql
-- Accounts above average balance — no self-join needed
SELECT account_id, balance
FROM accounts
WHERE balance > (SELECT AVG(balance) FROM accounts WHERE status = 'ACTIVE');
-- Inner query runs ONCE → single average value

Problem 2: Existence Without Row Duplication

sql
-- Customers with at least one active account — no 1:N join duplication
SELECT customer_id, email
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM accounts a
    WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
);

Problem 3: Filter by Dynamic Set

sql
-- Accounts for customers in APAC region
SELECT account_id, balance
FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id IN (
    SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE region = 'APAC'
);
-- Inner query produces set of IDs — outer filters by membership

Problem 4: Inline Transformation (Derived Table)

sql
-- Filter on aggregated result without HAVING on outer entity
SELECT customer_id, total_balance
FROM (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) AS total_balance
    FROM accounts GROUP BY customer_id
) agg
WHERE total_balance > 50000;
-- Subquery in FROM = temporary result set

Problem 5: Per-Row Lookup (Correlated)

sql
-- Each account with customer's email in same row (join is better — but pattern exists)
SELECT a.account_id, a.balance,
       (SELECT c.email FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = a.customer_id) AS email
FROM accounts a;
-- Correlated: inner query runs per account row (or unnested to join by optimizer)

Unified Problem Statement

Subqueries express filters, comparisons, and intermediate results that depend on other query parts — especially existence checks, scalar comparisons, and inline aggregations — without always materializing a full join.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Not Always Use JOIN?

Expressiveness

Some logic maps naturally to subqueries:

text
"Balance greater than the average"     → scalar subquery
"Customers who have any account"       → EXISTS
"Customers with no orders"             → NOT EXISTS
"Top customer per region" (legacy)   → correlated subquery (now: window fn)

Semi-Join Semantics

sql
-- JOIN version — may duplicate customers
SELECT DISTINCT c.customer_id
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id;

-- EXISTS — one row per customer, clearer intent
SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id);

Layered Filtering

sql
-- Stage 1: aggregate in subquery
-- Stage 2: filter aggregated result
-- Cleaner than nested HAVING in some reporting queries
SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total FROM payments GROUP BY region
) r WHERE total > 1000000;

When JOIN Is Better

sql
-- ❌ Correlated scalar subquery per row (if not unnested)
SELECT c.name,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS cnt
FROM customers c;

-- ✅ Usually better as JOIN + GROUP BY (Lesson 16)
SELECT c.name, COUNT(a.account_id) AS cnt
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.name;

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Subqueries Execute Internally

Non-Correlated Subquery — InitPlan (Run Once)

sql
WHERE balance > (SELECT AVG(balance) FROM accounts WHERE status = 'ACTIVE')
text
EXECUTION (PostgreSQL InitPlan):

Step 1: Execute inner query ONCE
        → result: 12500.00 (single scalar)

Step 2: Substitute into outer query (constant folding)
        WHERE balance > 12500.00

Step 3: Index scan or seq scan on accounts with simple predicate

Plan node:
  InitPlan 1
    -> Aggregate: avg(balance)
  -> Seq Scan on accounts
       Filter: balance > InitPlan 1 result

Cost: cost of AVG + cost of filtered scan — efficient ✅

Correlated Subquery — Per Row (Naive) vs Unnest (Optimized)

sql
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM accounts a
    WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
)
text
NAIVE (uncorrelated execution — old engines):
  FOR each customer row c:
    RUN inner SELECT with c.customer_id bound
  → O(customers × accounts) — catastrophic

OPTIMIZED (semi-join unnesting — modern engines):
  Hash Semi Join:
    Build hash on accounts(customer_id) WHERE status='ACTIVE'
    Probe customers — emit if hash hit
  → O(customers + accounts) — same as INNER JOIN semi-join ✅

PostgreSQL EXPLAIN may show:
  Hash Semi Join
    -> Seq Scan customers
    -> Hash
         -> Index Scan accounts WHERE status='ACTIVE'

IN Subquery — Semi-Join Rewrite

sql
WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE region = 'APAC')
text
Optimizer rewrite:
  IN (subquery)  →  Semi Join  or  Hash Semi Join
  Equivalent to: EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM subquery s WHERE s.id = outer.id)

Materialization (sometimes):
  Execute subquery → store in temp hash table → probe outer
  InitPlan or CTE materialization

Derived Table in FROM

sql
FROM (SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) AS total FROM accounts GROUP BY customer_id) sub
text
Execution:
  1. Run inner query completely → materialize result (temp table or memory tuplestore)
  2. Outer query scans materialized result
  3. May not push outer WHERE into inner query (unless subquery flattening)

PostgreSQL 12+: often inlines simple subqueries (subquery pull-up)

Subquery Unnesting / Decorrelation

text
OPTIMIZER TRANSFORMATIONS:

  Correlated EXISTS     →  Semi Join
  Correlated IN         →  Semi Join
  Correlated NOT EXISTS →  Anti Join
  Scalar subquery (agg) →  InitPlan or Join
  IN (constant list)    →  OR expansion or hash

When unnesting fails:
  SubPlan node — correlated loop per outer row — slow
  Look for "SubPlan" or "InitPlan" in EXPLAIN — investigate rewrite

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Subqueries and Storage

Non-Correlated: Minimal Extra I/O

text
Scalar AVG subquery:
  Reads accounts table (or index-only) once for aggregate
  Result cached in InitPlan — no repeated reads

Same I/O as running AVG in application then second query — but one round trip

Correlated Without Unnesting: Repeated Index Probes

text
If optimizer falls back to nested correlated loop:
  Outer: 50,000 customers
  Inner each time: index scan accounts(customer_id)
  50,000 index lookups — may still be OK if index selective
  vs one hash semi-join: one scan of accounts + hash build — usually better

Materialized Subquery (Temp Storage)

text
Derived table with large inner result:
  Inner GROUP BY 1M customers → spool to temp file
  Outer filters total > 50000

Temp file location:
  PostgreSQL: pgsql_tmp
  Oracle: TEMP tablespace
  SQL Server: tempdb

Same storage concern as sort/hash spill — work_mem, temp tablespace sizing

IN List vs Subquery

sql
WHERE customer_id IN (1001, 1002, 1003)           -- constants in plan
WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT ... FROM big_table)  -- hash semi-join or materialize
-- Large IN lists (1000+ values) — sometimes temp table or array scan
-- Subquery often better for large dynamic sets

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Subquery Memory Impact

PatternMemory
Scalar InitPlanSingle value — negligible
EXISTS unnested to semi-joinHash table on inner side — work_mem
IN (subquery) materializedFull inner result in hash — work_mem
Derived table in FROMTuplestore / temp — work_mem or disk
Correlated SubPlan loopMinimal per iteration — high CPU/I/O
Large IN list (10000 literals)Plan cache, parse memory

work_mem and Hash Semi-Join

sql
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id)
-- Unnested to hash semi-join:
-- Build hash on accounts (all customer_ids) — may be large
-- work_mem exceeded → hash batches to disk

Application N+1 vs Subquery

java
// ❌ N+1 — NOT a SQL subquery but analogous anti-pattern
for (Customer c : customers) {
    accountRepo.countByCustomerId(c.getId());  // N queries
}

// ✅ One EXISTS or JOIN query
// Memory: one result set vs N round trips + N small result sets

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Subquery Execution Flows

Flow 1: Scalar Non-Correlated

sql
SELECT account_id, balance
FROM accounts
WHERE balance > (SELECT AVG(balance) FROM accounts WHERE status = 'ACTIVE')
AND status = 'ACTIVE';
text
1. InitPlan: compute AVG(balance) WHERE status='ACTIVE' → 8500.00
2. Scan accounts WHERE status='ACTIVE' AND balance > 8500.00
3. Return matching rows

Single inner execution — fast

Flow 2: EXISTS (Decorrelated)

sql
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM accounts a
    WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
);
text
1. Hash inner: active accounts → hash on customer_id
2. Scan customers — probe hash
3. Emit customer if probe hit (semi-join — once per customer)
4. No account columns in output

Plan: Hash Semi Join — mirrors INNER JOIN existence check

Flow 3: NOT EXISTS (Anti-Join)

sql
SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id
);
text
1. Hash all account customer_ids
2. Scan customers — probe hash
3. Emit customer if NO probe hit

Plan: Hash Anti Join or Hash Left Anti Join

Flow 4: Correlated Scalar in SELECT (Risky)

sql
SELECT a.account_id,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM transactions t WHERE t.account_id = a.account_id) AS txn_count
FROM accounts a;
text
IF NOT unnested:
  SubPlan per account row:
    For account 5001: COUNT transactions WHERE account_id=5001
    For account 5002: COUNT ...
  N subplan executions

IF unnested (PG may use LEFT JOIN + GROUP BY or aggregate pushdown):
  Single join + group — efficient

Always check EXPLAIN — avoid SubPlan on large outer sets

Flow 5: Derived Table + Filter

sql
SELECT customer_id, total
FROM (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) AS total
    FROM accounts WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
    GROUP BY customer_id
) x
WHERE total > 10000
ORDER BY total DESC
LIMIT 20;
text
1. HashAggregate: group by customer_id → materialize (customer_id, total)
2. Filter total > 10000
3. Sort by total DESC
4. Limit 20

Alternative: same with HAVING SUM(balance) > 10000 — often identical plan

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Subquery Performance Rules

Performance Hierarchy

text
FASTEST → SLOWEST:

1. Non-correlated scalar InitPlan (runs once)
2. EXISTS / NOT EXISTS unnested to hash semi/anti join
3. IN (subquery) unnested to semi-join
4. Derived table inlined / pulled up by optimizer
5. Correlated SubPlan with index on correlation column
6. Correlated SubPlan without index — nested loop hell
7. Correlated scalar in SELECT list for millions of rows
8. NOT IN with NULLs in subquery — wrong + potentially slow

Subquery vs Join Decision Guide

PatternPrefer
Exists any related row?EXISTS
Not exists?NOT EXISTS
Need columns from both tables?JOIN
Compare to global aggregate?Scalar subquery (InitPlan)
Filter on grouped aggregate?Derived table or HAVING
Per-group rankingWindow function (Lesson 19)
IN list < 100 constantsIN (...) OK
IN from large subqueryEXISTS or JOIN often same plan

Anti-Patterns

sql
-- ❌ NOT IN with possible NULL
WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM blocked WHERE active = false);
-- NULL in subquery → UNKNOWN → zero rows

-- ✅ NOT EXISTS
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM blocked b WHERE b.customer_id = c.customer_id AND b.active = false);

-- ❌ Correlated COUNT in SELECT for 1M rows (if SubPlan)
SELECT a.*, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t WHERE t.account_id = a.account_id) FROM accounts a;

-- ✅ JOIN + GROUP BY or window COUNT OVER (Lesson 19)

-- ❌ Nested subqueries 5 levels deep — hard to optimize
WHERE id IN (SELECT ... IN (SELECT ... IN (SELECT ...)));

-- ✅ Flatten with JOINs or CTEs (Lesson 18)

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

Subquery TypeNaive ExecutionOptimized (Unnested)
Scalar non-correlatedO(m) onceO(m) InitPlan
EXISTS correlatedO(n × m)O(n + m) semi-join
NOT EXISTSO(n × m)O(n + m) anti-join
IN (subquery)O(n × m)O(n + m) semi-join
Scalar correlated per rowO(n × log m) with indexO(n + m) if decorrelated
Derived tableO(inner) + O(outer)Same; pull-up may merge
Nested k levelsProduct of scansOptimizer may flatten

n = outer rows, m = inner rows

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Subquery Masterclass Examples

Scalar Subquery in WHERE

sql
-- Above average balance
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE balance > (SELECT AVG(balance) FROM accounts WHERE status = 'ACTIVE');

-- Maximum balance customer(s) — scalar subquery in comparison
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE balance = (SELECT MAX(balance) FROM accounts);

-- Subquery with ALL / ANY
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE balance > ALL (
    SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_type = 'LOAN'
);
-- Greater than every loan account balance

WHERE balance > ANY (SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = 1001);
-- Greater than at least one of customer 1001's balances

IN and NOT IN

sql
-- IN with subquery
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id IN (
    SELECT customer_id FROM customers
    WHERE region IN ('APAC', 'EMEA') AND status = 'ACTIVE'
);

-- NOT IN — only safe if subquery column NOT NULL
SELECT customer_id, email FROM customers
WHERE customer_id NOT IN (
    SELECT customer_id FROM accounts WHERE status = 'SUSPENDED'
    AND customer_id IS NOT NULL  -- defensive
);
-- Prefer NOT EXISTS

EXISTS and NOT EXISTS

sql
-- Active account exists
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM accounts a
    WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
);

-- No accounts at all
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id
);

-- Complex existence
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM transactions t
    JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = t.account_id
    WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id
    AND t.amount > 10000
    AND t.created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'
);

Correlated Subquery in WHERE

sql
-- Accounts with balance above their customer's average
SELECT a.account_id, a.balance, a.customer_id
FROM accounts a
WHERE a.balance > (
    SELECT AVG(a2.balance)
    FROM accounts a2
    WHERE a2.customer_id = a.customer_id
    AND a2.status = 'ACTIVE'
);
-- Correlated: inner references a.customer_id
-- Optimizer may decorrelate to window AVG or self-join

Subquery in SELECT List

sql
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.email,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS account_count,
    (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(balance), 0) FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS total_balance
FROM customers c
WHERE c.status = 'ACTIVE';
-- Two correlated subqueries per row — consider JOIN + GROUP BY instead

Subquery in FROM (Derived Table)

sql
SELECT region, avg_customer_balance
FROM (
    SELECT c.region, c.customer_id, SUM(a.balance) AS cust_total
    FROM customers c
    JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
    WHERE a.status = 'ACTIVE'
    GROUP BY c.region, c.customer_id
) customer_totals
GROUP BY region
HAVING AVG(cust_total) > 5000;

-- Oracle inline view — same concept
-- SQL Server derived table — requires alias (sub)

Subquery in HAVING

sql
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM payments
WHERE status = 'COMPLETED'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(amount) > (
    SELECT AVG(total) FROM (
        SELECT SUM(amount) AS total
        FROM payments WHERE status = 'COMPLETED'
        GROUP BY customer_id
    ) t
);
-- Above average paying customer

Row Subquery

sql
-- PostgreSQL row constructor
SELECT account_id FROM accounts
WHERE (customer_id, account_type) = (
    SELECT customer_id, account_type FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 5001
);
-- Single row returned from subquery required

INSERT / UPDATE with Subquery

sql
-- Archive closed accounts
INSERT INTO accounts_archive
SELECT * FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'CLOSED'
AND closed_at < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7 years';

UPDATE accounts SET status = 'SUSPENDED'
WHERE customer_id IN (
    SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE status = 'FRAUD_FLAGGED'
);
-- MySQL: may need same-table update workaround

Part 12 — Production Usage

Subqueries in Production

Banking — Above-Threshold Detection

sql
-- Transactions above daily average for that account type
SELECT t.transaction_id, t.amount, t.account_id
FROM transactions t
WHERE t.amount > (
    SELECT AVG(t2.amount) * 3
    FROM transactions t2
    JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = t2.account_id
    WHERE a.account_type = (
        SELECT account_type FROM accounts WHERE account_id = t.account_id
    )
    AND t2.created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '90 days'
);
-- Nested subqueries — verify EXPLAIN; consider rewriting with JOINs

Payments — Idempotency Existence Check

sql
-- Before insert — check duplicate client_request_id
SELECT CASE WHEN EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM payments WHERE client_request_id = :requestId
) THEN 'DUPLICATE' ELSE 'OK' END;
-- Or rely on UNIQUE constraint + catch exception — preferred in app

E-Commerce — Customers Who Never Ordered

sql
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email, c.created_at
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
)
AND c.created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '90 days';
-- Marketing re-engagement cohort

Reporting — Regional Rollup via Derived Table

sql
-- Run on read replica
SELECT region, SUM(customer_total) AS region_total
FROM (
    SELECT c.region, c.customer_id, SUM(a.balance) AS customer_total
    FROM customers c
    JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
    WHERE a.status = 'ACTIVE'
    GROUP BY c.region, c.customer_id
) sub
GROUP BY region
ORDER BY region_total DESC;

Subqueries in Spring Data JPA

java
@Query("""
    SELECT c FROM Customer c
    WHERE EXISTS (
        SELECT 1 FROM Account a
        WHERE a.customer.customerId = c.customerId
        AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
    )
    """)
List<Customer> findCustomersWithActiveAccounts();

    WHERE a.balance > (

JPQL Subquery Restrictions

text
JPQL subqueries supported in:
  WHERE, HAVING
  Sometimes FROM (entity subquery — limited)

JPQL subqueries NOT in SELECT list (JPA 2.1+ allows in some providers — avoid)

Correlated: inner query references outer alias c, a

Native Subquery

java
@Query(value = """
    SELECT c.customer_id, c.email
    FROM customers c
    WHERE NOT EXISTS (
        SELECT 1 FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id
    )
    """, nativeQuery = true)
List<Object[]> findCustomersWithoutAccountsNative();

Specification with Subquery (Criteria API)

java
public static Specification<Customer> hasActiveAccount() {
    return (root, query, cb) -> {
        Subquery<Long> sq = query.subquery(Long.class);
        Root<Account> account = sq.from(Account.class);
        sq.select(account.get("customer").get("customerId"));
        sq.where(
            cb.equal(account.get("customer").get("customerId"), root.get("customerId")),
            cb.equal(account.get("status"), AccountStatus.ACTIVE)
        );
        return cb.exists(sq);
    };
}

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

ORM and Subqueries

N+1 Is Not SQL Subquery — But Related

java
// Hibernate lazy load — generates repeated queries (like correlated subquery cost)
Customer c = customerRepo.findById(1001L);
c.getAccounts().size();  // SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE customer_id=1001

// Fix: JOIN FETCH — single query (Lesson 16)
@Query("SELECT c FROM Customer c JOIN FETCH c.accounts WHERE c.customerId = :id")

Hibernate @Subselect (Entity from Subquery)

java
@Entity
@Subselect("SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) AS total FROM accounts GROUP BY customer_id")
@Synchronize({"accounts"})
public class CustomerBalanceSummary {
    @Id
    private Long customerId;
    private BigDecimal total;
}
// Read-only entity backed by subquery — advanced pattern

DTO Projection Beats SELECT List Subqueries

java
// ❌ Hibernate loads entities + implicit correlated queries
// ✅ Explicit JPQL with JOIN + GROUP BY
@Query("""
    SELECT new com.bank.dto.CustomerSummaryDto(
        c.customerId, c.email, COUNT(a), SUM(a.balance))
    FROM Customer c LEFT JOIN c.accounts a
    WHERE c.status = 'ACTIVE'
    GROUP BY c.customerId, c.email
    """)
List<CustomerSummaryDto> getSummaries();

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

Subquery Architecture Decisions

EXISTS vs JOIN vs Application Filter

text
Decision tree:

Need columns from both tables in result?
  YES → JOIN
  NO ↓

Checking existence or absence only?
  YES → EXISTS / NOT EXISTS
  NO ↓

Comparing to single aggregate value?
  YES → scalar subquery (InitPlan)
  NO ↓

Intermediate aggregation then filter?
  YES → derived table in FROM or CTE (Lesson 18)
  NO ↓

Per-row ranking / running total?
  YES → window functions (Lesson 19)

Microservices — No Cross-Service Subqueries

sql
-- ❌ Impossible
WHERE order_id IN (SELECT id FROM order_service.orders ...)

-- ✅
-- 1. Call Order Service API → get IDs → parameter IN (:ids)  (small sets)
-- 2. Replicate read data to local DB via events
-- 3. CQRS read model with pre-joined data

Caching Scalar Subquery Results

java
// Average balance changes infrequently — cache InitPlan equivalent
@Cacheable("avgActiveBalance")
public BigDecimal getAverageActiveBalance() {
    return accountRepo.findAverageBalanceByStatus(ACTIVE);
}
// Application compares in memory for simple dashboards — trade staleness for speed

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: NOT IN with NULL

sql
-- ❌ Returns zero rows if subquery has ANY NULL
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM blocked);

-- ✅
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM blocked b WHERE b.customer_id = customers.customer_id);

Mistake 2: Scalar Subquery Returns Multiple Rows

sql
-- ❌ ERROR: more than one row returned by a subquery
WHERE balance = (SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE status = 'ACTIVE');
-- Multiple rows

-- ✅ Add LIMIT 1 only if business rule guarantees one — usually MAX/MIN/aggregate
WHERE balance = (SELECT MAX(balance) FROM accounts WHERE status = 'ACTIVE');

Mistake 3: Correlated Subqueries in SELECT for Large Sets

sql
-- ❌ Two counts per customer row if not unnested
SELECT c.*,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM accounts ...) ,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders ...)
FROM customers c;

-- ✅ One query with JOINs + GROUP BY or subquery in FROM

Mistake 4: Assuming Subquery Always Runs Per Row

text
Modern optimizers unnest — always EXPLAIN
"Correlated" in SQL text ≠ correlated loop in execution

Mistake 5: Deep Nesting Instead of CTE

sql
-- ❌ Hard to read and optimize
WHERE id IN (SELECT ... IN (SELECT ... IN (SELECT ...)))

-- ✅ CTE (Lesson 18) — same logic, clearer

Mistake 6: IN List with 10,000 Bind Parameters

java
// ❌ WHERE id IN (:ids) — 10000 params — plan instability
// ✅ Temp table JOIN, or EXISTS subquery from staged table, or batch

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is a subquery?

A SELECT nested inside another SQL statement — in WHERE, FROM, HAVING, etc.

Q2: Difference between IN and EXISTS?

IN checks membership in a set. EXISTS checks if subquery returns any row. EXISTS often preferred; NULL-safe for NOT case.

Q3: Can subquery return multiple rows for = operator?

No — scalar comparison requires exactly one row and one column; otherwise error.

Q4: What is correlated subquery?

Inner query references outer query row — e.g. WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id.

Q5: Subquery in FROM vs WHERE?

FROM: creates derived table for outer query. WHERE: filters using subquery result.

Mid-Level

Q6: NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS with NULL?

NOT IN: if subquery returns NULL, result is UNKNOWN — no rows match. NOT EXISTS: NULL-safe.

Q7: How does optimizer handle EXISTS?

Often unnests to hash semi-join — same cost class as join, not per-row loop.

Q8: Scalar subquery execution — how many times run?

Non-correlated: once (InitPlan). Correlated naive: per outer row; optimized: decorrelated.

Q9: EXISTS vs INNER JOIN for existence?

EXISTS: no duplication, don't need DISTINCT. JOIN: need DISTINCT if selecting left columns only.

Q10: Derived table vs CTE?

Similar semantics; CTE (Lesson 18) clearer, may be optimization fence in some DBs.

Senior

Q11: Rewrite correlated scalar COUNT in SELECT for performance.

JOIN + GROUP BY, or window COUNT() OVER, or lateral join. Verify EXPLAIN removes SubPlan.

Q12: Subquery unnesting — when does it fail?

Volatile functions, LIMIT in subquery, DISTINCT ON, writeable CTE conflicts, complex aggregation — SubPlan remains.

Q13: ANY vs IN?

IN = = ANY for single column. ANY allows operators: > ANY, < ANY (compare to any subquery value).

Q14: Update with subquery same table — MySQL pitfall?

MySQL restricts updating table while selecting from same table in subquery — use derived table wrapper.

Staff / Architect

Q15: ORM generates N+1 — relate to subqueries.

N+1 = application-level correlated query pattern. Fix: JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, batch size, DTO query — not more subqueries.

Q16: Payment service checks order exists in Order DB — design?

No SQL subquery across DBs. Synchronous API call, cached order existence, or local replica of order IDs via Kafka.

Scenario

Scenario: "EXISTS query slow; plan shows Nested Loop with SubPlan."

Optimizer failed to unnest. Add index on correlated columns, update statistics, simplify subquery, rewrite as explicit semi-join, or use CTE materialization hint (database-specific). PostgreSQL: check enable_hashjoin, subquery pull-up limitations.
