1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why This Exists5Internal Working6Storage Internals7Memory Usage8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Complexity Analysis11Code / SQL Examples12Production Usage13Spring Boot Integration14Hibernate/JPA Integration15Architect Perspective16Decision Matrix17Comparison Tables18Common Mistakes19Interview Questions20Revision Sheet21Summary Table*Practice

Part 1 — Concept

What Is a CTE?

A Common Table Expression (CTE) is a named temporary result set defined with the WITH clause and referenced in the main query. It improves readability, enables multi-stage pipelines, and supports recursive queries (hierarchies, graphs).

sql
WITH active_accounts AS (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) AS total_balance
    FROM accounts
    WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email, aa.total_balance
FROM customers c
JOIN active_accounts aa ON aa.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE aa.total_balance > 50000
ORDER BY aa.total_balance DESC;

CTE vs Subquery in FROM

sql
-- Subquery in FROM (anonymous)
SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) AS total FROM accounts GROUP BY customer_id
) sub WHERE total > 50000;

-- CTE (named, reusable in same statement)
WITH customer_totals AS (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) AS total FROM accounts GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT * FROM customer_totals WHERE total > 50000;

Same logical result — CTE is named, readable, and can be referenced multiple times in one query.

CTE Classification

text
COMMON TABLE EXPRESSIONS (WITH)

├── Non-recursive CTE
│   ├── Single CTE
│   ├── Multiple CTEs (chained pipeline)
│   └── CTE referenced multiple times in main query
│
├── Recursive CTE
│   ├── Anchor member (base case)
│   ├── Recursive member (references CTE itself)
│   └── UNION ALL between them
│
├── By mutability (PostgreSQL)
│   ├── Read-only CTE (default)
│   └── Writable CTE (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE in WITH — advanced)
│
└── By optimization behavior
    ├── Inlined (merged into main query — no materialization)
    ├── Materialized (explicit or optimizer choice)
    └── Optimization fence (PostgreSQL ≤11 default for some cases)

CTE Anatomy

sql
WITH
  cte_name [(column1, column2, ...)] AS (
    -- CTE query body (SELECT, sometimes INSERT/UPDATE)
  ),
  second_cte AS ( ... )
SELECT ... FROM cte_name ... ;

Part 2 — History

Evolution of CTEs in SQL

text
1999    SQL:1999 standard introduces WITH clause (CTE)
        Recursive queries standardized for hierarchies

2005    SQL Server 2005 — full CTE support including recursive
        Oracle 9i Release 2 — WITH clause (non-recursive first)

2008    PostgreSQL 8.4 — WITH RECURSIVE
        DB2 — recursive CTE support

2010s   CTEs become standard for readable reporting SQL
        "Optimization fence" debate — PG materialized CTEs by default (≤11)

2016    PostgreSQL 9.1+ improved CTE inlining in some cases
        MySQL 8.0 — finally adds WITH clause (major gap closed)

2019    PostgreSQL 12 — NOT MATERIALIZED / MATERIALIZED hints
        Default: CTEs can be inlined (optimizer merges) unless marked MATERIALIZED

2020s   Recursive CTEs for org charts, bill of materials, graph traversal
        Writable CTEs for upsert pipelines (PostgreSQL)
        ORMs still weak on CTE — native SQL common in analytics

Historical Lesson

CTEs were invented for readability and recursion, not performance. PostgreSQL ≤11 always materialized CTEs — a surprise performance trap. Modern PostgreSQL inlines by default unless you force materialization. Always EXPLAIN — CTE is not free abstraction.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Do CTEs Solve?

Problem 1: Unreadable Nested Subqueries

sql
-- ❌ Lesson 17 — 4 levels deep
SELECT region, AVG(cust_total) FROM (
    SELECT c.region, c.customer_id, SUM(a.balance) AS cust_total
    FROM customers c JOIN accounts a ON ...
    GROUP BY c.region, c.customer_id
) x GROUP BY region;

-- ✅ CTE pipeline — each stage named
WITH per_customer AS (
    SELECT c.region, c.customer_id, SUM(a.balance) AS cust_total
    FROM customers c JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
    WHERE a.status = 'ACTIVE'
    GROUP BY c.region, c.customer_id
),
per_region AS (
    SELECT region, AVG(cust_total) AS avg_customer_balance
    FROM per_customer
    GROUP BY region
)
SELECT * FROM per_region WHERE avg_customer_balance > 10000;

Problem 2: Reuse Same Subquery Multiple Times

sql
-- Without CTE: duplicate subquery text or temp table
WITH high_value AS (
    SELECT customer_id FROM accounts
    GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(balance) > 100000
)
SELECT c.email FROM customers c JOIN high_value h ON ...
UNION
SELECT c.phone FROM customers c JOIN high_value h ON ...;
-- high_value defined once, used twice

Problem 3: Hierarchies (Recursive)

sql
-- Branch hierarchy: HQ → Region → Branch
-- Cannot express with simple JOIN — need recursion
WITH RECURSIVE branch_tree AS (
    SELECT branch_id, parent_branch_id, name, 1 AS depth
    FROM branches WHERE parent_branch_id IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT b.branch_id, b.parent_branch_id, b.name, bt.depth + 1
    FROM branches b
    JOIN branch_tree bt ON b.parent_branch_id = bt.branch_id
)
SELECT * FROM branch_tree;

Problem 4: Pagination with Stable Ranking

sql
-- Stage 1: rank accounts; Stage 2: filter page
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT account_id, balance,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY balance DESC) AS rn
    FROM accounts WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
)
SELECT account_id, balance FROM ranked WHERE rn BETWEEN 21 AND 40;
-- Window function detail in Lesson 19 — CTE stages the pipeline

Problem 5: Deduplication Before Join

sql
WITH latest_payment AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id) customer_id, amount, created_at
    FROM payments
    ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC
)
SELECT c.email, lp.amount
FROM customers c
JOIN latest_payment lp ON lp.customer_id = c.customer_id;

Unified Problem Statement

CTEs name intermediate query stages, eliminate duplicate subquery text, enable recursive graph traversal, and structure complex analytics pipelines — without necessarily creating permanent objects like views.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why WITH Instead of Views or Temp Tables?

vs Permanent View

CTEView
ScopeSingle statementPersistent schema object
Reuse across sessionsNoYes
PermissionsInherits querySeparate GRANT
Version controlIn application SQLDDL migration

Use CTE when logic is query-local; use view when many queries share same definition.

vs Temp Table

CTETemp Table
Explicit CREATENoYes
Statistics/indexNo (usually)Can CREATE INDEX
Cross-statementNoYes (session scope)
TransactionPart of one queryCOMMIT behavior varies

Use temp table when millions of rows need index for repeated access in same session.

vs Subquery

CTE wins on readability, multiple references, and recursive queries. Optimizer may treat them identically (inlined).

Readability as Engineering Value

text
Solution Architect perspective:
  Complex SQL in production = maintenance cost
  Named CTE stages = self-documenting pipeline
  Code review: "per_customer → per_region → filter" vs nested parens

Part 5 — Internal Working

How CTEs Execute Internally

Inlining (Default — PostgreSQL 12+, Modern Optimizers)

sql
WITH active AS (SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE status = 'ACTIVE')
SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) FROM active GROUP BY customer_id;
text
OPTIMIZER REWRITE (conceptual):

  WITH active AS (subquery)
  SELECT ... FROM active

  →  SELECT ... FROM (SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE status='ACTIVE') active
  →  Pulled up: SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) FROM accounts
               WHERE status='ACTIVE' GROUP BY customer_id

No separate materialization — single unified plan
CTE name disappears in execution — zero overhead if inlined

Materialization (Explicit or Forced)

sql
WITH active AS MATERIALIZED (
    SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
)
SELECT ... FROM active a1 JOIN active a2 ON ...;
text
EXECUTION:

  Step 1: Run CTE query → write all rows to tuplestore (memory or temp disk)
  Step 2: Main query reads from materialized result (like scanning temp table)

When used:
  - CTE referenced multiple times AND optimizer chooses materialize-once-read-twice
  - MATERIALIZED hint (PostgreSQL)
  - Old PostgreSQL (≤11): always materialized
  - Volatile functions in CTE — must materialize once

Multiple CTEs — Dependency Order

sql
WITH
  a AS (SELECT ...),
  b AS (SELECT ... FROM a),  -- depends on a
  c AS (SELECT ... FROM b)
SELECT * FROM c;
text
Execution order:
  1. Evaluate a (or inline entire chain)
  2. Evaluate b using a's result
  3. Evaluate c using b's result
  4. Main query

Optimizer may merge entire chain into one plan if no materialization fence

Recursive CTE Internals

sql
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
    SELECT ... FROM branches WHERE parent IS NULL     -- anchor
    UNION ALL
    SELECT ... FROM branches b JOIN tree t ON ...     -- recursive
)
SELECT * FROM tree;
text
WORKING ALGORITHM (iterative fixpoint):

  Iteration 0 (anchor):
    Execute anchor query → result set R0
    Insert into working table

  Iteration 1:
    Execute recursive member with working table = R0
    → new rows R1 (exclude duplicates per UNION ALL rules)
    Append to working table

  Iteration 2:
    Execute recursive member with new rows from R1 only (PostgreSQL optimization)
    → R2

  Stop when recursive member returns 0 rows
  Final: UNION ALL of all iterations

Index on join columns (parent_branch_id) critical for performance
Cycle detection: PostgreSQL — CYCLE clause (PG 14+)

Writable CTE (PostgreSQL)

sql
WITH moved AS (
    DELETE FROM payments_staging WHERE processed = true RETURNING *
)
INSERT INTO payments_archive SELECT * FROM moved;
text
Single statement — CTE side effects + main query
Execution order defined by CTE dependencies
Useful for atomic ETL in one round trip

Part 6 — Storage Internals

CTE and Storage

Inlined CTE — No Extra Storage

text
Same as subquery pull-up:
  Reads base tables directly
  No intermediate persistence
  Spills only if sort/hash in unified plan exceeds work_mem

Materialized CTE — Tuplestore

text
Storage path:
  Memory tuplestore (under work_mem)
  → spill to temp files if large

PostgreSQL: base/pgsql_tmp/
Oracle: TEMP tablespace (GLOBAL TEMPORARY TABLE analogy)
SQL Server: tempdb (when materialized as work table)

Size = full CTE result row count × row width
Repeated scan of materialized CTE = sequential read from tuplestore (fast in memory)

Recursive CTE Working Table

text
Each iteration appends rows to working table:
  Anchor: 1 row (HQ branch)
  Iter 1: 5 regional branches
  Iter 2: 50 city branches
  Iter 3: 500 leaf branches

Working table grows until fixpoint
Deep/wide hierarchies → large working table → memory + temp I/O

Cycle without guard → infinite loop until max recursion (database limit)

CTE vs Physical Temp Table

sql
CREATE TEMP TABLE tmp_active AS SELECT ... FROM accounts WHERE status='ACTIVE';
CREATE INDEX ON tmp_active(customer_id);
SELECT ... FROM tmp_active JOIN ...;

-- Temp table: persists for session, supports indexes, ANALYZE statistics
-- CTE: no index on materialized result (PostgreSQL) — full scan each reference

For very large intermediate sets accessed multiple times with joins, explicit temp table + index may beat materialized CTE.

Part 7 — Memory Usage

CTE Memory Impact

ScenarioMemory
Inlined single-use CTESame as equivalent subquery — no extra
MATERIALIZED CTE, 100K rowsTuplestore — work_mem then disk
CTE referenced 3×, materialized onceOne materialization — amortized reads
CTE referenced 3×, inlined 3×3× subquery execution — may be worse or better
Recursive CTE, depth 10, 10K nodesWorking table in memory/temp
Writable CTE + INSERTBuffer pool for target table + CTE tuplestore

PostgreSQL work_mem

text
Materialized CTE sort/hash:
  Same work_mem budget as regular query nodes
  Multiple materialized CTEs in one query — each may allocate work_mem
  SET work_mem too high × many connections = OOM risk

Recursive CTE Memory

text
PostgreSQL:
  recursive_worktable_factor (GUC) — tuning recursive execution
  max recursion depth limits (work_mem, statement timeout)

Wide org tree (100K employees):
  Consider closure table or ltree extension instead of runtime recursion

Part 8 — Execution Flow

CTE Execution Flows

Flow 1: Simple Inlined Pipeline

sql
WITH totals AS (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) AS total
    FROM accounts WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.email, t.total
FROM customers c
JOIN totals t ON t.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE t.total > 50000;
text
1. Parser: register CTE name "totals"
2. Optimizer: inline totals into main query
3. Plan: HashAggregate on accounts → Hash Join with customers
4. Filter total > 50000
5. Return rows

No CTE-specific execution step — unified plan

Flow 2: Materialized Multi-Reference

sql
WITH big AS MATERIALIZED (
    SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01'
)
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM big), (SELECT SUM(amount) FROM big);
text
1. Scan transactions (date filter) → materialize to tuplestore
2. Subquery 1: count rows in tuplestore
3. Subquery 2: sum amount from tuplestore

Single scan of base table — two scans of in-memory result
Better than scanning transactions twice if base table huge

Flow 3: Chained CTEs

sql
WITH
  step1 AS (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM accounts GROUP BY customer_id),
  step2 AS (SELECT customer_id FROM step1 WHERE cnt > 5),
  step3 AS (SELECT c.* FROM customers c JOIN step2 s ON s.customer_id = c.customer_id)
SELECT * FROM step3 WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';
text
Logical: step1 → step2 → step3 → main filter
Optimized: may flatten to one join + group + filter if inlined
Or: materialize each stage if fences exist

Flow 4: Recursive Branch Tree

sql
WITH RECURSIVE branch_tree AS (
    SELECT branch_id, name, 0 AS depth FROM branches WHERE branch_id = 1
    UNION ALL
    SELECT b.branch_id, b.name, bt.depth + 1
    FROM branches b JOIN branch_tree bt ON b.parent_branch_id = bt.branch_id
    WHERE bt.depth < 10
)
SELECT * FROM branch_tree;
text
1. Anchor: branch_id=1 → (1, 'HQ', 0)
2. Recurse: children of 1 → depth 1
3. Recurse: children of those → depth 2
4. ... until depth 10 or no children
5. Return full tree

Index: branches(parent_branch_id) — each iteration probes index

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

CTE Performance Rules

Performance Hierarchy

text
GENERALLY FAST:
  Single-use CTE inlined by optimizer
  Recursive CTE with indexed join columns, shallow depth
  MATERIALIZED CTE referenced many times on expensive base scan

WATCH OUT:
  MATERIALIZED CTE on huge result — memory/disk spill
  Recursive CTE on deep graph without cycle guard
  PostgreSQL ≤11 — all CTEs materialized (upgrade or hint)
  Assuming CTE = "cache" — it often isn't

SLOW:
  Recursive CTE replacing precomputed closure table at scale
  Multiple MATERIALIZED CTEs each scanning millions of rows
  CTE preventing predicate pushdown (optimization fence — rare modern PG)

When to Force MATERIALIZED

sql
-- Expensive CTE used twice — force single evaluation
WITH expensive AS MATERIALIZED (
    SELECT ... FROM transactions t
    JOIN accounts a ON ... JOIN customers c ON ...
    WHERE t.created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 year'
)
SELECT ... FROM expensive e1 JOIN expensive e2 ON ...;

When to Force NOT MATERIALIZED

sql
-- Small CTE — let optimizer merge for predicate pushdown
WITH recent AS NOT MATERIALIZED (
    SELECT * FROM payments WHERE created_at >= :since
)
SELECT * FROM recent WHERE customer_id = :id AND amount > 1000;
-- Outer filter on customer_id may push into payments scan

CTE vs View vs Temp Table

NeedChoice
One-off readable queryCTE
Shared across app queriesView
Session-long, indexed intermediateTemp table
Recursive hierarchy (moderate size)Recursive CTE
Hierarchy queried constantlyClosure table / ltree

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

PatternTime (typical)Space
Inlined single CTESame as subquery — O(scan)O(1) extra
Materialized CTE (n rows)O(build) + O(reads × scans)O(n)
k chained CTEs (inlined)O(unified plan)O(1)
k chained (each materialized)O(Σ build_i)O(Σ n_i)
Recursive, depth d, branching bO(rows visited) ≈ O(b^d) worstO(total nodes)
CTE referenced r times (materialized once)O(build) + r × O(n)O(n)
CTE referenced r times (inlined r times)r × O(subquery cost)O(1)

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

CTE Masterclass Examples

Basic Pipeline

sql
WITH
  active_accounts AS (
    SELECT account_id, customer_id, balance, account_type
    FROM accounts
    WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
  ),
  customer_exposure AS (
    SELECT customer_id,
           SUM(balance) AS total_balance,
           COUNT(*) AS account_count
    FROM active_accounts
    GROUP BY customer_id
  )
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email, c.region, ce.total_balance, ce.account_count
FROM customers c
JOIN customer_exposure ce ON ce.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE ce.total_balance > 100000
ORDER BY ce.total_balance DESC
LIMIT 100;

Multiple References

sql
WITH fraud_candidates AS (
    SELECT customer_id
    FROM transactions t
    JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = t.account_id
    WHERE t.created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7 days'
    GROUP BY customer_id
    HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN t.amount > 50000 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) >= 3
)
SELECT 'EMAIL' AS channel, c.email AS contact
FROM customers c JOIN fraud_candidates f ON f.customer_id = c.customer_id
UNION ALL
SELECT 'SMS', c.phone
FROM customers c JOIN fraud_candidates f ON f.customer_id = c.customer_id;

Recursive — Branch Hierarchy

sql
WITH RECURSIVE branch_hierarchy AS (
    -- Anchor: root branches (no parent)
    SELECT branch_id, parent_branch_id, name, name AS path, 1 AS level
    FROM branches
    WHERE parent_branch_id IS NULL

    UNION ALL

    -- Recursive: children
    SELECT b.branch_id, b.parent_branch_id, b.name,
           bh.path || ' > ' || b.name,
           bh.level + 1
    FROM branches b
    JOIN branch_hierarchy bh ON b.parent_branch_id = bh.branch_id
    WHERE bh.level < 20  -- depth guard
)
SELECT branch_id, name, path, level
FROM branch_hierarchy
ORDER BY path;

Recursive — Account Transfer Chain (Fraud)

sql
WITH RECURSIVE transfer_chain AS (
    SELECT t.transaction_id, t.from_account_id, t.to_account_id,
           t.amount, 1 AS hop, ARRAY[t.transaction_id] AS path
    FROM transactions t
    WHERE t.transaction_id = :seed_txn_id

    UNION ALL

    SELECT t.transaction_id, t.from_account_id, t.to_account_id,
           t.amount, tc.hop + 1, tc.path || t.transaction_id
    FROM transactions t
    JOIN transfer_chain tc ON t.from_account_id = tc.to_account_id
    WHERE tc.hop < 5
      AND NOT t.transaction_id = ANY(tc.path)  -- cycle guard
)
SELECT * FROM transfer_chain;

PostgreSQL Cycle Detection (14+)

sql
WITH RECURSIVE branch_tree AS (
    SELECT branch_id, parent_branch_id, name
    FROM branches WHERE branch_id = 1
    UNION ALL
    SELECT b.branch_id, b.parent_branch_id, b.name
    FROM branches b
    JOIN branch_tree bt ON b.parent_branch_id = bt.branch_id
) CYCLE branch_id SET is_cycle USING path
SELECT * FROM branch_tree WHERE NOT is_cycle;

Deduplication Pattern

sql
-- Latest payment per customer (PostgreSQL DISTINCT ON)
WITH latest_payment AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id)
           customer_id, payment_id, amount, status, created_at
    FROM payments
    ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC
)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email, lp.amount, lp.status
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN latest_payment lp ON lp.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.status = 'ACTIVE';

Oracle — CTE with Hints

sql
WITH customer_totals AS (
    SELECT /*+ MATERIALIZE */ customer_id, SUM(balance) AS total
    FROM accounts
    WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT * FROM customer_totals WHERE total > 50000;
-- Oracle MATERIALIZE hint forces CTE materialization

SQL Server — Recursive with MAXRECURSION

sql
WITH RECURSIVE_EMP AS (
    SELECT employee_id, manager_id, 1 AS level
    FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.employee_id, e.manager_id, r.level + 1
    FROM employees e
    JOIN RECURSIVE_EMP r ON e.manager_id = r.employee_id
)
SELECT * FROM RECURSIVE_EMP
OPTION (MAXRECURSION 100);

Writable CTE — Archive Pipeline (PostgreSQL)

sql
WITH deleted AS (
    DELETE FROM payments_staging
    WHERE status = 'PROCESSED'
      AND processed_at < CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'
    RETURNING payment_id, customer_id, amount, created_at
)
INSERT INTO payments_archive (payment_id, customer_id, amount, created_at)
SELECT payment_id, customer_id, amount, created_at FROM deleted;

Part 12 — Production Usage

CTEs in Production

Banking — Risk Dashboard Pipeline

sql
-- Read replica — multi-stage risk report
WITH
  daily_outflow AS (
    SELECT account_id, DATE(created_at) AS txn_date, SUM(amount) AS outflow
    FROM transactions
    WHERE direction = 'DEBIT'
      AND created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'
    GROUP BY account_id, DATE(created_at)
  ),
  spike_days AS (
    SELECT account_id, txn_date, outflow
    FROM daily_outflow d
    WHERE outflow > (
      SELECT AVG(outflow) * 3 FROM daily_outflow d2 WHERE d2.account_id = d.account_id
    )
  ),
  flagged_accounts AS (
    SELECT account_id, COUNT(*) AS spike_count
    FROM spike_days
    GROUP BY account_id
    HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
  )
SELECT a.account_id, c.email, fa.spike_count
FROM flagged_accounts fa
JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = fa.account_id
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = a.customer_id;

Logistics — Route Expansion (Recursive)

sql
WITH RECURSIVE route_stops AS (
    SELECT stop_id, next_stop_id, warehouse_id, 1 AS seq
    FROM route_segments WHERE warehouse_id = :origin
    UNION ALL
    SELECT rs.stop_id, s.next_stop_id, rs.warehouse_id, rs.seq + 1
    FROM route_stops rs
    JOIN route_segments s ON s.stop_id = rs.next_stop_id
    WHERE rs.seq < 50
)
SELECT * FROM route_stops;

E-Commerce — Cohort Retention Stages

sql
WITH
  cohort AS (
    SELECT customer_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(created_at)) AS cohort_month
    FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id
  ),
  activity AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', o.created_at) AS activity_month
    FROM orders o
  )
SELECT c.cohort_month, a.activity_month,
       COUNT(DISTINCT c.customer_id) AS customers
FROM cohort c
JOIN activity a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.cohort_month, a.activity_month
ORDER BY 1, 2;

When NOT to Use CTE in Production

text
❌ Hot OLTP path — 1ms SLA — keep SQL flat and indexed
❌ ORM-generated CRUD — CTE not portable in JPQL
❌ Billion-row recursive traversal — precompute hierarchy
✅ Analytics, reporting, batch jobs, read replicas
✅ Complex admin/fraud queries maintained as .sql files

Part 13 — Spring Boot Integration

CTEs in Spring Boot

Native Query with CTE

java
@Repository
public interface CustomerAnalyticsRepository extends JpaRepository<Customer, Long> {

    @Query(value = """
        WITH customer_totals AS (
            SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) AS total_balance
            FROM accounts
            WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
            GROUP BY customer_id
        )
        SELECT c.customer_id, c.email, ct.total_balance
        FROM customers c
        JOIN customer_totals ct ON ct.customer_id = c.customer_id
        WHERE ct.total_balance > :minBalance
        ORDER BY ct.total_balance DESC
        LIMIT :limit
        """, nativeQuery = true)
    List<Object[]> findHighValueCustomers(
        @Param("minBalance") BigDecimal minBalance,
        @Param("limit") int limit);
}

JdbcTemplate for Complex CTE Reports

java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class FraudReportService {

    private final JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate;

    private static final String FRAUD_PIPELINE = """
        WITH spike_accounts AS (
            SELECT account_id FROM transactions
            WHERE created_at >= ? AND amount > ?
            GROUP BY account_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= ?
        )
        SELECT a.account_id, c.email FROM spike_accounts sa
        JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = sa.account_id
        JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = a.customer_id
        """;

    public List<FraudAlertDto> generateReport(Instant since, BigDecimal threshold, int minCount) {
        return jdbcTemplate.query(
            FRAUD_PIPELINE,
            (rs, rowNum) -> new FraudAlertDto(
                rs.getLong("account_id"),
                rs.getString("email")),
            Timestamp.from(since),
            threshold,
            minCount);
    }
}

External SQL Files (Best Practice)

text
src/main/resources/sql/
  fraud-spike-report.sql
  branch-hierarchy.sql
  cohort-retention.sql

// Load with @Value or ResourceLoader — version CTE pipelines in Git
// Flyway/Liquibase for views; CTE for ad-hoc/reporting queries

JPQL Limitation

text
JPQL does NOT support WITH clause (JPA standard)
Options:
  1. nativeQuery = true
  2. @NamedNativeQuery
  3. Database view wrapping CTE logic (if reused heavily)
  4. jOOQ / MyBatis for complex SQL-first projects

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

CTE Architecture Decisions

CTE vs View vs Materialized View

text
Decision tree:

Same logic used in 10+ queries across services?
  YES → VIEW or MATERIALIZED VIEW (Flyway DDL)
  NO ↓

Logic specific to one report/query?
  YES → CTE in native SQL file
  NO ↓

Result must be precomputed for dashboard SLA?
  YES → MATERIALIZED VIEW + refresh job
  NO ↓

Recursive hierarchy queried on every request?
  YES → Closure table / path enumeration column / graph DB
  NO → Recursive CTE OK for admin/batch

Team Standards

text
Architect guidelines:

1. Name CTEs as pipeline stages: staged_payments → aggregated → filtered
2. Max 5 CTEs per query — beyond that, split or use view
3. All production CTEs in version-controlled .sql with EXPLAIN baseline
4. Document MATERIALIZED vs NOT MATERIALIZED choice in comment
5. No CTE in ORM entity load path — native reporting layer only
6. PostgreSQL version documented — CTE inlining behavior differs by version

Microservices

text
CTE spans tables in ONE database only
Cross-service analytics:
  → Data warehouse (Snowflake/BigQuery) with ETL
  → Local read replica fed by Kafka events
  → Not CTE across API boundaries

Read Replica Strategy

text
Heavy CTE pipelines → route to read replica
  @Transactional(readOnly = true) on reporting service
  Connection pool: reportingDataSource
Avoid CTE on primary during peak OLTP

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: CTE as Performance Silver Bullet

sql
-- ❌ Assumption: WITH = cached result
WITH big AS (SELECT * FROM transactions)  -- PG 12+ may inline — full scan anyway
SELECT * FROM big WHERE account_id = 5001;

-- ✅ Filter early in CTE or rely on pushdown
WITH big AS (
    SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE account_id = 5001
)
SELECT * FROM big;

Mistake 2: PostgreSQL 11 Production Surprise

text
Upgraded app, same SQL, slower reports?
  Old PG: CTE materialized (accidentally helped duplicate-scan cases)
  New PG: inlined (sometimes faster, sometimes not)
  Fix: EXPLAIN both; use MATERIALIZED where needed

Mistake 3: Recursive CTE Without Cycle Guard

sql
-- ❌ Circular parent_branch_id → infinite recursion until limit
WITH RECURSIVE t AS (
    SELECT branch_id, parent_branch_id FROM branches WHERE branch_id = 1
    UNION ALL
    SELECT b.branch_id, b.parent_branch_id
    FROM branches b JOIN t ON b.parent_branch_id = t.branch_id
)
-- ✅ Add path array, depth limit, or CYCLE clause
WHERE b.branch_id <> ALL(path_array) AND depth < 100

Mistake 4: UNION vs UNION ALL in Recursive

sql
-- ❌ UNION (dedup) in recursive — expensive dedup each iteration
-- ✅ UNION ALL + cycle detection — standard pattern

Mistake 5: JPQL WITH Attempt

java
// ❌ Invalid JPQL
@Query("WITH x AS (SELECT ...) SELECT ...")  // Parse error

// ✅ nativeQuery = true or database view

Mistake 6: Too Many CTE Stages Without Documentation

sql
-- ❌ a, b, c, d, e — opaque
-- ✅ named by business meaning: raw_txns → daily_agg → spike_filter → final

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is a CTE?

A named temporary result set defined with WITH, used in the following SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE.

Q2: CTE vs subquery in FROM?

Same idea; CTE is named, can be referenced multiple times, supports recursion.

Q3: Can you use multiple CTEs in one query?

Yes — comma-separated in WITH clause; later CTEs can reference earlier ones.

Q4: What is recursive CTE?

CTE that references itself — anchor member + recursive member joined with UNION ALL.

Q5: Does CTE create a permanent table?

No — statement-scoped unless written as view or temp table separately.

Mid-Level

Q6: PostgreSQL CTE materialization — PG 11 vs 12+?

PG ≤11 always materialized (optimization fence). PG 12+ inlines by default; MATERIALIZED/NOT MATERIALIZED hints available.

Q7: When force MATERIALIZED?

Expensive CTE referenced multiple times — evaluate once, read many from tuplestore.

Q8: Recursive CTE execution model?

Iterative fixpoint: anchor result, then recursive member runs on new rows until empty.

Q9: CTE vs view?

CTE: query-local, no DDL. View: persistent, shared, permissions, used across sessions.

Q9: UNION vs UNION ALL in recursive CTE?

UNION ALL standard — UNION deduplicates each iteration (costly). Use cycle guards instead.

Senior

Q10: Recursive CTE for org chart — when to stop using it?

Deep/wide trees, frequent queries, SLA pressure → closure table, path column, ltree, or graph DB.

Q11: CTE preventing predicate pushdown?

Was issue on old PG (materialization fence). Modern PG inlines — verify with EXPLAIN. Use NOT MATERIALIZED if needed.

Q12: Writable CTE use case?

Atomic DELETE...RETURNING + INSERT in one statement — staging cleanup pipelines.

Q13: How to use CTE with Spring Data JPA?

Native query only — JPQL has no WITH. Or wrap in database view.

Staff / Architect

Q14: Reporting architecture — CTE in app vs warehouse?

App DB: moderate CTE on read replica for operational reports. Heavy analytics → ETL to warehouse; don't run 10-CTE pipelines on OLTP primary.

Q15: MySQL 5.7 → 8.0 migration and CTEs?

5.7 had no WITH — subqueries only. Migration enables CTE syntax; verify MySQL 8 recursive optimizer limits vs PostgreSQL.

Scenario

Scenario: "Report query slow after PostgreSQL upgrade 11 → 15."

CTE inlining changed plan shape. EXPLAIN ANALYZE before/after. If CTE was accidentally helping (materialized once, used twice), add AS MATERIALIZED. If inlining helps pushdown, keep default. Update SQL comments documenting choice.

Part 20 — Revision Sheet

Syntax

sql
WITH name AS (SELECT ...)           -- single
WITH a AS (...), b AS (...)         -- chain
WITH RECURSIVE r AS (anchor UNION ALL recursive)  -- tree/graph
WITH x AS MATERIALIZED (...)      -- PG 12+ force materialize
WITH x AS NOT MATERIALIZED (...)  -- PG 12+ force inline

Rules

text
✅ Name stages by business meaning
✅ EXPLAIN after PG version change
✅ Cycle guard + depth limit on recursive
✅ Native SQL in Spring for CTE reports
✅ Read replica for heavy pipelines
❌ Assume CTE = cache
❌ Recursive CTE at billion-row scale
❌ JPQL WITH clause
❌ UNION (dedup) in recursive member

vs Alternatives

text
One query readability     → CTE
Many queries reuse        → VIEW
Precomputed dashboard     → MATERIALIZED VIEW
Session + index           → TEMP TABLE
Hierarchy OLTP              → Closure table

Lesson 19

Window Functions

Phase 2: SQL MASTERCLASS | Previous: CTE (Common Table Expressions) | Next: Views

SQL
1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why This Exists5Internal Working6Storage Internals7Memory Usage8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Complexity Analysis11Code / SQL Examples12Production Usage13Spring Boot Integration14Hibernate/JPA Integration15Architect Perspective16Decision Matrix17Comparison Tables18Common Mistakes19Interview Questions20Revision Sheet21Summary Table*Practice

Part 1 — Concept

What Is a Window Function?

A window function computes a value for each row using a window of related rows — without collapsing the result set like GROUP BY. Rows stay intact; a new computed column is added.

sql
SELECT
    account_id,
    customer_id,
    balance,
    SUM(balance) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS customer_total_balance,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY balance DESC) AS balance_rank
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';

Window Function vs Aggregate

text
GROUP BY (Lesson 14):
  Input:  10 account rows for customer 1001
  Output: 1 row — SUM(balance) = 85000
  Detail rows LOST

Window function:
  Input:  10 account rows for customer 1001
  Output: 10 rows — each row keeps account_id, balance
           + customer_total_balance = 85000 on EVERY row
  Detail rows PRESERVED

Anatomy of Window Function

sql
function_name(args) OVER (
    [ PARTITION BY partition_columns ]   -- groups rows into windows (like GROUP BY groups)
    [ ORDER BY sort_columns ]           -- orders rows within each window
    [ frame_clause ]                    -- which rows in window contribute (ROWS/RANGE/GROUPS)
)

Window Function Categories

text
WINDOW FUNCTIONS

├── Ranking
│   ├── ROW_NUMBER()     → unique rank 1,2,3... (no ties)
│   ├── RANK()             → ties share rank, gaps after (1,2,2,4)
│   ├── DENSE_RANK()       → ties share rank, no gaps (1,2,2,3)
│   └── NTILE(n)           → divide into n buckets
│
├── Offset (navigation)
│   ├── LAG(col, n)        → previous row value
│   ├── LEAD(col, n)       → next row value
│   ├── FIRST_VALUE(col)   → first row in frame
│   └── LAST_VALUE(col)    → last row in frame (needs explicit frame)
│
├── Aggregate as window
│   ├── SUM(), AVG(), COUNT(), MIN(), MAX()
│   └── Running totals, moving averages
│
├── Statistical (PostgreSQL, SQL Server)
│   ├── PERCENT_RANK(), CUME_DIST()
│   └── STDDEV(), VARIANCE()
│
└── Named WINDOW clause
    WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)
    → reuse same window definition

ASCII — Window Concept

text
All rows (no PARTITION BY):
┌─────┬─────────┬──────────────────────────────┐
│ row │ balance │ SUM(balance) OVER ()         │
├─────┼─────────┼──────────────────────────────┤
│  1  │  1000   │ 6000  ← sum of ALL rows      │
│  2  │  2000   │ 6000                         │
│  3  │  3000   │ 6000                         │
└─────┴─────────┴──────────────────────────────┘

PARTITION BY customer_id:
Customer 1001 window          Customer 1002 window
┌─────┬─────────┬──────────┐  ┌─────┬─────────┬──────────┐
│ acct│ balance │ SUM OVER │  │ acct│ balance │ SUM OVER │
├─────┼─────────┼──────────┤  ├─────┼─────────┼──────────┤
│ 501 │  5000   │  15000   │  │ 601 │  8000   │  12000   │
│ 502 │ 10000   │  15000   │  │ 602 │  4000   │  12000   │
└─────┴─────────┴──────────┘  └─────┴─────────┴──────────┘
     ↑ same partition total         ↑ separate window

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Window Functions

text
1990s   Vendor extensions:
        Oracle ANALYTIC functions (RANK, LAG, LEAD)
        SQL Server ranking functions

2003    SQL:2003 standard — OVER clause formalized
        PARTITION BY, ORDER BY, frame clause

2008    PostgreSQL 8.4 — window functions added
        DB2, Oracle full standard support

2010s   Window functions replace correlated subqueries for top-N-per-group
        Running totals in reporting without self-joins

2014    PostgreSQL 9.4 — ordered-set aggregates (PERCENTILE_CONT as aggregate)
        MySQL still missing window functions

2018    MySQL 8.0 — window functions finally available
        Major portability milestone

2020s   Standard pattern: ROW_NUMBER for dedup, LAG for sessionization
        Stream processing (Flink, Kafka) mirrors window semantics
        ORMs lag — native SQL / jOOQ for window-heavy analytics

Historical Lesson

Before window functions, top-N per group required correlated subqueries or self-joins — O(n²) nightmares. ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...) is one of the highest-ROI SQL patterns for architects and senior developers.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Do Window Functions Solve?

Problem 1: Top-N Per Group (Classic)

sql
-- Latest account balance per customer — keep ONE row per customer (highest balance acct)
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT account_id, customer_id, balance,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY customer_id
               ORDER BY balance DESC, account_id
           ) AS rn
    FROM accounts
    WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
)
SELECT account_id, customer_id, balance
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1;
-- Replaces correlated subquery from Lessons 17–18

Problem 2: Running Total (Cumulative Sum)

sql
-- Running balance of transactions per account
SELECT
    transaction_id,
    account_id,
    amount,
    created_at,
    SUM(amount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id
        ORDER BY created_at, transaction_id
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS running_balance
FROM transactions
WHERE account_id = 5001
ORDER BY created_at;

Problem 3: Compare Row to Previous/Next (LAG/LEAD)

sql
-- Detect balance drops > 50% from previous day snapshot
SELECT
    snapshot_date,
    account_id,
    balance,
    LAG(balance) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY snapshot_date) AS prev_balance,
    balance - LAG(balance) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY snapshot_date) AS delta
FROM account_daily_snapshots
WHERE account_id = 5001;

Problem 4: Percent of Total

sql
-- Each payment as % of customer's total payments
SELECT
    payment_id,
    customer_id,
    amount,
    amount * 100.0 / SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS pct_of_customer_total
FROM payments
WHERE status = 'COMPLETED';

Problem 5: Dedup — Keep Latest Row

sql
-- Latest payment status per customer (dedup duplicate events)
DELETE FROM payments_staging p
WHERE payment_id IN (
    SELECT payment_id FROM (
        SELECT payment_id,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
                   PARTITION BY client_request_id
                   ORDER BY created_at DESC
               ) AS rn
        FROM payments_staging
    ) x WHERE rn > 1
);
-- Or use in SELECT for idempotent ingest views

Unified Problem Statement

Window functions answer row-level questions that depend on neighboring rows or group context — ranking, running totals, deltas, percent-of-total, deduplication — while preserving every detail row.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Not GROUP BY or Self-Join?

GROUP BY Loses Detail

sql
-- GROUP BY: how many accounts per customer — OK
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) FROM accounts GROUP BY customer_id;

-- Window: each account row + customer's account count — detail preserved
SELECT account_id, customer_id,
       COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS accounts_for_customer
FROM accounts;

Self-Join Is Fragile and Slow

sql
-- ❌ Top balance account per customer via self-join
SELECT a.*
FROM accounts a
JOIN (
    SELECT customer_id, MAX(balance) AS max_bal
    FROM accounts GROUP BY customer_id
) m ON a.customer_id = m.customer_id AND a.balance = m.max_bal;
-- Tie problem: two accounts same max balance → duplicate rows

-- ✅ ROW_NUMBER — exactly one row per customer (with tie-breaker)
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY balance DESC, account_id)

Correlated Subquery vs Window

sql
-- ❌ Lesson 17 — correlated COUNT per row
SELECT c.customer_id,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id)
FROM customers c;

-- ✅ Window or JOIN+GROUP BY
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) ...
-- Or GROUP BY if only one row per customer needed

Stream and Event Semantics

text
LAG/LEAD model event streams:
  Session boundaries (gap > 30 min → new session)
  Fraud: amount > 3× LAG(amount)
  Same pattern in Flink SQL OVER windows — conceptual alignment for architects

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Window Functions Execute Internally

Execution Model — Sort and Scan

text
General algorithm:

1. PARTITION BY → split rows into independent windows
2. ORDER BY     → sort rows within each window (often external sort)
3. Frame         → for each row, determine contributing rows in window
4. Compute       → apply function over frame rows
5. Emit          → attach result to current row

Plan nodes (PostgreSQL):
  WindowAgg
    → Sort (if not index-ordered)
    → WindowAgg on sorted input

ROW_NUMBER Internals

text
PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY balance DESC

For each partition:
  Sort rows by balance DESC
  Assign 1, 2, 3... sequentially — no tie logic

Cost: O(n log n) per partition for sort
If index matches (customer_id, balance DESC) → skip sort (Index Scan + WindowAgg)

RANK vs DENSE_RANK Internals

text
Values: 100, 200, 200, 300

ROW_NUMBER:   1, 2, 3, 4
RANK:         1, 2, 2, 4  (gap after tie)
DENSE_RANK:   1, 2, 2, 3  (no gap)

Implementation: single sorted pass, track previous value for tie detection

Frame Clause — ROWS vs RANGE

sql
SUM(amount) OVER (
    PARTITION BY account_id
    ORDER BY created_at
    ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
)  -- exactly 4 physical rows (moving window)

SUM(amount) OVER (
    PARTITION BY account_id
    ORDER BY created_at
    RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '7 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
)  -- all rows with created_at in 7-day range (peer rows may differ count)
text
ROWS  → physical row offset — predictable count
RANGE → logical value range — peers (same ORDER BY value) included
GROUPS → PostgreSQL 11+ — groups of peer rows

Default frame (with ORDER BY):
  RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
  → running aggregate from start of partition to current row

Default frame (no ORDER BY):
  entire partition — all rows in window

LAG/LEAD Internals

text
LAG(balance, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY snapshot_date)

After sort within partition:
  Row i gets value from row i-1
  Row 0 gets NULL (or default)

O(1) per row after sort — no self-join
Single pass over sorted partition

Multiple Window Functions — One Sort?

sql
SELECT
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY balance DESC),
    SUM(balance) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id),
    RANK() OVER (ORDER BY balance DESC)
FROM accounts;
text
Optimizer may:
  - Use one WindowAgg with multiple functions if same PARTITION/ORDER
  - Or multiple WindowAgg nodes if different sort keys — expensive

Tip: named WINDOW clause helps optimizer recognize identical windows
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY balance DESC)

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Window Functions and Storage

Sort Spill

text
Window functions require ordered input per partition:
  Sort fits in work_mem → quicksort in memory
  Sort exceeds work_mem → external merge sort → temp files

Same temp storage as ORDER BY / GROUP BY hash spill
pgsql_tmp / tempdb

Large partition (1M transactions for one account):
  Sort 1M rows for running total — heavy
  Index on (account_id, created_at) → index scan in order → avoid sort

Index-Only Window Path

sql
-- Index: accounts(customer_id, balance DESC)
SELECT account_id, balance,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY balance DESC) AS rn
FROM accounts WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';

Plan may show:
  Index Scan using idx_accounts_cust_bal
  WindowAgg — no Sort node ✅

No Persistent Storage

text
Window results computed at query time — not stored
Unlike materialized view — each query recomputes

Exception: you persist into table via INSERT...SELECT with window fn

LAST_VALUE Gotcha

sql
-- Default frame ends at CURRENT ROW — LAST_VALUE = current row!
SELECT LAST_VALUE(balance) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at)
-- Usually wrong for "last in partition"

-- Fix: explicit frame
LAST_VALUE(balance) OVER (
    PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
)

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Window Function Memory

ComponentMemory
Sort bufferwork_mem per sort node
WindowAgg stateO(1) per partition for ROW_NUMBER/LAG
Running SUM frameO(1) for default cumulative frame
Moving avg ROWS 100 PRECEDINGO(100) frame buffer
Multiple partitionsSort may process all rows — one big sort or partitioned sort
RANGE frameMay need peer group tracking — more than ROWS

work_mem Tuning

text
Many concurrent window queries on reporting replica:
  Each WindowAgg + Sort allocates work_mem
  50 connections × 256MB work_mem = disaster

Reporting role: moderate work_mem + statement_timeout
Batch reports: increase work_mem for session only
SET LOCAL work_mem = '512MB';  -- transaction scope

Parallel Window Execution

text
PostgreSQL 9.6+ parallel query:
  Partial WindowAgg on workers
  Gather → Finalize WindowAgg

Large table scan + window — may parallelize scan, finalize window on leader
Not all window functions parallelize equally — check EXPLAIN

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Window Function Execution Flows

Flow 1: ROW_NUMBER Top-1 Per Group

sql
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT payment_id, customer_id, amount, created_at,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY customer_id
               ORDER BY created_at DESC
           ) AS rn
    FROM payments
)
SELECT payment_id, customer_id, amount, created_at
FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;
text
1. Seq/Index Scan payments
2. Sort by (customer_id, created_at DESC) — or use index
3. WindowAgg ROW_NUMBER — assign rn within each customer_id
4. Filter rn = 1
5. Return latest payment per customer

Often wrapped in CTE (Lesson 18) — filter in outer query

Flow 2: Running Total

sql
SELECT transaction_id, amount, created_at,
       SUM(amount) OVER (
           PARTITION BY account_id
           ORDER BY created_at, transaction_id
       ) AS running_total
FROM transactions
WHERE account_id = 5001;
text
1. Filter account_id = 5001
2. Sort by created_at, transaction_id
3. WindowAgg SUM — cumulative from first row to current
4. Emit each row with running_total

Flow 3: LAG for Delta Detection

sql
SELECT transaction_id, amount,
       LAG(amount, 1, 0) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY created_at) AS prev_amount,
       amount - LAG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY created_at) AS change
FROM transactions;
text
1. Sort per account_id by created_at
2. For each row: read previous row's amount from sorted buffer
3. Compute delta
4. First row per partition: LAG returns NULL (or default 0)

Flow 4: Percent of Partition

sql
SELECT payment_id, amount,
       amount / SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS share
FROM payments;
text
1. Two window computations possible:
   - SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) — no ORDER BY → whole partition
   - Division per row
2. Or single pass WindowAgg with multiple functions

Flow 5: NTILE for Quartiles

sql
SELECT customer_id, total_balance,
       NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY total_balance DESC) AS wealth_quartile
FROM (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) AS total_balance
    FROM accounts GROUP BY customer_id
) sub;
-- Quartile 1 = top 25% by balance — marketing segments

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Window Function Performance Rules

Performance Hierarchy

text
FAST:
  ROW_NUMBER / RANK with index matching PARTITION BY + ORDER BY
  LAG/LEAD after index-ordered scan
  SUM/AVG with small partition sizes

SLOW:
  Window over full table scan + huge sort spill
  Multiple WindowAgg with different sort orders
  ROW_NUMBER on billions of rows then filter rn=1 (consider DISTINCT ON or lateral)
  RANGE frame on high-cardinality ORDER BY column

Top-N Per Group — Pattern Comparison

PatternWhen Best
ROW_NUMBER ... WHERE rn=1General, tie-break control
DISTINCT ON (PostgreSQL)Top-1 per group, index-friendly
LATERAL JOIN + LIMIT 1Top-N small N, good index
Correlated subqueryAvoid — legacy
GROUP BY + MAX + joinTie issues
sql
-- PostgreSQL DISTINCT ON — often fastest for top-1
SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id)
       customer_id, payment_id, amount, created_at
FROM payments
ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC;
-- Requires sort matching ORDER BY — index (customer_id, created_at DESC)

Filter Placement

sql
-- ❌ Window over all rows then filter
SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) rn
    FROM payments  -- 100M rows
) x WHERE rn = 1 AND created_at >= '2024-01-01';

-- ✅ Filter first when business rules allow
SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) rn
    FROM payments WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01'
) x WHERE rn = 1;
-- Window still per customer — but fewer input rows

Index Recommendations

sql
-- Pattern: PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_cust_created
    ON payments (customer_id, created_at DESC);

-- Pattern: PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY created_at
CREATE INDEX idx_txn_acct_created
    ON transactions (account_id, created_at, transaction_id);

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

OperationTimeSpace
Window over n rows, k partitionsO(n log n) sort dominantO(n) sort buffer
ROW_NUMBER / RANK after sortO(n) single passO(1) extra
LAG/LEAD after sortO(n)O(1)
Running SUM default frameO(n)O(1)
Moving ROWS k PRECEDINGO(n × k) naive; O(n) with ring bufferO(k)
Top-1 via ROW_NUMBERO(n log n) + filter O(n)Same as window
vs Self-join top-NO(n × m) worstHigher

n = total rows, k = partition count, frame size w = O(n) for ROWS w PRECEDING

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Window Function Masterclass

Ranking — Top 3 Accounts Per Customer

sql
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT
        account_id,
        customer_id,
        balance,
        account_type,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY customer_id
            ORDER BY balance DESC, account_id
        ) AS rn,
        RANK() OVER (
            PARTITION BY customer_id
            ORDER BY balance DESC
        ) AS rnk,
        DENSE_RANK() OVER (
            PARTITION BY customer_id
            ORDER BY balance DESC
        ) AS dense_rnk
    FROM accounts
    WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
)
SELECT account_id, customer_id, balance, rn, rnk, dense_rnk
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 3;

Running and Moving Aggregates

sql
SELECT
    transaction_id,
    account_id,
    created_at,
    amount,
    -- Cumulative sum
    SUM(amount) OVER w AS running_total,
    -- 7-row moving average
    AVG(amount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id
        ORDER BY created_at
        ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS moving_avg_7,
    -- Month-to-date (RANGE)
    SUM(amount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id
        ORDER BY created_at
        RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '1 month' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS mtd_sum
FROM transactions
WINDOW w AS (
    PARTITION BY account_id
    ORDER BY created_at, transaction_id
    ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
);

LAG / LEAD — Payment Gaps

sql
SELECT
    customer_id,
    payment_id,
    created_at,
    amount,
    LAG(created_at) OVER (
        PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at
    ) AS prev_payment_at,
    created_at - LAG(created_at) OVER (
        PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at
    ) AS days_since_last,
    LEAD(amount, 1) OVER (
        PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at
    ) AS next_amount
FROM payments
WHERE status = 'COMPLETED';

FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE — Benchmark Row

sql
SELECT
    transaction_id,
    account_id,
    amount,
    created_at,
    FIRST_VALUE(amount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY created_at
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
    ) AS first_txn_amount,
    LAST_VALUE(amount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY created_at
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
    ) AS last_txn_amount
FROM transactions;

Percent Rank — Customer Balance Standing

sql
SELECT
    customer_id,
    total_balance,
    PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total_balance) AS pct_rank,
    CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY total_balance) AS cumulative_dist
FROM (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(balance) AS total_balance
    FROM accounts WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
    GROUP BY customer_id
) t;
-- pct_rank: 0 to 1 — relative standing in customer base

Dedup Idempotent Ingest

sql
-- Keep earliest row per client_request_id
WITH deduped AS (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY client_request_id
               ORDER BY created_at ASC, payment_id ASC
           ) AS rn
    FROM payments_staging
)
INSERT INTO payments (payment_id, client_request_id, amount, ...)
SELECT payment_id, client_request_id, amount, ...
FROM deduped WHERE rn = 1
ON CONFLICT (client_request_id) DO NOTHING;

Sessionization (Gap and Islands)

sql
-- New session if gap > 30 minutes between transactions
WITH ordered AS (
    SELECT
        account_id,
        transaction_id,
        created_at,
        LAG(created_at) OVER (
            PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY created_at
        ) AS prev_at
    FROM transactions
),
flagged AS (
    SELECT *,
           CASE
               WHEN prev_at IS NULL
                    OR created_at - prev_at > INTERVAL '30 minutes'
               THEN 1 ELSE 0
           END AS new_session
    FROM ordered
),
sessionized AS (
    SELECT *,
           SUM(new_session) OVER (
               PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY created_at
               ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
           ) AS session_id
    FROM flagged
)
SELECT account_id, session_id, COUNT(*) AS txns_in_session,
       SUM(amount) AS session_total
FROM sessionized s
JOIN transactions t USING (transaction_id)
GROUP BY account_id, session_id;

Named WINDOW Reuse

sql
SELECT
    account_id,
    balance,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER w AS rn,
    RANK() OVER w AS rk,
    balance - AVG(balance) OVER w AS diff_from_avg
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY balance DESC);

Part 12 — Production Usage

Window Functions in Production

Banking — Daily Limit Monitoring

sql
-- Cumulative outbound transfer amount per account today
SELECT
    account_id,
    transaction_id,
    amount,
    created_at,
    SUM(amount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id, DATE(created_at)
        ORDER BY created_at
        ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
    ) AS daily_outbound_running
FROM transactions
WHERE direction = 'DEBIT'
  AND created_at >= CURRENT_DATE
HAVING SUM(amount) OVER (
    PARTITION BY account_id, DATE(created_at)
    ORDER BY created_at ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
) > 100000;  -- Note: filter in outer query in practice
sql
-- Better: wrap in CTE then filter
WITH running AS (
    SELECT *, SUM(amount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id, DATE(created_at)
        ORDER BY created_at ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING
    ) AS daily_running
    FROM transactions
    WHERE direction = 'DEBIT' AND created_at >= CURRENT_DATE
)
SELECT * FROM running WHERE daily_running > 100000;

Payments — Reconciliation Ranking

sql
-- Match each bank statement line to best candidate payment
WITH candidates AS (
    SELECT
        bs.line_id,
        p.payment_id,
        ABS(bs.amount - p.amount) AS amount_diff,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY bs.line_id
            ORDER BY ABS(bs.amount - p.amount), p.created_at
        ) AS match_rank
    FROM bank_statement_lines bs
    JOIN payments p ON p.customer_id = bs.customer_id
        AND p.created_at BETWEEN bs.txn_date - INTERVAL '1 day'
                              AND bs.txn_date + INTERVAL '1 day'
)
SELECT line_id, payment_id, amount_diff
FROM candidates WHERE match_rank = 1;

Healthcare — Patient Visit Sequence

sql
SELECT
    patient_id,
    visit_date,
    visit_type,
    LAG(visit_type) OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_date) AS prev_visit,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY visit_date) AS visit_number
FROM patient_visits;

E-Commerce — Cohort Month Index

sql
SELECT
    customer_id,
    order_month,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_month) AS month_index,
    -- month_index = 1 → first order month, 2 → second active month
    COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id, order_month) AS orders_in_month
FROM (
    SELECT customer_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', created_at) AS order_month
    FROM orders
) t;

java
@Query(value = """

JdbcTemplate — Running Balance Report

java
private static final String RUNNING_BALANCE = """
    SELECT transaction_id, amount, created_at,
           SUM(amount) OVER (
               PARTITION BY account_id
               ORDER BY created_at, transaction_id
               ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
           ) AS running_balance
    FROM transactions
    WHERE account_id = ?
    ORDER BY created_at
    """;

public List<TransactionBalanceDto> getRunningBalance(Long accountId) {
    return jdbcTemplate.query(RUNNING_BALANCE,
        (rs, n) -> new TransactionBalanceDto(
            rs.getLong("transaction_id"),
            rs.getBigDecimal("amount"),
            rs.getTimestamp("created_at").toInstant(),
            rs.getBigDecimal("running_balance")),
        accountId);
}

dsl.select(PAYMENTS.fields())

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

ORM and Window Functions

JPQL Has No OVER Clause

text
JPA/JPQL standard: no window functions
Hibernate HQL: no native OVER support

Solutions:
  1. @Query nativeQuery = true
  2. @NamedNativeQuery + SqlResultSetMapping
  3. Database view encapsulating window logic
  4. jOOQ / MyBatis for analytics layer
  5. Compute in application (avoid for large datasets)

View Encapsulation Pattern

sql
-- Flyway migration V42__latest_payment_view.sql
CREATE VIEW v_latest_payment AS
SELECT payment_id, customer_id, amount, created_at
FROM (
    SELECT *,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC
           ) AS rn
    FROM payments WHERE status = 'COMPLETED'
) t WHERE rn = 1;
java
@Entity
@Immutable
@Subselect("SELECT * FROM v_latest_payment")
public class LatestPaymentView {
    @Id
    private Long paymentId;
    private Long customerId;
    private BigDecimal amount;
    // read-only entity for reports
}

java
// ❌ Load all payments for all customers — OOM
List<Payment> all = paymentRepo.findAll();
Map<Long, Payment> latest = all.stream()
    .collect(groupingBy(Payment::getCustomerId,
        collectingAndThen(maxBy(comparing(Payment::getCreatedAt)), opt -> opt.orElseThrow())));

// ✅ SQL window or DISTINCT ON in database

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

Window Function Architecture

Analytics Layer Separation

text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  OLTP Service (Spring Boot + JPA)                       │
│  Simple CRUD, EXISTS, JOIN — no window functions        │
└──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                           │ events / CDC
┌──────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐
│  Reporting DB / Read Replica                            │
│  Native SQL: window functions, CTEs, views              │
│  Flyway views: v_latest_*, v_running_*                  │
└──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                           │ ETL
┌──────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐
│  Warehouse (Snowflake/BigQuery)                         │
│  Window functions at scale — pre-aggregated marts       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

When to Push to DB vs Stream Processor

Use CaseDB WindowFlink/Kafka Streams
Batch nightly report✅Overkill
Real-time fraud (ms SLA)❌✅
Account running daily limit✅ with careful indexing✅ for high throughput
Historical analytics✅ read replica✅ for very large scale

Standard View Library

text
Architect deliverable — catalog of window-based views:

v_customer_latest_payment     ROW_NUMBER dedup
v_account_running_balance     cumulative SUM (snapshot table better for OLTP)
v_customer_wealth_quartile    NTILE on aggregated balance
v_payment_sequence            LAG days_since_last

Version in Flyway; document refresh semantics (view = live query)
For heavy dashboards → materialized view + REFRESH

Top-N Per Group at Scale

text
< 1M rows: ROW_NUMBER in SQL — fine
> 10M rows, frequent: consider precomputed "latest" table maintained by trigger/event
Microservice: "latest" as cached field updated on write — CQRS read model

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Forgetting ORDER BY in ROW_NUMBER

sql
-- ❌ Non-deterministic ranking — random rn each run
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)

-- ✅ Deterministic tie-break
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id)

Mistake 2: RANK When You Need Exactly One Row

sql
-- ❌ RANK = 1 can return MULTIPLE rows (ties)
WHERE RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY balance DESC) = 1

-- ✅ ROW_NUMBER for exactly one

Mistake 3: LAST_VALUE Without Frame

sql
-- ❌ LAST_VALUE returns current row with default frame
-- ✅ ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING

Mistake 4: Window in WHERE (Invalid SQL)

sql
-- ❌ WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) = 1  -- syntax error

-- ✅ Subquery / CTE / QUALIFY (Oracle/Snowflake)
SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) rn FROM payments
) t WHERE rn = 1;

Mistake 5: Mixing Global and Partitioned Windows Incorrectly

sql
-- SUM without PARTITION — whole table total on every row
-- SUM with PARTITION — per-group total on each row in group
-- Know which you intend

Mistake 6: RANGE vs ROWS Confusion

sql
-- RANGE with TIMESTAMP — peers within range included — may double-count logical duplicates
-- Moving 7-row avg: use ROWS not RANGE

Mistake 7: N+1 in App Instead of Window

java
// ❌ Fetch latest payment per customer in loop
// ✅ One query with ROW_NUMBER or view

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is a window function?

Computes per-row values over a window of rows defined by PARTITION BY, ORDER BY, and frame — without collapsing groups like GROUP BY.

Q2: Difference between ROW_NUMBER and RANK?

ROW_NUMBER: unique 1,2,3. RANK: ties get same rank, gaps after (1,2,2,4).

Q3: What does PARTITION BY do?

Divides rows into independent windows — like GROUP BY groups but rows stay separate.

Q4: Can you use window functions in WHERE?

No — wrap in subquery/CTE or use QUALIFY where supported.

Q5: LAG vs LEAD?

LAG: previous row's value. LEAD: next row's value. Requires ORDER BY.

Mid-Level

Q6: Top-3 per customer — write the pattern.

ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ...), filter rn <= 3 in outer query.

Q7: Running total SQL?

SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY created_at ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).

Q8: Default window frame with ORDER BY?

RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW — cumulative through peers.

Q9: ROW_NUMBER vs DISTINCT ON (PostgreSQL)?

Both top-1 per group; DISTINCT ON often cleaner; ROW_NUMBER more portable.

Q10: Why is LAST_VALUE tricky?

Default frame ends at current row — need explicit UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING frame.

Senior

Q11: Window function execution plan — what to look for?

WindowAgg node; Sort before it; check if index eliminates sort; work_mem spills.

Q12: Gap and islands problem — approach?

LAG to detect gap → flag new group → SUM flags as session_id → GROUP BY session.

Q13: Window vs GROUP BY + JOIN back?

Window: one pass, no join inflation. GROUP BY + join: two steps, also valid.

Q14: MySQL 5.7 vs 8.0 migration impact?

5.7: no windows — used user variables (fragile). 8.0: proper OVER — rewrite.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Real-time daily limit — DB window or stream processor?

High-volume payment rail: stream state store or Redis counter. Moderate volume: indexed running SUM on replica with CTE filter. OLTP primary: avoid heavy window.

Q16: How to expose window logic to JPA services?

Database views + read-only entities, or dedicated reporting service with native SQL — not JPQL.

Scenario

Scenario: "Query with ROW_NUMBER slow on 50M payments table."

Check index (customer_id, created_at DESC). Consider DISTINCT ON. Filter date range before window. Partial index on recent data. Precompute latest_payment table via CDC. EXPLAIN ANALYZE for sort spill — tune work_mem for batch job.

Core Syntax

sql
func() OVER (PARTITION BY cols ORDER BY cols [frame])
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)

Key Functions

text
ROW_NUMBER  → unique rank, top-N, dedup

Frames

Rules

text

✅ Index matches PARTITION + ORDER BY

❌ LAST_VALUE without full frame
❌ Load-all rank in Java

Part 1 — Concept

What Is a View?

A view is a named, stored SQL query in the database catalog. It looks like a table when queried, but has no independent stored data (unless it is a materialized view — preview for Lesson 21 patterns). The database expands the view definition into the calling query at runtime.

sql
CREATE VIEW v_active_customer_balances AS
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.email,
    c.region,
    SUM(a.balance) AS total_balance,
    COUNT(a.account_id) AS account_count
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.status = 'ACTIVE'
  AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.email, c.region;

-- Use like a table
SELECT customer_id, email, total_balance
FROM v_active_customer_balances
WHERE region = 'APAC'
ORDER BY total_balance DESC
LIMIT 100;

View vs Table vs CTE

text
┌──────────────┬─────────────────┬──────────────────┬─────────────────┐
│              │ TABLE           │ VIEW             │ CTE (WITH)      │
├──────────────┼─────────────────┼──────────────────┼─────────────────┤
│ Data stored  │ Yes (physical)  │ No (definition)  │ No (in query)   │
│ Scope        │ Permanent       │ Permanent (DDL)  │ One statement   │
│ DDL          │ CREATE TABLE    │ CREATE VIEW      │ WITH ...        │
│ Reuse        │ All sessions    │ All sessions     │ Same query only │
│ Permissions  │ GRANT on table  │ GRANT on view    │ N/A             │
│ ORM map      │ @Entity         │ @Immutable @Subselect │ Native only │
└──────────────┴─────────────────┴──────────────────┴─────────────────┘

View Classification

text
VIEWS

├── Simple view
│   └── Single table, no aggregation — often updatable
│
├── Complex view
│   └── JOINs, GROUP BY, DISTINCT, window functions — read-only usually
│
├── Updatable view
│   └── INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE allowed (rules apply)
│
├── Security view
│   └── Hide columns/rows — expose subset to apps/roles
│
├── Compatibility view
│   └── Legacy schema alias after migration
│
├── Materialized view (Lesson 21 territory)
│   └── Stored snapshot — REFRESH required
│
└── System/catalog views
    └── information_schema, pg_catalog, ALL_* (Oracle)

Anatomy

sql
CREATE [OR REPLACE] VIEW view_name [(column_aliases)]
AS
    select_statement
[WITH [CASCADE | LOCAL] CHECK OPTION]
[WITH READ ONLY];   -- Oracle / some DBs

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Views in SQL

text
1970s   Early relational systems — views as external schemas (IMS, early System R ideas)
        Goal: logical data independence — change base table, view shields apps

1980s   SQL standard includes CREATE VIEW
        Oracle: updatable view rules; view merging into query plan
        DB2: nested views, dependency tracking

1990s   Materialized views (Oracle snapshots) — precomputed for performance
        Security: GRANT SELECT on view without base table access

2000s   ORMs map entities to tables — views used for read models, reporting
        "View hell" — deep view stacks hard to optimize

2010s   PostgreSQL: simple view inlining (rewrite as subquery)
        Updatable views via INSTEAD OF triggers
        Database migrations (Flyway/Liquibase) version views as code

2020s   Microservices: views within service DB boundary only
        CQRS read models — table or materialized view, not cross-service view
        Cloud RDS: views for row-level security patterns (with RLS)

Historical Lesson

Views were invented for logical independence and security, not speed. Treating views as a performance cache without materialization is a common architect mistake. A view is a saved query — performance equals that query plus your outer filters, every time.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Do Views Solve?

Problem 1: Hide Complexity from Applications

sql
-- App developers query one object — not 4-table join every time
CREATE VIEW v_customer_360 AS
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.email,
    c.region,
    COUNT(DISTINCT a.account_id) AS account_count,
    COALESCE(SUM(a.balance), 0) AS total_balance,
    MAX(p.created_at) AS last_payment_at
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id AND p.status = 'COMPLETED'
WHERE c.status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.email, c.region;

-- Application: SELECT * FROM v_customer_360 WHERE customer_id = ?

Problem 2: Column-Level Security

sql
-- Call center role sees no PII columns
CREATE VIEW v_customer_support AS
SELECT customer_id, email, phone, status, region
FROM customers;
-- GRANT SELECT ON v_customer_support TO support_role;
-- No access to tax_id, date_of_birth on base table

Problem 3: Row-Level Security (Filter View)

sql
-- Regional managers see only their region
CREATE VIEW v_customers_emea AS
SELECT customer_id, email, region, status
FROM customers
WHERE region = 'EMEA';
-- Combine with GRANT per role — or use DB RLS policies (PostgreSQL)

Problem 4: Schema Migration Compatibility

sql
-- Renamed column accounts.acct_bal → accounts.balance
-- Old app still works via view
CREATE VIEW legacy_accounts AS
SELECT
    account_id,
    balance AS acct_bal,   -- alias restores old name
    customer_id,
    status
FROM accounts;

Problem 5: Encapsulate Window Logic (Lesson 19)

sql
CREATE VIEW v_latest_payment AS
SELECT payment_id, customer_id, amount, created_at, status
FROM (
    SELECT p.*,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC
           ) AS rn
    FROM payments p
    WHERE status = 'COMPLETED'
) t
WHERE rn = 1;
-- Reused by many reports and Spring @Subselect entities

Unified Problem Statement

Views provide a stable, permissioned, reusable logical table interface over complex or sensitive base data — decoupling application queries from physical schema evolution.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Views Instead of Application-Layer Abstraction?

Logical Data Independence

text
Without view:
  50 microservices embed same 4-table JOIN
  Schema change → 50 deployments

With view:
  Change base tables → CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW
  Apps unchanged if view columns stable

Security at Data Layer

text
Application bugs can leak SQL construction errors
View + GRANT = database enforces column/row subset
Defense in depth with RLS (PostgreSQL) or Oracle VPD

vs ORM @Formula / DTO Queries

Database ViewApp-Layer Query
Reuse across toolsBI, SQL clients, ETLApp only
PermissionsDB rolesApp auth only
ConsistencySingle definitionDuplicated in services
VersioningFlyway migrationCode deploy

vs CTE (Lesson 18)

text
CTE:  one statement, not shared, not permissioned separately
View: many queries, GRANT, catalog object, ORM-mappable

Rule: query used once → CTE
      query used across apps/reports → view

vs Copy-Paste SQL in Repositories

text
10 Spring @Query copies of same JOIN → drift, bug in one repo only
1 view + simple SELECT → single source of truth

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Views Execute Internally

View Expansion (View Merging)

sql
-- User query
SELECT customer_id, total_balance
FROM v_active_customer_balances
WHERE region = 'APAC';

-- Internal rewrite (conceptual)
SELECT customer_id, total_balance
FROM (
    SELECT c.customer_id, ..., SUM(a.balance) AS total_balance
    FROM customers c JOIN accounts a ...
    GROUP BY ...
) AS v_active_customer_balances
WHERE region = 'APAC';
text
OPTIMIZER (view merging):

  Outer WHERE region = 'APAC' may push into inner scan
  Outer LIMIT 100 may short-circuit if planner supports it
  View is NOT materialized — merged into one plan

PostgreSQL: "simple subquery" pull-up
Oracle: view merging (mergeable view)
SQL Server: view expansion in optimization

Non-Mergeable Views

text
Optimizer may NOT merge when:
  - DISTINCT in view + outer join
  - UNION in view
  - GROUP BY + outer references ambiguous
  - Volatile functions (random(), now() in some contexts)
  - WITH CHECK OPTION complications
  - Materialized view (separate stored data)

Result: scan view as subquery block — optimization fence (similar to old CTE)
Always EXPLAIN queries through views

Updatable View — Rewrite Rules

sql
CREATE VIEW v_account_balances AS
SELECT account_id, customer_id, balance, status
FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';

UPDATE v_account_balances SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE account_id = 5001;
text
PostgreSQL updatable view rules (simplified):
  - Single base table in FROM
  - No DISTINCT, GROUP BY, HAVING, UNION, window functions
  - All NOT NULL columns without default must appear if INSERT

Rewrite:
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100
  WHERE account_id = 5001 AND status = 'ACTIVE';

WITH CHECK OPTION:
  UPDATE balance such that status becomes 'CLOSED'
  → rejected if row would disappear from view

INSTEAD OF Triggers (Complex Views)

sql
-- View with JOIN — not auto-updatable
CREATE VIEW v_account_customer AS
SELECT a.account_id, a.balance, c.email
FROM accounts a JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = a.customer_id;

CREATE TRIGGER trg_instead_update
INSTEAD OF UPDATE ON v_account_customer
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION ...;
-- Application updates view → trigger updates base tables

Dependency Tracking

text
Catalog stores view definition + dependencies:
  v_customer_360 depends on customers, accounts, payments

DROP TABLE accounts CASCADE → drops dependent views (dangerous)
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW → must preserve column types/names or break dependents

Tools: pg_depend, Oracle ALL_DEPENDENCIES, Flyway ordering

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Views and Storage

Standard View — Zero Data Storage

text
System catalog stores:
  - View name, schema, owner
  - View definition text (parse tree)
  - Column metadata (names, types)
  - Dependencies, permissions

No heap file for view data
Query reads base tables every time

Query Through View — Same I/O as Underlying SQL

sql
SELECT * FROM v_active_customer_balances WHERE customer_id = 1001;

Plan:
  Index scan customers PK customer_id=1001
  Index scan accounts by customer_id
  Aggregate — minimal I/O if indexed

View adds zero storage — does not reduce I/O either

View Stack Depth

sql
CREATE VIEW v1 AS SELECT ... FROM accounts;
CREATE VIEW v2 AS SELECT ... FROM v1;
CREATE VIEW v3 AS SELECT ... FROM v2;

Query v3 → optimizer may flatten v1+v2+v3 into one plan
Or may expand nested definitions — parse/plan time grows
Avoid >3 levels without reason

Materialized View Contrast (Preview)

text
Standard view:     no storage, live data
Materialized view: disk blocks, stale until REFRESH
Lesson 21 deep dive — architect must choose consciously

Statistics

text
Standard view has no statistics of its own
Optimizer uses base table statistics
CREATE STATISTICS on expressions in base tables helps merged plans

PostgreSQL 15+: extended statistics on correlated columns

View Memory Impact

AspectStandard ViewMaterialized View
CatalogDefinition bytesDefinition + table data
Query memorySame as equivalent SQLScan materialized heap
Plan cacheParsed view mergedMay cache mat view scan
Connection poolNo extraNo extra

Deep View Trees

text
Many nested views:
  Longer parse/rewrite phase — CPU, plan cache memory
  Not row data memory — planning overhead

Symptom: slow planning, fast execution — simplify view chain

ORM + View

java
@Entity
@Immutable
@Subselect("SELECT * FROM v_customer_360")
public class Customer360View { ... }

// Hibernate loads like table — memory = result set size, not view definition

Part 8 — Execution Flow

View Execution Flows

Flow 1: Simple Filter Through View

sql
-- View exists in catalog
SELECT email, total_balance
FROM v_active_customer_balances
WHERE customer_id = 1001;
text
1. Parser: resolve v_active_customer_balances → expand definition
2. Rewriter: merge outer WHERE customer_id = 1001 into inner query
3. Optimizer: plan index scan on customers PK + accounts FK index
4. Executor: return rows
5. No view-specific execution step — unified plan

Flow 2: BI Tool Queries View

text
Tableau / Metabase → SELECT * FROM v_customer_360 WHERE region = 'APAC'

1. JDBC to read replica
2. DB expands view
3. Full aggregation may run — expensive if BI adds no filters
4. Architect: add indexes on base tables; consider materialized view for dashboard SLA

Flow 3: UPDATE Updatable View

sql
UPDATE v_account_balances SET balance = 9000 WHERE account_id = 5001;
text
1. Rule checker: view is updatable (single table, simple SELECT)
2. Rewrite to UPDATE accounts SET balance=9000 WHERE account_id=5001 AND status='ACTIVE'
3. Execute on base table — row locks on accounts
4. WAL flush, index update on accounts PK
5. WITH CHECK OPTION: verify row still visible in view

Flow 4: CREATE OR REPLACE Deployment

text
Flyway V55__update_customer_360_view.sql runs on deploy:

1. CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_customer_360 AS ... (new JOIN to branches)
2. Catalog updates definition — instant, no data copy
3. Dependent views re-validated
4. Running apps: next query uses new definition — no restart
5. Risk: column rename breaks @Subselect entities — coordinate app + DB migration

Flow 5: Security Boundary

text
User support_role executes:
  SELECT * FROM v_customer_support WHERE customer_id = 1001;

1. Permission check: GRANT on view — OK
2. Permission check: base table customers — not required if no SELECT on base
3. View runs with view owner's privileges (PostgreSQL SECURITY DEFINER possible via functions; default INVOKER)
4. Returns subset of columns — tax_id never exposed

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

View Performance Rules

Key Truth

text
Standard view does NOT cache results
Performance = merged SQL performance
Bad view + bad indexes on base tables = bad performance
Good view + predicate pushdown + indexes = good performance

Performance Hierarchy

text
FAST:
  Simple view on indexed columns — full merge, pushdown works
  View encapsulates window logic — same cost as inline window query
  App queries view with selective WHERE (customer_id, PK)

SLOW:
  SELECT * FROM heavy aggregation view with no filter — full scan + group
  Stack of 5 non-mergeable views — optimization fence
  BI tool full-table scan through view on primary OLTP DB
  View hiding missing index problem — "view is slow" = base query is slow

FIX slow views:
  Index base tables — not "optimize the view"
  Materialized view for read-heavy aggregates (Lesson 21)
  Move to read replica
  Restrict view definition (pre-filter status = 'ACTIVE')

Predicate Pushdown Test

sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM v_customer_360 WHERE customer_id = 1001;

-- Good: Index Scan on customers, nested loop accounts
-- Bad:  Seq Scan customers → Hash Join entire tables → Filter customer_id

View vs Application Cache

text
View: fresh data every query
Redis cache of customer_360: stale but fast

Architect: view for correctness + simplicity
           cache for hot read path with TTL/event invalidation
           materialized view for predictable report latency

Updatable Simple View

CREATE VIEW v_active_accounts AS

FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
WITH LOCAL CHECK OPTION;

-- Valid update

PostgreSQL INSTEAD OF (Complex View)

sql
CREATE VIEW v_account_email AS
SELECT a.account_id, a.balance, c.email
FROM accounts a
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = a.customer_id;

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION fn_update_account_email()
RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
BEGIN
    UPDATE accounts SET balance = NEW.balance WHERE account_id = OLD.account_id;
    UPDATE customers SET email = NEW.email
    WHERE customer_id = (SELECT customer_id FROM accounts WHERE account_id = OLD.account_id);
    RETURN NEW;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER trg_v_account_email_update
INSTEAD OF UPDATE ON v_account_email
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION fn_update_account_email();

FROM branches b
LEFT JOIN accounts a ON a.branch_id = b.branch_id AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY b.branch_id, b.name
