Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Trigger Masterclass

Standard updated_at (PostgreSQL)

sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION trg_fn_set_updated_at()
RETURNS TRIGGER
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
BEGIN
    NEW.updated_at := NOW();
    RETURN NEW;
END;
$$;

CREATE TRIGGER trg_accounts_updated_at
BEFORE UPDATE ON accounts
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE FUNCTION trg_fn_set_updated_at();

Comprehensive Audit Trigger

sql
CREATE TABLE payments_audit (
    audit_id        BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    payment_id      BIGINT NOT NULL,
    operation       VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
    old_amount      NUMERIC(18,2),
    new_amount      NUMERIC(18,2),
    old_status      VARCHAR(20),
    new_status      VARCHAR(20),
    changed_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    changed_by      TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT current_user,
    application     TEXT DEFAULT current_setting('app.name', true)
);

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION trg_fn_payments_audit()
RETURNS TRIGGER
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO payments_audit (
        payment_id, operation,
        old_amount, new_amount, old_status, new_status,
        changed_by, application
    ) VALUES (
        COALESCE(NEW.payment_id, OLD.payment_id),
        TG_OP,
        OLD.amount, NEW.amount,
        OLD.status, NEW.status,
        current_user,
        current_setting('app.name', true)
    );
    RETURN COALESCE(NEW, OLD);
END;
$$;

CREATE TRIGGER trg_payments_audit
AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON payments
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE FUNCTION trg_fn_payments_audit();

Spring Sets Application Context (PostgreSQL)

java
@Transactional
public void updatePayment(Payment p) {
    jdbcTemplate.execute("SET LOCAL app.name = 'payment-service'");
    paymentRepo.save(p);
}
// Trigger reads current_setting('app.name', true)

BEFORE — Enforce Non-Negative Balance

sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION trg_fn_check_balance()
RETURNS TRIGGER
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
BEGIN
    IF NEW.balance < 0 AND NEW.status = 'ACTIVE' THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION 'BALANCE_NEGATIVE' USING ERRCODE = '23514';
    END IF;
    RETURN NEW;
END;
$$;

CREATE TRIGGER trg_accounts_balance_check
BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OF balance ON accounts
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE FUNCTION trg_fn_check_balance();
-- Note: CHECK (balance >= 0 OR status <> 'ACTIVE') possible for simpler case

Delta Summary (Better Than Full Recalc)

sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION trg_fn_customer_balance_delta()
RETURNS TRIGGER
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
DECLARE
    v_delta NUMERIC(18,2) := 0;
    v_cid BIGINT;
BEGIN
    IF TG_OP = 'INSERT' THEN
        v_delta := NEW.balance; v_cid := NEW.customer_id;
    ELSIF TG_OP = 'DELETE' THEN
        v_delta := -OLD.balance; v_cid := OLD.customer_id;
    ELSIF TG_OP = 'UPDATE' THEN
        v_delta := NEW.balance - OLD.balance;
        v_cid := NEW.customer_id;
        IF OLD.customer_id <> NEW.customer_id THEN
            RAISE EXCEPTION 'customer_id change not allowed';
        END IF;
    END IF;

    INSERT INTO customer_balance_summary (customer_id, total_balance)
    VALUES (v_cid, v_delta)
    ON CONFLICT (customer_id) DO UPDATE
    SET total_balance = customer_balance_summary.total_balance + EXCLUDED.total_balance;

    RETURN COALESCE(NEW, OLD);
END;
$$;

CREATE TRIGGER trg_accounts_balance_summary
AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON accounts
FOR EACH ROW
EXECUTE FUNCTION trg_fn_customer_balance_delta();

Statement Trigger with Transition Table (PostgreSQL 10+)

sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION trg_fn_reject_bulk_status_change()
RETURNS TRIGGER
LANGUAGE plpgsql
AS $$
BEGIN
    IF EXISTS (
        SELECT 1 FROM new_rows WHERE status = 'FRAUD_FLAGGED'
    ) AND (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM new_rows) > 100 THEN
        RAISE EXCEPTION 'Bulk fraud flag requires batch job';
    END IF;
    RETURN NULL;
END;
$$;

CREATE TRIGGER trg_payments_bulk_guard
AFTER UPDATE ON payments
REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS new_rows
FOR EACH STATEMENT
EXECUTE FUNCTION trg_fn_reject_bulk_status_change();

Oracle — Compound Trigger (Simplified Concept)

sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER trg_accounts_audit
FOR UPDATE ON accounts
COMPOUND TRIGGER
    TYPE t_audit IS TABLE OF accounts_audit%ROWTYPE INDEX BY PLS_INTEGER;
    g_audit t_audit;
    idx PLS_INTEGER := 0;

    AFTER EACH ROW IS
    BEGIN
        idx := idx + 1;
        g_audit(idx).account_id := :OLD.account_id;
        g_audit(idx).old_balance := :OLD.balance;
        g_audit(idx).new_balance := :NEW.balance;
    END AFTER EACH ROW;

    AFTER STATEMENT IS
    BEGIN
        FORALL i IN 1..idx
            INSERT INTO accounts_audit VALUES g_audit(i);
    END AFTER STATEMENT;
END;
/
-- Batches audit writes — reduces row-by-row INSERT overhead

SQL Server — Audit Trigger

sql
CREATE TRIGGER trg_payments_audit ON dbo.payments
AFTER INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
AS
BEGIN
    SET NOCOUNT ON;
    INSERT INTO dbo.payments_audit (payment_id, operation, changed_at)
    SELECT payment_id, 'I', SYSUTCDATETIME() FROM inserted
    UNION ALL
    SELECT payment_id, 'D', SYSUTCDATETIME() FROM deleted;
    -- Use inserted/deleted pseudo-tables
END;

Guard Against Recursion

sql
IF pg_trigger_depth() > 1 THEN
    RETURN NEW;
END IF;

Part 12 — Production Usage

Triggers in Production

PCI / SOX Audit — Common Legitimate Use

text
AFTER trigger on payments, accounts, privilege tables
Immutable audit store (INSERT only, no UPDATE on audit table)
Retention 7 years — partition by month
App name via SET LOCAL per connection

updated_at on All Domain Tables

text
Flyway template:
  trg_fn_set_updated_at() shared function
  One BEFORE UPDATE trigger per table
Complements JPA @UpdateTimestamp — covers non-JPA writers

When Teams Use CDC Instead

text
High-throughput payments:
  Debezium → Kafka → audit service → S3/warehouse
  No AFTER trigger on hot INSERT path
  Trigger only on low-volume admin tables

Operational Runbook

text
□ Trigger inventory in Flyway + architecture catalog
□ Never DISABLE TRIGGER in prod without ticket
□ Bulk migration: explicit audit backfill plan
□ Monitor audit table size — partition strategy
□ Test trigger + Hibernate batch insert in CI
□ Document RAISE error codes for app mapping

Anti-Patterns

text
❌ Business workflow in trigger (approve payment → trigger creates transfer)
❌ Trigger sends email (UTL_HTTP, pg_notify without consumer)
❌ 15 triggers on one table
❌ Audit trigger that UPDATEs audit row (defeats immutability)
❌ Same validation in @Valid and BEFORE trigger — drift

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

Trigger Architecture Policy

Recommended Tier List

text
Tier 0 — Standard (approve by default):
  BEFORE UPDATE updated_at
  AFTER INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE audit (narrow tables, compliance)

Tier 1 — Needs ADR:
  Derived summary table maintenance
  BEFORE validation not in CHECK/FK
  INSTEAD OF view DML

Tier 2 — Avoid / migrate away:
  Cross-table business workflows
  Outbox/event publish in trigger
  More than 2 triggers per table per event

Audit Architecture Comparison

┌────────────────┬───────────────┬──────────────┬─────────────────┐
│                │ DB Trigger    │ App Envers   │ CDC (Debezium)  │
├────────────────┼───────────────┼──────────────┼─────────────────┤
│ All writers    │ ✅            │ ❌           │ ✅              │

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Business Logic in Trigger

sql
-- ❌ AFTER INSERT payment → trigger creates transfer, sends notification
-- ✅ PaymentService @Transactional + domain events

Mistake 2: Full Recalc Per Row

sql
-- ❌ AFTER UPDATE accounts: SELECT SUM(balance) ... into summary
-- ✅ Delta trigger or async aggregate job

Mistake 3: Mutating Table (Oracle Classic)

sql
-- ❌ Cannot SELECT from accounts in row trigger on accounts without compound/autonomous
-- ✅ Compound trigger batch or AFTER STATEMENT

Mistake 4: Duplicate Validation

java
@Min(0) amount in DTO + BEFORE trigger check — rules diverge
-- ✅ One owner: constraint or app, not both without sync tests

Mistake 5: Audit Table Without Partitioning

text
payments_audit grows 500M rows — queries slow, backups huge
-- ✅ Partition by changed_at monthly; archive to cold storage

Mistake 6: Ignoring Trigger on Bulk Migration

sql
-- COPY 10M rows → 10M audit INSERTs — migration takes days
-- Plan: disable audit trigger + separate audit backfill OR use CDC

Mistake 7: RETURN NULL Confusion (PostgreSQL)

sql
-- BEFORE INSERT RETURN NULL skips row silently — surprising partial insert
-- Use RAISE for explicit reject

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is a database trigger?

Stored program auto-fired on DML events (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) without explicit CALL.

Q2: BEFORE vs AFTER trigger?

BEFORE: before row written, can modify NEW. AFTER: after row written, good for audit.

Q3: Row vs statement trigger?

Row: once per affected row. Statement: once per SQL command.

Q4: Can triggers replace foreign keys?

No — use declarative FK; triggers for what constraints cannot express simply.

Q5: Do triggers run in the same transaction?

Yes — failure rolls back triggering DML and trigger side effects.

Mid-Level

Q6: Why audit in AFTER not BEFORE?

Audit should record committed intent on final row values; AFTER sees successful row change.

Q7: Trigger vs application audit service?

Trigger covers DBA/batch/all writers; app audit only covers app path.

Q8: Hibernate batch insert + audit trigger impact?

Each row still fires trigger — audit INSERT per row; reduces batch benefit.

Q9: INSTEAD OF trigger use case?

Updatable view over JOIN — trigger decomposes DML to base tables.

Q10: How prevent trigger recursion?

pg_trigger_depth(), guard flags, avoid trigger updating same table carelessly.

Senior

Q11: Design audit for 5K TPS payment table.

CDC to Kafka + async audit store; or narrow AFTER trigger + partitioned audit; avoid heavy per-row logic.

Q12: Delta vs full recalc summary trigger?

Delta O(1) per row with ON CONFLICT; full SUM O(n) per fire — unacceptable at scale.

Q13: Envers vs trigger audit for SOX?

SOX often needs all-writer coverage → trigger or CDC; Envers insufficient if ETL/DBA writes exist.

Q14: DISABLE TRIGGER in production migration?

Change control, time window, compensating audit, re-enable verification.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Enterprise trigger policy?

Tier 0/1/2 approval, inventory, max triggers per table, forbid external I/O, prefer constraints/CDC.

Q16: Replace trigger-maintained summary with event-driven read model.

Account events → Kafka → consumer updates summary table; eventual consistency; remove AFTER trigger after dual-write validation.

Scenario

Scenario: "Account update slow after adding balance summary trigger."

EXPLAIN trigger body — likely full SUM recalc. Rewrite delta upsert, index summary PK, measure row lock waits on hot customer_id. Consider async aggregate.

Part 1 — Concept

What Is a Sequence?

A sequence is a database object that generates a stream of numeric values — typically used for primary keys and surrogate identifiers. It guarantees uniqueness and monotonic increase (usually), but not contiguous values without gaps.

sql
-- PostgreSQL
CREATE SEQUENCE seq_payment_id
    START WITH 1
    INCREMENT BY 1
    NO MINVALUE
    NO MAXVALUE
    CACHE 50;

CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT nextval('seq_payment_id'),
    customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    amount NUMERIC(18,2) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

INSERT INTO payments (customer_id, amount) VALUES (1001, 250.00);
-- payment_id assigned automatically via nextval()

Sequence vs Identity vs UUID vs Application ID

text
IDENTIFIER STRATEGIES

├── Database sequence
│   ├── CREATE SEQUENCE + DEFAULT nextval()
│   ├── IDENTITY column (SQL standard — auto sequence)
│   └── SERIAL / BIGSERIAL (PostgreSQL sugar)
│
├── UUID / GUID
│   ├── gen_random_uuid() (PostgreSQL)
│   ├── UUID v4 random, v7 time-ordered
│   └── CHAR(36) or native UUID type
│
├── Application-generated
│   ├── Snowflake / Sonyflake (64-bit time + machine + sequence)
│   ├── ULID (lexicographically sortable)
│   └── Hi/Lo, pooled optimizer (Hibernate)
│
└── Natural key
    └── client_request_id, ISIN, account_number (business meaning)

Core Properties

text
SEQUENCE BEHAVIOR

  nextval('seq')  → returns next value, advances counter
  currval('seq')  → last value in THIS session (after nextval)
  setval('seq', n) → reset (admin — dangerous in prod)

  Guarantees:
    ✅ Unique (within sequence scope)
    ✅ Increasing (INCREMENT BY positive)
    ❌ No gaps-free guarantee
    ❌ Not transactional with INSERT rollback (most DBs)
    ❌ Not globally ordered across shards without design

ASCII — Sequence Flow

text
Session A                          Sequence Object (catalog)
┌──────────────────┐              ┌─────────────────────────┐
│ INSERT payment   │  nextval()   │ last_value: 90042       │
│                  │ ──────────►  │ increment: 1            │
│ payment_id=90043 │ ◄──────────  │ cache: 50 (pre-alloc)   │
└──────────────────┘              └─────────────────────────┘
                                         │
                                         ▼
                                  90043 returned to session
                                  (90044..90092 may be cached in memory)

Part 2 — History

Evolution of ID Generation in Databases

text
1970s   IMS/VSAM relative record — not SQL sequences
1980s   Oracle SEQUENCE — independent of table; widely adopted in banking
        Sybase IDENTITY column pattern

1990s   SQL:2003 IDENTITY columns standardized
        PostgreSQL SERIAL (sequence + default + owned by column)
        Gaps on rollback understood as normal Oracle behavior

2000s   UUID RFC 4122 — distributed systems without central sequence
        Hibernate @GeneratedValue strategies: AUTO, SEQUENCE, IDENTITY, TABLE

2010s   Twitter Snowflake — 64-bit sortable IDs at scale
        PostgreSQL 10: IDENTITY column syntax (standard)
        PostgreSQL 13: GENERATED AS IDENTITY preferred over SERIAL

2020s   UUID v7 (time-ordered UUID) — index-friendly random IDs
        Microservices: per-service ID ranges or global Snowflake service
        Cloud Spanner / CockroachDB sequences with different gap semantics
        Hi/Lo and pooled-lo optimizers for reducing sequence round trips

Historical Lesson

Oracle sequences predate identity columns — banking cores still use SEQ_PAYMENT_ID.NEXTVAL explicitly. Architects must understand gaps are a feature of performance and crash recovery, not bugs. Demanding gapless IDs leads to table-level locking and throughput collapse.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Do Sequences Solve?

Problem 1: Surrogate Primary Key Without Business Meaning

sql
-- payment_id has no business semantics — stable, compact, join-friendly
-- client_request_id remains UNIQUE for idempotency (natural key separate)
CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    client_request_id VARCHAR(64) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
    ...
);

Problem 2: Single Writer Generates Unique IDs Efficiently

sql
-- One nextval() call — O(1), no SELECT MAX(id)+1 race
INSERT INTO transactions (...) VALUES (...);
-- MAX(id)+1 ❌ race condition under concurrent inserts

Problem 3: Pre-allocate IDs Before INSERT (Batch, ORM)

java
// Hibernate allocates 50 IDs from sequence in one nextval burst (CACHE 50)
// Batch insert 50 payments without 50 sequence round trips

Problem 4: Distributed Systems Need Non-Colliding IDs

text
Single PostgreSQL sequence → OK for one database
Multi-region active-active → sequence fails globally
Solutions: Snowflake ID service, UUID v7, range per shard (1001→ shard 1)

Problem 5: Ordered IDs for Index Locality (Time Correlation)

text
BIGINT sequence → recent IDs clustered in B-tree right edge (insert hot spot)
UUID v4 random → index page splits scattered — insert heavy
UUID v7 / Snowflake → time prefix → better locality than v4

Unified Problem Statement

Sequences (and their modern successors) provide fast, unique, surrogate identifiers decoupled from business keys — with explicit trade-offs between gaplessness, global uniqueness, sort order, and index performance.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Not Natural Keys or MAX+1?

Natural Key Alone

text
client_request_id as PK — OK for idempotency
But: VARCHAR PK on child FK indexes — wider, slower joins
Pattern: BIGINT surrogate PK + UNIQUE business key

SELECT MAX(id) + 1

sql
-- ❌ Two transactions read MAX=9000 simultaneously → both insert 9001 → PK violation
-- ❌ Table lock on PostgreSQL without sequence
-- ✅ nextval() — atomic increment in sequence machinery

UUID Everywhere

text
✅ Globally unique without coordination
✅ Client can generate before INSERT (offline mobile)
❌ 16 bytes vs 8 bytes BIGINT
❌ Random UUID v4 hurts B-tree index locality
❌ Sort order not time-correlated (v4)

Application Snowflake Service

text
✅ 64-bit, sortable, no DB round trip per insert
❌ Another infrastructure component to operate
❌ Clock skew handling required
Use when: multi-master writes, high TPS ID generation outside DB

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Sequences Execute Internally

PostgreSQL Sequence Internals

text
Sequence stored in pg_class / pg_sequence catalog
Not a normal table row — lightweight counter object
nextval():
  1. Lock sequence (lightweight — not full table lock)
  2. Return current + increment
  3. If CACHE n: allocate n values in memory for session/connection
  4. Persist last_value periodically (not every nextval if cached)

ROLLBACK of INSERT does NOT rollback sequence value in PostgreSQL
  → gap on failed transaction — by design

CACHE Parameter

sql
CREATE SEQUENCE seq_payment_id CACHE 50;
-- Server pre-reserves 50 values in memory
-- Crash may lose unused cached values → gaps
-- CACHE 1 → safest against gaps, slowest (disk sync each nextval in some DBs)

Oracle default CACHE 20 for sequences
PostgreSQL: CACHE 1 default until PG 15+ discussions; often set 50+ in prod

IDENTITY Column Binding

sql
CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY (
        SEQUENCE NAME seq_payment_id
        INCREMENT BY 1
        CACHE 50
    ) PRIMARY KEY,
    ...
);
-- Standard SQL — sequence owned by column
-- GENERATED ALWAYS vs BY DEFAULT (allow explicit insert of id)

SERIAL (PostgreSQL Legacy)

sql
CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    ...
);
-- Equivalent to:
-- CREATE SEQUENCE payments_payment_id_seq;
-- CREATE TABLE ... payment_id BIGINT DEFAULT nextval('payments_payment_id_seq');
-- ALTER SEQUENCE OWNED BY payments.payment_id;
-- Prefer IDENTITY in new schemas (PG 10+)

Oracle SEQUENCE.NEXTVAL

sql
CREATE SEQUENCE seq_payment_id START WITH 1 INCREMENT BY 1 CACHE 50 NOCYCLE;

INSERT INTO payments (payment_id, ...) VALUES (seq_payment_id.NEXTVAL, ...);
-- Or trigger/default populating ID
-- NOCACHE for gap-minimal (slow) — rare
-- CYCLE dangerous for PK — reuse IDs after MAX

SQL Server IDENTITY

sql
CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id BIGINT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
    ...
);
-- Not a separate sequence object until SQL Server 2012 SEQUENCE added
-- IDENTITY is table-bound; SEQUENCE is independent object

Hibernate Sequence Optimizer

text
pooled-lo (preferred):
  hi/lo variant — one sequence call allocates "increment" block
  Application: id = (next_hi * increment) + local_counter
  Reduces DB round trips dramatically

enhanced-sequence with allocationSize must match DB INCREMENT BY / CACHE semantics
Mismatch → duplicate key or huge gaps

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Sequences and Storage

Sequence Catalog Footprint

text
Negligible disk — one catalog row per sequence
Not stored in user tablespace heap (implementation-specific)
Millions of sequences possible — avoid one sequence per row (anti-pattern)

Primary Key Index — BIGINT Sequence

text
B-tree index on payment_id (BIGINT):
  Sequential inserts → right-edge leaf page growth
  Hot spot on single monotonic sequence at extreme TPS
  Mitigation: HASH partition PK rare; Snowflake/UUID v7 spread; batch inserts

Index size: 8-byte key + overhead vs 16-byte UUID
Child FK indexes also 8 vs 16 bytes — compounding savings

UUID Primary Key Index

text
UUID v4 random:
  Inserts land on random B-tree pages → splits, fragmentation, buffer churn
  PostgreSQL: fillfactor tuning; consider UUID v7 for monotonic prefix

UUID stored as uuid type (16 bytes) vs CHAR(36) (36 bytes)

WAL Impact

text
nextval() generates WAL for sequence update (unless heavily cached batch)
Much smaller than INSERT WAL for full row
Sequence not bottleneck vs row data + indexes for typical OLTP

Table per Service — One Sequence per Table

text
payments → seq_payment_id
accounts   → seq_account_id
Normal — independent counters, no collision
Global ID service: one logical namespace across entities

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Sequence Memory Impact

AspectImpact
CACHE 50Up to 49 values in session/server memory un persisted
nextval()Minimal CPU — counter increment
Hibernate poolPre-allocated ID block in JVM heap
Snowflake generatorStateless — few bytes per generated ID
Connection pool × CACHEEach connection may cache — more gaps, faster

CACHE Tuning Trade-off

text
CACHE 1:   minimal gaps on crash, more sync I/O
CACHE 50:  fewer round trips, larger gap on crash/restart
CACHE 1000: batch systems, accept large gap jumps

Oracle RAC: CACHE must be large enough per instance — ORDER/NOCACHE options for strict ordering (slow)

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Sequence Execution Flows

Flow 1: Simple INSERT with DEFAULT

sql
INSERT INTO payments (customer_id, amount, client_request_id)
VALUES (1001, 250.00, 'req-uuid-abc');
text
1. Parser: payment_id omitted → apply DEFAULT nextval('seq_payment_id')
2. nextval(): lock sequence → return 90043 → advance to 90044 (or cache block)
3. INSERT row with payment_id=90043
4. UPDATE PK index, any FK indexes on referencing tables (none on insert)
5. COMMIT — row durable; sequence 90043 never reused even if ROLLBACK later

Flow 2: Hibernate @SequenceGenerator

java
@Entity
public class Payment {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "payment_seq")
    @SequenceGenerator(name = "payment_seq", sequenceName = "seq_payment_id", allocationSize = 50)
    private Long paymentId;
}
text
1. Session.persist(payment) — needs ID
2. Hibernate: if no pooled IDs left, SELECT nextval('seq_payment_id') — may advance by 50
3. Assign paymentId from local pool in JVM
4. INSERT on flush with known ID
5. One sequence call per 50 entities (allocationSize=50, DB INCREMENT aligned)

Flow 3: Rollback Creates Gap

text
1. nextval() → 90044
2. INSERT payment_id=90044
3. Constraint violation on client_request_id duplicate
4. ROLLBACK — row gone
5. Sequence stays at 90045+ — 90044 never reused
6. Finance audit: "missing payment_id 90044" → explain gap semantics

Flow 4: Bulk Import with Explicit IDs

sql
-- GENERATED BY DEFAULT allows override
INSERT INTO payments (payment_id, customer_id, amount)
VALUES (5000001, 1001, 100.00);

-- Must setval after import to avoid collision
SELECT setval('seq_payment_id', (SELECT MAX(payment_id) FROM payments));
-- Migration runbook step — critical

Flow 5: Distributed Snowflake (Application)

text
1. Payment service requests ID from Snowflake generator (in-process or sidecar)
2. ID encodes: timestamp | datacenter | worker | sequence bits
3. INSERT with explicit payment_id — no DB sequence call
4. Global uniqueness without DB coordination
5. Clock backward → generator waits or errors

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Sequence Performance Rules

Performance Hierarchy (ID Generation)

text
FAST:
  BIGINT IDENTITY/SEQUENCE with CACHE 50+
  Hibernate pooled-lo allocationSize matched to DB
  Snowflake in-process generation — no DB call

MODERATE:
  UUID gen_random_uuid() per row — DB CPU, index spread cost
  CACHE 1 sequence — sync overhead

SLOW:
  MAX(id)+1 subquery
  TABLE generator (Hibernate hilo table) — row lock on hi value
  Global single sequence for ALL tables contended by 100 services — rare bottleneck

INDEX COST (separate from generation):
  Monotonic BIGINT → right-edge insert contention at extreme scale
  UUID v4 → random insert spread — page splits
  UUID v7 / Snowflake → compromise

Oracle Banking Pattern

sql
-- Explicit NEXTVAL in INSERT — one per row
INSERT INTO GL_ENTRY (entry_id, ...) VALUES (seq_gl_entry.NEXTVAL, ...);
-- High volume GL: batch allocator in proc pre-fetching range

PostgreSQL Sequence Contention

text
Single sequence at 100K inserts/sec:
  PostgreSQL 10+ improved sequence scalability — sharded sequences rare
  If bottleneck: increase CACHE; use IDENTITY; batch inserts

Multiple tables — separate sequences — no cross-contention

alignment Checklist

text
Hibernate allocationSize = 50
PostgreSQL INCREMENT BY 1 on sequence (Hibernate uses hi/lo math)
OR use @SequenceGenerator with optimizer=pooled-lo and proper config

❌ allocationSize=50 but DB INCREMENT BY 50 without understanding → broken IDs
Read Hibernate + dialect docs for your version

OperationTimeNotes
nextval()O(1)Light lock
nextval() CACHE 1O(1) + possible disk syncDB-dependent
INSERT with PKO(log n) indexn = table size
MAX(id)+1O(n) scan or O(log n) index scan + race❌
Snowflake generateO(1) CPU
UUID v4 insertO(log n) random index posfragmentation

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Sequence Masterclass

PostgreSQL — Modern IDENTITY

sql
CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id BIGINT GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY (
        SEQUENCE NAME seq_payment_id
        INCREMENT BY 1
        START WITH 1
        CACHE 50
    ) PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id     BIGINT NOT NULL,
    amount          NUMERIC(18,2) NOT NULL,
    currency        CHAR(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'USD',
    client_request_id VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    status          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING',
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE INDEX idx_payments_customer_created ON payments (customer_id, created_at DESC);

Separate Sequences per Entity

sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    balance NUMERIC(18,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE'
);

CREATE TABLE transactions (
    transaction_id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(account_id),
    amount NUMERIC(18,2) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

UUID Alternative (PostgreSQL)

sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgcrypto;

CREATE TABLE payments_uuid (
    payment_id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    amount NUMERIC(18,2) NOT NULL,
    client_request_id VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

-- PostgreSQL 18+ / pg_uuidv7 extension for time-ordered UUID
-- payment_id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuid_generate_v7();

Oracle Sequence

sql
CREATE SEQUENCE seq_payment_id
    START WITH 1
    INCREMENT BY 1
    CACHE 50
    NOCACHE  -- only if gap-intolerant (performance hit)
    NOCYCLE
    NOORDER;  -- RAC: NOORDER faster, may assign out-of-order

CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id NUMBER(19) PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id NUMBER(19) NOT NULL,
    amount NUMBER(18,2) NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO payments (payment_id, customer_id, amount)
VALUES (seq_payment_id.NEXTVAL, 1001, 250.00);

SQL Server — IDENTITY and SEQUENCE

sql
-- Table-bound IDENTITY
CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id BIGINT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    amount DECIMAL(18,2) NOT NULL
);

-- Independent sequence (SQL Server 2012+)
CREATE SEQUENCE dbo.seq_payment_id AS BIGINT START WITH 1 INCREMENT BY 1 CACHE 50;
INSERT INTO payments (payment_id, customer_id, amount)
VALUES (NEXT VALUE FOR dbo.seq_payment_id, 1001, 250.00);

Post-Migration setval

sql
-- After loading CSV with explicit IDs
SELECT setval(
    pg_get_serial_sequence('payments', 'payment_id'),
    COALESCE((SELECT MAX(payment_id) FROM payments), 1)
);

Hi/Lo Concept (Illustrative)

text
Sequence "hi" value = 100  (one nextval)
Application allocates IDs:
  100 * 50 + 0  = 5000
  100 * 50 + 1  = 5001
  ...
  100 * 50 + 49 = 5049
Next nextval → hi=101 → IDs 5050..5099

One DB call per 50 IDs — Hibernate pooled-lo similar idea

Snowflake-Style 64-bit Layout (Conceptual)

text
| 1 bit sign (0) | 41 bits timestamp ms | 10 bits machine | 12 bits sequence |
Total: 64-bit BIGINT — fits Java long and SQL BIGINT
Sortable by time — index friendly vs UUID v4
Requires unique (datacenter, worker) assignment per JVM/pod

Part 12 — Production Usage

Sequences in Production

Banking — Standard Pattern

text
Surrogate BIGINT PK on all core tables
Business keys UNIQUE NOT NULL separately:
  client_request_id, account_number (external), transaction_ref
Oracle: SEQ_* naming convention — SEQ_PAYMENT_ID
PostgreSQL: IDENTITY or seq_<table>_id
Never expose raw sequence to customer-facing APIs — use opaque IDs or UUIDs externally

Payment Idempotency + Sequence

sql
CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    client_request_id VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT uq_payments_client_request UNIQUE (client_request_id)
);
-- Idempotency on business key — not on sequence
-- Retry same client_request_id → UNIQUE violation → return existing row

Gap Management — Finance Auditors

text
Auditors ask: "Why is payment_id 90045 missing?"
Answer template:
  - Failed transaction after nextval
  - CACHE pre-allocation
  - Rollback does not recycle IDs
  - Not indicative of missing money — reconcile on business keys + ledger

Do NOT use NOCACHE everywhere to please auditors — performance cost

Multi-Region Considerations

text
Active-passive DR:
  Primary generates IDs — standby read-only — OK

Active-active same table two regions:
  ❌ Single sequence — not shared across independent writes
  ✅ UUID v7, Snowflake, or range sharding:
     Region US: IDs ending 0-4
     Region EU: IDs ending 5-9
  ✅ Separate databases per region — global ID in application layer

Operational Runbook

text
□ Document every sequence + current max + CACHE setting
□ After bulk import: setval verification script
□ Monitor sequence exhaustion (BIGINT practically never; INT rare legacy)
□ Hibernate allocationSize matches Flyway sequence definition
□ Load test ID generation under expected TPS
□ External API IDs may differ from internal BIGINT PK

StrategyDB SupportBatch InsertGapsPortable

allocationSize Pitfall

Persist Order

java

Testing IDs

java
@Test
void idsAreUniqueConcurrent() throws Exception {
    int threads = 20;
    ExecutorService ex = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(threads);
    Set<Long> ids = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
        ex.submit(() -> ids.add(paymentRepo.save(new Payment(...)).getPaymentId()));
    }
    ex.shutdown();
    ex.awaitTermination(1, MINUTES);
    assertThat(ids).hasSize(1000);
}

Mistake 1: Expecting Gapless Sequence

text
Finance: "Renumber payments to remove gaps"
❌ Breaks FK references, audit trail, external systems
✅ Explain gaps normal; report by business date not contiguous ID

Mistake 2: allocationSize Mismatch

java
@SequenceGenerator(allocationSize = 50)
// DB sequence INCREMENT BY 50 without hi/lo understanding → duplicate PKs
// Fix: use pooled-lo, INCREMENT BY 1 on sequence

Mistake 3: Forgot setval After Migration

sql

-- Sequence still at 1000 → next insert collision
SELECT setval('seq_payment_id', (SELECT MAX(payment_id) FROM payments));

Mistake 4: UUID v4 as PK on Billion-Row Table

text
Index bloat, slow inserts, buffer churn
✅ BIGINT sequence or UUID v7 / Snowflake

Mistake 5: Public Sequential API IDs

text
GET /payments/90043 → enumerate competitors scrape all payments
✅ Opaque UUID in API; internal BIGINT OK in DB

Mistake 6: Single Natural Key as PK

sql
-- client_request_id VARCHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY
-- All child FK indexes wide
✅ BIGINT PK + UNIQUE(client_request_id)

Mistake 7: MAX(id)+1 in Concurrent Code

java
Long nextId = jdbcTemplate.queryForObject("SELECT COALESCE(MAX(id),0)+1 FROM payments", Long.class);

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is a database sequence?

Object generating unique numeric values via nextval — typically for primary keys.

Q2: Why gaps in sequence values?

Rollback after nextval, CACHE pre-allocation, failed inserts — IDs not reused by design.

Q3: SEQUENCE vs IDENTITY?

Sequence is independent object; IDENTITY is column-bound auto-increment standard syntax.

Q4: Can rolled-back transaction reuse same ID?

No in PostgreSQL/Oracle — gap remains.

Q5: Why surrogate key + unique business key?

Compact join index on BIGINT; idempotency on natural key like client_request_id.

Mid-Level

Q6: UUID vs BIGINT PK tradeoffs?

UUID globally unique, larger index, v4 random hurts locality; BIGINT compact, DB-local sequence.

Q7: Hibernate allocationSize purpose?

Batch pre-allocate IDs from sequence — fewer nextval round trips.

Q8: What is CACHE 50 on sequence?

Pre-reserve 50 values in memory — faster, larger gaps on crash.

Q9: How fix sequence after bulk import?

setval to MAX(id) — verify next nextval > max existing.

Q10: IDENTITY vs SEQUENCE for batch insert?

SEQUENCE with pooling batches better; IDENTITY may disable batch optimization.

Senior

Q11: Active-active multi-region ID strategy?

Not single DB sequence — Snowflake, UUID v7, or shard ranges per region.

Q12: Snowflake ID structure benefits?

64-bit, time-sortable, no DB coordination, fits BIGINT — vs UUID v4 random index cost.

Q13: Hi/Lo / pooled-lo Hibernate?

One sequence call allocates block; app assigns IDs from block — align config with DB INCREMENT BY 1.

Q14: External API ID vs internal PK design?

Internal BIGINT sequence; external opaque ULID/UUID — prevent enumeration; map if needed.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Greenfield payment microservice ID policy?

BIGINT IDENTITY + UNIQUE client_request_id; pooled sequence; external ULID in API response optional.

Q16: Auditor demands gapless payment numbers?

Separate human-readable document_number table with pessimistic lock or serial — not PK sequence; explain performance.

Scenario

Scenario: "Duplicate payment_id after Hibernate upgrade."

Check allocationSize vs sequence INCREMENT; pooled-lo config; flyway sequence definition; concurrent test — fix alignment.

❌ Gapless sequence obsession
❌ MAX(id)+1 concurrent
❌ UUID v4 on huge OLTP without reason
❌ allocationSize mismatch
❌ Cross-region single sequence

Spring/JPA

text
PostgreSQL/Oracle → GenerationType.SEQUENCE + allocationSize
MySQL → GenerationType.IDENTITY
Pre-insert ID → UUID / Snowflake / nextval in service
Idempotency → UNIQUE natural key, not sequence

EXPLAIN & Query Execution Plans

Phase 3: QUERY OPTIMIZATION & EXECUTION PLANS | Previous: — | Next: Indexes Deep Dive

Performance
1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why This Exists5Internal Working6Storage Internals7Memory Usage8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Complexity Analysis11Code / SQL Examples12Production Usage13Spring Boot Integration14Hibernate/JPA Integration15Architect Perspective16Decision Matrix17Comparison Tables18Common Mistakes19Interview Questions20Revision Sheet21Summary Table*Practice

Part 1 — Concept

What Is EXPLAIN?

EXPLAIN asks the database how it would execute a query (or how it did execute, with ANALYZE) without necessarily returning full result data. The output is a query execution plan — a tree of operators (scan, join, sort, aggregate) chosen by the optimizer.

sql
-- PostgreSQL: plan only (no execution)
EXPLAIN
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email, SUM(a.balance) AS total
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.region = 'APAC'
  AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.email
HAVING SUM(a.balance) > 50000
ORDER BY total DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- PostgreSQL: actually run + real timings
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE, FORMAT TEXT)
SELECT ... ;

Plan as a Tree

text
LIMIT (20 rows)
  └── Sort (total DESC)
        └── HashAggregate (GROUP BY customer_id, email)
              Filter: SUM(balance) > 50000
              └── Hash Join
                    ├── Seq Scan on customers  (filter: region = 'APAC')
                    └── Hash
                          └── Index Scan on accounts  (status = 'ACTIVE')

Each node = an operator. Rows flow bottom-up (children → parent). The optimizer picks operators to minimize estimated cost (I/O + CPU).

EXPLAIN Variants by Database

text
PostgreSQL   EXPLAIN | EXPLAIN ANALYZE | BUFFERS | VERBOSE | JSON
Oracle       EXPLAIN PLAN FOR ... + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY
SQL Server   SET SHOWPLAN_TEXT ON | Actual Execution Plan (SSMS)
MySQL        EXPLAIN | EXPLAIN ANALYZE (8.0.18+)
DB2          EXPLAIN PLAN FOR ... + db2exfmt

Core Vocabulary

text
OPERATOR TYPES (conceptual — names vary by DB)

Scan:
  Seq Scan / Table Scan     → read entire table (or partition)
  Index Scan                → traverse B-tree index, fetch heap rows
  Index Only Scan           → index has all columns (covering)
  Bitmap Index Scan         → build bitmap from index, then heap fetch

Join:
  Nested Loop               → for each outer row, probe inner
  Hash Join                 → build hash on inner, probe outer
  Merge Join                → both inputs sorted, merge

Other:
  Sort, HashAggregate, GroupAggregate
  Materialize, CTE Scan
  Filter, Limit

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Query Optimizers and EXPLAIN

text
1970s   System R — cost-based optimization (CBO) foundation
        Rule-based optimizers (RBO) — fixed rules, predictable but dumb

1980s   Oracle cost-based optimizer; EXPLAIN PLAN table
        DB2 optimizer; statistics on tables

1990s   PostgreSQL Query Optimizer (GEQO for large joins)
        SQL Server showplan; histogram statistics

2000s   PostgreSQL EXPLAIN ANALYZE — actual row counts vs estimates
        Extended statistics, auto-vacuum stats collection

2010s   PostgreSQL JSON plans for tooling (pev2, explain.depesz.com)
        Oracle SQL Monitor, Real-Time SQL Monitoring
        Adaptive query plans (Oracle, SQL Server)

2020s   PostgreSQL: parallel query in plans, JIT nodes
        Hypothetical indexes (pg_hypo, some clouds)
        ORM logging: spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics
        AI-assisted plan analysis — still requires human verification

Historical Lesson

Early optimizers used rules ("if index exists, use it"). Modern engines use cost models driven by statistics. EXPLAIN shows the optimizer's belief about your data — when beliefs are wrong, plans are wrong. Lesson 25 teaches you to read that belief.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does EXPLAIN Solve?

Problem 1: Query Is Slow — Where Is Time Spent?

sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM transactions
WHERE account_id = 5001
  AND created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '90 days'
ORDER BY created_at DESC;
-- Answer: Seq Scan on 50M rows? Missing index? Sort spilling to disk?

Problem 2: Wrong Plan — Nested Loop on Large Tables

text
Estimated: 100 rows from customers
Actual:    2,000,000 rows (stale stats)
Plan:      Nested Loop → 2M index probes → timeout

EXPLAIN ANALYZE reveals: actual rows >> estimated rows
Fix: ANALYZE table; better index; rewrite query

Problem 3: Index Exists but Not Used

sql
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM payments WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01';
-- Seq Scan — why?
-- Function on column, low selectivity, stats say most rows match, wrong datatype cast

Problem 4: Production-Safe Investigation

text
EXPLAIN without ANALYZE → no query execution (safe on prod for many queries)
EXPLAIN ANALYZE → runs query — use read replica or off-peak with LIMIT care

Problem 5: Release Validation

text
Flyway adds index idx_payments_customer_created
Before/after EXPLAIN on critical report — verify Index Scan appears
CI: pg_query or explain plan regression tests for top 10 queries

Unified Problem Statement

EXPLAIN makes the optimizer's execution strategy visible — enabling diagnosis of slow queries, missing indexes, bad estimates, and regressions before and after schema or query changes.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Not Just "Add an Index"?

Indexes Are Not Always the Answer

text
EXPLAIN shows:
  - Seq Scan chosen because 80% of table matches — index + heap fetch worse
  - Sort cost dominates — work_mem spill
  - Hash Join cheaper than Nested Loop at this cardinality
Without plan: blind index creation wastes write amplification

Cost-Based Reasoning

text
Optimizer compares:
  Nested Loop cost = outer_rows × inner_probe_cost
  Hash Join cost = build_hash(inner) + probe(outer)

EXPLAIN exposes which branch won and estimated costs
Architect validates: does plan match data distribution?

Developer–DBA Common Language

text
"This report does Seq Scan + HashAggregate on 10M payments"
DBA: "Add partial index WHERE status = 'COMPLETED'"
Dev: EXPLAIN after — Index Scan, 200ms → 2ms

ORM Hides SQL

java
// Hibernate generates:
select ... from payments p0_ cross join customers c0_ ...  -- accidental cartesian
// EXPLAIN the logged SQL — ORM bugs visible only in plan

Part 5 — Internal Working

How EXPLAIN Works Internally

Pipeline: SQL → Plan

text
1. Parse SQL → query tree
2. Rewrite (rules):
     - View expansion (Lesson 20)
     - RLS policy injection
     - Subquery pull-up / flattening (Lessons 17–18)
3. Optimize (cost-based):
     - Generate candidate paths (join orders, scan methods)
     - Use statistics: row counts, distinct values, histograms
     - Pick minimum total cost plan
4. EXPLAIN → serialize plan tree to text/JSON
5. EXPLAIN ANALYZE → execute + instrument each node with actual rows/time

PostgreSQL Cost Units

text
cost=0.00..1234.56
      ↑      ↑
   startup  total

Arbitrary units — not milliseconds
Compare relative costs within same plan
seq_page_cost, cpu_tuple_cost, random_page_cost GUCs tune model

EXPLAIN ANALYZE adds:
  actual time=0.045..892.123 rows=50000 loops=1
  BUFFERS: shared hit=1000 read=5000  (cache vs disk)

Statistics the Optimizer Uses

text
pg_stats / ALL_TAB_STATISTICS:
  n_distinct (distinct values)
  most_common_vals, most_common_freqs
  histogram_bounds (value distribution)
  correlation (physical order vs logical)

Stale stats → wrong row estimates → wrong join algorithm
ANALYZE / DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATS refreshes

Join Algorithm Selection (Simplified)

text
Nested Loop:
  Good: outer small, inner indexed on join key
  Bad:  large outer × large inner

Hash Join:
  Good: equi-join, build side fits work_mem
  Bad:  hash too big → disk batches

Merge Join:
  Good: both inputs pre-sorted on join key
  Bad:  need sort first if unsorted

Plan Caching

text
Prepared statements / JDBC bind params:
  Generic plan vs custom plan per parameter values (PostgreSQL)
  EXPLAIN with literal vs $1 may show different plans

Oracle: bind peeking, adaptive cursor sharing
SQL Server: parameter sniffing — plan good for first value, bad for others

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Plans and Physical Storage

Seq Scan I/O

text
Reads heap pages sequentially or via bitmap
EXPLAIN BUFFERS:
  shared read=10000  → pages from disk
  shared hit=50000   → pages from buffer cache

Cold cache first run slow; warm cache misleading — test twice

Index Scan I/O

text
Index Scan:
  Traverse B-tree index pages (random I/O)
  For each matching entry → heap fetch (random) unless Index Only Scan

Index Only Scan:
  Visibility map check (PostgreSQL) — skip heap if all-visible page
  Covering index includes all SELECT columns

Sort/Materialize Spill

text
Sort node:
  Fits work_mem → quicksort in memory
  Exceeds work_mem → external sort → temp files (pgsql_tmp)

EXPLAIN ANALYZE:
  Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 2048kB
Architect signal: increase work_mem for session OR reduce rows sorted

Parallel Query (PostgreSQL)

text
Gather
  ├── Parallel Seq Scan (workers 2-4)
  └── Partial HashAggregate
        └── Gather Merge

Workers share I/O — plan shows parallelism chosen for large scans

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Plan Operators and Memory

OperatorMemorySpill if exceeded
Hash Join (build side)work_memHash batches to disk
HashAggregatework_memDisk
Sortwork_memExternal merge
Materializework_memTuplestore disk
Nested LoopMinimalN/A
Bitmap Heap ScanBitmap pagesUsually in memory

work_mem Scope

text
Per operation per query — not per connection total
4 Hash Joins in one query → up to 4 × work_mem (simplified)
50 concurrent queries × 256MB work_mem → OOM risk

Reporting session: SET LOCAL work_mem = '512MB';
OLTP pool: keep moderate default (4–64MB)

EXPLAIN ANALYZE Does Not Show All Memory

text
Shows sort/hash spill via Disk: kB
Full memory: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, SETTINGS) in PG 12+

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Reading a Plan Top to Bottom

Flow 1: Simple Index Lookup

sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 5001;
text
Index Scan using accounts_pkey on accounts
  Index Cond: (account_id = 5001)
  Buffers: shared hit=3
Planning Time: 0.1 ms
Execution Time: 0.05 ms

Flow: root → index scan → 1 row returned
PK lookup — optimal OLTP pattern

Flow 2: Join Report Query

sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT c.email, SUM(a.balance)
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.region = 'APAC' AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY c.email;
text
HashAggregate
  -> Hash Join
        Hash Cond: (a.customer_id = c.customer_id)
        -> Seq Scan on accounts (filter: status = 'ACTIVE')
        -> Hash
              -> Index Scan on customers (region = 'APAC')

Execution flow:
1. Scan APAC customers → build hash
2. Scan active accounts → probe hash (or reverse depending on plan)
3. Aggregate by email
Actual rows at each node vs estimate — check for 10× mismatch

Flow 3: Bad Nested Loop (Diagnosis)

text
Nested Loop
  -> Seq Scan on customers (actual rows=2000000)
  -> Index Scan on accounts (loops=2000000, actual rows=3 each)

Problem: 2M outer loops × index probe
Fix: join order swap, Hash Join, filter customers earlier, stats refresh

Flow 4: Sort + Limit (Top-N)

sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
ORDER BY balance DESC LIMIT 20;
text
Limit
  -> Sort (top-N heapsort if optimizer smart)
        -> Index Scan on idx_accounts_status_balance

Ideal: Index Scan backward on (status, balance DESC) — no full sort
Bad: Seq Scan all active + sort millions

Flow 5: Subquery InitPlan

text
InitPlan 1
  -> Aggregate: avg(balance)
  -> Index Scan ...
  -> Seq Scan on accounts
    Filter: (balance > (InitPlan 1).col1)

Inner aggregate runs once — Lesson 17 scalar subquery
Look for InitPlan vs SubPlan (per-row) — performance cliff

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

How to Analyze Plans Systematically

The 5-Step EXPLAIN Workflow

text
1. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on representative query + bind values
2. Find highest "actual time" node (usually largest child)
3. Compare actual rows vs estimated rows at that node (10× = stats problem)
4. Check scan type: Seq Scan on large filtered table → index candidate?
5. Check Sort/Hash Disk spill → work_mem or reduce rows

Red Flags in Plans

Red FlagLikely Cause
Seq Scan on huge table + selective WHEREMissing/partial index
Nested Loop + high loops=Wrong join order/cardinality
actual rows >> rows estimateStale statistics
External Sort Disk: largework_mem / missing index for ORDER BY
Hash Batches: >1Hash too big for work_mem
SubPlan per rowCorrelated subquery not unnested
Parallel not used on big scanmax_parallel_workers, cost threshold
Bitmap Heap Scan + high recheckLow index selectivity

Good Patterns for Banking OLTP

text
PK lookup:              Index Scan on PK — sub-ms
FK lookup:              Index Scan on FK index
Recent transactions:    Index Scan (account_id, created_at DESC)
Aggregation report:     HashAggregate on replica — acceptable

Production EXPLAIN Safety

text
Safe:  EXPLAIN (no ANALYZE) on prod — planning only
Risk:  EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs DML side effects, locks, load
Use:   read replica, sanitized query, transaction READ ONLY
PostgreSQL: EXPLAIN in transaction without ANALYZE for DDL check

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

OperatorTypical TimeNotes
Index Scan PKO(log n)n = table rows
Seq ScanO(n) pagesParallel: O(n/workers)
Nested LoopO(outer × inner_probe)Disaster if outer large
Hash JoinO(a + b)Build + probe
Merge JoinO(a + b) or + sort cost
SortO(n log n)Spill increases I/O
HashAggregateO(n) average

Plan choice changes asymptotic class — Nested Loop vs Hash Join is the classic interview and production trap.

EXPLAIN Masterclass (PostgreSQL-Focused)

Basic EXPLAIN Options

sql

Before/After Index

sql
-- Before: Seq Scan

FROM payments
WHERE customer_id = 1001
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 10;

ON payments (customer_id, created_at DESC);

-- After: Index Scan + Limit — no Sort node
EXPLAIN ANALYZE ... ;

Join Order and Hash Join

sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT t.transaction_id, t.amount, c.email
FROM transactions t
JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = t.account_id
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = a.customer_id
WHERE t.created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7 days'
  AND c.region = 'APAC';
-- Look for: date filter on transactions early, join method, buffer reads

Detect Stale Statistics

sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM accounts WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';
-- rows estimate vs actual

ANALYZE accounts;
EXPLAIN ANALYZE ... ;
-- Re-compare estimates

Oracle Pattern

sql
EXPLAIN PLAN FOR
SELECT /*+ INDEX(p payments_customer_idx) */
       payment_id, amount
FROM payments p
WHERE customer_id = 1001;

SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY(NULL, NULL, 'ALLSTATS LAST'));
-- DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR for executed SQL in V$SQL

SQL Server Pattern

sql
SET STATISTICS IO ON;
SET STATISTICS TIME ON;

SELECT p.payment_id, p.amount
FROM dbo.payments p
WHERE p.customer_id = 1001;

-- Actual plan from SSMS or:
-- SET SHOWPLAN_XML ON;

MySQL 8

sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT payment_id, amount
FROM payments
WHERE customer_id = 1001
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 10;
-- Extra column in plain EXPLAIN: Using filesort, Using temporary

Force Plan Comparison (Test Only)

sql
-- PostgreSQL: disable seq scan to test index path (test env only!)
SET enable_seqscan = off;
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ... ;
RESET enable_seqscan;
-- Never leave disabled in prod

Part 12 — Production Usage

EXPLAIN in Production Operations

Slow Query Triage Runbook

text
1. Capture SQL from pg_stat_statements / APM / slow log
2. Normalize parameters → EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on replica
3. Identify top time node
4. Check waits (PG: pg_stat_activity.wait_event_type)
5. Fix: index, rewrite, stats, partition prune, cache
6. Re-EXPLAIN — document baseline in ticket
7. Monitor p95 latency post-deploy

pg_stat_statements

sql
SELECT query, calls, mean_exec_time, rows, shared_blks_read
FROM pg_stat_statements
WHERE query LIKE '%payments%'
ORDER BY mean_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 10;
-- Then EXPLAIN top offenders

Banking Report SLA

text
Report: v_customer_360 style aggregation
Baseline EXPLAIN stored in Git: reports/customer-360.explain
Flyway index migration must update baseline in PR review
SLA: p95 < 2s on read replica — plan shows HashAggregate < 500ms

When EXPLAIN ANALYZE Is Forbidden

text
Destructive DML EXPLAIN ANALYZE — never on prod
DELETE without WHERE accident risk with ANALYZE
Large cartesian product — can run hours
Use: EXPLAIN only, or BEGIN READ ONLY + LIMIT wrapper for SELECT subset

java
@Repository
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class QueryPlanDiagnostics {

    private final JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate;

    public String explainAnalyze(String sql, Object... args) {
        String explainSql = "EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT TEXT) " + sql;
        return String.join("\n", jdbcTemplate.queryForList(explainSql, String.class, args));
    }
}
// Secure behind admin role — never public API

    assertThat(plan).contains("Index Scan");
    assertThat(plan).doesNotContain("Seq Scan on payments");
}

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

ORM and Execution Plans

N+1 Visible in EXPLAIN

text
Hibernate generates 1001 queries:
  1 × SELECT customers
  1000 × SELECT accounts WHERE customer_id = ?

EXPLAIN each — 1000 Index Scans OK individually but 1000 round trips kill latency
Fix: JOIN FETCH — one plan with Hash Join

Cartesian Product

java
// Bad JPQL
SELECT c FROM Customer c, Account a WHERE c.customerId = a.customerId

EXPLAIN shows:
  Nested Loop
    Seq Scan customers
    Materialize Seq Scan accounts  -- or cross join explosion

Batch Fetch vs Plan

java
@BatchSize(size = 50)
@OneToMany ...
// Hibernate IN (?,?,...) batch — EXPLAIN shows Index Scan with IN list
// Better than N+1, worse than JOIN FETCH for full load

Pagination OFFSET in Plan

sql
-- Hibernate: setFirstResult(100000), setMaxResults(20)
EXPLAIN ANALYZE ... OFFSET 100000 LIMIT 20;
-- Seq Scan or Index Scan still reads/skips 100000 rows — Lesson 11
Plan proves keyset pagination need

Native Query — Full Control

java
@Query(value = """
    SELECT payment_id, amount FROM payments
    WHERE customer_id = :cid ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20
    """, nativeQuery = true)
// EXPLAIN-friendly — explicit SQL matches plan tuning

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

EXPLAIN in Architecture Governance

Performance Baseline Library

text
Repository: perf-baselines/
  payment-by-customer.sql
  payment-by-customer.explain.json   (ANALYZE on seeded data)
  payment-by-customer.notes.md

PR checklist:
  □ EXPLAIN diff attached for changed queries

Read Replica Strategy

text
OLTP primary: EXPLAIN (no ANALYZE) for quick checks only
Reporting replica: EXPLAIN ANALYZE for heavy reports
Different data volume on replica — stats should match prod (same ANALYZE schedule)

Multi-Tenant and RLS

text
EXPLAIN shows RLS policy as Filter or SubPlan

Bad: policy function prevents index use — architect review

Cloud Managed DB

text
RDS/Aurora Performance Insights → top SQL
Click plan or pull from pg_stat_statements
Auto EXPLAIN extensions (auto_explain log nested statements > 1s)
Architect enables auto_explain on staging, sample on prod

Decision: Index vs Rewrite vs Cache

text
EXPLAIN shows Seq Scan 10M rows for 10 rows returned → index
EXPLAIN shows Hash Join OK but 5s sort spill → rewrite + work_mem or index for ORDER BY
EXPLAIN shows plan optimal but still slow → read replica, cache, materialized view
EXPLAIN wrong estimates persist → extended statistics, increase default_statistics_target

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: EXPLAIN ANALYZE on Production DML

sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM payments WHERE status = 'PENDING';
-- Actually deletes — disaster
-- ✅ EXPLAIN without ANALYZE for DML shape only

Mistake 2: Trusting Cold-Cache First Run Only

text
First ANALYZE: shared read=1M (slow)
Second run: shared hit=1M (fast)
Report both or warm cache intentionally

Mistake 3: Different Bind Values, Different Plan

sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE ... WHERE customer_id = 1001;  -- Index Scan
-- customer_id rarely selective value → Seq Scan in prod
Test with typical AND worst-case parameters

Mistake 4: Adding Index Without EXPLAIN Verification

text
CREATE INDEX — plan still Seq Scan because:
  query wraps column in function, wrong column order, OR low selectivity
Always EXPLAIN after

Mistake 5: Ignoring Planning Time

text
Planning Time: 45 ms on simple query × 10K QPS = problem
Generic plan vs custom plan issues — prepared statement tuning

Mistake 6: Reading Only Top Node

text
Limit 0.1ms at top
  Sort 8000ms below — real problem hidden
Drill to highest actual time child

Mistake 7: ORM SQL Not EXPLAIN'd

text
Optimize Java code while DB runs cartesian join
Always EXPLAIN the actual SQL Hibernate emits

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What does EXPLAIN do?

Shows planned execution strategy for SQL — operators, join order, scan types, estimated costs.

Q2: EXPLAIN vs EXPLAIN ANALYZE?

EXPLAIN plans only; ANALYZE executes and shows actual rows and timings.

Q3: What is Seq Scan?

Full table scan — reads heap pages; OK for small/unselective, bad for selective filters on large tables.

Q4: Index Scan vs Index Only Scan?

Index Scan fetches heap rows; Index Only Scan answers from index when covering + visibility allows.

Q5: Why do plans change after data grows?

Statistics and selectivity change; optimizer picks different join/scan algorithms.

Mid-Level

Q6: actual rows much larger than estimated — cause?

Stale statistics, missing histogram, correlated columns not captured, skewed data.

Q7: Nested Loop vs Hash Join — when each?

NL: small outer + indexed inner. Hash: larger equi-joins, build side fits memory.

Q8: Red flag in EXPLAIN ANALYZE for OLTP?

Seq Scan on million-row table returning few rows; SubPlan per row; sort spill on small LIMIT query.

Q9: How investigate slow ORDER BY LIMIT?

Check for Index Scan matching ORDER BY columns; Sort node with high cost; top-N optimization.

Q10: Safe EXPLAIN on production?

EXPLAIN without ANALYZE for SELECT; use replica for ANALYZE; never ANALYZE destructive DML.

Senior

Q11: Parameter sniffing / bind variable plan instability?

Plan optimized for first bind value; bad for others — fix with adaptive plans, hints, rewrite, OR literals on skewed values (careful).

Q12: BUFFERS interpretation?

shared hit = cache; read = disk I/O — high read on warm cache indicates working set exceeds memory.

Q13: InitPlan vs SubPlan?

InitPlan runs once; SubPlan per outer row — scalar subquery performance cliff.

Q14: How validate index migration?

Before/after EXPLAIN ANALYZE on replica; compare node types, execution time, buffer reads; pg_stat_user_indexes idx_scan increase.

Staff / Architect

Q15: EXPLAIN governance in 20-team org?

Baseline library, pg_stat_statements, PR plan diff for critical SQL, auto_explain on slow threshold, read replica analysis pipeline.

Q16: Plan good but query slow — next steps?

Lock contention, vacuum bloat, hardware I/O, synchronous replication lag, network, connection pool wait — not optimizer issue.

Scenario

Scenario: "Report timeout after deploy; no code change in report SQL."

Stats auto-analyzed poorly after bulk load; EXPLAIN shows Nested Loop vs yesterday Hash Join; ANALYZE; compare estimates; check new data volume crossing threshold; consider extended stats or join hint temporarily while fixing stats job.

PostgreSQL Commands

sql

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE) SELECT ...;
EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON, ANALYZE) SELECT ...;
ANALYZE table_name;

Reading Plans

text
Top node = last step (LIMIT, Sort)
Drill down to highest actual time
Compare actual rows vs rows estimate
Check: Scan type, Join type, Sort spill, SubPlan
Buffers: hit vs read

Workflow

text
1. Capture SQL (log, pg_stat_statements)
2. EXPLAIN ANALYZE on replica
3. Find slowest node
4. Fix index / stats / rewrite
5. Re-EXPLAIN + monitor

Red Flags

text
Seq Scan large + selective WHERE
Nested Loop huge loops
actual >> estimated
External Sort Disk
SubPlan per row
OFFSET huge cost
