Part 1 — Concept

What Is an Index?

An index is a secondary data structure that speeds up lookup, filter, join, and sort operations by maintaining an ordered mapping from index key values → row locations (heap TID, ROWID, or clustered key). It is not free: every index adds storage, write amplification, and maintenance on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE.

sql
-- PostgreSQL: B-tree index (default)
CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_customer_status
ON accounts (customer_id, status);

-- Query that can use it
SELECT account_id, balance
FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001
  AND status = 'ACTIVE';

Index vs Full Table Scan

text
Without index on customer_id:
  Seq Scan → read every page of accounts → filter customer_id = 1001
  Cost: O(n) pages

With index on customer_id:
  Index Scan → traverse B-tree to customer_id = 1001 entries → fetch matching heap rows
  Cost: O(log n) index + k heap fetches (k = matching rows)

Index Classification

text
INDEX TYPES

├── By structure (PostgreSQL common set)
│   ├── B-tree (default)     → =, <, >, <=, >=, BETWEEN, LIKE 'prefix%'
│   ├── Hash                 → equality only (=)
│   ├── GiST / SP-GiST       → geometry, full-text, ranges
│   ├── GIN                    → arrays, JSONB, full-text
│   └── BRIN                   → very large, naturally ordered tables (time series)
│
├── By column count
│   ├── Single-column
│   └── Composite (multi-column)
│
├── By predicate
│   ├── Full index           → all rows
│   ├── Partial index        → WHERE clause subset
│   └── Expression index     → ON (lower(email))
│
├── By coverage
│   ├── Non-covering         → index + heap fetch for other columns
│   └── Covering / INCLUDE   → index contains all needed columns
│
└── By constraint role
    ├── Primary key index    → unique + not null
    ├── UNIQUE index
    └── Plain secondary index

ASCII — B-Tree Concept

text
                    [ 5000 | 12000 ]
                   /               \
        [1000|3000]                 [8000|15000]
        /    |    \                 /    |     \
   leaf pages (sorted keys + pointers to heap rows)

Search customer_id = 1001:
  Root → left branch → leaf → entries (1001, ...) → heap fetch

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Database Indexes

text
1970s   B-tree (Bayer, McCreight) — balanced tree, O(log n) search/insert
        IBM System R uses B-tree indexes

1980s   Oracle indexes: B-tree, bitmap indexes (warehouse)
        Clustered index (SQL Server) — table data in index order

1990s   Covering indexes concept — index-only access
        Composite index column order rules established
        Partial indexes in PostgreSQL emerging

2000s   PostgreSQL GIN/GiST for non-scalar types
        Online index creation (CONCURRENTLY) — reduce lock impact
        Index skip scan (Oracle) — composite index partial use

2010s   PostgreSQL BRIN for time-series / append-only
        INCLUDE columns (covering) — PG 11
        Index-only scans with visibility map optimization

2020s   Automatic index advisors (cloud consoles, HypoPG)
        UUID v7 / time-ordered PK discussion — index locality
        Over-indexing backlash — write amplification in high-TPS OLTP

Historical Lesson

Indexes were invented to avoid full scans on disk-resident data. In the SSD era, random I/O is cheaper but write amplification and buffer cache pollution remain real. Modern architects index proven query patterns, not every column — and use partial/covering indexes surgically.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Do Indexes Solve?

Problem 1: Point Lookup (OLTP Primary Key / FK)

sql
SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 5001;
-- PK index → microseconds vs seq scan millions of rows

Problem 2: Selective Filter

sql
SELECT * FROM payments
WHERE customer_id = 1001
  AND created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days';
-- Composite (customer_id, created_at DESC) avoids scanning all payments

Problem 3: Join Acceleration

sql
SELECT c.email, a.balance
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id;
-- Index on accounts(customer_id) → nested loop or hash build efficient

Problem 4: ORDER BY Avoiding Sort

sql
SELECT account_id, balance FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'
ORDER BY balance DESC
LIMIT 20;
-- Index (status, balance DESC) → read top 20 in order, no Sort node

Problem 5: Uniqueness Enforcement

sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_payments_client_request
ON payments (client_request_id);
-- Fast lookup + constraint — idempotency key (Lesson 24)

Unified Problem Statement

Indexes trade extra storage and write cost for faster reads on specific access paths — lookups, joins, sorts, and uniqueness — when predicates are selective enough to beat sequential scan.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Not Scan Every Table?

Disk and Memory Economics

text
Table: 50M payments × 200 bytes ≈ 10 GB
Index on customer_id: perhaps 1–2 GB additional

Query: 100 payments for one customer
  Seq Scan: touch ~10 GB
  Index Scan: touch ~log(50M) index pages + 100 heap pages

Constraint Enforcement

text
UNIQUE index:
  INSERT checks index — O(log n) duplicate detection
  Without index: full scan per insert — impossible at scale

Sort Elimination

text
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10
Without matching index: sort all matching rows → work_mem or disk spill
With index: read first 10 entries in order — O(10)

When Indexes Fail to Help

text
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'  -- 95% of rows ACTIVE → seq scan often cheaper
WHERE amount > 0         -- not selective
LOWER(email) = 'x'       -- function prevents index unless expression index
SELECT *                 -- wide rows, heap fetch heavy even with index

Part 5 — Internal Working

B-Tree Index Internals

Structure

text
B-Tree (PostgreSQL B-tree implementation — Lehman-Yao variant)

Internal nodes: keys + child pointers
Leaf nodes: keys + TIDs (heap row pointers) [+ INCLUDE columns]
Balanced height: typically 3–4 levels for millions of rows
Page size: 8 KB default (PostgreSQL) — keys per page depends on key width

Search Algorithm

text
Lookup key K:
  1. Start at root page
  2. Binary search keys in page → follow child pointer
  3. Repeat until leaf
  4. Leaf: find K or range start
  5. For each matching entry: TID → heap page fetch (unless index-only)

Insert:
  Find leaf → insert key+TID
  Page full → split → propagate up (rarely root split increases height)

Delete:
  Mark dead / remove key → page may underflow → merge/borrow

Composite Index — Left-to-Prefix Rule

sql
CREATE INDEX idx ON accounts (customer_id, status, balance);

Usable for:
  WHERE customer_id = 1001                           ✅ (leading column)
  WHERE customer_id = 1001 AND status = 'ACTIVE'     ✅
  WHERE customer_id = 1001 ORDER BY status, balance ✅

NOT usable for (typically):
  WHERE status = 'ACTIVE' alone                      ❌ (skip leading column)
  WHERE balance > 10000 alone                        ❌

Column order matters: most selective / equality first, range last
Pattern: (customer_id, created_at DESC) for customer + recent range

Index-Only Scan (Covering)

sql
CREATE INDEX idx_cover ON payments (customer_id, created_at DESC)
INCLUDE (amount, status);  -- PostgreSQL INCLUDE

SELECT amount, status, created_at
FROM payments
WHERE customer_id = 1001
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 10;

Plan: Index Only Scan — no heap fetch if visibility map says all-visible pages
Requires: all SELECT/WHERE columns in index (+ heap visibility check)

Partial Index

sql
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_pending
ON payments (created_at)
WHERE status = 'PENDING';

-- Smaller index — only pending rows
-- Used only when query predicate implies status = 'PENDING'
SELECT * FROM payments
WHERE status = 'PENDING'
  AND created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '1 hour';

Bitmap Index Scan (PostgreSQL)

text
For medium selectivity OR multiple conditions:
  1. Bitmap Index Scan on idx1 → bitmap of TIDs
  2. Bitmap Index Scan on idx2 → AND/OR bitmaps
  3. Bitmap Heap Scan → fetch heap pages in physical order (reduces random I/O)

Clustered vs Heap (Database Differences)

text
PostgreSQL: table heap unordered — all indexes secondary (except cluster one-time reorder)
SQL Server clustered index: table data in index order — PK often clustered
Oracle Index Organized Table (IOT): similar concept
Architect impact: clustered PK → range scans on PK are sequential I/O

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Index Physical Storage

Index Size Formula (Approximate)

text
Index size ≈ row_count × (key_bytes + pointer_bytes + overhead) / fillfactor

BIGINT key + TID: ~16–24 bytes per entry + page overhead
UUID PK index: 16 bytes key — nearly 2× wider than BIGINT
Composite (BIGINT, TIMESTAMPTZ, VARCHAR(20)): wider → fewer keys per page → taller tree

Fillfactor

sql
CREATE INDEX idx ON accounts (customer_id) WITH (fillfactor = 90);
-- Leave 10% page space for HOT updates (PostgreSQL) — reduce index bloat on updated columns
-- Default 90 for btree — trade space for update performance

Bloat and Vacuum

text
UPDATE account balance → new row version in heap → index entries updated (unless HOT)
DELETE → dead tuples — index entries dead until VACUUM
Bloated index: more pages than necessary — EXPLAIN shows more buffer reads
REINDEX CONCURRENTLY / pg_repack — operational maintenance

Write Amplification

text
INSERT 1 payment row with 5 secondary indexes:
  1 heap insert + 5 index inserts + WAL for each
UPDATE indexed column:
  Old index entry delete + new insert (or HOT if same page, no indexed col change)
DELETE:
  Mark heap dead + index cleanup on vacuum

High-TPS OLTP: every unnecessary index costs write throughput

Partial Index Storage Win

text
payments: 100M rows, 1M PENDING
Full index on (status, created_at): 100M entries
Partial WHERE status = 'PENDING': 1M entries — 100× smaller

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Indexes and Memory

ComponentMemory Role
Shared buffersIndex pages cached like heap — hot index stays in RAM
Index-only scanNo heap fetch — less cache pollution
Wide covering indexMore pages — may evict other data from cache
Hash join buildSeparate from index — index speeds probe side
SortIndex matching ORDER BY avoids sort memory entirely

Buffer Cache Strategy

text
OLTP hot path:
  PK + critical FK indexes always in cache after warm-up
EXPLAIN BUFFERS:
  shared hit on index pages — good
  shared read on index — cold cache or working set too large

Over-indexing:
  15 indexes on payments — INSERT evicts useful pages from cache
Architect caps secondary indexes per table (e.g. 5–7 without ADR)

work_mem vs Index

text
Index eliminates Sort node → work_mem irrelevant for that query
No index → Sort spills → work_mem matters (Lesson 25)

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Index Usage Execution Flows

Flow 1: Primary Key Lookup

sql
SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 5001;
text
1. Planner: account_id is PK → Index Scan using accounts_pkey
2. Load root → internal → leaf for 5001
3. TID → heap page → row version (MVCC check)
4. Return row
Buffers: ~3–5 pages typical

Flow 2: Composite Index Range + ORDER BY

sql
SELECT payment_id, amount, created_at
FROM payments
WHERE customer_id = 1001
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
text
Index: (customer_id, created_at DESC)

1. Index Scan: seek customer_id = 1001
2. Read leaf entries in created_at DESC order
3. Stop after 20 rows (Limit) — top-N optimization
4. Heap fetch 20 rows for amount if not INCLUDE
No Sort node in plan

Flow 3: Index Only Scan

sql
-- covering index includes amount, status
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT amount, status FROM payments
WHERE customer_id = 1001 AND created_at > '2024-01-01';
text
1. Index Only Scan on idx_cover
2. Visibility map check per page — all-visible → skip heap
3. Return columns from index leaf
Fewer buffer reads than Index Scan

Flow 4: Index Not Used — Low Selectivity

sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';
-- 95% rows ACTIVE

Plan: Seq Scan on accounts
  Filter: status = 'ACTIVE'
Reason: optimizer estimates reading index + 95% heap worse than one seq scan
Partial index rarely helps if most rows match

Flow 5: Foreign Key Without Index (Disaster)

sql
DELETE FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 1001;
-- Child accounts: FK check must find referencing rows
-- No index on accounts(customer_id):
Plan: Seq Scan accounts for each delete or lock escalation — slow, blocks
Fix: CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_customer ON accounts(customer_id);

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Index Design and Performance Rules

Index Design Checklist

text
1. Identify query patterns (pg_stat_statements, APM)
2. EXPLAIN ANALYZE — Seq Scan on large table? (Lesson 25)
3. Leading column = equality filter columns first
4. Range/sort columns last in composite
5. Consider partial index for skewed subsets (PENDING, FAILED)
6. INCLUDE columns for index-only scan on hot SELECT
7. UNIQUE on idempotency / business keys
8. Index all FK columns (child side)
9. Measure write impact on INSERT TPS
10. REINDEX/monitor bloat quarterly

Selectivity Rule of Thumb

text
Index likely wins when matching rows < ~5–15% of table (heuristic, not law)
Highly selective: customer_id = one value on 100M payments ✅
Low selective: status = 'ACTIVE' on 95% rows ❌ seq scan

Combine with table size: small tables always seq scan (cheaper to read whole table)
PostgreSQL: random_page_cost vs seq_page_cost tuning affects decision

Composite Column Order Examples

sql
-- Query: WHERE customer_id = ? AND created_at BETWEEN ? AND ?
-- ✅ (customer_id, created_at)
-- ❌ (created_at, customer_id) — range on leading column blocks customer filter in index

-- Query: WHERE region = ? AND status = ? (both equality)
-- Order by lower cardinality first? Debate — test EXPLAIN
-- Often: (region, status) if region has fewer distinct values

Anti-Patterns

sql
-- ❌ Index every column
CREATE INDEX ON payments (amount);
CREATE INDEX ON payments (status);
CREATE INDEX ON payments (currency);
-- Write amplification; optimizer may pick wrong index

-- ❌ Redundant indexes
CREATE INDEX idx1 ON accounts (customer_id);
CREATE INDEX idx2 ON accounts (customer_id, status);
-- idx1 redundant if idx2 exists — drop idx1

-- ❌ Wrong column order
CREATE INDEX ON transactions (created_at, account_id);
-- WHERE account_id = ? AND created_at > ? — put account_id first

-- ❌ Function without expression index
WHERE LOWER(email) = 'user@bank.com'
-- Need: CREATE INDEX ON customers (lower(email));

Drop Unused Indexes

sql
-- PostgreSQL
SELECT schemaname, relname, indexrelname, idx_scan, idx_tup_read
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
WHERE idx_scan = 0
  AND indexrelname NOT LIKE '%pkey%'
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(indexrelid) DESC;
-- idx_scan = 0 since stats reset — verify over weeks before drop

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

OperationWithout IndexWith B-Tree Index
Point lookupO(n) pagesO(log n) index + O(1) heap
Range scan k rowsO(n)O(log n + k)
INSERTO(1) heapO(log n) per index
DELETEO(1) heap markO(log n) per index entry
UNIQUE checkO(n)O(log n)

n = table rows, m = number of secondary indexes — INSERT cost O(m log n)

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Index Masterclass

Essential Banking Indexes

sql
-- Primary keys (automatic)
-- accounts(account_id), payments(payment_id), customers(customer_id)

-- Foreign keys — ALWAYS index child side
CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_customer_id
ON accounts (customer_id);

CREATE INDEX idx_payments_customer_id
ON payments (customer_id);

CREATE INDEX idx_transactions_account_id
ON transactions (account_id);

-- Idempotency
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_payments_client_request
ON payments (client_request_id);

-- Hot OLTP: recent payments per customer
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_customer_created
ON payments (customer_id, created_at DESC);

-- Covering index for list screen (PostgreSQL)
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_customer_list
ON payments (customer_id, created_at DESC)
INCLUDE (amount, status, currency);

-- Partial: pending payment sweeper job
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_pending_created
ON payments (created_at)
WHERE status = 'PENDING';

-- Partial: active accounts only (if majority closed/archived)
CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_active_customer
ON accounts (customer_id, balance DESC)
WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';

-- Expression: case-insensitive email login
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_customers_email_lower
ON customers (lower(email));

-- Transactions: account statement
CREATE INDEX idx_transactions_acct_created
ON transactions (account_id, created_at DESC, transaction_id);
-- transaction_id tie-breaker for keyset pagination (Lesson 11)

Online Index Creation (Production)

sql
-- PostgreSQL: avoid long write locks
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_payments_customer_created
ON payments (customer_id, created_at DESC);
-- Cannot run inside transaction block
-- Failed run may leave INVALID index — REINDEX CONCURRENTLY

-- Oracle
CREATE INDEX idx_name ON payments(customer_id) ONLINE;

-- SQL Server
CREATE INDEX idx_name ON payments(customer_id) WITH (ONLINE = ON);

Verify Index Usage

sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT payment_id, amount, status, created_at
FROM payments
WHERE customer_id = 1001
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
-- Expect: Index Scan or Index Only Scan on idx_payments_customer_list

Keyset Pagination Index

sql
-- Query: WHERE (created_at, payment_id) < (:ts, :id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_keyset
ON payments (customer_id, created_at DESC, payment_id DESC);

SELECT payment_id, amount, created_at
FROM payments
WHERE customer_id = 1001
  AND (created_at, payment_id) < ('2024-06-01', 90001)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC
LIMIT 20;

BRIN for Append-Only Time Series (Archival)

sql
-- transactions_archive: billions of rows, inserted by time
CREATE INDEX idx_txn_archive_created_brin
ON transactions_archive USING brin (created_at)
WITH (pages_per_range = 128);
-- Tiny index size — good for wide time-range scans on cold data

Oracle Function-Based Index

sql
CREATE INDEX idx_cust_upper_email ON customers (UPPER(email));
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE UPPER(email) = 'USER@BANK.COM';

Part 12 — Production Usage

Indexes in Production Banking / Payments

OLTP Payment Service — Minimal Index Set

text
payments:
  PK (payment_id)
  UNIQUE (client_request_id)
  (customer_id, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (amount, status)
  PARTIAL (created_at) WHERE status = 'PENDING'  -- sweeper only

Avoid:
  INDEX (amount) — low selectivity, fraud queries use replica with different index
  INDEX (status) alone — useless if low cardinality

Reconciliation Batch (Read Replica)

sql
-- Different workload — additional index OK on replica only (logical replication)
-- Or same index if query runs on primary off-peak
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_value_date_status
ON payments (value_date, status)
WHERE status IN ('COMPLETED', 'PENDING_SETTLEMENT');

Index Migration Runbook

text
1. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on replica first — measure build time
2. EXPLAIN critical queries on replica
3. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on primary during low traffic
4. Monitor: idx_scan, insert TPS delta, replication lag
5. Drop redundant old index CONCURRENTLY after 7 days
6. Document in Flyway Vxx__idx_payments_customer_created.sql

PCI / Audit Tables

text
payments_audit:
  INDEX (payment_id, changed_at DESC) — lookup history per payment
  No index on changed_by alone unless proven query
  Partition by changed_at monthly — index per partition smaller

Part 13 — Spring Boot Integration

Indexes and Spring Data JPA

Repository Queries Drive Indexes

java
public interface PaymentRepository extends JpaRepository<Payment, Long> {

    // Needs: (customer_id, created_at DESC) index
    List<Payment> findByCustomerIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc(
        Long customerId, Pageable pageable);

    // Needs: UNIQUE client_request_id (also idempotency)
    Optional<Payment> findByClientRequestId(String clientRequestId);

    // Needs: partial index on PENDING + created_at if high volume
    List<Payment> findByStatusAndCreatedAtBefore(
        PaymentStatus status, Instant before);
}

@Query Native — Match Index

java
@Query(value = """
    SELECT payment_id, amount, created_at
    FROM payments
    WHERE customer_id = :customerId
      AND (created_at, payment_id) < (:cursorTime, :cursorId)
    ORDER BY created_at DESC, payment_id DESC
    LIMIT :limit
    """, nativeQuery = true)
List<PaymentSummaryProjection> keysetPage(...);
// Flyway index must match WHERE + ORDER BY columns exactly

Flyway Index Migration

sql
-- V45__idx_payments_customer_created.sql
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS idx_payments_customer_created
ON payments (customer_id, created_at DESC);

COMMENT ON INDEX idx_payments_customer_created IS
    'Supports PaymentRepository.findByCustomerIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc and keyset pagination';

Hibernate DDL Auto — Production Forbidden

yaml
spring:
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate  # NOT update — indexes managed by Flyway only

Integration Test — Index Exists

java
@Test
void requiredIndexesExist() {
    Integer count = jdbcTemplate.queryForObject("""
        SELECT COUNT(*) FROM pg_indexes
        WHERE tablename = 'payments'
          AND indexname = 'idx_payments_customer_created'
        """, Integer.class);
    assertThat(count).isEqualTo(1);
}

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

ORM and Index Interaction

@Index and @Table Annotations (Documentation)

java
@Entity
@Table(name = "payments", indexes = {
    @Index(name = "idx_payments_customer_created",
           columnList = "customer_id, created_at DESC"),
    @Index(name = "uq_payments_client_request",
           columnList = "client_request_id", unique = true)
})
public class Payment { ... }
// Hibernate may generate in ddl-auto=update — use Flyway as source of truth
// Annotation documents intent for developers

@Column(unique = true) → UNIQUE Index

java
@Column(name = "client_request_id", nullable = false, unique = true)
private String clientRequestId;
// One unique index — do not duplicate with manual + annotation

FK Without Index — Hibernate Won't Warn

java
@ManyToOne
@JoinColumn(name = "customer_id")
private Customer customer;
// JPA creates FK constraint — NOT automatic index on customer_id in all DBs
// PostgreSQL: YOU must CREATE INDEX on customer_id — Flyway

Optimistic Lock + Index

java
@Version
private Long version;
// Updates version column — indexed column in PK only usually
// HOT update if indexed columns unchanged — good for balance updates on non-indexed columns only

Avoid Defeating Index

java
// ❌ JPQL function prevents index unless expression index exists
@Query("SELECT p FROM Payment p WHERE LOWER(p.clientRequestId) = LOWER(:id)")

// ✅ match index
@Query("SELECT p FROM Payment p WHERE p.clientRequestId = :id")

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

Index Architecture Governance

Index Review Board Criteria

text
New index proposal must include:
  □ Query SQL + pg_stat_statements call frequency
  □ EXPLAIN before (Seq Scan cost) and after (Index Scan cost)
  □ Estimated index size (pg_relation_size projection)
  □ Write path impact (INSERT/UPDATE TPS on table)
  □ Redundancy check against existing indexes
  □ Partial vs full justification
  □ Drop plan for replaced indexes

Per-Table Index Budget

text
OLTP fact tables (payments, transactions):
  Target: PK + 2–4 secondary indexes
  Exception ADR for more

Dimension tables (customers):
  PK + UNIQUE business keys + FK targets

Audit/history:
  Partition + minimal indexes per partition

Read Replica Index Strategy

text
Option A: Same indexes primary + replica (simple, replication applies DDL)
Option B: Extra indexes on replica only — requires logical replication or ETL
  Not physical streaming replication with different indexes easily
Architect: usually same schema, tune queries to shared index set

UUID PK Index Locality

text
UUID v4 PK on payments:
  Random inserts → B-tree page splits, fragmentation
Mitigations:
  UUID v7 (time-ordered prefix)
  BIGINT sequence PK + UUID external id column with unique index
  BRIN not for PK — only time-range on archive tables

Index vs Denormalization vs Cache

text
Repeated expensive JOIN aggregate:
  Index on FK + covering index may suffice
  Still slow at scale → summary table (Lesson 9) or mat view
  Hot point lookup → cache (Redis) with TTL — not duplicate of index, complementary

Index Type Selection

Access PatternIndex Type
PK / FK lookupB-tree on key columns
Equality + rangeComposite B-tree (eq cols first)
ORDER BY + LIMITComposite including sort columns DESC
SELECT few colsINCLUDE covering index
Skewed subset (PENDING)Partial index
LOWER(col) =Expression index
JSONB containsGIN
Time-series archive scanBRIN on timestamp
Full text searchGIN tsvector
Low cardinality aloneUsually skip — bitmap scan or seq

Composite Column Order

Query PatternColumn Order
col1 = ? AND col2 > ?(col1, col2)
col1 = ? AND col2 = ?(col1, col2) either eq order OK
col1 > ? AND col2 = ?(col2, col1) — equality leading
ORDER BY col2 DESC LIMIT N with col1 = ?(col1, col2 DESC)

Create vs Skip Index

SignalDecision
EXPLAIN Seq Scan, >1M rows, <1% matchCreate
idx_scan = 0 for 90 daysDrop candidate
INSERT TPS critical, read rareSkip
FK child columnAlways create
UNIQUE business keyAlways create
Column updated frequentlyAvoid indexing unless essential

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Missing FK Index

sql
-- accounts.customer_id FK → customers
-- No index on accounts(customer_id)
-- DELETE customer / JOIN from customer side — seq scan child table

Mistake 2: Redundant Indexes

sql
INDEX (customer_id)
INDEX (customer_id, created_at)
-- Drop standalone (customer_id) — composite covers prefix

Mistake 3: Wrong Composite Order

sql
INDEX (created_at, customer_id)
WHERE customer_id = 1001 AND created_at > '2024-01-01'
-- Fix: (customer_id, created_at)

Mistake 4: Index Low-Cardinality Column Alone

sql
CREATE INDEX ON payments (status);  -- 5 values, 20M rows each
-- Seq scan wins — wasted write cost

Mistake 5: SELECT * With Wide Covering Attempt

sql
-- Covering index with 20 INCLUDE columns — index bigger than heap
-- Include only columns SELECT actually needs

Mistake 6: CREATE INDEX Without CONCURRENTLY in Prod

sql
CREATE INDEX idx ... ON payments (...);
-- Locks writes — use CONCURRENTLY on PostgreSQL production

Mistake 7: Function on Column Without Expression Index

sql
WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2024-01-01'
-- Fix: range predicate created_at >= ... AND created_at < ...
-- Or index on (date(created_at)) — less ideal

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is a database index?

Secondary ordered structure mapping key values to row locations — speeds lookups at cost of storage and write overhead.

Q2: Default index type in PostgreSQL?

B-tree — supports equality and range.

Q3: Why index foreign key columns?

Speed JOINs and DELETE/UPDATE parent checks — avoid full child table scan.

Q4: Composite index column order?

Leading columns must match query equality filters; range/sort columns later; left-prefix rule.

Q5: UNIQUE index purpose?

Enforce uniqueness + fast duplicate detection — idempotency keys.

Mid-Level

Q6: Index Scan vs Index Only Scan?

Index Scan fetches heap; Index Only Scan reads index alone when covering + visibility map allows.

Q7: Partial index when?

Queries always filter subset (status = 'PENDING') — smaller index, faster, less write cost.

Q8: When does optimizer ignore index?

Low selectivity, function on column, wrong column order, small table, stale stats.

Q9: Covering index / INCLUDE?

Index contains all columns needed by query — avoids heap fetch, enables index-only scan.

Q10: Write amplification from indexes?

Each INSERT/UPDATE on indexed columns maintains every index — O(number of indexes × log n).

Senior

Q11: Design index for WHERE customer_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20.

(customer_id, created_at DESC) optionally INCLUDE selected columns.

Q12: Redundant index detection?

(a) redundant if (a, b) exists; pg_stat_user_indexes idx_scan; index size vs benefit.

Q13: UUID v4 PK index problems?

Random insertion → page splits, poor cache locality; prefer BIGINT or UUID v7.

Q14: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY failure handling?

Invalid index state — REINDEX CONCURRENTLY; monitor pg_index.indisvalid.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Index governance for 50-team org?

Flyway-only DDL, proposal template with EXPLAIN evidence, per-table budget, quarterly unused index review.

Q16: Extra indexes on read replica?

Physical replication same schema; logical/ETL for divergent indexes; usually shared index set.

Scenario

Scenario: "Added index but query still Seq Scan."

EXPLAIN ANALYZE — check selectivity, function on column, wrong bind values, generic plan, enable_seqscan not issue — run ANALYZE; verify index valid; matching predicate to partial index WHERE clause.

Part 20 — Revision Sheet

Design Rules

text
Index FK columns (child side)
UNIQUE on idempotency keys
Composite: equality cols first, range/sort last
Partial index for skewed subsets
INCLUDE for covering hot SELECTs
Expression index for LOWER(email) etc.

Verify

text
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) — Index Scan / Index Only Scan
pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan
Drop idx_scan = 0 after observation period
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in prod

Avoid

text
Index every column
Redundant (a) when (a,b) exists
(status) alone on low cardinality
Functions on columns without expression index
DATE(column) = ... sargability break
Missing FK index
Too many indexes on hot INSERT table

Trade-off

text
Read faster  ↔  Write slower + storage + bloat maintenance

Lesson 27

Statistics & Cost-Based Optimization

Phase 3: QUERY OPTIMIZATION & EXECUTION PLANS | Previous: Indexes Deep Dive | Next: Query Tuning Methodology

Performance
1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why This Exists5Internal Working6Storage Internals7Memory Usage8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Complexity Analysis11Code / SQL Examples12Production Usage13Spring Boot Integration14Hibernate/JPA Integration15Architect Perspective16Decision Matrix17Comparison Tables18Common Mistakes19Interview Questions20Revision Sheet21Summary Table*Practice

Part 1 — Concept

What Is Cost-Based Optimization (CBO)?

The cost-based optimizer chooses a query execution plan by estimating how many rows each operator will process and assigning a cost (I/O + CPU) to alternative strategies — then picking the lowest-cost plan. Those estimates come from statistics collected about tables, columns, and data distribution.

text
SQL Query
    ↓
Rewrite (views, subqueries)
    ↓
Optimizer generates candidate plans
    ↓
For each plan: estimate rows at each node using STATISTICS
    ↓
Assign cost (seq_page_cost, cpu_tuple_cost, join algorithms…)
    ↓
Pick minimum cost plan
    ↓
Execute (EXPLAIN shows this plan — Lesson 25)

If statistics lie, row estimates lie → wrong join algorithm → slow query even with perfect indexes.

Statistics vs Indexes

text
INDEX (Lesson 26)  → physical access path ("how to find rows quickly")
STATISTICS         → cardinality estimates ("how many rows match")

Index exists + wrong stats → optimizer may still choose Seq Scan + Hash Join wrongly
Good stats + no index     → optimizer knows Seq Scan is cheapest (low selectivity)
Both aligned              → optimal plan

Core Statistics Objects

text
TABLE STATISTICS (per table)
  row count (reltuples / num_rows)
  pages (relpages / blocks)
  visibility / dead tuple ratio

COLUMN STATISTICS (per indexed/analyzed column)
  n_distinct (distinct value count)
  null_frac (fraction NULL)
  most_common_vals / frequencies (MCV list)
  histogram_bounds (equi-depth buckets)

EXTENDED STATISTICS (PostgreSQL 10+)
  multivariate n-distinct
  functional dependencies (col A → col B)
  ndistinct combinations

WORKLOAD / RUNTIME (advanced)
  Oracle SQL Plan Directives, Adaptive Statistics
  SQL Server ascending key / cardinality estimator updates
  pg_stat_statements — actual vs estimated feedback loops (manual)

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Optimizer Statistics

text
1980s   Oracle rule-based optimizer (RBO) — fixed rules, no stats
        DB2 early cost models with RUNSTATS

1990s   Oracle CBO becomes default — DBMS_STATS
        SQL Server statistics auto-create on indexed columns
        PostgreSQL ANALYZE — simpler stats, reltuples sampling

2000s   Histograms in all major DBs — handle skewed columns (status, region)
        PostgreSQL autovacuum also triggers ANALYZE

2010s   Extended statistics (PG 10) — correlated columns
        Oracle adaptive plans, SQL Server cardinality estimator v120+
        Column groups (SQL Server CREATE STATISTICS …)

2020s   Increasing default_statistics_target in PG for skewed OLTP
        Cloud auto-tuning "index advisor" + stats health dashboards
        pg_stat_statements + hypothetical indexes (HypoPG) workflows
        Still no substitute for DBA/architect understanding skew and correlation

Historical Lesson

Optimizers did not get "smarter" only through code — they got smarter by better guessing row counts. A 10× underestimate on a join inner side turns a Hash Join into a catastrophic Nested Loop. Statistics maintenance is production operations, not optional DBA trivia.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Do Statistics Solve?

Problem 1: How Many Rows Match WHERE region = 'APAC'?

text
Without stats: guess 10% of table (generic)
With stats:    APAC = 8.2% (histogram + MCV)
With bad stats: table grew 10× since last ANALYZE → guess 8.2% of old size → wrong

Problem 2: Join Cardinality Explosion

sql
SELECT *
FROM accounts a
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = a.customer_id
WHERE c.region = 'APAC' AND a.status = 'ACTIVE';
-- Optimizer must estimate:
--   rows from customers (APAC filter)
--   rows from accounts (ACTIVE filter)
--   join result size — assumes independence unless extended stats say otherwise

Problem 3: Skewed Column — status = 'PENDING'

text
payments.status:
  COMPLETED  92%
  PENDING     5%
  FAILED      3%

Uniform assumption: each status ~33% — catastrophic
MCV list: PENDING = 5% — accurate → partial index + correct plan

Problem 4: Correlated Columns

sql
-- region and country_code highly correlated
WHERE region = 'APAC' AND country_code = 'SG'
-- Independent assumption: P(APAC) × P(SG) << actual
-- Extended stats: functional dependency or ndistinct pair fixes estimate

Problem 5: Plan Regression After Bulk Load

text
Sunday ETL loads 5M new payments
Monday morning: reports timeout
ANALYZE not run → stats stale → Nested Loop on 5M rows
Fix: ANALYZE payments; or increase autovacuum analyze threshold

Unified Problem Statement

Statistics tell the optimizer how data is distributed so it can estimate row counts at each plan node — choosing the right scan, join, and sort strategy. Stale or incomplete statistics cause cardinality misestimates and wrong plans.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Not Fixed Rules or Always Seq Scan?

Cost Comparison Requires Row Counts

text
Nested Loop cost ≈ outer_rows × inner_cost_per_probe
Hash Join cost   ≈ build(inner) + probe(outer)

If outer estimated 100 but actual 1,000,000:
  Optimizer picks Nested Loop — disaster

Correct estimate → Hash Join chosen

Histograms Handle Non-Uniform Data

text
Without histogram on balance:
  WHERE balance > 100000 assumed uniform → 50% rows

With histogram:
  Only 2% above 100000 → Index Scan wins

Extended Stats Handle Correlation

text
Real banking data: account_type and product_code correlated
Independent multiplication underestimates or overestimates join sizes
Extended statistics capture dependency

Trade-off: ANALYZE Cost

text
ANALYZE reads sample of table — CPU + I/O
Too frequent on 500M row table — load spike
Too rare — bad plans
Architect balances: autovacuum thresholds, post-ETL jobs, manual ANALYZE on critical tables

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Statistics Are Collected and Used

PostgreSQL ANALYZE Pipeline

text
ANALYZE payments;  (or autovacuum ANALYZE)

1. Sample pages (default_statistics_target × 300 rows sample cap per column)
2. For each column:
   - Compute null_frac, avg_width, n_distinct
   - Build MCV list (most common values) if distinct count low enough
   - Build histogram (equi-depth) for remaining value range
3. Update pg_class.reltuples, relpages
4. Store in pg_statistic → visible via pg_stats view
5. Invalidate plan cache for affected tables (new plans use new stats)

Reading pg_stats

sql
SELECT
    tablename,
    attname,
    n_distinct,
    null_frac,
    most_common_vals,
    most_common_freqs,
    histogram_bounds
FROM pg_stats
WHERE tablename = 'payments'
  AND attname IN ('status', 'customer_id', 'created_at');
text
n_distinct:
  positive N  → ~N distinct values
  negative f  → fraction of table (~f × rows distinct)

most_common_vals / freqs:
  status = 'COMPLETED' → 0.92

histogram_bounds:
  created_at split into buckets — estimates range queries

Selectivity Estimation (Simplified)

text
Equality: status = 'PENDING'
  If in MCV: use most_common_freqs
  Else: 1 / n_distinct (uniform fallback)

Range: created_at >= '2024-01-01'
  Use histogram: sum fraction of buckets >= boundary

AND independence (default):
  sel(A AND B) = sel(A) × sel(B)  ← often wrong for correlated cols

JOIN:
  rows ≈ rows_outer × rows_inner / max(n_distinct(join_key))
  (simplified — varies by DB)

Extended Statistics (PostgreSQL)

sql
-- Functional dependency: country_code determines region?
CREATE STATISTICS stat_cust_region (dependencies)
ON region, country_code FROM customers;

ANALYZE customers;

-- Multivariate ndistinct for join pairs
CREATE STATISTICS stat_acct_cust (ndistinct)
ON customer_id, status FROM accounts;

ANALYZE accounts;
text
dependencies:
  If region functionally depends on country_code,
  optimizer uses sel(APAC AND SG) ≈ sel(SG) not sel(APAC)×sel(SG)

ndistinct:
  Better distinct count for (customer_id, status) combination

Oracle DBMS_STATS

sql
EXEC DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATS('BANK', 'PAYMENTS', estimate_percent => DBMS_STATS.AUTO_SAMPLE_SIZE);
-- Histograms: METHOD_OPT => 'FOR ALL COLUMNS SIZE AUTO'
-- Extended stats: CREATE_EXTENDED_STATS for column groups

SQL Server Statistics

sql
UPDATE STATISTICS dbo.payments WITH FULLSCAN;
-- Auto-created on index key; column stats for predicates
-- Filtered statistics on partial indexes
-- Cardinality estimator version affects estimates (DB compatibility level)

Plan Stability Mechanisms

text
PostgreSQL: generic vs custom plan for prepared statements (plan_cache_mode)
Oracle: SQL Plan Baselines, SQL Profiles, Adaptive Plans
SQL Server: Plan Guides, Query Store force plan
Use when: upgrade changes estimator → known-good plan regression

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Where Statistics Live

PostgreSQL Catalog

text
pg_class:     reltuples, relpages (table-level)
pg_statistic: internal stats per column (not readable directly)
pg_stats:     view exposing human-readable stats
pg_statistic_ext: extended statistics definitions + values

Disk: kilobytes per table — negligible vs table data

Histogram Size

text
default_statistics_target = 100 (PostgreSQL default)
  → up to 100 histogram buckets per column
  → larger target = better skew accuracy, longer ANALYZE time

Increase for skewed OLTP columns:
ALTER TABLE payments ALTER COLUMN status SET STATISTICS 1000;
ANALYZE payments;

Statistics Invalidation

text
INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE accumulate until autovacuum ANALYZE threshold:
  autovacuum_analyze_threshold + autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor × reltuples

Example: 50M rows, scale_factor 0.05 → analyze after ~2.5M changes
High-churn payments table may need lower scale_factor or manual post-batch ANALYZE

Oracle Statistics History

text
SYS.WRI$_OPTSTAT_HISTHEAD_HISTORY — restore stats after bad gather
Architect: lock stats before ETL mistake; restore prior version

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Statistics and Runtime Memory

AspectImpact
Stats storageCatalog — negligible RAM
Plan cacheEach distinct plan cached — bad stats → wrong plan cached
Hash Join buildSized from estimated rows — underestimate → work_mem OK; overestimate → spill
ANALYZE runReads sample pages — temporary sort for MCV/histogram — moderate I/O
Extended statsSlightly more planner CPU — negligible vs query execution

work_mem and Cardinality

text
Hash Join chosen because estimate says inner fits work_mem
Actual rows 10× larger → Hash Batches: 4 → disk spill (Lesson 25)
Fix stats, not just work_mem — root cause is wrong algorithm choice

autovacuum Worker Memory

text
ANALYZE during autovacuum on large table — concurrent with OLTP
maintenance_work_mem affects ANALYZE speed — not query work_mem
Tune autovacuum_naptime, analyze thresholds per table (PostgreSQL storage params)

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Statistics → Plan → Execution Flows

Flow 1: Accurate Stats — Good Plan

sql
-- 50M payments, customer_id = 1001 returns ~200 rows (MCV/histogram accurate)
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM payments
WHERE customer_id = 1001
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
text
Planner:
  Estimate customer_id=1001 → 200 rows (accurate)
  Index idx_payments_customer_created cost < Seq Scan cost
Plan:
  Index Scan → Limit
EXPLAIN ANALYZE: actual rows ≈ estimated rows ✅

Flow 2: Stale Stats — Nested Loop Disaster

sql
SELECT c.email, t.amount
FROM customers c
JOIN transactions t ON t.account_id IN (
    SELECT account_id FROM accounts WHERE customer_id = c.customer_id
)
WHERE c.region = 'APAC';
text
Stats stale on accounts:
  Estimated APAC customers: 500
  Estimated accounts per customer: 3
  Actual after data growth: 50,000 customers, 10 accounts each

Plan: Nested Loop with correlated subplan
Actual: timeout

Fix:
  ANALYZE customers; ANALYZE accounts; ANALYZE transactions;
  Re-EXPLAIN — likely Hash Join + HashAggregate or JOIN rewrite

Flow 3: Correlated Columns — Independent Guess

sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers
WHERE region = 'EMEA' AND currency = 'EUR';
-- All EMEA rows are EUR — 100% overlap
-- Optimizer guesses sel = sel(EMEA) × sel(EUR) = 0.25 × 0.30 = 7.5%
-- Actual: 25% of table

CREATE STATISTICS stat_region_currency (dependencies) ON region, currency FROM customers;
ANALYZE customers;
-- Estimate improves

Flow 4: Post-ETL ANALYZE Job

text
1. ETL COPY 5M rows into payments (Sunday 02:00)
2. pg_class.reltuples still reflects pre-load count until ANALYZE
3. Monday 09:00 reports run — underestimate total table, wrong join order
4. Cron: ANALYZE payments; ANALYZE transactions; (or VACUUM ANALYZE)
5. pg_stats refreshed — plans stabilize

Flow 5: Parameter Sniffing (SQL Server / Oracle)

text
First execution: WHERE customer_id = 1001 (highly selective) → Index Scan plan cached
Second execution: WHERE customer_id IS NULL or rare bulk customer → same plan bad

SQL Server: OPTION (RECOMPILE), OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN, Query Store force plan
PostgreSQL: custom vs generic plan for prepared statements
Architect: document skewed parameters; separate queries or plan hints as last resort

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Diagnosing Statistics Problems

Smoking Gun in EXPLAIN ANALYZE

text
rows=100 loops=1          ← estimate
actual rows=850000 loops=1  ← reality

Ratio > 10× at join node → investigate stats at that node's inputs
Multiple nodes wrong → table-level stale ANALYZE
One column predicate wrong → histogram/MCV issue or correlation

Systematic Workflow

text
1. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) — find worst row mismatch
2. Identify filter columns at that node
3. SELECT * FROM pg_stats WHERE tablename=... AND attname=...
4. Check reltuples vs SELECT COUNT(*) — table stats stale?
5. ANALYZE table; increase STATISTICS target on skewed column
6. If correlated columns: CREATE STATISTICS ... ANALYZE
7. Re-EXPLAIN — compare estimates
8. If still wrong: rewrite query, partial index, hint (last resort), extended stats

When ANALYZE Is Not Enough

text
Very high cardinality join keys — independence assumption still fails
Ultra-skewed tail (fraud 0.01%) — increase statistics target
Join across uneven distributions — consider materialized stats / constrained stats (Oracle)
Query touches partitioned table — per-partition stats (Oracle, PG 11+ partitionwise)

autovacuum Tuning for Stats Freshness

sql
-- PostgreSQL: per-table aggressive analyze on payments
ALTER TABLE payments SET (
    autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor = 0.02,
    autovacuum_analyze_threshold = 1000
);
-- Analyze after 2% of 50M = 1M changes — tune to SLA

Anti-Patterns

text
❌ Never ANALYZE after bulk load
❌ default_statistics_target=100 on ultra-skewed status column
❌ Ignore extended stats for region+country correlated filters
❌ Increase work_mem forever instead of fixing cardinality
❌ Force index hint without fixing stats — brittle
❌ Disable autovacuum on OLTP tables

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

OperationCostNotes
ANALYZE sampleO(sample size) per columnNot full table scan (usually)
Plan selectionO(candidates × nodes)Planner CPU — ms typically
Wrong Nested LoopO(outer × inner)Cardinality error multiplier
Correct Hash JoinO(a + b)Depends on accurate estimates
Extended stats ANALYZE+O(columns²) sample workSmall overhead

Cardinality error is multiplicative through join trees — small error at base → explosion at top.

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Statistics Masterclass

Check Staleness

sql
-- PostgreSQL: compare stats row count to actual
SELECT
    c.relname AS table_name,
    c.reltuples::bigint AS stats_rows,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM payments) AS actual_rows,
    ABS(c.reltuples - (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM payments)) / NULLIF((SELECT COUNT(*) FROM payments), 0) AS drift_ratio
FROM pg_class c
WHERE c.relname = 'payments';

-- drift_ratio > 0.1 → ANALYZE recommended

Inspect Column Stats

sql
SELECT
    attname,
    n_distinct,
    null_frac,
    most_common_vals,
    most_common_freqs,
    array_length(histogram_bounds, 1) AS histogram_buckets
FROM pg_stats
WHERE tablename = 'payments'
ORDER BY attname;

Manual ANALYZE

sql
ANALYZE payments;
ANALYZE VERBOSE payments (customer_id, status, created_at);
VACUUM ANALYZE payments;  -- also reclaims dead tuples + stats

Increase Statistics Target (Skewed Column)

sql
ALTER TABLE payments ALTER COLUMN status SET STATISTICS 500;
ALTER TABLE payments ALTER COLUMN customer_id SET STATISTICS 500;
ANALYZE payments;

Extended Statistics — Dependencies

sql
CREATE STATISTICS stat_customers_region_country (dependencies)
ON region, country_code FROM customers;

ANALYZE customers;

-- View extended stats
SELECT * FROM pg_statistic_ext_data
WHERE stxname = 'stat_customers_region_country';

Extended Statistics — ndistinct

sql
CREATE STATISTICS stat_accounts_cust_status (ndistinct)
ON customer_id, status FROM accounts;

ANALYZE accounts;
-- Improves: GROUP BY customer_id, status and join cardinality estimates

Bulk Insert Job + Post-Analyze Hook

java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PaymentBulkImportService {

    private final PaymentImportRepository importRepo;

    @Transactional
    public ImportResult importBatch(List<PaymentRow> rows) {

Read Replica Routing

@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public List<ReportRow> runReport() {

    // Physical replication: ANALYZE on primary propagates stats via WAL?

}

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

Statistics Governance

Statistics Health Dashboard

text
Metrics (per Tier 1 table):
  reltuples vs COUNT(*) drift %
  last_analyze timestamp (pg_stat_all_tables.last_analyze)
  autovacuum analyze count
  Top queries: EXPLAIN rows vs actual rows ratio (sampled weekly)

Alerts:
  drift > 20%
  last_analyze > 7 days on payments with daily bulk load
  mean_exec_time spike on known report SQL

CBO vs Rule-Based Legacy

text
Oracle shops migrating off RBO hints:
  Systematic DBMS_STATS + remove obsolete /*+ INDEX */ hints
  SQL Plan Baselines preserve known-good plans during transition

Plan Stability Policy

text
1. Prefer fixing stats and SQL rewrite over hints
2. Hints require ADR + expiry review date
3. PostgreSQL: avoid pg_hint_plan unless emergency
4. SQL Server Query Store: force plan only after stats fix failed
5. Document every forced plan owner and removal criteria

Multi-Tenant Skew

text
tenant_id = large enterprise → 40% of rows
tenant_id = small SaaS → 0.001%

Single plan for prepared statement fails one tenant
Architect patterns:
  separate schema per tier
  tenant_id leading column in composite index + partition by tenant
  literal sniff for known mega-tenant reports (careful)

Cost Model Tuning (Advanced)

sql
-- PostgreSQL: SSD storage
SET random_page_cost = 1.1;  -- default 4.0 assumes HDD
SET effective_cache_size = '24GB';  -- planner assumes cache hits
-- Session-level on reporting role — not global without testing

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Index Added, Never ANALYZE

text
New index exists but planner still Seq Scan — stats say 80% rows match
ANALYZE → planner switches to Index Scan

Mistake 2: ANALYZE Primary Only, Reports on Replica

text
Replica has stale pg_stats — slow reports despite healthy primary
Fix: ANALYZE on replica schedule

Mistake 3: Uniform Assumption on status

text
92% COMPLETED — query for COMPLETED needs MCV not 1/n_distinct
Increase statistics target on status

Mistake 4: Fixing work_mem Instead of Stats

text
Hash Batches spill — because Hash Join chosen on wrong estimate
Correct estimates → Nested Loop or different join might win; or correct hash size

Mistake 5: Over-Hinting Instead of Stats

sql
/*+ HashJoin(c t) */  -- frozen bad plan after next month's data growth
Fix stats; remove hint when plan stable

Mistake 6: CREATE STATISTICS Without ANALYZE

sql
CREATE STATISTICS ...;
-- forgot ANALYZE → extended stats empty → no benefit

Mistake 7: Truncate + Reload Without Stats Job

text
TRUNCATE payments; COPY ...;
Stats still show old reltuples until ANALYZE — plans wildly wrong

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is cost-based optimization?

Optimizer picks lowest-cost plan using estimated row counts and I/O/CPU costs from statistics.

Q2: What does ANALYZE do?

Samples table data to update planner statistics: row counts, distinct values, histograms, MCV lists.

Q3: EXPLAIN shows rows=100, actual rows=500000 — meaning?

Cardinality misestimate — often stale stats or missing histogram; investigate ANALYZE.

Q4: What is a histogram in database stats?

Buckets dividing column value range — estimates selectivity of range predicates.

Q5: Statistics vs indexes?

Statistics estimate how many rows; indexes provide access paths — both needed.

Mid-Level

Q6: MCV list purpose?

Stores most frequent values and frequencies — accurate equality selectivity on skewed columns like status.

Q7: Why correlated columns break estimates?

Optimizer multiplies selectivities assuming independence — over/under-estimates AND conditions.

Q8: PostgreSQL extended statistics types?

dependencies (functional deps), ndistinct (multivariate distinct), mcv (multivariate MCV PG 14+).

Q9: When increase default_statistics_target?

Skewed columns where 100 buckets insufficient — status, region, type codes on large tables.

Q10: ANALYZE on replica needed?

Yes — PostgreSQL stats are per-instance; replica planner needs local ANALYZE for accurate reports.

Senior

Q11: Parameter sniffing — cause and fix?

Plan cached for first parameter values; bad for others — recompile, separate queries, OPTIMIZE FOR, Query Store.

Q12: Post-ETL plan regression triage steps?

EXPLAIN ANALYZE mismatch → check reltuples drift → ANALYZE → extended stats if correlated → re-baseline.

Q13: Hash Join spill despite work_mem increase?

Wrong join algorithm from bad stats — fix cardinality first; then memory if algorithm correct.

Q14: Plan stability mechanisms Oracle vs PostgreSQL?

Oracle SQL Plan Baselines/Profiles; PostgreSQL pg_stat_statements + plan_cache_mode, hints last resort.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Statistics governance for payments platform?

Tier table watchlist, post-ETL ANALYZE, drift monitoring, replica stats, hint policy, upgrade re-analyze.

Q16: Multi-tenant cardinality skew handling?

Partitioning, leading tenant_id in indexes, separate plans, extended stats, avoid one generic plan for all.

Scenario

Scenario: "Monday slowdown after Sunday 5M payment load; indexes unchanged."

reltuples stale; run ANALYZE payments on primary and replica; verify estimates in EXPLAIN; tune autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor; add post-ETL cron; document in runbook.

Query Tuning Methodology

Part 1 — Concept

What Is Query Tuning Methodology?

Query tuning methodology is a repeatable, evidence-based process to diagnose and fix slow database queries in production — not random index creation or parameter tweaking. It connects symptoms (latency, timeouts) to root causes (bad plan, lock wait, pool exhaustion, N+1) using measurements at each layer.

text
SLOW QUERY IS NOT ONE DISEASE

Layer 1: Application     → N+1, wrong API, missing cache, pool wait
Layer 2: SQL / ORM       → bad SQL shape, cartesian join, OFFSET pagination
Layer 3: Optimizer       → wrong plan, stale stats (Lessons 25–27)
Layer 4: Storage / I/O   → seq scan, cache miss, bloat, temp spill
Layer 5: Concurrency     → lock wait, deadlock, hot row
Layer 6: Infrastructure  → replica lag, CPU saturation, disk queue depth

Methodology: top-down OR bottom-up — always with DATA at each step

The Tuning Loop

text
┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐
│ 1. MEASURE  │ → │ 2. ISOLATE  │ → │ 3. DIAGNOSE │ → │ 4. FIX      │
│ p95, QPS    │    │ one query   │    │ EXPLAIN     │    │ index/SQL   │
│ wait events │    │ one txn     │    │ locks, pool │    │ stats/config│
└─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └──────┬──────┘
                                                                 │
                    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐          │
                    │ 6. DOCUMENT│ ← │ 5. VERIFY   │ ←──────────┘
                    │ runbook     │    │ before/after│
                    └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘

Tuning vs Optimization vs Scaling

ActivityScopeExample
Query tuningOne SQL / access patternAdd index, rewrite JOIN
Schema designTables, normalizationPartition payments by month
ConfigurationDB + pool GUCswork_mem, random_page_cost
ScalingMore hardware / replicasRead replica for reports
ArchitectureService boundariesCQRS, cache, event read model

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Performance Troubleshooting

text
1980s   EXPLAIN + rule-based hints — trial and error
        Oracle UTLBSTAT/UTLESTAT — wait event precursors

1990s   Oracle Statspack — time model + top SQL
        SQL Server Profiler — trace heavy queries

2000s   AWR/ASH (Oracle) — active session history
        pg_stat_statements (PostgreSQL 8.4+) — aggregated query stats
        Methodology: "find top SQL by elapsed_time" becomes standard

2010s   APM (Datadog, New Relic) — trace SQL from Spring Boot
        ORM N+1 discovered via trace waterfall
        VividCortex / PMM — database-specific wait analysis

2020s   OpenTelemetry JDBC instrumentation
        Cloud Performance Insights (RDS, Aurora)
        AI query advisors — still require human validation loop
        FinOps: tune before scale-out — cost discipline

Historical Lesson

The industry moved from "tune by intuition" to "tune by top-N SQL + wait events + EXPLAIN evidence." Solution Architects own the methodology and governance — not every index proposal — so teams stop cargo-cult tuning (adding indexes that never get used).

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does Methodology Solve?

Problem 1: "The Database Is Slow" (No Specifics)

text
Without methodology:
  DBA adds 3 indexes — no improvement
  Dev increases connection pool to 200 — worse
  Ops scales RDS 2× — cost up, latency same

With methodology:
  APM shows 80% time in lock:transactionid on payments row
  Fix: shorten txn, row-level lock ordering — not index

Problem 2: Symptom vs Root Cause Confusion

text
Symptom:  report timeout at 30s
Cause A:  Seq Scan 50M rows (missing index)
Cause B:  plan OK (200ms) but 29s waiting for connection from pool
Cause C:  plan OK but blocked by EOD batch lock on accounts

Same symptom — three different fixes

Problem 3: Regression After Release

text
Friday deploy → Monday p99 spike
Methodology:
  1. pg_stat_statements diff: new query or mean_time change?
  2. EXPLAIN plan diff vs baseline (Lesson 25)
  3. Hibernate SQL log diff
  4. Flyway migration index/stats impact

Problem 4: ORM Hides SQL Shape

text
API latency 2s — one HTTP call
Trace: 501 JDBC calls — N+1 on accounts
Methodology: APM span count → find entity load pattern → JOIN FETCH fix
Not: EXPLAIN one query that is fast individually

Problem 5: Production Safety

text
Developer runs EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE on prod — incident
Methodology defines:
  safe EXPLAIN (no ANALYZE) on prod
  ANALYZE on replica with same schema/stats refresh
  read-only transaction for SELECT investigation

Unified Problem Statement

Query tuning methodology turns vague slowness into a measured diagnosis chain — isolating whether the bottleneck is SQL plan, concurrency, application pattern, or infrastructure — before applying targeted fixes with verified before/after evidence.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Not "Just Add an Index"?

Indexes Fix Only Plan-Class Problems

text
Lesson 26: index helps selective lookup/join/sort
Does NOT help:
  Lock wait on hot summary row
  Connection pool queue 500ms
  N+1 × 1000 round trips (each query fast)
  Replica lag reading stale + retry storm
  work_mem spill if plan already correct but memory tight (secondary)

Statistics Fix Estimator-Class Problems

text
Lesson 27: ANALYZE fixes wrong Nested Loop choice
Does NOT help:
  Inherently expensive report scanning 2 years of data without partition prune
  Fix: partition, archive, materialized view, replica — architecture

Methodology Prevents Harm

text
Unbounded work_mem × 200 connections = OOM kill
Index on (status) low cardinality — write cost, no read benefit
Hint frozen plan — breaks next month after data growth
Methodology includes: risk assessment, rollback, monitor

Team Scalability

text
20 developers — without methodology, 20 different tuning styles
Architect publishes:
  triage runbook
  EXPLAIN baseline library
  index proposal template (Lesson 26)
  when to escalate to DBA vs fix in app

Part 5 — Internal Working

The Systematic Tuning Workflow (Internal Steps)

Phase A — Measure (Where Is Time Going?)

text
Sources:
  APM trace:     HTTP → Service → JDBC span duration
  pg_stat_statements: total_time, mean_time, calls, rows
  pg_stat_activity: wait_event_type, wait_event, state, query
  Cloud PI:      DB load by wait type (CPU, IO, Locks)

Classify wait:
  Client: ClientRead / ClientWrite — app not consuming results
  IO:     DataFileRead, read — disk/cache miss
  Lock:   transactionid, relation — blocking
  CPU:    on CPU — sort/hash/compute heavy
  LWLock: internal contention — rare OLTP

Phase B — Isolate (One Variable)

text
Reproduce with:
  Same bind parameters as slow execution (parameter sniffing)
  Same data volume (prod stats on replica)
  Same connection path (through PgBouncer vs direct)

Remove:
  concurrent load for controlled test (staging)
  OR capture active session during incident (prod)

Phase C — Diagnose SQL Plan

text
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on replica — Lesson 25
Check:
  highest actual time node
  rows vs actual rows — Lesson 27
  Seq Scan on large selective table — Lesson 26
  Sort/Hash Disk spill
  SubPlan per row

Phase D — Diagnose Non-Plan Causes

text
Locks:
  SELECT * FROM pg_locks JOIN pg_stat_activity ...

Pool:
  HikariCP metrics: threads awaiting connection, timeout count

N+1:
  JDBC statement count per HTTP request in trace

Replication:
  pg_stat_replication lag on replica used for reads

Phase E — Fix, Verify, Document

text
Fix one primary cause — avoid changing 5 variables at once
Verify:
  p50/p95/p99 latency
  pg_stat_statements mean_time for queryid
  EXPLAIN plan diff attached to ticket
Document:
  runbook entry
  Flyway migration link
  monitor alert threshold

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Storage-Related Tuning Signals

Buffer Cache vs Disk Read

text
EXPLAIN BUFFERS:
  shared hit=5000 read=8000  → cold or working set > shared_buffers

Tuning path:
  Not always "add RAM" — reduce rows read (index, rewrite)
  Increase shared_buffers only after evidence (typically 25% RAM PG guideline)
  Partition pruning — fewer pages touched

Table / Index Bloat

text
UPDATE balance frequently → dead tuples → seq scan reads bloat
EXPLAIN shows more buffers than expected for row count

Check:
  pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup
  pgstattuple extension — bloat percentage

Fix:
  autovacuum tuning (scale_factor, threshold)
  VACUUM (FULL last resort — locks)
  REINDEX CONCURRENTLY bloated index

Temp File Spill

text
EXPLAIN ANALYZE: Sort Method: external merge Disk: 2048576kB
Storage: pgsql_tmp on disk — I/O storm

Fix:
  index for ORDER BY (eliminate sort)
  reduce rows before sort (filter earlier)
  SET LOCAL work_mem for reporting session only

Partition Pruning Failure

sql
WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01'
-- Plan scans ALL monthly partitions → 24× I/O
Fix: ensure constraint exclusion / declarative partition key in predicate

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Memory in Tuning Context

SymptomMemory-Related CauseFix Class
Hash Batches: >1Hash join > work_memStats fix OR work_mem (session) OR rewrite
Sort spill DiskSort > work_memIndex for ORDER BY OR fewer rows
OOM on DB serverwork_mem × active queriesLower work_mem; fix plans; limit parallelism
Pool exhaustionApp threads block waitingRight-size pool; fix slow queries; async
Hibernate L1 cacheLarge persistence contextclear(); DTO projection; pagination

HikariCP Sizing (Spring Boot)

text
connections = ((core_count × 2) + effective_spindle_count)  — rough starting point
PostgreSQL: often 20–50 per service instance — NOT 200

Too many connections:
  Each connection = backend process memory
  Lock contention on PostgreSQL internal structures
  Context switching — everyone slow

Tuning: fix query duration first — then pool size

work_mem Global Trap

sql
-- 100 active queries each allocate 256MB work_mem for hash — theoretical 25GB
-- Tuning methodology: session-level for batch role only
ALTER ROLE reporting SET work_mem = '512MB';

Part 8 — Execution Flow

End-to-End Tuning Flows (Case Patterns)

Flow 1: Slow SELECT — Plan Problem

text
1. APM: GET /payments?customerId=1001 — 4.2s
2. Trace: single JDBC query 4.1s
3. pg_stat_statements: mean 4s for SELECT ... payments WHERE customer_id = $1
4. EXPLAIN ANALYZE on replica:
     Seq Scan payments (actual rows=50M filter to 200)
5. Root cause: missing index (Lesson 26)
6. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_payments_customer_created ...
7. EXPLAIN: Index Scan — 12ms
8. Deploy index; APM p95 → 25ms
9. Document in Flyway V47 + baseline explain file

Flow 2: Slow API — N+1 Problem

text
1. APM: GET /customers/1001/accounts — 1.8s
2. Trace: 401 JDBC spans (1 + 400)
3. Each SELECT accounts WHERE customer_id=? — 4ms × 400 = 1.6s
4. EXPLAIN one query — fast — red herring if only one query tuned
5. Root cause: Hibernate lazy load loop
6. Fix: @Query JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph
7. Trace: 1 JDBC span — 15ms total
8. No index change needed

Flow 3: Timeout — Lock Wait

text
1. APM: POST /transfer — timeout 30s
2. pg_stat_activity: wait_event=transactionid, state=active
3. Blocker: UPDATE accounts SET balance ... (EOD batch job)
4. pg_locks: blocked_pid → blocking_pid
5. Root cause: batch job long txn + OLTP row overlap
6. Fix: batch in smaller commits; schedule off-peak; consistent lock order
7. NOT: new index on accounts

Flow 4: Pool Wait

text
1. APM: all endpoints slow uniformly + threads awaiting connection
2. HikariCP: connectionTimeout exceptions
3. DB CPU 30% — not DB saturated
4. Root cause: pool size 10, 50 Tomcat threads, each holds conn during slow external HTTP call
5. Fix: shorten txn; don't hold DB conn during Kafka/HTTP; pool 20; fix slow query releasing conn

Flow 5: Post-Deploy Regression

text
1. pg_stat_statements compare: new queryid after deploy
2. Hibernate log: new JOIN without WHERE tenant_id
3. EXPLAIN: rows estimate 1000, actual 4M — cross-tenant leak + seq scan
4. Fix: add tenant predicate + index (tenant_id, customer_id)
5. Add integration test asserting tenant filter in SQL

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

The Master Triage Decision Tree

text
Query slow?
│
├─ APM shows many JDBC calls per request?
│   YES → N+1 / chatty ORM → JOIN FETCH, batch, DTO query
│   NO ↓
│
├─ Waiting for DB connection (pool metrics)?
│   YES → pool sizing, conn held too long, fix longest queries
│   NO ↓
│
├─ pg_stat_activity wait_event = Lock/*?
│   YES → lock analysis, txn duration, batch overlap, deadlock graph
│   NO ↓
│
├─ EXPLAIN: rows << actual rows (10×)?
│   YES → ANALYZE, extended stats (Lesson 27)
│   NO ↓
│
├─ EXPLAIN: Seq Scan large table selective WHERE?
│   YES → index, rewrite sargable predicate (Lesson 26)
│   NO ↓
│
├─ EXPLAIN: Sort/Hash spill Disk?
│   YES → index for ORDER BY; filter earlier; session work_mem
│   NO ↓
│
├─ Plan looks good (<200ms) but query slow in prod?
│   YES → cold cache, replica lag, network, sync replication, CPU steal
│   NO ↓
│
└─ Inherently large result / report?
    YES → replica, partition, mat view, pre-aggregate, async export

Key Metrics to Track

MetricSourceIndicates
mean_exec_timepg_stat_statementsQuery-specific regression
calls × mean_timepg_stat_statementsTotal DB load contribution
wait_eventpg_stat_activityLock vs IO vs CPU
blk_read_timepg_stat_statementsI/O heavy query
shared_blks_readEXPLAIN BUFFERSCache miss
p95 API latencyAPMUser impact
pool waiting threadsHikariCPApp-side bottleneck
replication lagpg_stat_replicationStale read / load

pg_stat_statements Workflow

sql
SELECT
    queryid,
    LEFT(query, 120) AS query_snippet,
    calls,
    round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 2) AS mean_ms,
    round(total_exec_time::numeric, 2) AS total_ms,
    rows,
    shared_blks_read,
    shared_blks_hit
FROM pg_stat_statements
WHERE dbid = (SELECT oid FROM pg_database WHERE datname = current_database())
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
LIMIT 20;
-- Pick top total_ms offenders — not just mean_ms (rare slow vs constant moderate)

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Tuning Toolkit SQL

Active Session + Wait Events (PostgreSQL)

sql
SELECT
    pid,
    usename,
    application_name,
    client_addr,
    state,
    wait_event_type,
    wait_event,
    now() - query_start AS query_duration,
    LEFT(query, 200) AS query_snippet
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state != 'idle'
  AND pid != pg_backend_pid()
ORDER BY query_start;

Lock Blocking Chain

sql
SELECT
    blocked.pid AS blocked_pid,
    LEFT(blocked.query, 100) AS blocked_query,
    blocking.pid AS blocking_pid,
    LEFT(blocking.query, 100) AS blocking_query,
    now() - blocked.query_start AS blocked_duration
FROM pg_stat_activity blocked
JOIN pg_locks blocked_locks ON blocked.pid = blocked_locks.pid
JOIN pg_locks blocking_locks
    ON blocked_locks.locktype = blocking_locks.locktype
    AND blocked_locks.database IS NOT DISTINCT FROM blocking_locks.database
    AND blocked_locks.relation IS NOT DISTINCT FROM blocking_locks.relation
    AND blocked_locks.page IS NOT DISTINCT FROM blocking_locks.page
    AND blocked_locks.tuple IS NOT DISTINCT FROM blocking_locks.tuple
    AND blocked_locks.virtualxid IS NOT DISTINCT FROM blocking_locks.virtualxid
    AND blocked_locks.transactionid IS NOT DISTINCT FROM blocking_locks.transactionid
    AND blocked_locks.classid IS NOT DISTINCT FROM blocking_locks.classid
    AND blocked_locks.objid IS NOT DISTINCT FROM blocking_locks.objid
    AND blocked_locks.objsubid IS NOT DISTINCT FROM blocking_locks.objsubid
    AND blocked_locks.pid != blocking_locks.pid
JOIN pg_stat_activity blocking ON blocking.pid = blocking_locks.pid
WHERE NOT blocked_locks.granted;

Reset Stats Baseline (Controlled)

sql
SELECT pg_stat_statements_reset();  -- after deploy, measure fresh week
-- Requires pg_stat_statements extension

Identify Bloat Candidate

sql
SELECT
    schemaname,
    relname,
    n_live_tup,
    n_dead_tup,
    round(100.0 * n_dead_tup / NULLIF(n_live_tup + n_dead_tup, 0), 2) AS dead_pct,
    last_autovacuum,
    last_autoanalyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE relname IN ('payments', 'transactions', 'accounts')
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC;

Long-Running Transactions (Lock Risk)

sql
SELECT
    pid,
    application_name,
    now() - xact_start AS xact_duration,
    now() - query_start AS query_duration,
    LEFT(query, 150) AS query_snippet
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL
  AND state != 'idle'
ORDER BY xact_start;
-- xact_duration > 30s on OLTP — investigate

Safe Production EXPLAIN Wrapper

sql
BEGIN READ ONLY;
SET statement_timeout = '5s';
EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON)
SELECT payment_id, amount FROM payments WHERE customer_id = 1001 LIMIT 20;
ROLLBACK;
-- No ANALYZE on prod primary for risky queries

Part 12 — Production Usage

Banking Case Studies

Case Study 1: Payment History API Timeout

text
Symptom:  GET /payments/history p99 = 8s (SLA 500ms)
Measure:  APM — 1 JDBC query 7.9s
SQL:      SELECT * FROM payments WHERE customer_id=? ORDER BY created_at DESC OFFSET 50000 LIMIT 20
EXPLAIN:  Index Scan + Sort or Seq Scan; OFFSET cost dominates
Fix:      Keyset pagination (Lesson 11) + index (customer_id, created_at DESC, payment_id DESC)
Result:   p99 = 18ms
Lesson:   OFFSET pagination — not fixed by bigger instance

Case Study 2: Transfer API Lock Wait Monday Morning

text
Symptom:  POST /transfer timeouts 09:00–11:00
Measure:  wait_event=transactionid; blocker = interest_accrual batch
SQL:      batch UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance * 1.0001 — full table scan
Fix:      batch by account_id ranges + commit every 5K; schedule 02:00; SKIP LOCKED for non-critical paths
Result:   transfer p99 stable
Lesson:   tuning ≠ index — workflow scheduling

Case Study 3: Customer 360 Report After ETL

text
Symptom:  report 45 min (was 3 min)
Measure:  EXPLAIN rows=1M est, actual=40M on join
Stats:    reltuples drift 50% after Sunday load
Fix:      ANALYZE payments, accounts, customers on replica; extended stats region+country
Result:   2.5 min — further architect: mat view refresh hourly
Lesson:   Lesson 27 before Lesson 26

Case Study 4: Connection Pool Death Spiral

text
Symptom:  all APIs slow; CPU low; connectionTimeout spikes
Measure:  HikariCP active=50/50; threads blocked on external fraud API inside @Transactional
Fix:      move fraud check before txn; reduce pool wait; circuit breaker
Result:   latency normal
Lesson:   don't hold DB connection across network I/O

Production Runbook Snippet

text
1. Check APM error rate + p99 by endpoint
2. Check HikariCP pool metrics
3. pg_stat_activity wait events top 5
4. pg_stat_statements top total_time last 1h (if reset policy allows)
5. If single query: EXPLAIN on replica
6. If locks: identify blocker pid → application_name → kill only with approval
7. Escalate to DBA with: query text, EXPLAIN, wait_event, deploy correlation

@Transactional Scope Discipline

java
// ❌ Holds connection during external call
@Transactional
public void pay(PaymentRequest req) {
    var payment = paymentRepo.save(new Payment(...));
    fraudClient.check(req);  // 2s HTTP — conn held
    ledgerClient.post(payment);
}

// ✅ Minimize txn scope
public void pay(PaymentRequest req) {
    fraudClient.check(req);
    Payment payment = txTemplate.execute(status ->
        paymentRepo.save(new Payment(...)));
    ledgerClient.post(payment);
}

Read Replica Routing

@Transactional(readOnly = true)
@Target(DataSourceType.REPORTING)
public List<PaymentDto> getHistory(Long customerId, Pageable page) {
    return paymentQueryService.findHistory(customerId, page);
}
// Tune on replica; protect primary; ANALYZE replica separately

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: First step when user reports slow API?

Measure with APM/trace — identify if DB-bound, how many queries, which query duration.

Q2: EXPLAIN vs EXPLAIN ANALYZE production safety?

EXPLAIN safe; ANALYZE runs query — use replica, not destructive DML on primary.

Q3: What is N+1?

One query loads parent rows, N queries load children — fix with JOIN FETCH or batch.

Q4: pg_stat_statements purpose?

Aggregated query performance — calls, mean time, total time — find top offenders.

Q5: Index always fixes slow query?

No — locks, pool, N+1, full scan intentional, stale stats may be root cause.

Mid-Level

Q6: wait_event Lock vs IO?

Lock: blocked by another txn. IO: reading data pages — different fixes.

Q7: OFFSET pagination tuning path?

EXPLAIN shows skip cost — keyset pagination + matching composite index.

Q8: Pool exhausted but DB CPU low?

Connections held too long — long txn, external calls inside txn, or pool too small for thread count.

Q9: Post-ETL regression triage?

Stats drift → ANALYZE; EXPLAIN row mismatch; compare pg_stat_statements mean time.

Q10: Tuning workflow steps?

Measure → isolate → diagnose (plan/lock/pool/ORM) → fix → verify → document.

Senior

Q11: Plan good 50ms but query 30s in prod?

Lock wait, pool wait, network, sync replication, cold cache on first run — check pg_stat_activity and app metrics.

Q12: When not to add index?

Low selectivity, write-heavy table already over-indexed, problem is lock/N+1, report needs architecture fix.

Q13: Design idempotent payment insert tuning?

UNIQUE(client_request_id) index + single INSERT — not MAX(id)+1; measure duplicate path.

Q14: Batch job blocks OLTP — architect options?

Schedule off-peak, smaller commits, SKIP LOCKED, separate replica for batch reads, queue-based processing.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Enterprise slow query program components?

APM, pg_stat_statements, runbooks, EXPLAIN baselines, index governance, post-ETL ANALYZE, RACI, finops gate before scale.

Q16: When accept 10-minute report runtime?

Regulatory full export inherently large — async job + object storage; don't block OLTP tuning budget on it.

Scenario

Scenario: "Payment list API p99 6s after mobile app launch."

Trace: 1 query but OFFSET 10000 — keyset + index. Check pool and replica if read path. EXPLAIN on replica. Not: add cache before pagination fix.
