Lesson 29

Join Optimization

Phase 3: QUERY OPTIMIZATION & EXECUTION PLANS | Previous: Query Tuning Methodology | Next: Partitioning

SQL
1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why This Exists5Internal Working6Storage Internals7Memory Usage8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Complexity Analysis11Code / SQL Examples12Production Usage13Spring Boot Integration14Hibernate/JPA Integration15Architect Perspective16Decision Matrix17Comparison Tables18Common Mistakes19Interview Questions20Revision Sheet21Summary Table*Practice

Part 1 — Concept

What Is Join Optimization?

Join optimization is the process of making multi-table queries fast by ensuring the optimizer picks the right join algorithm, join order, and supporting indexes — and by rewriting SQL when the default join plan is wrong. Joins dominate reporting and many OLTP read paths; they are often the largest cost node in an execution plan.

sql
-- Typical banking join
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email, a.account_id, a.balance, p.amount
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN payments p ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.region = 'APAC'
  AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
  AND p.created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days';

Join in the Plan Tree

text
Hash Join (c ⋈ a)
  ├── Hash Join (intermediate ⋈ p)
  │     ├── Seq/Index Scan customers (region = APAC)
  │     └── Hash
  │           └── Index Scan accounts (status = ACTIVE)
  └── Hash
        └── Index Scan payments (created_at range)

OR (bad plan):

Nested Loop
  ├── Seq Scan customers (2M rows)
  └── Index Scan accounts (loops=2M)

Join Optimization Dimensions

text
JOIN OPTIMIZATION

├── Algorithm     → Nested Loop | Hash Join | Merge Join
├── Order         → which table is outer vs inner (build vs probe)
├── Access path   → Seq Scan vs Index Scan per table
├── Cardinality     → row estimates drive algorithm choice (Lesson 27)
├── Semi/Anti join  → EXISTS, IN, NOT EXISTS (Lesson 17)
├── Physical design → FK indexes, covering indexes, partitioning
└── SQL rewrite     → filter early, avoid cross join, subquery → join

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Join Optimization

text
1970s   System R — dynamic programming join order enumeration
        Nested loop only — memory for hash not assumed

1980s   Oracle hash join; sort-merge join for warehouse
        Star transformation (Oracle) — fact + dimension joins

1990s   PostgreSQL merge join + hash join
        "Join order matters" becomes DBA folklore

2000s   Cost-based join reordering standard
        FK indexing rules in OLTP schema design
        ORM accidental cartesian joins discovered via EXPLAIN

2010s   PostgreSQL join_collapse_limit, GEQO for many tables
        Semi-join deduplication from IN/EXISTS (Lesson 17)
        Columnar warehouses — different join engine (broadcast, shuffle)

2020s   Adaptive join (SQL Server, Oracle) — runtime switch NL ↔ Hash
        Parallel hash join (PostgreSQL)
        Microservices: "no cross-service JOIN" — join optimization becomes **intra-DB** discipline

Historical Lesson

Join optimization was the first major victory of cost-based optimizers over rule-based systems. Today the hard problems are wrong cardinality estimates and ORM-generated join explosions — not missing hash join support. Architects optimize joins inside service boundaries and use read models when cross-domain data is needed.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Join Problems Must We Solve?

Problem 1: Wrong Algorithm — Nested Loop at Scale

text
Estimated: 500 APAC customers
Actual:    500,000 (stale stats)
Plan:      Nested Loop → 500K × index probe on accounts
Fix:       ANALYZE + Hash Join or filter pushdown

Problem 2: Wrong Join Order — Large Table First

text
Build hash on payments (50M rows) instead of customers (500 rows filtered)
Memory: hash spills to disk — 10× slower
Fix:       stats + optimizer usually fixes; else rewrite subquery to filter first

Problem 3: Missing FK Index — Join Becomes Seq Scan

sql
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
-- No index on accounts(customer_id)
-- Nested Loop degenerates to Seq Scan accounts per customer OR hash on full accounts heap

Problem 4: Accidental Cross Join (Cartesian Product)

java
// JPQL missing join condition
SELECT c FROM Customer c, Payment p WHERE c.region = 'APAC'
-- 50K × 20M rows intermediate — timeout

Problem 5: EXISTS vs JOIN Duplication

sql
-- INNER JOIN without DISTINCT duplicates customers with 10 accounts
SELECT c.email FROM customers c JOIN accounts a ON ...
-- Semi-join (EXISTS) returns one row per customer — clearer and sometimes faster

Unified Problem Statement

Join optimization ensures multi-table queries use efficient algorithms and orders on correctly estimated row sets — with indexes on join keys — avoiding cartesian explosions, unnecessary duplication, and nested-loop disasters.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Joins Dominate Performance

Relational Model Core Operation

text
Normalized schema (Lessons 8–10) → data split across tables
Every customer 360 view, payment report, reconciliation → JOIN
Bad join plan = full pipeline slow even if each table indexed individually

Algorithm Complexity Difference

text
Nested Loop:  O(n × m) worst case
Hash Join:    O(n + m) average
Merge Join:   O(n + m) with sorted inputs

Wrong choice at n=1M → minutes vs seconds

Semi-Join Saves Work

text
"Customers with any payment" — don't need payment columns
EXISTS / IN semi-join stops at first match — no row multiplication
JOIN + DISTINCT adds sort/hash dedup cost

Microservices Boundary

text
Join optimization applies WITHIN Payment DB:
  payments ⋈ customers (same DB)

Cross-service:
  Payment API + Order API — application-side join or read model — NOT SQL JOIN

Part 5 — Internal Working

Join Algorithms In Depth

Nested Loop Join

text
FOR each row r in OUTER:
    FOR each row s in INNER where join condition matches r:
        emit (r, s)

Inner typically: Index Scan on join key — O(log m) per outer row
Total: O(n × log m) if indexed — OK when n small (100)

Nested Loop with Materialize:
  Inner cached if cheap — rare optimization
text
Best:  outer 100 rows, inner indexed on FK
Worst: outer 1M rows, inner seq scan each loop

Hash Join

text
Phase 1 BUILD: scan smaller/build side → hash table in memory (work_mem)
Phase 2 PROBE: scan probe side → hash lookup → emit matches

Cost: O(build + probe)
Spill: Hash Batches > 1 if build side > work_mem → disk

Best: medium/large equi-joins, no useful sort order
Requires: equality join condition (a.id = b.id)

Merge Join

text
Both inputs sorted on join key
Merge like merge-sort: advance pointers, emit matches

Cost: O(n + m) if already sorted
Else: sort both sides first — expensive

Best: both inputs index-ordered on join key, large sorted scans
Common: merge join on PK-FK when planner chooses index scans on both sides

Semi-Join (EXISTS / IN)

sql
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id)
text
Hash Semi Join:
  Build hash on accounts(customer_id)
  Scan customers — probe — emit customer if hit ONCE (no duplication)

Anti-Join (NOT EXISTS):
  Hash Anti Join — emit outer row if NO probe hit
text
PostgreSQL: IN (subquery) → semi-join rewrite (Lesson 17)
NOT IN with NULL → broken semantics — use NOT EXISTS

Join Order Enumeration

text
3 tables: A, B, C
Possible orders (bushy vs left-deep): optimizer explores via dynamic programming
Cost = sum of intermediate result sizes + join algorithm costs

PostgreSQL join_collapse_limit (default 8):
  Tables beyond limit → GEQO genetic optimizer (less optimal)

Many-table report: consider simplifying view or staged CTEs (Lesson 18)

Selectivity Pushdown

text
WHERE c.region = 'APAC' AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'

Ideal plan:
  Filter customers APAC first (small)
  Join accounts with index on (customer_id) + filter ACTIVE
  NOT: full accounts hash then filter

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Joins and Physical Storage

Index on Join Column — Critical

sql
CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_customer_id ON accounts (customer_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_customer_id ON payments (customer_id);

Nested Loop: index probe O(log n) per outer row
Hash Join: full scan build side — sequential I/O — still needs stats for order
Merge Join: index scan provides order — avoid sort

Heap Fetch Amplification

text
Index Scan join:
  Each match → random heap page fetch
  Covering index (INCLUDE) on join query → reduce heap fetches (Lesson 26)

Join 3 tables all non-covering:
  Random I/O storm — buffer cache churn

Partition-Wise Join (PostgreSQL 11+)

text
payments partitioned by month
customers not partitioned
Join on customer_id:
  partition pruning on payments.created_at filter reduces partitions scanned
Architect: align partition key with common filter (time) on fact tables

Cluster / Physical Order

text
CLUSTER accounts USING idx_accounts_customer_id;  -- one-time PG
Subsequent range scans on customer_id more sequential — rare in OLTP
Normal: rely on index not cluster

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Join Memory Dynamics

AlgorithmMemorySpill Signal
Nested LoopMinimalNone (I/O bound)
Hash Join buildwork_mem for hash tableHash Batches: n
Merge JoinMinimal if pre-sortedSort children spill
Hash Semi JoinHash on inner sideSame as hash join
Materialize (CTE)TuplestoreDisk in EXPLAIN

Build Side Selection

text
Optimizer picks smaller estimated side as hash build
Wrong estimate → build on 50M row table → spill
Fix cardinality (Lesson 27) not just work_mem

Parallel Hash Join (PostgreSQL)

text
Gather
  Parallel Hash Join
    Parallel Seq Scan (build workers share)
    Parallel Seq Scan (probe)
Uses shared memory — complex but faster on large scans

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Join Execution Flows

Flow 1: OLTP — Customer + Active Accounts

sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email, a.account_id, a.balance
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.customer_id = 1001
  AND a.status = 'ACTIVE';
text
1. Filter customer_id = 1001 — 1 row (PK)
2. Nested Loop or Hash (1 row → NL always wins)
3. Index Scan accounts(customer_id) — few rows
4. Filter ACTIVE — or index (customer_id, status)
Time: sub-ms

Flow 2: Report — Region + Accounts + Payments

sql
SELECT c.region, COUNT(DISTINCT p.payment_id), SUM(p.amount)
FROM customers c
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
JOIN payments p ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE p.created_at >= '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY c.region;
text
1. Often: Hash Join payments (date filter) → customers
   OR Hash Join accounts → payments → aggregate
2. HashAggregate by region
3. Check EXPLAIN: which table scanned first — payments filter should reduce early
4. Indexes: payments(created_at), payments(customer_id), accounts(customer_id)

Flow 3: Semi-Join — Customers With Payments

sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM payments p
    WHERE p.customer_id = c.customer_id
      AND p.created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '90 days'
);
text
Plan: Hash Semi Join
  Build: hash payments (filtered by date) on customer_id
  Probe: customers
No duplicate customer rows — vs JOIN + DISTINCT

Flow 4: Anti-Join — Customers Without Accounts

sql
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id
);
text
Hash Anti Join:
  Build hash all account customer_ids
  Scan customers — emit if NOT in hash
Index on accounts(customer_id) helps build scan

Flow 5: Bad Cartesian — ORM Bug

sql
-- Accidental cross join
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers c, payments p WHERE c.region = 'APAC';
-- Missing c.customer_id = p.customer_id
Plan: Nested Loop with Seq Scan both — product of rows

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Join Optimization Playbook

Step-by-Step

text
1. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) — identify join nodes
2. Check algorithm: NL vs Hash vs Merge — appropriate for row counts?
3. Compare actual vs estimated rows at each join input (Lesson 27)
4. Verify indexes on ALL FK / join columns (Lesson 26)
5. Push filters as early as possible — rewrite if optimizer doesn't
6. EXISTS vs JOIN+DISTINCT — use semi-join when no inner columns needed
7. Avoid SELECT * — narrower rows faster hash build
8. Many tables — simplify or staged CTE with filter early
9. Re-test on replica with production-like stats

Join Algorithm Selection Guide

ShapePrefer
Outer 1–1000 rows, inner indexed FKNested Loop
Both large, equi-joinHash Join
Both large, sorted on join keyMerge Join
Existence onlyEXISTS semi-join
AbsenceNOT EXISTS anti-join
Inequality join (rare)Nested Loop or special

Star Schema vs OLTP Joins

text
STAR (warehouse / reporting):
  Fact (payments) center — JOIN many dimensions (customer, branch, product, date)
  Optimizer: filter fact by date first — partition prune
  Broadcast small dimensions or hash join
  Denormalized dim tables OK

OLTP (microservice DB):
  Few joins (2–3 tables) per query
  Highly selective filters — index nested loop common
  Avoid 8-table join in API path — split query or denormalize read model

Rewrite Patterns

sql
-- ❌ JOIN + DISTINCT when only existence needed
SELECT DISTINCT c.customer_id FROM customers c
JOIN payments p ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE ...;

-- ✅ Semi-join
SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM payments p WHERE p.customer_id = c.customer_id AND ...);

-- ❌ Filter after join
SELECT * FROM customers c JOIN payments p ON ...
WHERE p.created_at >= '2024-01-01';
-- Often OK if optimizer pushes — verify EXPLAIN

-- ✅ Subquery/CTE filter fact first (if optimizer fails)
WITH recent_p AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM payments WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01'
)
SELECT c.* FROM customers c JOIN recent_p rp ON rp.customer_id = c.customer_id;

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

PatternTime (typical)Notes
NL, outer n, inner indexedO(n log m)n small
NL, outer n, inner seqO(n × m)disaster
Hash JoinO(a + b)+ spill if large
Merge Join sortedO(a + b)+ sort if unsorted
Semi-join EXISTSO(a + b)no row multiply
JOIN + DISTINCTO(join output) + dedupoften worse than semi
Cross joinO(n × m)always avoid

Join output size can exceed either input — selectivity of join condition matters as much as algorithm.

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Join Optimization Masterclass

Index Package for Join-Heavy Schema

sql
-- FK indexes (mandatory)
CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_customer_id ON accounts (customer_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_customer_id ON payments (customer_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_transactions_account_id ON transactions (account_id);

-- Composite for join + filter
CREATE INDEX idx_accounts_customer_status ON accounts (customer_id, status);
CREATE INDEX idx_payments_customer_created ON payments (customer_id, created_at DESC);

-- Parent side filters
CREATE INDEX idx_customers_region ON customers (region) WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';

Hash Join Friendly Report

sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.email,
    COUNT(p.payment_id) AS payment_count,
    SUM(p.amount) AS total_paid
FROM customers c
JOIN payments p ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE c.region = 'APAC'
  AND p.status = 'COMPLETED'
  AND p.created_at >= DATE '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.email;
-- Expect: filtered scan payments or customers → Hash Join → HashAggregate

Semi-Join Rewrite

sql
-- Before
SELECT c.email
FROM customers c
JOIN payments p ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE p.amount > 10000
GROUP BY c.email;  -- implicit dedup if multiple payments

-- After
SELECT c.email
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM payments p
    WHERE p.customer_id = c.customer_id
      AND p.amount > 10000
);

Anti-Join — Orphan Customers

sql
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email, c.created_at
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM accounts a WHERE a.customer_id = c.customer_id
)
AND c.status = 'ACTIVE';
-- Hash Anti Join — marketing re-engagement

Filter Early with CTE

sql
WITH apac_customers AS (
    SELECT customer_id, email, region
    FROM customers
    WHERE region = 'APAC' AND status = 'ACTIVE'
),
recent_payments AS (
    SELECT customer_id, amount, created_at
    FROM payments
    WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days'
      AND status = 'COMPLETED'
)
SELECT ac.email, rp.amount, rp.created_at
FROM apac_customers ac
JOIN recent_payments rp ON rp.customer_id = ac.customer_id;
-- Smaller hash inputs — helps if optimizer doesn't push filters

LATERAL for Top-N Per Group (Join Alternative)

sql
SELECT c.customer_id, c.email, lp.payment_id, lp.amount
FROM customers c
CROSS JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT payment_id, amount
    FROM payments p
    WHERE p.customer_id = c.customer_id
    ORDER BY created_at DESC
    LIMIT 1
) lp
WHERE c.region = 'APAC';
-- Index (customer_id, created_at DESC) — efficient per customer
-- vs JOIN all payments + window ROW_NUMBER (Lesson 19)

Oracle Star Transformation Hint (Warehouse)

sql
SELECT /*+ STAR_TRANSFORMATION */
    d.region, SUM(f.amount)
FROM payments f
JOIN customers d ON d.customer_id = f.customer_id
JOIN branches b ON b.branch_id = f.branch_id
WHERE f.created_at >= DATE '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY d.region;
-- Warehouse only — not typical OLTP API

Part 12 — Production Usage

Join Optimization in Banking Production

OLTP API — Max 2–3 Table Joins

text
GET /customer/{id}/summary:
  customers ⋈ accounts (aggregate in SQL or app)
  NOT: customers ⋈ accounts ⋈ transactions ⋈ payments ⋈ branches in one API query

Separate:
  /payments?customerId= — indexed list
  /accounts?customerId= — indexed list
Architect: join depth budget per endpoint

Reconciliation — Controlled 4-Table Join

sql
-- Read replica, off-peak OK
SELECT
    bs.line_id,
    p.payment_id,
    p.amount,
    c.email
FROM bank_statement_lines bs
JOIN payments p ON p.external_ref = bs.reference
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = p.customer_id
JOIN accounts a ON a.account_id = p.account_id
WHERE bs.batch_id = :batchId
  AND bs.status = 'UNMATCHED';
-- Indexes: external_ref UNIQUE, batch_id partial on UNMATCHED
-- EXPLAIN baseline in perf-baselines/

N+1 Is Repeated Join Failure

text
501 queries = 501 single-table "joins" in application loop
Fix: one JOIN FETCH — one Hash Join or NL with batch
Join optimization at ORM layer first

Microservices — Application Join

java
// Order totals + Payment status — two DBs
List<Order> orders = orderClient.getOrders(customerId);
List<Payment> payments = paymentRepo.findByCustomerId(customerId);
Map<Long, Payment> byOrderId = payments.stream()...;
// O(n) memory join — NOT SQL cross-DB join
// At scale: PaymentReadModel fed by OrderPaid events

Joins in Spring Data JPA

JOIN FETCH — Fix N+1

java

    JOIN FETCH c.accounts a
    WHERE c.region = :region
      AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
    """)
List<Customer> findActiveCustomersWithAccounts(@Param("region") String region);
// EXPLAIN: Hash Join or NL — verify DISTINCT not causing extra sort

EntityGraph

java
@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"accounts"})
List<Customer> findByRegion(String region);

Projection DTO — Narrower Join

java
@Query("""
    SELECT new com.bank.dto.CustomerAccountDto(

    FROM Customer c
    JOIN c.accounts a
    WHERE c.customerId = :id AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
    """)
List<CustomerAccountDto> findCustomerAccounts(@Param("id") Long id);
// No entity hydration — less memory — same join plan

Native Join Report

java
@Query(value = """
    SELECT c.email, COUNT(p.payment_id), SUM(p.amount)
    FROM customers c
    JOIN payments p ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id
    WHERE c.region = :region AND p.created_at >= :since

    """, nativeQuery = true)
List<Object[]> paymentSummaryByEmail(@Param("region") String region, @Param("since") Instant since);

Avoid Cartesian in Criteria API

java
// ❌ accidental cross join — missing join predicate
root.join("accounts", JoinType.INNER);  // must link ON customer_id

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

ORM Join Pitfalls

Fetch Join + Pagination Bug

java
@Query("SELECT c FROM Customer c JOIN FETCH c.accounts WHERE c.region = :r")
List<Customer> findPage(Pageable pageable);  // Hibernate may warn — in-memory pagination
// Join fetch all then slice in memory — disaster
// Fix: separate query for IDs with pagination, then JOIN FETCH WHERE id IN (:ids)

Multiple Bag Fetch Exception

java
// Cannot JOIN FETCH two @OneToMany collections in one query
JOIN FETCH c.accounts JOIN FETCH c.payments  // Hibernate error
// Fix: two queries or DTO native join

@BatchSize vs Join Fetch

java
@OneToMany @BatchSize(size = 50)
private List<Account> accounts;
// 1 + ceil(n/50) queries — middle ground
// EXPLAIN each — vs 1 join query for full load

Lazy + Open Session In View

yaml
spring.jpa.open-in-view: false  # recommended
# Forces explicit join in service layer — join plan visible in one EXPLAIN
# OSIV hides N+1 until production load

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

Join Architecture Decisions

Join Depth Budget

text
API endpoint max join tables: 3 (team standard)
Report query max: 6 — replica only
Warehouse: unlimited star joins — ETL schema designed for it

Violations require ADR with EXPLAIN evidence

Read Model vs Runtime Join

text
If API always returns customer + latest payment + account totals:
  Option A: 3-table join every request — tune indexes
  Option B: customer_summary table updated by events — 0 joins
Choose B when p99 SLA tight and join cost high

Cross-Service Data

text
❌ Federated query engine joining Payment DB + Order DB in production OLTP
✅ Saga + local cache of order_id list
✅ Data warehouse for analytics joins
✅ CQRS read store with pre-joined documents

Denormalization Trigger

text
When EXPLAIN shows 4-way join on hot path > 50ms after index/stats tuning:
  Consider denormalized column (Lesson 9): payment.customer_region copied on insert
  Trade: storage + consistency on region change vs join elimination

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: No Index on FK

sql
JOIN accounts a ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
-- Missing idx_accounts_customer_id — #1 join performance bug

Mistake 2: JOIN When EXISTS Suffices

sql
SELECT DISTINCT c.* FROM customers c JOIN payments p ...  -- sort/hash dedup
-- Use EXISTS

Mistake 3: Trust Optimizer Filter Pushdown Without EXPLAIN

text
Filter not pushed — huge hash on full payments
Fix: CTE with explicit filter first

Mistake 4: ORM Cartesian

java
FROM Customer c, Payment p  -- missing ON

Mistake 5: Cross-Database Join in Microservices

sql
-- dblink foreign table join — latency, coupling, failure blast radius

Mistake 6: DISTINCT After JOIN to Fix Duplication

text

Mistake 7: Fetch Join + Pageable on Large Set

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: Three main join algorithms?

Nested Loop, Hash Join, Merge Join.

Q2: When Nested Loop is ideal?

Small outer result set, inner table indexed on join key.

Q3: Why index foreign key columns?

Speed nested loop probes and hash build scans on joins.

Q4: EXISTS vs INNER JOIN for "customers with payments"?

EXISTS semi-join — no duplicate customer rows.

Q5: What is cartesian product?

Join without condition — every row paired with every row — O(n×m).

Mid-Level

Q6: Hash Join spill symptom in EXPLAIN?

Hash Batches: >1, Disk temp — build side exceeded work_mem.

Q7: Semi-join vs INNER JOIN + DISTINCT performance?

Semi-join stops at first match; JOIN materializes all matches then dedups.

Q8: Wrong join order symptom?

Building hash on largest table — spill, slow; often stats issue.

Q9: Fix N+1 from join perspective?

Single JOIN FETCH — one join plan instead of N single-table lookups.

Q10: NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS?

NOT EXISTS anti-join NULL-safe; NOT IN fails with NULL in subquery.

Senior

Q11: Star schema join optimization?

Filter fact table by date/partition first; hash join dimensions; avoid scanning full fact.

Q12: Merge join when chosen?

Both inputs sorted on join key — index scans on PK/FK both sides.

Q13: Microservice needs order + payment data — SQL join?

No cross-DB join — API composition, events, or warehouse.

Q14: EXPLAIN shows Hash Join but still slow?

Large true result set — legitimate work; partition, pre-aggregate, read model, not always wrong algorithm.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Join depth policy for OLTP APIs?

Max 3 tables; reports on replica; read models when join cost exceeds SLA after tuning.

Q16: When denormalize instead of join?

Hot path 4+ table join after index/stats exhausted; copy stable attributes with event-driven sync.

Scenario

Scenario: "Customer search with accounts slow after data doubling."

EXPLAIN join node — NL loops doubled? ANALYZE; check idx on accounts(customer_id); consider Hash Join; verify ORM not N+1; semi-join if only filtering customers with accounts.

Algorithms

text
Nested Loop  → small outer + indexed inner
Hash Join    → equi-join, large tables, build smaller side
Merge Join   → sorted inputs on join key
Semi Join    → EXISTS / IN — no dup
Anti Join    → NOT EXISTS — not NOT IN with NULL

Rules

text
✅ Index every FK join column
✅ EXPLAIN join nodes + row estimates
✅ EXISTS when no inner columns needed
✅ Filter early — CTE if needed
✅ JOIN FETCH for ORM N+1
✅ Max join depth on OLTP API

❌ Fetch join + pagination all rows

text
NL loops= huge     → stats, index, hash
Hash Batches > 1   → build too big
Seq Scan on FK     → missing index
Many JDBC calls    → N+1 not join tuned

Part 1 — Concept

What Is Table Partitioning?

Partitioning splits one logical table into multiple physical segments (partitions) by a partition key — typically date, region, or hash bucket. Queries that filter on the partition key can skip irrelevant partitions (partition pruning), reducing I/O and maintenance scope.

sql
-- PostgreSQL declarative partitioning (range by month)
CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id     BIGINT NOT NULL,
    customer_id    BIGINT NOT NULL,
    amount         NUMERIC(18,2) NOT NULL,
    status         VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    created_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (payment_id, created_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

CREATE TABLE payments_2024_01 PARTITION OF payments
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2024-02-01');

CREATE TABLE payments_2024_02 PARTITION OF payments
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-02-01') TO ('2024-03-01');
-- Parent table: no rows stored — partitions hold data

Logical vs Physical View

text
Application / ORM:
  SELECT * FROM payments WHERE created_at >= '2024-06-01'
  → still queries "payments" — one table name

Database internally:
  payments_2024_06, payments_2024_07, ... only scanned
  payments_2023_* pruned — never opened

Partitioning Classification

text
PARTITIONING STRATEGIES

├── RANGE          → dates, numeric ranges (created_at, payment_id ranges)
├── LIST           → discrete values (region, status bucket, tenant_id)
├── HASH           → even spread by hash(key) — no natural prune filter
│
├── Single-level   → one partition key column
├── Composite      → (region, month) — multi-column partition key
│
├── Local objects  → index per partition (default PG)
├── Global index   → Oracle global index spanning partitions (special)
│
└── Lifecycle      → DETACH old → archive; ATTACH new monthly

Partitioning vs Sharding vs Archive Table

text
┌──────────────┬─────────────────┬─────────────────┬─────────────────┐
│              │ PARTITION       │ SHARD           │ ARCHIVE TABLE   │
├──────────────┼─────────────────┼─────────────────┼─────────────────┤
│ Scope        │ One database    │ Multiple DBs    │ Separate table  │
│ App sees     │ One table       │ Router logic    │ Two table names │
│ Prune key    │ Usually yes     │ Shard key       │ Manual routing  │
│ Cross-part   │ Easy JOIN       │ Hard            │ App/ETL move    │
│ Use case     │ Large single DB │ Horizontal scale│ Cold data       │
└──────────────┴─────────────────┴─────────────────┴─────────────────┘

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Partitioning

text
1990s   Oracle Partitioning — range for data warehouse fact tables
        Very expensive option — enterprise only

2000s   PostgreSQL inheritance partitioning — manual, brittle
        MySQL partitioning (5.1) — limited
        DB2 table partitioning

2010s   PostgreSQL 10 — native declarative partitioning (major)
        Automatic partition creation scripts / pg_partman
        Cloud RDS makes partition management operational focus

2010s   PostgreSQL 11 — partition-wise join, improved pruning
        PostgreSQL 12 — ATTACH/DETACH CONCURRENTLY

2020s   Billions-row OLTP fact tables (payments, events) partitioned by month
        Time-series BRIN + partition hybrid
        Microservices: partition within service DB before sharding
        Compliance: DETACH + archive old partitions to cold storage

Historical Lesson

Partitioning was born for data warehouses (scan one month of sales). It is now standard for OLTP fact tables at scale — but wrong partition key (e.g. hash when all queries filter by date) gives zero pruning benefit with extra planner complexity. Partition when access patterns match the key, not because the table "feels big."

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does Partitioning Solve?

Problem 1: Time-Range Queries on Billion-Row Table

sql
-- Without partition: scan/index 5 years of payments for "last 30 days"
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(amount) FROM payments
WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '30 days';

-- With monthly partitions: only 1–2 child tables scanned
-- 50× less data touched

Problem 2: Index Bloat and Size on Monolithic Table

text
Single payments PK index: 100M entries — deep B-tree, cache unfriendly
Per-month partition indexes: 2M entries each — shallower, hot partitions in cache

Problem 3: Retention and Compliance (GDPR / PCI)

text
Delete data older than 7 years:
  Without partition: DELETE ... WHERE created_at < X — massive WAL, bloat, long lock
  With partition: DROP TABLE payments_2017_01 — instant metadata operation (after DETACH)

Problem 4: Maintenance Windows

text
REINDEX entire 500M row table — hours
REINDEX one monthly partition — minutes
VACUUM one hot partition — targeted

Problem 5: Bulk Load Isolation

text
ETL loads June partition only — less lock contention with reads on other months
ATTACH pre-loaded partition — swap data quickly

Unified Problem Statement

Partitioning divides large tables along a key aligned with query and lifecycle patterns — enabling partition pruning, faster maintenance, and efficient archival — without changing the logical table name seen by applications.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Not One Big Table + Index?

Index Alone Has Limits

text
Index on created_at helps range query — but:
  Index still spans all years — large, cache pressure
  DELETE old rows — marks dead tuples across heap — vacuum pain
  Partition prune + smaller indexes per month wins at scale

When Single Table Is Fine

text
< 50–100M rows (rule of thumb — workload dependent)
Queries need full table scan analytics without partition key filter
No retention drop requirement
Team lacks partition operational maturity

Partition Key Must Match Queries

text
Partition by created_at:
  ✅ WHERE created_at >= ...
  ✅ Recent OLTP inserts hit current partition (hot spot manageable)
  ❌ WHERE customer_id = 1001 only — all partitions scanned unless sub-partition strategy

Composite: PARTITION BY LIST (region) SUBPARTITION BY RANGE (created_at)
  ✅ APAC + last month queries prune both dimensions

vs Read Replica / Sharding

text
Partition: one PostgreSQL instance, operational split
Shard: multiple instances — app routing, cross-shard queries hard
Architect: partition first on single DB; shard when CPU/IO ceiling hit

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Partitioning Works Internally

Declarative Partitioning (PostgreSQL)

text
Parent table: partition definition + CHECK constraints on children
Child tables: inherit schema, hold rows
Constraint exclusion / partition pruning:
  Planner examines WHERE clause against partition bounds
  Eliminates partitions that cannot contain matching rows

INSERT:
  Router evaluates partition key → targets one child heap

UPDATE changing partition key:
  DELETE from old partition + INSERT to new — expensive
  Avoid updating partition key column in design

Partition Pruning

sql
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM payments
WHERE created_at >= '2024-06-01' AND created_at < '2024-07-01';

Plan may show:
  Append
    -> Seq Scan on payments_2024_06
  Partitions pruned: 2024_01..05, 2024_07.. (not in plan)

Pruning requires:
  Predicate matches partition key (no function on column: bad DATE(created_at))
  enable_partition_pruning = on (default)
  Stable bounds on partitions

Partition-Wise Join (PostgreSQL 11+)

sql
-- Both tables partitioned compatibly on created_at
SELECT p.payment_id, t.transaction_id
FROM payments p
JOIN transactions t ON t.account_id = p.account_id
   AND t.created_at = p.created_at
WHERE p.created_at >= '2024-06-01';
-- Optimizer may join matching partitions pairwise — smaller hash tables
Requires: compatible partition strategy and join includes partition key

HASH Partitioning

sql
CREATE TABLE events PARTITION BY HASH (customer_id);
CREATE TABLE events_p0 PARTITION OF events FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 4, REMAINDER 0);
-- ... p1, p2, p3

Pruning: only when customer_id = X or IN list — hash remainder known
No prune: full table aggregate without customer filter — all 4 partitions scanned
Use: write spread, not time-range reports

LIST Partitioning

sql
CREATE TABLE payments PARTITION BY LIST (region);
CREATE TABLE payments_apac PARTITION OF payments FOR VALUES IN ('APAC');
CREATE TABLE payments_emea PARTITION OF payments FOR VALUES IN ('EMEA');

Prune: WHERE region = 'APAC' → one partition
Multi-tenant: LIST (tenant_id) — strong isolation per tenant partition

Constraint Exclusion (Legacy / Fallback)

text
Pre-PG10 inheritance tables used CHECK (created_at >= ... AND < ...)
Planner constraint exclusion — same pruning idea, more manual

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Partition Physical Storage

Separate Heap Files per Partition

text
payments_2024_06: own heap file, own indexes, own FSM/VM
Drop partition: unlink files — fast vs DELETE millions of rows
Each partition: separate autovacuum, bloat, statistics (ANALYZE per partition)

Primary Key on Partitioned Table

sql
-- PostgreSQL: PK must include partition key
PRIMARY KEY (payment_id, created_at)

-- payment_id alone not globally unique across partitions unless guaranteed — 
-- usually (payment_id, created_at) or use global UUID + partition key

Index Strategies

text
LOCAL index (default):
  idx_payments_2024_06_customer ON payments_2024_06(customer_id)
  Pruned with partition — smaller per child

Global concept (Oracle):
  One index entry across partitions — different operational model
PostgreSQL: no true global index — unique constraints must include partition key

TOAST, Bloat, WAL

text
DELETE 50M old rows monolithic table:
  50M dead tuples, massive WAL, autovacuum backlog

DROP partition:
  Minimal WAL — catalog change + file delete
Architect: retention via DROP/DETACH not DELETE at scale

ATTACH / DETACH

sql
-- Pre-load new month
CREATE TABLE payments_2025_01 (LIKE payments INCLUDING ALL);
COPY payments_2025_01 FROM ...;
ALTER TABLE payments ATTACH PARTITION payments_2025_01
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2025-01-01') TO ('2025-02-01');

-- Archive old month
ALTER TABLE payments DETACH PARTITION payments_2018_01;
ALTER TABLE payments_2018_01 SET SCHEMA archive;
-- or pg_dump archive schema to S3, DROP TABLE

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Partitioning and Memory

AspectEffect
Buffer cacheHot recent partition stays cached — old partitions cold
Hash join per partitionPartition-wise join — smaller hashes fit work_mem
Planner memoryMany partitions (1000+) — planning time increases
StatisticsPer-partition reltuples — accurate prune if ANALYZE each child
Connection poolUnchanged — logical one table

Too Many Partitions Problem

text
Daily partitions × 10 years = 3650 children
Planner prune loop cost — milliseconds to seconds planning
Guideline: monthly for payments common; daily only if proven need
pg_partman manages retention — don't hand-roll 500 partitions without automation

work_mem and Partition-Wise Hash Join

text
Join June payments ⋈ June transactions:
  Two 2M row partitions vs two 100M monolithic tables
  Hash build 2M fits work_mem — no spill
  Monolithic: Hash Batches 8 — disk

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Partition Query Execution Flows

Flow 1: Pruned Range Scan

sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT payment_id, amount FROM payments
WHERE created_at >= '2024-06-15' AND created_at < '2024-06-16';
text
1. Planner: prune to payments_2024_06 only
2. Index Scan idx_2024_06_customer_created if exists
3. Return rows — single partition Append child
Buffers: fraction of full table

Flow 2: No Prune — Full Scan All Partitions

sql
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM payments
WHERE customer_id = 1001
GROUP BY customer_id;
-- Partition key created_at not in WHERE
text
Append
  -> Seq Scan payments_2024_01 ... (filter customer_id)
  -> Seq Scan payments_2024_02 ...
  ... all months
Unless: subpartition by customer hash or BRIN+partition hybrid design

Fix: different partition strategy OR accept index on customer_id on each partition
Index Scan each partition — still N partition index scans — better than one huge index sometimes

Flow 3: Partition DROP for Retention

text
1. ALTER TABLE payments DETACH PARTITION payments_2017_06;
2. pg_dump archive OR move to cold tablespace
3. DROP TABLE payments_2017_06;
4. No VACUUM on parent — instant space reclaim
Compliance audit: archive manifest logged

Flow 4: INSERT Routing

text
INSERT INTO payments (...) VALUES (..., '2024-06-20', ...);
1. Evaluate created_at partition bound
2. Route insert to payments_2024_06 heap only
3. Update indexes on that partition only
Current month partition: insert hot spot — right edge B-tree growth (acceptable)

Flow 5: Partition-Wise Join

sql
-- payments and transactions both RANGE(created_at)
EXPLAIN SELECT ...
FROM payments p JOIN transactions t
  ON p.account_id = t.account_id AND p.created_at = t.created_at
WHERE p.created_at >= '2024-06-01' AND p.created_at < '2024-07-01';
text
Append Nested Loop or Hash Join per partition pair:
  payments_2024_06 ⋈ transactions_2024_06
Prune + smaller joins — win

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Partitioning Performance Rules

When Partitioning Helps

text
✅ Time-range queries on fact table (payments, transactions, audit)
✅ Retention DROP/DETACH by month/year
✅ Bulk load into current partition
✅ Maintenance REINDEX/VACUUM scoped
✅ Partition-wise join when both facts share time key
✅ Table > 100M rows with clear time filter pattern

When Partitioning Hurts or Fails

text
❌ Queries rarely filter on partition key
❌ Too many partitions (planning overhead)
❌ UPDATE partition key frequently — row migration between heaps
❌ Global uniqueness on non-partition column without including key in PK
❌ Small table "future proofing" — operational burden only
❌ Expecting partition to fix missing index on customer_id

Performance Hierarchy

text
BEST:
  Range partition by created_at + query filters created_at + local index (customer_id, created_at)
  Retention via DETACH not DELETE

GOOD:
  List tenant_id + range month for multi-tenant SaaS

MIXED:
  Hash only for insert spread — full scans hit all partitions

WORST:
  5000 daily partitions, no prune in queries — planner tax for nothing

Monitoring

sql
-- PostgreSQL: partition sizes
SELECT
    child.relname AS partition,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(child.oid)) AS size
FROM pg_inherits
JOIN pg_class parent ON pg_inherits.inhparent = parent.oid
JOIN pg_class child ON pg_inherits.inhrelid = child.oid
WHERE parent.relname = 'payments'
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(child.oid) DESC;

-- Prune verification: EXPLAIN must show Append with subset of children

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

OperationMonolithicPartitioned (pruned)
Range scan 1 month / 5 years dataO(n) or O(log n) wide indexO(n/60) approx
INSERTO(log n) indexO(log n_part) — smaller n
DELETE old yearO(rows) WALO(1) DROP partition
Query by customer_id onlyO(log n) one indexO(k × log n_part) k partitions
Planner timeO(1) tablesO(partitions) prune check
JOIN same time keyO(a+b)O(a_part+b_part) partition-wise

k = partitions scanned when prune fails — can erase benefit

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Partitioning Masterclass

Monthly Range — Payments (PostgreSQL)

sql
CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id      BIGINT NOT NULL,
    customer_id     BIGINT NOT NULL,
    amount          NUMERIC(18,2) NOT NULL,
    status          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    client_request_id VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (payment_id, created_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

-- Template for automation (pg_partman or Flyway monthly job)
CREATE TABLE payments_2024_06 PARTITION OF payments
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-06-01') TO ('2024-07-01');

CREATE INDEX idx_payments_2024_06_cust_created
ON payments_2024_06 (customer_id, created_at DESC);

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_payments_2024_06_client_request
ON payments_2024_06 (client_request_id);
-- UNIQUE on partition — global uniqueness if client_request_id never repeats across time
-- OR include created_at in unique scope — business rule dependent

Transactions Partition + BRIN Optional

sql
CREATE TABLE transactions (
    transaction_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    account_id     BIGINT NOT NULL,
    amount         NUMERIC(18,2) NOT NULL,
    created_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (transaction_id, created_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

CREATE TABLE transactions_2024_06 PARTITION OF transactions
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-06-01') TO ('2024-07-01');

CREATE INDEX idx_txn_2024_06_acct_created
ON transactions_2024_06 (account_id, created_at DESC);

-- Optional wide time scan within partition
CREATE INDEX idx_txn_2024_06_created_brin
ON transactions_2024_06 USING brin (created_at);

LIST — Multi-Region (Regulatory Data Residency)

sql
CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    region      VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
    email       TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (customer_id, region)
) PARTITION BY LIST (region);

CREATE TABLE customers_apac PARTITION OF customers FOR VALUES IN ('APAC');
CREATE TABLE customers_emea PARTITION OF customers FOR VALUES IN ('EMEA');
CREATE TABLE customers_amer PARTITION OF customers FOR VALUES IN ('AMER');

HASH — Event Ingest Spread

sql
CREATE TABLE payment_events (
    event_id     UUID NOT NULL,
    payment_id   BIGINT NOT NULL,
    payload      JSONB NOT NULL,
    created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (event_id, created_at)
) PARTITION BY HASH (payment_id);

CREATE TABLE payment_events_p0 PARTITION OF payment_events
    FOR VALUES WITH (MODULUS 8, REMAINDER 0);
-- ... p1 through p7

Default Partition (Catch-All — Use Carefully)

sql
CREATE TABLE payments_default PARTITION OF payments DEFAULT;
-- Rows not matching any bound land here — prevents INSERT fail
-- Risk: becomes bloated junk drawer — monitor and split

Retention Job

sql
-- Detach and drop older than 7 years
ALTER TABLE payments DETACH PARTITION payments_2017_06;
ALTER TABLE payments DETACH PARTITION payments_2017_07;
-- Move to archive schema or S3 export then:
DROP TABLE payments_2017_06;
DROP TABLE payments_2017_07;

Oracle Range Partition (Reference)

sql
CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id NUMBER,
    created_at TIMESTAMP,
    amount NUMBER(18,2)
)
PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at) (
    PARTITION p2024_01 VALUES LESS THAN (TO_DATE('2024-02-01','YYYY-MM-DD')),
    PARTITION p2024_02 VALUES LESS THAN (TO_DATE('2024-03-01','YYYY-MM-DD'))
);
-- Local index on (customer_id, created_at) per partition

Part 12 — Production Usage

Partitioning in Banking Production

Payments Table — Standard Pattern

text
Trigger: > 200M rows OR retention DROP required OR monthly report SLA miss
Key: created_at RANGE monthly
PK: (payment_id, created_at)
Indexes per partition: (customer_id, created_at DESC), UNIQUE(client_request_id) if scoped
Automation: pg_partman or K8s CronJob Flyway monthly partition
Retention: 7 years PCI — DETACH + glacier

Audit Log — High Insert, Time Query Only

text
PARTITION BY RANGE (changed_at) weekly or monthly
No UPDATE on audit rows — ideal for partition
Queries: WHERE payment_id = ? AND changed_at > ? — index (payment_id, changed_at) per partition

When NOT to Partition customers

text
customers: 10M rows — index on PK/email sufficient
Wide queries by region without list partition — single table + index
Partition customers only for regulatory LIST(region) isolation

ETL / Reconciliation

text
Load bank_statement_lines monthly partition matching statement cycle
JOIN payments same month partition — partition-wise join
Cross-month reconciliation: two-partition Append — still bounded

Operational Calendar

text
1st of month 00:05 UTC: CREATE next month partition + indexes
1st of month 01:00: ANALYZE new empty partition (cheap)
Quarterly: review default partition row count
Annually: DETACH year N-7 partitions after legal sign-off

Part 13 — Spring Boot Integration

Partitioned Tables and JPA

Entity Maps to Parent Table

java
@Entity
@Table(name = "payments")  // parent — not child partition name
public class Payment {

    @Id
    private Long paymentId;

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private Instant createdAt;  // partition key — required on insert

    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true)  // verify unique scope with DBA
    private String clientRequestId;

    private BigDecimal amount;
    private Long customerId;
}
// Hibernate INSERT INTO payments — DB routes to child partition
// PK in JPA: consider @IdClass or composite if (paymentId, createdAt) both PK

Composite Primary Key for Partitioned Table

java
@Embeddable
public class PaymentId implements Serializable {
    private Long paymentId;
    private Instant createdAt;
}

@Entity
@Table(name = "payments")
public class Payment {
    @EmbeddedId
    private PaymentId id;
    // ...
}

Queries Must Include Partition Key (When Possible)

java
@Query("""
    SELECT p FROM Payment p
    WHERE p.customerId = :customerId
      AND p.createdAt >= :from
      AND p.createdAt < :to
    ORDER BY p.createdAt DESC
    """)
List<Payment> findRecentPayments(
    @Param("customerId") Long customerId,
    @Param("from") Instant from,
    @Param("to") Instant to);
// Prune: from/to bound months — architect documents required date window default (90 days)

Native SQL — Explicit Partition (Rare)

java
// Usually avoid — bypasses prune if wrong partition name
// jdbcTemplate.query("SELECT * FROM payments_2024_06 WHERE ...") — only admin tools

Flyway Partition Automation

sql
-- V100__payments_partition_2025_01.sql (scheduled monthly via pipeline)
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS payments_2025_01 PARTITION OF payments
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2025-01-01') TO ('2025-02-01');
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_payments_2025_01_cust_created
    ON payments_2025_01 (customer_id, created_at DESC);

Service Default Date Window

java
@Service
public class PaymentQueryService {
    private static final Duration MAX_LOOKBACK = Duration.ofDays(90);

    public List<PaymentDto> history(Long customerId, Instant from) {
        Instant effectiveFrom = from.isBefore(Instant.now().minus(MAX_LOOKBACK))
            ? Instant.now().minus(MAX_LOOKBACK) : from;
        return repo.findRecentPayments(customerId, effectiveFrom, Instant.now());
    }
}
// API enforces prune-friendly queries

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

ORM Partition Considerations

Hibernate Unaware of Partitions

text
Hibernate treats parent table as normal @Entity
No @Partition annotation in standard JPA — DB handles routing
DDL: ddl-auto=validate — Flyway creates partitions, not Hibernate

Unique Constraint Scope

java
@Column(unique = true)
private String clientRequestId;
// On partitioned table PostgreSQL: unique must include partition key
// unless client_request_id is globally unique by design (UUID) enforced app-side
// Architect: UNIQUE(client_request_id, created_at) or global UUID idempotency key

Avoid Updating Partition Key

java
payment.setCreatedAt(newTime);  // ❌ may move row across partitions — expensive
// created_at immutable after insert — business rule + @Column(updatable = false)

Bulk Delete Anti-Pattern

java
@Modifying
@Query("DELETE FROM Payment p WHERE p.createdAt < :cutoff")
// Deletes row-by-row all partitions — WAL storm
// ✅ DETACH/DROP partition via admin job — not JPA

Batch Insert Current Month

yaml
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size: 50
# Inserts hit one hot partition — monitor index bloat on current child
# Consider fillfactor 90 on current partition index

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Partition Key Not in Queries

sql
SELECT * FROM payments WHERE customer_id = 1001;
-- Scans all monthly partitions — worse than monolithic single index scan
-- Fix: default 90-day window OR subpartition strategy OR accept cost

Mistake 2: PK Without Partition Key

sql
PRIMARY KEY (payment_id)  -- fails on PostgreSQL partitioned table
-- Must include created_at in PK or use unique per partition only

Mistake 3: Too Many Partitions

text
Daily partitions for 20 years — planner slow
Use monthly unless daily DROP/legal requirement

Mistake 4: Forgetting Future Partition

text
INSERT June 2025 — no partition → ERROR
Automation must create N+1 month ahead
Default partition hides error — then bloats

Mistake 5: UPDATE Partition Key

sql
UPDATE payments SET created_at = ... WHERE payment_id = ...;
-- Row migration — slow, breaks HOT, doubles index work

Mistake 6: Function on Partition Column

sql
WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2024-06-01'  -- prune may fail
WHERE created_at >= '2024-06-01' AND created_at < '2024-06-02'  -- prune ✅

Mistake 7: Partition Small Table Prematurely

text
5M payments — operational overhead without measurable win

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is table partitioning?

Splitting one logical table into physical segments by a key — queries skip irrelevant partitions via pruning.

Q2: RANGE vs LIST partition?

RANGE: continuous bounds (dates). LIST: discrete values (regions).

Q3: What is partition pruning?

Optimizer excludes partitions that cannot match WHERE clause on partition key.

Q4: Why include partition key in primary key (PostgreSQL)?

Uniqueness enforced per partition; global PK requires partition key in unique constraints.

Q5: DROP partition vs DELETE old rows?

DROP instant file removal; DELETE massive WAL and vacuum.

Mid-Level

Q6: When partition payments by created_at?

Large row count, time-filtered queries, retention needs, maintenance scope.

Q7: Query by customer_id only on time-partitioned payments — problem?

All partitions scanned — need date filter default or different design.

Q8: Partition-wise join benefit?

Join matching partitions only — smaller inputs, better hash join memory.

Q9: HASH partition when?

Write spread; not when queries need time prune without hash key filter.

Q10: How automate monthly partitions?

pg_partman, Flyway cron, ATTACH pre-loaded, CREATE ahead of calendar.

Senior

Q11: client_request_id UNIQUE on partitioned payments?

PostgreSQL needs partition key in unique constraint OR global UUID guaranteed unique app-wide — design idempotency accordingly.

Q12: Too many partitions symptom?

Slow planning, long EXPLAIN — consolidate granularity.

Q13: Partition vs read replica for reports?

Complementary — partition reduces I/O; replica isolates load — use both.

Q14: DETACH CONCURRENTLY use case?

Archive old partition without blocking reads on parent — PG 14+.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Payment platform 500M rows — partition strategy?

RANGE monthly created_at, PK (payment_id, created_at), per-partition indexes, pg_partman, 7-year DETACH, API default 90-day query window.

Q16: Multi-tenant erasure (GDPR) with partitioning?

LIST(tenant_id) or tenant-scoped partition DROP vs DELETE — legal + performance win.

Scenario

Scenario: "After partitioning, customer payment history API slower."

API queries customer_id without created_at — all partitions scanned. Fix: require date range, default 90 days, index (customer_id, created_at) per partition, EXPLAIN Append count.

Part 1 — Concept

What Is Database Locking & Concurrency?

Locking and concurrency control how multiple transactions read and write the same data simultaneously without corrupting business invariants (balance never negative, double spend, lost updates). Databases combine MVCC (multi-version concurrency control) for reads with explicit locks for conflicting writes.

sql
-- Transfer: debit + credit must be atomic and isolated
BEGIN;

SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 5001 FOR UPDATE;  -- row lock
-- verify balance >= 1000

UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 1000 WHERE account_id = 5001;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1000 WHERE account_id = 5002;

INSERT INTO transfers (from_account_id, to_account_id, amount) VALUES (5001, 5002, 1000);

COMMIT;

Concurrency Problem Taxonomy

text
CLASSIC ANOMALIES

├── Dirty read       → read uncommitted data from another txn (rolled back)
├── Non-repeatable read → same row read twice, value changed by other txn
├── Phantom read     → same query twice, different row set (new rows inserted)
├── Lost update      → two txns overwrite each other — last writer wins
├── Write skew       → two txns read overlapping state, write inconsistently
└── Double spend     → two txns both pass balance check on stale read

Isolation vs Locking

text
ISOLATION LEVEL     → transaction-wide visibility rules (SQL standard)
LOCK                → physical mechanism (row, table, advisory)
MVCC                → snapshot versions — readers don't block writers (usually)

PostgreSQL default: READ COMMITTED + MVCC
Oracle default: READ COMMITTED (no READ UNCOMMITTED)
SQL Server default: READ COMMITTED (with locking/blocking variants)

Lock Types (Conceptual)

text
LOCKS

├── Row-level        → FOR UPDATE, UPDATE, DELETE on row
├── Table-level      → ACCESS SHARE, ROW EXCLUSIVE, ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (PostgreSQL)
├── Predicate / gap  → next-key locks (InnoDB REPEATABLE READ — phantoms)
├── Transaction id   → waiting on another txn's uncommitted row version
├── Advisory         → application-defined pg_advisory_xact_lock
└── Deadlock         → circular wait — DB picks victim, aborts one txn

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Concurrency Control

text
1970s   Two-phase locking (2PL) theory — serializable schedules
        System R introduces MVCC concepts

1980s   Oracle multi-version read consistency — readers non-blocking
        SQL standard isolation levels defined (SQL-92)

1990s   PostgreSQL MVCC — xmin/xmax, no UNDO tablespace (unlike Oracle)
        MySQL InnoDB row locks + gap locks for REPEATABLE READ

2000s   Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) — PostgreSQL 9.1
        Optimistic concurrency @Version in JPA/Hibernate

2010s   Distributed locks (Redis, ZooKeeper) — often misused vs DB txn
        "Hold DB connection during HTTP call" antipatterns at scale

2020s   Saga / outbox for microservice concurrency across services
        SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for job queues
        CockroachDB/Spanner serializable by default — different model
        Banking: row-level pessimistic lock still standard for balances

Historical Lesson

MVCC solved read/write blocking but did not eliminate write/write conflicts. Transfer APIs still need explicit row locks or atomic UPDATE … WHERE balance >= amount — optimistic @Version alone fails under concurrent debit unless the business logic handles retry. Architects choose pessimistic for hot financial rows, optimistic for low-contention entities.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Do Locks and Isolation Solve?

Problem 1: Lost Update on Balance

text
Txn A: read balance 1000 → subtract 100 → write 900
Txn B: read balance 1000 → subtract 200 → write 800
Result: 800 — should be 700 (lost A's or B's update)

Fix: SELECT FOR UPDATE, or UPDATE balance = balance - 100 WHERE id=5001 (atomic)

Problem 2: Double Spend

text
Txn A: read balance 1000 → OK for 800 transfer
Txn B: read balance 1000 → OK for 700 transfer
Both commit — balance -500 — overdraft

Fix: lock row before check, or conditional UPDATE returning row count

Problem 3: Phantom Inventory / Limit Breach

text
Daily limit 100K: SUM today's debits = 95K
Two txns each add 10K concurrently — both pass check — 115K total

Fix: SERIALIZABLE, advisory lock per account-day, or single-row counter with FOR UPDATE

Problem 4: Deadlock on Transfer

text
Txn A: lock account 5001 → wait for 5002
Txn B: lock account 5002 → wait for 5001
Database aborts one — application must retry

Problem 5: Long Transaction Blocks OLTP

text
EOD batch UPDATE accounts holds row locks 30 minutes
Transfer API waits — timeout

Fix: shorter txns, batch in chunks, schedule off-peak, SKIP LOCKED for non-critical

Unified Problem Statement

Locking and isolation preserve correctness when many sessions mutate the same rows — preventing lost updates, double spends, and inconsistent reads — while MVCC keeps readers from blocking writers where possible.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Not Single-Threaded Database Access?

Throughput Requirement

text
10K TPS payment rail — must process concurrently
Serial execution: 1 txn at a time — unusable
Concurrency with rules: maximum throughput + correctness

MVCC Benefits

text
READ COMMITTED reader:
  Sees snapshot as of statement start — no dirty read
  Does not block writer's INSERT/UPDATE (different row versions)
Writer creates new row version — old visible to old snapshots until vacuum

When MVCC Is Not Enough

text
Read-modify-write in application:
  SELECT balance;  // MVCC snapshot
  if (balance >= amt) UPDATE ...
  Another txn commits between SELECT and UPDATE — race

Must: FOR UPDATE (pessimistic) OR atomic UPDATE WHERE OR optimistic version OR SERIALIZABLE

Isolation Level Trade-off

text
Higher isolation → fewer anomalies → more blocking / aborts / serialization failures
Financial hot rows: targeted pessimistic locks often beat SERIALIZABLE whole txn

Part 5 — Internal Working

MVCC Internals (PostgreSQL Model)

Row Versions

text
Each row has system columns:
  xmin — inserting transaction id
  xmax — deleting/updating transaction id (0 if live)

UPDATE: creates NEW row version — old marked dead
Readers with snapshot_id < xmax see old version until vacuum

Snapshot Isolation (READ COMMITTED)

text
Each statement gets fresh snapshot (PG READ COMMITTED):
  Visible rows: committed before statement start, xmin valid

REPEATABLE READ (PG):
  Snapshot at transaction start — non-repeatable read prevented within txn
  Phantom: prevented for PG RR (unlike standard — PG uses snapshot)

SERIALIZABLE (SSI)

text
Serializable Snapshot Isolation:
  Tracks read/write dependencies — detects dangerous structures
  May raise: could not serialize access due to concurrent update
  Application: retry transaction

Row Lock: FOR UPDATE

sql
SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 5001 FOR UPDATE;
-- Acquires RowExclusive lock on row — blocks other FOR UPDATE / UPDATE / DELETE
-- Other SELECT (no lock) still reads committed snapshot — MVCC
-- Waits if another txn holds conflicting lock

Lock Modes (PostgreSQL Simplified)

text
FOR UPDATE          → exclusive row lock for update
FOR NO KEY UPDATE   → weaker — FK checks still allowed on key
FOR SHARE           → shared row lock — blocks writers, not other readers FOR SHARE
FOR KEY SHARE       → weakest row lock

UPDATE/DELETE       → implicit row exclusive lock

Deadlock Detection

text
Wait-for graph cycle:
  T1 waits T2 waits T1
PostgreSQL deadlock_timeout (default 1s) — checks cycle — aborts one txn
ERROR: deadlock detected
Spring: @Retryable or catch and retry idempotent transfer

Consistent Lock Ordering

text
Transfer accounts 5001 → 5002:
  Always lock lower account_id first (both directions)
  Prevents deadlock between A→B and B→A transfers

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Locks and Storage Interaction

Row Lock Storage

text
Locks stored in memory (lock tables) — not on disk row
Heavy contention: many sessions waiting — CPU + memory for lock manager
pg_locks view — granted vs waiting

HOT Updates (Heap-Only Tuple)

text
UPDATE column NOT in any index → same heap page new version
  No index update — faster, less lock time on indexes
UPDATE indexed column (balance often indexed? usually not PK only) — index update + wider locks duration
Keep hot financial UPDATE on non-indexed columns where possible — balance may be heavily read — index rarely on balance alone

WAL and Locks

text
Held lock until COMMIT — WAL flush at commit
Long txn = long lock hold = long WAL retention (Pg: xmin horizon blocks vacuum)
Monitoring: pg_stat_activity.xact_start, age(datfrozenxid)

Index Row Locks

text
FOR UPDATE on row locks row — index entries for that row involved in update
Gap/next-key (InnoDB): locks index range — phantom prevention — different engine behavior

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Concurrency Memory Impact

ComponentMemory
Lock managerPer lock object — scales with contention
MVCC versionsDead row versions until vacuum — bloat if long txns
SnapshotPer transaction snapshot map — active txns block cleanup
Connection × txnEach waiting connection holds backend RAM
Advisory locksLightweight — integer keys

Long Transaction Problem

text
One open txn for 2 hours:
  Prevents vacuum from reclaiming dead tuples — table bloat
  Holds row locks — blocked sessions pile up
  Increases snapshot age — wraparound risk (extreme)

Banking: statement_timeout, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout

Connection Pool × Lock Wait

text
50 threads, 50 connections — all waiting on same hot row
Pool exhausted — unrelated APIs timeout (Lesson 28)
Fix: reduce lock hold time, shard hot account, queue per account

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Concurrency Execution Flows

Flow 1: Pessimistic Transfer (Correct)

text
1. BEGIN (@Transactional)
2. SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id=5001 FOR UPDATE  → lock 5001
3. SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id=5002 FOR UPDATE  → lock 5002 (ordered IDs)
4. Validate balance >= amount
5. UPDATE both accounts
6. INSERT transfer
7. COMMIT → release locks
Concurrent transfer on 5001: blocks at step 2 until commit

Flow 2: Optimistic Lock (@Version)

text
1. BEGIN
2. SELECT account version=5, balance=1000
3. Business logic
4. UPDATE accounts SET balance=900, version=6 WHERE id=5001 AND version=5
5. If row count 0 → OptimisticLockException → retry
6. COMMIT
Concurrent: second txn gets version=6 on re-read — one wins, one retries
Good: low contention read-heavy entities
Risk: high contention hot account — retry storm

Flow 3: Atomic Conditional UPDATE (No Explicit SELECT)

sql
UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - 1000
WHERE account_id = 5001
  AND status = 'ACTIVE'
  AND balance >= 1000
RETURNING balance;
-- 0 rows → insufficient funds — no separate read race
-- Single statement atomic — still need lock on row during UPDATE internally

Flow 4: Deadlock

text
Txn A: lock 5001, wait 5002
Txn B: lock 5002, wait 5001
~1s: deadlock detected → abort B (victim)
B's Spring: rollback, retry transfer idempotently
A: completes commit

Flow 5: SKIP LOCKED Job Queue

sql
UPDATE payments_staging
SET status = 'PROCESSING', worker_id = 'pod-3'
WHERE payment_id = (
    SELECT payment_id FROM payments_staging
    WHERE status = 'PENDING'
    ORDER BY created_at
    FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
    LIMIT 1
)
RETURNING *;
-- Workers don't block each other — take next available row

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Locking Performance Rules

Performance Hierarchy

text
FAST (low contention):
  MVCC read-only SELECT — no locks held long
  Short txn pessimistic lock — microsecond hold
  Atomic UPDATE … WHERE balance >= amt — one round trip

SLOW:
  Long @Transactional with HTTP inside — lock held seconds
  SERIALIZABLE on hot table — frequent serialization failures + retries
  Lock accounts in random order — deadlocks + retries
  Table-level lock from DDL/migration during peak
  Missing index on FOR UPDATE lookup — seq scan + lock many rows

DISASTER:
  SELECT * FROM accounts FOR UPDATE — locks entire table scan rows
  EOD batch UPDATE without chunking on OLTP tables

Tuning Contention

text
1. Minimize transaction scope — lock late, release early
2. Consistent lock ordering — account_id ascending
3. Index PK lookup for FOR UPDATE — always point row lock
4. Retry with exponential backoff on deadlock (idempotent)
5. Queue per hot account (Kafka partition key = account_id)
6. Split hot ledger row — sharded balance counters (advanced)
7. idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = 60s
8. statement_timeout on OLTP role

Isolation Level Selection

LevelBanking Use
READ COMMITTEDDefault OLTP — most APIs
REPEATABLE READReport in one txn — consistent snapshot
SERIALIZABLERare — limit checks needing SSI — retry logic
READ UNCOMMITTEDNot PG — avoid

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

PatternContentionCorrectness
Read + write no lockLow❌ lost update
FOR UPDATEMedium✅
Atomic UPDATE WHEREMedium✅ if single statement check
@Version optimisticLow–Medium✅ with retry
SERIALIZABLEHigh abort rate✅
Application synchronized blockN/A single JVM❌ multi-instance

Deadlock probability increases with number of locks per txn and random lock order — O(n!) ordering paths without discipline.

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Locking Masterclass

Pessimistic Lock — Spring + JPA

java
@Repository
public interface AccountRepository extends JpaRepository<Account, Long> {

    @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
    @Query("SELECT a FROM Account a WHERE a.accountId = :id")
    Optional<Account> findByIdForUpdate(@Param("id") Long id);
}

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class TransferService {

    private final AccountRepository accountRepo;
    private final TransferRepository transferRepo;

    @Transactional
    public void transfer(long fromId, long toId, BigDecimal amount) {
        long first = Math.min(fromId, toId);
        long second = Math.max(fromId, toId);

        Account firstAcct = accountRepo.findByIdForUpdate(first).orElseThrow();
        Account secondAcct = first == second ? firstAcct
            : accountRepo.findByIdForUpdate(second).orElseThrow();

        Account from = fromId == first ? firstAcct : secondAcct;
        Account to = toId == first ? firstAcct : secondAcct;

        if (from.getBalance().compareTo(amount) < 0) {
            throw new InsufficientFundsException();
        }
        from.debit(amount);
        to.credit(amount);
        transferRepo.save(new Transfer(fromId, toId, amount));
    }
}

Native FOR UPDATE

java
@Query(value = """
    SELECT account_id, balance, status FROM accounts
    WHERE account_id = :id FOR UPDATE
    """, nativeQuery = true)
Optional<AccountLockRow> lockAccount(@Param("id") Long id);

Atomic Debit (No Prior SELECT)

java
@Modifying
@Query("""
    UPDATE Account a SET a.balance = a.balance - :amount
    WHERE a.accountId = :id AND a.status = 'ACTIVE' AND a.balance >= :amount
    """)
int debitIfSufficient(@Param("id") Long id, @Param("amount") BigDecimal amount);

@Transactional
public void transferAtomic(long fromId, long toId, BigDecimal amount) {
    if (accountRepo.debitIfSufficient(fromId, amount) != 1) {
        throw new InsufficientFundsException();
    }
    accountRepo.credit(toId, amount);  // separate UPDATE — consider ordering locks for credit leg too
    transferRepo.save(new Transfer(fromId, toId, amount));
}
// Note: two UPDATEs without explicit lock — gap between debits possible for complex invariants
// Full transfer: lock both rows or single SERIALIZABLE txn

Optimistic Lock

java
@Entity
public class Account {
    @Id
    private Long accountId;

    @Version
    private Long version;

    private BigDecimal balance;
}
// Concurrent updates → OptimisticLockException

Advisory Lock — Daily Limit

sql
-- Serialize all debits for account 5001 for this transaction
SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(5001);

SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) FROM transactions
WHERE account_id = 5001 AND created_at >= CURRENT_DATE AND direction = 'DEBIT';

-- check limit + insert — released at COMMIT

SKIP LOCKED Worker

sql
SELECT payment_id FROM payments_staging
WHERE status = 'PENDING'
ORDER BY created_at
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
LIMIT 10;

Deadlock Retry

java
@Retryable(retryFor = DeadlockLoserDataAccessException.class, maxAttempts = 3, backoff = @Backoff(delay = 50))
@Transactional
public void transferWithRetry(...) { ... }

Monitor Locks

sql
SELECT
    blocked.pid AS blocked_pid,
    blocking.pid AS blocking_pid,
    blocked.wait_event_type,
    now() - blocked.query_start AS wait_time,
    LEFT(blocked.query, 80) AS blocked_q,
    LEFT(blocking.query, 80) AS blocking_q
FROM pg_stat_activity blocked
JOIN pg_locks bl ON bl.pid = blocked.pid AND NOT bl.granted
JOIN pg_locks bk ON bk.locktype = bl.locktype
    AND bk.database IS NOT DISTINCT FROM bl.database
    AND bk.relation IS NOT DISTINCT FROM bl.relation
    AND bk.pid != bl.pid
JOIN pg_stat_activity blocking ON blocking.pid = bk.pid
WHERE bk.granted;

Part 12 — Production Usage

Locking in Banking Production

Transfer API Standard

text
Pattern: pessimistic FOR UPDATE both accounts (ordered IDs)
Txn scope: < 50ms — no external HTTP inside
Idempotency: client_request_id UNIQUE — retry after deadlock safe
Isolation: READ COMMITTED (default)
Metrics: lock wait time, deadlock count, transfer p99

Payment Insert vs Balance

text
Option A: ledger double-entry — no UPDATE balance column — append-only entries (less row lock on balance)
Option B: balance column + FOR UPDATE — simpler, hot row contention
Architect: high-throughput → event sourcing / ledger; traditional → row lock

EOD Batch vs OLTP

text
Batch: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance * factor — row locks millions
Schedule 02:00 UTC; chunk 5000 + COMMIT; or use SKIP LOCKED for non-overlapping subsets
Never: single txn update all accounts on primary during business hours

Reconciliation Job

text
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on staging rows — parallel workers
Avoid: SELECT status='PENDING' then UPDATE in app without lock — duplicate processing

Migration DDL

text
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY — doesn't block writes long
ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN — brief lock — use flyway maintenance window
ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locks block all writes — schedule carefully

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

Concurrency Architecture

Within Service DB

text
Financial invariants: ACID transaction + row locks
Idempotency keys: UNIQUE constraint — deadlock retry safe
Outbox pattern: INSERT outbox in same txn as payment — no cross-service lock

Cross-Service

text
❌ Distributed lock only without local txn — split brain risk
✅ Saga: reserve → capture → release with compensating txns
✅ Kafka partition key = account_id — serializes events per account
✅ 2PC/XA — avoided in modern microservices (complexity)

Ledger vs Balance Column

text
Append-only ledger:
  INSERT ledger_entry — less UPDATE contention on single balance cell
  Balance = SUM(entries) or materialized cache updated async
Architect at scale: ledger + projection; small bank: FOR UPDATE balance OK

Hot Account Mitigation

text
Celebrity account / treasury settlement account:
  Single row millions TPS impossible on one balance UPDATE
  Queue: all mutations serialized per account_id in single-thread consumer
  Sharded sub-accounts aggregated periodically

Isolation Policy Document

text
Default: READ COMMITTED
REPEATABLE READ: finance reports in txn
SERIALIZABLE: only with explicit ADR + retry framework
No READ UNCOMMITTED
FOR UPDATE required for: transfer, reservation, inventory-style debit

Mistake 1: Read Balance Without Lock

text

Transfer B→A locks B then A

text

text

sql

text

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is MVCC?

Multi-version concurrency control — readers see snapshot versions; writers create new versions; reduces read/write blocking.

Q2: Default isolation in PostgreSQL?

READ COMMITTED — each statement sees committed data as of statement start.

Q3: What does SELECT FOR UPDATE do?

Locks selected rows for update — blocks other transactions from updating them until commit.

Q4: Lost update problem?

Two transactions read same value, both write — one update lost — fix with lock or version.

Q5: What is a deadlock?

Circular lock wait — DB aborts one transaction — app should retry.

Mid-Level

Q6: Pessimistic vs optimistic locking?

Pessimistic: FOR UPDATE blocks. Optimistic: @Version checks at commit — retry on conflict.

Q7: Prevent deadlock on transfer between two accounts?

Always lock accounts in consistent order (e.g. ascending account_id).

Q8: Atomic UPDATE vs SELECT FOR UPDATE?

Atomic UPDATE WHERE balance >= amt — single statement; FOR UPDATE — read-modify-write with explicit lock across statements.

Q9: SKIP LOCKED use case?

Job queue workers — each takes unlocked pending row — no mutual blocking.

Q10: Why long transaction bad beyond locks?

Blocks vacuum — bloat — holds connections — snapshot age increases.

Senior

Q11: SERIALIZABLE when in banking?

Rare — strict invariants without explicit locks — requires retry; often advisory lock or row lock targeted instead.

Q12: Transfer across microservices without 2PC?

Saga + outbox + idempotency; local txn per service; compensate on failure.

Q13: Hot account single row limit?

Serialize via queue partition; ledger append; sharded balance — not infinite FOR UPDATE throughput.

Q14: READ COMMITTED enough for transfer?

Yes with pessimistic row lock or atomic conditional UPDATE — isolation alone doesn't prevent lost update without lock/version.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Ledger vs balance column architecture?

Ledger: append-only, audit-friendly, scales writes differently; balance: simpler, hot row risk — choose by TPS and audit needs.

Q16: Lock monitoring production stack?

pg_locks, wait_event, APM txn duration, deadlock metric, idle_in_transaction alert, statement_timeout policy.

Scenario

Scenario: "Transfer timeouts 9am — DB CPU low, wait_event Lock."

Identify blocker txn (batch job); shorten batch; lock order; index FOR UPDATE path; move batch off-peak; not add index on unrelated column.

Optimistic@Version — low contention; retry on conflict
Atomic UPDATEWHERE balance >= — single-statement check
SKIP LOCKEDParallel job consumers
DeadlockDB aborts victim — idempotent retry
SpringShort txn; no I/O inside lock; lock timeout
ArchitectSaga cross-service; ledger at scale; hot account queue

Connection Pooling & Timeouts
