Part 1 — Concept

What Is Connection Pooling?

A connection pool is a cache of reusable database connections managed by the application (or middleware). Opening a TCP/TLS connection + PostgreSQL authentication is expensive (milliseconds to tens of ms); pools borrow connections for the duration of a transaction or statement and return them for reuse.

text
Without pool:
  Request → new Connection → query → close
  1000 req/s → 1000 connects/sec — DB melts

With pool (HikariCP):
  Request → borrow from pool (10–50 connections) → query → return
  Same 50 physical connections serve 1000 req/s sequentially

Pool in the Stack

text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Spring Boot API (50 Tomcat threads)                        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │ HikariCP (maxPoolSize=20)                           │    │
│  │  idle connections waiting in pool                   │    │
│  └──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘    │
└─────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┘
                          │ JDBC (max 20 sessions)
┌─────────────────────────▼───────────────────────────────────┐
│  Optional: PgBouncer / RDS Proxy (transaction pooling)      │
└─────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘
                          │
┌─────────────────────────▼───────────────────────────────────┐
│  PostgreSQL (max_connections = 200, shared by all services)   │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Timeout Taxonomy

text
TIMEOUT LAYERS

├── Connection acquisition   → pool waits for free connection (HikariCP connectionTimeout)
├── Statement execution      → DB kills long query (statement_timeout)
├── Lock wait                → give up waiting for row lock (lock_timeout)
├── Idle in transaction      → kill txn open but idle (idle_in_transaction_session_timeout)
├── Socket / network         → TCP read timeout (socketTimeout in JDBC URL)
├── HTTP / client            → Spring MVC, load balancer idle timeout
└── ORM                      → jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout, query timeout

Why This Lesson Matters After Locking (Lesson 31)

text
Lock wait 30s × 50 threads = all pool connections held
Unrelated APIs: "Cannot get JDBC connection" — looks like DB down
Root cause: pool exhaustion from long transactions, not PostgreSQL capacity

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Connection Pooling

text
1990s   JDBC introduced — apps open/close per request — performance disaster
        Early pools: DBCP, C3P0

2000s   Tomcat JDBC pool, JBoss datasources
        Rule of thumb: connections = ((core×2)+spindle) — Brett Wooldridge

2010s   HikariCP — fast, minimal overhead — default in Spring Boot 2+
        PgBouncer widespread for PostgreSQL connection multiplexing
        Cloud RDS: too many microservices × pool size > max_connections crisis

2015+   AWS RDS Proxy, Azure flexible server proxy — IAM, failover, pooling
        Serverless (Lambda) + RDS Proxy mandatory pattern

2020s   FinOps: right-size pools before scaling DB instance
        Observability: HikariCP metrics + pg_stat_activity correlation standard
        PgBouncer transaction mode vs prepared statement friction with ORMs

Historical Lesson

The #1 production PostgreSQL incident in microservice era is connection storms: 30 services × maximumPoolSize=50 = 1500 connections vs max_connections=300. Pooling middleware (PgBouncer/RDS Proxy) + smaller Hikari pools beat upgrading RDS instance size.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Do Pools and Timeouts Solve?

Problem 1: Connection Establishment Cost

text
New connection: TCP + TLS + auth + memory for backend process (~5–10 MB RAM each PG backend)
Pool: amortize cost across thousands of requests

Problem 2: Database Connection Limit

sql
SHOW max_connections;  -- e.g. 500
-- 10 pods × 50 pool × 3 services = 1500 demanded — FATAL: too many connections

Problem 3: Hung Query Consumes Connection Forever

text
Report query runs 6 hours — holds pool connection
Without statement_timeout: connection never returns until kill
With statement_timeout = '30s': query aborted, connection returned to pool

Problem 4: Idle Transaction Holds Lock + Connection

text
BEGIN; SELECT ...; developer goes to lunch; connection idle in transaction
Locks row; pool drains; idle_in_transaction_session_timeout kills after 60s

Problem 5: Pool Exhaustion Cascade

text
All 20 connections waiting on lock (Lesson 31)
Thread 21: connectionTimeout 30s — API timeout — user retries — thundering herd
Fix: shorter txns + lock tuning + right pool size — not always bigger pool

Unified Problem Statement

Connection pools bound application concurrency to sustainable database sessions; timeouts ensure connections, locks, and queries fail fast instead of exhausting resources and cascading outages.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Not One Connection Per Thread Unbounded?

PostgreSQL Process Model

text
Each connection = one backend OS process (traditionally)
500 connections = 500 processes — context switch + memory pressure
CPU spent managing connections, not running queries

Queuing at the Pool Is Cheaper

text
Better: 20 DB connections, 50 threads queue 5ms for borrow
Than: 50 DB connections all waiting 30s on locks anyway
Pool size ≈ sustainable concurrent **active** queries, not thread count

Timeouts as Circuit Breakers

text
statement_timeout: protects DB from runaway JOIN
connectionTimeout: fail fast when pool starved — trigger alert
lock_timeout: don't wait forever behind batch job
Together: predictable failure vs platform-wide stall

Middleware Pooling (PgBouncer)

text
1000 client connections → PgBouncer → 50 server connections to PostgreSQL
Multiplexes **non-overlapping** transaction windows
Critical when many short-lived clients (serverless, huge pod counts)

Part 5 — Internal Working

HikariCP Internals

Pool Lifecycle

text
Startup:
  minimumIdle connections created (or on demand)
  Housekeeping thread: keepalive, idle timeout, maxLifetime rotation

Borrow (getConnection):
  1. Thread requests connection
  2. If idle in pool → hand off (microseconds)
  3. If pool at max and all in use → wait up to connectionTimeout
  4. Timeout → SQLException "Connection is not available, request timed out"

Return (close() in try-with-resources):
  Connection reset (rollback if needed) → back to pool
  NOT closed on DB server if pool still open

Key HikariCP Settings

yaml
spring:
  datasource:
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 20        # max concurrent DB connections per JVM
      minimum-idle: 5              # idle connections maintained
      connection-timeout: 5000     # ms to wait for connection from pool
      idle-timeout: 600000         # ms — retire idle connection (10 min)
      max-lifetime: 1800000        # ms — recycle connection (30 min) — below DB/network limit
      validation-timeout: 5000
      pool-name: payment-service-pool
text
maxLifetime: rotate before firewall/load balancer drops silent connections
maximumPoolSize: per instance — multiply by pod count for total demand

JDBC Connection ≠ Transaction

text
@Transactional start → borrow connection (may already be bound to thread)
Commit/rollback → connection returned to pool (Spring transaction manager)
Leak: forget to close session, long @Transactional — connection not returned

PgBouncer Pool Modes

text
SESSION pooling (default):
  Client connection tied to one PG backend for whole session
  Prepared statements OK — Hibernate/JPA happy
  Less multiplexing benefit

TRANSACTION pooling:
  PG backend assigned only during transaction — high multiplexing
  Prepared statements break unless disabled (prepareThreshold=0)
  SET parameters don't persist across transactions

STATEMENT pooling:
  Rare — one statement per backend — most ORMs broken

RDS Proxy

text
Managed connection pool between apps and Aurora/RDS
Features: IAM auth, failover pinning reduction, connection multiplexing
Still need reasonable Hikari pool — proxy not infinite capacity

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Connections and Database Storage

Backend Memory per Connection

text
PostgreSQL each backend:
  work_mem (per operation, not per connection permanently)
  maintenance_work_mem
  temp_buffers
  Catalog cache, prepared statement cache

Rough: 5–15 MB baseline per connection — 500 conn = 2.5–7.5 GB RAM before queries

Prepared Statement Cache

text
PgBouncer transaction mode + ORM prepared statements:
  "prepared statement s_1 already exists" errors
Fix: prepareThreshold=0 in JDBC URL, or session pooling, or ORM setting
Spring Boot 3 + PostgreSQL: understand driver prepare behavior

Connection Storm on DB Restart

text
All pods lose connections simultaneously
HikariCP validates + reconnects — thundering herd auth
Stagger deploys; connectionTimeout fail fast; RDS Proxy absorbs spike

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Memory at Each Layer

LayerMemory Impact
HikariCP pool objectSmall JVM heap per Connection wrapper
PostgreSQL backend~5–15 MB × active connections
Idle in pool (app)DB still has backend if not using PgBouncer multiplex
PgBouncerLightweight — thousands client conns, few server conns
Too large poolRAM exhaustion on DB — OOM killer — total outage

Sizing Formula (Starting Point)

text
Per service instance:
  maximumPoolSize = min(
    (expected concurrent DB-bound requests),
    (PostgreSQL max_connections - admin reserve) / (instances × services)
  )

Example:
  max_connections=300, reserve 50, 5 services, 10 pods each
  250 / (5 × 10) = 5 connections per pod maximum average
  Reality: uneven load — payment service gets 15, config service gets 3

Threads vs Pool Size

text
50 Tomcat threads, pool 20:
  OK — not all threads hit DB simultaneously
  Bad if all 50 enter @Transactional and block — 30 wait on pool
Align: pool ≤ threads that can concurrently need DB, but don't auto-set pool = threads

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Connection Borrow Flows

Flow 1: Happy Path OLTP

text
1. HTTP request → Tomcat thread
2. @Transactional service method starts
3. HikariCP getConnection — idle conn #7 — 0.2ms
4. PreparedStatement execute — 5ms
5. Commit — connection reset — return to pool
6. HTTP response — total 25ms
Connection held ~20ms

Flow 2: Pool Exhaustion

text
1. 20 connections all in 30s lock wait (batch job blocker)
2. Thread 21: getConnection — waits connectionTimeout 5000ms
3. SQLException → Spring 500 → user retry
4. 50 retry threads amplify load
5. Alert: hikaricp.connections.pending > 0 sustained
Fix: kill blocker txn, lock_timeout, batch schedule — Lesson 31

Flow 3: statement_timeout Abort

text
1. Borrow connection
2. Run heavy report — Seq Scan 10M rows
3. At 30s PostgreSQL cancels query — ERROR: canceling statement due to statement timeout
4. Spring: QueryTimeoutException / PSQLException
5. Connection returned to pool (if txn handled)
6. User gets error — platform stable

Flow 4: idle_in_transaction_session_timeout

text
1. BEGIN; SELECT FOR UPDATE account — lock held
2. Developer debugging breakpoint 5 minutes
3. PostgreSQL terminates session at 60s idle in txn
4. Connection broken — HikariCP evicts — new connection on next borrow
5. Lock released — other transfers proceed

Flow 5: PgBouncer Transaction Multiplexing

text
Client A: BEGIN → borrow PG backend #3 → COMMIT → release backend
Client B: BEGIN → reuse PG backend #3 (different client TCP)
1000 clients, 30 backends — serializes if all txns long; wins for short OLTP txns

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Pool and Timeout Tuning

Performance Hierarchy

text
HEALTHY:
  Pool size matches sustained concurrent queries (10–30 per instance typical)
  Short transactions (<100ms hold time)
  statement_timeout on OLTP role (5–30s)
  lock_timeout for interactive (2–5s)
  maxLifetime rotation — no stale connection errors

UNHEALTHY:
  maximumPoolSize=100 "just in case"
  connectionTimeout=120000 — hides pool starvation 2 minutes
  No statement_timeout — one report kills platform
  @Transactional spans HTTP/Kafka — minutes hold
  50 pods × 30 pool without PgBouncer

DIAGNOSIS ORDER (Lesson 28 extended):
  1. HikariCP pending connections?
  2. pg_stat_activity count by application_name?
  3. idle in transaction sessions?
  4. wait_event Lock vs Client vs IO?
  5. Then EXPLAIN query plan

HikariCP Metrics (Micrometer)

text
hikaricp.connections.active
hikaricp.connections.idle
hikaricp.connections.pending   ← critical alert
hikaricp.connections.timeout   ← acquisition failures
hikaricp.connections.usage     ← borrow duration histogram

PostgreSQL Monitoring

sql
SELECT
    application_name,
    state,
    COUNT(*) AS cnt,
    MAX(now() - state_change) AS max_state_duration
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = current_database()
GROUP BY application_name, state
ORDER BY cnt DESC;

-- idle in transaction
SELECT pid, application_name, now() - xact_start AS xact_age, query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'idle in transaction'
ORDER BY xact_age DESC;

Recommended Timeout Stack (OLTP Payment Service)

sql

ALTER ROLE payment_app SET statement_timeout = '30s';
ALTER ROLE payment_app SET lock_timeout = '5s';
ALTER ROLE payment_app SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s';

spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout: 5000
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size: 20

TransactionTemplate — Minimal Scope

private final TransactionTemplate txTemplate;

public PaymentResult process(PaymentCommand cmd) {
    fraudService.validate(cmd);  // outside txn — no connection held

    return txTemplate.execute(status -> {
        accountRepo.findByIdForUpdate(cmd.accountId());
        return paymentRepo.save(new Payment(cmd));
    });
}

Part 12 — Production Usage

Banking Production Patterns

Service Tier Pool Budget

text
Platform max_connections: 400
Reserve: 50 (admin, replication, monitoring)
Available: 350

payment-service:    10 pods × 15 pool = 150
account-service:    8 pods × 10 pool  = 80
reporting-service:  3 pods × 10 pool  = 30  (read replica separate instance)
other:                             = 90
Total primary demand: 260 — headroom OK

RDS Proxy + Aurora

text
Apps → HikariCP (pool 10–15) → RDS Proxy → Aurora cluster
Failover: proxy reduces connection storm on writer change
IAM auth: rotate secrets without redeploy
Still tune Hikari — proxy multiplexes but not magic for long txns

Reporting Isolation

text
Separate read replica + separate datasource + separate pool
statement_timeout = '5min' on reporting role only
Never share pool with OLTP primary — blast radius isolation

Deploy / Scale Events

text
Scale pods 10 → 20: double connection demand — update pool math before HPA
Rolling deploy: maxLifetime jitter prevents simultaneous recycle
Load test: watch hikaricp.connections.pending at peak RPS

Incident Runbook: "Cannot Get JDBC Connection"

text
1. Check HikariCP pending/timeouts in Grafana
2. pg_stat_activity: count by state — idle in transaction?
3. Find blockers (Lesson 31 lock query)
4. statement_timeout / idle_in_transaction killing stuck?
5. Temporary: scale pods down OR kill idle txns OR pause batch — not blindly raise pool
6. Post-incident: fix txn scope, batch schedule, pool budget doc

Part 13 — Spring Boot Integration

Spring Boot Connection Management

Default HikariCP (Spring Boot 2+)

text
spring-boot-starter-jdbc / spring-boot-starter-data-jpa
→ auto-configures HikariDataSource unless other pool on classpath

Actuator Health

yaml
management.health.db.enabled: true
# Reports UP if getConnection succeeds — doesn't detect pool exhaustion under load
# Custom health: alert on pending > 0

Custom Pool Exhaustion Health Indicator

java
@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class HikariPoolHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {

    private final DataSource dataSource;

    @Override
    public Health health() {
        if (dataSource instanceof HikariDataSource hikari) {
            var pool = hikari.getHikariPoolMXBean();
            int pending = pool.getThreadsAwaitingConnection();
            if (pending > 0) {
                return Health.down()
                    .withDetail("threadsAwaitingConnection", pending)
                    .withDetail("active", pool.getActiveConnections())
                    .build();
            }
        }
        return Health.up().build();
    }
}

Graceful Shutdown

yaml
server:
  shutdown: graceful
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 30s
# Allows in-flight txns to complete — return connections cleanly

text

ORM and Connection Hold Time

Session Lifetime

saveAll(10000):

Mistake 1: maximumPoolSize = 100 Default

Mistake 3: No statement_timeout on App Role

Intermittent "prepared statement already exists" — prepareThreshold=0

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: Why connection pool?

Reuse DB connections — avoid expensive connect/auth per request; cap concurrent DB sessions.

Q2: Spring Boot default pool?

HikariCP.

Q3: connectionTimeout vs statement_timeout?

connectionTimeout: wait for free pool connection. statement_timeout: max query execution time in DB.

Q4: What happens when pool exhausted?

Threads block until connectionTimeout — then SQLException — requests fail.

Q5: maximumPoolSize vs Tomcat threads?

Pool can be smaller than threads — not every thread uses DB simultaneously.

Mid-Level

Q6: Size HikariCP for 10 pods, max_connections=300, 5 services?

Divide available connections across services and pods — e.g. 250/50 = 5 avg per pod — adjust by load.

Q7: idle_in_transaction_session_timeout purpose?

Kill sessions with open txn but no activity — release locks and pool connections.

Q8: PgBouncer transaction vs session mode?

Transaction: multiplex aggressively — breaks prepared statements. Session: one PG backend per client session — ORM-safe.

Q9: Why separate pool for reporting?

Long queries don't exhaust OLTP pool; different statement_timeout; read replica isolation.

Q10: socketTimeout in JDBC URL?

Network-level read timeout — client stops waiting if DB/network hangs — complements statement_timeout.

Senior

Q11: Pool exhausted but DB CPU low?

Connections waiting on locks (Lesson 31) or idle in transaction — not CPU — diagnose pg_stat_activity.

Q12: RDS Proxy when?

Many short-lived clients, Lambda, connection storm risk, Aurora failover — not substitute for fixing long txns.

Q13: Prepared statement issue with PgBouncer?

prepareThreshold=0 or session pooling or disable server-side prepare in Hibernate.

Q14: leak-detection-threshold use?

Debug connection leaks in non-prod — stack trace when held too long — fix unclosed resources or long @Transactional.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Platform connection governance?

Central budget registry, max pool approval, PgBouncer/RDS Proxy layer, per-role timeouts, alerts on pending connections.

Q16: FinOps: scale DB vs tune pool?

Prove connection math and timeout policy first — scale when active queries saturate CPU/IO after pool optimized.

Scenario

Scenario: "After HPA scale-out, FATAL too many connections."

Recalculate Σ(pods × maximumPoolSize); reduce per-pod pool; add PgBouncer; or increase max_connections temporarily with RAM check — document budget.

ALTER ROLE app SET lock_timeout = '5s';
ALTER ROLE app SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '60s';

JDBC URL

text
?connectTimeout=5&socketTimeout=30&prepareThreshold=0  # if PgBouncer txn mode

Diagnosis

text
hikaricp.connections.pending > 0  → alert
pg_stat_activity idle in transaction
Σ(pods × pool) vs max_connections
connectionTimeout storm → lock or long txn — not always bigger pool

Rules

text
✅ Central connection budget
✅ Short @Transactional
✅ statement_timeout on OLTP role
✅ Separate reporting pool + replica
✅ PgBouncer/RDS Proxy at scale
❌ maximumPoolSize=100 default
❌ Long connectionTimeout hiding starvation
❌ Hold connection during HTTP
❌ Scale pods without pool math

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why This Exists5Internal Working6Storage Internals7Memory Usage8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Complexity Analysis11Code / SQL Examples12Production Usage13Spring Boot Integration14Hibernate/JPA Integration15Architect Perspective16Decision Matrix17Comparison Tables18Common Mistakes19Interview Questions20Revision Sheet21Summary Table*Practice

Part 1 — Concept

What Is ACID?

ACID is the four-property contract that makes a database transaction reliable: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability. Together they guarantee that a unit of work either completes fully, respects business rules, behaves predictably under concurrency, and survives crashes.

sql
BEGIN;  -- start transaction

UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 1000 WHERE account_id = 5001;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1000 WHERE account_id = 5002;
INSERT INTO transfers (from_account_id, to_account_id, amount) VALUES (5001, 5002, 1000);

COMMIT;  -- all three succeed together — or none do (ROLLBACK)

ACID at a Glance

text
A — ATOMICITY
    All operations in the transaction succeed, or all are undone.
    "Transfer debit + credit + audit row" — no half transfer.

C — CONSISTENCY
    Database moves from one valid state to another.
    Business rules hold: balance ≥ 0, FK valid, totals preserved.

I — ISOLATION
    Concurrent transactions don't interfere in forbidden ways.
    Controlled by isolation level + locks (Lesson 31).

D — DURABILITY
    After COMMIT, data survives power loss / crash.
    Implemented via WAL (write-ahead log) + disk flush.

ACID vs BASE (Architect Context)

text
ACID (RDBMS OLTP):     strong guarantees — banking core, payments
BASE (some NoSQL):     Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency
                       — Cassandra, Dynamo at scale — different trade-off

Solution Architect: money movement → ACID local txn default;
cross-service → Saga + eventual consistency (not single ACID txn)

Transaction Boundary

text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TRANSACTION                                            │
│  ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐                   │
│  │ Op 1    │ │ Op 2    │ │ Op 3    │  → COMMIT or ROLLBACK
│  └─────────┘ └─────────┘ └─────────┘                   │
│  Atomic unit — one connection, one isolation context    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Transaction Guarantees

text
1970s   System R — transaction concepts, logging for recovery
        Gray & Reuter — transaction processing fundamentals

1980s   ACID term popularized with commercial RDBMS (Oracle, DB2)
        Two-phase commit (2PC) for distributed transactions

1990s   SQL standard TRANSACTION, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, isolation levels
        PostgreSQL MVCC — snapshot isolation without read locks

2000s   Spring @Transactional — declarative ACID in Java enterprise
        NoSQL movement challenges ACID at scale — CAP theorem discourse

2010s   Microservices: "avoid distributed transactions" — Saga pattern
        Amazon Aurora / cloud — durability via replicated storage

2020s   ACID still default for ledger/payment DB per service
        Spanner/Cockroach "serializable globally" — ACID across regions at cost
        Outbox pattern — atomic DB write + event intent in one local ACID txn

Historical Lesson

ACID was defined when the database was the system of record for a monolith. In microservices, each service keeps ACID inside its database; cross-service consistency uses Sagas, outbox, and idempotency — not one giant 2PC transaction. Architects must not confuse local ACID with global consistency.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does ACID Solve?

Problem 1: Partial Failure (Atomicity)

text
Debit succeeds, server crashes before credit:
Without atomicity: money vanishes from source, never arrives
With atomicity: ROLLBACK on failure — both undone

Problem 2: Invalid Business State (Consistency)

text
Transfer leaves total system balance changed (fee miscalculation)
Negative balance on ACTIVE account
Orphan payment without customer FK
Constraints + application logic enforce consistency

Problem 3: Concurrent Corruption (Isolation)

text
Two transfers read same balance, both pass check, both debit — overdraft
Isolation + locks prevent forbidden interleavings (Lesson 31)

Problem 4: Lost Commit (Durability)

text
COMMIT returned to app, power fails before log flushed:
User thinks payment succeeded — data lost
WAL fsync before COMMIT ack — durability guarantee

Problem 5: Application Exception Mid-Flow

java
@Transactional
void transfer() {
    debit();
    credit();
    throw new RuntimeException();  // Spring rolls back entire txn
}

Unified Problem Statement

ACID ensures grouped database operations behave as a single reliable unit — correct under failure, concurrency, and crash — which is the foundation of trustworthy banking and payment systems.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Not Auto-Commit Every Statement?

Auto-Commit Mode

text
Each INSERT/UPDATE is its own transaction — immediate COMMIT
Transfer debit COMMIT → crash → credit never runs — money lost
Multi-step business workflows require explicit transaction boundary

Application vs Database Consistency

text
Consistency (C) is split:
  Database constraints: NOT NULL, FK, CHECK, UNIQUE
  Application rules: sufficient funds, daily limit, fraud score
Both must hold at COMMIT — DB cannot know "sufficient funds" without app or CHECK/trigger

Isolation Is Not Infinite

text
Serializable perfection vs performance trade-off
Banking: targeted pessimistic locks on hot rows + READ COMMITTED default
Not all anomalies eliminated at lowest isolation — by design

Durability Has Cost

text
Every COMMIT waits for WAL flush (synchronous_commit=on)
Throughput vs durability tunable (async commit — risk on crash window)
Financial systems: synchronous durability on primary

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Each ACID Property Is Implemented

Atomicity — Undo via WAL

text
Transaction ID assigned (xid)
Changes written to heap + WAL records (before/after images)

COMMIT:
  WAL flush → mark xid committed in clog (commit log)

ROLLBACK / crash before commit:
  Discard uncommitted changes — old row versions visible via MVCC
  Or replay WAL only committed xids on recovery

PostgreSQL: abort = transaction status aborted — changes invisible to others

Consistency — Constraints + Triggers + App

text
At COMMIT time PostgreSQL checks:
  NOT NULL, CHECK, FK, UNIQUE deferred constraints

Application in @Transactional:
  if (balance < amount) throw — triggers rollback

Invariant example:
  SUM(all account balances) + bank equity = constant (double-entry ledger)
Enforced by ledger design + txn, not single CHECK on one table

Isolation — MVCC + Locks

text
READ COMMITTED (PG default):
  Each statement new snapshot — no dirty read
  Write/write conflicts: row locks, deadlock detection

REPEATABLE READ / SERIALIZABLE:
  Stronger snapshot / SSI predicates (Lesson 31)

Anomalies vs isolation level — SQL standard matrix

Durability — Write-Ahead Logging

text
Rule: WAL record flushed to disk BEFORE data page commit visible

Process:
  1. UPDATE account row in shared_buffers (memory)
  2. Write WAL record to wal_buffers
  3. COMMIT → wal_flush (fsync) — disk
  4. Return success to client
  5. Data pages written later (checkpoint) — crash recovery replays WAL

PostgreSQL: pg_wal directory
Oracle: redo log
SQL Server: transaction log

Crash Recovery Flow

text
Database restart:
  1. Read WAL from last checkpoint
  2. REDO committed transactions not yet in data files
  3. UNDO uncommitted (abort) changes
  4. Database consistent — ACID restored

Part 6 — Storage Internals

ACID and On-Disk Structures

WAL Segments

text
PostgreSQL WAL: 16 MB segments (default), sequential append
High COMMIT rate → WAL I/O bottleneck — monitor wal_write, wal_sync
Replication: WAL shipped to standby — durability + HA (sync replication)

Commit Log (pg_clog / pg_xact)

text
Stores transaction status: in progress, committed, aborted
Visibility: tuple xmin/xmax checked against clog for MVCC

Double-Write / Full Page Writes

text
PostgreSQL full_page_writes — first page change after checkpoint written to WAL as full page — torn page protection
Part of durability on crash during partial page write

Sync Replication Durability

sql
-- synchronous_commit = on (default)
-- synchronous_standby_names = 'standby1'  -- commit waits for replica ack
-- Trade: higher commit latency, lower data loss risk on primary failure

Tablespace and fsync

text
Durability requires reliable storage:
  Local SSD with fsync honored
  Network storage — verify latency on COMMIT path
  cloud: provisioned IOPS on WAL volume

Part 7 — Memory Usage

ACID Runtime Memory

ComponentRole
Shared buffersDirty pages — flushed via checkpoint + WAL
wal_buffersWAL in memory before disk
ProcArrayActive transaction IDs — snapshot computation
Lock tablesRow/table locks (Lesson 31)
ConnectionOne transaction context per connection from pool (Lesson 32)

Long Transaction Impact

text
Open txn prevents vacuum of dead tuples — bloat
Holds xmin — freezes horizon — storage growth
Holds connection from pool — exhaustion
Violates atomicity intent if txn scope too wide — not memory but operational ACID break

work_mem Inside Transaction

text
Sort/hash in txn — same work_mem rules (Lesson 25)
Rollback releases temp files — atomicity cleans up failed txn temp

Part 8 — Execution Flow

ACID Execution Flows

Flow 1: Successful Transfer (Full ACID)

text
1. Spring @Transactional begin — borrow connection
2. BEGIN (implicit)
3. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE — isolation lock
4. UPDATE debit, UPDATE credit, INSERT transfer — atomicity unit
5. Constraint checks pass — consistency
6. COMMIT — WAL fsync — durability
7. Connection returned to pool
Client receives success — data survives crash after step 6

Flow 2: Rollback on Business Rule

text
1. BEGIN
2. Debit UPDATE in memory
3. if insufficient funds → throw InsufficientFundsException
4. Spring rollback — ROLLBACK
5. Debit undone — atomicity
6. No COMMIT — durability unchanged for this attempt

Flow 3: Crash Mid-Transaction

text
1. BEGIN
2. Debit flushed to WAL (uncommitted)
3. Power loss before COMMIT WAL record
4. Recovery: txn not in clog committed → abort — debit invisible
Atomicity + durability together: neither half-visible after restart

Flow 4: Concurrent Transfers (Isolation)

text
Txn A: lock 5001, debit 800
Txn B: wait on lock 5001 (Lesson 31)
Txn A: COMMIT — release lock
Txn B: acquire lock, read updated balance, proceed or fail
Isolation serializes conflicting access — no lost update

Flow 5: Constraint Violation (Consistency)

text
1. INSERT payment duplicate client_request_id
2. UNIQUE violation — ERROR
3. Entire @Transactional scope rolls back if not caught incorrectly
4. Database consistent — no duplicate row

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

ACID Performance Trade-offs

Durability vs Latency

text
synchronous_commit = off:
  COMMIT returns before WAL flush — faster — risk last ~100ms txns on crash
Payment OLTP: keep on for primary writer

synchronous_commit = on + sync replica:
  Commit latency = WAL flush primary + network ack standby
  Typical: 1–5ms per commit — budget in transfer SLA

Atomicity Scope Size

text
Large @Transactional:
  More locks held longer — isolation contention
  Bigger rollback cost
  Keep atomic unit minimal — only what must be atomic together

Isolation Level Cost

text
READ COMMITTED: baseline
SERIALIZABLE: serialization failures — retry overhead
Match lowest isolation that correctness allows

Batch vs ACID

text
10K inserts one COMMIT:
  Atomicity: all or nothing — one failure rolls back all
  Performance: one WAL flush — fast
  Risk: long lock duration, huge rollback — chunk batches (5000 + COMMIT each chunk)

Metrics

text
COMMIT rate vs tps
wal_sync wait_event — durability bottleneck
transaction rollback rate — app errors
idle in transaction — ACID boundary discipline (Lesson 32)

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

PropertyImplementation CostFailure Without It
AtomicityWAL + rollbackPartial updates, money loss
ConsistencyConstraints + app logicInvalid business state
IsolationMVCC + locksLost update, double spend
DurabilityWAL fsyncSilent data loss after COMMIT

Distributed ACID (2PC): O(participants) round trips, blocking on coordinator failure — avoided in modern microservices.

Local ACID: O(1) COMMIT with fsync — standard OLTP path.

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

ACID Masterclass

SQL Transaction — Explicit

sql
BEGIN;

SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 5001 FOR UPDATE;

UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 1000
WHERE account_id = 5001 AND balance >= 1000;

-- Check ROW_COUNT or use RETURNING
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 1000 WHERE account_id = 5002;

INSERT INTO transfers (from_account_id, to_account_id, amount, created_at)
VALUES (5001, 5002, 1000, NOW());

COMMIT;
-- ROLLBACK; on any error

Spring @Transactional — Atomicity + Rollback Rules

java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class TransferService {

    private final AccountRepository accountRepo;
    private final TransferRepository transferRepo;

    @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)
    public TransferResult transfer(TransferCommand cmd) {
        Account from = accountRepo.findByIdForUpdate(cmd.fromId()).orElseThrow();
        Account to = accountRepo.findByIdForUpdate(cmd.toId()).orElseThrow();

        if (from.getBalance().compareTo(cmd.amount()) < 0) {
            throw new InsufficientFundsException();  // triggers rollback
        }

        from.debit(cmd.amount());
        to.credit(cmd.amount());
        Transfer transfer = transferRepo.save(new Transfer(cmd));

        return new TransferResult(transfer.getId());
    }
}
// RuntimeException → rollback by default
// Checked Exception → no rollback unless rollbackFor specified

Consistency — DB Constraints

sql
ALTER TABLE accounts
ADD CONSTRAINT chk_balance_active CHECK (
    status <> 'ACTIVE' OR balance >= 0
);

ALTER TABLE payments
ADD CONSTRAINT uq_client_request UNIQUE (client_request_id);

ALTER TABLE accounts
ADD CONSTRAINT fk_accounts_customer
FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(customer_id);
-- DB-enforced consistency — survives any app bug bypassing service layer

Idempotency + Atomicity

java
@Transactional
public PaymentResult createPayment(CreatePaymentCommand cmd) {
    return paymentRepo.findByClientRequestId(cmd.clientRequestId())
        .map(p -> new PaymentResult(p.getId(), DUPLICATE))
        .orElseGet(() -> {
            Payment p = paymentRepo.save(new Payment(cmd));
            return new PaymentResult(p.getId(), CREATED);
        });
}
// UNIQUE on client_request_id — consistency under retry
// Entire method atomic — no duplicate partial state

Outbox Pattern — Local ACID + Event Intent

java
@Transactional
public void placeOrder(Order order) {
    orderRepo.save(order);
    outboxRepo.save(new OutboxEvent("OrderCreated", order.getId(), payload));
    // Same COMMIT — atomicity: order + outbox row together
    // Separate process publishes to Kafka — eventual cross-service
}

Durability Configuration (PostgreSQL — DBA)

sql
SHOW synchronous_commit;
SHOW wal_level;  -- replica for streaming replication

-- Do NOT disable synchronous_commit on payment primary without ADR

Savepoint — Partial Rollback (Rare)

sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE account_id = 5001;
SAVEPOINT sp1;
INSERT INTO audit_log ...;  -- fails
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp1;  -- undo audit only
COMMIT;  -- debit still commits — use carefully

Part 12 — Production Usage

ACID in Banking Production

Payment Service Boundary

text
Single ACID transaction includes:
  INSERT payment
  UPDATE account balance (or INSERT ledger entries)
  INSERT outbox event
  INSERT audit row (optional same txn)

NOT in same txn:
  Call to fraud HTTP service
  Send Kafka message directly (use outbox)
  Update Order DB in other microservice

Double-Entry Ledger Consistency

text
Invariant: debits = credits per transaction
INSERT ledger_entry debit 1000 account A
INSERT ledger_entry credit 1000 account B
Same @Transactional — atomicity preserves invariant
Consistency checked by batch reconciliation job

Reconciliation and ACID

text
Nightly job compares SUM(ledger) vs external statements
ACID ensures internal consistency; reconciliation catches external drift
Not a substitute for ACID — complementary

Disaster Recovery and Durability

text
RPO (recovery point objective): sync replication → seconds of WAL max loss
RTO (recovery time objective): failover automation
Test: simulate primary failure — verify committed payments visible on standby
Durability is operational — not only code

Anti-Patterns

text
❌ @Transactional on controller spanning user think time
❌ Cross-database @Transactional XA for microservices "simplicity"
❌ Cassandra QUORUM claimed as ACID transfer without design
❌ COMMIT then best-effort side effect without outbox — inconsistency on crash
✅ Local ACID + idempotency + Saga cross-service

Part 13 — Spring Boot Integration

@Transactional as ACID Facade

Propagation and Atomicity Scope

java
@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRED)  // default — join or create txn
@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)  // new independent atomic unit
@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.NEVER)  // forbid txn — read-only utility
text
REQUIRES_NEW:
  Outer rollback does NOT undo inner if inner committed
  Use: audit log that must persist even if outer fails — rare, careful design

Rollback Rules

java
@Transactional(rollbackFor = {InsufficientFundsException.class, FraudException.class})
@Transactional(noRollbackFor = {BusinessWarningException.class})
// Default: RuntimeException + Error → rollback
// Checked Exception → commit unless rollbackFor

Programmatic Transaction

java
TransactionTemplate txTemplate;

txTemplate.executeWithoutResult(status -> {
    // atomic block
    if (fail) status.setRollbackOnly();  // manual rollback mark
});

Read-Only Optimization

java
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public List<PaymentDto> listPayments() { ... }
// PostgreSQL: default_transaction_read_only — no writes allowed
// Hint to Hibernate — no flush — no accidental INSERT
// Does NOT replace isolation — still MVCC reads

Connection and Transaction

text
One @Transactional method ≈ one connection from pool (Lesson 32)
Nested REQUIRED joins same transaction — same atomicity unit
Commit at method exit (success) — durability at COMMIT

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

JPA and ACID Semantics

Flush Timing and Atomicity

text
Hibernate queues DML in persistence context
flush() before commit — sends SQL to DB — still in same DB transaction
rollback() — discard queued changes — atomicity preserved

Constraint Violation

java
try {
    paymentRepo.save(payment);
} catch (DataIntegrityViolationException e) {
    // UNIQUE client_request_id — txn marked rollback-only if still active
}
// Don't catch and swallow inside @Transactional without rethrow — silent commit of other changes

OptimisticLockException and Atomicity

java
@Version
private Long version;
// Stale update → OptimisticLockException at flush
// @Transactional rolls back entire unit — atomicity
// Retry at service layer with idempotency key

Entity State vs Committed State

text
Persistence context (L1 cache) within txn — REPEATABLE READ-like for entities
Other transactions invisible until commit (committed isolation level dependent)
clear() / detach after rollback before retry

No JPA Cross-PU Transaction

text
Two EntityManagerFactory / two databases — two transactions
No single ACID across without XA — architect uses Saga

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

ACID in System Design

Local ACID vs Distributed Consistency

text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Payment Service DB          │ Order Service DB              │
│ ┌─────────────────────┐     │ ┌─────────────────────┐       │
│ │ ACID txn:           │     │ │ ACID txn:           │       │
│ │ payment + balance   │     │ │ order status        │       │
│ └─────────────────────┘     │ └─────────────────────┘       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         │                              ▲
         └──────── Kafka / Saga ────────┘
Global consistency: eventual — not single ACID

When to Weaken Durability (Rare)

text
Analytics replica async — OK
Primary payment writer — never async commit without explicit risk acceptance

CAP at Architect Level

text
Network partition:
  CP (consistent + partition tolerant): RDBMS primary may reject writes to avoid split brain
  AP: Cassandra accepts writes — resolve later — not for ledger without design

Banking ledger on PostgreSQL: CP on single primary — scale read replicas

ACID Checklist for New Service

text
□ What is the atomic unit? (list SQL operations)
□ What constraints enforce consistency on DB?
□ What isolation + locks for hot rows?
□ Durability: sync commit + replication SLA?
□ Cross-service: outbox/Saga/idempotency documented?
□ Rollback behavior on each exception type?

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Confusing Atomicity with Isolation

text
"We use @Transactional so we're isolated" — isolation is separate property
Need locks/@Version for write conflicts at READ COMMITTED

Mistake 2: Consistency = Only Application

text
No FK on payments.customer_id — orphan rows — DB consistency missing
Defense in depth: constraints + service checks

Mistake 3: COMMIT Then Kafka

java
paymentRepo.save(p);  // commits at method end
kafka.send(...);      // outside txn — crash after commit, before send — lost event
// Use outbox in same txn

Mistake 4: Swallow Exception in @Transactional

java
try { risky(); } catch (Exception e) { log.error(...); }
// Method completes — COMMIT — partial atomicity break if risky partially flushed
// Rethrow or setRollbackOnly()

Mistake 5: XA Across Microservices

text
Atomikos 2PC across Payment + Order DB — fragile, slow, blocked on failure
Use Saga

Mistake 6: Assuming Cassandra Row Write = ACID Transfer

text
Transfer needs debit+credit atomicity — design explicitly — not default CQL

Mistake 7: Huge Transaction for "Performance"

text
One txn 100K rows — atomicity yes — lock duration, rollback risk, vacuum harm
Chunk with per-chunk atomicity

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What does ACID stand for?

Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.

Q2: Atomicity in transfer example?

Debit, credit, and transfer record all commit or all roll back — no partial transfer.

Q3: What is durability?

Committed data survives crash — via write-ahead log flushed to disk.

Q4: @Transactional default rollback?

RuntimeException and Error rollback; checked exceptions commit unless configured.

Q5: Consistency vs constraints?

Consistency means valid state; DB constraints are one enforcement mechanism.

Mid-Level

Q6: How does PostgreSQL implement atomicity?

WAL logging; uncommitted changes aborted on ROLLBACK/crash; MVCC hides uncommitted rows.

Q7: Isolation level for banking OLTP default?

READ COMMITTED with explicit row locks for transfers — not always SERIALIZABLE.

Q8: Outbox pattern and ACID?

Business row + outbox row in same transaction — atomic local commit; async publish after.

Q9: synchronous_commit trade-off?

on: safer durability, higher commit latency; off: faster, risk recent commits on crash.

Q10: Local ACID vs distributed transaction?

Local: single DB COMMIT. Distributed: Saga/outbox — avoid 2PC in microservices.

Senior

Q11: Double-entry ledger and ACID?

Debit and credit entries in one transaction — atomicity preserves balanced books.

Q12: REQUIRES_NEW when appropriate?

Rare independent commit unit — audit that must survive outer failure — understand trade-offs.

Q13: How crash recovery relates to ACID?

REDO committed WAL, UNDO uncommitted — restores atomicity and durability after restart.

Q14: CAP and ACID for architects?

Partition tolerance forces choice; RDBMS primary favors consistency; design cross-service as eventual.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Design payment flow ACID boundaries across 3 services.

Each service local ACID; Saga orchestration; idempotency keys; outbox events; no XA.

Q16: When weaken ACID intentionally?

Analytics batch async replica; never primary payment without documented risk; not for core ledger.

Scenario

Scenario: "Payment saved but customer says money gone, no credit on destination."

Check if two updates in same txn; partial commit from separate autocommit statements; missing rollback on exception; or two different services without Saga compensation — triage txn logs and application code boundary.

Part 20 — Revision Sheet

ACID Definitions

text

Part 1 — Concept

What Is Transaction Isolation?

Transaction isolation is the I in ACID: it defines which effects of concurrent transactions are visible to each other and which interleavings are allowed. Higher isolation reduces anomalies but increases blocking, aborts, and latency.

sql
-- PostgreSQL session A
BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 5001;  -- 1000

-- Session B (concurrent): UPDATE balance to 500; COMMIT;

-- Session A (same txn, READ COMMITTED):
SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 5001;  -- 500  ← non-repeatable read

-- Session A (REPEATABLE READ):
-- second SELECT still 1000 within same transaction

SQL Standard Isolation Levels (Weakest → Strongest)

text
1. READ UNCOMMITTED   → dirty reads possible (PostgreSQL treats as READ COMMITTED)
2. READ COMMITTED     → default most OLTP databases
3. REPEATABLE READ    → stable read snapshot per transaction
4. SERIALIZABLE       → as if transactions ran one-at-a-time

Anomaly Matrix (Conceptual)

text
ANOMALY              │ READ UNCOMMITTED │ READ COMMITTED │ REPEATABLE READ │ SERIALIZABLE
─────────────────────┼──────────────────┼────────────────┼─────────────────┼──────────────
Dirty read           │ Possible         │ No             │ No              │ No
Non-repeatable read  │ Possible         │ Possible       │ No              │ No
Phantom read         │ Possible         │ Possible       │ Possible*       │ No
Write skew           │ Possible         │ Possible       │ Possible**      │ No
Serialization anom.  │ Possible         │ Possible       │ Possible        │ No

* PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ prevents phantoms (snapshot) — stricter than SQL standard
** PostgreSQL RR prevents some write skew via snapshot — not all; SERIALIZABLE (SSI) needed

Isolation vs Locking

text
ISOLATION LEVEL     → declarative guarantee (what you must not see)
LOCK (FOR UPDATE)   → explicit mechanism (how to serialize writes)
Both together: READ COMMITTED + FOR UPDATE = common banking pattern

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Isolation Levels

text
1970s   Theory: serializable schedules — conflict serializability
        Lock-based 2PL for serializability — heavy blocking

1980s   SQL-92 standardizes four isolation levels + anomaly definitions
        Oracle MVCC — readers don't block writers; READ COMMITTED default

1990s   Snapshot isolation (SI) — REPEATABLE READ in PostgreSQL, InnoDB
        Phantom problem understood — gap locks in InnoDB RR

2000s   Anomalies under SI: write skew, fuzzy read — not in original SQL matrix
        PostgreSQL 9.1: Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) — true serializable

2010s   MVCC default industry-wide for OLTP
        JPA isolation attribute maps to JDBC — often misunderstood
        Microservices: default RC + explicit locks vs SERIALIZABLE whole app

2020s   CockroachDB/Spanner serializable default — different cost model
        Documenting per-endpoint isolation policy standard for architects
        "Use SERIALIZABLE everywhere" rejected — targeted use + retries

Historical Lesson

SQL standard isolation names do not mean the same thing on every database. PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation (stronger than standard RR on phantoms). Always verify engine behavior — interview answers and production design depend on it.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Do Isolation Levels Solve?

Problem 1: Dirty Read

text
Txn A: UPDATE balance = 9000 (not committed)
Txn B: READ balance = 9000
Txn A: ROLLBACK — balance was 10000
Txn B acted on dirty data — fraud decision on fake balance
Fix: READ COMMITTED or higher — MVCC hides uncommitted rows

Problem 2: Non-Repeatable Read

text
Txn A: READ balance 1000 — approve 800 transfer
Txn B: debit 500, COMMIT
Txn A: READ balance 500 — inconsistent decision within same report txn
Fix: REPEATABLE READ for consistent read snapshot in one report transaction

Problem 3: Phantom Read

text
Txn A: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM payments WHERE status='PENDING' → 10
Txn B: INSERT new PENDING payment, COMMIT
Txn A: SELECT COUNT(*) → 11 — phantom row appeared
Fix: SERIALIZABLE or engine-specific RR snapshot (PostgreSQL RR prevents this)

Problem 4: Write Skew

text
Two doctors on call — rule: at least one must be on call
Txn A: read both off-call → set self on-call
Txn B: read both off-call → set self on-call
Both commit — nobody on call — invariant violated
Fix: SERIALIZABLE (SSI) or explicit row locks on all involved rows
Banking analog: dual limit checks on overlapping aggregate counters

Problem 5: Lost Update (Not Always "Fixed" by Isolation Alone)

text
Two txns read balance 1000, both write 900 and 800 — last writer wins
Fix: FOR UPDATE, @Version optimistic lock, or atomic UPDATE — not isolation level alone at READ COMMITTED

Unified Problem Statement

Isolation levels define which concurrent phenomena applications can observe — trading off correctness guarantees against performance, blocking, and serialization failure rates.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Four Levels Instead of One Serializable?

Performance Spectrum

text
SERIALIZABLE everywhere:
  SSI predicate locks — serialization failures — retry storms on hot OLTP
  More blocking in lock-based engines

READ COMMITTED:
  Minimal reader/writer blocking — MVCC — highest throughput
  Application uses targeted locks for money rows

Not All Workloads Need Strong Isolation

text
Single-row transfer with FOR UPDATE: READ COMMITTED sufficient
Multi-row invariant without locking all rows: may need SERIALIZABLE
Read-only dashboard snapshot: REPEATABLE READ or READ ONLY replica snapshot

Database Implementation Differences

text
Same JDBC constant ISOLATION_REPEATABLE_READ:
  PostgreSQL: snapshot for transaction
  Oracle: consistent read snapshot
  SQL Server: depends on READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT setting
Architect must read engine docs — not only JDBC enum

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Each Level Works Internally

READ COMMITTED (PostgreSQL)

text
Each STATEMENT gets fresh snapshot:
  Visible: rows committed before statement start
  UPDATE sees latest committed version on conflict — "read committed update conflict" re-evaluate

No dirty read: uncommitted xmin invisible
Non-repeatable read: next statement sees B's commit
Implementation: MVCC tuple visibility + row locks on write

REPEATABLE READ (PostgreSQL = Snapshot Isolation)

text
One snapshot for entire TRANSACTION (first statement):
  All reads in txn see consistent point-in-time
  Non-repeatable read: prevented
  Phantom: prevented for snapshot reads (new inserts by others not visible if started before)

Write skew still possible:
  Two txns read overlapping sets, write disjoint rows — both commit
  Example: two account limit counters updated without locking each other

SERIALIZABLE (PostgreSQL SSI)

text
Serializable Snapshot Isolation:
  Tracks read/write dependencies — detects dangerous structures
  May abort with: could not serialize access due to concurrent update
  Application MUST retry transaction

Predicate locking (SIREAD locks) — memory overhead
True serializable — no write skew (that SSI catches)

READ UNCOMMITTED

text
PostgreSQL: mapped to READ COMMITTED — no dirty reads
SQL Server: can read uncommitted with NOLOCK hint — dirty read possible
MySQL InnoDB: effectively READ COMMITTED for InnoDB tables
Banking: never use dirty read semantics

Oracle Snapshot

text
Default READ COMMITTED (consistent read per statement)
SERIALIZABLE isolation: snapshot + extra checks — ORA-08177 possible (can't serialize access)
Multi-version undo segments — long txn can cause undo retention issues

SQL Server Models

text
Default READ COMMITTED with locking (shared locks on read — blocks writers)
READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT (RCSI): row versioning — similar MVCC — less blocking
SNAPSHOT isolation: statement-level consistent read — separate from SERIALIZABLE
SERIALIZABLE: full locking — range locks — phantoms prevented — blocking heavy

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Isolation and Storage Interaction

MVCC Versions and Snapshots

text
Each row version: xmin, xmax
Snapshot: set of active xids at snapshot time
Long REPEATABLE READ txn:
  Holds xmin horizon — prevents vacuum — dead tuple bloat (Lesson 31)
  storage growth if RR reports run hours

Undo / Old Versions

text
PostgreSQL: old versions in heap until vacuum
Oracle: undo tablespace — long serializable query — ORA-01555 snapshot too old
SQL Server RCSI: version store in tempdb — long txn — version store bloat

SSI Tracking (PostgreSQL)

text
pg_readonly_predicates / serialization conflicts
WAL records for conflicts
Slight CPU + memory overhead vs READ COMMITTED

Lock Escalation (SQL Server Serializable)

text
Range locks on index — phantom prevention
Lock memory — blocking chains — different from PG MVCC SSI abort model

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Isolation Memory Impact

LevelExtra Memory
READ COMMITTEDBaseline snapshot per statement
REPEATABLE READSnapshot held whole txn — blocks vacuum
SERIALIZABLE (SSI)Dependency graph + predicate locks
SQL Server version storetempdb growth under RCSI
Oracle undoUndo blocks for consistent read

Long Report Transaction

java
@Transactional(isolation = REPEATABLE_READ, readOnly = true)
public Report generate() {
    // 30 minute report — holds snapshot — bloat + connection pool hold
}
// Prefer: READ ONLY replica + READ COMMITTED + snapshot export
// Or: materialized view / warehouse

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Isolation Level Execution Flows

Flow 1: READ COMMITTED Transfer (Standard Banking)

text
Txn A: BEGIN (RC default)
Txn A: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE account 5001 — lock row
Txn B: UPDATE account 5001 — waits on lock
Txn A: UPDATE debit; COMMIT — release lock
Txn B: acquires lock, reads committed state, continues
Isolation: no dirty read; write serialized by lock
Non-repeatable read irrelevant — single consistent lock path for transfer

Flow 2: Non-Repeatable Read Demo (RC)

text
Txn A: BEGIN; SELECT sum(balance) FROM accounts WHERE customer_id=1001 → 5000
Txn B: UPDATE account balance; COMMIT
Txn A: SELECT sum(balance) ... → 4500  ← different within same txn
Expected for RC — document if report needs RR

Flow 3: REPEATABLE READ Report

text
Txn A: BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
Txn A: SELECT ... aggregates at T0
Txn B: INSERT payment; COMMIT
Txn A: same SELECT — same result — snapshot at T0
Txn A: COMMIT
Consistent financial snapshot for report PDF

Flow 4: SERIALIZABLE Abort + Retry

text
Txn A: BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
Txn B: BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
Both read overlapping predicate, write conflicting rows
Txn A: COMMIT — success
Txn B: COMMIT — ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update
Spring: catch, retry transfer idempotently

Flow 5: Write Skew (RR Not Enough)

text
On-call doctors table — two rows
Txn A RR: read both off-call; update self on-call
Txn B RR: read both off-call; update self on-call
Both COMMIT — RR allows — write skew
SSI SERIALIZABLE: one aborts on commit
Alternative: SELECT FOR UPDATE all rows in rule set

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Choosing Isolation by Performance

Throughput Ranking (Typical OLTP)

text
Highest throughput → lowest:

READ COMMITTED (+ explicit row locks where needed)
REPEATABLE READ (snapshot — vacuum pressure if long)
SERIALIZABLE SSI (aborts + tracking overhead)
Lock-based SERIALIZABLE (SQL Server classic — blocking)

When to Use Each (Banking)

Use CaseIsolationAdditional
Transfer debit/creditREAD COMMITTEDFOR UPDATE ordered locks
Payment insert + idempotencyREAD COMMITTEDUNIQUE constraint
Balance report in one PDFREPEATABLE READreadOnly, short duration
Daily limit across rowsSERIALIZABLE or advisory lockretry logic
Read API list paymentsREAD COMMITTEDno txn or readOnly
Inventory-style reservationSERIALIZABLE or SELECT FOR UPDATE all SKUs

Serialization Failure Rate

text
Monitor: SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization_failure) in PostgreSQL
High rate → too hot for SERIALIZABLE — row locks or redesign
Retry with exponential backoff + jitter — max 3 attempts

Default Policy

text
Platform default: READ COMMITTED for all @Transactional
Escalate per method with ADR:
  @Transactional(isolation = Isolation.REPEATABLE_READ) on named report services
  SERIALIZABLE: explicit approval + retry framework
Never: READ UNCOMMITTED

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

LevelRead BlockingWrite BlockingAbort/RetryAnomalies Prevented
READ COMMITTEDLowRow lock conflictsDeadlock retryDirty read
REPEATABLE READLowWrite conflictsDeadlock retry+ non-repeatable, phantoms (PG)
SERIALIZABLE (SSI)Low-MedMedSerialization failure+ write skew (detected)
RC + FOR UPDATEWaits on lockWaitsDeadlockLost update on locked rows

Correctness for transfer: O(1) lock contention per account — isolation level less important than lock discipline.

Isolation Level Masterclass

Set Session Isolation (PostgreSQL)

sql
-- Per transaction
BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY;
SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at) AS day, SUM(amount)
FROM payments
WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
COMMIT;

BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
-- limit enforcement logic
COMMIT;

Role Default

sql
ALTER ROLE reporting_app SET default_transaction_isolation = 'repeatable read';
ALTER ROLE payment_app SET default_transaction_isolation = 'read committed';

Spring Isolation per Method

java
@Service
public class ReportingService {

    @Transactional(readOnly = true, isolation = Isolation.REPEATABLE_READ)
    public MonthlyReport generateMonthlyReport(YearMonth month) {
        BigDecimal total = paymentRepo.sumByMonth(month);
        BigDecimal fees = feeRepo.sumByMonth(month);
        return new MonthlyReport(total, fees);  // consistent snapshot
    }
}

@Service
public class DailyLimitService {

    @Transactional(isolation = Isolation.SERIALIZABLE)
    @Retryable(retryFor = CannotSerializeTransactionException.class, maxAttempts = 3)
    public void debitWithDailyLimit(DebitCommand cmd) {
        // multi-row read + insert — SSI protects invariant
    }
}

@Service
public class TransferService {

    @Transactional  // READ COMMITTED default
    public void transfer(TransferCommand cmd) {
        // FOR UPDATE locks — sufficient for transfer
    }
}

java
connection.setTransactionIsolation(Connection.TRANSACTION_READ_COMMITTED);
// TRANSACTION_REPEATABLE_READ
// TRANSACTION_SERIALIZABLE

Detect Serialization Failure (PostgreSQL)

java
catch (PSQLException ex) {
    if ("40001".equals(ex.getSQLState())) {
        throw new RetryableConcurrencyException(ex);
    }
    throw ex;
}
// Spring 6: CannotSerializeTransactionException

Write Skew Fix Without SERIALIZABLE

sql
BEGIN;
SELECT account_id FROM accounts
WHERE customer_id = 1001
FOR UPDATE;  -- lock ALL accounts for customer before limit check
-- check sum debits + new debit <= limit
INSERT INTO transactions ...;
COMMIT;

Oracle Serializable Reference

sql
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
-- ORA-08177: can't serialize access for this transaction — retry

SQL Server Snapshot

sql
ALTER DATABASE BankDb SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON;
-- Row versioning for READ COMMITTED — reduces blocking
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SNAPSHOT;

Part 12 — Production Usage

Isolation in Banking Production

Payment Platform Standard

yaml
# Documented platform policy
default_isolation: READ_COMMITTED
exceptions:
  - service: reporting-api
    methods: generateRegulatoryReport
    isolation: REPEATABLE_READ
    max_duration: 120s
  - service: limits-api
    methods: enforceDailyDebitLimit
    isolation: SERIALIZABLE
    retry: 3

Transfer Path — Do Not Over-Isolate

text
Anti-pattern: @Transactional(isolation = SERIALIZABLE) on all transfers
Result: serialization failures on hot accounts — p99 latency spikes
Correct: READ COMMITTED + findByIdForUpdate + ordered account locks

Regulatory Report

text
REPEATABLE READ read-only on replica:
  Consistent numbers in all sections of PDF
  Run during low lag window — replica snapshot lag documented in footer

Monitoring

text
Metrics:
  txn rollback rate by sqlstate 40001
  ORA-08177 / SQL Server deadlock graph
  idle in transaction by isolation level (pg_stat_activity)
Alerts:
  serialization_failure rate > 1% on endpoint

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

JPA Isolation Mapping

Standard Mapping

java
@Transactional(isolation = Isolation.REPEATABLE_READ)
// Hibernate passes to Connection.setTransactionIsolation at txn begin
// Must match database-supported levels

Persistence Context and Snapshot

text
REPEATABLE READ:
  Hibernate L1 cache + DB snapshot — entity reads consistent within txn
  clear() if handling retry after serialization failure

READ COMMITTED:
  flush() may see newer committed data on subsequent query — by design

OptimisticLockException vs Serialization

text
@Version failure: OptimisticLockException — concurrent write conflict
SSI abort: CannotSerializeTransactionException / SQLSTATE 40001
Different retry policies — don't conflate

Read-Only Hint

java
@Transactional(readOnly = true, isolation = Isolation.REPEATABLE_READ)
// Hibernate: flushMode MANUAL, no dirty checking writes
// PostgreSQL: SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY

No JPA Standard for SSI Retry

text
Implement @Retryable or Resilience4j on service methods using SERIALIZABLE
Idempotency keys mandatory on retries

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

Isolation Architecture Policy

Decision Tree

text
Need consistent multi-statement read without writes?
  YES → REPEATABLE READ read-only (short) on replica
  NO ↓

Need multi-row invariant without locking all rows?
  YES → SERIALIZABLE + retry OR redesign with explicit locks
  NO ↓

Single-row or locked-row write path?
  YES → READ COMMITTED + FOR UPDATE / @Version
  NO ↓

Default READ COMMITTED + code review

Cross-Service Is Not Isolation Level

text
Order service READ COMMITTED + Payment READ COMMITTED ≠ global isolation
Saga compensations — eventual consistency — document separately from ACID I

Engine Migration Risk

text
Oracle → PostgreSQL migration:
  Re-test all REPEATABLE READ reports — snapshot behavior similar but not identical
  SERIALIZABLE: Oracle ORA-08177 vs PG 40001 — retry code must handle both during migration

Documentation Template

text
Endpoint: POST /transfer
Isolation: READ COMMITTED (default)
Concurrency control: PESSIMISTIC_WRITE on accounts (ordered IDs)
Anomalies accepted: non-repeatable read on unrelated reads — N/A
Anomalies prevented: lost update on debited accounts
Retry: deadlock only (40P01), not serialization

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: SERIALIZABLE on All @Transactional

text
Hot payment rows — constant 40001 — retry storm — use RC + locks

Mistake 2: Assume RR Fixes Lost Update Without Lock

text
Two txns read balance in RR, both write — last writer still wins on same row unless @Version or FOR UPDATE
RR prevents read change — not write conflict on same row automatically

Mistake 3: Long REPEATABLE READ on Primary

text
Blocks vacuum — bloat — pool hold — use replica

Mistake 4: Ignore SQLSTATE 40001 Retry

text
SERIALIZABLE without retry — user sees random failures

Mistake 5: READ UNCOMMITTED for "Speed"

text
PostgreSQL ignores; SQL Server NOLOCK — dirty reads — forbidden in finance

Mistake 6: Confuse SQL Server SNAPSHOT with SERIALIZABLE

text
Different semantics — RCSI reduces blocking — not full serializable

Mistake 7: Different Isolation per Layer Undocumented

text
Service RR, repository RC — confusion — isolation on outermost @Transactional wins for connection

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: Four isolation levels in order?

READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE (weakest to strongest).

Q2: Default PostgreSQL isolation?

READ COMMITTED.

Q3: What is dirty read?

Reading another transaction's uncommitted changes — prevented at READ COMMITTED in PostgreSQL.

Q4: Non-repeatable read example?

Two reads of same row in one txn return different values — possible in READ COMMITTED.

Q5: Transfer service isolation recommendation?

READ COMMITTED with SELECT FOR UPDATE — not necessarily SERIALIZABLE.

Mid-Level

Q6: Phantom read vs non-repeatable read?

Non-repeatable: same row changes. Phantom: new rows appear matching prior query predicate.

Q7: PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ vs SQL standard?

PG uses snapshot — prevents phantoms; standard RR may allow phantoms.

Q8: What is write skew?

Concurrent txns read overlapping state, write disjoint rows, break global invariant — RR allows; SSI SERIALIZABLE detects.

Q9: SQLSTATE 40001?

serialization_failure — retry transaction (PostgreSQL SSI).

Q10: Does isolation alone prevent lost update?

Not at READ COMMITTED without locks or optimistic versioning.

Senior

Q11: SSI vs lock-based serializable?

SSI: MVCC + abort on dangerous conflicts — less blocking. Lock-based: range locks — more blocking, fewer aborts.

Q12: When REPEATABLE READ on replica for report?

Consistent multi-query snapshot; short duration; document replication lag.

Q13: Fix write skew without SERIALIZABLE?

Lock all rows involved in invariant (FOR UPDATE all customer accounts) or materialize counter row with lock.

Q14: Oracle ORA-08177 vs PG 40001?

Both serialization failures — retry; different engines, same architectural response.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Platform isolation policy for 20 services?

Default READ COMMITTED; registry of SERIALIZABLE/RR exceptions with ADR, retry, idempotency, monitoring.

Q16: Migrate SQL Server locking RC to PostgreSQL MVCC — test focus?

Blocking differences, phantom behavior, report RR snapshots, deadlock vs serialization rates.

Scenario

Scenario: "Daily limit exceeded under concurrent debits though each check passed."

Write skew — RR insufficient — use SERIALIZABLE with retry, advisory lock per account-day, or single locked counter row updated atomically.

Part 20 — Revision Sheet

Levels (weak → strong)

text
READ UNCOMMITTED  → PG acts as RC
READ COMMITTED    → default OLTP; statement snapshot
REPEATABLE READ   → txn snapshot (PG); consistent reads
SERIALIZABLE      → SSI (PG); abort 40001; retry required

Banking Defaults

text
Transfer/payment     → READ COMMITTED + FOR UPDATE
Report snapshot      → RR read-only short on replica
Multi-row invariant  → SERIALIZABLE or lock all rows
Never                → READ UNCOMMITTED / NOLOCK

Anomalies

text
Dirty read           → RC+
Non-repeatable       → RR+
Phantom (PG RR)      → RR+
Write skew           → SERIALIZABLE or lock all
Lost update          → FOR UPDATE / @Version

Banking transferRC + FOR UPDATE — not global SERIALIZABLE
Spring@Transactional(isolation=) per service method
Engines differVerify PG vs Oracle vs SQL Server behavior
ArchitectDefault RC; documented exceptions; idempotent retry
