Lesson 35

Pessimistic vs Optimistic Locking

Phase 4: TRANSACTIONS, CONCURRENCY & RELIABILITY | Previous: Transaction Isolation Levels — Deep Dive | Next: Deadlocks

Transactions
1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why This Exists5Internal Working6Storage Internals7Memory Usage8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Complexity Analysis11Code / SQL Examples12Production Usage13Spring Boot Integration14Hibernate/JPA Integration15Architect Perspective16Decision Matrix17Comparison Tables18Common Mistakes19Interview Questions20Revision Sheet21Summary Table*Practice

Part 1 — Concept

What Are Pessimistic and Optimistic Locking?

Two strategies to prevent lost updates and write conflicts when multiple transactions modify the same data:

text
PESSIMISTIC LOCKING
  "Lock before you change."
  Block other writers until commit.
  DB: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
  JPA: @Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)

OPTIMISTIC LOCKING
  "Assume no conflict; detect at commit."
  No lock during read; verify version at UPDATE.
  JPA: @Version column
  DB: UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ?

Side-by-Side Mental Model

text
PESSIMISTIC (transfer on account 5001):

  Txn A: FOR UPDATE → holds row lock
  Txn B: FOR UPDATE → WAITS
  Txn A: UPDATE, COMMIT → releases
  Txn B: proceeds with fresh balance

OPTIMISTIC (update customer profile):

  Txn A: read entity version=5
  Txn B: read entity version=5
  Txn A: UPDATE WHERE version=5 → version=6, COMMIT ✅
  Txn B: UPDATE WHERE version=5 → 0 rows → OptimisticLockException → retry

Related Patterns (Not the Same Thing)

text
SKIP LOCKED       → don't wait — take next row (job queues)
NOWAIT            → fail immediately if lock held
Atomic UPDATE     → UPDATE ... WHERE balance >= amt (conditional, no explicit SELECT lock)
SERIALIZABLE      → isolation level — detects conflicts at commit (Lesson 34)
Advisory lock     → app-defined serialization key (pg_advisory_xact_lock)

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Concurrency Control Strategies

text
1980s   Two-phase locking (2PL) — pessimistic standard in RDBMS
        MVCC readers — writers still use row locks for UPDATE

1990s   Optimistic concurrency in client-server apps — version columns
        Hibernate 3+ @Version — industry pattern for JPA entities

2000s   Web scale: optimistic preferred for read-heavy CRUD
        Financial cores remain pessimistic on balance rows
        SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED — PostgreSQL 9.5 — queue workers

2010s   Microservices retry + idempotency — optimistic retry safe only with keys
        Redis distributed locks — often misapplied vs DB row lock
        @Retryable on OptimisticLockException and deadlock

2020s   Event sourcing / ledger — append-only reduces UPDATE contention
        Hot account queue serialization — beyond classic lock choice
        Architect policy: pessimistic money rows, optimistic reference data

Historical Lesson

Optimistic locking became fashionable with ORMs and REST APIs — but hot financial rows (balances, inventory SKU with flash sales) still need pessimistic or atomic conditional UPDATE. Choosing optimistic on a treasury account is a production incident waiting for a retry storm.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Do Locking Strategies Solve?

Problem 1: Lost Update

text
Txn A and B read balance 1000
Both write 900 and 800 — last commit wins — wrong balance
Fix: pessimistic FOR UPDATE OR optimistic @Version OR atomic UPDATE

Problem 2: Double Spend (Check-Then-Act Race)

text
Txn A: read 1000, approve 800 debit
Txn B: read 1000, approve 700 debit
Both commit — overdraft
Fix: pessimistic lock before check OR single atomic UPDATE with balance >= condition

Problem 3: Queue Duplicate Processing

text
Two workers pick same PENDING payment row
Both process — double charge
Fix: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED or UPDATE ... WHERE status='PENDING' RETURNING with row lock

Problem 4: Optimistic Retry Storm

text
100 concurrent updates on same product inventory row — all version conflict — all retry
Throughput collapses — pessimistic or queue per SKU better

Problem 5: Pessimistic Deadlock

text
Transfer A→B locks 5001 then 5002; transfer B→A locks 5002 then 5001
Deadlock — one victim aborted — need ordering + retry

Unified Problem Statement

Pessimistic and optimistic locking coordinate concurrent writers on shared rows — pessimistic blocks early, optimistic detects late — each suited to different contention profiles and business workflows.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Two Strategies Instead of One?

Contention Profile Drives Choice

text
Low contention, read-mostly entity (customer address):
  Optimistic — no lock wait — rare conflict — simple retry

High contention hot row (account balance, ticket inventory):
  Pessimistic — serialize writers — predictable latency vs retry chaos

User Experience

text
Pessimistic: second user waits (or lock_timeout fails fast)
Optimistic: second user succeeds on retry or gets conflict error — UX must handle
Payment API: often fail fast insufficient funds — pessimistic path clearer

Database Already Serializes Writes

text
Single UPDATE is atomic — combining check+update in one SQL avoids read-modify-write race
Lock strategy choice applies when logic spans multiple statements or ORM entity graph

ORM Entity State

text
JPA load-modify-save benefits from @Version — detects stale entity in persistence context
Native atomic SQL may skip ORM — different pattern same correctness goal

Part 5 — Internal Working

Internal Mechanisms

Pessimistic — PostgreSQL Row Lock

sql
SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 5001 FOR UPDATE;
-- Lock mode: RowExclusive on row until transaction end
-- Other FOR UPDATE / UPDATE / DELETE block
-- Plain SELECT (MVCC) still reads committed snapshot — no block
text
Lock wait queue — FIFO-ish — lock_timeout aborts waiter
NOWAIT: immediate ERROR if not granted
SKIP LOCKED: row skipped in scan — worker takes different row

Optimistic — Version Column

sql
-- Hibernate generates:
UPDATE accounts
SET balance = 900, version = 6
WHERE account_id = 5001 AND version = 5;

-- 0 rows updated → StaleStateException / OptimisticLockException
text
Version increment at flush time — not at read
Concurrent txn committed version=6 between read and flush → conflict detected
No lock held during business logic between read and update

JPA LockModeType

java
PESSIMISTIC_WRITE   → SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
PESSIMISTIC_READ    → FOR SHARE (PostgreSQL)
OPTIMISTIC          → version check at flush (mode on read — schedules check)
OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT → version++ even if no field change
PESSIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT → lock + version bump

Atomic Conditional UPDATE (Third Path)

sql
UPDATE accounts
SET balance = balance - :amount
WHERE account_id = :id AND balance >= :amount AND status = 'ACTIVE';
-- Row locked during UPDATE internally — short duration
-- No prior SELECT — no OptimisticLockException — check rows affected

SKIP LOCKED Internals

sql
SELECT payment_id FROM payments_staging
WHERE status = 'PENDING'
ORDER BY created_at
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
LIMIT 1;
-- Skips rows already locked by other workers — no wait
-- Ideal work queue — not for transfer same account

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Locking and Storage

Row Lock — Not On-Disk Flag

text
Lock in shared memory lock table — released at COMMIT/ROLLBACK
Uncommitted row version visible only to owning txn (MVCC)
FOR UPDATE locks latest committed version + waits for concurrent uncommitted writer

@Version Column Storage

text
Extra BIGINT column per entity table — 8 bytes per row
Every successful UPDATE increments version — WAL includes version column
Index not required on version — PK in WHERE clause sufficient

HOT Update and Locks

text
UPDATE without indexed column change — same page HOT — shorter lock window
@Version always changes on update — if version indexed unnecessarily — extra index maintenance
Don't index version column alone

Skip Locked Scan

text
Index scan on (status, created_at) — locked rows skipped — may scan many rows to find unlocked
Monitor: workers idle while rows pending but all locked — need more workers or smaller batch lock scope

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Locking Memory and Pool Impact

PatternConnection HoldLock Memory
Pessimistic long txnEntire txn — pool risk (L32)Row lock until commit
Optimistic short txnShorter — no waitNo lock until UPDATE instant
Optimistic retry loopMultiple txns — multiplies loadBurst of conflicts
SKIP LOCKED workersShort per rowMinimal wait queue

Retry Amplification

text
10 optimistic conflicts → 10 full transactions — 10× COMMIT WAL
Pessimistic: 1 wait chain — 1 COMMIT each serially — predictable for hot row

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Execution Flows

Flow 1: Pessimistic Transfer

text
1. @Transactional BEGIN
2. findByIdForUpdate(5001) — acquire lock or wait
3. findByIdForUpdate(5002) — ordered IDs — avoid deadlock
4. validate balance, mutate entities
5. flush, COMMIT — release locks
Concurrent transfer on 5001: blocks at step 2 until step 5 completes

Flow 2: Optimistic Profile Update

text
1. @Transactional BEGIN
2. findById(customer) — version=3
3. setEmail(...)
4. save — flush UPDATE ... WHERE version=3
5. If 0 rows → OptimisticLockException → rollback
6. Service retry: reload version=4, merge user intent, save again

Flow 3: Atomic Debit (Minimal Lock Window)

text
1. @Transactional BEGIN
2. debitIfSufficient(accountId, amount) → UPDATE ... WHERE balance >= amount
3. if rowsUpdated==0 → InsufficientFundsException
4. credit(toAccount)
5. COMMIT
No explicit SELECT FOR UPDATE — UPDATE acquires row lock briefly
Gap between debit and credit: another txn could read middle state within same txn isolation — both in one txn OK

Flow 4: SKIP LOCKED Worker

text
Worker 1: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED → locks payment 9001
Worker 2: same query → skips 9001 → locks 9002
Both process in parallel — no duplicate — no blocking on same row

Flow 5: Optimistic Failure → User Message

text
User A and B edit same config row
B commits first
A save → OptimisticLockException
Controller: 409 Conflict — "Data changed, refresh and retry"
Not silent overwrite

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

When to Use Which

Decision Matrix (Primary)

ProfileStrategyPattern
Hot row, financial debitPessimisticFOR UPDATE ordered
Hot row, single UPDATE ruleAtomic SQLUPDATE WHERE balance >=
Low contention CRUDOptimistic@Version + retry
Job queue / workersSKIP LOCKEDFOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
Must not waitNOWAITfail fast to user
Flash inventory (same SKU)Pessimistic or queuenot blind optimistic

Performance Comparison

text
Low contention (conflict rate < 1%):
  Optimistic wins — no lock wait — fewer round trips than FOR UPDATE

High contention (same row > 10 TPS writes):
  Pessimistic wins — serial latency < optimistic retry multiplication
  Measure conflict rate — switch if optimistic retries > 5%

Anti-Patterns

text
❌ @Version on account balance with 500 TPS — retry storm
❌ FOR UPDATE on report query scanning 1M rows
❌ No retry on OptimisticLockException in batch job
❌ Pessimistic lock in Redis + DB update without same txn — split brain
❌ SKIP LOCKED for transfer between two accounts — wrong tool

Metrics

text
optimistic_lock_failures_total
lock_wait_time_ms (pg_stat_activity wait_event=Lock)
deadlock_count
transfer_p99 with pessimistic vs optimistic A/B

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

StrategyConflict HandlingLatency Under ContentionImplementation
PessimisticBlock O(wait)Linear queueFOR UPDATE
OptimisticFail O(1) detectRetries O(k) conflicts@Version
Atomic UPDATEBlock on UPDATE onlyLow for single stmtJDBC/JPQL
SKIP LOCKEDSkip O(1)High parallelism queueNative SQL

k = retry count under conflict — unbounded retries forbidden — max 3 with backoff.

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Locking Masterclass

Pessimistic — JPA

java
public interface AccountRepository extends JpaRepository<Account, Long> {

    @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
    @Query("SELECT a FROM Account a WHERE a.accountId = :id")
    Optional<Account> findByIdForUpdate(@Param("id") Long id);

    @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
    @QueryHints(@QueryHint(name = "jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout", value = "3000"))
    Optional<Account> findByIdForUpdateWithTimeout(@Param("id") Long id);
}

Optimistic — Entity

java
@Entity
@Table(name = "customers")
public class Customer {

    @Id
    private Long customerId;

    @Version
    private Long version;

    private String email;
    private String phone;
}

@Service
public class CustomerService {

    @Transactional
    public void updateEmail(Long id, String email) {
        Customer c = customerRepo.findById(id).orElseThrow();
        c.setEmail(email);
        // version checked at flush
    }

    @Transactional
    @Retryable(retryFor = OptimisticLockingFailureException.class, maxAttempts = 3,
               backoff = @Backoff(delay = 50, multiplier = 2))
    public void updateEmailWithRetry(Long id, String email) {
        updateEmail(id, email);
    }
}

Atomic Conditional Update

java
public interface AccountRepository extends JpaRepository<Account, Long> {

    @Modifying
    @Query("""
        UPDATE Account a SET a.balance = a.balance - :amount, a.version = a.version + 1
        WHERE a.accountId = :id AND a.balance >= :amount AND a.status = 'ACTIVE'
        """)
    int debitIfSufficient(@Param("id") Long id, @Param("amount") BigDecimal amount);
}
// Note: mixing @Version manual increment — prefer entity load or native SQL without broken version semantics
// Cleaner native:
java
@Modifying
@Query(value = """
    UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - :amount
    WHERE account_id = :id AND balance >= :amount AND status = 'ACTIVE'
    """, nativeQuery = true)
int debitNative(@Param("id") Long id, @Param("amount") BigDecimal amount);

SKIP LOCKED — Payment Processor

java
@Query(value = """
    SELECT payment_id FROM payments_staging
    WHERE status = 'PENDING'
    ORDER BY created_at
    FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
    LIMIT :batch
    """, nativeQuery = true)
List<Long> claimPendingBatch(@Param("batch") int batch);

@Transactional
public void processBatch() {
    List<Long> ids = repo.claimPendingBatch(10);
    for (Long id : processWithLockHeld(ids)) { ... }
}

NOWAIT — Fail Fast

sql
SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE account_id = 5001 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;
-- ERROR: could not obtain lock on row — return 409 to user "Account busy"

Conflict Response — REST

java
@ExceptionHandler(OptimisticLockingFailureException.class)
public ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> handleOptimisticLock(OptimisticLockingFailureException ex) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CONFLICT)
        .body(ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(CONFLICT, "Record was modified by another user"));
}

Inventory — Pessimistic for Flash Sale

java
@Transactional
public void purchase(Long skuId, int qty) {
    Inventory inv = inventoryRepo.findByIdForUpdate(skuId).orElseThrow();
    if (inv.getAvailable() < qty) throw new OutOfStockException();
    inv.decrement(qty);
}
// Optimistic on same SKU during flash sale → mass OptimisticLockException

Part 12 — Production Usage

Banking & Payments Production Patterns

Standard Ledger Choices

text
Account transfer:           PESSIMISTIC_WRITE + lock ordering
Customer master data:       OPTIMISTIC @Version
Payment idempotency insert: UNIQUE key — no lock on read path
Staging worker:             SKIP LOCKED
Config/fee table admin:     OPTIMISTIC + 409 Conflict UI
Treasury hot account:         per-account message queue OR pessimistic accept wait

Retry Policy

yaml
# Platform standard
optimistic_lock:
  max_attempts: 3
  backoff_ms: [50, 100, 200]
  jitter: true

deadlock:
  max_attempts: 3
  sqlstate: [40P01]  # PostgreSQL deadlock

# Never infinite retry on payment without idempotency key

Idempotency + Retry

java
@Transactional
@Retryable(retryFor = {DeadlockLoserDataAccessException.class}, maxAttempts = 3)
public PaymentResult createPayment(CreatePaymentCommand cmd) {
    return paymentRepo.findByClientRequestId(cmd.clientRequestId())
        .map(p -> PaymentResult.duplicate(p))
        .orElseGet(() -> PaymentResult.created(doCreate(cmd)));
}
// Retry after deadlock safe — duplicate path on second attempt

Monitoring Alerts

text
Alert: optimistic_lock_failure_rate > 5% on any endpoint → review strategy
Alert: avg lock wait > 500ms on transfer → hot account or batch blocker
Dashboard: SKIP LOCKED queue depth vs workers

TransactionTemplate Retry Wrapper

java
public <T> T withOptimisticRetry(Supplier<T> action) {
    int attempts = 0;
    while (true) {
        try {
            return txTemplate.execute(status -> action.get());
        } catch (OptimisticLockingFailureException e) {
            if (++attempts >= 3) throw e;
        }
    }
}

Separate Lock Service Bean

java
@Service
public class AccountLockService {
    @Transactional
    public <T> T withLockedAccounts(long id1, long id2, BiFunction<Account, Account, T> fn) {
        long first = Math.min(id1, id2), second = Math.max(id1, id2);
        Account a1 = accountRepo.findByIdForUpdate(first).orElseThrow();
        Account a2 = (first == second) ? a1 : accountRepo.findByIdForUpdate(second).orElseThrow();
        Account from = id1 == first ? a1 : a2;
        Account to = id1 == first ? a2 : a1;
        return fn.apply(from, to);
    }
}

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

JPA Locking Details

@Version Rules

text
Every entity update increments version automatically
DELETE with version check optional
Primitive int version — overflow theoretical — use Long
Don't manually set version in application code

Pessimistic and Lazy Loading

java
@Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
@Query("SELECT c FROM Customer c JOIN FETCH c.accounts WHERE c.id = :id")
// Lock customer + fetched accounts — know what's locked
// Lazy load accounts after lock customer — separate queries — account rows not locked unless fetched with lock

EntityManager Lock

java
em.find(Account.class, id, LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE);
em.lock(account, LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE);  // on already loaded entity

Optimistic on Detached Entity

java
// merge detached entity with stale version → OptimisticLockException at flush
Customer detached = ...; // version=3 from API payload
customerRepo.save(detached); // DB already version=5 → conflict
// API must send version from client If-Match header — ETag pattern

REST ETag Pattern

text
GET /customers/1001 → ETag: "v-7"
PUT /customers/1001 If-Match: "v-7"
@Version mismatch → 412 Precondition Failed
Architect standard for optimistic admin UIs

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

Locking Strategy Architecture

Platform Decision Tree

text
Money movement on balance row?
  YES → Pessimistic FOR UPDATE (ordered) OR ledger append-only
  NO ↓

Work queue row claim?
  YES → SKIP LOCKED
  NO ↓

Same row write TPS > 20 sustained?
  YES → pessimistic or queue — not optimistic
  NO ↓

Admin CRUD / reference data?
  YES → optimistic @Version + 409

Redis Distributed Lock vs DB Row Lock

text
❌ Redis lock then DB read without txn coordination — crash between — inconsistent
✅ DB row lock inside @Transactional — single source of truth
Redis: leader election, cron singleton — not money row replacement
Redlock controversy — avoid for financial correctness without DB backing

Event Sourcing Alternative

text
Append ledger entry — no UPDATE balance version conflict
Balance = projection — optimistic on projection row or single-thread per account consumer
Architect choice at scale — Lesson 33 ACID on append txn still required

Documentation per Aggregate

text
Aggregate: Account
  Locking: PESSIMISTIC_WRITE on transfer
  Ordering: ascending accountId
  Retry: deadlock only, max 3
  Idempotency: transfer client_request_id

Aggregate: Customer
  Locking: OPTIMISTIC @Version
  Retry: optimistic max 3
  API: If-Match ETag

Mistake 1: Optimistic on Balance

java
@Version on Account.balance hot row — mass failures — use pessimistic

Mistake 2: FOR UPDATE Without Transaction

java
// @Lock on repository method without @Transactional — lock released immediately — race returns

Mistake 3: No Lock Ordering

text
Transfer opposite directions deadlock — always min/max account id order

Mistake 4: Retry Without Idempotency

java
@Retryable on payment create without client_request_id — duplicate payments

Mistake 5: SKIP LOCKED for Balance

text
Cannot skip — must serialize same account — wrong pattern

Mistake 6: Client Doesn't Send Version

text
PUT without If-Match — last writer wins despite @Version if merge wrong — always overwrite

Mistake 7: Long Pessimistic Hold

text
FOR UPDATE then external API — pool + lock exhaustion (L31–32)

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: Pessimistic vs optimistic locking?

Pessimistic locks row before update; optimistic detects conflict at commit via version.

Q2: JPA optimistic implementation?

@Version column — UPDATE includes version — 0 rows → OptimisticLockException.

Q3: SELECT FOR UPDATE purpose?

Exclusive row lock until commit — blocks concurrent writers on same row.

Q4: When optimistic appropriate?

Low contention updates — customer profile, config — with retry or 409 UX.

Q5: What is SKIP LOCKED?

Skip rows locked by others — parallel workers claim different queue rows.

Mid-Level

Q6: Transfer — pessimistic or optimistic?

Pessimistic FOR UPDATE with ordered account IDs — or atomic conditional UPDATE in one txn.

Q7: OptimisticLockException handling?

Retry max 3 with backoff for batch; 409 Conflict for user-facing admin UI.

Q8: Deadlock vs optimistic conflict?

Deadlock: circular lock wait — DB aborts one — retry. Optimistic: version mismatch — retry or fail.

Q9: lock_timeout vs NOWAIT?

Timeout: wait up to N ms. NOWAIT: fail immediately if lock unavailable.

Q10: Does optimistic eliminate need for transaction?

No — still need @Transactional for atomicity of multi-step update.

Senior

Q11: Hot account 1000 TPS — design?

Per-account queue partition; ledger append; pessimistic accept serial latency — not optimistic retry.

Q12: Redis lock + DB update anti-pattern?

Not same atomic unit — use DB row lock in transaction or Saga with idempotency.

Q13: ETag + @Version REST pattern?

GET returns ETag version; PUT If-Match — 412 on stale — explicit optimistic concurrency API.

Q14: Atomic UPDATE vs FOR UPDATE then UPDATE?

Atomic: shorter lock, single round trip if logic simple. FOR UPDATE: multi-step validation in txn.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Platform locking policy for 15 services?

Registry: money aggregates pessimistic; reference optimistic; queue SKIP LOCKED; retry/idempotency standards.

Q16: Metrics to switch optimistic → pessimistic?

Optimistic failure rate > 5%, p99 retry latency, CPU on retry storms — A/B evidence.

Scenario

Scenario: "Flash sale — 50% orders fail OptimisticLockException."

Switch SKU row to pessimistic FOR UPDATE or pre-reserve with SKIP LOCKED inventory chunks; not more retries.

Deadlocks

Part 1 — Concept

What Is a Deadlock?

A deadlock occurs when two or more transactions wait forever for each other’s locks — a circular wait. The database detects the cycle and aborts one transaction (the victim). The application must retry safely, usually with idempotency.

sql
-- Session A                          -- Session B
BEGIN;                                 BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100
  WHERE account_id = 5001;             UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50
                                       WHERE account_id = 5002;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 100
  WHERE account_id = 5002;  -- waits B  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 50
                                       WHERE account_id = 5001;  -- waits A

-- ~1s later (PostgreSQL deadlock_timeout):
-- ERROR: deadlock detected
-- DETAIL: Process 12345 waits for ShareLock on transaction 67890; blocked by process 54321...
-- One session ROLLBACK; other proceeds

Deadlock vs Lock Wait vs Timeout

text
┌─────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 │ DEADLOCK          │ LOCK WAIT        │ LOCK TIMEOUT       │
├─────────────────┼───────────────────┼──────────────────┼────────────────────┤
│ Cause           │ Circular wait     │ Another txn holds│ Wait exceeded limit│
│                 │ A→B→A             │ row (not circle) │ lock_timeout       │
│ DB action       │ Abort victim txn  │ Keep waiting     │ Abort waiter       │
│ Fix             │ Lock ordering     │ Shorten blocker  │ Fail fast / tune   │
│ Retry           │ Yes (idempotent)  │ Maybe            │ User retry         │
└─────────────────┴───────────────────┴──────────────────┴────────────────────┘

Four Conditions (Coffman)

text
Deadlock requires ALL four:

1. Mutual exclusion   → row lock held exclusively
2. Hold and wait      → txn holds lock while waiting for another
3. No preemption      → DB doesn't steal locks mid-txn
4. Circular wait      → A waits B waits A

Break any condition → prevent deadlock
Banking standard: break circular wait via LOCK ORDERING

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Deadlock Handling

text
1970s   Two-phase locking theory — deadlocks inevitable without ordering
        Wait-for graph analysis in transaction managers

1980s   Commercial DBs: deadlock detector daemon (Oracle, DB2)
        Victim selection: youngest transaction, least work

1990s   PostgreSQL deadlock_timeout (default 1s) — cycle check on lock wait
        Application retry becomes standard pattern

2000s   ORM multi-table updates increase deadlock surface
        "Always lock in primary key order" — DBA folklore codified

2010s   Microservices: deadlocks WITHIN service DB still common
        Cross-service "deadlock" is really distributed saga stuck state — different problem
        Spring @Retryable on DeadlockLoserDataAccessException

2020s   pg_stat_database.deadlocks monitoring
        Connection pool exhaustion mistaken for deadlock epidemic (Lesson 32)
        Skip locked queues eliminate worker-worker deadlocks on same table pattern

Historical Lesson

Deadlocks are normal in systems with multi-row pessimistic locking — not a bug if rare and retried idempotently. They become an incident when rate spikes (bad lock order, missing index causing row lock explosion, or batch job overlapping OLTP).

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Do Deadlocks Create?

Problem 1: Transfer A↔B Concurrent

text
Txn A: lock 5001 → wait 5002
Txn B: lock 5002 → wait 5001
Circle → one transfer fails with deadlock error
User sees intermittent 500 unless retry works

Problem 2: Multi-Table Update Order

text
Txn A: lock payments row → lock accounts row
Txn B: lock accounts row → lock payments row
Different code paths — same circular wait

Problem 3: Foreign Key Lock Ordering

text
Insert payment (locks parent customer) + update account
Another txn: update account + insert payment for same customer
FK checks acquire locks in different orders — subtle deadlocks

Problem 4: Batch + OLTP Overlap

text
Batch: UPDATE accounts ... WHERE branch_id = X (many row locks)
OLTP: transfer locks two accounts in branch — waits batch — batch waits OLTP
Extended waits — may form cycles with other sessions

Problem 5: Retry Without Idempotency

text
Deadlock victim rolls back — client retries POST /transfer
First txn actually committed after victim aborted? No — victim rolled back
But if first txn committed and client retries duplicate — double transfer
Idempotency key mandatory on retry (Lesson 24, 33)

Unified Problem Statement

Deadlocks abort in-progress work when transactions lock resources in incompatible orders — applications must prevent cycles where possible, detect via database errors, and retry with idempotent semantics.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Not Prevent All Blocking?

Blocking Is Required for Correctness

text
Without waiting on locks — lost updates return (Lesson 35)
Deadlock is the **price of fine-grained row locking** vs table-level locks
Table lock: no deadlock — no concurrency — unacceptable for OLTP

Detection vs Prevention Trade-off

text
Prevention (global lock order): zero deadlock — requires discipline everywhere
Detection: occasional deadlock — simpler code paths — retry
Industry: detection + ordering for hot paths

Victim Abort Preserves Liveness

text
Without detector: circular wait forever — hung transactions — pool exhaustion
Detector: kill one — other completes — system live

Not Same as Distributed Deadlock

text
Service A waits Service B HTTP; B waits A Kafka — no unified detector
Saga timeout + compensation — Lesson 33 architect patterns
This lesson: **single database** deadlock

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Deadlock Detection Works

Wait-For Graph

text
Nodes: transactions (or processes)
Edge T1 → T2: T1 waits for lock held by T2

Deadlock: cycle in graph
  T1 → T2 → T1

PostgreSQL:
  On lock wait, check periodically (deadlock_timeout default 1000ms)
  DFS for cycle — if found → cancel one transaction

Victim Selection (PostgreSQL Simplified)

text
Generally: transaction with **less work undone** / easier rollback
  Smaller number of changes
  Not always predictable — treat any participant as possible victim

ERROR:
  SQLSTATE 40P01 (deadlock_detected)
  Message: deadlock detected

What Gets Rolled Back

text
Victim: entire transaction ROLLBACK
  All locks released
  All changes in txn discarded
Winner: proceeds — acquires lock — completes

Spring @Transactional: DataAccessException — rollbackOnly already applied
Connection returned to pool — clean state on retry

Lock Types in Deadlock

text
Row-level ShareLock / ExclusiveLock on tuple
Transaction id waits (waiting for other txn to commit/rollback)
Multiple tables — any lock type in cycle counts

Index page locks rare in row-level engines — but possible with page splits

deadlock_timeout vs lock_timeout

sql
SHOW deadlock_timeout;  -- 1s — how often to check for cycle while waiting
SHOW lock_timeout;      -- 0 = wait forever until deadlock detected or commit
-- lock_timeout: max wait for ANY lock — abort waiter — not necessarily deadlock

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Deadlocks and Storage

Rollback of Victim Work

text
Victim's uncommitted heap changes:
  Dead tuples remain until vacuum — same as ROLLBACK (Lesson 33)
  WAL records abort — no durable commit

No permanent corruption — atomicity preserved
Performance: wasted work on victim — CPU + I/O thrown away

Index and FK Side Effects

text
Victim rolled back INSERT:
  Unique index entry removed from visibility
  FK locks on parent released

High deadlock rate → repeated rollback → write amplification without business progress

Long Transactions Expand Cycle Window

text
Batch holding 10K row locks:
  Larger wait-for graph — more cycle opportunities
  Shorter batch chunks reduce graph size (Lesson 28)

Monitoring Catalog

sql
-- PostgreSQL cumulative
SELECT deadlocks FROM pg_stat_database WHERE datname = current_database();

-- Reset stats carefully — use rate not single counter in prod

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Deadlock and Resource Impact

EffectImpact
Lock managerWait-for graph in memory — grows with waiting txns
Victim rollbackCPU — discard work
Retry storm2×–3× connections, queries, WAL if many concurrent deadlocks
PoolVictim releases conn; retry borrows again — brief spike
Application threadsBlocked until deadlock_timeout (~1s) before detection

Retry Amplification

text
100 concurrent opposing transfers:
  Without ordering: many deadlocks — each waits ~1s detection — p99 terrible
  With ordering: serial lock acquisition — fewer deadlocks — slightly more wait — predictable

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Deadlock Execution Flows

Flow 1: Classic AB-BA Account Deadlock

text
T0: Txn A locks account 5001
T1: Txn B locks account 5002
T2: Txn A requests lock 5002 — waits B
T3: Txn B requests lock 5001 — waits A
T4: deadlock_timeout elapses — detector finds cycle
T5: Victim B aborted — ERROR 40P01 to app
T6: Txn A acquires 5002 — completes COMMIT
T7: App B @Retryable — new txn — locks 5001 then 5002 ordered — succeeds

Flow 2: Fixed Lock Ordering Prevention

text
Both txns:
  first = min(5001, 5002); second = max(5001, 5002);
  lock first, then second

Txn A: lock 5001, lock 5002 — proceed
Txn B: lock 5001 (wait A), then lock 5002
Serial on first account — no cycle — no deadlock
Trade: contention on min(id) — still possible wait — not circular

Flow 3: Deadlock vs Lock Wait (Batch)

text
Txn OLTP: FOR UPDATE account 5001 — waits batch txn
Txn Batch: holds lock 5001, wants 5002 — OLTP holds 5002? 
If no cycle — OLTP waits until batch commits — slow but not deadlock
If cycle forms — victim chosen
Fix batch: smaller transactions — consistent order

Flow 4: Spring Retry Path

text
1. transfer() @Transactional @Retryable(DeadlockLoser...)
2. Deadlock on attempt 1 — rollback — exception
3. Spring Retry intercept — backoff 50ms
4. Attempt 2 — idempotency check client_request_id — new or duplicate
5. Success COMMIT — return 200
6. Metric: deadlock_retry_success_total++

Flow 5: FK-Induced Subtle Deadlock

text
Txn A: INSERT payment (locks customer PK share) → UPDATE account 5001
Txn B: UPDATE account 5001 → INSERT payment same customer
Cycle on customer + account locks
Fix: consistent order — always lock account before payment insert
Or defer FK: NOT VALID constraint rare — prefer order discipline

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Deadlock Prevention and Tuning

Prevention Hierarchy (Best → Fallback)

text
1. LOCK ORDERING — all code paths lock resources in global order (account_id ASC)
2. REDUCE LOCK SCOPE — shorter txn, fewer rows, no HTTP in txn
3. CONSISTENT ACCESS PATH — same indexes → same lock order
4. SKIP LOCKED — workers don't compete for same row lock
5. SINGLE ROW AGGREGATE — advisory lock per business key before multi-row work
6. RETRY with idempotency — accept rare deadlock
7. NEVER ignore — log and alert on rate spike

Lock Ordering Rules (Banking)

text
Multiple accounts:
  Sort account IDs ascending — lock in order

Account + customer:
  Document: lock account before customer OR always customer_id order first

Multiple payments:
  Lock by payment_id ASC if touching multiple

Same row:
  No ordering issue — single lock

When Retry Is Acceptable

text
Deadlock rate < 0.1% of txns: retry max 3 — OK
Rate > 1%: fix ordering or design — retry masks systemic bug
Alert threshold: deadlocks per minute > baseline × 3

Index Impact on Deadlock

text
UPDATE without index:
  Locks many rows (seq scan) — increases deadlock probability with other txns
Index precise row lock — smaller graph

Metrics Dashboard

text
pg_stat_database.deadlocks rate
Application: deadlock_exceptions / transfer_attempts
p99 transfer latency (deadlock wait ~1s before detect hurts tail)
lock_wait_time from pg_stat_activity
Correlation with batch job schedule

ScenarioDeadlock ProbabilityMitigation Cost

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Deadlock Masterclass

Ordered Transfer (Prevention)

java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class TransferService {

    private final AccountRepository accountRepo;
    private final TransferRepository transferRepo;

    @Transactional
    @Retryable(
        retryFor = DeadlockLoserDataAccessException.class,
        maxAttempts = 3,
        backoff = @Backoff(delay = 50, multiplier = 2, random = true)
    )
    public TransferResult transfer(TransferCommand cmd) {
        long firstId = Math.min(cmd.fromId(), cmd.toId());
        long secondId = Math.max(cmd.fromId(), cmd.toId());

        Account first = accountRepo.findByIdForUpdate(firstId).orElseThrow();
        Account second = (firstId == secondId) ? first
            : accountRepo.findByIdForUpdate(secondId).orElseThrow();

        Account from = cmd.fromId() == firstId ? first : second;
        Account to = cmd.fromId() == firstId ? second : first;

        if (from.getBalance().compareTo(cmd.amount()) < 0) {
            throw new InsufficientFundsException();
        }

        from.debit(cmd.amount());
        to.credit(cmd.amount());

        Transfer transfer = transferRepo.save(
            new Transfer(cmd.fromId(), cmd.toId(), cmd.amount(), cmd.clientRequestId()));

        return new TransferResult(transfer.getId());
    }
}

Idempotency Before Retry-Safe Logic

java
@Transactional
@Retryable(retryFor = DeadlockLoserDataAccessException.class, maxAttempts = 3)
public PaymentResult createPayment(CreatePaymentCommand cmd) {
    return paymentRepo.findByClientRequestId(cmd.clientRequestId())
        .map(p -> PaymentResult.alreadyExists(p.getId()))
        .orElseGet(() -> doCreatePayment(cmd));
}
// Victim rollback: nothing committed — retry runs full create — OK
// After success + client retry duplicate: UNIQUE path — OK

Explicit Lock Order Utility

java
public final class LockOrdering {

    public static <T> T withOrderedAccountLocks(
            long accountId1,
            long accountId2,
            AccountRepository repo,
            BiFunction<Account, Account, T> action) {

        long a = Math.min(accountId1, accountId2);
        long b = Math.max(accountId1, accountId2);

        Account accA = repo.findByIdForUpdate(a).orElseThrow();
        Account accB = (a == b) ? accA : repo.findByIdForUpdate(b).orElseThrow();

        Account firstArg = (accountId1 <= accountId2) ? accA : accB;
        Account secondArg = (accountId1 <= accountId2) ? accB : accA;

        return action.apply(firstArg, secondArg);
    }
}

PostgreSQL — Inspect Deadlock (Log)

sql
-- postgresql.conf
-- deadlock_timeout = 1s
-- log_lock_waits = on
-- log_line_prefix with session id

-- Live blocked queries
SELECT
    blocked.pid AS blocked_pid,
    blocking.pid AS blocking_pid,
    blocked.wait_event_type,
    now() - blocked.query_start AS blocked_for,
    LEFT(blocked.query, 100) AS blocked_query,
    LEFT(blocking.query, 100) AS blocking_query
FROM pg_stat_activity blocked
JOIN pg_locks bl ON bl.pid = blocked.pid AND NOT bl.granted
JOIN pg_locks bk ON bk.locktype = bl.locktype
    AND bk.database IS NOT DISTINCT FROM bl.database
    AND bk.relation IS NOT DISTINCT FROM bl.relation
    AND bk.page IS NOT DISTINCT FROM bl.page
    AND bk.tuple IS NOT DISTINCT FROM bl.tuple
    AND bk.virtualxid IS NOT DISTINCT FROM bl.virtualxid
    AND bk.transactionid IS NOT DISTINCT FROM bl.transactionid
    AND bk.classid IS NOT DISTINCT FROM bl.classid
    AND bk.objid IS NOT DISTINCT FROM bl.objid
    AND bk.objsubid IS NOT DISTINCT FROM bl.objsubid
    AND bk.pid != bl.pid
JOIN pg_stat_activity blocking ON blocking.pid = bk.pid
WHERE NOT bl.granted;

Part 12 — Production Usage

Deadlocks in Banking Production

Expected Baseline

text
Well-ordered transfer API:
  Deadlocks < 0.05% of transfer attempts — retry transparent
  Alert if > 10 deadlocks/minute on payment service

Log sample on 40P01:
  from_account, to_account, duration, attempt number
  Never log full PAN/PII

Runbook: Deadlock Spike

text
1. Check pg_stat_database deadlocks delta (last 15 min)
2. Correlate with deploy, batch job cron, marketing event traffic
3. pg_stat_activity blocked chains — identify blocking application_name
4. Compare new code paths — new lock order inversion?
5. EXPLAIN batch UPDATE — row lock count explosion?
6. Mitigate: pause batch, kill idle in transaction, hotfix lock order
7. Post-mortem: add integration test for lock ordering contract

Batch Job Guidelines

text
Chunk UPDATE accounts WHERE ... LIMIT 5000 COMMIT
Same lock order within chunk as OLTP (account_id ASC)
Schedule off peak — not 09:00 transfer peak
Consider SKIP LOCKED for non-critical background claims only

Load Test Acceptance

text
JMeter: 50% transfers A→B, 50% B→A concurrent
Without ordering: deadlock rate high — fail test
With ordering: zero deadlocks — p99 stable
Document as regression gate in CI nightly

@Configuration
@EnableRetry
public class RetryConfig {}

@Service
public class PaymentService {

    @Retryable(
        retryFor = {
            DeadlockLoserDataAccessException.class,

        },

Manual Retry with Idempotency

java
public TransferResult transferWithManualRetry(TransferCommand cmd) {
    int attempts = 0;
    while (true) {
        try {
            return transferService.transfer(cmd);
        } catch (DeadlockLoserDataAccessException e) {
            if (++attempts >= 3) throw e;
            sleep(jitter(50, attempts));
        }
    }
}

Observability

java
@Aspect
@Component
public class DeadlockMetricsAspect {

    @AfterThrowing(
        pointcut = "@annotation(org.springframework.retry.annotation.Retryable)",
        throwing = "ex")
    public void recordDeadlock(Exception ex) {
        if (ex instanceof DeadlockLoserDataAccessException) {
            meterRegistry.counter("db.deadlock", "service", "payment").increment();
        }
    }
}

Don't Retry at Controller for Non-Idempotent POST

text
Only retry inside service with idempotency key
Blind HTTP client retry on 500 without key — duplicate risk if first txn actually committed after timeout confusion
Return 503 with Retry-After only if idempotent GET — not blind POST retry

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

ORM Deadlock Surfaces

Flush Order and Lock Order

text
Hibernate flush order: inserts → updates → deletes (simplified)
Entity save order in code may differ from account lock order
Explicit findByIdForUpdate BEFORE mutate — don't rely on flush order for locks

Cascade Operations

java
@OneToMany(cascade = CascadeType.ALL)
// Saving parent may lock/update children in undefined order — deadlock risk
// Financial aggregates: avoid deep cascade writes — explicit ordered locks

Pessimistic Lock Scope

java
@Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
@Query("SELECT a FROM Account a WHERE a.customerId = :cid")
List<Account> lockAllCustomerAccounts(@Param("cid") Long cid);
// Locks multiple rows — ensure query ORDER BY accountId ASC
@Query("... WHERE a.customerId = :cid ORDER BY a.accountId ASC")

Optimistic vs Deadlock

text
OptimisticLockException ≠ deadlock — different retry policy
Don't merge retry handlers blindly — idempotency rules differ

Session Clear on Retry

java
@Recover
public TransferResult recover(DeadlockLoserDataAccessException e, TransferCommand cmd) {
    throw new ServiceUnavailableException("Transfer failed after retries", e);
}
// New retry attempt starts new @Transactional — new persistence context — OK
// Same txn retry after catch without rethrow — broken — let @Retryable open new txn

Deadlock Architecture

Platform Standards Document

text
MANDATORY:

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is a deadlock?

Two transactions wait for each other's locks in a cycle — neither can proceed.

Q2: What does database do on deadlock?

Detects cycle, aborts one transaction (victim), rolls it back.

Q3: PostgreSQL deadlock SQLSTATE?

40P01 deadlock_detected.

Q4: How prevent transfer deadlock?

Lock accounts in consistent order — e.g. ascending account_id.

Q5: Should you retry deadlock?

Yes — with limit and idempotency — victim txn did not commit.

Mid-Level

Q6: Deadlock vs lock wait?

Deadlock is circular — detector aborts. Lock wait is one-way — wait until release or timeout.

Q7: deadlock_timeout purpose?

How long to wait before checking wait-for graph for cycle while blocked.

Q8: Why idempotency with deadlock retry?

Client may also retry; ensures at-most-once business effect if commit succeeded on ambiguous timeout.

Q9: Spring exception for PostgreSQL deadlock?

DeadlockLoserDataAccessException — use @Retryable.

Q10: SKIP LOCKED and deadlocks?

Workers skip locked rows — avoids waiting — reduces worker deadlock on same queue row.

Senior

Q11: Three-account transfer lock strategy?

Sort all three account IDs ascending — lock in order — or advisory lock on business key first.

Q12: FK-related deadlock example?

Insert child locks parent; concurrent path locks parent then child — fix with consistent lock order.

Q13: Acceptable deadlock rate?

Near zero with ordering; <0.1% with retry OK — spike needs investigation.

Q14: Victim selection predictable?

No — always code for either txn being victim — idempotent retry both sides.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Platform policy for financial POST retry?

Idempotency key mandatory; 40P01/40001 max 3 jitter; lock order standard; metrics/alerts.

Q16: Deadlock spike after deploy — triage steps?

Metrics, blocked queries, batch overlap, new code lock paths, EXPLAIN row locks, rollback batch or hotfix order.

Scenario

Scenario: "Intermittent transfer failures 09:00 daily, message deadlock detected."

Correlate EOD interest batch; check batch lock order vs transfer; chunk batch; order account_id ASC in both; verify retry idempotency; reduce batch window overlap.

Short transactions
Same index access path
Batch jobs chunked + ordered
SKIP LOCKED for queues only

Don't infinite retry

Transactional Outbox Pattern

Phase 4: TRANSACTIONS, CONCURRENCY & RELIABILITY | Previous: Deadlocks | Next: Saga Pattern

Transactions
1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why This Exists5Internal Working6Storage Internals7Memory Usage8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Complexity Analysis11Code / SQL Examples12Production Usage13Spring Boot Integration14Hibernate/JPA Integration15Architect Perspective16Decision Matrix17Comparison Tables18Common Mistakes19Interview Questions20Revision Sheet21Summary Table*Practice

Part 1 — Concept

What Is the Transactional Outbox Pattern?

The transactional outbox ensures business data and an event/message intent are persisted in the same database transaction. A separate relay process reads the outbox and publishes to Kafka, a queue, or another service — avoiding dual-write inconsistency (DB committed, message never sent).

java
@Transactional
public PaymentResult createPayment(CreatePaymentCommand cmd) {
    Payment payment = paymentRepo.save(new Payment(cmd));

    outboxRepo.save(new OutboxEvent(
        UUID.randomUUID(),
        "PaymentCreated",
        payment.getPaymentId().toString(),
        toJson(new PaymentCreatedEvent(payment)),
        Instant.now(),
        OutboxStatus.PENDING
    ));

    return PaymentResult.created(payment.getId());
    // Single COMMIT — payment row + outbox row together (atomicity)
}
// Separate relay: read PENDING outbox → publish Kafka → mark PUBLISHED

Dual-Write Problem (Why Outbox Exists)

text
❌ WRONG ORDER — both can fail independently:

  1. COMMIT payment to DB
  2. kafka.send(PaymentCreated)  ← crash here → DB has payment, no event

  OR:

  1. kafka.send(...)
  2. COMMIT payment  ← crash here → event sent, no payment (worse)

✅ OUTBOX — one atomic write:

  1. INSERT payment + INSERT outbox (same txn)
  2. COMMIT
  3. Relay publishes later (at-least-once) + idempotent consumers

Pattern Components

text
TRANSACTIONAL OUTBOX

├── Business table(s)     → payments, orders, accounts
├── Outbox table            → event payload, status, metadata
├── Same @Transactional    → atomic INSERT/UPDATE both
├── Relay / Publisher       → poll, CDC, or Debezium
├── Message broker          → Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ
└── Consumer                → idempotent processing + dedup

ASCII — Flow

text
┌──────────────┐     one txn      ┌─────────────────────────┐
│ Payment      │ ───────────────► │ payments + outbox rows  │
│ Service      │     COMMIT       │ (same PostgreSQL DB)    │
└──────────────┘                  └───────────┬─────────────┘
                                              │
                              relay (poll/CDC)│
                                              ▼
                                  ┌───────────────────────┐
                                  │ Kafka: payment.created│
                                  └───────────┬───────────┘
                                              │
                                              ▼
                                  ┌───────────────────────┐
                                  │ Notification Service  │
                                  │ Ledger / Analytics    │
                                  └───────────────────────┘

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Reliable Event Publishing

text
2000s   Enterprise integration: XA/2PC across DB + JMS — fragile, slow
        "Write DB then send message" — operational default — inconsistent on failure

2010s   Microservices anti-pattern recognized: dual write without distributed txn
        Transactional outbox described (Chris Richardson, microservices.io)
        Polling publisher: simple SELECT FROM outbox WHERE status=PENDING

2015+   Debezium CDC: read PostgreSQL WAL → Kafka — lower latency than poll
        Kafka transactions / idempotent producer — broker-side dedup aids
        Eventuate Tram, Axon — framework outbox in Java ecosystem

2018+   AWS DMS, RDS logical replication — managed CDC paths
        "Exactly-once" marketing — architect reality: at-least-once + idempotent

2020s   Standard pattern in payment/order microservices
        Outbox + Saga choreography replaces cross-DB 2PC
        Spring lack of native outbox — custom, Debezium, or libraries (Transactional Outbox libs)

Historical Lesson

There is no magic exactly-once end-to-end across DB + Kafka + consumer without cooperation. Outbox gives atomic intent in the DB; relay and consumers provide at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing — the industry-standard "exactly-once-ish" compromise.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does the Outbox Solve?

Problem 1: Payment Created but Notification Never Sent

text
DB COMMIT success → JVM crash before kafka.send
Customer charged — no email — support ticket
Outbox: relay eventually publishes PENDING row

Problem 2: Event Sent but DB Rolled Back

text
kafka.send succeeds → DB constraint violation → ROLLBACK
Downstream acts on ghost payment event
Outbox: event row only commits with business row

Problem 3: Cross-Service Consistency Without 2PC

text
Payment DB + Order DB — cannot one ACID txn
Payment commits + outbox PaymentCompleted → Order service consumes — eventual consistency
Saga compensations if downstream fails

Problem 4: Retry After Deadlock (Lesson 36)

text
@Transactional retry creates payment + outbox again
Idempotency on payment + outbox dedup by business key or unique event id

Problem 5: Ordering Events per Aggregate

text
PaymentCreated must publish before PaymentSettled
Outbox relay ORDER BY created_at, id per aggregate_key
Kafka partition key = payment_id — per-payment order

Unified Problem Statement

The transactional outbox atomically records message intent alongside business state changes, enabling reliable asynchronous integration without distributed two-phase commit.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Not Kafka Transactions Alone?

Kafka Transactional Producer Limits

text
kafka transaction spans produce + consume offset — not your PostgreSQL COMMIT
Cannot atomically commit Postgres payment INSERT and Kafka message in one true ACIT txn without external protocol (XA — avoided)
Outbox: DB is source of truth for "what must be published"

Why Not Change Data Capture Only?

text
CDC on payments table publishes every column change — noisy
Outbox: explicit event schema, event type, routing metadata
Can still use CDC **on outbox table** — best of both

Why Not Inbox on Consumer Only

text
Inbox dedupes consumer side — doesn't fix producer never sending
Outbox fixes producer side — inbox complements consumer idempotency

ACID Locality (Lesson 33)

text
Atomicity: payment + outbox — all or nothing
Durability: after COMMIT, relay can crash and retry — outbox row durable
Isolation: concurrent payments don't corrupt outbox — normal row locks
Consistency: business constraints + outbox NOT NULL on payment_id

Part 5 — Internal Working

Outbox Internal Mechanics

Write Phase (Application)

text
1. BEGIN transaction
2. INSERT INTO payments (...)
3. INSERT INTO outbox (event_type, aggregate_id, payload, status='PENDING')
4. COMMIT — WAL fsync — both rows durable
5. Return HTTP 201 to client (payment exists — event may publish milliseconds later)

Relay Phase — Polling

text
Loop every N ms (or scheduled job):
  BEGIN;
  SELECT * FROM outbox
  WHERE status = 'PENDING'
  ORDER BY created_at
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  LIMIT 100;

  For each row:
    kafka.send(topic, key=aggregate_id, value=payload)
    UPDATE outbox SET status='PUBLISHED', published_at=NOW()
  COMMIT;
text
SKIP LOCKED: multiple relay workers without duplicate publish attempt same row
Still at-least-once if crash after send before mark PUBLISHED — consumer idempotent

Relay Phase — CDC (Debezium)

text
PostgreSQL logical replication / pgoutput
Debezium connector reads WAL INSERT on outbox table
Publishes to Kafka topic outbox.events
Optional: separate process marks PUBLISHED or rely on compacted topic + consumer offset
Lower latency than poll — no SELECT load on DB for relay

Delivery Semantics

text
Producer to Kafka: at-least-once (retries)
Outbox mark PUBLISHED: at-least-once (retry relay)
Consumer: at-least-once (offset commit after process)

End-to-end: at-least-once
Effective business: exactly-once if consumer dedupes by event_id

Ordering

text
Relay ORDER BY created_at, outbox_id
Kafka key = payment_id → same partition → order per payment preserved
Global order across payments — not guaranteed — usually not required

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Outbox Table Storage

Schema Design

sql
CREATE TABLE outbox_events (
    outbox_id       BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    event_id        UUID NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    aggregate_type  VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    aggregate_id    VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    event_type      VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    payload         JSONB NOT NULL,
    status          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING',
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    published_at    TIMESTAMPTZ,
    retry_count     INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    last_error      TEXT
);

CREATE INDEX idx_outbox_pending_created
ON outbox_events (created_at)
WHERE status = 'PENDING';

-- Partition by month if volume huge (Lesson 30)

Growth and Retention

text
Every payment → 1+ outbox rows — high volume
PUBLISHED rows accumulate — archive or DELETE WHERE published_at < NOW()-7d
Partition DETACH old months — compliance may require event audit retention in warehouse first

WAL Impact

text
Same COMMIT WAL as business row — minimal extra — one INSERT
CDC reads WAL — replication slot retains WAL until consumed — monitor disk (pg_replication_slots)

Payload Size

text
Large JSON payloads bloat table and Kafka — store reference (S3 key) for big blobs
Payload: essential fields only — version, event_type, ids, amounts

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Outbox Memory and Load

ComponentImpact
Application INSERTOne row — negligible
Polling relayBatch 100 rows — memory in relay JVM
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKEDShort lock per batch
CDC DebeziumKafka Connect JVM — WAL buffer — separate from app pool
Pending backlogLarge PENDING count — relay lag — not app heap — monitor lag metric

Connection Pool (Lesson 32)

text
Relay uses separate small pool — don't share payment API pool
Payment API: 20 connections — relay: 2–5 connections
CDC: no app polling connections — replication connection on DB

Backpressure

text
Kafka down → PENDING grows → table bloat → index scan slower
Alert: outbox_pending_count > 10000 or oldest_pending_age > 60s
Circuit: pause payment? No — business commits — async catch-up — unless regulatory real-time requirement

Part 8 — Execution Flow

End-to-End Execution Flows

Flow 1: Happy Path — Poll Relay

text
1. POST /payments → @Transactional → payment + outbox PENDING → COMMIT
2. Relay (500ms later): SKIP LOCKED batch → publish Kafka → mark PUBLISHED → COMMIT
3. Notification consumer: consume event_id → send email → commit offset
4. Total user-visible: payment instant, email +2s

Flow 2: Crash After COMMIT, Before Relay

text
1. Payment + outbox committed
2. Relay JVM crash
3. Restart relay → poll PENDING → publish — eventual delivery — durability OK

Flow 3: Crash After Kafka Send, Before PUBLISHED Mark

text
1. Relay sends to Kafka — success
2. Crash before UPDATE outbox PUBLISHED
3. Relay retries same row (still PENDING) → duplicate Kafka message
4. Consumer: INSERT processed_events(event_id) UNIQUE — skip duplicate — OK

Flow 4: Deadlock on Payment Txn (Lesson 36)

text
1. Transfer + outbox in same txn — deadlock victim — rollback — no payment, no outbox
2. Retry with idempotency — success — one outbox row — OK

Flow 5: Debezium CDC Path

text
1. COMMIT outbox INSERT → WAL record
2. Debezium reads WAL → produces to kafka.outbox topic
3. Optional stream processor: route by event_type to payment.created topic
4. Mark PUBLISHED via separate consumer or tombstone/compaction strategy

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Outbox Performance

Polling vs CDC

PollingCDC (Debezium)
Latencypoll interval (500ms–5s)sub-second
DB loadSELECT on outboxreplication slot WAL
Complexitylowmedium (Kafka Connect)
Opscron/workerconnector monitoring
Multi-DBsame codeconnector per DB

Throughput Tuning

text
Batch size 50–500 SKIP LOCKED
Multiple relay instances — SKIP LOCKED scales horizontally
Kafka idempotent producer + acks=all — durability vs latency
Partition outbox table by month — keep PENDING index small
Async publish parallel within batch — careful ordering per aggregate_id

Anti-Patterns

text
❌ kafka.send inside @Transactional before COMMIT — not outbox — dual-write risk if txn rolls back after send
❌ DELETE outbox before Kafka ack — lose message
❌ No consumer dedup — duplicate charges on relay retry
❌ Poll without SKIP LOCKED — relay workers deadlock or duplicate work
❌ Giant payload — slow relay — Kafka message limit 1MB default

SLAs

text
Payment API: sync 200ms — outbox COMMIT included
Event delivery: async p99 < 5s — relay lag metric
Regulatory real-time reporting: may need CDC not 5s poll

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

OperationTimeNotes
Outbox INSERT in txnO(1) + payment INSERTSame COMMIT cost
Poll batch k rowsO(k log n) index scanPENDING partial index
Publish k eventsO(k × Kafka latency)network bound
Consumer dedupO(1) UNIQUE insertper event_id
CDC lagO(WAL volume)replication catch-up

Consistency model: strong local ACID + eventual cross-service — O(relay_lag) delay.

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Transactional Outbox Masterclass

Outbox Entity + Payment (Spring/JPA)

java
@Entity
@Table(name = "outbox_events")
public class OutboxEvent {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long outboxId;

    @Column(nullable = false, unique = true)
    private UUID eventId;

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String aggregateType;

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String aggregateId;

    @Column(nullable = false)
    private String eventType;

    @Column(nullable = false, columnDefinition = "jsonb")
    private String payload;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    private OutboxStatus status = OutboxStatus.PENDING;

    private Instant createdAt = Instant.now();
    private Instant publishedAt;
}

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PaymentService {

    private final PaymentRepository paymentRepo;
    private final OutboxEventRepository outboxRepo;
    private final ObjectMapper objectMapper;

    @Transactional
    public PaymentResult createPayment(CreatePaymentCommand cmd) {
        paymentRepo.findByClientRequestId(cmd.clientRequestId())
            .ifPresent(p -> { throw new DuplicatePaymentException(p.getId()); });

        Payment payment = paymentRepo.save(Payment.from(cmd));

        OutboxEvent event = new OutboxEvent();
        event.setEventId(UUID.randomUUID());
        event.setAggregateType("Payment");
        event.setAggregateId(payment.getId().toString());
        event.setEventType("PaymentCreated");
        event.setPayload(writeJson(new PaymentCreatedEvent(
            payment.getId(), payment.getCustomerId(), payment.getAmount(), cmd.clientRequestId())));

        outboxRepo.save(event);

        return PaymentResult.created(payment.getId());
    }
}

Polling Relay

java
@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class OutboxRelay {

    private final JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate;
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafkaTemplate;

    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 500)
    @Transactional
    public void publishPending() {
        List<OutboxRow> batch = jdbcTemplate.query("""
            SELECT outbox_id, event_id, aggregate_id, event_type, payload
            FROM outbox_events
            WHERE status = 'PENDING'
            ORDER BY created_at, outbox_id
            FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
            LIMIT 100
            """, outboxRowMapper);

        for (OutboxRow row : batch) {
            try {
                kafkaTemplate.send(
                    topicFor(row.eventType()),
                    row.aggregateId(),
                    envelope(row)
                ).get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

                jdbcTemplate.update("""
                    UPDATE outbox_events
                    SET status = 'PUBLISHED', published_at = NOW()
                    WHERE outbox_id = ?
                    """, row.outboxId());
            } catch (Exception e) {
                jdbcTemplate.update("""
                    UPDATE outbox_events
                    SET retry_count = retry_count + 1, last_error = ?
                    WHERE outbox_id = ?
                    """, e.getMessage(), row.outboxId());
            }
        }
    }
}

Idempotent Consumer

java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PaymentCreatedHandler {

    private final ProcessedEventRepository processedRepo;
    private final NotificationService notificationService;

    @Transactional
    public void handle(PaymentCreatedEvent event) {
        if (processedRepo.existsByEventId(event.eventId())) {
            return;  // duplicate from at-least-once relay
        }

        notificationService.sendPaymentConfirmation(event.customerId(), event.paymentId());
        processedRepo.save(new ProcessedEvent(event.eventId(), Instant.now()));
    }
}

@Entity
@Table(name = "processed_events")
public class ProcessedEvent {
    @Id
    private UUID eventId;
    private Instant processedAt;
}

Part 12 — Production Usage

Outbox in Banking / Payments Production

Standard Architecture

text
Payment Service (PostgreSQL):
  payments + outbox_events — same Flyway migration
  Relay: Debezium → Kafka topic payment.events
  Consumers: Notification, Ledger projection, Fraud analytics (read models)

Never: kafka.send in PaymentService @Transactional without outbox row
Idempotency: client_request_id on payment + event_id on consumer
Monitoring: outbox_pending_age_seconds, relay_errors, consumer_lag

Event Catalog

text
PaymentCreated   → partition key payment_id
PaymentSettled   → same key — order preserved per payment
PaymentFailed    → compensation triggers in Saga
Schema: CloudEvents or internal JSON version field "schemaVersion": 2

Failure Runbook

text
1. Kafka cluster down → PENDING grows → alert → fix Kafka → relay catches up
2. Poison message → retry_count > 10 → move to outbox_dead_letter status manual review
3. WAL disk full (CDC slot lag) → increase disk or fix connector → pg_replication_slots
4. Duplicate consumer processing → verify processed_events UNIQUE

Compliance / Audit

text
Outbox row is intent audit trail until archived to warehouse
Do not DELETE PENDING — fix relay
PUBLISHED rows retained 90 days then partition drop after S3 archive

JPA Outbox Considerations

Same Persistence Context

@Transactional

Flush Order

text

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

Outbox Architecture Decisions

Outbox vs Saga vs 2PC

PatternUse
OutboxReliable publish after local commit
SagaMulti-service workflow + compensations
2PC/XAAvoid in microservices
Outbox + SagaLocal outbox per step — choreography via Kafka

Per-Service Outbox

text
Each microservice owns:
  Its business tables
  Its outbox table
  Its relay (or shared Debezium connector per DB)
Never share outbox table across services — boundary violation

Exactly-Once-ISH Recipe

text
1. Local txn: business + outbox (atomicity)
2. Relay: at-least-once publish (SKIP LOCKED + retry)
3. Kafka: idempotent producer (reduce broker dupes)
4. Consumer: processed_events(event_id) UNIQUE (dedup)
5. Business idempotency: client_request_id on side effects
= Effective exactly-once business outcome

When Skip Outbox

text
Truly fire-and-forget metrics — loss OK
Read replica cache invalidation — loss OK — not payments
Synchronous REST where caller polls until done — no event needed

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: kafka.send Inside @Transactional

java
@Transactional
void pay() {
    paymentRepo.save(p);
    kafkaTemplate.send(...);  // if txn rolls back, message may exist — ghost event
}

Mistake 2: No Consumer Dedup

text
Relay retry → duplicate PaymentCreated → double email charge — processed_events missing

Mistake 3: Mark PUBLISHED Before Kafka Ack

text
Update status then send — crash — lost event — always send then mark (accept dup) or use Kafka txn outbox mark in same external store carefully
Standard: send → ack → mark PUBLISHED

Mistake 4: Shared API Pool with Heavy Relay

text
Relay starves payment API connections — separate deployment + pool

Mistake 5: No Pending Index

text
Seq scan on 100M outbox rows — relay slow — partial index WHERE status='PENDING'

Mistake 6: CDC Slot Lag Unmonitored

text
WAL disk fills — DB read-only — production halt

Mistake 7: Outbox Without Version in Payload

text
Consumer breaks on schema change — include schemaVersion in JSON

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is transactional outbox?

Insert event into outbox table in same DB transaction as business data; separate process publishes to Kafka.

Q2: What dual-write problem does it solve?

DB committed but message not sent (or vice versa) when write and publish are separate.

Q3: Is delivery exactly-once?

Not end-to-end by default — at-least-once relay + idempotent consumer ≈ exactly-once effect.

Q4: Why not send Kafka in @Transactional?

Transaction may roll back after send — inconsistent; outbox ties commit together.

Q5: What is relay?

Process that reads PENDING outbox rows and publishes to message broker.

Mid-Level

Q6: Polling vs CDC for outbox?

Poll: SELECT SKIP LOCKED on schedule — simple. CDC: Debezium reads WAL — lower latency, more ops.

Q7: Why FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on relay?

Multiple relay workers without blocking; each claims different rows.

Q8: Crash after Kafka send before PUBLISHED?

Duplicate message on retry — consumer dedup by event_id.

Q9: Kafka partition key for payments?

payment_id — preserve order of events per payment.

Q10: Outbox vs AFTER_COMMIT listener?

Outbox durable in DB; AFTER_COMMIT send can fail with no record to retry.

Senior

Q11: Design outbox schema fields?

event_id UUID, aggregate_id, event_type, payload JSON, status, created_at, published_at, retry_count.

Q12: Outbox + Saga together?

Each service local outbox publishes step events; choreography; compensating events on failure.

Q13: Retention strategy for PUBLISHED rows?

Archive to warehouse; partition drop; keep PENDING forever until published.

Q14: pg_replication_slots risk?

CDC lag prevents WAL recycle — disk full — monitor lag_bytes.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Exactly-once-ish recipe across payment platform?

Local atomic outbox + idempotent producer + consumer processed_events + business idempotency keys.

Q16: Separate relay deployment rationale?

Isolate Kafka slowness from API pool; scale relay independently; blast radius.

Scenario

Scenario: "Payments succeed but downstream ledger hours behind."

Check outbox_pending count, relay errors, Kafka lag, Debezium connector status; not payment API — outbox backlog triage runbook.

Pattern

text
Same @Transactional:

  COMMIT → both durable

Relay:
  Poll: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED

Consumer:
  processed_events(event_id) UNIQUE dedup

Semantics

text
Local write:     ACID atomic
Relay:           at-least-once
Consumer:        idempotent
Business effect: exactly-once-ish

Avoid

No consumer dedup
PUBLISHED before Kafka ack
Unmonitored CDC slot lag
No partial index on PENDING
