Backup & Recovery

Phase 5: DATABASE DESIGN & AVAILABILITY | Previous: Replication & High Availability | Next: Disaster Recovery

Availability
1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why This Exists5Internal Working6Storage Internals7Memory Usage8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Complexity Analysis11Code / SQL Examples12Production Usage13Spring Boot Integration14Hibernate/JPA Integration15Architect Perspective16Decision Matrix17Comparison Tables18Common Mistakes19Interview Questions20Revision Sheet21Summary Table*Practice

Part 1 — Concept

What Is Backup & Recovery?

Backup is a durable copy of database data (and often transaction logs) stored outside the live system — on object storage, tape, or another region — so you can restore after failure, corruption, or human error.

Recovery is the process of rebuilding a database to a usable state from backups — optionally to an exact point in time.

text
LIVE DATABASE                         BACKUP STORE (immutable, off-site)
┌─────────────────────┐               ┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ accounts            │  ── backup ─► │ full_2026-07-01.tar         │
│ payments            │  ── archive ─►│ wal_000001 ... wal_000099   │
│ transactions        │               │ rman_backup_piece_abc       │
└─────────────────────┘               └─────────────────────────────┘
         │                                         │
         │ crash / DELETE mistake / ransomware     │
         └──────────── restore / PITR ◄────────────┘

Backup Types (Conceptual)

TypeWhat it capturesRestore speedStorage
FullEntire database at a momentBaseline — slower to createLargest per snapshot
IncrementalChanges since last backupFaster backups; restore chainsSmaller
DifferentialChanges since last fullMiddle groundMedium
LogicalSQL or rows (pg_dump)Portable, slow restoreFlexible
PhysicalData files + WAL/redoFast restore at scaleEngine-specific

Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)

PITR restores a base backup then replays archived WAL/redo until a target timestamp or LSN — recovering to one second before an accidental DELETE.

text
Timeline:
  ────●────────●────────●────────●────────●────► time
      Full      WAL      WAL      OOPS!    target
      backup    arch     arch     DELETE   (PITR stop)

Backup vs Replication (Lesson 40)

text
REPLICATION                    BACKUP
───────────                    ──────
Near-real-time mirror          Point-in-time snapshots
Survives node/AZ failure       Survives corruption, DELETE, ransomware
Bad change replicates too      Independent copy — can restore yesterday
Not a substitute for backup    Not a substitute for HA failover

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Database Backup

text
1970s   Tape backups of flat files — offline batch windows
        Banking: end-of-day close → backup → reopen next day

1980s   Oracle hot backup — tablespaces while database open
        Archive log mode — continuous redo for recovery

1990s   RMAN (Recovery Manager) — Oracle standard physical backup
        SQL Server BACKUP DATABASE + transaction log backups
        PostgreSQL pg_dump logical backups

2000s   WAL archiving to NFS/S3 — PostgreSQL PITR matures
        Incremental forever strategies in enterprise backup tools
        EMC NetBackup, Veritas — integrated with RMAN

2010s   Cloud managed backups:
        AWS RDS automated snapshots + PITR window
        Aurora continuous backup to S3
        pgBackRest, Barman — PostgreSQL physical backup standard

2015+   Immutable backups — WORM, Object Lock — ransomware defense
        Banking regulators: restore testing, retention, encryption
        Dev/test clones from snapshots — masked data

2020s   Zero-trust backup access — separate account, air-gapped copy
        Application-level export insufficient for Tier 0 ledger
        Kubernetes Velero for cluster; DB still needs native backup

Historical Lesson

Replication gave us uptime; backups gave us time travel. A bank that only replicated still cannot undo DELETE FROM payments WHERE created_at > '2020-01-01' — only PITR from independent backup can.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Do Backups Solve?

Problem 1: Human Error

text
Analyst runs UPDATE accounts SET balance = 0 without WHERE
Replication copies zero balances to all replicas instantly
Need: restore to 5 minutes before mistake

Problem 2: Application Bug

text
Payment service double-credits accounts for 6 hours
Bug deployed Friday — discovered Monday
Need: PITR to Thursday 23:59 + replay good changes or selective fix

Problem 3: Corruption / Storage Failure

text
Silent disk corruption on primary data files
Replica may have same corruption if replicated after bad page write
Need: clean physical backup from before corruption detected

Problem 4: Ransomware / Malicious Insider

text
Attacker encrypts database volume or drops schemas
Replication propagates destruction
Need: immutable off-site backup in separate AWS account

Problem 5: Compliance & Audit Retention

text
Regulator: retain payment records 7 years — provable recoverability
Need: encrypted backups, retention policy, tested restore evidence

Problem 6: Disaster Recovery (Preview Lesson 42)

text
Entire region lost — replication in same region insufficient
Need: cross-region backup copies + DR runbook

Unified Problem Statement

Backups provide independent, restorable history of data — enabling recovery from logical errors and catastrophes that replication amplifies rather than fixes.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Backups Exist

Durability Beyond Single Instance (Lesson 33 — D)

text
WAL fsync protects crash on one machine
Backup protects fire, ransomware, operator error, multi-node logical failure

Time Travel

text
Business needs "state as of end of quarter close"
PITR or snapshot restore to exact timestamp

Clone Environments

text
Restore masked backup to staging for performance testing
Spring Boot integration tests against realistic volume

Regulatory Proof

text
SOX, PCI, RBI-style audits ask: "Show you can restore"
Documented restore drills — not just backup job success emails

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Backups Work Internally

Physical Backup (PostgreSQL pgBackRest / base backup)

text
1. CHECKPOINT — consistent starting point
2. Copy data directory files (or use filesystem snapshot)
3. Copy WAL generated during backup (backup_label file tracks start LSN)
4. Result: base backup + WAL chain for PITR

Restore:
  Stop postgres → restore data files → configure recovery
  → replay WAL from archive until recovery_target_time

Logical Backup (pg_dump)

text
1. Read catalog + table data via SQL protocol
2. Emit CREATE TABLE + COPY or INSERT statements
3. No WAL replay — restore = psql/pg_restore runs DDL+DML
4. Slow for TB scale; good for schema migration, subset export

Oracle RMAN

text
Full backup: backup database — copies data blocks (incrementally with change tracking)
Archive log backup: backup archivelog all delete input
Incremental level 0 = full; level 1 = changed blocks since level 0/1

Restore:
  STARTUP NOMOUNT → restore controlfile → restore database → recover database
  RECOVER UNTIL TIME '...' — PITR
  OPEN RESETLOGS — new incarnation after incomplete recovery

MySQL / InnoDB

text
mysqldump: logical — consistent with --single-transaction (InnoDB)
Percona XtraBackup: physical hot backup — copies ibd files + redo
Binlog archiving enables PITR: restore backup + mysqlbinlog replay

WAL Archiving (PostgreSQL)

text
archive_mode = on
archive_command = 'cp %p /wal_archive/%f'  (or aws s3 cp)

Each filled WAL segment copied to archive before recycled
PITR needs: base backup + continuous archive chain — no gaps

Incremental Backup Internals

text
Track changed blocks since last backup (bitmap, change tracking file)
Backup only changed pages — faster, less I/O
Restore: apply full + incr1 + incr2 ... in order
pgBackRest, RMAN, XtraBackup all implement variants

Part 6 — Storage Internals

What Gets Stored On Disk

PostgreSQL Layout

text
$PGDATA/
  base/           — heap + index files (table data)
  pg_wal/         — WAL segments (16MB each)
  pg_xact/        — commit status
  global/         — catalog

Backup store:
  /backups/full-20260701/     — copy of base/ + partial pg_wal
  /wal_archive/0000000100000000000000AB  — archived segments

Oracle Layout

text
Datafiles (.dbf) — tablespaces
Control file — structural metadata
Redo log groups — online redo
Archive log destination — ARCH process copies filled redo

RMAN backup piece — compressed block images + metadata in recovery catalog

Snapshot-Based Backup (EBS, ZFS)

text
Storage-level snapshot = point-in-time block copy
Crash-consistent unless DB quiesced or uses backup API
PostgreSQL: pg_start_backup() / pg_stop_backup() for consistency
Aurora: storage snapshot continuous — managed PITR window

Immutability

text
S3 Object Lock (Compliance mode) — cannot delete until retention expires
Separate AWS account — attacker cannot wipe backups from prod credentials
WORM tape — air-gapped copy for Tier 0 banking

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Backup Impact on Running Database

PhasePrimary memory/CPUNotes
Full physical backupRead I/O from buffer cacheEvicts hot pages — OLTP latency spike
pg_dumpSequential scanswork_mem for sorts; long MVCC snapshots
RMAN backupBackup buffers, change trackingOften throttled with RATE
WAL archiveMinimal per segmentarchive_command failure → WAL bloat
RestoreOff productionSeparate instance — no prod impact

Banking Operations Window

text
Schedule heavy full backups off peak (02:00–04:00 local)
Use incremental during week, full on weekend
RDS: backup window configurable — avoid month-end close
Long pg_dump holds xmin horizon — can block vacuum (Lesson 40 replica conflict similar)

Part 8 — Execution Flow

End-to-End Flows

Flow 1: Nightly Automated RDS Snapshot

text
T0: AWS snapshot job starts — storage layer incremental snapshot
T1: No application change — same endpoint
T2: Snapshot completes — 35-day retention (configurable)
T3: PITR available to any second within retention window

Flow 2: pgBackRest Full + Continuous WAL (Self-Managed PG)

text
Sunday 02:00: pgbackrest backup full
Mon–Sat 02:00: pgbackrest backup incr
Continuous: archive_push to S3
Daily: verify backup integrity (pgbackrest check)

Incident Wednesday 14:32: accidental truncate payments
Recovery:
  1. Provision new PG instance
  2. pgbackrest restore — target time '2026-07-01 14:31:00'
  3. Validate row counts vs reconciliation
  4. Cutover application JDBC URL
  5. Replay outbox/Kafka gap analysis (Lesson 37)

Flow 3: Oracle RMAN PITR

text
RMAN> RUN {
  SET UNTIL TIME "TO_DATE('2026-07-01 14:31:00','YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS')";
  RESTORE DATABASE;
  RECOVER DATABASE;
}
SQL> ALTER DATABASE OPEN RESETLOGS;
-- Rebuild standby, reconfigure Data Guard after PITR (Lesson 40)

Flow 4: Logical Export for Migration (Not DR)

text
pg_dump -Fc payments_db > payments.dump
Restore to new RDS for upgrade test
NOT sufficient alone for Tier 0 RPO — use physical + WAL for production DR

Flow 5: Restore Drill (Quarterly — Banking)

text
1. Pick random backup from 30 days ago
2. Restore to isolated VPC subnet — no prod routing
3. Run validation SQL: SUM(payments.amount), COUNT(accounts)
4. Compare to known audit totals for that date
5. Measure elapsed RTO — document gaps
6. Sign compliance attestation

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Backup Performance Trade-offs

Backup Method Comparison

MethodBackup duration (1TB)Restore durationPITRProd impact
pg_dumpHours–daysHours–daysNoHigh CPU/IO
pgBackRest full1–4 hr30–90 minYesModerate IO
pgBackRest incr10–30 minChain dependentYesLower
RMAN full+incrTunableFastYesThrottle RATE
RDS snapshotManagedManagedYesMinimal visible
EBS snapshot rawFastFastIf WAL archivedRisk if not quiesced

RPO from Backups

text
Daily full only:
  RPO up to 24 hours — unacceptable for payments

Full + continuous WAL/binlog:
  RPO = minutes to seconds (archive lag)

Sync replication (Lesson 40):
  RPO ~ 0 for failover — still need backup for logical errors

Cost

text
S3 Glacier for 7-year retention — pennies/GB/month
Cross-region replication of backups — 2× storage + egress
Cheaper than regulatory fine or brand damage from unrecoverable ledger

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

OperationTime complexity (ops)Space
Full backupO(database size)O(database size)
IncrementalO(changes since last)O(changes)
PITR restoreO(base) + O(WAL replay)Temp space for replay
Logical restoreO(rows)O(rows)
Retention N daysO(1) per day policyO(N × daily increment)

Restore chain depth: k incrementals → restore O(k) merge steps — cap chain length with periodic full.

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Backup & Recovery Commands

PostgreSQL — Enable Archiving (postgresql.conf)

ini
wal_level = replica          # or logical if needed
archive_mode = on
archive_command = 'pgbackrest --stanza=payments archive-push %p'
max_wal_senders = 10

pgBackRest — Backup & Restore

bash
# Full backup
pgbackrest --stanza=payments backup --type=full

# Incremental
pgbackrest --stanza=payments backup --type=incr

# PITR restore to new data directory
pgbackrest --stanza=payments --delta restore \
  --type=time --target='2026-07-01 14:31:00' \
  --target-action=promote

pg_dump — Logical (Dev / Schema)

bash
# Custom format — parallel restore
pg_dump -h primary.db.internal -U app -d payments -Fc -f payments_20260701.dump

pg_restore -h staging.db.internal -U app -d payments_staging -j 4 payments_20260701.dump

PostgreSQL — Validate After Restore

sql
-- Banking sanity checks post-restore
SELECT COUNT(*) AS payment_count, SUM(amount) AS total_amount
FROM payments
WHERE created_at < TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-07-01 14:31:00';

SELECT account_id, balance
FROM accounts
WHERE account_id IN (5001, 5002, 5003);

-- Reconcile branch totals
SELECT b.branch_code, SUM(a.balance) AS branch_liability
FROM branches b
JOIN accounts a ON a.branch_id = b.branch_id
GROUP BY b.branch_code;

Oracle RMAN — Backup & PITR

sql
-- Backup (RMAN)
RMAN> BACKUP DATABASE PLUS ARCHIVELOG DELETE INPUT;
RMAN> BACKUP INCREMENTAL LEVEL 1 DATABASE;

-- List backups
RMAN> LIST BACKUP SUMMARY;

-- PITR
RMAN> RUN {
  SET UNTIL TIME "TO_DATE('2026-07-01 14:31:00','YYYY-MM-DD HH24:MI:SS')";
  RESTORE DATABASE;
  RECOVER DATABASE;
}
SQL> ALTER DATABASE OPEN RESETLOGS;

MySQL — XtraBackup + Binlog PITR

bash
# Hot physical backup
xtrabackup --backup --target-dir=/backup/full --user=root --password=***

# Prepare
xtrabackup --prepare --target-dir=/backup/full

# PITR: restore files, start mysql, apply binlog
mysqlbinlog --stop-datetime="2026-07-01 14:31:00" /var/log/mysql/binlog.* | mysql -u root -p

AWS RDS — CLI Snapshot

bash
aws rds create-db-snapshot \
  --db-instance-identifier payments-prod \
  --db-snapshot-identifier payments-prod-manual-20260701

# Restore to new instance (DR test)
aws rds restore-db-instance-from-db-snapshot \
  --db-instance-identifier payments-restore-drill \
  --db-snapshot-identifier payments-prod-manual-20260701

Accidental DELETE — Recovery Decision SQL (On Primary — Before Restore)

sql
-- Identify damage scope (if rows still visible in MVCC — sometimes too late)
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM payments WHERE deleted_at IS NOT NULL;

-- If hard DELETE — only PITR helps
-- Document: last good time from audit table / application logs
SELECT MAX(changed_at) FROM payments_audit WHERE operation = 'DELETE';

Part 12 — Production Usage

Backup Strategy in Production

3-2-1 Rule (Banking Standard)

text
3 copies of data
2 different media types (EBS + S3)
1 off-site / separate account (cross-region, immutable)

Tiered Retention

TierSystemFullIncremental/WALRetention
0Core ledgerDaily + WALContinuous7 yr (regulatory)
1Payments OLTPDaily + WALContinuous1 yr online, 7 yr archive
2Customer CRMWeeklyDaily90 days
3AnalyticsETL snapshotN/A30 days

Monitoring

text
□ Backup job success/failure alerts
□ WAL archive lag (minutes behind)
□ Backup age (last successful full < 24h)
□ Restore drill calendar (quarterly minimum)
□ Backup size anomaly (ransomware may shrink/encrypt)
□ Encryption at rest + in transit verified
□ RTO/RPO actual vs target from last drill

Banking Incident Playbook (Truncate / Bad Deploy)

text
1. STOP writes — disable payment API or read-only mode
2. Assess scope — which tables, time window
3. Choose recovery: PITR vs selective fix vs saga compensate
4. Restore to NEW instance — never overwrite prod in place first
5. Validate financial totals vs audit/reconciliation
6. Cutover JDBC + update secrets
7. Reconcile Kafka/outbox events since divergence (Lesson 37)
8. Post-mortem + backup policy review

What Managed RDS Gives You

text
Automated daily snapshot + transaction log archiving
PITR to any second within retention (default 7 days — extend to 35)
Manual snapshot before major migration
Cross-region snapshot copy for DR (Lesson 42)
Still run restore drills — "managed" ≠ "tested"

Part 13 — Spring Boot Integration

Application Layer During Backup & Recovery

Normal Operation — No Special Code

yaml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://payments-prod.xxxx.rds.amazonaws.com:5432/payments
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 30
# Backups run transparently on RDS — app unaware

Read-Only Mode During Incident

java
@Component
public class MaintenanceModeFilter implements Filter {
    @Override
    public void doFilter(ServletRequest req, ServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws IOException, ServletException {
        if (maintenanceProperties.isReadOnly()) {
            if (isWriteRequest((HttpServletRequest) req)) {
                ((HttpServletResponse) res).sendError(503, "System in recovery mode");
                return;
            }
        }
        chain.doFilter(req, res);
    }
}

Cutover to Restored Database

yaml
# Blue/green cutover — change endpoint after validation
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://payments-restored.xxxx.rds.amazonaws.com:5432/payments
# Rolling restart pods — Hikari picks new target
# Idempotent payment APIs essential — clients may retry during outage

Flyway/Liquibase After PITR

text
PITR to T-5min may restore schema BEFORE migration V47 applied
If migration ran at T-3min — schema drift vs code
Rule: note migration timestamp vs PITR target
After restore: verify flyway_schema_history version matches deployed app

Connection Pool After Restore

yaml
spring:
  datasource:
    hikari:
      connection-test-query: SELECT 1
      max-lifetime: 600000   # recycle connections after cutover

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

ORM Considerations for Backup/Recovery

No JPA Backup API

text
Backups are infrastructure — not @Entity concern
Never implement "backup" in application code for Tier 0 — use native tools

Audit Tables Help PITR Target Selection

java
@Entity
@Table(name = "payments_audit")
public class PaymentAudit {
    @Id
    private Long auditId;
    private String operation;   // INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
    private Instant changedAt;
    private String changedBy;
    // Helps identify "last good time" for PITR target
}

Envers / Hibernate Audit

text
Envers revision tables show when row changed
PITR still needed for hard DELETE without audit trail
Combine: audit for forensics + backup for recovery

Restore Validation in Integration Tests

java
@SpringBootTest
@ActiveProfiles("restore-drill")
class RestoreValidationIT {
    @Test
    void paymentsTotalMatchesExpectedAuditSnapshot() {
        BigDecimal total = paymentRepo.sumAmountBefore(Instant.parse("2026-07-01T14:31:00Z"));
        assertThat(total).isEqualByComparingTo("9845721.33");
    }
}

Sequence Gaps After PITR

text
PITR to past → sequences may reuse IDs if new writes after restore
Use UUID primary keys for payments (recommended) — avoids ID collision
Oracle sequences: ALTER SEQUENCE ... RESTART or INCREMENT BY large gap

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

Solution Architect View

Defense in Depth

text
Layer 1: HA replication (Lesson 40)     — node failure, seconds RTO
Layer 2: Continuous backup + PITR       — logical errors, minutes RPO
Layer 3: Cross-region immutable backup  — regional disaster (Lesson 42)
Layer 4: Audit + reconciliation         — detect drift, compensate (Lesson 38)

When Replication Hurts Recovery

text
DELETE propagated → all replicas wrong
Only independent backup predating DELETE succeeds
Architect policy: backups in separate security boundary

RPO/RTO Matrix (Backup-Specific)

ScenarioReplication aloneBackup + PITR
AZ failureFailover — OKNot first line
Bad UPDATE 2hr agoReplicas wrongPITR to T-2hr+1min
RansomwareEncrypted replicaImmutable backup
Regulatory restoreN/A7-year archive

Logical vs Physical — Architect Choice

text
Tier 0 production DR:     physical + WAL (pgBackRest, RMAN, RDS PITR)
Schema migration:         logical pg_dump subset
Developer laptop:           logical dump masked
Vendor export requirement:  logical CSV — not DR substitute

Cost vs Risk

text
Skipping restore drills saves engineer hours
One failed audit or lost ledger costs millions
Quarterly drill is non-negotiable for payment platforms

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Replication = Backup

text
DELETE replicates — no recovery — incident escalates to P0

Mistake 2: Never Testing Restore

text
Backup job green for 2 years — restore fails missing WAL segment

Mistake 3: WAL Archive Gaps

text
archive_command fails silently — disk full on archive mount — PITR impossible
Monitor every segment push

Mistake 4: Restoring Over Production

text
pgbackrest restore on live $PGDATA — destroys production
Always restore to NEW instance first

Mistake 5: pg_dump Only for Tier 0

text
No PITR — 23 hours of payments lost — regulatory breach

Mistake 6: Backups in Same Account as Prod

text
Ransomware deletes S3 backups with stolen IAM role
Separate account + Object Lock

Mistake 7: Ignoring RESETLOGS / Incarnation (Oracle)

text
After PITR OPEN RESETLOGS — standby must be rebuilt — Data Guard broken until fixed

Mistake 8: No Pre-Migration Snapshot

text
Flyway V48 fails halfway — need snapshot from before migration attempt

Mistake 9: Long-Running pg_dump on Primary Peak

text
Vacuum blocked — bloat — payment latency spike
Use replica for dump or off-peak + physical backup

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: Difference between backup and replication?

Backup is independent copy for restore/time travel; replication mirrors live changes including mistakes.

Q2: Full vs incremental backup?

Full copies everything; incremental copies changes since last backup.

Q3: What is PITR?

Restore base backup + replay logs to specific timestamp.

Q4: Why WAL archiving?

Enables continuous recovery between full backups.

Q5: 3-2-1 backup rule?

3 copies, 2 media types, 1 off-site.

Mid-Level

Q6: pg_dump vs pgBackRest?

Logical SQL export vs physical files + WAL; pgBackRest for production PITR at scale.

Q7: RPO with daily backup only?

Up to 24 hours data loss — need WAL for better RPO.

Q8: DELETE mistake — replication running — recovery?

PITR from backup before DELETE to new instance; cannot use replica alone.

Q9: RMAN incremental level 0 vs 1?

Level 0 = full block backup; level 1 = changed blocks since prior.

Q10: RDS automated backup vs manual snapshot?

Automated enables PITR window; manual snapshot pinned until deleted — pre-change safety.

Senior

Q11: Design backup for payment DB RPO 5 min, RTO 2 hr.

Continuous WAL to S3, daily full, cross-region copy, quarterly drill, restore to new RDS, validation SQL, cutover runbook.

Q12: Immutable backup against ransomware?

S3 Object Lock compliance, separate account, MFA delete, air-gapped copy.

Q13: After PITR, Kafka/outbox gap?

Events after recovery point missing — replay from outbox or reconciliation job (Lessons 37–38).

Q14: pg_dump --single-transaction purpose?

Consistent InnoDB/PG snapshot in one transaction — avoids partial export.

Staff / Architect

Q15: Tier 0 banking backup architecture diagram elements?

HA sync replica, pgBackRest/RMAN, WAL archive, cross-region immutable, drills, audit retention 7yr, separate IAM.

Q16: Logical backup sufficient for DR?

No for large Tier 0 — too slow RTO; physical + PITR required.

Scenario

Scenario: "Ops says we have Multi-AZ RDS so backups unnecessary."

Reject — Multi-AZ is HA not protection from logical errors or ransomware; enable PITR, cross-region snapshots, restore drills.

Disaster Recovery

Part 1 — Concept

What Is Disaster Recovery (DR)?

Disaster recovery is the planned capability to restore critical systems after a large-scale failure — entire data center, AWS region outage, prolonged network partition, or catastrophic corruption — within agreed RTO (Recovery Time Objective) and RPO (Recovery Point Objective).

text
LOCAL HA (Lesson 40)              DISASTER RECOVERY (Lesson 42)
────────────────────              ─────────────────────────────
Single AZ / node fails            Entire region unavailable
Failover seconds–minutes          Restore hours (or warm standby minutes)
Same geography usually            Cross-region / cross-site
Replication primary→standby       Backups + DR site + runbooks + people
RPO ~ 0 (sync Multi-AZ)           RPO often minutes–hours (async cross-region)

DR vs HA vs Backup

text
┌─────────────┬──────────────────┬─────────────────────┬──────────────────────┐
│             │ HA (L40)         │ Backup (L41)        │ DR (L42)             │
├─────────────┼──────────────────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────────────┤
│ Scope       │ Node/AZ          │ Any failure type    │ Region/site disaster │
│ Mechanism   │ Sync/async repl  │ Snapshots + PITR    │ Cross-region restore │
│ RTO         │ 1–5 min typical  │ Hours (cold)        │ Minutes–hours        │
│ RPO         │ ~0 in-region     │ Seconds–hours       │ Minutes–hours typical│
│ Undo DELETE │ No               │ Yes (PITR)          │ Yes (if backup OK)   │
│ Runbook     │ Automated        │ Restore procedure   │ Full org playbook    │
└─────────────┴──────────────────┴─────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘

Active-Passive vs Active-Active (Regional)

text
ACTIVE-PASSIVE (most banking DR)
  us-east-1 PRIMARY ──async repl/backup──► us-west-2 STANDBY (cold/warm)
  Normal: 100% traffic east
  DR:     declare disaster → promote/restore west → redirect traffic

ACTIVE-ACTIVE (multi-region writes — rare for core ledger)
  us-east-1 WRITES ◄──► us-west-2 WRITES
  Conflict resolution, split-brain risk, regulatory complexity
  Used selectively: read paths, stateless APIs, Cassandra-style (Phase 7)

Key DR Terms

TermMeaning
Primary siteNormal production region
DR siteSecondary region ready for failover
Cold standbyBackups only — restore on declare
Warm standbyDB restored/running, minimal traffic
Hot standbyActive replica, fast promotion
FailoverSwitch production to DR site
FailbackReturn to primary after repair
Game dayScheduled DR exercise — no real disaster
BCPBusiness Continuity Plan — people, ops, comms beyond DB

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Disaster Recovery

text
1970s   Mainframe DR — hot site with tape restore — RTO measured in days
        Banking: alternate data center, manual switch

1980s   IBM GDPS, remote copy — synchronous distance limits (~100km)
        Oracle standby database — redo shipping cross-site

1990s   DR as insurance — expensive idle hardware
        RTO/RTO SLAs in outsourcing contracts

2000s   Active/passive clusters — VMware SRM, Oracle Data Guard far sync
        9/11 and regional outages — regulatory push for tested DR

2010s   Cloud DR — AWS cross-region RDS snapshot copy, Route53 failover
        "Pilot light" and "warm standby" Well-Architected patterns
        Cheap object storage — 7-year backup retention feasible

2015+   Aurora Global Database — sub-second cross-region replication (reads)
        Kubernetes multi-cluster — DB still the hard part
        ransomware — DR must include immutable backups (L41)

2020s   us-east-1 outages teach: DR region must be truly independent
        Regulators (RBI, ECB, OCC-style): annual DR drill evidence
        Payment systems: strict max downtime + reconciliation post-DR
        Architects accept: perfect zero-RPO cross-region is expensive

Historical Lesson

HA solved the failing server. DR solves the failing city. Cloud makes DR cheaper, but only if backups, runbooks, and game days exist — not if you merely checked "Multi-AZ enabled."

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problem Does DR Solve?

Problem 1: Regional Cloud Outage

text
AWS us-east-1 degraded 6 hours — RDS, EKS, networking impacted
Multi-AZ within region does not help — whole region impaired
Need: payments run from us-west-2 with defined RTO

Problem 2: Natural Disaster / Data Center Loss

text
Flood/fire destroys primary facility
Local replication and backups in same building lost together
Need: geographically separated immutable backups

Problem 3: Prolonged Primary Unavailability

text
Primary region technically up but unreliable 48 hours
Business decision: graceful DR failover vs wait
Need: pre-decided thresholds and authority to declare

Problem 4: Regulatory Minimum Continuity

text
Payment system license requires proof of DR capability
Audit asks: RTO/RPO targets, last successful drill, evidence
Need: documented architecture + signed drill reports

Problem 5: Cascading Failure After Partial Recovery

text
Restore DB in DR region — Kafka, secrets, DNS still point to primary
Apps connect to wrong region — split brain or total outage
Need: end-to-end DR runbook, not DB-only

Unified Problem Statement

DR ensures the organization can resume critical data services after regional catastrophe — within contractual RTO/RPO — using cross-region redundancy, backups, runbooks, and tested procedures that span database, application, and operations.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why DR Exists

Single Region Is a Single Bet

text
Even 99.99% regional SLA → ~52 min/year downtime
Payment license may require higher effective availability via DR

HA Does Not Escape Geography

text
Sync Multi-AZ: two AZs, **one region**
Regional control-plane failure affects both AZs
Cross-region DR is separate insurance layer

Backups Alone Are Insufficient Without Process

text
S3 backups in us-west-2 exist — but:
  Who restores? How long? Who approves cutover?
DR = backup + capacity + runbook + practice + governance

Business Continuity

text
DB restored but no staff roles, customer comms, fraud monitoring → failed DR
DR architecture includes downstream reconciliation (Lesson 38)

Part 5 — Internal Working

How DR Works Internally

DR Pattern 1: Backup-Restore (Cold DR)

text
Primary us-east-1:
  Continuous backups → S3 cross-region replication → us-west-2 bucket (immutable)

DR declare:
  1. Restore RDS/Aurora from latest cross-region snapshot or PITR
  2. Restore secrets, deploy K8s manifests to west cluster
  3. Update Route53 / Global Accelerator to west endpoints
  4. Validate financial totals
  5. Open read/write traffic

RTO: hours (restore size dependent)
RPO: backup/WAL lag (minutes if continuous archive replicated)

DR Pattern 2: Warm Standby (Read Replica Promotion)

text
Primary: Aurora/RDS writer us-east-1
DR:      cross-region read replica OR Aurora secondary cluster us-west-2
         (async replication — lag monitored)

Failover:
  aws rds promote-read-replica / Aurora global failover
  Promote replica to writer — minutes RTO
  RPO = replication lag at failover instant (often 1–60 sec Aurora Global; longer RDS async)

Internal:
  Async redo/WAL shipped cross-region
  Promotion breaks replication link — rebuild after failback

DR Pattern 3: Pilot Light

text
Minimal west footprint: VPC, IAM, small RDS from recent snapshot, AMIs
Normal traffic: 0% west
DR: scale up west RDS, restore to latest, deploy full app tier
Lower cost than warm — higher RTO

DR Pattern 4: Active-Passive Hot Standby

text
West cluster runs same schema, receives async replication
Health checks + manual/auto failover via DNS
Connection strings pre-configured in Spring (profile-based)
Some teams run shadow read-only traffic for validation

Active-Active Multi-Region Writes (Advanced — Usually Not Core Ledger)

text
Two writable regions — conflict resolution:
  Last-write-wins (dangerous for balances)
  Region-owned shards (customer_id % region)
  CRDT / specialized stores

Core banking ledger: avoid — use active-passive + saga reconciliation

Failback Internals

text
Primary region repaired:
  1. Re-establish replication west → east OR fresh restore east from west
  2. Sync drift during DR period — reconciliation job
  3. Planned maintenance window — failback traffic
  4. Re-test replication and backup chains both directions

Part 6 — Storage Internals

DR and Cross-Region Storage

Cross-Region Backup Replication

text
S3 CRR (Cross-Region Replication) or AWS Backup copy jobs
Object Lock on destination — ransomware protection
WAL/archive segments must replicate with no gap — same as L41 monitoring

RDS:
  automated snapshot copy to DR region
  manual snapshot copy before major release

Aurora Global Database Storage

text
Storage volume replicated cross-region at storage layer (~<1s typical)
Secondary cluster can promote in ~1 minute (AWS claims — verify in drills)
Unshared storage model — different from traditional redo apply
After failover: old primary must rejoin carefully — avoid split brain

Oracle Data Guard Far Sync / MaxAvailability

text
Far sync instance receives redo synchronously without opening DB
Standby applies async — balances RPO vs distance latency
DR site standby open read-only for reporting

PostgreSQL DR Storage

text
pgBackRest repo on S3 with CRR to DR region
Restore in DR VPC: new EC2 + EBS from restore
Archive-get pulls WAL from DR bucket during recovery

Metadata and Catalog

text
Don't forget DR copies of:
  RMAN recovery catalog
  pgBackRest stanza config
  Flyway migration history
  KMS keys (multi-region keys MRK)
  Parameter groups, security groups (IaC in git)

Part 7 — Memory Usage

DR Site Resource Planning

ModeDR memory/CPUCost
ColdZero until restoreLowest
Pilot lightSmall RDS instanceLow
Warm replicaFull-size replica (often scaled down)Medium
Hot/activeFull production mirrorHighest

Restore Burst

text
Cold restore: high I/O + CPU during WAL replay — provision larger instance class temporarily
Then scale down post-validation
Spring app tier: pre-provision max replicas in DR — scale from 0 on declare

Connection Storm on Failover

text
All Hikari pools reconnect simultaneously — DR DB max_connections spike
Use connection pooler (PgBouncer/RDS Proxy) in DR runbook
Rate-limit pod rollout during DR

Part 8 — Execution Flow

End-to-End DR Flows

Flow 1: Regional Outage — Warm Standby Failover (Payments)

text
T+0:    AWS us-east-1 status degraded — error rate >50%
T+5m:   Incident commander convenes — confirm not transient
T+10m:  Declare DR — execute runbook section 4.2
T+12m:  Promote Aurora secondary cluster us-west-2 to writer
T+15m:  Update Route53 health checks — point api.bank.com → west ALB
T+18m:  Rolling restart payment-service pods (Spring profile dr-active)
T+25m:  Smoke test: idempotent test payment + rollback
T+30m:  Open customer traffic — comms team notifies
T+2h:   Reconciliation batch: compare east outage window vs west ledger
RTO achieved: 30 min | RPO: ~5 sec async lag at promotion

Flow 2: Cold Restore from Cross-Region Backup

text
T+0:    Primary region declared lost (not just degraded)
T+30m:  Restore RDS PostgreSQL from cross-region snapshot to us-west-2
T+2h:   PITR complete — WAL replay from DR bucket
T+2h30m: Validation SQL — SUM(payments), branch totals
T+3h:   Application cutover
RTO: 3h | RPO: last archived WAL received (e.g. 8 min gap if replication delayed)

Flow 3: Game Day (No Real Disaster)

text
Week -4:  Announce game day — no customer impact
Week -2:  Deploy DR environment from IaC — isolated DNS test.bank-internal.com
Day 0:    Team executes full failover playbook against test namespace
          Measure RTO/RPO — document gaps
Day +1:   Failback exercise — restore replication
Report:   Sign for auditors — gaps → remediation tickets

Flow 4: DR with Kafka / Outbox Gap (Lessons 37–38)

text
DB promoted in west — Kafka cluster still east (unavailable)
Outbox relay in payment-service:
  1. Pause consumers or enable DR Kafka cluster (MirrorMaker2 / cluster link)
  2. Replay outbox events from DR DB from last processed offset
  3. Idempotent consumers in ledger-service handle duplicates
  4. Saga timeouts trigger compensations for in-flight workflows

Flow 5: Failback to Primary

text
Primary region healthy after 72h
  1. Establish replication west → east (or restore east from west snapshot)
  2. Reconcile 72h of DR-only writes
  3. Maintenance window: read-only → sync → DNS back to east
  4. Monitor lag — restore normal HA

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

DR Configuration & Validation Examples

AWS — Cross-Region Automated Backup Copy

bash
# Enable cross-region copy for RDS automated backups
aws rds start-db-instance-automated-backups-replication \
  --region us-west-2 \
  --source-db-instance-arn arn:aws:rds:us-east-1:123456789:db:payments-prod

# Manual snapshot copy to DR region
aws rds copy-db-snapshot \
  --source-db-snapshot-identifier arn:aws:rds:us-east-1:123456789:snapshot:payments-pre-release \
  --target-db-snapshot-identifier payments-pre-release-west \
  --region us-west-2 \
  --kms-key-id arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:123456789:key/dr-key-id

Aurora Global Database — Failover (CLI)

bash
aws rds failover-global-cluster \
  --global-cluster-identifier payments-global \
  --target-db-cluster-identifier payments-cluster-west

PostgreSQL — DR Restore from pgBackRest (DR Region)

bash
# In us-west-2 DR VPC — repo already replicated via S3 CRR
pgbackrest --stanza=payments --delta restore \
  --target=/var/lib/postgresql/16/main

# recovery.conf / postgresql.auto.conf
# restore_command = 'pgbackrest --stanza=payments archive-get %f "%p"'
# recovery_target_timeline = 'latest'

Post-Failover Validation SQL

sql
-- 1. Latest transaction timestamp vs expected outage start
SELECT MAX(created_at) AS last_payment_time, COUNT(*) AS payment_count
FROM payments;

-- 2. Branch liability snapshot (compare to pre-DR audit file)
SELECT b.branch_code, SUM(a.balance) AS total_balance
FROM branches b
JOIN accounts a ON a.branch_id = b.branch_id
WHERE a.status = 'ACTIVE'
GROUP BY b.branch_code
ORDER BY b.branch_code;

-- 3. Detect possible duplicate payments during overlap window
SELECT idempotency_key, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM payments
WHERE created_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-07-01 10:00:00+00'
GROUP BY idempotency_key
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- 4. Outbox unprocessed events for relay catch-up
SELECT COUNT(*) AS pending_outbox
FROM outbox_events
WHERE published_at IS NULL;

Route53 Failover Record (Conceptual)

json
{
  "Type": "A",
  "SetIdentifier": "primary-east",
  "Failover": "PRIMARY",
  "HealthCheckId": "abc-primary-health",
  "AliasTarget": { "DNSName": "payments-east.example.com" }
}
{
  "Type": "A",
  "SetIdentifier": "dr-west",
  "Failover": "SECONDARY",
  "AliasTarget": { "DNSName": "payments-west.example.com" }
}

Oracle Data Guard — Switchover vs Failover

sql
-- Planned switchover (primary healthy) — preferred for maintenance
DGMGRL> SWITCHOVER TO payments_standby;

-- Failover (primary lost) — data loss possible per lag
DGMGRL> FAILOVER TO payments_standby;

Part 12 — Production Usage

DR in Production Banking

Well-Architected DR Tiers (AWS Mapping)

text
Backup & Restore     → Cold — RTO hours
Pilot Light          → Small DR footprint
Warm Standby         → Scaled-down replica + scale on declare
Hot Standby/Multi-site → Active-passive near-real-time
Active-Active        → Multi-region writes — selective use

Governance

text
DR Steering Committee:
  - RTO/RPO per system documented in service catalog
  - Incident commander authority to declare DR
  - Communication templates (customers, regulators, partners)
  - Post-DR mandatory reconciliation sign-off from Finance

Evidence pack for audit:
  - Architecture diagram (primary + DR + backup flows)
  - Last 4 game day reports
  - Cross-region backup immutability config
  - Signed RTO/RPO achievement vs target

Regulatory Expectations (Conceptual — Jurisdiction Varies)

text
Payment / banking regulators commonly expect:
  ✓ Documented DR strategy aligned to business impact
  ✓ Periodic testing (annual minimum — quarterly for Tier 0)
  ✓ Defined RTO/RPO for critical payment processing
  ✓ Data integrity validation after failover
  ✓ Incident reporting timelines if DR invoked in production
  ✓ Geographic separation of primary and DR

Not sufficient:
  ✗ "We use Multi-AZ"
  ✗ "Backups exist but never restored"
  ✗ DR plan in wiki — never exercised

Multi-Service DR Checklist

text
□ Database promoted/restored in DR region
□ Secrets Manager / Vault DR copies
□ Kafka MirrorMaker or DR cluster + offset mapping
□ IAM roles for DR account/region
□ Spring profile switches JDBC + Kafka bootstrap
□ Idempotency keys on all payment APIs
□ Fraud/risk systems receiving events from DR
□ DNS TTL lowered before planned DR tests
□ Customer-facing status page process
□ Reconciliation jobs scheduled post-DR

bash
# Emergency deploy — CI/CD or kubectl
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod-west-dr kubectl rollout restart deployment/payment-service

Resilience During DR Cutover

java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PaymentCaptureService {

    @Retryable(
        retryFor = { TransientDataAccessException.class, SQLTransientConnectionException.class },
        maxAttempts = 5,
        backoff = @Backoff(delay = 2000, multiplier = 2)
    )
    @Transactional
    public PaymentResult capture(PaymentCommand cmd) {
        paymentRepo.saveIfAbsent(cmd.idempotencyKey(), cmd.toPayment());
        outboxRepo.save(OutboxEvent.paymentCreated(cmd));
        return PaymentResult.accepted(cmd.idempotencyKey());
    }
}

    boolean active,
    boolean writesEnabled
) {}

@Transactional
public PaymentResult capture(PaymentCommand cmd) {
    if (drProperties.active() && !drProperties.writesEnabled()) {
        throw new ServiceUnavailableException("DR validation in progress");

Health Check for Route53

java
@RestController
public class DrHealthController {
    @GetMapping("/actuator/dr-ready")
    public ResponseEntity<Map<String, String>> drReady(
            DataSource dataSource,
            @Value("${dr.writes-enabled:false}") boolean writesEnabled) {
        try (Connection c = dataSource.getConnection()) {
            c.createStatement().execute("SELECT 1");
            if (!writesEnabled) return ResponseEntity.status(503).body(Map.of("status", "DB up, writes disabled"));
            return ResponseEntity.ok(Map.of("status", "ready"));
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            return ResponseEntity.status(503).body(Map.of("status", "db-down"));
        }
    }
}

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

Solution Architect DR Framework

Layered Resilience Model

text
Layer 1: In-region Multi-AZ (L40)     — AZ failure
Layer 2: Continuous backup + PITR (L41) — logical errors
Layer 3: Cross-region DR (L42)        — regional disaster
Layer 4: Business continuity          — people, fraud, comms
Layer 5: Reconciliation (L38)         — financial truth after chaos

When NOT to Use Active-Active Ledger

text
Double-spend risk across regions
Regulatory reporting on single timeline
Saga compensations explode in complexity
Prefer: single writer region + DR promotion

DR Region Selection

text
Avoid adjacent failure domains:
  Primary us-east-1 → DR us-west-2 ✓
  Primary us-east-1 → DR us-east-2 ✗ (same region)

Consider:
  Data residency (EU customer data → DR in EU)
  Latency for ops team during incident
  Service availability history of DR region

CAP at Regional Scale

text
Regional partition:
  Active-passive async: choose AP for availability in DR region
                        accept RPO > 0
  Sync cross-region CP: commits block if link down — rarely chosen globally

Cost-Optimized DR for Mid-Size Bank

text
Tier 0: Aurora Global or warm replica
Tier 1–2: cross-region backup copy + pilot light IaC
Quarterly game day on Tier 0 — annual on Tier 2
Immutable backups in separate account — mandatory all tiers

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: DR vs HA?

HA handles node/AZ failure in-region; DR handles regional/site disaster with cross-region recovery.

Q2: RTO vs RPO in DR context?

RPO: max data loss on failover. RTO: max downtime until service restored.

Q3: Active-passive vs active-active?

Passive: one region serves writes normally. Active-active: multiple regions write — complex consistency.

Q4: Cold vs warm DR?

Cold: restore from backup on declare. Warm: replica/pre-built stack ready to promote/scale.

Q5: Why cross-region backups?

Regional disaster destroys primary and in-region copies — need geographically separate immutable backups.

Mid-Level

Q6: Multi-AZ sufficient for DR audit?

No — same region risk — need cross-region strategy and tested restore/failover.

Q7: Aurora Global vs cross-region RDS replica?

Aurora Global: storage-level replication, faster failover. RDS replica: async promotion, longer RTO/RPO typically.

Q8: What happens to replication lag on failover?

Transactions not yet replicated may be lost — RPO = lag at promotion instant.

Q9: Game day purpose?

Prove runbook, measure RTO/RPO, train teams, satisfy audit — without real disaster.

Q10: Post-DR reconciliation why needed?

Async gap, duplicate retries, partial sagas — finance must verify ledger integrity.

Senior

Q11: Design DR for payment platform RPO 1 min, RTO 30 min on AWS.

Aurora Global or cross-region replica us-west-2, Route53 failover, Spring profiles, idempotent APIs, outbox replay to DR Kafka, quarterly game day, immutable S3 CRR.

Q12: When declare DR vs wait through degradation?

Pre-defined error budget, duration threshold, customer impact, irreversibility of promote — incident commander decision matrix.

Q13: Failback strategy after 3 days in DR?

Read-only east, sync/rebuild, reconcile, planned DNS cutover, validate replication.

Q14: Active-active for core ledger — your view?

Generally reject — use region-sharded ownership or active-passive with promoted writer — unless specialized DB (Spanner) with explicit model.

Staff / Architect

Q15: DR evidence pack for regulator?

Architecture, RTO/RPO matrix, game day reports, immutability config, reconciliation process, incident comms plan.

Q16: Cost-optimize DR without violating Tier 0 RPO?

Aurora Global for Tier 0 only; pilot light + backup for Tier 2; automate IaC scale-up; avoid full hot mirror everywhere.

Scenario

Scenario: "us-east-1 down 4 hours — promote west replica — customers complain duplicate charges."

Missing idempotency + retry storm during flaky cutover — fix API keys, reconcile duplicates, improve DR write-gate and pool config.

Schema Design for Payment Platforms

Phase 5: DATABASE DESIGN & AVAILABILITY | Previous: Disaster Recovery | Next: Sharding & Horizontal Scaling

Availability
1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why This Exists5Internal Working6Storage Internals7Memory Usage8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Complexity Analysis11Code / SQL Examples12Production Usage13Spring Boot Integration14Hibernate/JPA Integration15Architect Perspective16Decision Matrix17Comparison Tables18Common Mistakes19Interview Questions20Revision Sheet21Summary Table*Practice

Part 1 — Concept

What Is Schema Design for Payment Platforms?

Schema design is how you structure tables, keys, constraints, and relationships so a payment platform is correct, auditable, scalable, and recoverable under real-world failure modes — not just “tables that look right in an ER diagram.”

text
BUSINESS DOMAIN              BOUNDED CONTEXT (DB per service)     CORE TABLES
───────────────              ────────────────────────────────     ───────────
Customer onboarding    →     customer-service DB            →     customers, kyc_profiles
Account & balance      →     ledger-service DB              →     accounts, ledger_entries
Payment capture        →     payment-service DB             →     payments, idempotency_keys
Branch operations      →     branch-service DB              →     branches, branch_limits
Cross-service flow     →     events (outbox/saga)           →     outbox_events, saga_state

Payment Schema Principles

PrincipleMeaning
Single writer per aggregateOne service owns accounts.balance — no cross-DB updates
Append-only ledgerFinancial truth = immutable entries, not mutable balance alone
Idempotency firstEvery external command has a unique key — DR/retry safe
Audit everything materialWho changed what, when — regulatory requirement
Explicit money typesDECIMAL + ISO currency — never FLOAT
Time in UTCTIMESTAMPTZ — display converts in app layer
Soft delete selectivelyRegulatory records often cannot be hard-deleted

Ledger Pattern vs Balance Column

text
ANTI-PATTERN (mutable only)          LEDGER PATTERN (recommended)
───────────────────────────          ─────────────────────────────
accounts.balance = 5000              ledger_entries (append-only):
UPDATE balance = 4500                  +1000 DEPOSIT
                                       -500  PAYMENT
No history of why balance changed      balance = SUM(entries) or cached snapshot

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Payment Data Models

text
1970s   COBOL batch — sequential files, end-of-day balancing
        No online schema — correctness via batch reconciliation

1980s   Relational core banking — accounts + transactions tables
        Double-entry bookkeeping in GL separate from OLTP

1990s   ATM/card networks — authorization holds separate from settlement
        Status columns: PENDING → CAPTURED → SETTLED

2000s   ISO 8583 payment gateways — idempotency via STAN/RRN in messages
        Oracle/DB2 monolith schemas — shared database anti-pattern begins

2010s   Microservices — schema per service, saga/outbox
        Event sourcing in fintech startups — ledger as event log
        Stripe-style idempotency keys as first-class API concept

2015+   PSD2, open banking — payment_intents, consent tables
        Multi-currency wallets — amount + currency + FX metadata
        GDPR vs retention — soft delete + legal hold flags

2020s   Real-time payments (UPI, FedNow, SEPA Instant)
        High-volume idempotency + partitioning by date/customer
        Architects design for DR merge (UUID PKs), reconciliation jobs

Historical Lesson

Payment schemas evolved from “one big bank database” to “many bounded schemas connected by events.” Your job as architect is to draw the boundary lines so ACID stays local and reliability patterns (outbox, saga, DR) have tables to live in.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does Payment Schema Design Solve?

Problem 1: Double Spend / Duplicate Payment

text
Client retries POST /payments on timeout
Without idempotency_key UNIQUE → two rows, double debit

Problem 2: Lost Audit Trail

text
Regulator asks: "Show all balance changes for account X in March"
Only mutable balance column → cannot prove history

Problem 3: Cross-Service Join Hell

text
payment-service JOIN ledger-service.accounts in SQL
Breaks microservice autonomy — 2PC temptation (Lesson 39)

Problem 4: DR Merge Collisions

text
BIGINT sequences in east and west after split → duplicate PKs
Need UUID or snowflake IDs + idempotency

Problem 5: Currency Errors

text
FLOAT rounding: 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3
USD amount stored without currency code → silent FX bugs

Problem 6: Delete vs Retain

text
Developer DELETE FROM payments — replicates to all replicas (L40)
Backup can PITR (L41) but prevention beats recovery — soft delete + retention policy

Unified Problem Statement

Payment schema must enforce financial integrity at the database boundary, support idempotent distributed workflows, preserve auditability, and align table ownership with service boundaries for HA/DR and saga/outbox patterns.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Deliberate Schema Design Matters

Database as Last Line of Defense

text
Application bugs happen
CHECK constraints, UNIQUE, FK still reject invalid money movement

Compliance

text
PCI: minimize PAN storage — token references only
AML: transaction history retained 5–7 years — schema supports archival partition
SOX: segregation — audit tables immutable

Operational Scale

text
payments table 500M rows/year — schema supports partition key from day one
Index design follows access paths — not after firefighting

Enables Reliability Patterns

text
Outbox table co-located with payments — same transaction (L37)
Saga state table tracks step + compensation (L38)
Idempotency table survives retry storms in DR (L42)

Part 5 — Internal Working

Schema Internals — How Design Maps to Engine Behavior

Primary Key Choice

text
UUID v4/v7 (random/time-sortable):
  ✅ DR merge safe, global uniqueness
  ❌ Wider indexes, more B-tree fragmentation than BIGINT

BIGINT identity:
  ✅ Compact, fast joins
  ❌ Per-region sequences collide after DR unless coordinated

COMPOSITE (tenant_id, payment_id):
  ✅ Multi-tenant partition-friendly
  Used in B2B payment platforms

Ledger Internals

text
Each ledger_entry row:
  entry_id (PK), account_id (FK), amount DECIMAL(19,4),
  direction DEBIT/CREDIT, entry_type, reference_id,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ, correlation_id

accounts.balance = materialized snapshot
  Updated in SAME transaction as ledger insert
  OR computed view (too slow at scale for hot path)

Double-entry (strict GL):
  Every transaction → one DEBIT row + one CREDIT row
  SUM(debits) = SUM(credits) — database CHECK via trigger or app

Idempotency Table Internals

text
idempotency_keys (
  idempotency_key VARCHAR(128) PRIMARY KEY,
  request_hash    BYTEA,
  response_status INT,
  response_body   JSONB,
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ,
  expires_at      TIMESTAMPTZ
)

Flow:
  INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING → if conflict, return stored response
  Prevents duplicate side effects

Outbox Table Internals (Lesson 37)

text
outbox_events (
  event_id     UUID PK,
  aggregate_type VARCHAR(50),
  aggregate_id VARCHAR(100),
  event_type   VARCHAR(100),
  payload      JSONB NOT NULL,
  created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ,
  published_at TIMESTAMPTZ NULL
)
Index: (published_at NULLS FIRST, created_at) — relay polling

Audit Trail Internals

text
Option A: audit table per entity (payments_audit)
Option B: generic audit_log(entity_type, entity_id, old_json, new_json)
Option C: DB trigger → append-only (Lesson 23)

Immutable: REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE on audit tables from app role
INSERT-only application grant

Soft Delete Internals

text
deleted_at TIMESTAMPTZ NULL
Partial unique index: UNIQUE(email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL

Query default: WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
Retention job: archive then hard delete after legal period

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Physical Storage Implications

Table Layout (PostgreSQL Example)

text
payments (heap)
  PK index: payments_pkey (B-tree on payment_id UUID)
  UNIQUE:   ux_payments_idempotency_key
  INDEX:    ix_payments_account_created (account_id, created_at DESC)
  INDEX:    ix_payments_status_created (status, created_at) WHERE status = 'PENDING'

ledger_entries (append-heavy)
  PK: entry_id
  INDEX: ix_ledger_account_time (account_id, created_at)
  Consider BRIN on created_at for very large append-only tables

Partitioning Hook (Lesson 30)

text
payments partitioned by RANGE (created_at) monthly
  payments_2026_07, payments_2026_08
Archival: DETACH PARTITION → cold storage

JSONB for Payload vs Normalized

text
outbox payload JSONB — flexible event schema — GIN index if query inside
Payment core fields normalized — amount, currency, status — never only JSON
Architect rule: money always columns, metadata can JSONB

Multi-Currency Storage

text
amount_minor BIGINT     -- store in smallest unit (cents, paise) — integer avoids float
currency_code CHAR(3)   -- ISO 4217
OR
amount DECIMAL(19,4) + currency_code CHAR(3)

fx_rate DECIMAL(18,8) NULL  -- if converted at capture time
fx_source VARCHAR(50)       -- ECB, partner rate id

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Schema Impact on Memory & Cache

Design choiceBuffer cache effect
Wide payment rowFewer rows per page — more I/O for list queries
Separate ledger tableHot account: index range scan — keep narrow indexes
JSONB payloadLarger tuples — TOAST off-row storage in PG
Over-indexingIndex pages compete with heap in shared_buffers
Materialized balanceSingle row UPDATE — hot row lock contention (L31)

Banking Tuning

text
List payments by account: covering index (account_id, created_at) INCLUDE (amount, status, currency_code)
Avoid SELECT * on ledger for UI — paginate with keyset (created_at, entry_id)

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Schema in Runtime Flows

Flow 1: Idempotent Payment Capture

text
1. API receives Idempotency-Key header + body
2. BEGIN
3. INSERT idempotency_keys ... ON CONFLICT → return cached response
4. INSERT payments (status=PENDING)
5. INSERT outbox_events (PaymentCreated)
6. COMMIT
7. Relay publishes Kafka event → ledger-service consumes

Flow 2: Ledger Update (Separate Service)

text
1. Consume PaymentCreated (idempotent consumer table processed_events)
2. BEGIN
3. INSERT ledger_entries (DEBIT customer, CREDIT settlement)
4. UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - amount WHERE account_id = ?
5. INSERT saga_step COMPLETED or outbox PaymentSettled
6. COMMIT

Flow 3: Soft Delete Customer (GDPR vs Retention)

text
1. customer.status = 'CLOSED', deleted_at = NOW()
2. PII columns anonymized — name = 'REDACTED', email = hash
3. payments/ledger rows RETAINED — legal hold flag
4. Partial unique allows email reuse for new customer later

Flow 4: DR Failover Reconciliation

text
1. Compare SUM(ledger_entries.amount) per account vs accounts.balance
2. Find duplicate idempotency_key from retry window
3. saga_state INCOMPLETE → trigger compensation (L38)

Flow 5: Multi-Currency Payment

text
1. INSERT payments (amount=10000, currency='INR', amount_usd_equiv=NULL)
2. FX service returns rate → UPDATE amount_usd_equiv for reporting only
3. Ledger always in account's native currency

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Schema Performance Trade-offs

Balance Snapshot vs Ledger-Only

ApproachRead balanceWrite paymentAudit
Balance column onlyO(1)O(1) updatePoor
Ledger sum onlyO(n entries)O(1) insertPerfect
Both (recommended)O(1)O(1) insert + updatePerfect

Idempotency Table Growth

text
TTL 24–72 hours for API idempotency keys — scheduled purge job
UNIQUE constraint on hot path — acceptable — one index lookup per payment

Audit Trigger Cost

text
Every UPDATE payments → INSERT audit row — 2× write amplification
Accept for compliance tier — async audit via CDC for high TPS optional

Index Budget

text
Payment platform OLTP:
  3–5 indexes per hot table max — each index slows INSERT
  Add index only for proven query path (Lesson 28 methodology)

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

OperationSchema designNotes
Idempotent insertO(log n) UNIQUE checkn = idempotency rows in TTL window
Balance readO(1) with snapshotO(k) if sum ledger k entries
Account statementO(log n + m)Index range m rows
Outbox relay pollO(batch)Partial index on unpublished
Soft delete filterO(1) extra predicatePartial indexes help
Cross-service joinAvoidedO(services) API calls instead

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Reference Schema — Payment Platform

Customers (customer-service)

sql
CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id     UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    external_ref    VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
    email           VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    full_name       VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    status          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE'
                    CHECK (status IN ('ACTIVE', 'SUSPENDED', 'CLOSED')),
    kyc_level       SMALLINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    deleted_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NULL,
    version         BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0  -- optimistic lock (L35)
);

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_customers_email_active
    ON customers (email)
    WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_customers_external_ref
    ON customers (external_ref);

Branches (branch-service)

sql
CREATE TABLE branches (
    branch_id       UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    branch_code     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    region          VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    daily_limit     DECIMAL(19,4) NOT NULL CHECK (daily_limit >= 0),
    currency_code   CHAR(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'USD',
    status          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE',
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

Accounts + Ledger (ledger-service)

sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id      UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id     UUID NOT NULL,  -- logical ref — no FK cross-DB
    branch_id       UUID NOT NULL,
    account_number  VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    account_type    VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL CHECK (account_type IN ('CHECKING', 'SAVINGS')),
    currency_code   CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
    balance         DECIMAL(19,4) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    status          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE',
    version         BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    CONSTRAINT chk_balance_sign CHECK (balance >= 0 OR account_type = 'CHECKING')
);

CREATE TABLE ledger_entries (
    entry_id        UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id      UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(account_id),
    transaction_id  UUID NOT NULL,
    entry_type      VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,  -- PAYMENT, DEPOSIT, REVERSAL, FEE
    direction       CHAR(6) NOT NULL CHECK (direction IN ('DEBIT', 'CREDIT')),
    amount          DECIMAL(19,4) NOT NULL CHECK (amount > 0),
    currency_code   CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
    balance_after   DECIMAL(19,4) NOT NULL,
    correlation_id  UUID NOT NULL,
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE INDEX ix_ledger_account_time ON ledger_entries (account_id, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX ix_ledger_correlation ON ledger_entries (correlation_id);

Payments + Idempotency + Outbox (payment-service)

sql
CREATE TABLE payments (
    payment_id          UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    idempotency_key     VARCHAR(128) NOT NULL,
    account_id          UUID NOT NULL,
    branch_id           UUID NOT NULL,
    amount              DECIMAL(19,4) NOT NULL CHECK (amount > 0),
    currency_code       CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
    status              VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING'
                        CHECK (status IN ('PENDING','CAPTURED','FAILED','REVERSED')),
    failure_reason      VARCHAR(255),
    saga_id             UUID,
    correlation_id      UUID NOT NULL,
    created_at          TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at          TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    version             BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_payments_idempotency ON payments (idempotency_key);
CREATE INDEX ix_payments_account_created ON payments (account_id, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX ix_payments_saga ON payments (saga_id) WHERE saga_id IS NOT NULL;

CREATE TABLE idempotency_records (
    idempotency_key     VARCHAR(128) PRIMARY KEY,
    request_hash        BYTEA NOT NULL,
    http_status         SMALLINT NOT NULL,
    response_body       JSONB NOT NULL,
    created_at          TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    expires_at          TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE outbox_events (
    event_id        UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    aggregate_type  VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    aggregate_id    VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    event_type      VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    payload         JSONB NOT NULL,
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    published_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NULL
);

CREATE INDEX ix_outbox_unpublished
    ON outbox_events (created_at)
    WHERE published_at IS NULL;

Transactions (reporting / aggregate view — optional read model)

sql
CREATE TABLE transactions (
    transaction_id  UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    payment_id      UUID,
    from_account_id UUID NOT NULL,
    to_account_id   UUID,
    amount          DECIMAL(19,4) NOT NULL,
    currency_code   CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
    txn_type        VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    status          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);

Audit Table

sql
CREATE TABLE payments_audit (
    audit_id        BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    payment_id      UUID NOT NULL,
    operation       VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
    old_row         JSONB,
    new_row         JSONB,
    changed_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    changed_by      VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE ON payments_audit FROM payment_app_role;
GRANT INSERT, SELECT ON payments_audit TO payment_app_role;

Saga State (payment-service or orchestrator)

sql
CREATE TABLE saga_instances (
    saga_id         UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    saga_type       VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    current_step    VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    status          VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL
                    CHECK (status IN ('RUNNING','COMPLETED','COMPENSATING','FAILED')),
    payload         JSONB NOT NULL,
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

Part 12 — Production Usage

Production Schema Practices

Bounded Context Ownership

text
┌─────────────────┬──────────────────────┬─────────────────┐
│ Service         │ Owns tables          │ Never owns      │
├─────────────────┼──────────────────────┼─────────────────┤
│ payment-service │ payments, outbox,    │ accounts.balance│
│                 │ idempotency, saga    │                 │
│ ledger-service  │ accounts, ledger     │ payments.status │
│ customer-svc    │ customers            │ ledger          │
│ branch-svc      │ branches             │ payments        │
└─────────────────┴──────────────────────┴─────────────────┘
Cross-boundary: Kafka events + REST read APIs — not FK across DBs

Migration Discipline

text
Flyway/Liquibase versioned migrations only
Expand-contract pattern for zero-downtime:
  1. ADD column nullable
  2. Deploy app writing both
  3. Backfill
  4. NOT NULL + cutover
  5. DROP old column
Pre-DR snapshot before risky migration (L41)

Retention & Archival

text
payments hot: 13 months online partitioned
Archive to payments_archive_2025 — query via federation or warehouse
Legal hold column: prevents purge per account/investigation

PCI / Sensitive Data

text
No PAN/CVV in payments table — store payment_method_token_ref only
Encrypt column-level for national ID if required — KMS keys

Idempotency Service

java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class IdempotencyService {

    @Transactional
    public Optional<PaymentResult> findExisting(String key, byte[] requestHash) {
        return idempotencyRepo.findById(key)
            .filter(r -> Arrays.equals(r.getRequestHash(), requestHash))
            .map(r -> deserialize(r.getResponseBody()));
    }

    @Transactional
    public void store(String key, byte[] hash, PaymentResult result) {
        idempotencyRepo.save(new IdempotencyRecord(
            key, hash, 200, serialize(result), Instant.now().plus(Duration.ofHours(24))
        ));
    }
}

Outbox in Same Transaction

java
@Transactional
public PaymentResult capture(CaptureCommand cmd) {
    if (idempotencyService.findExisting(cmd.key(), cmd.hash()).isPresent()) {
        return idempotencyService.findExisting(cmd.key(), cmd.hash()).get();
    }
    Payment payment = paymentRepo.save(Payment.pending(cmd));
    outboxRepo.save(OutboxEvent.paymentCreated(payment));
    PaymentResult result = PaymentResult.from(payment);
    idempotencyService.store(cmd.key(), cmd.hash(), result);
    return result;
}

Mistake 1: Balance Without Ledger

text

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: Why idempotency_key on payments?

Prevent duplicate charges when clients retry API on timeout or DR failover.

Q2: ledger_entries vs accounts.balance?

Ledger is append-only history; balance is snapshot for fast read — both in sync.

Q3: Why UUID for payment_id in microservices?

Global uniqueness — safe for DR merge and distributed generation.

Q4: Soft delete use case?

Customer PII anonymization while retaining payment records for law.

Q5: Why outbox_events table?

Atomic DB write + event intent — Lesson 37 — no dual-write.

Mid-Level

Q6: Design payments table for capture flow.

UUID PK, idempotency UNIQUE, amount DECIMAL, currency, status CHECK, version, saga_id, correlation_id, indexes on account+created.

Q7: Double-entry in schema?

ledger_entries with DEBIT/CREIT pairs linked by transaction_id — debits sum = credits sum.

Q8: Cross-service account validation without FK?

ledger API or cached AccountReadModel — eventual sync — saga on failure.

Q9: Multi-currency column design?

amount DECIMAL + currency_code CHAR(3) — never add USD amounts without rate metadata.

Q10: Partial unique index example?

UNIQUE(email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL.

Senior

Q11: Schema support for saga compensation?

saga_instances status, payment status REVERSED, ledger REVERSAL entries, idempotent consumers.

Q12: Partition payments table?

RANGE(created_at) monthly — detach archive — index per partition.

Q13: Audit — trigger vs application?

Trigger: DB-enforced, harder to test. App: flexible. Hybrid for Tier 0.

Staff / Architect

Q14: Reject shared database — what schema split?

payment / ledger / customer / branch — outbox per writer — no cross-DB FK.

Q15: GDPR + 7-year payment retention?

Anonymize customer PII soft delete — retain payments/ledger — legal_hold flag.

Scenario

Scenario: "Team adds account balance column updated from payment-service via JDBC."

Reject — violates bounded context — payment emits event; ledger-service owns balance + ledger in one transaction.
