Lesson 44

Sharding & Horizontal Scaling

Phase 5: DATABASE DESIGN & AVAILABILITY | Previous: Schema Design for Payment Platforms | Next: JPA Fundamentals & the Persistence Model

Availability
1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why This Exists5Internal Working6Storage Internals7Memory Usage8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Complexity Analysis11Code / SQL Examples12Production Usage13Spring Boot Integration14Hibernate/JPA Integration15Architect Perspective16Decision Matrix17Comparison Tables18Common Mistakes19Interview Questions20Revision Sheet21Summary Table*Practice

Part 1 — Concept

What Is Sharding?

Sharding (horizontal partitioning) splits data across multiple independent database instances so each shard holds a subset of rows. Applications route reads and writes to the correct shard using a shard key.

text
SINGLE PRIMARY (vertical scale limit)          SHARDED CLUSTER
────────────────────────────────────          ────────────────
┌─────────────────────────┐                   ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐
│ ONE PostgreSQL          │                   │ Shard 0  │ │ Shard 1  │ │ Shard 2  │
│ 800M payments/year      │                   │ cust A-M │ │ cust N-Z │ │ cust ... │
│ Writes + indexes bound  │                   │ own CPU  │ │ own CPU  │ │ own CPU  │
│ one machine ceiling     │                   │ own disk │ │ own disk │ │ own disk │
└─────────────────────────┘                   └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘
         │                                           ▲            ▲            ▲
         │                                           └────────────┴────────────┘
         │                                                 Router / Proxy
         └─ Partitioning (L30) = split INSIDE one DB     (customer_id % 3)
            Sharding = split ACROSS many DBs

Sharding vs Partitioning vs Replication

TechniqueScopePurpose
Partitioning (L30)One database, one engineManage size, prune old data, partition-wise joins
Replication (L40)Copy same data to replicasHA, read scale same dataset
Sharding (L44)Split dataset across primariesWrite scale, storage scale beyond one node

Shard Key

The column(s) used to decide which shard owns a row.

text
Good shard keys for payments:
  customer_id     — co-locate customer accounts + payments
  account_id        — co-locate ledger for one account
  tenant_id         — B2B SaaS payment platform
  region + customer — geo-sharding for data residency

Bad shard keys:
  payment_id UUID random — every query cross-shard unless known ID
  created_at only       — hot shard for "today"
  status                — skew (all PENDING on few shards)

Co-Location Rule

All rows that must join in one ACID transaction must live on the same shard.
text
SAME SHARD (OK — local transaction):
  accounts + ledger_entries + payments for customer_id = hash % N

CROSS SHARD (avoid ACID — use saga):
  transfer from account on shard 1 → account on shard 2

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Sharding

text
1990s   Oracle RAC — shared disk, not app-level sharding
        MySQL manual sharding — mod(user_id) in PHP — painful ops

2000s   Google Bigtable paper — range partitions at scale
        Flickr/MySQL shards — celebrity user hot spots documented

2010s   MongoDB sharded cluster — mongos router + config servers
        Vitess (YouTube) — MySQL sharding layer for Kubernetes
        Citus — PostgreSQL extension — distribute by tenant

2015+   AWS Aurora Limitless / DynamoDB partitions — managed sharding
        CockroachDB, Yugabyte — auto-reshard, distributed SQL
        Payment fintech: shard by merchant_id or account_id

2020s   Hybrid: single PostgreSQL until 10TB / 50k TPS — then Citus/Vitess
        Architects prefer "shard-ready schema" early — UUID + tenant_id
        Cross-shard sagas standard for P2P transfers at scale
        DR: shard-aware failover — not one global promote button

Historical Lesson

Sharding was the answer when one Postgres could not hold Uber's payments table. Today you shard later with clear keys and routing — or choose distributed SQL — but the co-location and cross-shard saga rules remain universal.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

When Does Single-Primary Break?

Problem 1: Write Throughput Ceiling

text
50,000 payment INSERTs/sec — one primary WAL + index maintenance maxed
Need: N shards × M writes each

Problem 2: Storage Size

text
payments + ledger_entries = 15 TB — backup/restore windows exceed RTO
Need: 5 shards × 3 TB each

Problem 3: Hot Row / Hot Partition

text
Celebrity account — millions of txns — even with partitioning one partition hot
Need: shard by account or sub-shard strategy

Problem 4: Regional Data Residency

text
EU customers must stay in EU — US shard vs EU shard
Regulatory boundary = shard boundary

Problem 5: Connection & Lock Contention

text
Single primary — max_connections, single lock manager bottleneck
Shards isolate blast radius

When NOT to Shard Yet

text
< 2 TB, < 5k writes/sec, team < 5 engineers
Fix: indexes, partitioning, read replicas, connection pool (L32)
Shard too early → permanent ops tax

Unified Problem Statement

Sharding horizontally scales writes and storage by splitting ownership across database instances — trading single-database simplicity for routing complexity, cross-shard workflows, and shard-aware operations.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Architects Introduce Shards

Scale Beyond One Machine

text
CPU, disk IOPS, WAL throughput — physical limits
N independent primaries ≈ N × write capacity (if key distribution even)

Fault Isolation

text
Shard 2 corruption — shards 0,1 still serve other customers
Blast radius contained — if routing correct

Cost Steps

text
One monster RDS db.r6g.16xlarge vs ten db.r6g.xlarge shards
Sometimes cheaper at extreme scale

Geographic Placement

text
Shard EU-West, Shard US-East — latency + compliance
Pairs with DR per shard (L42)

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Sharding Works Internally

Application-Level Sharding (Most Common)

text
1. Request arrives with customer_id
2. shard_id = consistent_hash(customer_id) % num_shards
   OR jump consistent hash (minimal remapping on add shard)
3. DataSource router picks JDBC pool for shard_id
4. SQL executes on single shard only
5. Cross-shard: application orchestrates 2+ connections — no global 2PC (L39)

Proxy / Middleware Sharding

text
Vitess, Citus coordinator, ProxySQL, mongos
Client sends SQL → proxy parses → routes to backend shards
Transparent to app — complex queries may scatter-gather

Consistent Hashing

text
Shards as ring — key hashes to next node
Add shard 4: only ~1/4 keys remap (vs mod N remaps ~all keys)
Used in: Cassandra (L57 preview), DynamoDB, custom routers

Scatter-Gather Query

text
SELECT SUM(amount) FROM payments WHERE created_at > '2026-07-01'
No shard key in WHERE → router queries ALL shards → merge results
Expensive — avoid in OLTP — use warehouse/read model

Rebalancing

text
Add shard 4 — split range from shard 2
Background migration: copy rows → dual-write → cutover → delete old
Downtime-free rebalance is hard — plan capacity headroom

Distributed SQL (Alternative Internal Model)

text
CockroachDB / Spanner: shard = range partition — auto-managed
SQL looks single-database — geo-replication built-in
Trade-off: cross-range txn latency, cost, vendor model

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Physical Layout Per Shard

Independent Database Instances

text
Shard 0: $PGDATA_0 / full schema — customers A–M subset
Shard 1: $PGDATA_1 / same schema DDL — customers N–Z subset
Each shard: own WAL, backups (L41), replicas (L40), DR copy (L42)

Schema Per Shard

text
Identical DDL on all shards (Flyway runs N times or automation)
No cross-shard FK — enforced in application/saga only
Global uniqueness: UUID PK or (shard_id, local_seq)

Citus Example (PostgreSQL Extension)

text
CREATE TABLE payments (...)
  DISTRIBUTE BY HASH (customer_id);

Coordinator node → metadata: which worker holds which hash range
Worker shards: payments_102008, payments_102009 ...
Local indexes per worker — not one global B-tree

Global Secondary Index Problem

text
UNIQUE(email) across shards — no single index
Solutions:
  Lookup service (DynamoDB global table style)
  Coordinator table: email → shard_id (extra write on register)
  Accept non-global unique — email unique per tenant only

Outbox Per Shard

text
Each shard has own outbox_events table
Relay process per shard OR router-aware relay
Kafka partition key = customer_id — aligns with shard key

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Memory at Shard Level

LayerEffect
Per-shard buffer cacheHot customers fit in RAM on their shard — not competing globally
App connection poolsPool per shard — total connections = shards × pool_size — watch limits
Router cacheMap customer_id → shard_id in Redis/local Caffeine
Scatter-gatherN shard result sets in app memory — O(N × rowsize)

Banking Pool Math

text
5 shards × Hikari max 30 = 150 app connections per service instance
3 app pods = 450 connections cluster-wide — each shard sees subset
Size pools per shard DataSource — not one giant pool

Part 8 — Execution Flow

End-to-End Sharded Flows

Flow 1: Single-Shard Payment (Happy Path)

text
1. POST /payments — customer_id in JWT
2. shard = router.resolve(customer_id)  → Shard 2
3. @Transactional on Shard 2 DataSource:
     INSERT payments, INSERT outbox_events
4. COMMIT — local ACID — fast
5. Outbox relay shard-2 → Kafka partition keyed by customer_id
6. Ledger on same shard (if co-located) OR saga to ledger shard

Flow 2: Cross-Shard P2P Transfer (Saga — L38)

text
Debit account A (shard 1) ── step 1 local txn
Credit account B (shard 3) ── step 2 local txn
If step 2 fails ── compensate: credit back A on shard 1

Schema:
  payments.saga_id links steps
  saga_instances on orchestrator DB or shard of payer

NO XA across shard 1 and shard 3 (L39)

Flow 3: Admin Report — Global SUM (Anti-Pattern OLTP)

text
1. Report service queries shard 0..4 in parallel
2. Each: SELECT SUM(amount) FROM payments WHERE date = today
3. App reduces partial sums
4. Better: stream to Snowflake/BigQuery — query warehouse not shards

Flow 4: Customer Migration Between Shards

text
1. Mark customer IN_MIGRATION — read-only in app
2. Copy rows shard 1 → shard 4 (batch)
3. Dual-write brief window OR maintenance window
4. Update router: customer_id → shard 4
5. Delete from shard 1
6. Reconcile counts

Flow 5: DR Failover — One Shard Region Lost

text
Shard group EU: shards 2,3 in eu-west-1
Region failure → promote EU shard replicas only
US shards 0,1 unaffected — partial outage not total platform
Router disables EU customers until promoted
RPO per shard group — not single global RPO

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Sharding Performance Trade-offs

Write Scale (Ideal Even Distribution)

text
1 shard:   8k INSERT/s max
4 shards: ~28–32k INSERT/s (not perfect 4× — overhead)
Skew: one hot customer → one shard maxed — others idle

Latency

text
Single-shard txn: same as non-sharded
Cross-shard saga: 2× round trips + failure handling — 2–10× latency
Scatter-gather report: O(shards) × query time

Shard Key Skew (Celebrity Problem)

text
10% of customers = 90% payments → hash by customer_id still skewed
Mitigations:
  sub-shard by account_id
  isolate hot tenants to dedicated shard (noisy neighbor)
  rate limit per customer

When Sharding Beats Partitioning Alone

text
Partitioning: one WAL, one checkpoint, one vacuum — shared bottleneck
Sharding: separate WAL per shard — true parallel write paths

Cost of Operations

text
Migrations × N shards
Backup × N
Monitoring × N
On-call complexity ↑↑ — justify with metrics

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

OperationSingle DBSharded
Point read by shard keyO(log n)O(log n/s) — same per shard
Insert paymentO(log n)O(log n/s) — one shard
Cross-shard transferO(1) txnO(saga steps) — 2+ txns
Global aggregateO(n)O(n) + O(s) scatter overhead
Add shardN/AO(rebalance keys) — painful
ReconciliationO(1) DBO(s) shards

Routing: O(1) hash lookup with cached map.

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Sharding Examples — Banking Domain

Shard Key in Schema (Lesson 43 extension)

sql
-- Every sharded table carries shard routing column (denormalized OK)
ALTER TABLE payments ADD COLUMN shard_id SMALLINT NOT NULL;

CREATE INDEX ix_payments_shard_customer
    ON payments (shard_id, customer_id, created_at DESC);

-- Co-located on same shard
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id    UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id   UUID NOT NULL,
    shard_id      SMALLINT NOT NULL,
    balance       DECIMAL(19,4) NOT NULL,
    ...
);

CREATE TABLE ledger_entries (
    entry_id      UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id    UUID NOT NULL,
    shard_id      SMALLINT NOT NULL,
    ...
);
-- Enforce co-location in app: account.shard_id == ledger.shard_id

Router Logic (Java)

java
public final class ShardRouter {
    private final int shardCount;
    private final List<DataSource> dataSources;

    public int resolveShard(UUID customerId) {
        int hash = Math.floorMod(customerId.hashCode(), shardCount);
        return hash;
    }

    public DataSource dataSourceForCustomer(UUID customerId) {
        return dataSources.get(resolveShard(customerId));
    }
}

Spring Multi-Shard Transaction Template

java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class ShardedPaymentService {
    private final ShardRouter router;
    private final PlatformTransactionManager txManager; // per-shard — see config

    @Transactional  // binds to current shard DataSource via ThreadLocal
    public PaymentResult capture(UUID customerId, CaptureCommand cmd) {
        // Aspect sets shard before @Transactional opens connection
        Payment p = paymentRepo.save(Payment.pending(customerId, cmd));
        outboxRepo.save(OutboxEvent.paymentCreated(p));
        return PaymentResult.from(p);
    }
}
java
@Aspect
@Component
@Order(0)
public class ShardRoutingAspect {
    @Before("@annotation(com.bank.RequiresShard)")
    public void bindShard(JoinPoint jp) {
        UUID customerId = extractCustomerId(jp);
        ShardContext.set(router.resolveShard(customerId));
    }
    @After("@annotation(com.bank.RequiresShard)")
    public void clear() { ShardContext.clear(); }
}

Cross-Shard Transfer Saga

java
public void transfer(UUID fromCustomer, UUID toCustomer, Money amount) {
    UUID sagaId = UUID.randomUUID();
    sagaRepo.start(sagaId, "P2P_TRANSFER", payload);

    try {
        debitOnShard(fromCustomer, sagaId, amount);   // shard A — local @Transactional
        creditOnShard(toCustomer, sagaId, amount);    // shard B — local @Transactional
        sagaRepo.complete(sagaId);
    } catch (Exception e) {
        compensateDebit(fromCustomer, sagaId, amount); // reverse shard A
        sagaRepo.fail(sagaId);
        throw e;
    }
}

Citus Distributed Table DDL

sql
-- Coordinator
SELECT create_distributed_table('payments', 'customer_id');
SELECT create_distributed_table('accounts', 'customer_id');
SELECT create_distributed_table('ledger_entries', 'customer_id');
-- Co-located on same worker when same distribution column

Avoid Cross-Shard SQL

sql
-- BAD on sharded OLTP — hits all shards
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM payments WHERE status = 'PENDING';

-- GOOD — shard key present
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM payments
WHERE customer_id = '...' AND status = 'PENDING';

-- Global analytics → ETL to warehouse

Lookup Table for Non-Shard Key Access

sql
-- Global index service table (small, may be separate highly-available DB)
CREATE TABLE customer_shard_lookup (
    customer_id  UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    shard_id     SMALLINT NOT NULL,
    updated_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);
-- On customer create: insert lookup in same txn as customer row OR async with saga

Part 12 — Production Usage

Sharding in Production Payment Platforms

Decision Gates — Shard or Not?

text
Shard when ALL true (example thresholds — tune per org):
  □ Primary write CPU > 70% sustained after tuning
  □ Storage > 5–10 TB OR backup window > RTO
  □ Single-table INSERT rate exceeds benchmark
  □ Finance approved ops cost for N-fold infra
  □ Team has on-call for router/saga failures

Wait when:
  □ Slow queries fixable by indexes (L26–28)
  □ Read-heavy — use replicas (L40)
  □ Old data — partition DETACH (L30)

Part 13 — Spring Boot Integration

Spring Boot with Sharded DataSources

Dynamic Routing DataSource

java
@Bean
public DataSource routingDataSource(List<DataSource> shardDataSources) {
    Map<Object, Object> targets = new HashMap<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < shardDataSources.size(); i++) {
        targets.put(i, shardDataSources.get(i));
    }
    ShardRoutingDataSource ds = new ShardRoutingDataSource();
    ds.setTargetDataSources(targets);
    ds.setDefaultTargetDataSource(shardDataSources.get(0));
    return ds;
}

public class ShardRoutingDataSource extends AbstractRoutingDataSource {
    @Override
    protected Object determineCurrentLookupKey() {
        return ShardContext.get().orElseThrow(() ->
            new IllegalStateException("Shard not set"));
    }
}

Transaction Manager — One Per Shard or Chained (Avoid Chained for ACID)

java
@Bean
public PlatformTransactionManager transactionManager(
        @Qualifier("routingDataSource") DataSource ds) {
    return new DataSourceTransactionManager(ds);
}
// Cross-shard: separate programmatic transactions — saga — not @Transactional on both

Health Checks

java
@Component
public class ShardHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {
    public Health health() {
        for (int i = 0; i < shardCount; i++) {
            if (!pingShard(i)) return Health.down().withDetail("shard", i).build();
        }
        return Health.up().build();
    }
}

Flyway on N Shards

text
CI pipeline: for shard in 0..N-1; flyway migrate -url=shard$i
Schema version must match across shards — drift detection job

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

JPA with Sharded Databases

Single Persistence Unit, Routed DataSource

text
Hibernate sees one logical DataSource — routing transparent
Entities unchanged from L43 — add shardId column for debugging/audit

Never Lazy-Load Across Shards

java
// DANGEROUS if Payment and Account on different shards
@ManyToOne(fetch = LAZY)
Account account;  // may open wrong shard session

// RIGHT: store UUIDs only — load explicitly on correct shard

@Transactional Scope = One Shard

java
@RequiresShard
@Transactional
public void capture(UUID customerId, CaptureCommand cmd) {
    // entire method one shard — OK
}

// Cross-shard: two methods, two @Transactional with manual shard context switch
public void crossShardTransfer(...) {
    ShardContext.set(shardA);
    transactionalTemplateA.execute(status -> debit(...));
    ShardContext.set(shardB);
    transactionalTemplateB.execute(status -> credit(...));
}

Second-Level Cache Per Shard

text
Cache key must include shard_id — else collision
Prefer Redis cluster with key prefix shard:{id}:entity:{pk}

Hibernate @GeneratedValue on Sharded DB

text
Avoid global sequences — use UUID or (shard_id, local_bigserial)
Snowflake IDs embed datacenter + worker — shard-friendly

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: Sharding vs replication?

Sharding splits data across primaries for write scale; replication copies same data for HA/read scale.

Q2: What is a shard key?

Column determining which shard stores a row — e.g. customer_id.

Q3: Why co-locate account and ledger?

Same-shard local ACID — one transaction for debit + ledger entry.

Q4: Cross-shard transfer without 2PC?

Saga: debit shard A, credit shard B, compensate on failure.

Q5: Sharding vs partitioning?

Partitioning inside one DB; sharding across multiple DB instances.

Mid-Level

Q6: Celebrity skew problem?

Hot key overloads one shard — dedicated shard, sub-key, rate limits.

Q7: Global report on sharded DB?

Parallel scatter-gather or ETL to warehouse — not OLTP path.

Q8: How outbox works with sharding?

Table per shard; relay per shard; Kafka key aligns with shard key.

Q9: UUID payment_id routing issue?

Need customer_id in query or lookup table — don't shard by random UUID alone.

Q10: Add fifth shard — what breaks?

Hash mod N remaps keys — use consistent hashing or rebalance migration.

Senior

Q11: Design 4-shard payment platform for 40k TPS.

customer_id hash, co-locate payments/accounts/ledger/outbox, saga P2P, per-shard HA/backup, warehouse for reports, idempotency on API.

Q12: Sharding vs Cockroach for core ledger?

Sharding: control, Postgres, saga cost. Cockroach: global txn simpler, cost/latency trade-offs.

Q13: DR with sharded EU/US?

Independent shard groups, regional failover, router disables failed region, reconcile per shard.

Staff / Architect

Q14: When reject sharding proposal?

Data size 1 TB, team small, cross-shard join workload, no skew metrics — tune first.

Q15: Shard-ready schema without sharding?

UUID PKs, customer_id on all tables, no cross-service FK, outbox/saga tables day one.

Scenario

Scenario: "P2P transfer loses money — credit succeeded, debit compensated twice."

Saga idempotency missing on compensate step — add idempotency_key per saga step.

Part 1 — Concept

What Is JPA?

JPA (Java Persistence API) is the Java standard for object-relational mapping (ORM). It defines annotations, APIs, and rules for mapping Java objects (entities) to relational tables and for reading/writing them through a EntityManager.

Hibernate is the most widely used JPA implementation in Spring Boot. When you use Spring Data JPA, you are using JPA API + Hibernate engine under the hood.

text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Spring Boot Application                                         │
│  @RestController → @Service → @Repository (Spring Data)          │
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │
                             ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  JPA API (standard)                                              │
│  EntityManager · EntityTransaction · @Entity · @Id · JPQL       │
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │
                             ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Hibernate (implementation)                                      │
│  Session · Persistence Context · SQL generation · L2 cache       │
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │ JDBC
                             ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  PostgreSQL / Oracle / DB2  (+ routing: shard / replica)         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Core JPA Concepts

ConceptMeaning
EntityJava class mapped to a table row
EntityManagerPrimary JPA API — load, persist, merge, remove, query
Persistence ContextFirst-level cache of managed entities within a transaction
Persistence UnitSet of entities + DataSource config (persistence.xml or Spring auto-config)
JPQLObject-oriented query language — queries entities, not tables
ProviderHibernate, EclipseLink, etc.

Entity Lifecycle States (Preview — deep dive L46)

text
                    persist()
         NEW ─────────────────► MANAGED
          ▲                         │
          │                         │ flush / commit
          │ detach()                ▼
         DETACHED ◄────────────── REMOVED
          │                         ▲
          └─────── merge() ─────────┘

Part 2 — History

Evolution of JPA and ORM in Java

text
1990s   EJB Entity Beans — heavy, container-managed, widely hated
2001    Hibernate 2 — lightweight ORM — XML mappings, HQL
2006    JPA 1.0 (Java EE 5) — standardize ORM — annotations
        Hibernate becomes reference implementation via EntityManager
2009    JPA 2.0 — Criteria API, Bean Validation integration, `@ElementCollection`
2013    JPA 2.1 — stored procedures, entity graphs, converters
2017    JPA 2.2 — Java 8 time API, stream on Query
2020+   JPA 3.0/3.1 (Jakarta EE) — `jakarta.persistence.*` namespace
        Spring Boot 3 — Jakarta Persistence 3.1 + Hibernate 6.x
        Spring Data JPA — repository abstraction over EntityManager

Enterprise banking:
  2000s monolith EJB + Hibernate + Oracle
  2010s Spring Boot + JPA per microservice + one schema each (L43)
  2020s Hibernate 6 SQL AST, better batching — still need SQL fundamentals (Phase 2–3)

Historical Lesson

JPA succeeded because it standardized what Hibernate pioneered. As architect you still treat JPA as a persistence layer, not a substitute for schema design, transactions, indexes, and sharding — those remain your responsibility.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problem Does JPA Solve?

Problem 1: JDBC Boilerplate

text
Without JPA:
  map ResultSet → Payment object manually
  build INSERT with 15 columns
  handle nulls, timestamps, UUIDs

With JPA:
  paymentRepo.save(payment) — mapping declarative via @Entity

Problem 2: Object-Relational Impedance Mismatch

text
Java: inheritance, references, collections
SQL: tables, FKs, no real collections
JPA maps gap — @OneToMany, @Embedded, converters

Problem 3: Consistent Persistence Across Services

text
Standard annotations — developers portable between teams
Spring Data reduces repository boilerplate

Problem 4: Transaction-Scoped Consistency

text
EntityManager participates in Spring `@Transactional` (L33–34)
Same persistence context sees consistent snapshot within txn

What JPA Does NOT Solve

text
❌ Cross-shard ACID (L44) — routing is separate
❌ Read replica lag (L40) — routing DataSource
❌ Query optimization (Phase 3) — JPQL can still generate bad SQL
❌ Global idempotency — still schema + service design (L43)

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why the Industry Uses JPA

Developer Productivity

text
CRUD microservices — 80% boilerplate eliminated
Focus on payment rules, not JDBC string building

Maintainability

text
Schema change → update @Entity + Flyway — compile-time checks
Refactoring tools work on entity fields

Integration with Java Ecosystem

text
Bean Validation (@NotNull on entities)
Jackson DTO separation — entities not exposed on REST (best practice)
Spring `@Transactional` declarative boundaries

Portability (Theoretical)

text
Switch EclipseLink for Hibernate — rare in practice
Standard JPQL portable — native SQL is not

Part 5 — Internal Working

How JPA Works Internally (Hibernate)

Bootstrapping

text
1. Spring Boot scans @Entity classes
2. Builds SessionFactory (Hibernate) — metadata for all entities
3. Creates EntityManager proxy per `@Transactional` method (thread-bound)
4. EntityManager delegate = Hibernate Session

persist() Flow

text
1. paymentRepo.save(p)  →  em.persist(p) or merge if detached
2. Entity enters MANAGED persistence context (L1 cache)
3. SQL not sent yet — deferred until flush
4. @Transactional commit → flush() → INSERT SQL generated
5. JDBC via connection from DataSource (possibly routed shard/replica)
6. COMMIT

Flush Modes

text
AUTO (default): SQL before query if needed + at commit
COMMIT: SQL only at commit — surprise stale query reads in same txn
MANUAL: you call flush() — batch jobs

SQL Generation

text
Hibernate ORM 6 — SQL AST translator
@Entity Payment → INSERT INTO payments (payment_id, amount, ...) VALUES (?, ?, ...)
Dirty checking: compare managed entity field snapshots at flush → UPDATE changed columns only

Persistence Context (First-Level Cache)

text
Same @Transactional method:
  em.find(Payment.class, id)  — SELECT once
  em.find(Payment.class, id)  — returns cached MANAGED instance — no second SELECT

Different transaction:
  new persistence context — fresh SELECT

Spring Data JPA Layer

text
interface PaymentRepository extends JpaRepository<Payment, UUID> {}

Proxy implementation:
  @Transactional read methods → SimpleJpaRepository → EntityManager
  Derived query methods → parse method name → JPQL
  @Query → JPQL or native SQL

Integration with Phase 4–5 Infrastructure

text
@Transactional + routing DataSource (L40 read replica):
  readOnly=true → READER connection → EntityManager uses replica

ShardContext (L44) set before @Transactional:
  EntityManager gets connection from shard N only

Outbox (L37): same EntityManager/session persists Payment + OutboxEvent in one flush

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Entity Mapping → Physical Storage

Table Mapping

java
@Entity
@Table(name = "payments", indexes = {
    @Index(name = "ix_payments_account_created", columnList = "account_id, created_at")
})
public class Payment { ... }

Maps to heap file + B-tree indexes on disk (Lesson 4). JPA does not change storage — your DDL and indexes dominate performance.

ID Generation and Disk

java
@Id
@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.UUID)
private UUID paymentId;
// Random UUID — index page splits — acceptable at payment scale with L43 design

@Id
@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "pay_seq")
@SequenceGenerator(name = "pay_seq", sequenceName = "payments_seq", allocationSize = 50)
private Long id;
// Sequential — better index locality — allocationSize reduces round trips

Column Types

java
@Column(precision = 19, scale = 4)
private BigDecimal amount;   // → DECIMAL(19,4) — never double

@Column(columnDefinition = "TIMESTAMPTZ")
private Instant createdAt;   // → PostgreSQL timestamptz

Lob and JSON

java
@JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON)
private Map<String, Object> metadata;  // Hibernate 6 — JSONB in PostgreSQL
// TOAST storage for large JSON off-page in PG

Part 7 — Memory Usage

JPA Memory Model

ComponentScopeMemory
Persistence context (L1)Per EntityManager / txnOne managed copy per entity PK in txn
SessionFactory metadataJVM singletonEntity graphs, metamodel — fixed overhead
Query plan cacheSessionFactoryParsed JPQL/Criteria plans
Second-level cache (L52 preview)Cluster optionalShared entity regions — Redis/Ehcache
JDBC ResultSetDuring queryStreaming vs getResultList() loads all — O(n) heap

Banking Hot Path

text
@Transactional capture payment:
  1 Payment + 1 OutboxEvent in persistence context — tiny

Anti-pattern:
  findAll() on 2M payments for report — OOM
  Use pagination, projection DTO, or JDBC/replica (L40)

Dirty Checking Cost

text
Hibernate tracks dirty fields per managed entity at flush
Large persistence context (1000 entities in one txn) — flush slow
Keep transaction scope small (L33) — one payment + outbox, not batch 5000 without chunking

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Execution Flows with JPA in Payment Platform

Flow 1: Standard Capture (Single Shard, Primary)

text
1. Controller → PaymentService.capture()
2. @Transactional starts — EntityManager opened — ShardContext shard 2
3. DataSource routes to primary shard 2
4. idempotency check via repository.findByIdempotencyKey()
5. em.persist(new Payment(...))  — MANAGED
6. em.persist(new OutboxEvent(...)) — MANAGED
7. Method returns — flush → 2 INSERTs — COMMIT
8. EntityManager closed — entities DETACHED

Flow 2: Read Replica Report Query

text
1. @Transactional(readOnly = true) on BranchReportService
2. RoutingDataSource → READER
3. em.createQuery("SELECT ... FROM Payment p WHERE ...", Dto.class)
4. Hibernate: SELECT — no INSERT flush — connection read-only hint optional
5. Result may be stale vs primary (L40) — acceptable for branch summary

Flow 3: Optimistic Lock Failure (L35)

text
1. Account entity loaded — version = 5
2. Concurrent txn commits version = 6
3. This txn flush UPDATE ... WHERE version = 5 → 0 rows
4. OptimisticLockException — Spring wraps — retry or 409 to client

Flow 4: Lazy Loading Trap (Outside Transaction)

text
1. @Transactional method returns Payment entity (DETACHED)
2. Controller accesses payment.getLedgerEntries() — LAZY
3. LazyInitializationException — no Session
Fix: @Transactional(readOnly=true) on service returning DTO, or JOIN FETCH in query (L54 preview)

Flow 5: Sharded Wrong Context

text
1. ShardContext not set — defaults shard 0
2. Payment for customer on shard 3 written to shard 0
3. Data corruption — router aspect must run BEFORE EntityManager opens

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

JPA Performance Considerations

When JPA Is Fast Enough

text
Single-entity CRUD, simple JPQL by indexed columns
Batch insert with `hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50` + ordering
Spring Data pagination with LIMIT

When JPA Hurts

text
N+1 lazy loads (L53 preview) — 1 + N SELECTs
Cartesian product JOIN FETCH on two `@OneToMany` collections
Select entire entity when only 2 columns needed
Default flush before every JPQL query in long txn

Tuning Knobs (application.yml)

yaml
spring:
  jpa:
    properties:
      hibernate:
        jdbc:
          batch_size: 50
        order_inserts: true
        order_updates: true
        generate_statistics: false  # true only when profiling
    show-sql: false  # never true in prod — use logging bind params sampled

JPA vs JDBC for Hot Path

text
Architect rule:
  Default JPA for service CRUD + maintainability
  Native SQL / JDBC for bulk reconciliation, regulatory extract, COPY ingest
  Not either/or — hybrid in same service via @Query(nativeQuery=true) or JdbcTemplate

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

OperationJPA typicalNotes
em.find by PKO(1) cache hit / O(log n) index lookupn = table size
persist one entityO(1) memory + O(1) INSERT at flush
Dirty flush k entitiesO(k) field compare + O(k) SQL
JPQL without limitO(n) rows loadedMemory O(n)
Derived query parseO(1) after cachedFirst call parses method name

Transaction length: O(entities managed) — keep small.

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

JPA Mapping — Payment Schema (Lesson 43)

Payment Entity

java
@Entity
@Table(name = "payments")
public class Payment {

    @Id
    @Column(name = "payment_id", nullable = false, updatable = false)
    private UUID paymentId;

    @Column(name = "idempotency_key", nullable = false, unique = true, length = 128)
    private String idempotencyKey;

    @Column(name = "account_id", nullable = false)
    private UUID accountId;

    @Column(name = "branch_id", nullable = false)
    private UUID branchId;

    @Column(nullable = false, precision = 19, scale = 4)
    private BigDecimal amount;

    @Column(name = "currency_code", nullable = false, length = 3)
    private String currencyCode;

    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 20)
    private PaymentStatus status;

    @Column(name = "correlation_id", nullable = false)
    private UUID correlationId;

    @Column(name = "saga_id")
    private UUID sagaId;

    @Version
    @Column(nullable = false)
    private Long version;

    @Column(name = "created_at", nullable = false, updatable = false)
    private Instant createdAt;

    @Column(name = "updated_at", nullable = false)
    private Instant updatedAt;

    @PrePersist
    void onCreate() {
        if (paymentId == null) paymentId = UUID.randomUUID();
        Instant now = Instant.now();
        createdAt = now;
        updatedAt = now;
        if (status == null) status = PaymentStatus.PENDING;
    }

    @PreUpdate
    void onUpdate() {
        updatedAt = Instant.now();
    }
}

EntityManager Usage (Explicit — Rare with Spring Data)

java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class ManualPaymentWriter {
    @PersistenceContext
    private EntityManager em;

    @Transactional
    public Payment capture(CaptureCommand cmd) {
        Payment p = new Payment();
        p.setIdempotencyKey(cmd.key());
        p.setAccountId(cmd.accountId());
        p.setAmount(cmd.amount());
        p.setCurrencyCode(cmd.currency());
        em.persist(p);

        OutboxEvent evt = OutboxEvent.paymentCreated(p);
        em.persist(evt);

        return p; // flushed at commit
    }
}

Spring Data Repository

java
public interface PaymentRepository extends JpaRepository<Payment, UUID> {
    Optional<Payment> findByIdempotencyKey(String idempotencyKey);

    @Query("""
        SELECT p FROM Payment p
        WHERE p.accountId = :accountId
          AND p.createdAt >= :from
        ORDER BY p.createdAt DESC
        """)
    List<Payment> findRecentByAccount(
        @Param("accountId") UUID accountId,
        @Param("from") Instant from,
        Pageable pageable);
}

JPQL vs Native SQL

java
// JPQL — portable — uses entity names
@Query("SELECT COUNT(p) FROM Payment p WHERE p.status = :status")
long countByStatus(@Param("status") PaymentStatus status);

// Native — use for index-specific hints, window functions
@Query(value = """
    SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at) AS day, SUM(amount)
    FROM payments
    WHERE branch_id = :branchId
    GROUP BY 1
    """, nativeQuery = true)
List<Object[]> dailyTotals(@Param("branchId") UUID branchId);

Part 12 — Production Usage

JPA in Production Banking Microservices

Standard Service Layout

text
payment-service/
  domain/     — @Entity classes (Payment, OutboxEvent, IdempotencyRecord)
  repo/       — Spring Data interfaces
  service/    — @Transactional business logic
  api/        — REST DTOs — never expose @Entity directly
  config/     — DataSource routing, shard aspect, Flyway

ddl-auto Policy

yaml
spring:
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate   # PRODUCTION ONLY validate or none
  flyway:
    enabled: true
# NEVER update/create in prod — Flyway owns schema (L43)

One Persistence Unit Per Service

text
payment-service: entities Payment, OutboxEvent only
ledger-service:  entities Account, LedgerEntry only
No single persistence.xml spanning two databases

Observability

text
log Hibernate SQL at DEBUG only sampled
Micrometer + datasource metrics per shard
Trace span: @Transactional boundary — OpenTelemetry
Alert: OptimisticLockException rate, LazyInitializationException (bug indicator)

Production Checklist

text
□ ddl-auto=validate
□ Flyway version matches deployed entities
□ BigDecimal for money
□ UUID or sequence strategy documented for DR (L42)
□ No open-session-in-view (see below)
□ Batch size configured for bulk outbox relay if batch persist
□ open-in-view: false (Spring Boot 2.2+ default)

@Service

Open Session In View (OSIV) — Disabled

text
Default Spring Boot: spring.jpa.open-in-view=false

OSIV=true (legacy):
  Keeps EntityManager open entire HTTP request — lazy loads in view layer
  Hides N+1, long transactions, connection pool hold — BAD for payment APIs

Architect policy: OSIV false — fetch in service layer into DTO

Integration with Shard Router (L44)

java
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface RequiresShard {}

@Aspect
@Component
@Order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)
public class ShardAspect {
    @Before("@annotation(RequiresShard) && args(customerId,..)")
    public void setShard(UUID customerId) {
        ShardContext.set(router.resolveShard(customerId));
    }
    @After("@annotation(RequiresShard)")
    public void clear() { ShardContext.clear(); }
}

@Service
public class PaymentService {
    @RequiresShard
    @Transactional
    public PaymentResult capture(UUID customerId, CaptureCommand cmd) { ... }
}

Integration with Read Replica (L40)

java
public class RoutingDataSource extends AbstractRoutingDataSource {
    @Override
    protected Object determineCurrentLookupKey() {
        return TransactionSynchronizationManager.isCurrentTransactionReadOnly()
            ? DataSourceType.READER : DataSourceType.WRITER;
    }
}
// EntityManager inherits routed connection automatically

Solution Architect View

JPA in Microservice Boundaries

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: ddl-auto=update in Production

text
Hibernate alters schema unpredictably — Flyway bypassed — audit fail

Mistake 2: Exposing @Entity on REST

text
JSON infinite loop on bidirectional `@OneToMany`
LazyInitializationException or accidental N+1

Mistake 3: @Transactional on Repository Only

text
Service calls two repos without txn — two transactions — outbox not atomic with payment
Put `@Transactional` on service capture method

Mistake 4: Wrong Shard Before EM Opens

text
Routing aspect order wrong — data on wrong shard

Mistake 5: Read Replica + Write in Same readOnly Txn

text
readOnly=true routes to replica — UPDATE fails or worse read-only error storm

Mistake 6: Using double for Money

text
Rounding bugs — always BigDecimal

Mistake 7: Long @Transactional Including HTTP Call

text
Connection held — pool exhaustion (L32) — never call REST inside txn

Mistake 8: Assuming findById Always Hits DB

text
Same txn second find — cache — stale if native SQL updated same row bypassing EM

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is JPA?

Java standard ORM API — entities, EntityManager, JPQL. Hibernate is common implementation.

Q2: EntityManager vs SessionFactory?

SessionFactory is factory singleton; EntityManager is per-request/transaction persistence context API.

Q3: What does @Transactional do for JPA?

Starts transaction, binds EntityManager, commits/rollback at method end.

Q4: persist vs merge?

persist: NEW → MANAGED. merge: DETACHED → MANAGED copy, returns managed instance.

Q5: Why ddl-auto=validate in prod?

Schema owned by Flyway — Hibernate only verifies mapping matches DB.

Mid-Level

Q6: Persistence context first-level cache behavior?

Same txn repeated find by PK — one SELECT — same Java instance.

Q7: open-in-view false — why?

Avoid long transactions and lazy load in web layer — fetch in service to DTO.

Q8: Map Payment entity without @ManyToOne Account cross-service?

Store accountId UUID — ledger service owns Account — microservice boundary.

Q9: JPA with read replica routing?

readOnly @Transactional + routing DataSource — EntityManager uses replica connection.

Q10: Optimistic lock with @Version?

UPDATE checks version — concurrent modification → OptimisticLockException.

Senior

Q11: Outbox + payment same transaction in JPA?

One @Transactional service method — persist Payment + OutboxEvent — one flush — one COMMIT.

Q12: Sharding + JPA design?

Routing DataSource + ThreadLocal shard before txn — one EM one shard — cross-shard saga outside single @Transactional.

Q13: When native SQL over JPQL?

Reporting aggregates, DB-specific features, bulk operations, performance-critical paths with known plan.

Staff / Architect

Q14: JPA in every microservice — trade-offs?

Productivity vs SQL visibility — mandate EXPLAIN reviews for hot paths, hybrid JDBC, no OSIV, Flyway validate.

Q15: Entity design for idempotency + DR?

UUID PK, unique idempotencyKey, correlationId, version, no cross-DB FK — aligns L43 schema.

Scenario

Scenario: "LazyInitializationException on payment.getAccount() in controller."

OSIV off — lazy outside txn — fix: JOIN FETCH in service or load DTO with accountId only.

Part 1 — Concept

Entity Lifecycle States

Every JPA entity instance is in exactly one lifecycle state at any moment. The persistence context (Hibernate Session first-level cache) tracks MANAGED entities and synchronizes them with the database at flush time.

text
                         persist()
              ┌──────────────────────────────┐
              │                              ▼
         ┌────────┐                    ┌──────────┐
         │  NEW   │                    │ MANAGED  │◄────── merge()
         └────────┘                    └────┬─────┘         (detached → managed copy)
              ▲                             │
              │                             │ remove()
              │                             ▼
              │                        ┌──────────┐
              │     detach() /         │ REMOVED  │
              │     close txn          └────┬─────┘
              │                             │
              │         flush DELETE        │
              ▼                             │
         ┌──────────┐                       │
         │ DETACHED │───────────────────────┘
         └──────────┘   (removed entity often
                         becomes DETACHED after flush if txn continues)

State Definitions

StateIn persistence context?DB row exists?Dirty checking?
NEWNo (until persist)NoNo
MANAGEDYesUsually yesYes
DETACHEDNoUsually yesNo
REMOVEDYes (until flush)Until DELETE flushN/A

Persistence Context

text
One @Transactional method ≈ one persistence context (one EntityManager scope)

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Persistence Context (L1 cache)                          │
│  Map<PK, Managed Entity Instance>                        │
│  Identity guarantee: same PK → same Java object in txn   │
│                                                          │
│  paymentId=abc → Payment@7f3a  (MANAGED)                 │
│  eventId=xyz   → OutboxEvent@9b2c (MANAGED)              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         │ flush() at commit
         ▼
    INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE SQL

Part 2 — History

Why Lifecycle Management Exists

text
Early Hibernate (2001):
  Session as unit of work — entities attached/detached manually
  Developers confused when SQL ran

JPA 1.0 (2006):
  Standardized persist/remove/merge/detach
  EntityManager as Session wrapper

EJB 3.0 pattern:
  Extended persistence context — stateful — mostly abandoned in REST

Spring Boot era:
  Transaction-scoped EntityManager — request/service boundary
  open-in-view disabled — DETACHED errors exposed bad layering

Microservices + saga (2015+):
  Each saga step = new txn = new persistence context
  merge() bugs appear when reusing detached entities across Kafka consumers

DR failover (2020+):
  Client retries → idempotency + understanding NEW vs MANAGED prevents duplicate persist

Historical Lesson

Most production JPA bugs are lifecycle bugs — not missing annotations. Architects enforce transaction boundaries, DTO boundaries, and idempotency because DETACHED and duplicate MANAGED instances cause silent data corruption or duplicate payments.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does Lifecycle Understanding Solve?

Problem 1: LazyInitializationException

text
DETACHED entity → access lazy collection → no Session → crash

Problem 2: Duplicate INSERT on Retry

text
DR failover retry calls persist() on already-committed entity still NEW in memory
Or merge() creates unexpected INSERT

Problem 3: Lost Updates

text
Two DETACHED copies of Account — merge order wrong — last merge wins — balance wrong

Problem 4: Cascade Deletes Payment History

text
CascadeType.ALL on wrong association → DELETE customer cascades payments

Problem 5: SQL Surprises

text
Think save() immediately hits DB — actually flush at commit — constraint violation late

Problem 6: Saga Step State Confusion

text
Step 2 Kafka consumer loads entity — new persistence context — must idempotent merge not blind persist

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Not Hit DB on Every Setter?

Performance

text
Change 10 fields on MANAGED Payment → one UPDATE at flush with changed columns only
Not 10 UPDATE statements

Identity Map Consistency

text
Same txn:
  repo.findById(id) and repo.findByIdempotencyKey(key) same row
  Without identity map — two Java objects — inconsistent in-memory state

Write-Behind Semantics

text
Batch ordering: INSERT payment before INSERT outbox — FK order preserved at flush
hibernate.order_inserts helps

Atomic Unit of Work

text
All MANAGED changes flush → one COMMIT — ACID (L33) within single shard (L44)

Part 5 — Internal Working

Internal Mechanics (Hibernate)

EntityEntry / State Tracking

text
Each MANAGED entity has EntityEntry in persistence context:
  status: MANAGED | DELETED | ...
  loadedState[] snapshot at load time
  dirtyFields[] computed at flush by comparing current vs loadedState
  version field for optimistic lock

persist() Internals

text
1. Validate entity is NEW (not already MANAGED with same identity)
2. Assign ID if @GeneratedValue / @PrePersist UUID
3. Register in persistence context — MANAGED
4. Schedule INSERT at flush — not immediate unless flush() called
5. Cascade PERSIST to associated entities if configured

merge() Internals

text
Input: DETACHED (or NEW with existing PK) entity
1. Check persistence context for existing MANAGED instance by PK
2. If found: copy non-null fields from detached onto MANAGED instance
3. If not found: SELECT by PK — if row exists load MANAGED; else treat as new INSERT
4. Returns MANAGED instance — caller must use return value (input still DETACHED)

CRITICAL: paymentRepo.save(detached) in Spring Data → merge if id assigned

remove() Internals

text
1. Entity must be MANAGED (or merge first)
2. Mark REMOVED in context
3. DELETE at flush
4. After flush: often still in context as hollow or evicted depending on config

detach() / clear() / close

text
em.detach(payment)  — payment → DETACHED, evicted from context
em.clear()          — all entities DETACHED
txn commit/rollback — EntityManager closed — all DETACHED

Flush Algorithm (Simplified)

text
1. Before query (AUTO flush mode): flush dirty entities if query might stale-read
2. Order: INSERTs → UPDATEs → DELETEs (with dependency sorting)
3. Execute batch if batch_size configured
4. Increment @Version on successful UPDATE
5. Constraint violations throw here — txn may rollback

FlushModeType

text
AUTO   — default — flush before query + at commit
COMMIT — only at commit — risk: JPQL SELECT doesn't see unflushed changes in same txn
MANUAL — explicit flush() — bulk ETL patterns

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Lifecycle Events → Disk

NEW → MANAGED → Flush INSERT

text
Java: new Payment() — heap only
persist() — registered in persistence context heap structures
flush INSERT — WAL record on PostgreSQL — row in payments heap file + index pages
commit — WAL fsync durable (L33)

MANAGED Dirty Flush UPDATE

text
balance 1000 → 900 in memory
Dirty check at flush: UPDATE accounts SET balance=900, version=6 WHERE id=? AND version=5
Row-level lock held since transaction start if row was read for update (depends isolation L34)

REMOVED Flush DELETE

text
em.remove(payment) — logical REMOVED in context
flush DELETE FROM payments WHERE payment_id=?
Banking: prefer status=REVERSED UPDATE over remove() — L43

merge() Extra SELECT

text
DETACHED Payment with id — merge may SELECT first to load MANAGED copy
Extra round trip — performance cost on hot retry paths
Idempotent consumer: check exists first — avoid redundant merge SELECT

Identity vs UUID Storage (Lesson 45 preview — depth here)

text
IDENTITY / SEQUENCE:
  Sequential inserts — B-tree index friendly — fewer page splits on PK index
  IDENTITY: insert batching harder — Hibernate may defer until flush per row

UUID random:
  Insert random key order — index fragmentation — acceptable at moderate TPS
  UUID v7 (time-ordered): better locality — growing adoption

DR failover:
  UUID — no collision east/west merge
  IDENTITY — sequence gaps OK — collision if two DBs generate same id — dangerous

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Persistence Context Memory

FactorImpact
Entities in one txnEach MANAGED entity = object + snapshot array for dirty check
Large collections loaded@OneToMany eagerly loaded — all children in context
Long @TransactionalContext grows — GC pressure — connection held (L32)
clear() in batch jobem.flush(); em.clear(); every N rows — release memory

Banking Guideline

text
Payment capture txn: 2–5 entities typical — negligible memory
Anti-pattern: @Transactional on batch job processing 100k outbox rows without clear() — OOM
Pattern:
  for (chunk) { process; em.flush(); em.clear(); }

Duplicate Instance Memory Bug

text
Same PK two Java objects in one txn — should NOT happen if all access via EM
Bypass with new Payment(existingId) + persist — second instance — undefined behavior risk
Always load via find or getReference within txn

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Lifecycle Flows in Payment Platform

Flow 1: Happy Path Capture

text
1. @Transactional start — empty persistence context
2. new Payment() — NEW
3. em.persist(p) — MANAGED (no SQL yet)
4. em.persist(outbox) — MANAGED
5. Method exit — flush — INSERT payment, INSERT outbox
6. commit — EM close — both DETACHED (or discarded)

Flow 2: Spring Data save() on Existing ID

text
1. Controller retry sends same paymentId from client (bad) or load detached from cache
2. paymentRepo.save(detachedPayment) → SimpleJpaRepository.save → merge()
3. SELECT by PK — load MANAGED — copy fields — UPDATE at flush if dirty
4. If PK not in DB — INSERT — idempotency must prevent duplicate business key

Flow 3: Saga Step 2 — Ledger Consumer

text
1. Kafka delivers PaymentCaptured — consumer @Transactional NEW txn
2. processedEvents.find(eventId) — idempotent exit
3. ledgerRepo.find(accountId) — MANAGED Account
4. new LedgerEntry() + persist — MANAGED
5. account.setBalance(...) — MANAGED dirty
6. flush UPDATE account + INSERT ledger
7. commit — saga step complete
If failure before commit — rollback — all MANAGED changes discarded
Compensation txn — NEW persistence context — reverse entries

Flow 4: DR Failover Client Retry

text
1. First request: persist payment — commit succeeded on primary
2. Client timeout — no HTTP response — retries POST same Idempotency-Key
3. New txn: findByIdempotencyKey → MANAGED existing — return cached response
   NOT persist(new) — would violate UNIQUE or duplicate row if key check missed

Flow 5: Cascade Pitfall

text
1. em.remove(customer) with CascadeType.ALL including payments
2. flush DELETE payments... — regulatory catastrophe
Correct: no cascade remove on financial entities — soft delete customer only

Flow 6: Flush Before JPQL Query

text
1. persist(new Payment) — MANAGED not flushed
2. em.createQuery("SELECT COUNT(p) FROM Payment p").getSingleResult()
3. AUTO flush runs INSERT first — count includes new row
Surprise if you expected count before insert — use FlushMode.COMMIT or separate txn

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Lifecycle Performance Impact

OperationDB round tripsNotes
persist (new)0 until flush1 INSERT at flush
find by PK (cached)0Same txn second find
find by PK (cold)1 SELECTLoads snapshot
merge detached0–1 SELECT + 1 UPDATEAvoid in hot retry
dirty UPDATE1 UPDATE changed cols@DynamicUpdate optional
remove1 DELETEPrefer status update in banking

merge() on Hot Path

text
Idempotent retry calling merge 5000/sec — extra SELECT each time
Fix: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING native or check idempotency table first
Return early without merge

Cascade PERSIST Performance

text
persist Order with CascadeType.PERSIST on 50 LineItems
50 INSERTs at flush — batch_size=50 helps one JDBC batch
Without order_inserts — FK constraint order issues

Extended Persistence Context (Anti-Pattern REST)

text
Long-lived EM — huge identity map — memory leak pattern in stateful EJB
Not used in stateless Spring Boot payment APIs

ScenarioTimeSpace
n entities in one txnO(n) dirty check at flushO(n) snapshots
find by PKO(1) cache / O(log rows) DBO(1) entity
mergeO(1) + optional SELECTO(1)

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Lifecycle Code Examples

Correct Capture — persist NEW Entities

java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PaymentCaptureService {

    private final PaymentRepository paymentRepo;
    private final OutboxEventRepository outboxRepo;
    private final IdempotencyRepository idempotencyRepo;

    @Transactional
    public PaymentResult capture(CaptureCommand cmd) {
        return idempotencyRepo.findById(cmd.idempotencyKey())
            .map(r -> deserialize(r.getResponseBody()))
            .orElseGet(() -> {
                Payment payment = Payment.pending(cmd);  // NEW
                paymentRepo.save(payment);               // persist → MANAGED

                OutboxEvent event = OutboxEvent.paymentCreated(payment); // NEW
                outboxRepo.save(event);                    // MANAGED

                PaymentResult result = PaymentResult.from(payment);
                idempotencyRepo.save(IdempotencyRecord.of(cmd, result));
                return result;
            });
    }
}

merge() Trap — Wrong Retry Handling

java
// ❌ WRONG — client sends paymentId that already exists
@Transactional
public PaymentResult badRetry(Payment detachedFromJson) {
    paymentRepo.save(detachedFromJson); // merge → may UPDATE wrong fields
    return PaymentResult.from(detachedFromJson);
}

// ✅ RIGHT — business key idempotency
@Transactional
public PaymentResult goodRetry(CaptureCommand cmd) {
    return paymentRepo.findByIdempotencyKey(cmd.key())
        .map(PaymentResult::from)
        .orElseGet(() -> capture(cmd));
}

Using Return Value of merge

java
@Transactional
public void updateDetached(Payment detached) {
    // ❌ detached.setStatus(CAPTURED); — DETACHED — not synced
    Payment managed = entityManager.merge(detached);
    managed.setStatus(PaymentStatus.CAPTURED); // MANAGED — flushed at commit
}

remove() vs Soft Status (Banking)

java
// ❌ Regulatory risk
@Transactional
public void cancelPayment(UUID id) {
    paymentRepo.deleteById(id); // REMOVE → DELETE FROM payments
}

// ✅ Correct
@Transactional
public void reversePayment(UUID id) {
    Payment p = paymentRepo.findById(id).orElseThrow();
    p.setStatus(PaymentStatus.REVERSED); // MANAGED dirty → UPDATE
    outboxRepo.save(OutboxEvent.paymentReversed(p));
}

Cascade Configuration — Safe vs Dangerous

java
@Entity
public class Customer {
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "customer", cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST)
    private List<Account> accounts; // OK — create customer + accounts together

    // ❌ NEVER on payments in banking
    // cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true
}

@Entity
public class Payment {
    // No cascade to ledger — different service / aggregate
    @Column(name = "account_id")
    private UUID accountId;
}

Saga Consumer — New Context Each Message

java
@KafkaListener(topics = "payment-captured")
@Transactional
public void onPaymentCaptured(PaymentCapturedEvent event) {
    if (processedEventRepo.existsById(event.eventId())) {
        return; // idempotent — no duplicate MANAGED work
    }

    Account account = accountRepo.findById(event.accountId()).orElseThrow(); // MANAGED
    LedgerEntry entry = LedgerEntry.debit(account, event); // NEW
    ledgerRepo.save(entry); // persist

    account.debit(event.amount()); // dirty MANAGED
    processedEventRepo.save(new ProcessedEvent(event.eventId()));
    // single flush at commit — local ACID
}

Batch Outbox Relay — clear() Pattern

java
@Transactional
public void relayBatch() {
    List<OutboxEvent> batch = outboxRepo.findTop100ByPublishedAtIsNull();
    for (OutboxEvent e : batch) {
        kafka.send(e);
        e.setPublishedAt(Instant.now()); // MANAGED dirty
    }
    // flush at commit
}

// Large volume variant:
@Transactional
public void relayLarge() {
    Page<OutboxEvent> page = outboxRepo.findUnpublished(PageRequest.of(0, 500));
    for (OutboxEvent e : page) {
        kafka.send(e);
        e.setPublishedAt(Instant.now());
    }
    entityManager.flush();
    entityManager.clear(); // DETACH all — prevent identity map bloat
}

Explicit Flush for Constraint Timing

java
@Transactional
public void captureWithEarlyConstraintCheck(Payment p) {
    entityManager.persist(p);
    entityManager.flush(); // forces INSERT now — catch UNIQUE violation before outbox work
    outboxRepo.save(OutboxEvent.paymentCreated(p));
}

Part 12 — Production Usage

Lifecycle in Production

Transaction Boundary Rules

text
1. One business operation = one @Transactional method (service layer)
2. Never share entity instances across threads — persistence context not thread-safe
3. Kafka listener = new txn per message — entities DETACHED after commit
4. Do not store @Entity in Redis/session — serialize DTO only
5. DR retry = idempotency lookup — not blind persist

Identity Strategy in Production

text
Payment PK: UUID assigned @PrePersist — NEW persist safe on retries if idempotency guards business key
Ledger entry: UUID — append-only
Internal audit: BIGSERIAL OK — single DB shard only

Avoid merge-heavy IDENTITY entities on consumer hot paths

Cascade Policy (Banking)

text
Allowed: PERSIST on tightly owned aggregates (Order → OrderLine internal to one service)
Forbidden: REMOVE cascade on financial records
Forbidden: ALL cascade across bounded contexts
orphanRemoval=true — review as DELETE — usually reject for payments

Debugging Lifecycle Issues

text
logging.level.org.hibernate.engine.internal.StatisticalLoggingSessionEventListener=DEBUG (sampled)
hibernate.generate_statistics=true in staging only
Watch: UnexpectedRollbackException, OptimisticLockException, ConstraintViolationException at flush

Part 13 — Spring Boot Integration

Spring + Lifecycle

@Transactional Propagation and New Context

java
@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRED) // default — join or create
public void outer() {
    Payment p = paymentRepo.save(new Payment()); // MANAGED in outer context
    inner(); // same context by default — same persistence context
}

@Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
public void inner() {
    // NEW persistence context — outer entities DETACHED here
    // inner changes independent commit
}
// Use REQUIRES_NEW sparingly — saga compensation separate txn — outbox relay isolation

save() Implementation (Spring Data JPA)

java
// SimpleJpaRepository.save simplified:
public <S extends T> S save(S entity) {
    if (entityInformation.isNew(entity)) {
        em.persist(entity);
        return entity;
    } else {
        return em.merge(entity); // DETACHED or MANAGED with ID
    }
}
// isNew() — depends on Persistable.getId() override for UUID assigned pre-persist

Persistable for UUID Pre-Assigned

java
@Entity
public class Payment implements Persistable<UUID> {
    @Id
    private UUID paymentId;

    @Transient
    private boolean isNew = true;

    @PrePersist
    @PostLoad
    void markNotNew() { this.isNew = false; }

    @Override
    public UUID getId() { return paymentId; }

    @Override
    public boolean isNew() { return isNew; }
}
// Ensures save() uses persist() not merge() for new UUID payments — avoids extra SELECT

OSIV and DETACHED

text
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false (default)
Entity leaves service layer DETACHED
Controller must not touch lazy associations

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

Hibernate-Specific Lifecycle Details

getReference() vs find()

java
// find — SELECT immediately (or cache hit) — MANAGED with loaded state
Payment p = em.find(Payment.class, id);

// getReference — lazy proxy — no SELECT until access — MANAGED placeholder
Payment ref = em.getReference(Payment.class, id);
ref.getAmount(); // SELECT now — LazyInitializationException if EM closed

// Use getReference for FK assignment without loading full row:
LedgerEntry e = new LedgerEntry();
e.setPayment(em.getReference(Payment.class, paymentId));

@DynamicUpdate

java
@Entity
@DynamicUpdate
public class Account {
    // Hibernate generates UPDATE only changed columns
    // Smaller WAL — less lock time — good for hot balance row
}

Entity Graphs (Fetch Plan Control)

java
@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"metadata"})
Optional<Payment> findWithMetadata(UUID id);
// Loads MANAGED Payment + metadata in one SELECT — still within lifecycle rules

Hibernate Session Actions

java
Session session = em.unwrap(Session.class);
session.evict(payment);     // → DETACHED
session.refresh(payment);   // reload from DB — discard dirty changes
session.lock(payment, LockMode.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE); // Lesson 35

REMOVED Entity Access

text
After remove() before flush: some operations still allowed — undefined edge cases
After flush DELETE: accessing removed entity — error
Prefer status field over remove() in banking

Lifecycle + Distributed Patterns

text
┌─────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Pattern         │ Lifecycle implication                             │
├─────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Ignoring merge Return Value

text
Detached copy updated — MANAGED copy in context unchanged

Mistake 2: UUID Entity Without Persistable

text
Every save() → merge → SELECT — performance + wrong state on NEW

Mistake 3: Lazy Load After Commit

text
Payment returned from service — controller loads account — LazyInitializationException

Mistake 4: persist() with Existing Business Key

text
Second insert violates UNIQUE — should have checked idempotency first

Mistake 5: CascadeType.ALL on Customer → Payments

text
delete customer deletes payment history — regulatory disaster

Mistake 6: Same Entity Two Instances One Txn

text
em.persist(new Payment(sameId)) while find(id) exists — PersistenceException

Mistake 7: Saga Compensation Uses remove()

text
Physical DELETE — audit lost — use REVERSAL ledger + status

Mistake 8: Storing MANAGED Entity in Instance Field

text
Next request uses stale DETACHED/Managed wrong txn — thread safety + lifecycle horror

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: Four entity states?

NEW, MANAGED, DETACHED, REMOVED.

Q2: When does SQL execute for persist()?

At flush — typically commit — not necessarily immediately.

Q3: LazyInitializationException cause?

Access lazy association on DETACHED entity — no open persistence context.

Q4: persist vs merge?

persist: NEW to MANAGED. merge: reattach DETACHED, returns MANAGED copy.

Q5: What is persistence context?

First-level cache of MANAGED entities in one EntityManager/transaction scope.

Mid-Level

Q6: Spring Data save() with pre-assigned UUID?

Calls merge unless Persistable.isNew() returns true — implement Persistable for persist path.

Q7: Why identity map matters?

Same PK one Java instance in txn — consistent in-memory state.

Q8: FlushMode AUTO vs COMMIT?

AUTO flushes before queries; COMMIT only at commit — stale query risk.

Q9: Saga step lifecycle?

Each step new transaction — new persistence context — idempotent consumer — no shared entities across steps.

Q10: DR retry duplicate payment prevention?

Idempotency key lookup in new txn — return existing — don't persist NEW again.

Senior

Q11: Design capture to avoid merge SELECT?

Persistable UUID + idempotency table INSERT first ON CONFLICT pattern.

Q12: Cascade rules for payment platform?

PERSIST on owned children only — never REMOVE on financial — explicit outbox persist.

Q13: Batch outbox relay memory?

flush + clear every N events — prevent identity map growth.

Staff / Architect

Q14: Platform standard for entity lifecycle?

OSIV false, Persistable UUID, service txn boundary, DTO at edge, no REMOVE on money tables, idempotency before persist.

Scenario

Scenario: "Kafka consumer sometimes duplicates ledger entries on redelivery."

Missing processed_events idempotency — each redelivery new txn persists again — add EXISTS check or UNIQUE on eventId.

Part 1 — Concept

What Is Hibernate Architecture?

Hibernate is the JPA provider that sits between your @Entity objects and JDBC. It maintains metadata about mappings, tracks dirty field changes, builds SQL through an internal translator, and executes statements via JDBC at flush time.

text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  @Entity classes + annotations (@Table, @Column, @Id, ...)        │
└────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │ bootstrap (startup)
                             ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SessionFactory (immutable metadata — built once per JVM)         │
│  • Entity persisters (table/column mapping)                       │
│  • SQL generators (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE templates)                │
│  • Type system (BigDecimal ↔ DECIMAL, UUID ↔ uuid)               │
│  • Named query / filter definitions                               │
└────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │ opens per transaction
                             ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Session / EntityManager (runtime — one persistence context)      │
│  • Identity map (L1 cache)                                        │
│  • Dirty checking (field snapshots)                               │
│  • Action queue (insert/update/delete ordering)                   │
│  • Flush → SQL AST → JDBC                                         │
└────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │ JDBC
                             ▼
                      PostgreSQL / Oracle

Key Components

ComponentRole
SessionFactoryExpensive startup — caches all mapping metadata
Session / EntityManagerUnit of work for one transaction
Entity persisterKnows how to load/save one entity type
Action queueOrders DML before flush
Dirty checkingDetects changed fields vs load snapshot
SQL AST (Hibernate 6+)Tree representation → dialect-specific SQL
DialectPostgreSQL vs Oracle syntax differences

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Hibernate SQL Generation

text
2001–2005  Hibernate 2/3 — HQL → SQL string concatenation
           Dirty checking via field reflection
           XML mappings (.hbm.xml) dominant

2006–2013  JPA annotations — EntityManager wraps Session
           Hibernate 3.5+ JDBC batching improvements

2014–2019  Hibernate 5 — bytecode enhancement for lazy/dirty
           Criteria API peak then decline

2020+      Hibernate 6 (Spring Boot 3) — SQM (Semantic Query Model)
           SQL AST translator — cleaner SQL, better multi-tenant/sharding hooks
           Removal of legacy Criteria, javax → jakarta
           Better PostgreSQL JSON, UUID, enum STRING support

Enterprise payments:
  Teams still grep logs for "Hibernate: insert into payments"
  Performance incidents from unseen N+1 (L48 preview) and missing batch_size
  Architects require EXPLAIN on top 10 Hibernate SQL patterns per service

Historical Lesson

Hibernate hides SQL — but production latency is still SQL. Lesson 47 teaches you to predict what Hibernate will emit on payment hot paths before it hits pg_stat_statements.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does Understanding Hibernate Internals Solve?

Problem 1: Unexpected SQL Volume

text
paymentRepo.save() expected 1 INSERT — logs show 47 statements (N+1 cascade)

Problem 2: Slow flush()

text
500 MANAGED entities — dirty check O(n) + 500 UPDATEs — timeout

Problem 3: Wrong UPDATE Shape

text
UPDATE accounts SET col1=?, col2=?, ... col20=? WHERE id=? 
Updates all columns when one field changed — extra WAL (Lesson 33)

Problem 4: Batch Not Working

text
batch_size=50 configured — still 50 round trips — IDENTITY PK or flush per row

Problem 5: Optimizer Mismatch

text
JPQL looks simple — EXPLAIN shows seq scan — native SQL needed for report
Architect can't tune what team can't read in logs

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Not Raw SQL Everywhere?

Abstraction With Control Points

text
Hibernate generates SQL but exposes:
  @DynamicUpdate, batch_size, fetch plans, native @Query escape hatch
Understanding internals = knowing which knobs matter

Portable DML Generation

text
Same @Entity works PostgreSQL + Oracle — dialect adjusts types/limit syntax
Multi-cloud banking vendors — dialect per environment

Automatic Dirty Checking

text
Developer: account.setBalance(x) — Hibernate computes minimal UPDATE (with @DynamicUpdate)
Without ORM: manual "which fields changed" tracking boilerplate

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Hibernate Generates and Executes SQL

Bootstrap Phase (Application Start)

text
1. Scan @Entity classes
2. Build RuntimeMetamodels — tables, columns, associations, cascades
3. Compile named JPQL → SQM → SQL templates (or defer to runtime)
4. SessionFactory immutable — thread-safe
Spring Boot: LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean wraps SessionFactory
Startup time: seconds for 50 entities — acceptable once

Load Path (SELECT)

text
em.find(Payment.class, id):

1. Check persistence context identity map — hit → return MANAGED, no SQL
2. Miss → EntityPersister.load(id)
3. Generate SELECT ... FROM payments WHERE payment_id=?
4. JDBC PreparedStatement execute
5. Hydrate Payment — snapshot[] stored in EntityEntry for dirty check
6. Register MANAGED in context

Insert Path (persist → flush)

text
persist(new Payment):

1. ActionQueue.addInsert(entity)
2. At flush — EntityInsertAction
3. SQL AST InsertStatement:
     INSERT INTO payments (payment_id, amount, currency_code, status, ...)
     VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ...)
4. Optional: add to JDBC batch (BatchImpl)
5. Foreign key order: parent before child in queue sort

Dirty Checking Algorithm

text
At flush for each MANAGED entity:
  loadedState[] = field values at load/persist time
  currentState[] = current getter values
  For each property index i:
    if !Type.isEqual(loadedState[i], currentState[i]):
      mark property i dirty
  If any dirty OR force update:
    generate UPDATE with dirty columns only (@DynamicUpdate)
    OR all columns (default)

@Version: increment in UPDATE WHERE version=? — optimistic lock (L35)

Update Path

text
Default UPDATE (all columns):
  UPDATE payments SET amount=?, currency_code=?, status=?, updated_at=?, version=?
  WHERE payment_id=? AND version=?

@DynamicUpdate:
  UPDATE payments SET status=?, updated_at=?, version=?
  WHERE payment_id=? AND version=?
  (only changed columns — smaller WAL, shorter row lock)

Delete Path

text
remove(entity):
  ActionQueue.addDelete
  DELETE FROM payments WHERE payment_id=? AND version=?
Banking: rarely used — status UPDATE instead

Flush Order (Action Queue)

text
Before flush:
  1. Sort actions by type and FK dependencies
  2. Typical: INSERTs (parents first) → UPDATEs → DELETEs (children first)
  3. Execute JDBC batch groups per statement type if enabled
  4. AUTO flush before HQL/JPQL may trigger early flush

Example same txn:
  persist Payment (INSERT)
  persist OutboxEvent (INSERT)
  update Account (UPDATE)
→ 2 INSERTs + 1 UPDATE at commit (order preserved)

Hibernate 6 SQL AST Pipeline

text
JPQL/HQL → SQM (semantic) → SQL AST → SqlAstTranslator → final SQL string
Criteria → SQM same path
Benefits: consistent optimization, easier multi-tenant/sharding plugins
Logs: org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind (TRACE) shows bind values
      org.hibernate.SQL (DEBUG) shows SQL

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Generated SQL ↔ Disk Impact

INSERT Payment Row

text
SQL INSERT → PostgreSQL executor → heap page in payments partition
           → WAL record (durability L33)
           → B-tree insert on payments_pkey, ux_idempotency, ix_account_created
Wide row (many VARCHAR/JSONB) → larger page occupancy → more I/O

@DynamicUpdate on Hot Account Row

text
Without DynamicUpdate:
  UPDATE all 12 columns — full row WAL — longer row exclusive lock

With DynamicUpdate:
  UPDATE balance, version only — less WAL — better concurrent reads on account
Critical for ledger-service accounts table (L43)

JDBC Batching

text
hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50:
  50 INSERTs buffered → pg JDBC sendBatch() — one network round trip group
PostgreSQL: reWriteBatchedInserts=true (driver param) — multi-value INSERT optimization

IDENTITY generation:
  Hibernate must flush after each INSERT to get ID — batching breaks
  UUID @PrePersist — batching works (Lesson 46 Persistable)

Statement Cache

text
Prepared statement cache on PG (per connection)
Hibernate generates stable SQL shapes — good for prepare cache
@DynamicUpdate — variable column SET list — more unique SQL strings — slight prepare cache pressure
Trade-off usually worth it on wide tables

Hibernate Runtime Memory

StructureScopeSize driver
SessionFactory metadataJVMO(entities × properties) — fixed
EntityEntry per MANAGEDPer txnEntity + loadedState[] snapshot
Action queuePer txnPending inserts/updates/deletes
JDBC batch bufferPer txnbatch_size × row params

Payment Capture Txn

text
2 EntityEntry (Payment, OutboxEvent) — kilobytes
Action queue: 2 inserts — trivial
Problem: relay job 10k OutboxEvent UPDATE published_at without clear() — 10k entries
Fix: chunk + flush + clear (Lesson 46)

Dirty Checking CPU

text
Reflection or bytecode enhanced getters for snapshot compare
5000 entities/flus — measurable CPU — keep txn small

Part 8 — Execution Flow

End-to-End SQL Generation Flows

Flow 1: capture() — Expected SQL

text
@Transactional capture(CaptureCommand cmd):

1. SELECT idempotency_records WHERE id=?
2. (if miss) INSERT payments (...)
3. INSERT outbox_events (...)
4. INSERT idempotency_records (...)
COMMIT

Total: 1–4 statements — validate in staging with show_sql or datasource-proxy

Flow 2: Account Debit in Ledger Service

text
1. SELECT accounts WHERE account_id=? FOR UPDATE (if @Lock)
2. INSERT ledger_entries (...)
3. UPDATE accounts SET balance=?, version=? WHERE account_id=? AND version=?
@DynamicUpdate on Account → step 3 only changed columns

Flow 3: AUTO Flush Before COUNT Query

text
em.persist(payment);  // queued INSERT
em.createQuery("SELECT COUNT(p) FROM Payment p").getSingleResult();
→ AUTO flush runs INSERT first
→ COUNT includes new row
Surprise in same-txn validation — use FlushMode.COMMIT or separate read txn

Flow 4: Batched Outbox Publish

text
hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50, order_updates=true
Loop 50 events: setPublishedAt(now) — 50 UPDATEs batched
One flush at commit — pg logs show batched execution

Flow 5: Read Replica + readOnly

text
@Transactional(readOnly=true)
paymentRepo.findById(id):
  Single SELECT — no flush — routing to replica (L40)
Hibernate marks connection read-only — PG default_transaction_read_only optional

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Tuning Hibernate SQL on Payment Paths

High-Impact Settings

yaml
spring:
  jpa:
    properties:
      hibernate:
        jdbc:
          batch_size: 50
          batch_versioned_data: true
        order_inserts: true
        order_updates: true
        generate_statistics: false
        dialect: org.hibernate.dialect.PostgreSQLDialect

spring.datasource.hikari.data-source-properties:
  reWriteBatchedInserts: true   # PostgreSQL driver — batch INSERT rewrite

@DynamicUpdate When

text
✅ Wide entities — Account, Customer — few fields change per UPDATE
✅ Hot row contention — accounts.balance
❌ Tiny entities (3 columns) — negligible benefit
❌ Entities where almost all columns always change

Batch Size vs Allocation Size

java
@SequenceGenerator(name = "seq", allocationSize = 50)  // reduces SEQUENCE round trips
// Pair with jdbc.batch_size=50 for INSERT batches
// UUID PK — no sequence — batch_size alone matters

Reading Generated SQL in Production

text
❌ spring.jpa.show-sql=true in prod — bypasses logging framework, no bind values
✅ p6spy / datasource-proxy — sampled
✅ pg_stat_statements — normalized query patterns
✅ Hibernate STAT — staging load tests only

EXPLAIN Hibernate SQL (Phase 3)

sql
-- From log: SELECT ... FROM payments WHERE account_id=? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT ?
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT * FROM payments
WHERE account_id = '...'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
-- Expect: Index Scan on ix_payments_account_created

@Table(name = "accounts")
@DynamicUpdate

public class Account {

    @Id
    private UUID accountId;

    @Column(nullable = false, precision = 19, scale = 4)
    private BigDecimal balance;

    @Column(name = "currency_code", nullable = false, length = 3)
    private String currencyCode;

    @Column(length = 20)
    private String status;

    @Version
    private Long version;
}

// status, currency_code omitted from SET

@Modifying
@Query(value = """
    UPDATE outbox_events
    SET published_at = NOW()
    WHERE event_id IN (:ids)

int markPublished(@Param("ids") List<UUID> ids);

SQL Review Gate (Architect Process)

text
Before release of new repository method:

text

Mistake 1: show-sql=true in Production

text
Unstructured logs, no bind values, performance overhead — use pg_stat_statements
