Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: SessionFactory vs EntityManager?

SessionFactory: immutable metadata factory. EntityManager: per-txn persistence context API.

Q2: When does Hibernate send INSERT to DB?

At flush — usually transaction commit — not necessarily at persist().

Q3: What is dirty checking?

Compare current field values to load snapshot — generate UPDATE for changes at flush.

Q4: Purpose of jdbc.batch_size?

Batch multiple INSERT/UPDATE into fewer JDBC round trips.

Q5: What does dialect do?

Adapt SQL syntax and types for specific database (PostgreSQL vs Oracle).

Mid-Level

Q6: @DynamicUpdate benefit?

UPDATE only changed columns — less WAL and lock time on wide rows.

Q7: Why IDENTITY breaks batching?

Must flush immediately to retrieve generated ID — can't defer INSERT batch.

Q8: Flush order INSERT UPDATE DELETE?

Action queue sorts by dependency — parents before children on insert.

Q9: Hibernate 6 SQL AST?

SQM → SQL AST → translated SQL — cleaner generation pipeline.

Q10: readOnly @Transactional effect?

No flush of writes — optimization hint — replica routing in custom setup.

Senior

Q11: Optimize account balance UPDATE at 10k TPS.

@DynamicUpdate, @Version, batch if bulk, index on PK, short txn, PG connection pool, avoid pessimistic lock unless needed.

Q12: How verify capture API SQL budget?

Integration test + SQL logging + pg_stat_statements + EXPLAIN + statement count assert.

Q13: @Modifying bulk UPDATE vs load-update loop?

Bulk native/modifying — one SQL — clear persistence context — use for outbox mark published batch.

Staff / Architect

Q14: Hibernate on Tier 0 payment path — governance?

SQL review gate, EXPLAIN mandatory, batch/DynamicUpdate standards, native escape documented, no @Formula on OLTP.

Scenario

Scenario: "Outbox relay slow — 100 UPDATEs/sec each separate."

Enable batch_size, order_updates, batch_versioned_data, reWriteBatchedInserts, chunk in one @Transactional.

Fetch Strategies & the N+1 Problem

1Concept2History3Problem Statement4Why This Exists5Internal Working6Storage Internals7Memory Usage8Execution Flow9Performance Analysis10Complexity Analysis11Code / SQL Examples12Production Usage13Spring Boot Integration14Hibernate/JPA Integration15Architect Perspective16Decision Matrix17Comparison Tables18Common Mistakes19Interview Questions20Revision Sheet21Summary Table*Practice

Part 1 — Concept

What Are Fetch Strategies?

Fetch strategy defines when and how Hibernate loads associated data (@OneToMany, @ManyToOne, @ManyToMany, @ElementCollection). The wrong strategy causes N+1 queries — one query for parent rows plus N additional queries for each child — destroying payment API latency.

text
FETCH TYPE ON ASSOCIATION
─────────────────────────
LAZY  (default for collections)  → load on first access — needs open Session
EAGER (default @ManyToOne)        → load with parent — risk cartesian explosion

EXPLICIT FETCH IN QUERY (preferred in services)
───────────────────────────────────────────────
JOIN FETCH     → one SQL with join — watch duplicate rows
@EntityGraph   → declarative fetch plan on repository method
@BatchSize     → N+1 → 1 + ceil(N/batch) queries
DTO projection → SELECT only needed columns — no entity graph

The N+1 Problem

text
1 query:  SELECT * FROM payments WHERE account_id = ?     → 100 rows
100 queries: SELECT * FROM payment_lines WHERE payment_id = ?  (one per payment)

Total: 101 round trips — payment history API timeout at scale

ASCII — N+1 vs JOIN FETCH

text
N+1 (LAZY in loop):
  Payment₁ ──SELECT──► Lines₁
  Payment₂ ──SELECT──► Lines₂
  ...
  Payment₁₀₀ ──SELECT──► Lines₁₀₀

JOIN FETCH (single query):
  Payment₁..100 + Lines ── one SELECT with JOIN ──► hydrate in memory

Part 2 — History

Evolution of ORM Fetch Loading

text
2000s   Hibernate lazy proxies — LazyInitializationException drove OSIV pattern
        EAGER overused — huge joins — Hibernate forum "Don't use EAGER"

2008    JOIN FETCH in HQL — standard fix for N+1
        @BatchSize — hidden gem — 1 + N/batch

2013    JPA 2.1 @NamedEntityGraph / @EntityGraph — fetch plans on methods
        Spring Data @EntityGraph on repository interfaces

2015    Open Session In View anti-pattern documented widely
        Spring Boot 2.2+ open-in-view=false default push

2018    DTO projections / Blaze-Persistence / jOOQ for read models
        Microservices: no cross-service @ManyToOne — UUID refs only (L43)

2020+   Payment APIs: cursor pagination + DTO projection standard
        GraphQL DataLoader pattern — batch loading at API layer
        Hibernate 6 fail_on_pagination_over_collection_fetch — cartesian guard

Historical Lesson

N+1 survived because lazy loading "worked" with OSIV. With open-in-view=false, fetch strategy is explicit in the service layer — architects enforce query review like SQL review (L47).

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problem Do Fetch Strategies Solve?

Problem 1: Payment History API — 101 Queries

text
GET /accounts/{id}/payments?limit=50
Returns 50 payments each with status history lines — N+1 on lines

Problem 2: Branch Report — Cartesian Explosion

text
JOIN FETCH payments JOIN FETCH transactions — 50 payments × 200 txns = 10k rows in ResultSet
OOM and wrong COUNT in pagination

Problem 3: LazyInitializationException

text
Service returns List<Payment> entities — controller serializes JSON — lazy lines access — crash

Problem 4: EAGER Fetch Cascade

text
@ManyToOne EAGER Customer on Payment — every payment query joins customers — wasted I/O

Problem 5: Read Replica Heavy Join (L40)

text
Correct JOIN FETCH on replica OK for reports
Write path accidentally EAGER loads collections — primary overload

Unified Problem Statement

Fetch strategy controls SQL count and row shape. Payment platforms must load exactly the graph needed per use case — no accidental lazy loads, no blind EAGER, no unpaginated collection JOIN FETCH.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why LAZY and EAGER?

LAZY — Defer Cost

text
Don't load payment audit lines if API returns summary DTO only
Pay I/O cost only when association accessed
Requires MANAGED entity or explicit fetch in query

EAGER — Convenience (Dangerous)

text
@ManyToOne EAGER Account on Payment — always load account with payment
Seems simple — becomes join on every query — hard to override
JPA default: @ManyToOne EAGER, @OneToMany LAZY
Architect policy: explicit LAZY on @ManyToOne except rare cases

Explicit Fetch Plans Beat Defaults

text
Same entity Payment — different fetch per endpoint:
  capture(): no joins
  detail(): JOIN FETCH metadata only
  admin(): @EntityGraph with audit lines

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Hibernate Loads Associations

Lazy @ManyToOne Proxy

text
SELECT payment row — account_id FK present
account field = HibernateProxy — no SELECT yet
payment.getAccount().getName() → triggers SELECT account WHERE id=?
If Session closed → LazyInitializationException

Lazy @OneToMany Collection

text
Payment.lines = PersistentBag (uninitialized)
payment.getLines().size() → SELECT lines WHERE payment_id=?

JOIN FETCH Mechanics

java
@Query("SELECT p FROM Payment p JOIN FETCH p.lines WHERE p.accountId = :aid")
text
Hibernate generates:
  SELECT p.*, l.* FROM payments p
  INNER JOIN payment_lines l ON l.payment_id = p.payment_id
  WHERE p.account_id = ?

Single round trip — hydrates Payment + Lines in one persistence context
Duplicate Payment rows in ResultSet if multiple lines — Hibernate deduplicates by identity map

Multiple Bag Fetch Forbidden

text
Cannot JOIN FETCH two @OneToMany List collections in one query
Hibernate throws MultipleBagFetchException — use @BatchSize on one + JOIN FETCH other
Or two queries + assemble in service

@BatchSize Internals

java
@Entity
public class Payment {
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "payment")
    @BatchSize(size = 25)
    private List<PaymentLine> lines;
}
text
1. SELECT payments WHERE account_id=? → 100 payments
2. Access lines on each — Hibernate batches:
   SELECT * FROM payment_lines WHERE payment_id IN (?, ?, ... 25 ids)
   Repeat 4 times for 100 payments → 1 + 4 = 5 queries total vs 101

default_batch_fetch_size

yaml
hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size: 16
# Applies to lazy @ManyToOne too — batch load accounts for N payments

@EntityGraph

java
@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"lines"})
Optional<Payment> findWithLinesById(UUID id);
text
Translates to LEFT JOIN FETCH or separate batch per Hibernate version/plan
Declarative — reusable fetch plan on repository

DTO Projection (Constructor Expression)

java
@Query("""
    SELECT new com.bank.dto.PaymentSummaryDto(p.paymentId, p.amount, p.status, p.createdAt)
    FROM Payment p
    WHERE p.accountId = :accountId
    ORDER BY p.createdAt DESC
    """)
List<PaymentSummaryDto> summaries(@Param("accountId") UUID accountId, Pageable page);
text
No entity hydration — no lazy traps — no dirty checking — one SELECT columns only
Best for read APIs and branch reports

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Fetch Strategy and I/O

Index Use on N+1

text
Each lazy line query: SELECT * FROM payment_lines WHERE payment_id = ?
Requires index on payment_lines(payment_id) — PK/FK index — O(log n) per query
101 index lookups × network latency >> one JOIN with same index
pg_stat: 101 similar queries — smoking gun N+1

JOIN FETCH and Index

text
JOIN payments + lines ON payment_id
WHERE payments.account_id = ?
Ideal plan: Index Scan on ix_payments_account_created + Nested Loop index on lines FK

Wide ResultSet Cost

text
JOIN FETCH 50 payments × 10 lines = 500 logical rows in ResultSet
Memory in JDBC + Hibernate hydration — still better than 51 round trips usually
Pagination + JOIN FETCH collection = broken — fetch page wrong — see Part 9

Covering Index for DTO Projection

sql
CREATE INDEX ix_payments_acct_covering
  ON payments (account_id, created_at DESC)
  INCLUDE (amount, status, currency_code);
-- DTO projection avoids heap fetch — Index Only Scan possible

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Memory Impact of Fetch Choices

StrategyMemoryRisk
LAZY no accessMinimalLazyInitializationException
N+1 lazy loadModerate spreadConnection pool hold time
JOIN FETCH collectionAll rows at onceO(payments × lines) heap
@BatchSizeBatched chunksBetter than N+1
DTO projectionO(page size)Lowest for reads
EAGER two collectionsCartesian productOOM

Payment History Page (50 items)

text
DTO projection: 50 × ~100 bytes DTO — negligible
JOIN FETCH 50 payments + avg 5 lines: 250 entity objects + snapshots for dirty check
readOnly txn — no dirty check cost — still entity overhead vs DTO
Architect default: DTO for list endpoints

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Execution Flows — Banking Examples

Flow 1: N+1 Anti-Pattern (Broken)

java
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public List<PaymentDto> badHistory(UUID accountId) {
    List<Payment> payments = paymentRepo.findByAccountId(accountId); // 1 SELECT
    return payments.stream()
        .map(p -> new PaymentDto(p, p.getLines().size())) // N SELECTS — LAZY lines
        .toList();
}
// 1 + N SQL — fails SLA at N=100

Flow 2: JOIN FETCH Fix

java
@Query("""
    SELECT DISTINCT p FROM Payment p
    JOIN FETCH p.lines
    WHERE p.accountId = :accountId
    ORDER BY p.createdAt DESC
    """)
List<Payment> findWithLinesByAccount(@Param("accountId") UUID accountId, Pageable page);
// 1 SELECT — DISTINCT avoids duplicate Payment in JPQL result
// Pagination caveat: in-memory slice — use separate count query or batch fetch + page payments first

Flow 3: @BatchSize Fix (Pagination-Friendly)

java
// Page payments first — 1 SELECT with LIMIT
Page<Payment> page = paymentRepo.findByAccountId(accountId, PageRequest.of(0, 50));
page.forEach(p -> p.getLines().size()); // triggers batched IN queries — 1 + ceil(50/25)=3 total

Flow 4: DTO Projection (Recommended List API)

java
@Query("""
    SELECT new com.bank.api.PaymentListItem(
        p.paymentId, p.amount, p.currencyCode, p.status, p.createdAt)
    FROM Payment p
    WHERE p.accountId = :accountId
    """)
Page<PaymentListItem> listByAccount(@Param("accountId") UUID accountId, Pageable page);
// 1 SELECT + 1 COUNT — no entities — no N+1 possible

Flow 5: Branch Report on Read Replica (L40)

java
@Transactional(readOnly = true) // routes to replica
@Query(value = """
    SELECT b.branch_code, COUNT(p.payment_id), SUM(p.amount)
    FROM payments p
    JOIN branches b ON b.branch_id = p.branch_id
    WHERE p.created_at >= :start
    GROUP BY b.branch_code
    """, nativeQuery = true)
List<Object[]> branchTotals(@Param("start") Instant start);
// Single aggregate SQL — no JPA associations — best for reports

Flow 6: Cross-Service — No @ManyToOne

text
payment-service Payment has accountId UUID only — no Account entity
Need account name: call ledger API or denormalized read model — never JOIN FETCH across DB

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Performance Comparison

Query Count Comparison (100 payments, 5 lines each)

ApproachSQL countRound tripsPagination safe
N+1 LAZY101101Misleading
JOIN FETCH all11❌ with Pageable
@BatchSize(25)1 + 45✅ page then batch
DTO projection1 (+ count)2✅
Native aggregate11N/A

JOIN FETCH + Pageable Trap

text
@Query("SELECT p FROM Payment p JOIN FETCH p.lines ...")
Page<Payment> find(..., Pageable page);

Hibernate may:
  - Load ALL payments into memory — slice in app — disaster
  - Or ignore fetch join for page — inconsistent

Fix:
  Query 1: SELECT id FROM payments WHERE ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT/OFFSET
  Query 2: JOIN FETCH where p.id IN (:ids)
  Or use @BatchSize on lines instead

fail_on_pagination_over_collection_fetch

yaml
hibernate.query.fail_on_pagination_over_collection_fetch: true
# Fail fast in dev — prevents silent full load

EAGER @ManyToOne Cost

text
Every paymentRepo.findAll() adds JOIN customers or secondary SELECT
1000 payment list — 1000 customer rows loaded unnecessarily
Fix: @ManyToOne(fetch = LAZY) + JOIN FETCH only when needed

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Complete Examples — Payment Platform

Entity Mappings — Explicit LAZY

java
@Entity
@Table(name = "payments")
public class Payment {

    @Id
    private UUID paymentId;

    @Column(name = "account_id", nullable = false)
    private UUID accountId;

    // ❌ @ManyToOne(fetch = EAGER) Account — cross-service anyway
    // ✅ UUID only in payment-service

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "payment", fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    @BatchSize(size = 25)
    private List<PaymentLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "payment", fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    @BatchSize(size = 25)
    private List<PaymentStatusHistory> statusHistory = new ArrayList<>();
}

Two-Query Pagination Pattern (Safe JOIN FETCH)

java
@Repository
public interface PaymentRepository extends JpaRepository<Payment, UUID> {

    @Query("""
        SELECT p.id FROM Payment p
        WHERE p.accountId = :accountId
        ORDER BY p.createdAt DESC
        """)
    List<UUID> findIdsByAccount(@Param("accountId") UUID accountId, Pageable page);

    @Query("""
        SELECT DISTINCT p FROM Payment p
        JOIN FETCH p.lines
        WHERE p.paymentId IN :ids
        ORDER BY p.createdAt DESC
        """)
    List<Payment> findWithLinesByIds(@Param("ids") List<UUID> ids);
}

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PaymentHistoryService {
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public Page<PaymentDetailDto> history(UUID accountId, Pageable page) {
        List<UUID> ids = paymentRepo.findIdsByAccount(accountId, page);
        if (ids.isEmpty()) return Page.empty(page);
        List<Payment> loaded = paymentRepo.findWithLinesByIds(ids);
        List<PaymentDetailDto> dtos = loaded.stream().map(PaymentDetailDto::from).toList();
        long total = paymentRepo.countByAccountId(accountId);
        return new PageImpl<>(dtos, page, total);
    }
}

Part 12 — Production Usage

Fetch Strategy Standards — Production

Platform API Guidelines

text
LIST endpoints   → DTO projection + Pageable — no entity return
DETAIL endpoint  → @EntityGraph or JOIN FETCH — bounded associations
REPORT endpoints → native SQL or warehouse — no entity graph
WRITE endpoints  → no fetch joins — load by PK only
Cross-service    → UUID refs — no @ManyToOne across DB

Monitoring N+1

text
APM: JDBC query count per HTTP request — alert if > 10 for GET /payments
pg_stat_statements: same query pattern 1000×/min — parameter only differs
Code review: any .getXxx() in stream after query → require fetch plan

Read Replica (L40)

text
@Transactional(readOnly = true) on history/report services
Heavy JOIN FETCH OK on replica — protect primary for captures
Show "as of" timestamp if lag matters

Branch Report Production Pattern

text
Do NOT:
  Load all Branch entities → lazy load payments in loop

DO:
  Native SQL GROUP BY on replica
  Or materialized view refreshed hourly
  Or CDC to warehouse — Tableau on Snowflake

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is N+1 problem?

One query for N parent rows plus N queries for each child association — lazy load in loop.

Q2: Default fetch for @OneToMany and @ManyToOne?

OneToMany LAZY, ManyToOne EAGER — override ManyToOne to LAZY in practice.

Q3: LazyInitializationException?

Lazy association accessed outside open persistence context — OSIV off exposes it.

Q4: JOIN FETCH purpose?

Load association in same SQL query — avoid N+1.

Q5: Why open-in-view false?

Forces fetch in service layer — prevents hidden N+1 and long transactions.

Mid-Level

Q6: JOIN FETCH + Pageable problem?

Hibernate may load all rows before paging — use id query + IN fetch or @BatchSize.

Q7: @BatchSize how it works?

Batches lazy loads into WHERE id IN (...) — reduces N+1 to 1 + N/batch queries.

Q8: @EntityGraph vs JOIN FETCH?

EntityGraph declarative on method — Hibernate generates fetch plan — similar goal.

Q9: Fix N+1 on payment list without loading lines?

DTO projection — don't access lines — no lazy trigger.

Q10: Two @OneToMany JOIN FETCH?

Not allowed (multiple bags) — batch one, join other, or two queries.

Senior

Q11: Design GET /accounts/{id}/payments pagination.

DTO projection Pageable + index (account_id, created_at) — optional 2-query for detail with lines.

Q12: Branch report across payments/branches?

Native GROUP BY on read replica — not entity graph.

Q13: default_batch_fetch_size vs @BatchSize?

Default applies globally to lazy associations — @BatchSize overrides per collection.

Staff / Architect

Q14: Platform standard prevent N+1?

OSIV false, DTO list APIs, CI query count limits, no cross-service ORM relations, EXPLAIN reviews.

Scenario

Scenario: "GET /payments slow — APM shows 501 JDBC calls."

N+1 on lines — fix with DTO list or @BatchSize or JOIN FETCH on detail only — add ix on FK.

Part 1 — Concept

Cache Layers in JPA/Hibernate

Hibernate has three cache layers. Confusing them causes stale balances, wrong branch limits, and DR failover inconsistencies.

text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  APPLICATION (Spring @Cacheable, Redis, Caffeine)               │  ← You own invalidation
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │
┌────────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SECOND-LEVEL CACHE (L2) — SessionFactory scoped                │  ← Shared across EntityManagers
│  Entity regions: Account, Branch, Customer (read-mostly)         │
│  Optional: Redis, Infinispan, EhCache                           │
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │
┌────────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────────┐
│  FIRST-LEVEL CACHE (L1) — Persistence Context per @Transactional│  ← Lesson 46 — always on
│  Identity map — MANAGED entities in one transaction              │
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │
┌────────────────────────────▼────────────────────────────────────┐
│  QUERY CACHE (optional) — caches query RESULT IDs               │  ← Rare in payments OLTP
│  Invalidates when entity region changes                          │
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │ cache miss
                             ▼
                      DATABASE (source of truth)

What Each Layer Caches

LayerCachesScopePayment use case
L1Entity instancesOne transactionSame txn re-read payment
L2Dehydrated entity state by PKAll sessions in JVM/clusterBranch metadata, product config
Query cacheList of entity IDs per query keyClusterAlmost never for payments
Spring @CacheableDTOs, computed valuesApp-definedAccount summary for UI

Golden Rule for Banking

text
NEVER L2-cache mutable financial aggregates:
  ❌ Payment, LedgerEntry, Account.balance, running totals

OK to cache read-mostly reference data:
  ✅ Branch, fee schedule, currency list, country codes, static config
  ✅ Denormalized read model with TTL + event invalidation

Part 2 — History

Evolution of ORM Caching

text
2003    Hibernate 2 second-level cache — EhCache plugin
        Cluster invalidation via JGroups — fragile

2008    JPA standard silent on L2 — provider-specific
        Query cache popular — stale data incidents in e-commerce

2012    "Cache is hard" — Martin Fowler — eventual consistency accepted for catalogs only

2015    Microservices move caching to Redis at API layer — explicit TTL
        Hibernate L2 less common in greenfield REST services

2018    Spring Cache + Redis — @Cacheable on service methods — clearer ownership
        Payment platforms: Redis for idempotency + rate limits + reference data

2020+   Hibernate 6 + Infinispan/Redisson L2 region — still niche in banking OLTP
        Read replicas (L40) replace some cache needs for reports
        DR failover: all JVM caches cold — design for cache miss storm
        Architects document cache consistency per data class

Historical Lesson

Second-level cache caused more production bugs in financial OLTP than it saved in I/O. Modern payment platforms prefer Redis with explicit TTL/invalidation for reference data and no cache for balances — read from primary or accept replica lag (L40).

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does Caching Solve (and Create)?

Problem 1: Repeated Branch Lookups

text
Every payment validates branch_id → SELECT branches 5000/sec
Branch changes rarely — cache branch row — reduce DB load

Problem 2: Expensive Reference Joins

text
Fee calculation needs product + region rules — complex join — cache rule set

Problem 3: Read Replica Lag vs Cache

text
Replica 2s stale — OR L2 stale 60s stale — architect must pick consciously
Post-payment balance: neither cache nor replica — primary read (L40)

Problem 4: L2 After Payment Capture

text
Account balance updated in DB — L2 still holds old balance if mistakenly cached
Customer sees wrong balance — regulatory incident

Problem 5: DR Failover Cache Storm

text
All app pods cold cache — thundering herd on branches, accounts metadata
Database connection spike — need warming + circuit breaker

Problem 6: Multi-Instance Invalidation

text
Pod A updates branch daily_limit — Pod B L2 still old EhCache local
Need distributed invalidation or TTL short enough

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Hibernate Built Second-Level Cache

Reduce Read Load on Immutable/Slow-Changing Data

text
Entity load by PK: check L2 → skip SELECT
Good for reference tables — not transactional balances

Share Across Transactions

text
L1 dies at commit — L2 survives for next request
SessionFactory-scoped — all EntityManagers benefit

Query Cache (Narrow Use)

text
Caches "query key → list of entity IDs"
Still loads entities from L2 entity regions
Invalidates when any entity in regions changes — coarse
Payment OLTP: queries too dynamic (account_id, date range) — poor hit rate

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Hibernate L2 Works Internally

Entity Region

text
@Cache(usage = CacheConcurrencyStrategy.READ_ONLY)
@Entity Branch { ... }

Load branch_id=42:
  1. L1 miss (new txn)
  2. L2 region "com.bank.Branch" lookup key 42
  3. Hit → deserialize dehydrated state → build MANAGED entity in L1
  4. Miss → SELECT from DB → populate L2 → return

Update branch (rare admin txn):
  READ_ONLY strategy — exception on UPDATE — correct for true reference data
  READ_WRITE strategy — soft locks, timestamp versioning — complex cluster invalidation

CacheConcurrencyStrategy Options

StrategyUseWritesCluster safe
READ_ONLYImmutable referenceFail on updateYes with replication
NONSTRICT_READ_WRITERare updates, stale OK brieflyInvalidate lazyApproximate
READ_WRITERead-heavy, occasional updateSoft lockJGroups/invalidation
TRANSACTIONALJTA cacheFullRare, complex

Banking reference data: READ_ONLY + admin redeploy or explicit region evict on change.

Query Cache Internals

text
@QueryHints(@Cacheable true) on JPQL

First run: execute SQL → get IDs [1,5,9] → store in query cache region
Entity data in entity L2 regions

Second run same query params: get IDs from query cache → assemble from L2

Any UPDATE to Payment entity in region → entire query cache region may invalidate — unpredictable
Payment dynamic queries: cache pollution — disable

L1 vs L2 Interaction

text
Same txn:
  find Branch 42 → L2 hit → L1 MANAGED
  find Branch 42 again → L1 hit — no L2 check

After commit:
  L1 cleared — L2 still has Branch 42
Next txn: L2 hit — no SELECT

Spring @Cacheable (Separate from Hibernate L2)

java
@Cacheable(value = "branches", key = "#branchId")
public BranchDto getBranch(UUID branchId) {
    return branchRepo.findById(branchId).map(mapper::toDto).orElseThrow();
}

@CacheEvict(value = "branches", key = "#branch.branchId")
public BranchDto updateBranch(Branch branch) { ... }
text
Redis stores serialized BranchDto — not Hibernate entity
Clear invalidation contract — you write @CacheEvict on every update path
Preferred pattern in Spring Boot payment services vs Hibernate L2

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Where Cache Data Lives

Local EhCache / Caffeine (L2 Provider)

text
On-heap: Branch entities deserialized — MB scale OK
Off-heap/disk: larger regions — latency trade-off
Per JVM — DR failover new JVM — empty cache

Redis (Spring Cache or Redisson Hibernate L2)

text
Key: branch:42 → JSON or serialized DTO
TTL: 3600s for branch metadata
Memory: cluster shared — all pods consistent after TTL
Invalidation: pub/sub on branch update event from outbox consumer
Separate Redis cluster from idempotency keys — logical DB index separation

What NOT to Store

text
Account.balance in Redis without rigorous invalidation:
  capture() updates PG → forget Redis evict → stale 30s → wrong UI

If caching balance:
  write-through on capture txn + TTL 5s max + version check — still risky
Architect default: don't cache balance — query primary

Cache vs Read Replica

text
Replica: always fresh within lag — source = DB replication
L2: may be fresher than replica for reference if primary load cached before replicate
Balance: primary SELECT — no L2 — no replica
Branch: Redis cache — OK — invalidate on admin change

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Memory Planning

CacheTypical sizeEviction
L1 per txnKBEnd of txn
L2 Branch (500 rows)~1–5 MBLRU region maxEntries
Redis branch cache500 × 2KB = 1MBTTL + LRU maxmemory
Query cacheAvoid paymentsN/A
@Cacheable DTOControlled per keyTTL

Thundering Herd on Cold Start

text
1000 pods restart after deploy:
  Each requests branch list — cache miss — 1000 × SELECT branches
Mitigation:
  - Warm cache job on startup
  - Single-flight (only one thread loads key)
  - Stale-while-revalidate
  - Reasonable TTL + random jitter

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Cache Flows in Payment Platform

Flow 1: Branch Validation (Cache Hit)

text
1. capture() needs branch daily_limit
2. branchService.getBranch(branchId) — @Cacheable Redis
3. Redis HIT → return BranchDto — 0 DB queries
4. Validate amount ≤ daily_limit
5. persist payment on primary DB

Flow 2: Branch Admin Update (Invalidation)

text
1. Admin UPDATE branches SET daily_limit=...
2. @CacheEvict branchId on update method
3. Publish BranchUpdated outbox event (optional — other services evict)
4. Next capture → Redis MISS → SELECT primary → cache refresh

Flow 3: Payment Capture — No Balance Cache

text
1. capture() — load account from primary via accountRepo.findById
2. No @Cacheable on account — always fresh in txn
3. UPDATE balance in same txn — L1 only — no L2
4. Commit — L1 cleared — next read hits DB

Flow 4: Mistaken @Cache on Account (Incident)

text
1. getBalance() @Cacheable — cached 1000.00
2. capture() debits 250 — DB balance 750 — no cache evict
3. getBalance() returns 1000 from Redis — WRONG
Fix: remove cache OR evict on every write path + saga consumers — fragile

Flow 5: DR Failover — Cache + Replica

text
1. Failover to DR region — Redis cluster DR endpoint (or empty)
2. All caches cold — spike SELECT branches
3. Payment capture uses DR primary for accounts — no stale L2
4. Do NOT restore old region Redis snapshot into DR — stale branch limits
5. Warm critical reference caches from DR DB before full traffic

Flow 6: Hibernate L2 READ_ONLY Branch Entity (If Used)

text
1. em.find(Branch.class, id) — L2 hit after first load
2. Admin updates branch via native SQL bypassing Hibernate — L2 STALE
3. Risk: READ_ONLY won't auto-refresh — evict region after admin native update
Prefer Spring @Cacheable DTO over Hibernate L2 for clarity

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Cache Performance Trade-offs

Hit Rate Requirements

text
Cache worth it if:
  hit_rate > 90% AND load cost high AND staleness acceptable

Branch lookup: 5000/sec, 200 branches, changes 1/day → hit rate ~99.9% → excellent

Payment list by account: unique query per user → query cache hit rate ~0% → useless

Latency

text
Redis GET: 0.5–2 ms LAN
PostgreSQL PK SELECT (cached buffer): 0.1–1 ms
L2 local heap: microseconds

Reference data: Redis saves DB connection pool slots under peak — valuable
Balance: PG PK read on primary ~1ms — cache savings tiny vs correctness risk

Invalidation Cost

text
Every capture evicting account cache: defeats cache — write-heavy keys useless
Reference data: invalidate 1 key per day — cheap

Comparison Table

DataCache?Strategy
BranchYesRedis TTL 1h + evict on update
Currency codesYesREAD_ONLY / static
Account balanceNoPrimary read
Payment historyNoDTO query + replica (L48)
Idempotency recordOptional RedisShort TTL — not L2
Fee rulesYesVersioned key fee_rules:v3

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

OperationNo cacheRedis @CacheableHibernate L2
Branch readO(1) DBO(1) Redis + miss DBO(1) heap L2
InvalidationN/AO(1) key deleteO(1) entity evict or region clear
ConsistencyStrongTTL + explicitRegion strategy dependent
DR cold startO(n) DBO(n) missO(n) miss
Cluster coordNoneRedis centralJGroups/Infinispan complex

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Configuration & Code Examples

Spring Cache + Redis (Recommended Pattern)

yaml
spring:
  cache:
    type: redis
  data:
    redis:
      host: redis.internal
      port: 6379
      timeout: 200ms

app:
  cache:
    branch-ttl: 3600s
java
@Configuration
@EnableCaching
public class CacheConfig {

    @Bean
    public RedisCacheConfiguration branchCacheConfig() {
        return RedisCacheConfiguration.defaultCacheConfig()
            .entryTtl(Duration.ofHours(1))
            .disableCachingNullValues()
            .serializeValuesWith(
                RedisSerializationContext.SerializationPair.fromSerializer(
                    new GenericJackson2JsonRedisSerializer()));
    }

    @Bean
    public RedisCacheManager cacheManager(RedisConnectionFactory factory) {
        Map<String, RedisCacheConfiguration> configs = Map.of(
            "branches", branchCacheConfig(),
            "feeRules", branchCacheConfig().entryTtl(Duration.ofMinutes(15))
        );
        return RedisCacheManager.builder(factory)
            .cacheDefaults(RedisCacheConfiguration.defaultCacheConfig().entryTtl(Duration.ofMinutes(5)))
            .withInitialCacheConfigurations(configs)
            .build();
    }
}

Branch Service — Cache + Evict

java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class BranchService {

    private final BranchRepository branchRepo;
    private final BranchMapper mapper;

    @Cacheable(cacheNames = "branches", key = "#branchId")
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public BranchDto getBranch(UUID branchId) {
        return branchRepo.findById(branchId)
            .map(mapper::toDto)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new BranchNotFoundException(branchId));
    }

    @CacheEvict(cacheNames = "branches", key = "#dto.branchId")
    @Transactional
    public BranchDto updateDailyLimit(BranchUpdateCommand cmd) {
        Branch branch = branchRepo.findById(cmd.branchId()).orElseThrow();
        branch.setDailyLimit(cmd.newLimit());
        return mapper.toDto(branch);
    }
}

Payment Capture — Explicit No Cache on Account

java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PaymentCaptureService {

    @Transactional  // primary DB — no @Cacheable
    public PaymentResult capture(CaptureCommand cmd) {
        BranchDto branch = branchService.getBranch(cmd.branchId()); // cached OK
        validateLimit(branch, cmd.amount());

        Account account = accountRepo.findById(cmd.accountId()).orElseThrow(); // always DB
        account.debit(cmd.amount());

        Payment payment = paymentRepo.save(Payment.pending(cmd));
        outboxRepo.save(OutboxEvent.paymentCreated(payment));
        return PaymentResult.from(payment, account.getBalance());
    }
}

Part 12 — Production Usage

Caching Policy — Production Banking

Tiered Data Classification

ClassExamplesCacheInvalidation
Tier 0 mutablebalance, payment statusNever L2/RedisN/A
Tier 1 read-mostlybranch, product configRedis TTL + evictAdmin + event
Tier 2 staticISO country listREAD_ONLY / 24h TTLDeploy bump version
Tier 3 computeddashboard aggregatesShort TTL 60sTime-based only

Monitoring

text
Redis: hit rate, evicted keys, memory, latency p99
Application: @Cacheable miss ratio per cache name
Alerts: balance endpoint using cache (lint/static check)
Post-DR: cache warm job success
Hibernate stats: L2 hit ratio — if enabled — staging only

PCI / Security

text
Don't cache PAN, CVV, full account numbers in Redis plaintext
Encrypt Redis at rest + in transit — separate auth
Cache keys namespaced per environment — no prod key in staging

DR Runbook Cache Section

text
1. Failover apps to DR region
2. Point Redis to DR cluster (pre-replicated or empty)
3. Run cache warm: load all branches, fee rules from DR DB
4. Rate-limit if warm incomplete — degrade non-critical reads
5. Never copy primary Redis RDB snapshot after long outage — stale limits
6. Document RPO for cached reference data = TTL max staleness acceptable

Part 15 — Architect Perspective

Consistency Architecture with Cache + Replica + DR

text
                    ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
                    │         CONSISTENCY SPECTRUM         │
                    └─────────────────────────────────────┘
   STRONG ◄────────────────────────────────────────────► EVENTUAL

   Primary DB          None (default money)     Redis branch 1h TTL
   balance read        payment writes             fee rules versioned
   FOR UPDATE          outbox relay               static ISO list

   Read replica        Dashboard reports          Cross-region DR cache cold
   (lag 1-5s)          (L40 documented)             warm on failover

Decision Framework

text
Should we cache this data?
  1. Does it change after payment/ledger writes? → NO cache
  2. Is stale value legally acceptable for N seconds? → document N
  3. Can we invalidate all write paths? → if no, don't cache
  4. Is hit rate high enough? → if no, don't cache
  5. Does replica lag suffice for reads? → prefer replica over cache

L2 vs Redis vs Replica

NeedChoose
Branch metadataRedis @Cacheable
Payment listReplica + DTO query (L48)
Balance after payPrimary SELECT
Global reportWarehouse
Hibernate entity sharingAvoid L2 — use Redis DTO

Platform ADR Template

text
Title: No cache for Tier 0 financial mutable state
Decision: Redis only for Tier 1 reference; no Hibernate L2; no query cache
Consequences: Higher DB reads on accounts — acceptable for correctness
Exceptions: None for balance/payment status

Mistake 1: @Cacheable on Account.getBalance()

text
Stale balance after capture — customer trust destroyed

Mistake 2: Hibernate L2 on Payment Entity

text
Status updates don't invalidate properly — ghost PENDING payments

Mistake 3: Query Cache on Dynamic JPQL

text
Thrashing invalidation — zero benefit — CPU waste

Mistake 4: No @CacheEvict on Admin Update Path

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: L1 vs L2 cache?

L1 per transaction persistence context; L2 shared across sessions for entity state by PK.

Q2: Cache payment balance?

No — mutable financial state — must read primary after write.

Q3: What can be cached in banking?

Branch metadata, fee rules, static reference data — with TTL/eviction.

Q4: Spring @Cacheable vs Hibernate L2?

Spring caches method results (DTOs) with explicit Redis; Hibernate caches entities below JPA — less transparent.

Q5: Query cache?

Caches query result IDs — poor for dynamic payment queries — usually disabled.

Mid-Level

Q6: Invalidation after branch limit update?

@CacheEvict on admin service + optional Kafka event for other pods.

Q7: READ_ONLY cache strategy?

Immutable entities — throws on update — good for currency codes.

Q8: Post-payment balance read strategy?

Same txn return balance; subsequent GET from primary — no Redis.

Q9: Cache vs read replica for reports?

Replica for heavy reads; Redis for small hot reference — different tiers.

Q10: Thundering herd on deploy?

Warm cache, single-flight, TTL jitter, stagger pod restart.

Senior

Q11: Design caching for payment platform.

Tier 0 no cache; Redis for branch/fee with evict; no L2; no query cache; DR warm runbook; monitor hit rate.

Q12: DR failover cache consistency?

Empty/warm from DR DB; don't restore stale snapshot; document reference data RPO = TTL.

Q13: Natural id cache for branch_code?

OK for lookup optimization — evict on code change — rare.

Staff / Architect

Q14: ADR: prohibit balance caching — exceptions?

None Tier 0; read models with version check for marketing UI only — not authorization.

Scenario

Scenario: "Users see old daily limit after ops raised branch cap."

Redis @Cacheable without @CacheEvict on update path — fix evict + verify admin uses same service.

Part 1 — Concept

What Are Read Models and CQRS?

CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) splits writes (commands) from reads (queries) into separate models and often separate storage paths. A read model (projection) is a denormalized, query-optimized copy of data built from events or the write database.

text
WRITE SIDE (Command)                         READ SIDE (Query)
────────────────────                       ────────────────────
payment-service DB                         payment_read DB  OR  same DB read tables
  payments (normalized)                      payment_list_view
  outbox_events                              account_balance_view
  idempotency                                branch_daily_totals_mv
       │                                              ▲
       │  same txn: payment + outbox                   │
       ▼                                              │
  outbox relay ──► Kafka ──► projection consumer ─────┘
       │                              │
       └── saga / ledger-service       └── idempotent upsert read model

CQRS vs Cache vs Read Replica

text
READ REPLICA (L40)     Same schema, async copy, lag, OLTP SQL on replica
REDIS CACHE (L49)      Small hot keys, TTL, invalidation risk
READ MODEL / CQRS      Purpose-built tables/views for UI/search/reports
                       Fed by events — eventual consistency — explicit schema

Projection

A projection is a consumer that listens to PaymentCreated, PaymentCaptured, LedgerDebited and updates read tables optimized for queries:

sql
-- Read model example: customer payment history screen
CREATE TABLE payment_list_view (
    payment_id       UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id      UUID NOT NULL,
    account_id       UUID NOT NULL,
    branch_code      VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,  -- denormalized from branch-service
    amount           DECIMAL(19,4) NOT NULL,
    currency_code    CHAR(3) NOT NULL,
    status           VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    created_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX ix_plv_customer_time ON payment_list_view (customer_id, created_at DESC);

Part 2 — History

Evolution of CQRS and Read Models

text
2004    Greg Young — CQRS term — complex domains — separate read/write
2010    Event Sourcing + CQRS in DDD communities — Axon Framework
2012    Microservices — "API composition" pain — read models per UI
2014    Kafka adoption — projections as Kafka consumers — Kappa architecture
2016    Materialized views in PostgreSQL — native DB projections
2018    Stripe-style APIs — list endpoints backed by search indexes (Elasticsearch L58 preview)
2020+   Banking: core ledger stays normalized OLTP — read models for portals/AML dashboards
        Outbox (L37) makes projections reliable without dual-write
        Saga (L38) — projection marks saga step complete for ops UI
        Architects reject CQRS everywhere — apply per bounded context + query pain

Historical Lesson

CQRS is not "use Kafka instead of SQL." It is accept eventual consistency on reads in exchange for fast, simple queries — while commands stay ACID on the write model (L33, L43).

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Do Read Models Solve?

Problem 1: Cross-Service Join for UI

text
Payment history needs: payment + branch_code + customer_name
Microservices forbid cross-DB JOIN (L43) — API composition N+1 HTTP calls — slow
Read model denormalizes at write/event time

Problem 2: Heavy Report on OLTP

text
Branch daily totals scan payments table — hurts capture latency (L30, L48)
Projection maintains branch_daily_totals incrementally

Problem 3: Search and Filters

text
Find payments by status + date + branch + full-text reference
Normalized OLTP indexes awkward — read model or Elasticsearch side index

Problem 4: Read Replica Still Wrong Shape

text
Replica has same normalized schema — still needs 5-way join — replica lag + bad plan
Read model table = one SELECT for screen

Problem 5: Cache Invalidation Hell (L49)

text
Denormalized JSON in Redis — every payment invalidates many keys
Projection table + query = predictable vs cache whack-a-mole

When NOT to Use CQRS

text
Simple CRUD admin with low traffic — over-engineering
Strong read-your-writes on every field — stick to primary + DTO (L48)
Team lacks projection monitoring/reconciliation discipline

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Denormalize on Purpose (Lesson 9 Revisited)

Query Performance

text
GET /customers/{id}/payments — index-only scan on payment_list_view
No join — no N+1 (L48) — no scatter on shards (L44) if keyed by customer_id

Service Autonomy

text
payment-query-service owns read DB — scales independently from capture service
Write path protected from report load

Explicit Eventual Consistency

text
Document lag SLA: "History updated within 5 seconds"
Better than hidden replica lag or stale cache (L40, L49)

Audit and Rebuild

text
Replay Kafka from offset 0 — rebuild read model after bug
Impossible with ad-hoc cache — valuable for regulated corrections

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Projections Work Internally

Path A: Transactional Outbox → Kafka → Consumer

text
1. capture() txn: INSERT payments + INSERT outbox_events (L37)
2. Relay: poll outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL → publish Kafka → mark published
3. Projection consumer:
     @KafkaListener PaymentCreated
     @Transactional (read model DB)
     IF NOT processed_events.exists(eventId):
         UPSERT payment_list_view ...
         INSERT processed_events
4. Consumer offset commit after txn commit — at-least-once delivery
5. Idempotency on eventId — duplicate delivery safe

Path B: Same Database — Read Table Updated in Application

text
capture() txn:
  INSERT payments
  INSERT payment_list_view (same columns denormalized)
Single ACID — strong consistency read — no event lag
Trade-off: write amplification — coupling — simpler ops
Use when: one service, one DB, need read-your-writes immediately

Path C: PostgreSQL Materialized View

sql
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW branch_daily_totals AS
SELECT branch_id, date_trunc('day', created_at) AS day, SUM(amount)
FROM payments GROUP BY 1, 2;

REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY branch_daily_totals;
-- Batch refresh — lag minutes — OK for exec dashboard

Path D: CDC (Debezium) — Preview L51

text
WAL → Debezium → Kafka → projection
Write path unaware — ops complexity — preview next lesson

Saga Integration (L38)

text
saga_instances table — ops dashboard read model
Consumer listens PaymentFailed → update payment_list_view status + saga_status_view
Compensation events reverse projection: status=REVERSED, subtract branch_daily_total

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Read Model Storage Design

Table Shape — Wide vs Narrow

text
payment_list_view — one row per payment — list UI
account_balance_view — one row per account — balance widget (eventually consistent OR fed from ledger events only)
branch_daily_totals — aggregate — one row per branch per day

Denormalized Columns

text
branch_code copied into payment_list_view — avoid branch-service call on read
customer_name copied — update CustomerRenamed event rewrites projection rows
Storage cost << join cost at 100M payments

Indexes for Read Access Paths

sql
-- Customer app
CREATE INDEX ix_plv_customer_time ON payment_list_view (customer_id, created_at DESC);
-- Branch ops
CREATE INDEX ix_plv_branch_day ON payment_list_view (branch_code, created_at);
-- Status queue
CREATE INDEX ix_plv_status ON payment_list_view (status, created_at) WHERE status = 'PENDING';

Partitioning Read Tables (L30)

text
payment_list_view PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at) monthly
Detach old partitions to archive — same as OLTP strategy

Separate Database / Schema

text
payment_write schema — OLTP normalized
payment_read schema — projections — different connection pool — replica optional
Physical split on RDS: read replica fed by same primary OR separate consumer DB

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Projection Consumer Memory

PatternMemoryNotes
Single event upsertO(1)Standard consumer
Batch poll 500 eventsO(batch)flush + clear if JPA entities
Full replay rebuildO(chunk)TRUNCATE view + batch insert chunks
Materialized view refreshDB serverSpill to disk — schedule off-peak

JPA on Read Model

text
Prefer JdbcTemplate / @Modifying native UPSERT for projections — not full entity graph
If JPA: lightweight @Entity PaymentListView — no lazy collections — one table

Part 8 — Execution Flow

End-to-End Flows

Flow 1: Capture → Eventual List UI (5s SLA)

text
T0: POST /payments → write DB commit — payment row exists
T1: outbox relay publishes PaymentCreated (100ms–2s)
T2: projection consumer UPSERT payment_list_view (200ms)
T3: GET /payments?customerId=X → query-service reads payment_list_view
Customer may see new payment on write API response (return DTO from write txn)
List screen may lag 1–5s — document in UX

Flow 2: Same-DB Dual Write (Strong Read)

text
@Transactional capture():
  save Payment
  save PaymentListViewMapper.from(payment, branchCodeLookup)
Commit — list and detail immediately consistent on read model table
branchCodeLookup: cache branch (L49) or local branch table replica

Flow 3: Ledger Balance Projection

text
LedgerDebited event → account_balance_view SET balance = event.balanceAfter
Source of truth remains ledger-service accounts table
Read model balance is **eventually consistent** — NOT for authorization debit decision
Authorization uses ledger API primary — not projection

Flow 4: Compensation / Reversal

text
PaymentReversed event:
  UPDATE payment_list_view SET status='REVERSED'
  UPDATE branch_daily_totals SET total = total - amount (idempotent by payment_id ledger)
processed_events prevents double-subtract on redelivery

Flow 5: DR Failover

text
Write DB fails over — outbox relay resumes — Kafka retained
Projection consumers idempotent — continue from offset
Read model DB may failover separately — rebuild from Kafka if diverged
Reconciliation job: COUNT/SUM write vs read — alert drift

Flow 6: Shard Routing (L44)

text
Write payment on shard by customer_id
Projection keyed by customer_id — same shard OR dedicated query store per shard
Global search: Elasticsearch aggregate all shards — advanced

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

CQRS Performance Trade-offs

Write Amplification

text
Same-DB projection: +1 INSERT per capture — ~2× write I/O on payment path
Event path: +1 Kafka message + consumer UPSERT — async — doesn't block capture latency
Choose async when capture SLA tight

Read Improvement

text
Before: 3-table join + replica — 50ms p99
After:  index scan payment_list_view — 2ms p99
Report branch totals: O(1) row lookup vs O(n) scan

Lag vs Cache

text
Redis cache TTL 60s — stale arbitrary
Projection lag = outbox relay + consumer — measurable — target p99 < 5s
Strong consistency path: dual write same txn — 0 lag — higher write cost

When CQRS Beats Cache (L49)

FactorCacheRead model
Complex queryPoor hit ratePurpose-built index
High cardinality keysMemory explosionDisk cheap
InvalidationHardEvent-driven upsert
Rebuild after bugFlush Redis hopeReplay Kafka
Cross-service fieldsCompose APIsDenormalize on event

When Replica Beats CQRS

text
Ad-hoc analyst SQL on normalized schema — replica sufficient
Low traffic internal tools — CQRS ops not worth it

Part 10 — Complexity Analysis

OperationNormalized + joinRead model
List payments pageO(log n + k) joinO(log n + k) single table
Capture writeO(1)O(1) + O(1) projection or async O(1)
Branch daily totalO(n) scanO(1) lookup if maintained
Customer rename propagateN/AO(payments for customer) update — rare
Rebuild projectionN/AO(events) replay
ConsistencyStrong (same DB)Eventual (async)

Implementation Examples

Write Model — Outbox (payment-service)

java
@Transactional
public PaymentResult capture(CaptureCommand cmd) {
    Payment payment = paymentRepo.save(Payment.pending(cmd));
    outboxRepo.save(OutboxEvent.of("PaymentCreated", payment));
    return PaymentResult.from(payment); // strong — from write txn
}

Outbox Payload

json
{
  "eventId": "evt-uuid",
  "eventType": "PaymentCreated",
  "paymentId": "pay-uuid",
  "customerId": "cust-uuid",
  "accountId": "acct-uuid",
  "branchId": "branch-uuid",
  "branchCode": "NYC001",
  "amount": "250.00",

Projection Consumer (payment-query-service)

java
@KafkaListener(topics = "payment-events")
@Transactional
public void onPaymentEvent(PaymentEventEnvelope envelope) {
    if (processedEventRepo.existsById(envelope.eventId())) {
        return;
    }

    switch (envelope.eventType()) {
        case "PaymentCreated" -> upsertListView(envelope.payload());
        case "PaymentCaptured" -> updateStatus(envelope.payload(), "CAPTURED");
        case "PaymentReversed" -> reverse(envelope.payload());
        default -> log.warn("Unknown event {}", envelope.eventType());
    }

    processedEventRepo.save(new ProcessedEvent(envelope.eventId()));
}

private void upsertListView(PaymentCreatedPayload p) {
    jdbcTemplate.update("""
        INSERT INTO payment_list_view (
            payment_id, customer_id, account_id, branch_code,
            amount, currency_code, status, created_at
        ) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
        ON CONFLICT (payment_id) DO UPDATE SET
            status = EXCLUDED.status,
            amount = EXCLUDED.amount
        """,
        p.paymentId(), p.customerId(), p.accountId(), p.branchCode(),
        p.amount(), p.currencyCode(), p.status(), p.createdAt());
}

Same-DB Dual Write (Strong Consistency List)

java
@Transactional
public PaymentResult captureWithSyncProjection(CaptureCommand cmd) {
    BranchDto branch = branchService.getBranch(cmd.branchId());
    Payment payment = paymentRepo.save(Payment.pending(cmd));

    paymentListViewRepo.save(PaymentListView.from(payment, branch.branchCode()));
    outboxRepo.save(OutboxEvent.paymentCreated(payment));
    return PaymentResult.from(payment);
}

Incremental Aggregate Maintenance

java
private void onPaymentCaptured(PaymentCapturedPayload p) {
    jdbcTemplate.update("""
        UPDATE branch_daily_totals
        SET total_amount = total_amount + ?,
            payment_count = payment_count + 1
        WHERE branch_code = ? AND business_day = ?
        """, p.amount(), p.branchCode(), p.businessDay());

    jdbcTemplate.update("""
        INSERT INTO branch_daily_totals (branch_code, business_day, total_amount, payment_count)
        VALUES (?, ?, ?, 1)
        ON CONFLICT (branch_code, business_day) DO UPDATE
        SET total_amount = branch_daily_totals.total_amount + EXCLUDED.total_amount,
            payment_count = branch_daily_totals.payment_count + 1
        """, p.branchCode(), p.businessDay(), p.amount());
}

Reconciliation Job

sql
-- Nightly drift detection
SELECT w.payment_id
FROM payments w
LEFT JOIN payment_list_view r ON r.payment_id = w.payment_id
WHERE r.payment_id IS NULL
   OR w.status <> r.status
   OR w.amount <> r.amount;

SELECT SUM(w.amount) AS write_total, SUM(r.amount) AS read_total
FROM payments w
JOIN payment_list_view r ON r.payment_id = w.payment_id
WHERE w.created_at >= CURRENT_DATE;

JPA Read Entity (Query Service Only)

java
@Entity
@Table(name = "payment_list_view")
@Immutable
public class PaymentListView {
    @Id
    private UUID paymentId;
    private UUID customerId;
    private String branchCode;
    private BigDecimal amount;
    private String currencyCode;
    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
    private PaymentStatus status;
    private Instant createdAt;
}

public interface PaymentListViewRepository extends JpaRepository<PaymentListView, UUID> {
    Page<PaymentListView> findByCustomerIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc(UUID customerId, Pageable page);
}
// No writes through JPA — consumer uses JDBC UPSERT — repository read-only

Part 12 — Production Usage

CQRS in Production Banking

Choose Sync vs Async Projection

RequirementPattern
Receipt shows payment immediately on listSame-DB dual write OR return write DTO + async list
List lag ≤ 5s OKOutbox → Kafka → projection
Regulatory report EODMaterialized view refresh nightly
Fraud dashboard near-real-timeAsync projection + monitoring lag

Monitoring

text
□ Consumer lag (Kafka consumer group lag)
□ Projection processing latency (event createdAt → view updatedAt)
□ processed_events duplicate rate
□ Reconciliation drift count (nightly job)
□ Outbox unpublished backlog (L37)
□ Read model DB size / index bloat

Operational Runbook

text
Projection bug deployed:
  1. Stop consumer
  2. Fix code
  3. TRUNCATE payment_list_view OR delete affected range
  4. Reset consumer offset to replay start OR run backfill job from write DB
  5. Validate reconciliation
  6. Resume consumer

Multi-Service Denormalization

text
CustomerRenamed event → payment-query updates customer_name column in view
BranchMerged event → update branch_code mapping table + rewrite affected rows
Rare events — batch update acceptable

@RestController

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is CQRS?

Separate command (write) model from query (read) model — often optimized differently.

Q2: What is a projection?

Consumer that builds read tables from domain events.

Q3: CQRS vs read replica?

Replica copies OLTP schema; read model is purpose-built denormalized tables.

Q4: Why outbox with projections?

Atomic write + event intent — reliable delivery to Kafka without dual-write (L37).

Q5: Eventual consistency example?

Payment list shows new row 3 seconds after capture — projection lag.

Mid-Level

Q6: Idempotent projection consumer design?

processed_events table keyed by eventId — UPSERT — check before apply.

Q7: Same-DB dual write vs async projection trade-off?

Sync: strong list consistency, write cost. Async: lower capture coupling, lag SLA.

Q8: How handle PaymentReversed in projection?

UPDATE status — decrement aggregates idempotently — no DELETE.

Q9: Why not cache instead of read model for payment list?

High cardinality, complex invalidation, poor hit rate — table + index scales.

Q10: Reconciliation purpose?

Detect write vs read drift — mandatory for regulated systems.

Senior

Q11: Design payment history across payment + branch + customer microservices.

Capture emits PaymentCreated with denormalized fields; query-service projection; list API on payment_list_view; reconciliation nightly.

Q12: Saga + projection for support dashboard?

Consume saga step events → saga_status_view; link payment_id; compensate updates status.

Q13: DR with read model?

Failover write + read DB; consumer idempotent; replay Kafka if diverged; reconciliation.

Staff / Architect

Q14: When reject CQRS proposal?

Low traffic, strong consistency all reads, no cross-service compose pain — DTO + index sufficient.

Q15: Consistency matrix for payment platform APIs?

Document strong vs eventual per endpoint — authorization always primary ledger.

Scenario

Scenario: "List missing payments but detail by ID works."

Async projection lag or consumer stuck — check lag, outbox backlog, processed_events, reconciliation query.

Part 1 — Concept

What Is Change Data Capture (CDC)?

Change Data Capture is the process of detecting and streaming row-level changes from a database (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) to downstream systems — without the application explicitly publishing events.

text
OLTP DATABASE                         CDC PIPELINE                    CONSUMERS
─────────────                         ────────────                    ─────────
payments table                        Debezium connector              Read model projector
  INSERT row  ──► WAL/redo/binlog ──► parse change event ──► Kafka ──► Elasticsearch
  UPDATE row                          (after/before image)            Data warehouse
  DELETE row                                                          Fraud analytics
                                                                      Cache invalidation

CDC vs Transactional Outbox (Lesson 37)

text
OUTBOX (application-driven)              CDC (database-driven)
───────────────────────────              ─────────────────────
App writes business row + outbox row     App writes business row only
Explicit domain events in payload        Generic row change events
Full control of event shape              Schema/table oriented
Same txn as business write               Reads committed WAL — after commit
Best for: cross-service workflows        Best for: analytics, search, sync replicas
         saga, business semantics                 audit pipelines, read models at scale

Debezium

Debezium is the dominant open-source CDC platform — Kafka Connect connectors read database transaction logs and publish change events to Kafka topics (typically one topic per table).

text
PostgreSQL: logical decoding slot → pgoutput plugin → Debezium → Kafka
Oracle: LogMiner / XStream
MySQL: binlog
SQL Server: CDC tables / log reader

Part 2 — History

Evolution of CDC

text
2000s   ETL batch extracts nightly — stale analytics
        Oracle GoldenGate — commercial CDC — expensive, DBA-operated

2010s   LinkedIn Databus, Maxwell — MySQL binlog tailing
        Kafka Connect framework — pluggable connectors

2016    Debezium project (Red Hat) — unified CDC to Kafka
        PostgreSQL logical replication mature — pgoutput

2018    Event-driven microservices — debate: outbox vs CDC
        "Dual write problem" — CDC avoids app publishing code for analytics path

2020+   AWS DMS CDC, Confluent Oracle CDC, Aurora PostgreSQL logical replication
        Banking: core OLTP still uses outbox for PaymentCreated semantics
        CDC feeds Snowflake, Elasticsearch, read models, operational data stores
        Schema Registry (Avro/JSON Schema) for event evolution
        Exactly-once: idempotent consumers + Kafka transactions — not magic

Historical Lesson

CDC turns the database WAL into an event stream. It is powerful for integration and analytics, but business meaning (PaymentCaptured vs raw UPDATE status column) still needs careful mapping — often outbox for commands, CDC for mirrors.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does CDC Solve?

Problem 1: Analytics Without OLTP Load

text
BI team runs heavy JOINs on payments — crush capture latency
CDC stream to Snowflake — OLTP untouched

Problem 2: Avoid Dual-Write to Kafka from App

text
Every team implements outbox relay differently — inconsistent
CDC: one platform team operates Debezium — all tables available

Problem 3: Search Index Sync

text
Full-text search on payment reference, customer email — Elasticsearch
Maintaining sync via app code fragile — CDC keeps index aligned

Problem 4: Cross-Region Read Model

text
Global query store in another region — CDC + Kafka MirrorMaker
Not application publish burden

Problem 5: Legacy System Integration

text
Old Oracle core banking — cannot add outbox — CDC extracts changes for new microservices
Strangler pattern feed

When CDC Is Wrong Tool

text
Need rich domain event payload — use outbox (L37)
Need before-commit visibility — CDC is always after commit
DELETE semantics for compliance — CDC emits DELETE — downstream must handle tombstones
Low-volume simple app — outbox sufficient

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Stream WAL Instead of Polling?

Efficiency

text
SELECT * FROM payments WHERE updated_at > ? polling:
  Misses deletes, index scan cost, duplicates, lag

WAL CDC:
  Every committed change exactly once in order (per partition key)
  No extra read load on hot tables

Decoupling

text
Application unaware of downstream consumers
Add new projector without changing payment-service JAR

Near-Real-Time

text
Sub-second lag typical PostgreSQL → Kafka
Faster than nightly ETL — fraud rules, dashboards

Audit Trail

text
Immutable change log — before/after images — compliance reconstruction
Supplement payments_audit table (L43)

Part 5 — Internal Working

How CDC Works Internally

PostgreSQL Logical Replication Path

text
1. wal_level = logical on primary
2. CREATE PUBLICATION dbz_publication FOR TABLE payments, accounts, ...;
3. Debezium creates replication slot: pg_replication_slots
4. WAL records INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE decoded to logical change messages
5. Connector converts to Kafka Connect struct:
     {
       "op": "c",  // create
       "before": null,
       "after": { "payment_id": "...", "amount": "250.00", "status": "PENDING", ... },
       "source": { "table": "payments", "lsn": 12345678, ... },
       "ts_ms": ...
     }
6. Kafka producer sends to topic db.payments.payments (config dependent)
7. Slot retains WAL until consumer confirms — lagging consumer → WAL bloat (L40 slot risk)

Operation Codes

opMeaningKafka message
cINSERTafter only
uUPDATEbefore + after
dDELETEbefore only
rsnapshot readinitial load

Initial Snapshot + Streaming

text
Connector start:
  Phase 1: SNAPSHOT — consistent table export — all existing rows as 'r' or 'c' events
  Phase 2: STREAM — continuous WAL from snapshot LSN
Read model can bootstrap without one-time SQL dump job

Schema Changes

text
ALTER TABLE payments ADD COLUMN fee_amount:
  Debezium schema change event → Schema Registry new version
  Consumers must tolerate unknown fields — forward compatible readers
  Breaking renames: treat as new column + migrate — avoid in-flight CDC confusion

Ordering Guarantees

text
Kafka partition key = primary key (payment_id)
All changes for one payment ordered in one partition
Cross-table order NOT guaranteed — saga/outbox for cross-table atomic semantics
payment + outbox in same txn → two CDC events — may arrive interleaved with other tables
For outbox pattern with CDC: some teams CDC the outbox table only — relay still explicit

Exactly-Once-ish

text
True exactly-once end-to-end: hard across DB + Kafka + consumer DB
Practical pattern:
  At-least-once Kafka delivery
  Idempotent consumer: UPSERT by PK + processed offset per partition OR event source lsn
  Kafka transactions + read_committed — advanced — latency cost
Banking: idempotency table keyed by (topic, partition, offset) or source.lsn

Part 6 — Storage Internals

CDC Storage Impact on Source Database

Replication Slot WAL Retention

text
Laggy Debezium consumer OR stopped connector:
  pg_replication_slots.active = false but slot exists
  pg_wal grows — disk full — primary outage (Lesson 40 slot warning)

Monitor:
  SELECT slot_name, pg_wsize(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained
  FROM pg_replication_slots;

Publication Scope

text
Publish only needed tables — not entire database
  payments, accounts, ledger_entries — yes
  session_tokens — no PII leak to analytics

Kafka Topic Storage

text
Compacted topic optional for latest state per key — tombstones on DELETE
Append-only for audit — longer retention 7–30 days — replay projections
PCI: encrypt topics — mask PAN columns at Debezium SMT (Single Message Transform)

Consumer Read Model Storage

text
Same payment_list_view as L50 — fed by CDC consumer instead of domain event consumer
Additional metadata columns:
  source_lsn BIGINT — ordering/idempotency
  last_applied_at TIMESTAMPTZ

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Memory and Resource Usage

ComponentMemory/CPURisk
Debezium connectorJVM heap, decode buffersConnector crash → slot lag
Kafka brokersTopic retention sizeDisk
Consumer projectorBatch bufferO(batch) — flush chunks
PostgreSQL logical decodewalsender memoryMany slots multiply
Snapshot phaseTable scan I/ORun off-peak or use replica slot on standby (PG 16+ logical standby)

Banking Snapshot Strategy

text
Large payments table 500M rows:
  Snapshot from read replica connector (where supported) OR chunked snapshot signal
  Stagger initial load — avoid peak — coordinate with DBAs

Part 8 — Execution Flow

End-to-End CDC Flows

Flow 1: CDC → Read Model (Replace Domain Event Consumer)

text
1. capture() INSERT payments — commit — WAL record
2. Debezium emits op=c to Kafka topic db.payments.payments
3. Projector consumer:
     if processed_offsets contains (partition, offset): skip
     UPSERT payment_list_view from message.after
     record offset processed
4. GET /payments list reads payment_list_view — lag ~1–3s
No outbox row required for this read path — trade-off: no PaymentCreated business envelope

Flow 2: Outbox for Saga + CDC for Analytics (Hybrid — Recommended)

text
Write path:
  payment + outbox PaymentCreated (L37) — saga orchestration
CDC path:
  Debezium all tables → Snowflake + Elasticsearch + branch aggregates
Outbox: business events
CDC: mirrors and analytics — clear separation

Flow 3: UPDATE Status — Projection

text
1. UPDATE payments SET status='CAPTURED' WHERE payment_id=?
2. CDC op=u before={PENDING} after={CAPTURED}
3. Projector: UPDATE payment_list_view SET status='CAPTURED'
4. Increment branch_daily_totals if not already counted — idempotent by payment_id+status transition

Flow 4: DELETE (Should Be Rare)

text
Hard DELETE payments — CDC op=d
Projector: UPDATE status='DELETED' tombstone OR delete row — banking prefer no hard DELETE
Kafka compacted topic may emit tombstone — consumer removes from ES index

Flow 5: Schema Evolution

text
ALTER TABLE payments ADD COLUMN channel VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'MOBILE';
CDC after image includes channel
Old consumers ignore — new consumers use — Schema Registry version bump
Deploy order: backward compatible schema → consumers → producers (DDL)

Flow 6: DR Failover

text
Primary region fails — promote DR PostgreSQL (L42)
Debezium must reconnect to new primary — new replication slot or restore slot metadata
Kafka offsets retained — consumers resume — idempotent UPSERT heals gaps
Reconciliation still required — CDC lag during failover window

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

CDC vs Outbox Performance

AspectOutboxCDC
Write path overhead+1 INSERT outboxZero app overhead
Event semanticsRich domainRow-level
DB loadOutbox poll + relayWAL decode — separate CPU
LagRelay intervalTypically lower
Slot riskNoneWAL retention if lag
Table coverageExplicitAll published tables
PII controlPayload designMust filter in connector

Throughput

text
PostgreSQL logical decoding: 10k–50k events/sec possible — hardware dependent
Kafka partition count scales consumers
Hot payments table — partition key payment_id preserves order per payment

When CDC Replaces Outbox for Read Model (L50)

text
Replace when:
  ✅ Read model is 1:1 row mirror of payments table
  ✅ OK with column-level semantics not domain events
  ✅ Platform team operates Debezium + monitoring

Keep outbox when:
  ✅ Saga, PaymentCreated enrichment, cross-service contracts
  ✅ Need event before other systems without exposing full table CDC
  ✅ Smaller team without CDC ops maturity

Idempotent Projector (Spring Kafka + JDBC)

java
@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PaymentCdcProjector {

    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;
    private final CdcOffsetRepository offsetRepo;

    @KafkaListener(topics = "bank.payments.public.payments", groupId = "payment-list-cdc")
    @Transactional
    public void onPaymentChange(ConsumerRecord<String, Map<String, Object>> record) {
        String offsetKey = record.topic() + ":" + record.partition() + ":" + record.offset();
        if (offsetRepo.exists(offsetKey)) {
            return;
        }

        Map<String, Object> row = record.value();
        if ("d".equals(row.get("__op")) || "true".equals(String.valueOf(row.get("__deleted")))) {
            markDeleted(UUID.fromString((String) row.get("payment_id")));
        } else {
            upsertListView(row);
        }

        offsetRepo.save(new CdcOffset(offsetKey, Instant.now()));
    }

    private void upsertListView(Map<String, Object> row) {
        jdbc.update("""
            INSERT INTO payment_list_view (
                payment_id, account_id, branch_id, amount, currency_code, status, created_at
            ) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
            ON CONFLICT (payment_id) DO UPDATE SET
                amount = EXCLUDED.amount,
                status = EXCLUDED.status
            """,
            UUID.fromString((String) row.get("payment_id")),
            UUID.fromString((String) row.get("account_id")),
            UUID.fromString((String) row.get("branch_id")),
            new BigDecimal(row.get("amount").toString()),
            row.get("currency_code"),
            row.get("status"),
            Instant.parse(row.get("created_at").toString()));
    }
}

@Transactional
public PaymentResult capture(CaptureCommand cmd) {
    Payment p = paymentRepo.save(Payment.pending(cmd));
    outboxRepo.save(OutboxEvent.paymentCreated(p)); // keep for saga even with CDC read model
    return PaymentResult.from(p);
}

Error Handler + DLT

java
@Bean
public ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory<String, Map<String, Object>> cdcKafkaListenerContainerFactory(
        ConsumerFactory<String, Map<String, Object>> cf,
        KafkaTemplate<String, Object> template) {
    var factory = new ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory<String, Map<String, Object>>();
    factory.setConsumerFactory(cf);
    factory.setCommonErrorHandler(new DefaultErrorHandler(
        new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template),
        new FixedBackOff(1000L, 3)));
    return factory;
}

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

ORM Implications of CDC

Application Unaware — Good

text
Hibernate flush generates WAL changes automatically
CDC captures result — no @Entity listener required for analytics
Avoid @PostPersist publishing duplicate events if also using CDC for same purpose

Envers vs CDC

text
Hibernate Envers: audit tables in same DB — app-triggered revisions
CDC: external stream — all consumers — includes direct SQL DBA changes
Banking Tier 0: Envers optional — CDC + payments_audit (L43) + immutable log

Bypass Hibernate Native SQL

text
DBA or @Modifying native UPDATE bypasses L1 cache — correct in DB
CDC still captures — read model stays consistent
Hibernate L2 cache (L49) may stale — another reason no L2 on mutable entities

Schema Migration with Flyway + CDC

text
Flyway migration deploy:
  1. Add nullable column — backward compatible
  2. Deploy consumers understanding new field
  3. Backfill column
  4. SET NOT NULL
Debezium emits schema change — Schema Registry update
Never rename column in place — add new + deprecate old — CDC consumers break on renames

Snapshot and JPA Read Model Bootstrap

text
Initial snapshot events flood Kafka — consumer uses JDBC batch UPSERT — not entityManager.persist loop
Same guidance as L50 projections — JdbcTemplate for writes

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: CDC Instead of Outbox for Saga

text
Row UPDATE doesn't convey compensation intent — saga breaks — use domain events

Mistake 2: Ignoring Replication Slot Lag

text
WAL fills disk — primary down — entire payment platform out (L40)

Mistake 3: No Idempotency on Consumer

text
Kafka redelivery duplicates read model rows — double-count branch totals

Mistake 4: Publishing Entire Database

text
PII, secrets tables in CDC — compliance breach — table.include.list strict

Mistake 5: Column Rename Without Dual-Write Period

text
All projectors break — use expand-contract schema

Mistake 6: Assuming Cross-Table Transaction Order in Kafka

text
payment INSERT and outbox INSERT — events may interleave — consumer must handle
Outbox-only relay preserves pairing order if single table consumer processes by txn id (advanced)

Mistake 7: DELETE in OLTP Unexpectedly

text
CDC propagates DELETE — search index row gone — prefer soft status

Mistake 8: Duplicate Outbox + CDC Event Processing

text
Two projectors same read table — double apply — choose one primary path or dedupe key

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is CDC?

Capturing database row changes from transaction log and streaming to consumers.

Q2: CDC vs outbox?

Outbox: app-written domain events same txn. CDC: log-driven row changes after commit.

Q3: What is Debezium?

Kafka Connect-based CDC platform for PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, etc.

Q4: Why replication slot monitoring?

Lagging CDC holds WAL — disk full risk on primary.

Q5: At-least-once meaning?

Events may duplicate — consumers must be idempotent.

Mid-Level

Q6: PostgreSQL CDC internals?

logical wal_level, publication, replication slot, pgoutput decodes WAL to change events.

Q7: Idempotent CDC projector design?

UPSERT by PK + track Kafka offset or source LSN in processed table.

Q8: Initial snapshot purpose?

Bootstrap read models/historical warehouse before streaming live changes.

Q9: Schema ADD COLUMN with CDC?

New field in after image — backward compatible consumers — Schema Registry version.

Q10: When CDC over outbox for read model?

1:1 row mirror, platform CDC maturity, many downstream consumers — still keep outbox for saga.

Senior

Q11: Hybrid outbox + CDC architecture for bank payments.

Outbox for saga/ledger domain; Debezium payments/ledger to Snowflake+ES; idempotent projectors; reconciliation; slot monitoring.

Q12: DR failover with Debezium PostgreSQL.

Reconnect to promoted primary; recreate slot or restore; consumers idempotent; expect gap; reconcile.

Q13: Exactly-once claims?

End-to-end exactly-once impractical — idempotent consumers + reconciliation — honest architecture.

Staff / Architect

Q14: GDPR delete with CDC downstream?

DELETE event triggers purge in ES/Snowflake — retention policies — tombstone handling.

Q15: Legacy Oracle core CDC strangler pattern?

GoldenGate/Debezium to Kafka — new microservices consume — no big-bang rewrite.

Scenario

Scenario: "Read model lagged 6 hours, primary disk 95%."

Debezium consumer stuck — replication slot WAL retention — fix consumer, monitor slot, temporarily increase disk — post-mortem alert.
