Part 1 — Concept

What Is MongoDB?

MongoDB is a document-oriented NoSQL database. Data is stored as BSON documents (binary JSON) in collections, not rows in normalized tables.

text
RELATIONAL (PostgreSQL)                 MONGODB (Document)
───────────────────────                 ──────────────────
customers          accounts            customers collection
  │ row              │ row                └─ { _id, name, accounts: [ {...}, {...} ] }
  └──── FK ──────────┘                   payments collection
payments table (columns)                   └─ { _id, amount, metadata: { ... flexible } }

Core Terms

TermMongoDBRDBMS equivalent
DatabaseDatabaseDatabase
CollectionCollectionTable
DocumentJSON-like documentRow
FieldKey in documentColumn
_idPrimary key (ObjectId or UUID)PK
Embedded docNested object/arrayDenormalized / JSON column
ReferenceStore _id of another docForeign key (logical)

Where MongoDB Fits in Payment Platforms

text
TIER 0 CORE LEDGER          PostgreSQL / Oracle — ACID, constraints, money
TIER 1 PAYMENTS OLTP        PostgreSQL — payments, outbox, idempotency
TIER 2 METADATA / LOGS      MongoDB — KYC documents, payment metadata, audit blobs
TIER 3 SEARCH / ANALYTICS   Elasticsearch / warehouse — Lesson 58 preview

Golden rule: MongoDB is not your system of record for account balances or captured payments in regulated banking — PostgreSQL remains authoritative (Lessons 33, 43).

Part 2 — History

Evolution of MongoDB in Enterprise

text
2009    MongoDB 1.x — web scale JSON store — schema-less marketing
2010s   Early fintech misuse — payments in Mongo — consistency incidents
2012    WiredTiger storage engine preview — document-level locking improvement
2015    MongoDB 3.2+ — multi-document transactions absent — embed everything culture
2018    MongoDB 4.0 — multi-document ACID transactions on replica set
2020+   Document model accepted for ancillary data:
        payment request payloads, PSP webhooks, device fingerprint blobs
        PCI token metadata, case management (AML investigations)
        Polyglot persistence: Postgres money + Mongo context
2024+   MongoDB Atlas — global clusters, encryption, compliance certifications
        Architects document which aggregates live in Mongo vs SQL explicitly

Historical Lesson

MongoDB won where the data is semi-structured, high-volume, and eventually consistent OK — not where money invariants require strict relational constraints.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does MongoDB Solve in Payments?

Problem 1: Variable Payment Metadata

text
Card payment: { "3ds": {...}, "issuer": "..." }
UPI payment:  { "vpa": "...", "npciRef": "..." }
Wire:         { "swift": "...", "correspondentBank": "..." }
Fixed SQL columns = sparse NULL jungle — JSONB works too — Mongo if whole service is document-native

Problem 2: Audit / Evidence Blobs

text
Fraud investigation case file: documents, notes, timeline events — nested arrays
Regulatory export bundle — append-only event array in one document

Problem 3: Rapid Schema Evolution

text
New PSP integration adds fields weekly — no Flyway migration per field
Mongo schema flexibility — with discipline (schema validation)

Problem 4: High-Volume Append Logs

text
Webhook callback log from payment gateway — millions/day — TTL indexes auto-expire
Not ideal for core ledger — fine for operational logs

Problem 5: Read-Heavy Document Profiles

text
Customer KYC profile with nested identity documents — load one doc for onboarding UI

When PostgreSQL JSONB Is Enough

text
Same database, ACID with payments row, JSONB column metadata
Choose Mongo when separate scaling team, document-first API, or isolated failure domain

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Not Only SQL?

Impedance Mismatch for Nested Data

text
Java: PaymentRequest with nested DeviceInfo, RiskSignals, PspRawResponse
Mongo: one document maps naturally — one read for support screen
SQL normalized: 5 tables or JSONB — both valid

Horizontal Scale (Sharding)

text
MongoDB sharded cluster — shard key merchant_id — logs and metadata scale
Core ledger still often relational for ACID maturity (Lesson 44)

Developer Velocity for Non-Money Data

text
Product teams iterate metadata schema — Mongo + schema validation versioned
Money stays in Postgres with strict Flyway

Part 5 — Internal Working

How MongoDB Works Internally

Storage Engine (WiredTiger)

text
Document stored as BSON on disk — B-tree indexes on _id and index keys
Document-level locking (not early Mongo global lock)
Journal (WAL-like) — durability — crash recovery
Cache: WiredTiger cache — frequently accessed docs in RAM

_id and ObjectId

text
Default ObjectId: 12 bytes — timestamp + machine + pid + counter
Payment platforms prefer UUID string _id for cross-system correlation with Postgres payment_id
_id indexed uniquely by default

Indexes

text
Single field, compound, multikey (arrays), TTL, text, partial
Compound: { customerId: 1, createdAt: -1 }
Partial: { status: 1 } where status = "OPEN" — AML cases

Replica Set

text
Primary + secondaries — async replication — similar concepts to L40
Read preference: primary for writes, secondaryPreferred for analytics reads
Not cross-region sync substitute for DR planning (L42)

Multi-Document Transactions (4.0+)

text
Session.startTransaction() — multiple docs/collections atomic commit
Performance cost — use for small atomic updates — not cross Mongo + Postgres
Cannot replace Postgres payment capture ACID across databases

Change Streams

text
Real-time CDC-like API on oplog — alternative/complement to Debezium for Mongo-native pipelines
Watch collection for inserts — trigger notifications

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Document Storage Layout

BSON Document Structure

javascript
{
  "_id": "pay-uuid-001",
  "paymentId": "pay-uuid-001",      // same as Postgres PK — correlation
  "customerId": "cust-uuid",
  "amount": { "value": "250.00", "currency": "USD" },  // embedded value object
  "status": "CAPTURED",
  "channel": "MOBILE",
  "metadata": {
    "deviceId": "abc",
    "ip": "203.0.113.1",
    "psp": {
      "name": "STRIPE",
      "rawResponse": { /* large nested blob */ }
    }
  },
  "auditTrail": [
    { "at": ISODate("2026-07-01T14:30:00Z"), "action": "CREATED", "by": "api" },
    { "at": ISODate("2026-07-01T14:30:01Z"), "action": "CAPTURED", "by": "psp-webhook" }
  ],
  "createdAt": ISODate("2026-07-01T14:30:00Z"),
  "updatedAt": ISODate("2026-07-01T14:30:01Z")
}

Embedding vs Referencing

text
EMBED (auditTrail array in payment doc):
  ✅ Load payment + history one query
  ❌ Document grows — 16MB doc limit — hot array unbounded

REFERENCE (payment_metadata doc + payment_audit_events collection):
  ✅ Unbounded audit events — paginate separately
  ❌ Two queries or $lookup (join) — slower

Banking pattern:
  Core status in Postgres — Mongo stores enrichment + webhook logs
  Bounded embed (<100 events) OR separate audit_events collection with paymentId index

Document Size Limit

text
16 MB max per document — never embed unbounded PSP raw payloads — store S3 reference in doc

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Memory and Working Set

FactorImpact
Working setHot indexes + docs must fit RAM for low latency
Large embedded arraysWhole doc loaded on read — waste if only need summary
IndexesEach index duplicates key storage — compound index discipline
WiredTiger cacheDefault ~50% RAM — tune on dedicated Mongo nodes
Aggregation pipelineSpills to disk if allowDiskUse — monitor

Payment Metadata Service

text
Read one payment context doc per support ticket — 5–50 KB — cache friendly
Webhook log collection — millions docs — TTL 90 days — cold data on disk OK

Part 8 — Execution Flow

Flows in Payment Platform

Flow 1: Capture in Postgres + Metadata in Mongo (Polyglot)

text
1. POST /payments — @Transactional Postgres:
     INSERT payments, outbox PaymentCreated
2. Same request async or after commit:
     mongoTemplate.insert(PaymentMetadataDoc.from(cmd, pspResponse))
3. paymentId links both systems — correlation_id mandatory
4. Failure Mongo only: payment exists — reconciliation job backfills metadata
5. Failure Postgres only: no payment — Mongo doc orphaned — TTL cleanup or reconcile delete

Flow 2: Webhook Append Audit

text
1. PSP POST /webhooks/stripe — verify signature
2. INSERT webhook_events doc { paymentId, rawBody, headers, receivedAt }
3. Update Postgres payment status via capture service (authoritative)
4. Mongo webhook log for dispute evidence — not source of truth for balance

Flow 3: AML Case File

text
1. Fraud alert creates aml_cases doc { caseId, customerId, status: OPEN, notes: [] }
2. Analyst appends note: db.cases.updateOne({ _id }, { $push: { notes: note } })
3. Link paymentIds array grows — reference payments in Postgres for amounts
4. Close case — status CLOSED — retain 7 years — no hard delete

Flow 4: CDC from Postgres Enriches Mongo (Optional)

text
Debezium PaymentCreated → consumer upserts Mongo summary doc { paymentId, amount, status }
Mongo not primary writer — projector pattern (L50/L51) — idempotent by paymentId

Flow 5: Support UI Load

text
1. GET payment from Postgres — amount, status (authoritative)
2. GET payment_metadata from Mongo by paymentId — device, PSP raw, audit trail
3. Merge in API layer — DTO to UI
Never show Mongo amount without Postgres confirmation for money display

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

MongoDB vs PostgreSQL JSONB for Metadata

FactorPostgreSQL JSONBMongoDB
Same txn as payment✅ one ACID❌ separate unless saga
Nested queryJSON operatorsNative dot notation
Schema enforcementCHECK + JSON schemaJSON Schema validator
Scale writes separatelyCoupled to OLTP✅ separate cluster
Join with accountsSQL JOIN$lookup or app merge
Team skillDBA + SQLDocument modeling

Query Patterns

javascript
// Find recent metadata for customer — compound index (customerId, createdAt)
db.payment_metadata.find({ customerId: "cust-uuid" })
  .sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(20)

// Partial index — open AML cases only
db.aml_cases.find({ status: "OPEN", assignedTo: "analyst-1" })

Write Concern & Read Concern

text
w: majority — wait replica ack — durability for metadata
readConcern: majority — avoid stale reads after write for case updates
Not substitute for Postgres payment ACID

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

MongoDB Schema & Queries

Collection Schema Validation

javascript
db.runCommand({
  collMod: "payment_metadata",
  validator: {
    $jsonSchema: {
      bsonType: "object",
      required: ["paymentId", "customerId", "amount", "createdAt"],
      properties: {
        paymentId: { bsonType: "string", description: "UUID matching Postgres" },
        customerId: { bsonType: "string" },
        amount: {
          bsonType: "object",
          required: ["value", "currency"],
          properties: {
            value: { bsonType: "string", pattern: "^[0-9]+\\.[0-9]{2}$" },
            currency: { bsonType: "string", minLength: 3, maxLength: 3 }
          }
        },
        metadata: { bsonType: "object" }
      }
    }
  },
  validationLevel: "moderate"
});

Indexes

javascript
db.payment_metadata.createIndex({ paymentId: 1 }, { unique: true });
db.payment_metadata.createIndex({ customerId: 1, createdAt: -1 });
db.webhook_events.createIndex({ receivedAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 7776000 }); // 90 days TTL
db.aml_cases.createIndex(
  { status: 1, assignedTo: 1 },
  { partialFilterExpression: { status: "OPEN" } }
);

Spring Boot — Document Model

java
@Document(collection = "payment_metadata")
public class PaymentMetadataDoc {

    @Id
    private String paymentId;

    @Indexed
    private String customerId;

    private Money amount;

    private String status; // mirror for search — authoritative in Postgres

    private Map<String, Object> metadata;

    private List<AuditEntry> auditTrail;

    private Instant createdAt;
    private Instant updatedAt;
}

public record Money(String value, String currency) {}
public record AuditEntry(Instant at, String action, String by) {}

Repository

java
public interface PaymentMetadataRepository extends MongoRepository<PaymentMetadataDoc, String> {
    Optional<PaymentMetadataDoc> findByPaymentId(String paymentId);
    List<PaymentMetadataDoc> findByCustomerIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc(String customerId, Pageable page);
}

Service — Polyglot Write

java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PaymentEnrichmentService {

    private final PaymentCaptureService postgresCapture; // Postgres
    private final PaymentMetadataRepository mongoRepo;

    public PaymentResult captureWithMetadata(CaptureCommand cmd, Map<String, Object> metadata) {
        PaymentResult result = postgresCapture.capture(cmd); // ACID money

        try {
            mongoRepo.save(PaymentMetadataDoc.builder()
                .paymentId(result.paymentId().toString())
                .customerId(cmd.customerId().toString())
                .amount(new Money(cmd.amount().toPlainString(), cmd.currency()))
                .status("PENDING")
                .metadata(metadata)
                .auditTrail(List.of(new AuditEntry(Instant.now(), "CREATED", "api")))
                .createdAt(Instant.now())
                .build());
        } catch (DuplicateKeyException e) {
            log.warn("Mongo metadata exists for {}", result.paymentId());
        }
        return result;
    }
}

Append Audit with $push

java
public void appendAudit(String paymentId, AuditEntry entry) {
    mongoTemplate.updateFirst(
        Query.query(Criteria.where("paymentId").is(paymentId)),
        new Update().push("auditTrail", entry).set("updatedAt", Instant.now()),
        PaymentMetadataDoc.class);
}

Aggregation — Webhook Count by PSP (Report)

javascript
db.webhook_events.aggregate([
  { $match: { receivedAt: { $gte: ISODate("2026-07-01") } } },
  { $group: { _id: "$pspName", count: { $sum: 1 } } },
  { $sort: { count: -1 } }
]);

MongoDB in Production Banking

│ payment-service     │◄──────────────────►│ metadata-service    │
│ PostgreSQL          │                    │ MongoDB Atlas       │

Data Classification

CollectionSoR?RetentionEncrypted
payments (PG)Yes7 yrYes
payment_metadataNo7 yrYes
webhook_eventsNo90d TTLYes — mask PAN
aml_casesCase SoR7 yrYes — PII

Reconciliation

text
Nightly job:
  SELECT payment_id FROM payments WHERE created_at >= yesterday
  MINUS payment_ids in Mongo payment_metadata
Alert orphan or missing enrichment — backfill from outbox replay
Never reconcile money amounts from Mongo as authoritative

Atlas Production Settings

text
Replica set 3 nodes — multi-AZ
Encryption at rest + in transit
VPC peering to payment-service
Backup continuous + point-in-time
Avoid storing PAN — token references only — PCI scope reduction

Transactions — Mongo Only (Small Scope)

public void onPaymentCaptured(PaymentCapturedEvent event) {

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

JPA + MongoDB Together

Clear Boundary

text
JPA @Entity Payment — Postgres only — never @Document same class
Separate packages: com.bank.payment.domain vs com.bank.metadata.domain
No JPA @ManyToOne to Mongo document — store paymentId String/UUID

Hibernate JSON vs Mongo

text
If metadata small and must be same txn: @JdbcTypeCode(JSON) on Payment.metadata in Postgres
Move to Mongo when:
  document > 100KB average
  independent release cycle
  separate scaling
  nested arrays unbounded

Outbox Triggers Mongo Projector

text
Same as L50/L51 — PaymentCreated Kafka consumer writes Mongo doc
Idempotent findByPaymentId — upsert
JPA write path unchanged — Mongo async
Preferred over dual-write in same HTTP request

Read Merge Pattern

java
public PaymentDetailDto getDetail(UUID paymentId) {
    Payment payment = paymentRepo.findById(paymentId).orElseThrow(); // JPA Postgres
    PaymentMetadataDoc meta = mongoRepo.findByPaymentId(paymentId.toString())
        .orElse(PaymentMetadataDoc.empty());
    return PaymentDetailDto.merge(payment, meta);
}

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Payment Ledger in Mongo

text
Lost ACID guarantees — duplicate charges — regulatory failure

Mistake 2: Trusting Mongo Amount in UI

text
Postgres says 250, Mongo stale 200 — always merge with Postgres for money

Mistake 3: Unbounded auditTrail $push

text
16MB limit crash — archive to audit_events collection

Mistake 4: No Schema Validation

text
Typo amount: "250O" string — no type safety — use JSON Schema validator

Mistake 5: Cross-DB @Transactional Expectation

text
JPA + Mongo atomic — impossible — use after-commit or saga

Mistake 6: Storing PAN in webhook_events

text
PCI scope explosion — tokenize — redact body

Mistake 7: No Reconciliation

text
Postgres payments without Mongo metadata silent forever

Mistake 8: $lookup on Hot Path

text
Mongo join performance poor — denormalize customerId on metadata doc

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: Document vs relational?

Documents nest data in BSON; relational normalizes across tables with FKs.

Q2: MongoDB for payment amounts?

No — PostgreSQL system of record for money — Mongo for metadata/logs.

Q3: _id vs paymentId?

_id is Mongo PK — use same UUID as Postgres payment_id for correlation.

Q4: Embed vs reference?

Embed for bounded nested data loaded together; reference for unbounded/separate lifecycle.

Q5: TTL index?

Auto-delete documents after expireAfterSeconds — webhook logs 90 days.

Mid-Level

Q6: Polyglot capture flow?

Postgres ACID capture + after-commit or async Mongo metadata + reconciliation.

Q7: Mongo multi-doc transactions vs Postgres?

Mongo txn within cluster only — not cross-database with JPA — use events.

Q8: Schema validation in schemaless DB?

$jsonSchema validator on collection — enforce paymentId, amount shape.

Q9: Change streams vs Debezium?

Change streams Mongo-native; Debezium for Postgres CDC (L51) — different sources.

Q10: Reconciliation why?

Dual/async paths orphan docs — nightly paymentId set diff.

Senior

Q11: Design metadata service for multi-PSP payments.

Postgres payments SoR; Mongo payment_metadata + webhook_events TTL; after-commit projector; schema validation; no PAN; reconcile.

Q12: When Postgres JSONB instead of Mongo?

Same txn metadata, small payload, team single-DB ops, strong consistency with payment row.

Q13: 16MB document limit mitigation?

S3 for raw PSP payload, store URL in doc; separate collections.

Staff / Architect

Q14: Polyglot persistence ADR for bank payment platform.

Tier 0 Postgres; Tier 2 Mongo metadata; consistency matrix; prohibited Mongo money; reconciliation mandatory.

Scenario

Scenario: "Support UI shows captured but Mongo metadata missing."

After-commit listener failed — Postgres authoritative — backfill from outbox/Kafka — fix listener + reconciliation alert.

Part 1 — Concept

What Is Redis?

Redis is an in-memory data structure store used as cache, session store, message broker, and coordination layer. It is not a system of record for payment ledger data — it is a fast, ephemeral, explicitly managed sidecar to PostgreSQL.

text
PAYMENT HOT PATH                         REDIS (in-memory)
────────────────                         ────────────────
Spring Boot API                          ┌─────────────────────────┐
     │                                   │ STRING  idempotency:key │
     ├── cache branch metadata ─────────►│ HASH    branch:42       │
     ├── idempotency SET NX EX ─────────►│ STRING  lock:account:501│
     ├── rate limit counter ────────────►│ ZSET    rate:customer:x │
     └── authoritative money ──────────►│ (never balance SoR)     │
            │                             └─────────────────────────┘
            ▼
     PostgreSQL (payments, accounts, ledger)

Core Data Structures (Payment Platform Use)

StructureRedis commandPayment use
StringGET/SET/SET NX EXIdempotency, simple cache, locks
HashHGET/HSETBranch object fields, fee rule fields
ListLPUSH/BRPOPWork queues (careful — not Kafka replacement)
SetSADD/SISMEMBERProcessed event IDs (small sets)
Sorted SetZINCRBYRate limiting windows, leaderboards
StreamXADD/XREADLightweight event log ( niche )

Redis vs PostgreSQL vs MongoDB

text
PostgreSQL  SoR — money, payments, ledger — ACID — disk
MongoDB     Documents — metadata, logs — disk — flexible
Redis       Speed — cache, locks, idempotency window — RAM — TTL mandatory

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Redis in Enterprise Systems

text
2009    Redis open source — Salvatore Sanfilippo — single-threaded event loop
2010s   Memcached → Redis for richer structures + persistence options
2013    Redisson — Java distributed locks, collections on Redis
2015    Microservices — Redis session, cache, rate limits standard on AWS ElastiCache
2018    Payment APIs — idempotency keys in Redis with TTL (Stripe-style)
2020+   "Cache aside" + explicit TTL — architects ban balance in Redis
        Redis Cluster — sharding — replica failover — not financial SoR
        Banking: Redis for coordination; Postgres for truth; saga/outbox unchanged
2024+   Redis 7+ — functions, ACLs — ElastiCache/MemoryDB managed — multi-AZ

Historical Lesson

Redis wins on milliseconds and simplicity for ephemeral state. Treat every key as expiring and non-authoritative for money unless you have engineered write-through with version checks — which payment platforms usually reject (Lesson 49).

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does Redis Solve in Payments?

Problem 1: Idempotency Under Retry Storm

text
Client retries POST /payments on timeout — 10 identical requests in 2 seconds
Redis SET idempotency:key NX EX 86400 — first wins — others return cached response fast
Without hitting Postgres UNIQUE contention on every retry

Problem 2: Hot Reference Data

text
Branch daily_limit loaded 8000/sec — Postgres SELECT branches wasteful
Redis cache-aside — TTL 1h + @CacheEvict on admin update (Lesson 49)

Problem 3: Rate Limiting / Fraud Throttle

text
Max 10 payments/minute per customer — INCR with EXPIRE sliding window
Protect ledger and PSP from abuse

Problem 4: Short-Lived Coordination

text
Distributed lock during promotional debit cap — short hold — not cross-shard ledger substitute
Redisson lock with lease — better than homegrown SET NX without renewal

Problem 5: Session / OTP (Adjacent)

text
3DS challenge session, OTP codes — TTL 5 min — Redis natural fit
Not lesson focus but common in payment flows

What Redis Must NOT Solve

text
❌ Account balance source of truth
❌ Payment ledger replacement
❌ Long-term audit storage (no TTL = memory bomb)
❌ Cross-region strong consistency for money

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why In-Memory Sidecar?

Latency

text
Redis GET: sub-ms LAN
Postgres PK SELECT: 1–3 ms warm
Idempotency check on every API — Redis reduces DB read load 10×

Atomic Primitives

text
SET key value NX EX ttl — atomic "set if not exists with expiry"
INCR — atomic counter for rate limits
Compare-and-set patterns for lightweight coordination

Explicit Expiry

text
Idempotency keys expire after 24–72h — automatic memory reclaim
Forces architects to define retention — unlike forgotten cache tables

Horizontal Scale

text
Redis Cluster — hash slots — scale keys across nodes
Separate cluster from DB — failure isolation — cache miss OK (reference data)

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Redis Works Internally

Single-Threaded Event Loop

text
One thread executes commands — atomicity per command guaranteed
No race on INCR or SET NX within single command
Long commands block — avoid KEYS * in prod

Persistence (Know the Trade-offs)

ModeBehaviorPayment use
RDBSnapshots periodicCache OK — may lose last minutes
AOFAppend log fsyncStronger — still not money SoR
nonePure cacheIdempotency if Postgres also stores — OK

Architect default: ElastiCache cluster with replication for HA — treat as volatile — Postgres idempotency table is backup (L43).

Memory Eviction

text
maxmemory-policy: allkeys-lru — evict cache keys under pressure
Separate logical DB or key prefix:
  idempotency:* — volatile-lru or noeviction + alert
  cache:branch:* — allkeys-lru OK
noeviction on idempotency if evict causes duplicate payment risk — prefer Postgres UNIQUE as backstop

Replication & Failover

text
Primary + replica — async replication — brief data loss on failover possible
Not suitable for "only copy" of idempotency — dual-write Redis + Postgres idempotency_records

Redis Cluster

text
16384 hash slots — key hash tag {customerId}:lock — co-locate related keys
Cross-slot multi-key transactions limited — design keys accordingly

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Key Design for Banking

Key Naming Convention

text
idempotency:payment:{idempotencyKey}     → JSON response body
lock:account:{accountId}                   → lock token UUID
cache:branch:{branchId}                  → Hash or JSON string
rate:pay:customer:{customerId}:{minute}    → counter string
processed:event:{eventId}                → "1" with TTL 7d (optional dedup layer)

Idempotency Value Shape

json
{
  "httpStatus": 200,
  "paymentId": "pay-uuid",
  "bodyHash": "sha256-of-request",
  "response": { "status": "ACCEPTED", "paymentId": "pay-uuid" },
  "createdAt": "2026-07-01T14:30:00Z"
}

SET NX EX Atomic Idempotency

text
SET idempotency:payment:abc-123  <json>  NX  EX 86400

NX — only if key absent — first request wins
EX 86400 — auto delete after 24h
Second request: SET returns nil — read existing GET — return same response
Mismatch body hash: return 409 Conflict — same key different payload

Hash for Branch Cache

text
HSET cache:branch:42  code NYC001  dailyLimit 1000000  currency USD
HGETALL cache:branch:42
Field-level update without deserializing whole JSON — minor benefit

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Memory Planning

Key typeSize estimateTTL
Idempotency entry1–4 KB24–72h
Branch hash500 B1h
Lock key50 B30s lease
Rate limit counter100 B60s
1M idempotency keys/day~2 GB if 24h retentionrotate

Memory Risks

text
No TTL on idempotency — OOM — cluster down — duplicate payment risk if fallback weak
Huge response bodies in Redis — cap stored response size — store paymentId only + reload from PG
KEYS command in prod — blocks — use SCAN

Part 8 — Execution Flow

End-to-End Flows

Flow 1: Idempotency — Redis First, Postgres Authoritative

text
1. POST /payments Idempotency-Key: abc-123
2. Redis SET idempotency:payment:abc-123 NX EX 86400
   - FAIL (exists): GET → validate request hash → return cached response
   - OK (new): proceed
3. @Transactional Postgres:
     INSERT idempotency_records, INSERT payments, INSERT outbox
4. COMMIT
5. Redis SET idempotency:payment:abc-123 <full response> XX EX 86400  (update placeholder)
6. Return 202

If step 3 fails: DEL idempotency key OR leave placeholder with FAILED status — client retry safe

Postgres UNIQUE on idempotency_key — backstop if Redis evicted/failed

Flow 2: Cache-Aside Branch

text
1. getBranch(id): Redis GET cache:branch:{id}
2. MISS → SELECT branches FROM Postgres → SET Redis EX 3600
3. capture() uses branch daily_limit from cache
4. Admin update → @CacheEvict Redis + Postgres UPDATE

Flow 3: Rate Limit

text
1. Key: rate:pay:customer:{id}:{epochMinute}
2. INCR key → if == 1 EXPIRE 120
3. if count > 10 → 429 Too Many Requests
4. Else proceed capture
Optional: Redis Cell module or sliding window ZSET for smoother limit

Flow 4: Redisson Lock — Promotional Cap (Not Balance)

text
1. RLock lock = redisson.getLock("promo:branch:" + branchId);
2. if (lock.tryLock(5, 30, SECONDS)) { check promo quota; decrement quota hash; }
3. Always unlock in finally — lease expires if JVM dies
NOT for serializing all account debits — use Postgres row lock (L35)

Flow 5: DR Failover

text
1. Redis cluster failover — brief unavailability
2. Idempotency falls back to Postgres findByIdempotencyKey — slower but safe
3. Cache cold — branch loads hit Postgres — warm job
4. Do not restore stale Redis RDB from backup into prod without flush — idempotency collision risk

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Redis vs Database for Coordination

PatternRedisPostgreSQL
Idempotency check~0.5ms~2ms + pool
Idempotency guaranteeTTL + evict riskUNIQUE constraint strong
Distributed lockRedisson leaseSELECT FOR UPDATE local
Rate limitNative INCRToo heavy on DB
Branch cacheExcellentOK with replica
Balance lock❌ wrong tool✅ row lock / optimistic @Version

Dual Layer Idempotency (Recommended Tier 0)

text
Layer 1 Redis — fast path reject duplicates
Layer 2 Postgres UNIQUE — correctness if Redis miss
Same pattern as Lesson 49 — cache enhances, DB guarantees

Redisson Lock vs DB Pessimistic Lock

text
Redisson:
  ✅ Distributed across JVMs — promo quota, inventory-style
  ❌ Not in same txn as ledger UPDATE — split brain if lock released before commit
  ❌ Fencing token required for strict correctness (advanced)

Postgres FOR UPDATE:
  ✅ Same txn as balance debit — ACID
  ✅ Payment ledger standard (L35)
Use DB lock for money movement; Redis lock for non-money coordination only

Idempotency Service — SET NX EX

java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class RedisIdempotencyService {

    private static final String PREFIX = "idempotency:payment:";

    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;
    private final ObjectMapper mapper;

    public Optional<PaymentResult> begin(String key, byte[] requestHash, Duration ttl) {
        String redisKey = PREFIX + key;
        IdempotencyRecord placeholder = IdempotencyRecord.pending(requestHash);

        Boolean acquired = redis.opsForValue().setIfAbsent(
            redisKey, serialize(placeholder), ttl);

        if (Boolean.TRUE.equals(acquired)) {
            return Optional.empty(); // proceed with capture
        }

        IdempotencyRecord existing = deserialize(redis.opsForValue().get(redisKey));
        if (!Arrays.equals(existing.requestHash(), requestHash)) {
            throw new IdempotencyConflictException(key);
        }
        if (existing.completed()) {
            return Optional.of(existing.result());
        }
        throw new IdempotencyInProgressException(key); // first request still running
    }

    public void complete(String key, PaymentResult result, Duration ttl) {
        redis.opsForValue().set(PREFIX + key,
            serialize(IdempotencyRecord.done(result)), ttl);
    }

    public void abort(String key) {
        redis.delete(PREFIX + key);
    }
}

Capture with Redis + Postgres

java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PaymentCaptureService {

    private final RedisIdempotencyService idempotency;
    private final PaymentRepository paymentRepo;
    private final IdempotencyRecordRepository idempotencyRepo; // Postgres backstop

    @Transactional
    public PaymentResult capture(CaptureCommand cmd) {
        Duration ttl = Duration.ofHours(24);

        idempotency.begin(cmd.idempotencyKey(), cmd.hash(), ttl)
            .ifPresent(existing -> return existing);

        try {
            // Postgres UNIQUE — authoritative
            idempotencyRepo.insertIfAbsent(cmd.idempotencyKey(), cmd.hash());

            Payment payment = paymentRepo.save(Payment.pending(cmd));
            outboxRepo.save(OutboxEvent.paymentCreated(payment));

            PaymentResult result = PaymentResult.from(payment);
            idempotency.complete(cmd.idempotencyKey(), result, ttl);
            return result;
        } catch (Exception e) {
            idempotency.abort(cmd.idempotencyKey());
            throw e;
        }
    }
}

Rate Limiter

java
@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PaymentRateLimiter {

    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;

    public void checkAllowed(UUID customerId, int maxPerMinute) {
        long minute = Instant.now().getEpochSecond() / 60;
        String key = "rate:pay:customer:" + customerId + ":" + minute;
        Long count = redis.opsForValue().increment(key);
        if (count != null && count == 1L) {
            redis.expire(key, Duration.ofMinutes(2));
        }
        if (count != null && count > maxPerMinute) {
            throw new RateLimitExceededException(customerId);
        }
    }
}

Redisson Lock (Non-Money)

java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PromoQuotaService {

    private final RedissonClient redisson;
    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;

    public void consumePromoSlot(UUID branchId) throws InterruptedException {
        RLock lock = redisson.getLock("lock:promo:branch:" + branchId);
        if (!lock.tryLock(2, 15, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
            throw new PromoBusyException();
        }
        try {
            String quotaKey = "promo:quota:branch:" + branchId;
            Long remaining = redis.opsForValue().decrement(quotaKey);
            if (remaining != null && remaining < 0) {
                redis.opsForValue().increment(quotaKey);
                throw new PromoExhaustedException();
            }
        } finally {
            lock.unlock();
        }
    }
}

sql

    idempotency_key VARCHAR(128) PRIMARY KEY,
    request_hash    BYTEA NOT NULL,
    http_status     SMALLINT,
    response_body   JSONB,
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
    expires_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX ix_idempotency_expires ON idempotency_records (expires_at);

@Component
public class RedisHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {
    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;

JPA + Redis — No Native Integration

Separation of Concerns

text

Second-Level Cache vs Redis

text

text

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Redis-Only Idempotency

text
Failover loses keys — duplicate payment — always Postgres UNIQUE

Mistake 2: Caching Balance

text
Stale balance displayed or worse used for authorization — Lesson 49 incident

Mistake 3: Lock Without Lease

text
SET lock 1 NX — JVM crash — lock forever — use Redisson lease or EX on lock key

Mistake 4: Redis @Transactional with JPA

text
Assumes atomic rollback — Redis already committed

Mistake 5: Same Key Different Body

text
Return cached response without hash check — wrong payment linked to key

Mistake 6: evict idempotency keys

text
noeviction OOM — cluster down — have Postgres fallback ready

Mistake 7: Redisson for Account Debit

text
Lock released before DB commit — double spend race — use DB txn lock

Mistake 8: KEYS * in Production

text
Blocks Redis — outage — use SCAN or known key names

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is Redis used for in payments?

Idempotency, caching reference data, rate limiting, short-lived locks — not money ledger.

Q2: SET NX EX?

Set key only if not exists with expiry — atomic idempotency claim.

Q3: Redis vs Postgres idempotency?

Redis fast path; Postgres UNIQUE authoritative if Redis miss/evict.

Q4: Why TTL on idempotency keys?

Memory bound — keys expire after 24–72h — legal retention in Postgres.

Q5: Cache balance in Redis?

No — stale money risk — read primary Postgres.

Mid-Level

Q6: Idempotency dual-layer design?

Redis SET NX → Postgres INSERT UNIQUE → capture → Redis complete; 409 on hash mismatch.

Q7: Redisson vs SELECT FOR UPDATE?

Redisson distributed non-money coordination; DB lock in same txn for ledger debit.

Q8: Rate limit implementation?

INCR per customer per minute window EXPIRE — 429 if exceeded.

Q9: Redis down degradation?

Fall back Postgres idempotency; cache miss to DB; never skip dedup Tier 0.

Q10: @Cacheable vs idempotency key?

Cache for read reference; idempotency for write dedup — different purposes TTL/eviction differ.

Senior

Q11: Design idempotency for 5k TPS payment API.

Redis cluster noeviction + PG UNIQUE + request hash + in-progress state + TTL + monitoring evictions + DR Postgres-only mode.

Q12: Fencing token with Redis locks?

Lock token passed to DB conditional UPDATE — prevents stale lock holder writing — advanced; prefer DB lock for money.

Q13: Two Redis clusters why?

Separate idempotency (noeviction) from cache (LRU) — failure blast radius and policy isolation.

Staff / Architect

Q14: Redis prohibited uses policy?

Document forbidden balance/payment SoR; dual-layer idempotency mandatory; DR behavior defined.

Scenario

Scenario: "Duplicate payments after Redis failover."

Idempotency relied on Redis only — add Postgres UNIQUE + replay safety — noeviction + AOF + backstop.

Part 1 — Concept

What Is Apache Cassandra?

Apache Cassandra is a distributed wide-column store designed for massive write throughput, horizontal scale, and high availability across multiple data centers. It is not a replacement for PostgreSQL on your core payment ledger.

text
POSTGRESQL (OLTP SoR)                    CASSANDRA (Scale-out events)
─────────────────────                    ────────────────────────────
payments, accounts, ledger               payment_events (append-only)
ACID row transactions                    partition-scoped queries
JOIN, constraints, FK                    no JOIN — query by partition key
vertical + read replica scale            linear write scale — ring topology

Wide-Column Model (Conceptual)

text
Relational row:  payment_id | amount | status
Cassandra row:   PRIMARY KEY ((partition_key), clustering_columns...)
                 └── all columns stored together on one partition node set

Example partition:
  PRIMARY KEY ((customer_id, event_date), event_time, event_id)
  Columns: event_type, amount, channel, psp_ref, payload_hash

Core Terms

TermMeaning
KeyspaceDatabase namespace (like PostgreSQL database)
TableColumn family — rows grouped by partition key
Partition keyDetermines which nodes store the row — query boundary
Clustering columnsSort order within partition
Replication factor (RF)Copies of data per DC
Consistency level (CL)How many replicas must respond (ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM)
Tunable consistencyCAP trade-off per query — not global ACID

Where Cassandra Fits in Payment Platforms

text
✅ Payment event telemetry (status transitions, webhooks received)
✅ Device / session fingerprints at high volume
✅ Fraud feature store (recent behavior windows)
✅ Audit event stream (append-only, time-bucketed)
✅ IoT / POS terminal heartbeat logs

❌ Account balance ledger
❌ Idempotency authoritative store (use Postgres + Redis L53)
❌ Cross-partition transactional debit/credit pairs

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Cassandra

text
2008    Facebook open-sources Cassandra — Dynamo + Bigtable papers
2010s   Netflix, Apple at scale — "always on" multi-DC
        CQL (Cassandra Query Language) — SQL-like syntax — not SQL semantics

2012    Payment startups experiment — write payment logs to Cassandra — ledger stays Oracle/Postgres
2014    Lightweight transactions (LWT) — IF NOT EXISTS — limited — not 2PC

2016    Materialized views (deprecated path) — prefer explicit tables / dual-write projections
2018    Banking architects standardize polyglot: RDBMS money + Cassandra telemetry
2020+   Astra DB (DataStax) managed — AWS Keyspaces — multi-region active-active reads
        PCI: no PAN in wide columns — hash/token only
2024+   Kafka + Cassandra common for fraud pipelines — Postgres remains SoR

Historical Lesson

Cassandra optimizes for "write millions of events per day and query by known partition key." It punishes ad-hoc analytics JOINs — the opposite of PostgreSQL (Phase 2–3).

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does Cassandra Solve?

Problem 1: Event Volume Beyond Postgres Comfort

text
500M payment status events/year — TB scale — indexing cost on Postgres high
Append-only time-series — Cassandra natural — partition by customer + day

Problem 2: Multi-Region Always-On Writes

text
US + EU active writers — Cassandra multi-DC RF=3 LOCAL_QUORUM
Postgres cross-region sync harder (L42) — Cassandra built for this pattern (with caveats)

Problem 3: Write Spike Absorption

text
Black Friday 50k events/sec — Postgres WAL single primary bottleneck
Cassandra cluster add nodes — linear scale (theoretical — ops required)

Problem 4: Retention by Time Bucket

text
TTL on events 90 days — automatic compaction delete
Postgres DELETE expensive — partition DROP in Cassandra time buckets optional

Problem 5: Fraud "Recent History" Lookups

text
Last 50 events for customer_id in 7 days — single partition scan if modeled correctly

When Postgres + CDC (L51) Is Enough

text
< 100M events/year, strong correlation with payments table, team one-DB ops
Debezium → warehouse for analytics — skip Cassandra ops burden

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Wide-Column Distributed Store?

Partition-Oriented Scale

text
Hash partition key → token ring → nodes own ranges
Writes spread across cluster — no single WAL leader like Postgres primary

Availability Over Strong Global Consistency

text
AP system — tunable per operation — LOCAL_QUORUM in single DC typical
Survives node loss with RF≥3 — no single point of failure

Predictable Query Pattern Reward

text
Design table for query: "events by customer_id ordered by time"
Denormalize — duplicate data into multiple tables for different access paths (query-driven design)

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Cassandra Works Internally

Ring Architecture

text
         Node A (token 0–25%)
        /                    \
   Node D                      Node B
        \                    /
         Node C (token 50–75%)

Partition key hash → token → responsible nodes (replicas per RF)

Write Path (Simplified)

text
1. Client sends INSERT with CL=LOCAL_QUORUM
2. Coordinator node computes partition → replica nodes
3. Write to commit log (append) + memtable (in-memory)
4. Ack when QUORUM replicas acknowledge
5. Async flush to SSTable on disk — periodic compaction
6. Hinted handoff if replica down — repair later

Read Path

text
1. Coordinator → replica nodes per CL
2. Read from memtable + SSTables — merge (read repair possible)
3. Higher CL → more recent consistent read — latency cost

Compaction & SSTables

text
Immutable SSTables on disk — merged by compaction strategy
STCS — time-series — TWCS (Time Window) for event buckets — recommended for telemetry
Tombstones from DELETE — avoid heavy deletes — use TTL instead

Lightweight Transactions (LWT)

text
INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS — Paxos round — 4x slower — use sparingly
Not substitute for Postgres UNIQUE idempotency at payment capture scale
OK for rare coordination row — not hot path millions/sec

Consistency Levels (Payment Platform Guidance)

CLMeaningUse
ONEOne replicaMetrics only — stale OK
LOCAL_ONEOne local DC replicaLow-latency internal
LOCAL_QUORUMMajority in local DCDefault writes/reads Tier 2 events
QUORUMGlobal majorityCross-DC strong-ish — latency
ALLAll replicasAvoid — fragile

Part 6 — Storage Internals

Physical Storage & Data Modeling

Partition Key Design (Critical)

text
BAD:  PRIMARY KEY (event_id)           -- random UUID → hot spots avoided but query by customer impossible without ALLOW FILTERING
BAD:  PRIMARY KEY ((event_date))       -- entire day one partition → hotspot on Black Friday
GOOD: PRIMARY KEY ((customer_id, event_date), event_time DESC, event_id)
       -- one partition per customer per day — bounded size — efficient range scan within day

Time-Series Bucket Pattern

text
event_date = '2026-07-01'  -- clustering bucket prevents unbounded partition growth
If customer > 100k events/day → sub-bucket hour or merchant_id in partition key
16MB partition size guideline — monitor partition size

Duplicate Tables for Query Paths (Query-First Design)

text
Table payment_events_by_customer:
  PK ((customer_id, event_date), event_time, event_id)

Table payment_events_by_payment:
  PK ((payment_id), event_time, event_id)   -- support timeline for one payment

Same event written twice (dual insert) or async projector — trade storage for query speed
Like read models (L50) but in Cassandra

TTL

cql
INSERT INTO payment_events (...) VALUES (...) USING TTL 7776000;  -- 90 days
Automatic physical delete after TTL — good for telemetry — not regulatory ledger (keep Postgres)

Denormalization Example Document

text
One row stores everything needed for fraud feature read:
  customer_id, event_date, event_time, event_type, amount, device_id, geo, merchant_id
No JOIN to accounts table — account_id as column only — correlate in app with Postgres

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Memory & Disk at Scale

ComponentMemoryNotes
MemtableHeap per nodeFlush threshold
Row cacheOptionalKey cache for hot partitions — rare tuning
CompactionCPU + disk I/OTWCS reduces overlap
Partition sizeRead all into coordHuge partition OOM risk
CoordinatorMerges replicasWide rows hurt

Banking Sizing

text
10k events/sec × 1KB = ~864 GB/day raw — RF=3 → ~2.5 TB/day cluster gross
Compression (LZ4) ~3× reduction — plan nodes + TWCS windows
Separate keyspace fraud vs telemetry — different TTL/RF policies

Part 8 — Execution Flow

End-to-End Flows

Flow 1: Postgres Capture + Async Cassandra Event (Recommended)

text
1. POST /payments — Postgres ACID capture + outbox PaymentCreated
2. Kafka consumer (or outbox relay) — PaymentStatusChanged projector:
     INSERT INTO payment_events_by_customer ...
     INSERT INTO payment_events_by_payment ...   -- dual table
3. CL=LOCAL_QUORUM — idempotent by event_id LWT or INSERT with static event_id PK component
4. Fraud service reads last N events: SELECT ... WHERE customer_id=? AND event_date=? 
5. Money amount for decision still from Postgres ledger API — Cassandra features only

Flow 2: POS Terminal Telemetry

text
1. Terminal sends heartbeat + txn attempt every 30s — high volume
2. API writes Cassandra only — never Postgres per heartbeat
3. PK ((terminal_id, event_date), event_time)
4. TTL 30 days — ops dashboard
5. Actual payment still flows through payment-service Postgres when customer pays

Flow 3: Multi-DC Write

text
1. EU customer event — EU coordinator — LOCAL_QUORUM in eu-west DC
2. US DC async replication — eventual — RF per DC=3 NetworkTopologyStrategy
3. Fraud in EU reads LOCAL_QUORUM EU — doesn't need US sync for real-time rule
4. Global report batch job reads each DC or replicate to warehouse (Snowflake)

Flow 4: Rebuild / Backfill

text
1. Bug in projector — stop consumer
2. TRUNCATE table (expensive) or drop time partitions
3. Replay Kafka from offset — re-insert events idempotent
4. Reconcile count vs Postgres payments for audit window — not amount authority

Flow 5: DR Region Loss

text
1. US-East DC lost — LOCAL_QUORUM in US-West continues for US keyspace
2. Cassandra handles within designed NTS — unlike Postgres manual promote (L42)
3. Postgres payment SoR still needs separate DR runbook — Cassandra does not replace it
4. Repair / rebuild replicas when DC returns

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Cassandra vs PostgreSQL for Events

FactorPostgreSQLCassandra
Append event writeGood to ~5k/s single primaryCluster 50k+/s
Query by customer time rangeIndex (customer_id, time) OKExcellent if PK matches
Query by arbitrary filterSQL flexibleALLOW FILTERING forbidden prod
ACID txnFullPartition-limited LWT only
JOINNativeDenormalize
Ops complexityModerateHigh (compaction, repair, sizing)
Multi-DC activeHardNative NTS

Hot Partition Risk

text
Mega-merchant all events share merchant_id partition → single node hotspot
Mitigation: compound partition ((merchant_id, bucket_hour), ...)
Salt high-cardinality keys only with read merge penalty — advanced

When Cassandra Complements Postgres

text
Postgres: payment captured, balance correct, outbox, idempotency
Cassandra: every status transition, webhook receipt, device signal for ML/fraud
Analytics: CDC Postgres → warehouse; Cassandra optional real-time feature path
Elasticsearch (L55): full-text search on error messages — different tool

OperationComplexityNotes
Insert eventO(1) per partitionCoordinator + QUORUM
Read partition sliceO(k) rows in rangek = limit
Read wrong PKO(cluster) scanForbidden
Dual table write2× writeQuery optimization

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

CQL Schema & Queries

Keyspace & Network Topology

cql
CREATE KEYSPACE payment_events
WITH replication = {
  'class': 'NetworkTopologyStrategy',
  'us-east': 3,
  'eu-west': 3
};

USE payment_events;

Table — Events by Customer (Time-Series)

cql
CREATE TABLE payment_events_by_customer (
    customer_id   UUID,
    event_date    DATE,
    event_time    TIMESTAMP,
    event_id      UUID,
    payment_id    UUID,
    event_type    TEXT,       -- CREATED, CAPTURED, FAILED, REVERSED
    amount        DECIMAL,
    currency_code TEXT,
    channel       TEXT,
    device_id     TEXT,
    psp_ref       TEXT,
    payload_hash  TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY ((customer_id, event_date), event_time, event_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (event_time DESC, event_id ASC)
  AND compaction = {'class': 'TimeWindowCompactionStrategy',
                    'compaction_window_unit': 'DAYS',
                    'compaction_window_size': 1}
  AND default_time_to_live = 7776000;  -- 90 days

Table — Events by Payment

cql
CREATE TABLE payment_events_by_payment (
    payment_id  UUID,
    event_time  TIMESTAMP,
    event_id    UUID,
    event_type  TEXT,
    amount      DECIMAL,
    status      TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY (payment_id, event_time, event_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (event_time DESC)
  AND default_time_to_live = 7776000;

Insert Event

cql
INSERT INTO payment_events_by_customer (
    customer_id, event_date, event_time, event_id,
    payment_id, event_type, amount, currency_code, channel, device_id
) VALUES (
    ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, 'CAPTURED', ?, ?, 'MOBILE', ?
) USING TTL 7776000;

Query — Recent Customer Events (Single Partition)

cql
SELECT event_time, event_type, amount, payment_id
FROM payment_events_by_customer
WHERE customer_id = ?
  AND event_date = ?
  AND event_time >= ?
ORDER BY event_time DESC
LIMIT 50;
-- Must include partition key columns customer_id + event_date

Query — Payment Timeline

cql
SELECT event_time, event_type, status
FROM payment_events_by_payment
WHERE payment_id = ?
ORDER BY event_time DESC;

Anti-Pattern

cql
-- ❌ NEVER in production
SELECT * FROM payment_events_by_customer
WHERE event_type = 'FAILED' ALLOW FILTERING;
-- Scans all partitions — cluster meltdown

Spring Data Cassandra

java
@Table("payment_events_by_customer")
@PrimaryKeyClass
public class PaymentEventByCustomerKey implements Serializable {
    @PrimaryKeyColumn(name = "customer_id", type = PrimaryKeyType.PARTITIONED)
    private UUID customerId;
    @PrimaryKeyColumn(name = "event_date", type = PrimaryKeyType.PARTITIONED)
    private LocalDate eventDate;
    @PrimaryKeyColumn(name = "event_time", type = PrimaryKeyType.CLUSTERED, ordering = Ordering.DESCENDING)
    private Instant eventTime;
    @PrimaryKeyColumn(name = "event_id", type = PrimaryKeyType.CLUSTERED)
    private UUID eventId;
}

@Table("payment_events_by_customer")
public class PaymentEventByCustomer {
    @PrimaryKey
    private PaymentEventByCustomerKey key;
    private UUID paymentId;
    private String eventType;
    private BigDecimal amount;
    private String currencyCode;
    private String channel;
}

Kafka Projector Service

java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PaymentEventProjector {

    private final CassandraTemplate cassandra;
    private final ProcessedEventRepository processed; // Postgres optional dedup

    @KafkaListener(topics = "payment-events")
    public void onEvent(PaymentEventEnvelope env) {
        if (processed.exists(env.eventId())) return;

        PaymentEventPayload p = env.payload();
        LocalDate eventDate = p.eventTime().atZone(ZoneOffset.UTC).toLocalDate();

        PaymentEventByCustomer doc = mapToCustomerTable(p, eventDate);
        cassandra.insert(doc);

        PaymentEventByPayment byPay = mapToPaymentTable(p);
        cassandra.insert(byPay);

        processed.save(new ProcessedEvent(env.eventId()));
    }
}

application.yml

yaml
spring:
  cassandra:
    keyspace-name: payment_events
    local-datacenter: us-east
    contact-points: cassandra-1.internal,cassandra-2.internal
    session-name: payment-event-projector
    request:
      consistency: local_quorum

Part 12 — Production Usage

Cassandra in Production Banking

Architecture Pattern

text
┌──────────────────┐     outbox/Kafka      ┌─────────────────────┐
│ payment-service  │ ────────────────────► │ event-projector     │
│ PostgreSQL SoR   │                       │ → Cassandra cluster │
└──────────────────┘                       └─────────────────────┘
         │                                           │
         │ authoritative money                       │ telemetry / fraud features
         ▼                                           ▼
   capture API                                  fraud-service reads

Operational Checklist

text
□ Partition size monitoring (nodetool tablestats)
□ Compaction backlog / pending tasks
□ Repair schedule weekly (rf consistency)
□ Read/write latency p99 per table
□ Tombstone warnings — prefer TTL over DELETE
□ Backup (snapshots + commitlog) — separate from Postgres DR
□ Capacity plan: nodes added before 70% disk
□ CL documented per service — LOCAL_QUORUM default
□ No ALLOW FILTERING in code review linter
□ Dual-write tables kept in sync — reconciliation job

Regulatory Boundary

text
Cassandra events support fraud/investigation — not sole proof of payment
Legal record: Postgres payments + ledger + immutable audit (L43)
Export case: join Cassandra timeline with Postgres payment by payment_id in app

// ❌ Cannot atomically Postgres capture + Cassandra insert in one @Transactional

Health & Circuit Breaker

java
@CircuitBreaker(name = "cassandra", fallbackMethod = "fallbackRecentEvents")
public List<PaymentEventDto> recentEvents(UUID customerId, LocalDate date) {
    return cassandraRepo.findRecent(customerId, date, Instant.now().minus(7, DAYS));
}

List<PaymentEventDto> fallbackRecentEvents(...) {
    return List.of(); // fraud rules degrade — capture still works on Postgres
}

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

JPA vs Cassandra — Separate Worlds

No Hibernate for Cassandra Events

text
JPA @Entity Payment — Postgres only
Spring Data Cassandra @Table — event projections
Never map same Payment entity to both

Hibernate Write Path Unchanged

text
capture() JPA → Postgres — Lesson 45–47
Cassandra populated asynchronously — same as L50 read models / L51 CDC consumers

If Team Uses Single "Event" Concept

text
Domain event POJO (Java record) — serialized to Kafka
Projector maps record → Cassandra @Table entity — not JPA managed
Processed event dedup can stay Postgres (small table) even if events in Cassandra

Read Merge for Support UI

java
public PaymentInvestigationDto investigate(UUID paymentId) {
    Payment payment = paymentJpaRepo.findById(paymentId).orElseThrow(); // money truth
    List<PaymentEventByPayment> timeline = cassandraRepo.findByPaymentId(paymentId);
    return PaymentInvestigationDto.merge(payment, timeline);
}

Solution Architect Framework

Part 18 — Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Payment Balance in Cassandra

text
No cross-row ACID — double spend — use Postgres

Mistake 2: ALLOW FILTERING Reports

text
Ops fire entire cluster — use warehouse ETL

Mistake 3: Unbounded Partition

text
((customer_id), time) without date bucket — partition > 16MB — slow reads

Mistake 4: DELETE Instead of TTL

text
Tombstone accumulation — read performance death

Mistake 5: Single Table for All Queries

text
Forces filter scans — create second table by payment_id

Mistake 6: LWT Every Insert

text
Paxos bottleneck — use idempotent event_id + downstream dedup

Mistake 7: Ignoring Repair

text
Replica divergence silent — schedule nodetool repair

Mistake 8: Cassandra as Only Event Store Without Postgres Link

text
payment_id orphan events — always correlate to Postgres SoR

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: Cassandra vs PostgreSQL?

Cassandra scales wide-column writes horizontally; Postgres ACID relational OLTP.

Q2: Partition key purpose?

Determines node placement and query boundary — must include in WHERE.

Q3: Use Cassandra for payment ledger?

No — Postgres/Oracle for money SoR.

Q4: Replication factor?

Number of copies of data — RF=3 tolerates one node loss with QUORUM.

Q5: LOCAL_QUORUM?

Majority of replicas in local datacenter — common production CL.

Mid-Level

Q6: Hot partition problem?

Too many writes one partition key — add bucket (hour/date) or split key.

Q7: Why duplicate tables?

Query-first design — no JOIN — by_customer and by_payment timelines.

Q8: Cassandra + Postgres together?

Postgres capture authoritative; Kafka projector writes Cassandra telemetry.

Q9: TTL vs DELETE?

TTL auto expires without tombstones — preferred for events.

Q10: LWT IF NOT EXISTS when?

Rare dedup — not hot path idempotency — use Postgres UNIQUE.

Senior

Q11: Design event storage for 20k events/sec fraud features.

TWCS tables ((customer_id, event_date), time), RF=3 LOCAL_QUORUM, Kafka from outbox, dual by_payment table, 90d TTL, no filter scans, Postgres money separate.

Q12: Multi-DC Cassandra vs Postgres DR?

Cassandra NTS active-active events; Postgres separate promote runbook — don't conflate.

Q13: Rebuild projector after bug?

Stop consumer, truncate/replay Kafka, reconcile counts with Postgres window.

Staff / Architect

Q14: When reject Cassandra adoption?

Low volume, no ops, SQL analytics sufficient, team needs strong ACID only.

Scenario

Scenario: "Fraud dashboard slow after Black Friday."

Hot partition merchant_id or missing date bucket — check tablestats partition size — redesign PK + TWCS.

Part 1 — Concept

What Is Elasticsearch?

Elasticsearch is a distributed search and analytics engine built on Apache Lucene. It indexes documents as JSON, uses an inverted index for fast full-text search, and powers log analytics (ELK), observability, and investigation UIs in payment operations.

text
SQL LIKE / sequential scan              ELASTICSEARCH
──────────────────────────              ──────────────
WHERE psp_ref LIKE '%ERR-8842%'         Query: psp_ref:ERR-8842 OR message:"timeout"
Seq scan millions of rows — seconds     Inverted index — milliseconds
No relevance ranking                    Scoring, highlighting, aggregations
Poor for fuzzy "similar errors"         Analyzers, n-grams (careful with PCI)

ELK Stack

text
Elasticsearch  — store + search + aggregate
Logstash       — ingest, parse, enrich pipelines (or Fluent Bit / Beats)
Kibana         — dashboards, Discover, investigation UI
Often: App logs → Filebeat → Kafka → Elasticsearch (banking scale)

Where Elasticsearch Fits in Payment Platforms

text
✅ Ops search: "find all failed Stripe webhooks mentioning insufficient_funds today"
✅ Support investigation: correlation_id / trace_id across microservices
✅ PSP raw error text search (redacted — no PAN)
✅ Audit log centralization (application + gateway logs)
✅ Fraud analyst ad-hoc filters on enriched events

❌ System of record for payments or balances
❌ Authoritative idempotency or ledger
❌ Strong ACID updates to money state
❌ Primary transactional API read path for capture receipt

Part 2 — History

Evolution of Search in Enterprise Data

text
1999    Apache Lucene — inverted index library — Java
2010    Elasticsearch — distributed Lucene — JSON REST — near-real-time (NRT)
2013    ELK stack popular — replace grep across log files
2015    Payment ops teams index webhook logs — Postgres still SoR
2016    Elastic X-Pack — security, ML — commercial features
2020+   OpenSearch fork (AWS) — managed Amazon OpenSearch Service
        Banking: centralized observability — PCI log redaction pipelines
        CDC/Beats ship payment-service logs + enriched payment events to ES
        Architects: ES for "find needle" — warehouse for "sum everything"
2024+   Trace-native: OpenTelemetry trace_id in every log line — ES correlation

Historical Lesson

Elasticsearch answers "find and explore." PostgreSQL answers "correct and constrain." Using ES for money state repeats Mongo/Cassandra mistakes from Lessons 52–54.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problems Does Elasticsearch Solve?

Problem 1: LIKE '%term%' on OLTP

text
Support searches payment_reference partial match across 200M rows
Postgres seq scan or weak trigram index — timeouts — load on primary
ES index payment_events with analyzed reference field — fast

Problem 2: Cross-Service Investigation

text
Payment failed — need logs from payment-service, ledger-service, gateway, PSP adapter
trace_id=abc-123 search one Kibana query — not SSH four pods

Problem 3: Dispute Evidence Discovery

text
Chargeback case: "show all events for merchant X mentioning visa decline code 51 in June"
Full-text + filters + timeline histogram in Kibana

Problem 4: Operational Dashboards

text
Error rate by psp_name, by error_class, last 24h — terms aggregation
Not real-time ledger — ops metrics only

Problem 5: Semi-Structured Log Parsing

text
Unstructured stack traces — grok patterns in Logstash — structured fields in ES

When SQL / Warehouse Is Enough

text
Regulatory SUM(amount) by branch — Snowflake/BigQuery — not ES
Exact PK lookup payment_id — Postgres primary
List customer payments paginated — read model (L50) — not search engine

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Inverted Index?

Full-Text vs B-Tree

text
B-tree index (Postgres): good for equality, range, prefix — bad for contains/substring across large text
Inverted index: term → list of document IDs
  "timeout" → [doc1, doc47, doc892]
  "stripe"  → [doc1, doc2, ...]
Query intersects posting lists — fast for OR/AND text queries

Near-Real-Time (NRT)

text
Document indexed — refresh interval default 1s — searchable shortly after
Not immediate ACID — eventual visibility OK for logs/investigation

Aggregations

text
Bucket by branch_code, sub-aggregate avg latency — ops analytics without pre-built SQL reports
Not substitute for financial reconciliation totals — sampling/approximate awareness

Part 5 — Internal Working

How Elasticsearch Works Internally

Cluster Topology

text
Cluster
  └── Indices (payment-logs-2026.07.01 — daily rollover)
        └── Shards (primary + replica)
              └── Lucene segments (immutable inverted indexes)

Document JSON → analyzed tokens → stored in shard
Routing: shard = hash(_routing) % num_primary_shards
Routing key payment_id or customer_id — co-locate related docs optional

Analysis Pipeline

text
Field "message": "Payment CAPTURED for account 5001 FAILED timeout"

Standard analyzer (default):
  → [payment, captured, account, 5001, failed, timeout]

keyword subfield "message.keyword" — exact match — no analysis
Dual mapping: text for search, keyword for filters/sorts

Write Path

text
1. Index API POST /payment-logs/_doc
2. Primary shard — write to translog + memory buffer
3. Replicate to replica shards
4. Refresh (periodic) — segment visible for search
5. Flush to disk — translog commit

Read Path

text
1. Query DSL JSON → scatter to relevant shards
2. Each shard Lucene search → top N hits + aggregations
3. Coordinator merges — returns ranked results

Index Lifecycle Management (ILM)

text
Hot:  last 7 days — fast SSD — frequent search
Warm: 8–30 days — shrink replicas
Cold: 31–90 days — searchable snapshots
Delete: > 90 days — or archive to S3 — retention policy

Mapping (Schema)

json
{
  "mappings": {

      "timestamp":       { "type": "date" },
      "trace_id":        { "type": "keyword" },
      "correlation_id":  { "type": "keyword" },

    }
  }
}

PCI / PII Rules

text
Never index: PAN, CVV, full card number, raw Authorization headers with secrets
Tokenize: last4 only — card_last4 field if needed
Redact in Logstash/Filebeat pipeline BEFORE index
Separate index pattern without PII for wider access RBAC

Part 7 — Memory Usage

Memory & Disk Planning

ComponentResourceNotes
Heap50% RAM max (rule of thumb)Field data deprecated — use doc_values
SegmentsDiskMore shards = more overhead
Daily indicesRolloverpayment-logs-YYYY.MM.dd
Replicas2× storageRF=1 for hot — adjust
AggregationsHeap spikeLimit cardinality fields

Sizing Example

text
50 GB logs/day ingested — 3 primary shards — 1 replica — ~100 GB/day gross
90 day retention hot+warm — plan TB scale — ILM delete old
Force merge warm indices off-peak — trade CPU for fewer segments

Part 8 — Execution Flow

End-to-End Flows

Flow 1: Application Log → ELK with Trace Correlation

text
1. payment-service logs JSON: trace_id, correlation_id, payment_id, message
2. Filebeat → Kafka → Logstash enrich (service, env) → Elasticsearch
3. Analyst Kibana Discover: trace_id:"trace-abc-123" — all services timeline
4. Postgres still authoritative for payment status — ES for diagnosis only

Flow 2: CDC / Event Enrichment Index

text
1. Debezium payments table change (L51) OR PaymentCreated Kafka event
2. Stream processor maps row → ES document (status, amount, ids — no PAN)
3. Index payment-events-* for ops search by psp_ref, error_code
4. Lag seconds — label UI "search index — not financial truth"

Flow 3: Dispute Investigation

text
1. Chargeback references psp_ref pi_3NxAbC
2. Kibana query:
     psp_ref:"pi_3NxAbC" OR payment_id:"pay-uuid" 
     time range June 2026
3. Timeline visualization — correlate webhook FAILED + capture retry logs
4. Export PDF for case file — redacted fields only
5. Confirm amounts in Postgres reconciliation export — not ES sum

Flow 4: Replace SQL LIKE in Ops Tool

text
Before: SELECT * FROM payment_audit WHERE details LIKE '%timeout%' — 45s
After:  GET payment-logs-*/_search { "query": { "match": { "message": "timeout" } } } — 200ms
Guard: RBAC — ops role only — rate limit — no customer-facing API

Flow 5: DR / Index Failure

text
ES cluster degraded — investigation UI degraded — capture on Postgres continues
Do not block payments if ES down — async ingest buffer Kafka backlog
After recovery — replay Kafka offset — idempotent _id event_id

Part 9 — Performance Analysis

Elasticsearch vs SQL vs Cassandra vs Warehouse

NeedPostgresElasticsearchCassandraWarehouse
PK payment lookup✅ bestOverkillOverkillSlow
Full-text error search❌ LIKE✅ best❌Batch
trace_id log correlationgrep logs✅ bestPossibleETL delay
SUM revenue by branch✅ / replicaApprox aggs❌✅ best
Time-series events/secOKIngest heavy✅ bestBatch
Dispute keyword huntPoor✅PoorOK delayed

When ES Replaces SQL LIKE (Banking Ops)

text
✅ Replace: internal ops/support search across message, error_text, stack traces
✅ Replace: cross-service log correlation (trace_id)
✅ Replace: exploratory filters during incident ("all FAILED + stripe + today")
❌ Don't replace: customer payment history list (use read model L50)
❌ Don't replace: regulatory totals (warehouse)
❌ Don't replace: authorization balance check

Query Cost

text
Wildcard leading *term — slow — avoid
match_phrase on message — OK with time filter
Filter context on keyword fields (psp_name, status) — cached — fast
Always narrow time range — @timestamp last 24h — partition index pattern

Structured Logging (Micrometer / Logback JSON)

java
@Slf4j
@Service
public class PaymentCaptureService {
    public PaymentResult capture(CaptureCommand cmd) {
        MDC.put("trace_id", cmd.traceId());
        MDC.put("correlation_id", cmd.correlationId());
        MDC.put("payment_id", cmd.paymentId() != null ? cmd.paymentId().toString() : "pending");
        log.info("Payment capture started amount={} currency={}", cmd.amount(), cmd.currency());
        try {
            PaymentResult result = doCapture(cmd);
            log.info("Payment capture completed status={}", result.status());
            return result;
        } catch (Exception e) {
            log.error("Payment capture failed error={}", e.getMessage(), e);
            throw e;
        } finally {
            MDC.clear();
        }
    }
}

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/internal/ops/search")
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('PAYMENT_OPS')")
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PaymentInvestigationController {

    private final PaymentLogSearchRepository searchRepo;
    private final PaymentRepository paymentRepo; // Postgres truth

    @GetMapping("/by-trace/{traceId}")
    public InvestigationResponse byTrace(@PathVariable String traceId) {
        List<PaymentLogDocument> logs = searchRepo.findByTraceIdOrderByTimestampAsc(traceId);
        // Optional: load payment from Postgres if payment_id present in logs
        return InvestigationResponse.of(logs, disclaimer("Search index — verify amounts in core banking"));
    }
}

Part 14 — Hibernate/JPA Integration

JPA + Elasticsearch — Strict Separation

Postgres JPA — Source of Truth

java
@Entity Payment — capture, status, amount — authoritative

Elasticsearch — Read-Only Investigation Index

java
@Document — PaymentLogDocument — no @Transactional sync with JPA
Project via Kafka/logs — never Hibernate @PostPersist to ES on hot path (blocks capture)

Anti-Pattern: Hibernate Search on Payment Entity

text
Hibernate Search indexes JPA entities — couples OLTP to ES — reindex pain on schema change
Prefer log/event pipeline decoupling for microservices
Exception: small admin apps — still rare in Tier 0 payments

Investigation Merge Pattern

java
public DisputeCaseDto buildCase(String paymentId) {
    Payment payment = paymentJpaRepo.findById(UUID.fromString(paymentId)).orElseThrow();
    List<PaymentLogDocument> logs = esRepo.findByPaymentId(paymentId, PageRequest.of(0, 200));
    return DisputeCaseDto.mergeAuthoritativePayment(payment, logs);
}

Part 19 — Interview Questions

Junior

Q1: What is an inverted index?

Maps terms to document IDs — enables fast full-text search vs row scan.

Q2: Elasticsearch for payment ledger?

No — investigation/logs/search — Postgres is SoR.

Q3: trace_id purpose in ELK?

Correlate log lines across microservices for one payment request flow.

Q4: keyword vs text field?

keyword exact filter/sort; text analyzed for full-text search.

Q5: Why not SQL LIKE on production?

Seq scan load, slow, harms OLTP — ES offloads search.

Mid-Level

Q6: ELK stack components?

Elasticsearch store/search, Logstash/Beats ingest, Kibana UI.

Q7: Near-real-time meaning?

Document searchable ~1s after index — not instant ACID.

Q8: ILM purpose?

Hot/warm/cold/delete phases — manage retention and cost.

Q9: Design dispute search for psp_ref + error text?

keyword psp_ref filter + text message match + time range + daily indices + PCI redaction.

Q10: ES vs Cassandra for events?

ES search/analyze text; Cassandra write scale time-series — overlap possible — different strengths.

Senior

Q11: Architecture: ops search without touching Postgres primary.

Structured JSON logs trace_id → Kafka → Logstash redact → ES → Kibana RBAC; Postgres for verify amounts.

Q12: When ES replaces LIKE in ops?

Internal investigation full-text — not customer API — not financial totals.

Q13: Hibernate @PostPersist to ES risk?

Couples latency, failure to capture — async event pipeline preferred.

Staff / Architect

Q14: Polyglot tier table for payment platform?

Postgres money, Redis idempotency, Mongo metadata, Cassandra telemetry, ES investigation, warehouse regulatory.

Scenario

Scenario: "Support uses ES to tell customer final balance."

Wrong source — show Postgres balance — ES for timeline/logs only — fix process + UI disclaimer.

Part 1 — Concept

What Is Enterprise Payment Data Architecture?

Enterprise payment data architecture is the deliberate design of how data is stored, moved, secured, scaled, and recovered across relational, cache, document, wide-column, and search systems — with clear ownership, consistency tiers, and regulatory boundaries.

text
                         ENTERPRISE PAYMENT DATA PLATFORM
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  CHANNELS: Mobile · Web · POS · Partner API · Batch                            │
└───────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                    │
┌───────────────────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────────────────┐

The Architect’s Core Question

For each piece of data, answer in one line: Where is the source of truth? How fresh may reads be? What happens when it fails?

Part 2 — History

How Payment Data Architecture Evolved

text
1990s   Monolith Oracle — one schema — 2PC between modules — nightly batch
2000s   Service-oriented — still often shared database anti-pattern
2010s   Microservices + Kafka — outbox/saga — "no distributed transactions"
2015+   Polyglot persistence standard — Postgres money + Redis + ES logs
2020s   Cloud-native — RDS Multi-AZ + Aurora Global + managed Kafka + OpenSearch
        Regulators expect: DR drills, RPO/RTO evidence, data classification, reconciliation
2024+   Solution Architect owns **technology selection matrix** + **consistency catalog**
        Not "we use Postgres" — but **which tier each datum lives in and why**

Historical Lesson

Technology churn is constant; architectural invariants are not. ACID for money, idempotency for APIs, independent backups, no cross-service FK, reconciliation jobs — these survive every framework fad.

Part 3 — Problem Statement

What Problem Does Enterprise Architecture Solve?

Problem 1: Accidental Complexity

text
15 teams — 15 databases — no SoR map — duplicate balances in Mongo and Postgres

Problem 2: Wrong Tool for Tier

text
Elasticsearch as ledger — Cassandra for idempotency — Redis balance cache incidents

Problem 3: Consistency Surprises

text
Customer sees payment success but list screen empty — read model lag undocumented

Problem 4: Operational Gaps

text
Multi-AZ without cross-region DR — backups never restored — slot lag unknown

Problem 5: Regulatory Audit Failure

text
Cannot prove 7-year retention, PII handling, or recoverability evidence

Unified Problem Statement

Enterprise architecture makes trade-offs explicit — who owns what data, at what consistency, on what store, with what failure mode — so the platform scales without silent financial or compliance failure.

Part 4 — Why This Exists

Why Not “Best Database per Developer”?

Governance

text
Platform standards: Flyway validate, no ddl-auto update, UUID PKs, idempotency keys
Architecture review gate for new stores

Blast Radius

text
Telemetry in Cassandra failure ≠ payment capture down — tier isolation

Cost Control

text
Right-size: warehouse for reports — not 32 ES data nodes for one LIKE query

Onboarding

text
New engineer reads **data catalog + tier matrix** — not archaeology 50 repos

Part 5 — Internal Working

Reference Architecture — Logical Flow

Capture Path (Tier 0)

text
1. API Gateway — auth, rate limit (Redis L53)
2. payment-service:
     Redis SET NX idempotency (fast)
     @Transactional Postgres:
       INSERT idempotency_records
       INSERT payments
       INSERT outbox_events
     COMMIT
3. Response from write txn DTO — amount/status authoritative
4. Async: outbox relay → Kafka PaymentCreated
5. Consumers: ledger (saga), metadata (Mongo L52), events (Cassandra L54), ES (L55), warehouse (CDC L51)

Read Path (Tier 2)

text
GET /payments list → payment-query-service → payment_list_view (L50)
                   → eventual lag SLA 5s documented
GET /payments/{id} after POST → write DB or sync projection — strong
GET /investigation → ES trace_id — ops RBAC — disclaimer
GET /balance → ledger-service Postgres primary — never Redis cache (L49)

Failure Domains

text
Postgres primary down → Multi-AZ failover (L40) — RTO minutes
Redis down → Postgres idempotency fallback — slower OK
Kafka lag → read model stale — capture still OK
ES down → investigation degraded — not payment stop
Region loss → DR runbook (L42) + Cassandra NTS if used

Part 8 — Execution Flow

End-to-End Scenario — Customer Mobile Payment

text
T0  Customer initiates $250 payment — Idempotency-Key header
T1  Redis NX + Postgres capture txn (payment PENDING, outbox event)
T2  202 Accepted — body from write txn
T3  Outbox → Kafka PaymentCreated
T4  ledger-service saga: debit account, ledger_entries, PaymentSettled event
T5  Projectors: payment_list_view, Mongo metadata, Cassandra events, ES logs
T6  Customer opens history — read model may show payment at T5 (+2s lag)
T7  Balance screen — ledger API primary — strong
T8  Nightly reconciliation: SUM(payments) vs ledger vs read model vs warehouse
T9  Ops investigates failure: Kibana trace_id — Postgres confirms final status

Part 11 — Code / SQL Examples

Platform Standards (Copy-Paste Governance)

Tier 0 Capture Template (Spring)

java
@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PaymentCaptureService {

    private final RedisIdempotencyService redisIdempotency;
    private final PaymentRepository paymentRepo;
    private final OutboxEventRepository outboxRepo;
    private final IdempotencyRecordRepository idempotencyRepo;

    @Transactional
    public PaymentResult capture(CaptureCommand cmd) {
        redisIdempotency.begin(cmd.key(), cmd.hash(), Duration.ofHours(24))
            .ifPresent(r -> { throw new IdempotentReplayException(r); });

        idempotencyRepo.insertIfAbsent(cmd.key(), cmd.hash());

        Payment payment = paymentRepo.save(Payment.pending(cmd));
        outboxRepo.save(OutboxEvent.paymentCreated(payment));

        PaymentResult result = PaymentResult.from(payment);
        redisIdempotency.complete(cmd.key(), result, Duration.ofHours(24));
        return result;
    }
}

Consistency Catalog Entry (YAML-style documentation)

yaml
api: GET /customers/{id}/payments
consistency: eventual
source: payment_list_view (PostgreSQL read DB)
max_lag_sla_seconds: 5
authoritative_for: list display only
money_authority: payment-service PostgreSQL for disputes

api: POST /payments
consistency: strong
source: payment-service PostgreSQL primary
idempotency: Redis + UNIQUE idempotency_key

Reconciliation SQL (Nightly Tier 0)

sql
-- Write vs ledger (same business day)
SELECT
    (SELECT SUM(amount) FROM payments WHERE status = 'CAPTURED' AND created_at >= CURRENT_DATE) AS payments_total,
    (SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN direction = 'DEBIT' THEN amount ELSE 0 END)
     FROM ledger_entries WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE) AS ledger_debits_total;

-- Write vs read model drift
SELECT COUNT(*) AS missing_in_read_model
FROM payments p
LEFT JOIN payment_list_view r ON r.payment_id = p.payment_id
WHERE p.created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 day'
  AND r.payment_id IS NULL;

Architecture Decision Record (ADR) Skeleton

markdown
# ADR-042: Payment list served from CQRS read model

## Status: Accepted
## Context: List query JOIN load on primary OLTP
## Decision: payment-query-service + payment_list_view fed by outbox/Kafka
## Consequences: 5s eventual lag; reconciliation job; no cross-service JOIN
## Alternatives rejected: ES (wrong tool), replica normalized JOIN (still heavy)

ORM in Enterprise Architecture

Where JPA Lives

text
✅ Tier 0 OLTP capture in owned microservice Postgres
✅ Read-only @Immutable entities on read models

Platform JPA Checklist

text
□ Persistable UUID for pre-assigned IDs (L46)
□ @Version on contested aggregates
□ BigDecimal money — Instant UTC timestamps
□ No OSIV — DTO at API boundary
